docs.title: Z is Diophantine in Q
docs.text:
This blueprint formalizes Theorem 1.1 of the 11/5 manuscript ℤ is Diophantine in ℚ (diophantine_zq.tex in this repository), with its deep arithmetic inputs as explicit hypotheses and its finite computations checked by the Lean kernel.

Start reading

Every statement is fully proved.

18 of 22 source areas split into statements · 1 left for later · 3 out of scope What the sources cover Source notes

docs.title: Decomposed (18)
docs.text:
Section 1: main theorem and assembly

The first chapter states the target and the main theorem, proved from the minimal height hypothesis and four statements about L-series, none proved here: Gross–Zagier, the functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\) and Hecke's continuation (textbook theorems), and Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A, which no refereed text found by a literature search carried out by AI agents states explicitly and which Proposition N, reviewed only by AI models and never by a human, derives from a restatement of unambiguous results of their paper (the derivation is proved; only AI models have compared the restatement with the paper; supporting evidence, not a hypothesis). The chapter also states the main theorem from three hypotheses, the form closest to the manuscript's inputs, and the other forms; the assembly chapter decomposes Lemma 1.2.

Section 2 and Appendix C: literal finite specification

The specification chapter defines the expression language, every template, constant, constructor and recipe, and the polynomial; correctness of each template is assigned to the chapter that uses it.

Section 3: elliptic model, generator and addition

The elliptic model chapter covers the field, the descent, the heights and the finite search, membership and raw addition.

Section 4, last step: from \(h(J(u))\) to \(h(u)\), replaced (project notes wk-h §4.1, h-trust step F4)

The \(j\)-form section states the bound on the height of \(J(u)\) (not proved here), bounds the cancellation in \(J(u)\) by two polynomial identities, proves \(12h(u)\le h(J(u))+450\), which replaces the manuscript's \(h(u)<h(J(u))+74\) (that inequality is not proved here), and derives the minimal height hypothesis; the main theorem from the \(j\)-form and the L-series statements assumes the \(j\)-form in two of its three forms.

Section 5: pole predicate

Lemma 5.1 is the pole obstruction of the multiplication chapter and Theorem 5.2 is pole completeness in the first chapter, both for the Route K pole polynomial (curves \(x+\ell\) instead of \(x+3\ell\)); PC is proved in the Route K chapter from the hypothesis CR₃.

Section 6: multiplication and the false-triple guard

The multiplication chapter covers the template, soundness through the height estimate and the guard, and completeness; Proposition 6.2 is the hypothesis 22P in the first chapter, used only by the three-hypothesis form of the main theorem.

Proposition 6.2 replaced: route AP (project note nt-22p §3)

The route AP chapter covers Lemma P, the completeness of the multiplication template under the weakened slope representation, Proposition AP and the statement 22P_AP, and derives 22P_AP from Szemerédi's theorem in the primes and Proposition D; the main theorem from two hypotheses no longer assumes 22P.

Szemerédi's theorem in the primes (Green–Tao 2008, Theorems 1.1 and 1.2; project note gt-dense)

The Green–Tao chapter records the vendored Lean proof of Theorem 1.1 for all primes and its extension to sets of primes of positive relative upper density.

Proposition D: density of good slope primes (project note pd-paper)

The Proposition D chapter covers the character sums, the description of good primes, the residue set, the sieve bound with the vendored Selberg sieve, Theorem D and Proposition 5.3.

Proposition 0: the explicit system is the 2-Selmer group (project note nt-prop0)

The Proposition 0 chapter covers the 2-coverings, local solubility at every place, the Selmer group, Proposition 0, and CR₃ from its Selmer form CR₃^Sel, which is a hypothesis of a variant of the main theorem and is not proved here.

Row-5b determinant (project note tyz-5b §§2–4)

The row-5b chapter covers Smith's matrices, Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2, Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 4.4. It also covers the forest lemma and the forest expansion of determinants (forests section), and Rédei's \(g\), Lemma 2.2, Propositions 3.3–3.5 and Theorem 3.6, \(\det M_{5b}=T_{5b}(n)\) (genus-sum section). It derives CR₃^Sel from the hypothesis CR₃^5b, which follows from the hypothesis CR₃^TYZ in Tian–Yuan–Zhang's terms; with the minimal height hypothesis alone, CR₃^5b gives the main theorem from the Selmer form of the rank hypothesis. Neither hypothesis is proved here; they rest on Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A with Hecke's continuation and the functional equation, and on Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary field.

Rédei's formula (project note redei-plan §3.2; tyz-5b Proposition 2.3)

The Rédei chapter covers the field \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and its primes, ambiguous classes, genus characters and their surjectivity by Dirichlet's theorem, the principal genus theorem, Rédei's theorem on the 4-rank, and the translation of the Rédei matrix into the bits. It ends with Rédei's formula, which makes the class-number form CR₃^TYZ_Cl of the hypothesis equivalent to CR₃^TYZ.

Positive rank gives every Selmer class (project note pc-audit RK9), Mordell–Weil for \(C_d\), and the positive-rank forms of CR₃ (project note cr3-map-literature §8 N2)

The positive-rank chapter covers the complete 2-descent on \(C_d\) and RK9, and Mordell–Weil for \(C_d\) by the two-isogeny descent and heights. It states the hypotheses CR₃^Rk, CR₃^TYZ,Rk and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk, proves CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk ⇒ CR₃^TYZ,Rk ⇒ CR₃^Rk, and derives CR₃^Sel and CR₃ from CR₃^Rk, CR₃^TYZ from CR₃^TYZ,Rk, and CR₃^TYZ_Cl from CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk. These hypotheses are not proved here; they rest on Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A with Hecke's continuation and the functional equation, and on Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary field, with Kriz's 2-converse as an alternative that is not needed. They are the hypotheses of variants of the main theorem. CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk follows from three statements about L-series (literature section). The infinitely-many-points section restates CR₃^Rk, CR₃^TYZ,Rk, CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk and CR₃^DL,Rk with the conclusion that \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions, proves each equivalent to its positive-rank form, and gives the main theorem from each of them.

CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk from three statements about L-series (project notes wk-cr3, rv-lit)

The literature section defines entire continuations of \(L(E,s)\) and proves them unique, computes \(L(C_d,s)\) from its definition for odd squarefree \(d\) (minimality at every prime, reduction types, local polynomials and every Dirichlet coefficient, with the coefficient at a prime \(p\nmid2d\) as a point count; L-series subsection), states Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b, the functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) with conductor \(32d^2\) and root number \(-1\) on \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), and the positive-rank half of Gross–Zagier (none proved here); proves that the functional equation gives vanishing at the centre, that row 5b with vanishing at the centre gives analytic rank one and, with Gross–Zagier, CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk; and states Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A and Hecke's continuation (neither proved here), from which it proves row 5b. The main theorem assumes reading A, Hecke's continuation, the functional equation and Gross–Zagier, with the minimal height hypothesis; the main theorem from the \(j\)-form and the L-series statements assumes row 5b, the functional equation and Gross–Zagier in two of its three forms (with the minimal height hypothesis or with the \(j\)-form). Reading A rests on Tian–Yuan–Zhang in a reading that no refereed text found by a literature search carried out by AI agents states explicitly; Proposition N, reviewed only by AI models and never by a human, derives it from a restatement of unambiguous results of their paper that only AI models have compared with the paper, as supporting evidence, not a hypothesis.

CR₃ on the two curves of a slot choice (project notes rv-cr3-dl §1, cr3-map-needs §2)

The two-curves section states CR₃^DL,Rk and CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk, derives CR₃^DL,Rk from CR₃^Rk and from CR₃^TYZ,Rk, and proves pole completeness from each of the two. The main theorem from positive rank on the two curves assumes only the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^DL,Rk, or the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk; neither is proved here.

Section 10: precision computation and compilation

The natural compiler chapter covers the alpha and power formulas, the packed-history compiler, the universal interpreter and the natural precision polynomial (Sections 10.1–10.3); the translation chapter covers the rational translation (Section 10.4).

Section 11: variable-shift relation

The assembly chapter covers Close, the six local tests, Lemmas 11.1 and 11.2 and the ordinary-value relation.

Section 12: cutoff and polynomial size

The size chapter bounds the fixed constants, identifies the cutoff and bounds the degree and coefficients of the polynomial; the progression estimate is replaced by the catalogue bound with cutoff \(2^{W^8}\), which the progressions chapter proves from an effective Dirichlet theorem.

docs.title: Deferred (1)
docs.text:
Section 13: consequences

The three corollaries follow the main theorem and are scheduled after it.

docs.title: Out of scope (3)
docs.text:
Section 4: proof of the six-contact estimate

Needs Shimura curves, modularity and Arakelov geometry, which are not formalizable here; its conclusion is the hypothesis H in the first chapter. Its last step, from the height of the Hauptmodul value \(J(u)\) back to \(u\), is replaced by a proved inequality, \(12h(u)\le h(J(u))+450\) (\(j\)-form section), so the target also holds with H replaced by a bound on \(h(J(u))\) assembled from the section's earlier steps (the \(j\)-form, not proved here and not a published theorem), together with CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk or with the three statements about L-series (main theorem from the \(j\)-form and the L-series statements).

Section 5.1 and Sections 7–9, Appendices E–G: restricted converse

Uses Kato, Waldspurger, Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein, Nekovář and Gross–Zagier–Kolyvagin; replaced by Route K: the descent lemma is proved, and the deep input is the certified rank hypothesis CR₃, which rests on Proposition 0 (now proved) and on Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A with Hecke's continuation and the functional equation, and on Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary field (Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein), with Kriz's 2-converse as an alternative that is not needed (the trust statement for CR₃); CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk, from which CR₃ follows, is derived from three statements about L-series in the literature section; the main theorem from positive rank on the two curves replaces the restricted converse by the hypothesis that, for every input of the descent, the two curves of some slot choice have positive rank.

Appendix H: de Rham comparison in the height argument

Part of the proof of the six-contact estimate, replaced by the hypothesis H.

docs.title: Z is Diophantine in Q
docs.text:
This blueprint formalizes Theorem 1.1 of the 11/5 manuscript ℤ is Diophantine in ℚ: an integer polynomial in 292,890,231,905 variables, of degree below \(2\uparrow\uparrow 7\) and with coefficients below \(2\uparrow\uparrow 8\), whose rational zero projection to the first variable is exactly \(\mathbb Z\).

The main theorem proves it from five explicitly stated hypotheses, whose proofs lie far outside current formal libraries: the minimal form of the six-contact height estimate (the one instance of the manuscript's Theorem 4.1 that the proof uses; not a published theorem, its proof combines refereed theorems and exact computations with new arguments, the manuscript's and this project's, reviewed only by AI models), and four statements about L-series of elliptic curves over \(\mathbb Q\). Three of the four are textbook theorems: the positive-rank half of Gross–Zagier, the functional equation of the L-series of the congruent number curves \(C_d\) for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), with conductor \(32d^2\) and root number \(-1\), stated on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), and Hecke's continuation of \(L(C_d,s)\) to an entire function for every \(d\ne0\). No original source of Hecke's continuation was read, and the original source of the conductor and the functional equation has not been read in full. The fourth is a consequence of Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in one reading of its genus sums, reading A: for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), if \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes to order at least \(2\) at \(s=1\), two genus sums of class numbers are even. No refereed text found by the project's literature search, which AI agents carried out, states reading A explicitly; Tian–Yuan–Zhang's introductory theorem with the same parity criteria, read literally, is false; and their proof passes through their Proposition 3.4, whose proof is only sketched in the arXiv version; the journal's proof was not assessed on this point. A new argument written for this project, Proposition N, reviewed twice by AI models and never by a human, derives reading A from unambiguous results of that version; its derivation from a restatement of those results is proved here, but no proof checks that the restatement matches the paper, and only AI models have compared it with the paper, and it is supporting evidence, not a hypothesis of the theorem. From the four statements the proof derives a certified rank hypothesis for congruent number curves, CR₃; the theorem holds under the height hypothesis and CR₃ alone, and, in the form closest to the manuscript, under those two and the manuscript's twenty-two-prime pattern. The height hypothesis may also be assumed in its \(j\)-form, a bound on the height of the Hauptmodul value (not a published theorem) from which the minimal form is proved. The manuscript's other inputs are proved. Pole completeness follows from the certified rank hypothesis for a variant of the manuscript's pole polynomial, and also from positive rank of the congruent number curves that hypothesis covers, or of only the two curves the descent constructs; the bound for the prime catalogue follows from an effective Dirichlet theorem; the Mordell–Weil theorem for the generator curve, first stated as a hypothesis, is proved; and the twenty-two-prime pattern is not needed: a change in the completeness proof, route AP, uses long arithmetic progressions of good primes instead, which come from Szemerédi's theorem in the primes (from a Lean proof of the Green–Tao theorem) and a density theorem for those primes. The passage from positive rank to points in every Selmer class rests on the complete 2-descent and the Mordell–Weil theorem for these curves, and Smith's row-5b identity and Rédei's formula let the hypothesis be stated in Tian, Yuan and Zhang's terms; all four are proved. Everything else is proved, with every finite computation checked by the Lean kernel.

docs.title: Assembly and the ordinary-value relation
docs.text:
This chapter proves that the rational zero projection of the specified polynomial \(P_*\) is exactly \(\mathbb Z\), and assembles the target statement. It follows Section 11 of the manuscript (the variable-shift relation for ordinary values) and Lemma 1.2 (assembly).

The polynomial never sees an integer directly. A rational input \(t\) comes with a code \(N\in\mathbb Q^5\), which membership types as \(N=\iota(n)\) for an integer index \(n\); the value relation must then force \(t=n\). The point coordinates and the integer index play distinct roles throughout: the index is what the precision computation and the height estimate reason about, the coordinates are what the polynomial sees. For the six contact values \(n\in\mathcal C=\{0,-15,-20,-24,-30,-60\}\) an exceptional branch states \(t=n\) outright. For every other \(n\), the main branch chooses one shift \(\kappa\ne0\), a five-coordinate code shared by two relations: Close, which says that \(t\) lies within \(e^{-B(n,\kappa)}\) of \(n\) with \(B(n,\kappa)=H_6(S_{\rm ht})|\kappa F(n)|^{24}\), and Test, which through the height estimate bounds \(h(t)\le B(n,\kappa)\). A rational number of height at most \(B\) that is so close to an integer is that integer.

The constants \(D\), \(H_6(S_{\rm ht})\) and \(B(n,\kappa)\) are astronomically large. Every argument here treats them symbolically through their defining expressions; none is ever evaluated.

3 fully proved

docs.title: The value templates
docs.text:
The specification chapter defines the five templates of the value relation; their meaning is proved first. It rests on the elliptic model (input G: membership types arbitrary inputs, raw addition is the group law on canonical codes) and on multiplication (input M).

  • The value templates and their relations

docs.title: Approximation for every fixed shift
docs.text:
The relation Close links the five signed codes \(N,\mathcal K,A,L,J\) to the inputs of the compiled precision relation (input C) and imposes the coordinate window \(|t-r(a,j)|<\epsilon_l\). It is sound, \(|t-n|<e^{-B(n,\kappa)}\), and complete for every fixed nonzero shift, because positive multiples of \(P_0\) approach the identity at both real places and the derivative of \([n]\) at the identity is \(n\).

  • Approximation for every fixed shift

docs.title: The six local tests
docs.text:
The relation Test forms six field-valued tests from the shift, puts them over one common denominator \(F(t)\) into one product \(W\), one trace \(\Theta\) and one instance \(\Phi(R/\Theta^2)\) of the pole predicate. Soundness (Lemma 11.1) uses the pole obstruction and the formal groups at the primes above each contact prime to show \(M_{S_{\rm ht}}(t)\mid\kappa F(n)\). Completeness (Lemma 11.2) chooses \(\kappa\) deep in the formal groups above the primes of \(2730^6F(n)\) and applies pole completeness (PC).

  • The six local tests

docs.title: Exact ordinary value
docs.text:
In an accepting main branch, the divisibility lemma and the six-contact estimate (H) give \(h(t)\le B(n,\kappa)\), and soundness of Close gives \(|t-n|<e^{-B(n,\kappa)}\); a reduced fraction \(a/b\ne n\) has \(|t-n|\ge1/b\ge e^{-h(t)}\), so \(t=n\).

Conversely, for \(n\notin\mathcal C\) one suitable shift satisfies Test, Close holds for that same shift, and the two calls have disjoint private witness blocks, so they are satisfied simultaneously. Hence the value relation is exactly the graph \(t=n\), and projecting away the code gives ordinary \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\).

docs.title: An accepting main branch forces the exact value
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.main_branch_eq

Assume the minimal height hypothesis, pole completeness and the slope representation. Let \(n,\kappa\in\mathbb Z\) and \(t\in\mathbb Q\). If \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{close}}(\iota(n),\iota(\kappa),t)\) and \(\operatorname{Test}(n,\kappa,t)\), then \(t=n\).

Proof sketch. Soundness of Close gives \(n otin\mathcal C\), \(\kappa e0\) and \(|t-n|<e^{-B(n,\kappa)}\). The test gives \(t otin\mathcal C\) and, by the divisibility lemma, \(M_{S_{ m ht}}(t)\mid\kappa F(n)\); as \(\kappa F(n) e0\), \(M_{S_{ m ht}}(t)\le|\kappa F(n)|\). Apply the minimal height hypothesis at \(u=t otin\mathcal C\); since \(S_{ m ht}\subseteq S_{ m mul}\), \(M_{S_{ m mul}}(t)\) divides \(M_{S_{ m ht}}(t)\), so $\(h(t)\le H_6(D)\,M_{S_{ m mul}}(t)^{24}\le H_6(D)\,M_{S_{ m ht}}(t)^{24}\le A^{(0)}_{ m ht}\,|\kappa F(n)|^{24}=B(n,\kappa),\)$ where \(H_6(D)=H_6(S_{ m ht};D)=A^{(0)}_{ m ht}\) is the precision height constant. Suppose \(t=a/b e n\) in lowest terms, \(b>0\). Then \(|a-nb|\ge1\), so $\(|t-n|\ge1/b\ge e^{-h(t)}\ge e^{-B(n,\kappa)},\)$ contradicting soundness of Close. Hence \(t=n\). No numerical value of \(A^{(0)}_{ m ht}\) or \(D\) is needed.

docs.title: The exact ordinary-value relation
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.value_relation_iff ZInQ.Assembly.exists_value_relation_iff

Assume the minimal height hypothesis, pole completeness and the slope representation. Then for every \(N\in\mathbb Q^5\) and every \(t\in\mathbb Q\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value}}(N,t)\iff\exists\,n\in\mathbb Z:\ N=\iota(n)\ ext{and}\ t=n .\)$ Consequently, for every \(t\in\mathbb Q\), $\( igl(\exists\,N\in\mathbb Q^5:\ \mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value}}(N,t) igr)\iff t\in\mathbb Z .\)$

In the manuscript's notation, \(\operatorname{Val}(N,t)\) is membership of \(N\) together with \( igvee_{c\in\mathcal C}(N=\iota(c)\wedge t=c)\ \vee\ \exists\mathcal K\,(\operatorname{Close}(N,\mathcal K,t)\wedge\operatorname{Test}(N,\mathcal K,t))\), with the same five coordinates \(\mathcal K\) in both calls, and \(\operatorname{Val}(\iota(n),t)\) is exactly the graph \(t=n\).

Proof sketch. By the relations of the outer recipes, \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value}}(N,t)\) holds exactly when \(N\) is accepted by membership and either the exceptional relation holds or there is \(K\) with \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{close}}(N,K,t)\) and \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value.test}}(N,K,t)\).

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Membership gives \(N=\iota(n)\). In the exceptional branch, \(N=\iota(c)\) and \(t=c\) for some \(c\in\mathcal C\), and \(c=n\) by injectivity of \(\iota\). In the main branch, the value-test semantics gives \(N=\iota(n')\), \(K=\iota(\kappa)\) and \(\operatorname{Test}(n',\kappa,t)\) with \(n'=n\); then \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{close}}(\iota(n),\iota(\kappa),t)\) and \(\operatorname{Test}(n,\kappa,t)\) force \(t=n\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Let \(N=\iota(n)\) and \(t=n\); \(N\) is accepted by membership. If \(n\in\mathcal C\), the exceptional relation holds. If \(n otin\mathcal C\), choose \(\kappa e0\) with \(\operatorname{Test}(n,\kappa,n)\) (one suitable shift), then \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{close}}(\iota(n),\iota(\kappa),n)\) for that same shift (completeness of Close), and \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value.test}}(\iota(n),\iota(\kappa),n)\); the main relation holds with \(K=\iota(\kappa)\). The two calls have disjoint private blocks, so they are satisfied simultaneously, and the block of the inactive factor of the product takes arbitrary values.

For the consequence, project to \(t\): the right side becomes \(\exists n\in\mathbb Z,\ t=n\). For \(n\in\mathcal C\) the main branch is never accepted (Close requires \(n otin\mathcal C\)), so the six exceptional integers are given exactly by their displayed branches.

docs.title: Assembly
docs.text: The root recipe squares one call of the value relation with a fresh code, so the rational zero projection of \(P_*\) is the projection of the value relation; with the witness accounting and the size bounds of the specification and size chapters this proves the target statement for \(P_*\) under the four hypotheses. The main theorem follows directly.

docs.title: The assembly lemma
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.Pstar_spec ZInQ.Assembly.assembly

Assume the minimal height hypothesis, pole completeness and the slope representation. Then the specified polynomial \(P_*\in\mathbb Z[X_0,\dots,X_{292890231904}]\) satisfies:

  1. \(\deg P_*<2\uparrow\uparrow7\);
  2. every coefficient of \(P_*\) has absolute value less than \(2\uparrow\uparrow8\);
  3. for every \(q\in\mathbb Q\), $\(\bigl(\exists\,w\in\mathbb Q^{292890231904}:\ P_*(q,w)=0\bigr)\iff q\in\mathbb Z .\)$

In particular \(P_*\) witnesses the target statement, from which the main theorem follows at once.

This is the manuscript's Lemma 1.2 in the form used here, over the minimal form of H (the instance \(S=S_{\rm mul}\), \(R=D\) of the six-contact estimate), PC, and the slope representation, which is what the multiplication proof uses of 22P and which 22P and 22P₂ both give; the manuscript's fourth input CAT is a theorem here (the catalogue bound holds). Its inputs are: G, that canonical codes form \(2E(K_0)=\mathbb ZP_0\) with exact membership and raw addition (from the generator certificate, whose Mordell–Weil input is proved by the two-isogeny descent); M, multiplication (from the minimal height hypothesis, pole completeness and the slope representation); C, the semantics of the natural precision polynomial and its rational translation; B, the literal specification of \(P_*\) with its witness accounting and size bounds (the size bounds use the catalogue bound); and the hypotheses H (in its minimal form) and PC themselves. Besides the three hypotheses, the proof uses one finite computation, checked in the kernel: the node statistics of the universal halting circuit, on which the witness accounting and the size bounds of B depend.

Proof sketch. Part 3: by the rational zero projection of the specified polynomial, the left side holds exactly when \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value}}(N,q)\) for some \(N\in\mathbb Q^5\), and by the exact ordinary-value relation this holds exactly when \(q\in\mathbb Z\). Parts 1 and 2 are the variable, degree and coefficient bounds for the same \(P_*\); the constants \(D\), \(T\), \(H_{\rm cat}\) and the tower values are handled symbolically there and never evaluated. The witness accounting shows that \(P_*\) involves only \(X_0,\dots,X_{292890231904}\), with input \(X_0\) and \(292890231904\) witnesses, so \(P_*\), read in these variables, is a polynomial of the shape required by the target statement.

docs.title: Approximation for every fixed shift
docs.text:
The precision computation of the compiler chapter decides, for five integers \((n,\kappa,a,l,j)\) given by their signed encodings, whether \(n\notin\mathcal C\), \(\kappa\ne0\), \(a,l\ge1\), \(j=na\) and the two strict tests \(|r(a,j)-n|<\epsilon_l\) and \(4\epsilon_l<4^{-B(n,\kappa)}\) hold. All quantities are exact rationals and integers. The compiler chapter defines the precision relation, the local parameter and the window quantities, the signed encoding and the precision height constant, and proves that this constant is the six-contact constant \(H_6(S_{\rm ht})\), so that its bound is the \(B(n,\kappa)\) of the ordinary-value relation (identification). Its admissibility clause is automatic for nonzero indices, by the nonzero-multiples lemma.

Close chooses codes \(A,L,J\), links the five signed codes to the precision inputs in the order \((n,\kappa,a,l,j)\) and imposes \(|t-r(a,j)|<\epsilon_l\) on the same coordinates.

Soundness is the triangle inequality: \(|t-n|<2\epsilon_l<4^{-B}/2<e^{-B}\).

For completeness, positive multiples of \(P_0\) approach the identity simultaneously at both real places. The manuscript cites compactness of \(E(\mathbf R)\times E(\mathbf R)\); here the needed compactness and continuity of subtraction are proved by hand for real curves \(y^2=x^3-e^2x\).

Near the identity, \(z([n]Q)/z(Q)\) tends to \(n\); with the division-polynomial formulas this is a limit of rational functions at infinity.

Choosing \(l\) first so that \(\epsilon_l\) is small enough, and then \(a\) with \(r(a,na)\) within \(\epsilon_l\) of \(n\), gives Close for every fixed nonzero shift.

6 fully proved

docs.title: The relation Close
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.close_relation_iff

Assume the six-contact estimate, pole completeness and the twenty-two-prime pattern. Then for all \(N,K\in\mathbb Q^5\) and \(t\in\mathbb Q\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{close}}(N,K,t)\) holds exactly when there are \(n,\kappa,a,l\in\mathbb Z\) with $\(N=\iota(n),\quad K=\iota(\kappa),\quad\operatorname{Prec}(n,\kappa,a,l,na),\quad |t-r(a,na)|<\epsilon_l ,\)$ where, for integers \(n,\kappa,a,l,j\), \(\operatorname{Prec}(n,\kappa,a,l,j)\) abbreviates the precision relation \(\operatorname{accepts}(\operatorname{enc}n,\operatorname{enc}\kappa,\operatorname{enc}a,\operatorname{enc}l,\operatorname{enc}j)\) at the signed encodings, and \(r(a,j)\) and \(\epsilon_l\) are the quantities of the local parameter \(z\), defined because \(\operatorname{Prec}\) includes the admissibility of \(l,a,j\). This is the manuscript's \(\operatorname{Close}(N,\mathcal K,t)\): choose \(A,L,J\), link the five signed codes \(N,\mathcal K,A,L,J\) to the precision inputs in the order \((n,\kappa,a,l,j)\), and impose \(|t-r(a,j)|<\epsilon_l\) on the same coordinates.

Proof sketch. By the relations of the outer recipes, \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{close}}(N,K,t)\) holds exactly when there are \(A,L,J,E_0,\dots,E_4\) with five signed-encoding relations, the precision relation and the coordinate window. Input C is used as a chain of three equivalences. Let \(C\) be the natural precision polynomial. For all \(E_0,\dots,E_4\in\mathbb Q^5\):

  • by the semantics of the rational translation (which uses the multiplication statement M and so the three hypotheses of M), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{precision}}(E_0,\dots,E_4)\) holds exactly when there is \(c\in\mathbb N^5\) with \(E_i=\iota(c_i)\) for \(0\le i\le4\) and \(C(c,\mathbf z)=0\) for some \(\mathbf z\in\mathbb N^{1305806}\);
  • by the semantics of the natural precision polynomial, the existence of such \(\mathbf z\) is \(\operatorname{accepts}(c)\);
  • since \(\operatorname{enc}\circ\operatorname{dec}\) is the identity, \(\operatorname{accepts}(c)\) is \(\operatorname{Prec}(\operatorname{dec}c_0,\dots,\operatorname{dec}c_4)\).

Hence $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{precision}}(E_0,\dots,E_4)\iff\exists\,c\in\mathbb N^5:\ E_i=\iota(c_i)\ (0\le i\le4)\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{Prec}(\operatorname{dec}c_0,\dots,\operatorname{dec}c_4).\)$

(\(\Rightarrow\)) The signed encodings give \(\Sigma_i=\iota(m_i)\) and \(E_i=\iota(\operatorname{enc}m_i)\) with \((m_0,\dots,m_4)=(n,\kappa,a,l,j)\). By input C and injectivity of \(\iota\), \(c_i=\operatorname{enc}m_i\), so \(\operatorname{Prec}(n,\kappa,a,l,j)\), in particular \(j=na\). The coordinate window gives indices \(a',l',j'\) with \(A=\iota(a')\) etc. and \(|t-r(a',j')|<\epsilon_{l'}\); injectivity gives \((a',l',j')=(a,l,j)\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Put \(j=na\), \(A=\iota(a)\), \(L=\iota(l)\), \(J=\iota(j)\) and \(E_i=\iota(\operatorname{enc}m_i)\). The signed encodings hold, the precision relation holds by input C since \(\operatorname{dec}\circ\operatorname{enc}\) is the identity, and the coordinate window holds because \(a,l\ge1\) are nonzero.

Assume the six-contact estimate, pole completeness and the twenty-two-prime pattern. Let \(n,\kappa\in\mathbb Z\) and \(t\in\mathbb Q\). If \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{close}}(\iota(n),\iota(\kappa),t)\), then \(n otin\mathcal C\), \(\kappa e0\) and, in \(\mathbb R\), $\(|t-n|<e^{-B(n,\kappa)} .\)$

docs.title: Compactness and continuity of subtraction on a real curve
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.realCurve ZInQ.Assembly.RealCurve.TendstoPt ZInQ.Assembly.RealCurve.exists_subseq_tendstoPt ZInQ.Assembly.RealCurve.tendstoPt_sub_zero

Let \(e\in\mathbb R\), \(e e0\), and let \(E_e(\mathbb R)\) be the group of real points of \(y^2=x^3-e^2x\) (chord-and-tangent law, identity \(O\)). For a sequence \((P_m)\) in \(E_e(\mathbb R)\) and \(Q\in E_e(\mathbb R)\) write \(P_m o Q\) when

  • \(Q=(x_Q,y_Q)\) is affine, \(P_m\) is affine for all large \(m\), and \(x(P_m) o x_Q\), \(y(P_m) o y_Q\); or
  • \(Q=O\) and for every \(M\in\mathbb R\), for all large \(m\), either \(P_m=O\) or \(P_m\) is affine with \(x(P_m)>M\).

Then:

  1. every sequence in \(E_e(\mathbb R)\) has a subsequence converging to some point of \(E_e(\mathbb R)\);
  2. if \(P_m o Q\) and \(P'_m o Q\) for the same \(Q\), then \(P'_m-P_m o O\).

Proof sketch. Write \(f(x)=x^3-e^2x=(x+e)x(x-e)\); its roots \(0,\pm e\) are simple, with \(f'(c)=3c^2-e^2 e0\) at each root. Real points have \(f(x)\ge0\), so \(x\ge-|e|\).

(1) If infinitely many terms are \(O\), or the abscissas of the affine terms are unbounded above, a subsequence converges to \(O\). Otherwise the affine terms eventually lie in \([-|e|,M] imes[-\sqrt{\max f},\sqrt{\max f}]\), and Bolzano–Weierstrass gives a convergent subsequence; its limit satisfies \(y^2=f(x)\) by continuity.

(2) Discard the indices with \(P'_m=P_m\), where the difference is \(O\). Case \(Q\) affine with \(y_Q e0\): eventually \(y'+y o2y_Q e0\), so \(P' e-P\); if \(x'=x\) then \(P'=P\); otherwise \(P'-P=P'+(-P)\) has abscissa \(\lambda^2-x-x'\) with chord slope \(\lambda=(y'+y)/(x'-x)\), and \(|\lambda| o\infty\). Case \(Q=(c,0)\) with \(f(c)=0\): if \(x'=x\) then \(P'=-P\) and \(P'-P=-[2]P\) has abscissa \( igl(f'(x)/(2y) igr)^2-2x o\infty\) since \(f'(x) o f'(c) e0\) and \(y o0\); otherwise \(y'^2-y^2=(x'-x)\,g\) with \(g=x'^2+xx'+x^2-e^2 o f'(c) e0\), so eventually \(y' e y\) and \(\lambda=(y'+y)/(x'-x)=g/(y'-y)\) has \(|\lambda| o\infty\). Case \(Q=O\): translate by \(T=(0,0)\). For affine \(P=(x,y)\) with \(x e0\), \(P+T=(-e^2/x,\ e^2y/x^2)\), and \(|e^2y/x^2|^2=e^4f(x)/x^4 o0\) as \(x o\infty\), while \(O+T=T\); hence \(P_m+T o T\) and \(P'_m+T o T\), and \((P'_m+T)-(P_m+T)=P'_m-P_m o O\) by the previous case. In every case the abscissa of \(P'_m-P_m\) tends to \(+\infty\) (or the difference is \(O\)).

This is the elementary content of "\(E(\mathbb R)\) is a compact topological group"; the manuscript uses compactness of \(E(\mathbb R) imes E(\mathbb R)\) directly.

docs.title: Multiples of the generator approach the identity at both real places
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.exists_multiple_large_unconditional

For every \(M\in\mathbb R\) there is an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \([k]P_0=(x_k,y_k)\) is affine and $\(\sigma_+(x_k)>M\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma_-(x_k)>M .\)$ That is, positive multiples of \(P_0\) approach the identity simultaneously in the two real embeddings.

Proof sketch. Each real embedding \(\sigma_\pm\) maps \(E\) to the real curve \(y^2=x^3-e_\pm^2x\) with \(e_\pm=\sigma_\pm(d)=75\mp53\sqrt2\ne0\), and induces a group homomorphism \(E(K_0)\to E_{e_\pm}(\mathbb R)\), \((x,y)\mapsto(\sigma_\pm x,\sigma_\pm y)\), \(O\mapsto O\) (the chord-and-tangent formulas are rational and commute with ring homomorphisms). Apply the compactness statement to the sequence \(\sigma_+([k]P_0)\), \(k\ge1\), and then to \(\sigma_-([k]P_0)\) along the resulting subsequence: there are \(k_1<k_2<\cdots\) and points \(Q_\pm\) with \(\sigma_\pm([k_i]P_0)\to Q_\pm\). By continuity of subtraction, \(\sigma_\pm([k_{i+1}-k_i]P_0)=\sigma_\pm([k_{i+1}]P_0)-\sigma_\pm([k_i]P_0)\to O\) in both embeddings. For \(i\) large, \(k=k_{i+1}-k_i\ge1\) has both embedded points equal to \(O\) or with abscissa \(>M\); since \(P_0\) has infinite order, \([k]P_0\) is affine, so both abscissas exceed \(M\).

The manuscript's argument (partition the compact closure of the cyclic subgroup into small neighbourhoods and subtract two close multiples) is the same pigeonhole principle.

docs.text:

Let \( au\in\{\sigma_+,\sigma_-\}\) be a real embedding of \(K_0\) and \(n\) a nonzero integer. For every \(\eta>0\) there is \(M\in\mathbb R\) such that for every affine point \(Q=(x,y)\in E(K_0)\) with \( au(x)>M\):

  1. \(x e0\), \(y e0\), and \([n]Q\) is affine with nonzero abscissa and ordinate;
  2. \( igl| au igl(z([n]Q)/z(Q) igr)-n igr|<\eta\).

This is the statement that the derivative of \([n]\) at the identity is \(n\), read in the coordinate \(z=-x/y\) near \(O\) at the real place \( au\).

Proof sketch. Write \(f_m\) for the normalized division polynomials of \(y^2=x^3+Ax\), \(A=-d^2\), and \(\psi_m\) for the division polynomials. Since \(z(-P)=-z(P)\), it suffices to treat \(n\ge1\). By the multiplication-by-\(n\) formulas, if \(\psi_n(Q) e0\) then \([n]Q\) is affine with $\( rac{x([n]Q)}{x}= rac{\phi_n(x)}{x\,\psi_n^2(x)},\qquad rac{y([n]Q)}{y}= rac{f_{2n}(x)}{\psi_n^4(x)},\)$ where \(\phi_n=x\psi_n^2-\psi_{n+1}\psi_{n-1}\), and \(\psi_n^2\), \(\psi_n^4\) and \(\phi_n\) are polynomials in \(x\) after substituting \(y^2=x^3+Ax\) (the second identity is \(y([n]Q)=\psi_{2n}/(2\psi_n^4)\) with \(\psi_{2n}=2yf_{2n}\)). By the agreement with the classical division polynomials, the degrees and leading coefficients are: \(\phi_n\) degree \(n^2\), leading coefficient \(1\); \(\psi_n^2\) degree \(n^2-1\), leading coefficient \(n^2\); \(f_{2n}\) degree \(2n^2-2\), leading coefficient \(n\); \(\psi_n^4\) degree \(2n^2-2\), leading coefficient \(n^4\) (for odd \(n\) it is \(f_n^4\), for even \(n\) it is \(16(x^3+Ax)^2f_n^4\), and \(f_n\) has leading coefficient \(n\) or \(n/2\)). Apply \( au\) to the coefficients: as \( au(x) o+\infty\) the two quotients tend to \(1/n^2\) and \(1/n^3\), and \( au(\psi_n(x)^2) e0\), \( au(y^2)= au(x)( au(x)^2- au(d)^2)>0\) for \( au(x)\) large. Hence for \( au(x)>M\) all quantities are nonzero, and $\( au\Bigl( rac{z([n]Q)}{z(Q)}\Bigr)= au\Bigl( rac{x([n]Q)}{x}\Bigr)\Big/ au\Bigl( rac{y([n]Q)}{y}\Bigr)\longrightarrow rac{n^3}{n^2}=n .\)$ The polynomials depend only on \(n\) and \(A\), so \(M\) depends only on \(n\), \( au\) and \(\eta\).

docs.title: Completeness of Close for every fixed shift
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.close_complete

Assume the six-contact estimate, pole completeness and the twenty-two-prime pattern. For every \(n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\mathcal C\) and every nonzero \(\kappa\in\mathbb Z\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{close}} igl(\iota(n),\iota(\kappa),n igr).\)$ The shift \(\kappa\) is arbitrary: this holds for every already fixed nonzero \(\kappa\), whatever its size.

Proof sketch. Put \(B=B(n,\kappa)\in\mathbb N\) and \( heta=4^{-B}/4>0\). By the Close relation it suffices to find \(a,l\ge1\) with \(\operatorname{Prec}(n,\kappa,a,l,na)\) and \(|n-r(a,na)|<\epsilon_l\); the latter is one of the conditions of \(\operatorname{Prec}\).

Choice of \(l\). For an affine point with abscissa \(x\) and \( au(x)>| au(d)|\) in a real embedding \( au\), \( au(z)^2= au(x)/( au(x)^2- au(d)^2)\), which tends to \(0\) as \( au(x) o\infty\). Choose \(M_1\) such that \( au(x)>M_1\) gives \(| au(z)|< heta/2\) for both \( au=\sigma_\pm\), and by the accumulation statement choose \(l\ge1\) with \(\sigma_\pm(x([l]P_0))>M_1\). Since \(u_l=(\sigma_+z_l+\sigma_-z_l)/2\) and \(v_l=(\sigma_+z_l-\sigma_-z_l)/(2\sqrt2)\), $\(0<\epsilon_l=|u_l|+|v_l|\le|\sigma_+z_l|+|\sigma_-z_l|< heta,\)$ positivity because \(z_l e0\). Hence \(4\epsilon_l\cdot4^{B}<1\).

Choice of \(a\). Apply the real derivative statement to \(n\) with \(\eta=\epsilon_l\) in both embeddings, obtaining \(M_2\), and choose \(a\ge1\) by accumulation with \(\sigma_\pm(x([a]P_0))>M_2\). With \(Q=[a]P_0\) and \([n]Q=[na]P_0\), $\(|r(a,na)-n|=\Bigl| frac12\sum_\pm igl(\sigma_\pm(z_{na}/z_a)-n igr)\Bigr|<\epsilon_l .\)$

With \(j=na\) all conditions of \(\operatorname{Prec}(n,\kappa,a,l,j)\) hold (\(n otin\mathcal C\), \(\kappa e0\), \(a,l\ge1\), and \(l,a,j\) are admissible because they are nonzero), and the window \(|t-r(a,j)|<\epsilon_l\) holds for \(t=n\). The order of choices matters: \(l\) is fixed first, then \(a\) depending on \(\epsilon_l\).

The relation Test (defined with the value templates) puts the six tests \(D_1,\dots,D_6\) over the common denominator \(F(t)\), forms \(W=\prod(1+RC_j^2)\), the trace \(\Theta=\operatorname{Tr}(W^{-1})\) and one pole instance \(\Phi(R/\Theta^2)\). docs.title: Valuations and formal groups
docs.text:
Odd primes are unramified in \(\mathbb Z[s]\) and the trace of an element that is small at the primes above \(p\) is small at \(p\) (the primes above an odd prime); \(2\) is ramified, and at \((s)\) the trace gains one more power of \(2\).

At every prime, the points with negative abscissa valuation form a filtration by subgroups (the formal neighbourhood and its filtration), on which \(z=-x/y\) is additive up to terms of five times the depth. The manuscript uses the formal logarithm; the following elementary statement gives what is needed, including \(z([m]Q)=m\,z(Q)\cdot(\text{unit}\equiv1)\) at an odd prime.

docs.title: Valuation and trace at the prime \((s)\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.vS_star ZInQ.Assembly.vS_trace_ge

Let \(v_s\) be the valuation of \(K_0\) at the prime \((s)\), normalized by \(v_s(s)=1\) (so \(v_s(2)=2\)), \(\sigma\) the conjugation \(s\mapsto-s\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}x=x+\sigma x\in\mathbb Q\). Then:

  1. \(v_s(\sigma x)=v_s(x)\) for every \(x\in K_0\);
  2. if \(k\in\mathbb Z\) and \(v_s(x)\ge2k\), then \(v_2(\operatorname{Tr}x)\ge k+1\).

At an odd prime \(p\) the corresponding facts, with the bound \(v_p(\operatorname{Tr}x)\ge k\) when \(v_{\mathfrak p}(x)\ge k\) at every prime \(\mathfrak p\) above \(p\), are those of the primes above \(p\).

Proof sketch. (1) \(\sigma\) is a ring automorphism of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) and \(\sigma(s)=-s\) is associate to \(s\). (2) Write \(x=a+bs\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb Q\). By the valuation formula at \((s)\), \(v_s(x)=\min(2v_2(a),2v_2(b)+1)\ge2k\) gives \(v_2(a)\ge k\), so \(v_2(\operatorname{Tr}x)=v_2(2a)\ge k+1\).

docs.text:

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic \(0\) with a discrete valuation \(v\), \(v(K^ imes)=\mathbb Z\), whose residue field has characteristic \(p>0\). Let \(A\in K^ imes\) with \(v(A)\ge0\), \(W:y^2=x^3+Ax\), and let \(W_k(K)\) and \(z\) be as in the formal neighbourhood statement: \(W_k(K)\) is the subgroup of the points with \(v(z)\ge k\), that is \(v(x)\le-2k\), together with \(O\). Then:

  1. for \(k\ge1\) and \(P,Q\in W_k(K)\), $\(v igl(z(P+Q)-z(P)-z(Q) igr)\ge5k ;\)$
  2. for every affine \(Q\in W_1(K)\), with \(k=v(z(Q))\), and every \(n\in\mathbb Z\), \(v igl(z([n]Q)-n\,z(Q) igr)\ge5k\), hence \(v igl(z([n]Q)/z(Q)-n igr)\ge4k\);
  3. \([p]W_k(K)\subseteq W_{k+1}(K)\) for every \(k\ge1\); and if \(v(p)\le4\), then \([n]W_k(K)\subseteq W_{k+v(n)}(K)\) for every nonzero \(n\in\mathbb Z\) and every \(k\ge1\);
  4. if \(p\) is odd and \(v(p)=1\), then for every affine \(Q\in W_1(K)\), with \(k=v(z(Q))\), and every nonzero \(m\in\mathbb Z\), the point \([m]Q\) is affine, \(v(z([m]Q))=k+v_p(m)\), and $\(z([m]Q)=m\,z(Q)\,u_m\qquad ext{with }v(u_m-1)\ge1 .\)$

On \(K_0\), for a prime element \(\pi\) of \(\mathbb Z[s]\), write \(E_k(\pi)\) for the subgroup \(W_k(K_0)\) of \(E\) at \(v=v_\pi\), and \( u_\pi(P)=v_\pi(z(P))\) for affine \(P\in E_1(\pi)\). The hypotheses hold at every \(\pi\), including \(s\) and \(d\), because \(A=-d^2\) is integral everywhere; \(v_\pi(p)=1\) at a prime above an odd prime \(p\), and \(v_s(2)=2\).

Item 4 is the content of "\(\log([m]Q)=m\log(Q)\) and \(\log\) is an isometry with \(\log(Q)=z(Q)(1+e_Q)\), \(v(e_Q)\ge1\)" used in the manuscript, in the form actually needed. Item 3 is the elementary form of the logarithm isometry: the manuscript argues at \((s)\) with \(v_s(z([2]Q))=v_s(z(Q))+2\) for \(v_s(z(Q))\ge3\), and the inequality \(\ge\) given by item 3 is all that is used.

Proof sketch. (1) Use the coordinates \(z\) and \(\omega=-1/y\) of the formal neighbourhood statement. For affine \(P_1,P_2\in W_k(K)\) with \(P_2 e-P_1\), its chord construction gives the line \(\omega=\lambda z+ u\) through them (the tangent if \(P_1=P_2\)), with \(v(\lambda)\ge2k\) and \(v( u)\ge3k\), and by Vieta on the cubic \((1+A\lambda^2)z^3+2A\lambda u z^2+(A u^2-\lambda)z- u=0\), $\(z(P_1+P_2)=z(P_1)+z(P_2)+ rac{2A\lambda u}{1+A\lambda^2},\)$ where the last term has valuation at least \(5k\) because \(1+A\lambda^2\) is a unit. Sums involving \(O\), and \(P_2=-P_1\), are immediate since \(z(-P)=-z(P)\).

(2) The multiples \([j]Q\) lie in the subgroup \(W_k(K)\). By (1), \(z([j+1]Q)=z([j]Q)+z(Q)+e_j\) with \(v(e_j)\ge5k\); summing gives the claim for \(n\ge0\), and \(z(-P)=-z(P)\) gives \(n<0\). Divide by \(z(Q)\), which has valuation \(k\).

(3) Let \(Q\in W_k(K)\) be affine with \(v(z(Q))=k'\ge k\). By (2), \(v(z([p]Q))\ge\min(5k',k'+v(p))\), which is at least \(k'+1\), and equals \(k'+v(p)\) when \(v(p)\le4\); so \([p]Q\in W_{k+1}(K)\), and \([p]Q\in W_{k+v(p)}(K)\) when \(v(p)\le4\). Iterate for powers of \(p\), and note that \([n']W_k(K)\subseteq W_k(K)\) for \(n'\) prime to \(p\).

(4) Now \(v(p)=1\). For \(p mid m'\): by (2), \(z([m']Q)=m'z(Q)(1+\epsilon)\) with \(v(\epsilon)\ge4k\ge1\), so \(v(z([m']Q))=k\). For \(p\): \(z([p]Q)=p\,z(Q)(1+\epsilon)\) with \(v(\epsilon)\ge5k-(k+1)\ge3\), so \(v(z([p]Q))=k+1\). Write \(m=p^em'\) and compose, applying these to \([p^i]Q\) (of valuation \(k+i\)) and then to \([p^e]Q\); the units multiply and stay \(\equiv1\). In particular \(z([m]Q) e0\), so \([m]Q e O\).

docs.title: Soundness
docs.text: At a prime above a contact prime \(p\), the pole obstruction forces the pole input to have positive valuation, which makes all six tests small at one prime above \(p\). The first four put the four points in formal groups, and the last two, through the multiplication estimate, give \(s_0/h\equiv t\) and \((s_0-\kappa n)/(h-\kappa)\equiv t\), hence \(p\mid\kappa(n-c)\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.test_dvd

Let \(n,\kappa\in\mathbb Z\) and \(t\in\mathbb Q\). If \(\operatorname{Test}(n,\kappa,t)\) holds, then $\(M_{S_{ m ht}}(t)\ ig|\ \kappa F(n),\)$ where \(M_{S_{ m ht}}(t)\) is the product of the primes \(p>324\) for which \(v_p(t-c)\) is positive and odd for some \(c\in\mathcal C\). No unit assumption on \(\kappa\) is used, and no hypothesis is needed.

Proof sketch. Fix the data \(h,s_0,\eta,q\) of the test. Since \(M_{S_{ m ht}}(t)\) is squarefree, it suffices to show \(p\mid\kappa F(n)\) for every prime \(p>324\) with \(\delta=v_p(t-c)>0\) odd for some \(c\in\mathcal C\). For \(c' e c\) in \(\mathcal C\), \(0<|c-c'|\le60<p\), so \(v_p(t-c')=0\); hence \(v_p(F(t))=\delta\), and \(t\) is \(p\)-integral. The primes above \(p\) have \(v_\pi(p)=1\), and \(v_\pi\) restricts to \(v_p\) on \(\mathbb Q\).

Valuation of \(R\). \(\eta\) and \(2730^6\) are \(p\)-units, so \(v_p(R_0q^2)=\delta+2v_p(q)\) when \(q e0\). Put \(b=v_p(a_0)\). If \(q=0\) then \(b=0\); otherwise \(\delta+2v_p(q)\) is odd, hence nonzero, and \(b=\min(0,\delta+2v_p(q))\le0\). So \(\alpha=v_p(R)=\delta+2b\) is odd.

Valuation of \(W\). At each prime \(\pi\) above \(p\), \(v_\pi(RC_j^2)=\alpha+2(v_\pi(D_j)-\delta)\) is odd, hence nonzero, so \(v_\pi(1+RC_j^2)=\min igl(0,\alpha+2(v_\pi(D_j)-\delta) igr)\) (this is \(0\) if \(D_j=0\)). Let \(\lambda=\max_{\pi\mid p}v_\pi(W)\le0\). Since \(v_\pi(W^{-1})\ge-\lambda\) at every \(\pi\) above \(p\), the trace statement gives \(v_p(\Theta)\ge-\lambda\ge0\).

The pole input. \(B_{ m pole}=R/\Theta^2 e0\) has \(v_p(B_{ m pole})=\alpha-2v_p(\Theta)\), which is odd; since \(\Phi(B_{ m pole})\) and \(p otin\{2,3,5,7,13\}\), the one-sided pole obstruction says it is not negative, so it is positive. Hence \(\alpha>2v_p(\Theta)\ge-2\lambda\ge0\): \(\alpha>0\) and \(\lambda>-\alpha/2\).

All six tests are small at one prime. Take \(\pi\) above \(p\) with \(v_\pi(W)=\lambda\). The six terms \(\min(0,\alpha+2(v_\pi(D_j)-\delta))\) are \(\le0\) and sum to \(\lambda\), so each is \(\ge\lambda>-\alpha/2\); hence \(v_\pi(D_j)>\delta-3\alpha/4=\delta/4-3b/2>0\), so \(v_\pi(D_j)\ge1\) for \(j=1,\dots,6\). Let \(\pi'=\sigma(\pi)\), so \(v_\pi(\sigma(x))=v_{\pi'}(x)\).

Formal groups. \(v_\pi(D_1)\ge1\) and \(v_\pi(D_2)\ge1\) put \(H e O\) and \(U\) in \(E_1(\pi)\); \(v_\pi(D_3)\ge1\) and \(v_\pi(D_4)\ge1\) put \(V_0 e O\) and \(V_1\) in \(E_1(\pi')\). The fifth test makes \(z(U)/z(H)\) integral at \(\pi\) and congruent to \(t\) modulo \(\pi\). Let \(g=\gcd(h,s_0)>0\) and \(Q=[g]P_0\). The set of \(m\) with \([m]P_0\in E_1(\pi)\) is a subgroup of \(\mathbb Z\) containing \(h\) and \(s_0\), so \(Q\in E_1(\pi)\), and \(Q e O\) because \(H=[h/g]Q e O\). By the multiplication statement (\(p\) odd), \(z(H)=(h/g)z(Q)u\) and \(z(U)=(s_0/g)z(Q)u'\) with \(u,u'\equiv1\pmod\pi\) (for \(s_0=0\) take \(u'=1\)). Hence \(s_0/h=(z(U)/z(H))(u/u')\) is \(\pi\)-integral and congruent to \(t\), so \(v_p(s_0/h-t)\ge1\) and, \(h\) being an integer, \(s_0\equiv th\pmod p\) in \(\mathbb Z_{(p)}\). The same argument at \(\pi'\) with \(V_0=[h-\kappa]P_0\), \(V_1=[s_0-\kappa n]P_0\) and the sixth test gives \(s_0-\kappa n\equiv t(h-\kappa)\pmod p\). Subtracting, \(v_p(\kappa(t-n))\ge1\); since \(v_p(t-c)\ge1\), \(p\mid\kappa(n-c)\), and \(n-c\) divides \(F(n)\), so \(p\mid\kappa F(n)\).

docs.title: Completeness
docs.text:
Some multiple of \(P_0\) lies in any given formal neighbourhood: at the primes above an odd prime by the reduction orders of the size chapter (reduction orders of \(P_0\)), including the bad prime \(d\), and at \(s\) because \(P_0\) already lies in the dyadic formal group (the generator in the dyadic formal group).

With such a shift the tests are divisible by \(F(n)\) at every prime of \(R_0\), so \(W\equiv1\) and \(\Theta\equiv2\) there and the pole input has the local properties required by pole completeness; a rational \(q\) close to \(R_0^{-1/2}\) makes it lie in \((0,1/2)\).

docs.title: Deep multiples of the generator
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.exists_smul_mem_Ek ZInQ.Assembly.exists_common_smul_mem_Ek

For every prime element \(\pi\) of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) and every integer \(N\ge1\) there is an integer \(m\ge1\) with \([m]P_0\in E_N(\pi)\); then \([jm]P_0\in E_N(\pi)\) for every \(j\in\mathbb Z\). Consequently, for every finite set \(\Pi\) of prime elements and every \(N\ge1\) there is \(\kappa\ge1\) with \([j\kappa]P_0\in E_N(\pi)\) for all \(\pi\in\Pi\) and \(j\in\mathbb Z\).

This is the manuscript's "each sufficiently small local formal neighbourhood has finite index in the compact local group; a positive common multiple of the quotient orders gives \(\kappa\)", restricted to the cyclic group generated by \(P_0\).

Proof sketch. First find \(m_1\ge1\) with \([m_1]P_0\in E_1(\pi)\): if \(\pi\sim s\), \(m_1=1\) since \(P_0\in E_3(s)\); otherwise \(\pi\) lies above an odd prime \(p\), and the reduction orders of \(P_0\) (with \(N=p\)) give some \(m_1\le p^6\); at \(\pi\sim d\) this uses that \(P_0\) reduces to a nonsingular point of the cuspidal cubic. Let \(p\) be the rational prime below \(\pi\). Multiplying by \(p\) raises \(\nu_\pi\) by at least one, so \(m=p^{N-1}m_1\) works. Since \(E_N(\pi)\) is a subgroup, every multiple of \(m\) works too. For a finite set \(\Pi\), take \(\kappa=\prod_{\pi\in\Pi}m_\pi\).

docs.title: Local conditions on the pole input
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.poleInput_local

Let \(n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\mathcal C\), let \(\eta\in\{1,-1\}\) have the sign of \(F(n)\), and put \(R_0=\eta\cdot2730^6\cdot F(n)\), a positive integer. Let \(\kappa\ge1\) be such that for every prime element \(\pi\) of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) dividing \(R_0\), $\([\kappa]P_0\in E_N(\pi)\qquad\text{for some }N\ge\max\bigl(1,v_\pi(F(n))\bigr).\)$ Put \(h=2\kappa\), \(s_0=2\kappa n\), so that \(H=[2\kappa]P_0\), \(U=[2\kappa n]P_0\), \(V_0=[\kappa]P_0\), \(V_1=[\kappa n]P_0\), and let \(D_1,\dots,D_6\) and \(C_j=D_j/F(n)\) be the six tests at \(t=n\). Let \(q\in\mathbb Q\) with \(v_p(q)\ge0\) for every prime \(p\mid R_0\), and suppose that \(a_0=1-R_0q^2\), \(W\) and \(\Theta=\operatorname{Tr}(W^{-1})\) (formed with \(R=R_0a_0^2\)) are nonzero. Then \(B=R/\Theta^2\) satisfies $\(v_2(B)\ge4,\qquad v_p(B)\ge6\ \ (p=3,5,7,13),\qquad\text{and the reduced denominator of }B\text{ is a square.}\)$

Proof sketch. Let \(S'\) be the set of primes dividing \(R_0\); it contains \(2,3,5,7,13\), and \(e_p=v_p(R_0)=6+v_p(F(n))\) for those five primes.

The tests are small at \(S'\). Let \(\pi\) divide \(R_0\). All multiples of \([\kappa]P_0\) lie in \(E_N(\pi)\) and in \(E_N(\sigma(\pi))\), and \(\sigma(\pi)\) divides \(R_0\) too. Hence \(v_\pi(D_1),v_\pi(D_2)\ge2N\) (for \(w=1/x\)), \(v_\pi(D_3),v_\pi(D_4)\ge2N\) (at \(\sigma(\pi)\)), and, by the multiplication statement applied to \(Q=[2\kappa]P_0\) at \(\pi\) and to \(Q=[\kappa]P_0\) at \(\sigma(\pi)\), \(v_\pi(D_5),v_\pi(D_6)\ge4N\). So \(v_\pi(D_j)\ge v_\pi(F(n))\) for all \(j\).

\(W\equiv1\) and \(\Theta\equiv2\). At \(\pi\mid p\in S'\), \(q\) is integral and \(v_\pi(R_0q^2)\ge1\), so \(a_0\) is a unit and \(v_\pi(RC_j^2)=v_\pi(R_0)+2(v_\pi(D_j)-v_\pi(F(n)))\ge v_\pi(R_0)\). Hence \(v_\pi(W-1)\ge v_\pi(R_0)\), \(W\) is a unit and \(v_\pi(W^{-1}-1)\ge v_\pi(R_0)=e_pv_\pi(p)\). The trace statement gives \(v_p(\Theta-2)\ge e_p\) for odd \(p\), so \(\Theta\) is a \(p\)-unit, and \(v_2(\Theta-2)\ge e_2+1\ge7\), so \(v_2(\Theta)=1\).

Valuations of \(B\). For odd \(p\in S'\), \(v_p(B)=e_p\ge1\), and \(e_p\ge6\) for \(p=3,5,7,13\). At \(2\), \(v_2(B)=e_2-2=4+v_2(F(n))\ge4\). For \(p\notin S'\), \(v_p(R_0)=0\), so \(v_p(B)=2v_p(a_0)-2v_p(\Theta)\) is even. Thus every prime of the reduced denominator of \(B\) lies outside \(S'\) and occurs to an even power.

docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.poleInput_real

Let \(R_0>1\) be an integer and \(C_1,\dots,C_6\in K_0\). There is \(q\in\mathbb Q\) whose reduced denominator is coprime to \(R_0\) such that, with $\(a_0=1-R_0q^2,\qquad R=R_0a_0^2,\qquad W=\prod_{j=1}^6 igl(1+RC_j^2 igr),\qquad\Theta=\operatorname{Tr}(W^{-1}),\)$ one has \(a_0 e0\), \(W e0\), \(\Theta e0\) and $\(0<R/\Theta^2<1/2 .\)$

Proof sketch. Positivity. For any \(q\) with \(a_0 e0\), \(R>0\). In each real embedding \( au=\sigma_\pm\), \( au(RC_j^2)=R\, au(C_j)^2\ge0\), so \( au(W)\ge1\); hence \(W e0\), \(0< au(W^{-1})\le1\) and \(\Theta=\sigma_+(W^{-1})+\sigma_-(W^{-1})\in(0,2]\). So \(R/\Theta^2>0\).

Smallness. Let \(c=\max_{j,\pm}\sigma_\pm(C_j)^2\). If \(R\le r:=\min igl(1/4,\ 1/(10(c+1)) igr)\) then \( au(W)\le(1+Rc)^6\le e^{6/10}<2\), so \( au(W^{-1})>1/2\), \(\Theta>1\) and \(R/\Theta^2<R\le1/4\).

Choice of \(q\). For \(j\in\mathbb N\) put \(m_j=R_0j+1\), coprime to \(R_0\), and let \(k_j\) be the integer nearest to \(m_j/\sqrt{R_0}\), so \(q_j=k_j/m_j\) has \(|q_j-R_0^{-1/2}|\le1/(2m_j)\) and reduced denominator dividing \(m_j\). Then \(|a_0|=R_0\,|R_0^{-1/2}-q_j|\,|R_0^{-1/2}+q_j| o0\), so \(R=R_0a_0^2<r\) for \(j\) large. Finally \(a_0 e0\): \(R_0q_j^2=1\) would give \(R_0k_j^2=m_j^2\), so \(R_0\mid m_j^2\), impossible as \(\gcd(R_0,m_j)=1\) and \(R_0>1\). (The manuscript's "adjusting by one if equality occurs" is therefore never needed.)

docs.title: One suitable shift
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.test_complete

Assume pole completeness. For every \(n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\mathcal C\) there is a nonzero \(\kappa\in\mathbb Z\) with $\(\operatorname{Test}(n,\kappa,n).\)$

Proof sketch. \(F(n) e0\); choose \(\eta=\pm1\) with \(R_0=\eta\cdot2730^6F(n)>0\), so \(R_0>1\). Let \(\Pi\) be the finite set of prime elements of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) dividing \(R_0\) (one per associate class) and \(N=1+\max_{\pi\in\Pi}v_\pi(F(n))\). By the deep-multiples statement there is \(\kappa\ge1\) with \([\kappa]P_0\in E_N(\pi)\) for all \(\pi\in\Pi\).

Take \(h=2\kappa\), \(s_0=2\kappa n\), so that $\(H=[2\kappa]P_0,\quad U=[2\kappa n]P_0,\quad V_0=[\kappa]P_0,\quad V_1=[\kappa n]P_0 .\)$ Then \(\kappa e0\), \(h e0\) and \(h-\kappa=\kappa e0\), and \(t=n otin\mathcal C\). The six tests \(D_1,\dots,D_6\) and \(C_j=D_j/F(n)\) are now fixed elements of \(K_0\). By the real-conditions statement choose \(q\) with reduced denominator coprime to \(R_0\) (so \(v_p(q)\ge0\) for \(p\mid R_0\)) such that \(a_0,W,\Theta e0\) and \(0<B_{ m pole}<1/2\). By the local-conditions statement, \(v_p(B_{ m pole})\ge4\) for every \(p\in\{2,3,5,7,13\}\) and the reduced denominator of \(B_{ m pole}\) is a square. Pole completeness gives \(\Phi(B_{ m pole})\). All conditions of \(\operatorname{Test}(n,\kappa,n)\) hold.

Compared with the manuscript: its "integral trace justifies this also at the ramified place two" is the case \(p=2\) of the trace statement, and the guards hold because nonzero multiples of \(P_0\) are affine with nonzero coordinates.

docs.title: The value templates and their relations
The value templates and their relations
docs.text:
The value relation is assembled from the membership template, three value templates (signed encoding, coordinate window, value test), the exceptional-values template and the precision recipe, combined by five composition recipes. This section proves what each template expresses on arbitrary rational inputs. Every proof has the same shape: the template polynomial is the square of a compiled formula whose calls have disjoint private blocks, so the private-witness lemma replaces each call by its relation, and the model statements identify the relations on codes.

Nonzero multiples of \(P_0\) are affine with nonzero coordinates (nonzero multiples of the generator, in the model chapter); this makes every local parameter and inverse abscissa below well-defined.

7 fully proved

docs.title: Natural and signed codes
docs.text: The natural-code template types four untyped tuples by multiplication before adding their squares, so it accepts exactly \(\iota(\mathbb N)\) by Lagrange's theorem; this is the natural-code predicate of the compiler chapter, with M supplied by the multiplication template. The signed encoding links a signed code \(\iota(m)\) to the natural code \(\iota(\operatorname{enc}m)\), in which form the integer enters the precision relation.

docs.title: Semantics of the signed encoding
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.signedEncode_rel_iff

Assume the six-contact estimate, pole completeness and the twenty-two-prime pattern. Then for all \(N,C\in\mathbb Q^5\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value.signed\_encode}}(N,C)\iff\exists\,m\in\mathbb Z:\ N=\iota(m)\ \text{and}\ C=\iota(\operatorname{enc}(m)),\)$ equivalently, \(C=\iota(c)\) for some \(c\in\mathbb N\) and \(N=\iota(\operatorname{dec}(c))\).

Proof sketch. The template polynomial is the sum of the squares of the three generator equations and of \(\kappa(\varphi)\). By the rational-constant lemma the generator equations force \((c_1,c_2,c_3)=(1641/8,-15465/4,87483/32)\), so \(G=(0,c_1,-145,c_2,c_3)=\iota(1)\); they are outside the internal disjunction and constrain both branches. By the private-witness lemma, \(\mathrm{Rel}(N,C)\) holds exactly when there are points \(Q,Q_2,Q_+\) with \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{member}}(N)\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{member}}(C)\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{natural}}(Q)\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{raw\_add}}(Q,Q,Q_2)\) and one of the branches (i) \(N=Q\), \(C=Q_2\), or (ii) \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{raw\_add}}(Q,G,Q_+)\), \(N=\operatorname{neg}(Q_+)\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{raw\_add}}(Q_2,G,C)\).

(\(\Rightarrow\)) The natural-code predicate, with M from the multiplication template, gives \(Q=\iota(q)\) with \(q\in\mathbb N\), and raw addition on canonical codes gives \(Q_2=\iota(2q)\). In branch (i), \(N=\iota(q)\) and \(C=\iota(2q)=\iota(\operatorname{enc}q)\). In branch (ii), \(Q_+=\iota(q+1)\), \(N=\operatorname{neg}(\iota(q+1))=\iota(-(q+1))\) and \(C=\iota(2q+1)\); since \(-(q+1)<0\), \(\operatorname{enc}(-(q+1))=2q+1\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) For \(m\ge0\) take \(Q=\iota(m)\), \(Q_2=\iota(2m)\) and branch (i). For \(m<0\) take \(Q=\iota(-m-1)\), \(Q_2=\iota(-2m-2)\), \(Q_+=\iota(-m)\) and branch (ii); then \(\operatorname{neg}(Q_+)=\iota(m)\) and the last raw addition gives \(\iota(-2m-1)=\iota(\operatorname{enc}m)\). The membership, natural and raw-addition relations hold by the accepted-indices statement, the natural-code predicate (with M from the multiplication template) and raw addition; an inactive branch takes arbitrary witnesses.

docs.title: The coordinate window
docs.text: For nonzero \(a,l\) the coordinate-window template expresses the strict window \(|t-r(a,j)|<\epsilon_l\), with \(r(a,j)=\frac12\operatorname{Tr}(z_j/z_a)\) and \(\epsilon_l=|u_l|+|v_l|\).

docs.title: Semantics of the coordinate window
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.closeCoordinates_rel_iff

For all \(A,L,J\in\mathbb Q^5\) and \(t\in\mathbb Q\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value.close\_coordinates}}(A,L,J,t)\) holds exactly when there are \(a,l,j\in\mathbb Z\) with $\(A=\iota(a),\quad L=\iota(l),\quad J=\iota(j),\quad a e0,\quad l e0,\quad |t-r(a,j)|<\epsilon_l ,\)$ with \(r(a,j)= rac12\operatorname{Tr}(z_j/z_a)\) and \(\epsilon_l\) formed from the local parameter \(z\) on multiples of the generator, extended by \(z_0=0\) (so \(r(a,0)=0\)); \(a,l\) and every nonzero \(j\) are admissible by the nonzero-multiples lemma.

Proof sketch. The template is \(\kappa(\varphi)^2\); its calls (\(\mathtt{member}\) three times, \(\mathtt{value.abs}\) three times) have disjoint blocks occurring in no parameter, so by the private-witness lemma the relation holds exactly when there are pairs \(\zeta_A,\zeta_L,\zeta_J,q\) and rationals \(v,a_0,a_1,\delta,u_\epsilon,z_1,\dots,z_4\) and inverse witnesses making the following true: \(A,L,J\) are accepted by membership, \(A[0]=L[0]=0\) (first code coordinates), the gadgets \(Z(A,\zeta_A)\), \(Z(L,\zeta_L)\), \(Z(J,\zeta_J)\), \(\operatorname N(\zeta_A)v=1\) and \(\zeta_A\cdot q=\zeta_J\), \(a_0=|(\zeta_L)_0|\), \(a_1=|(\zeta_L)_1|\), \((a_0+a_1)u_\epsilon=1\), \(\delta=|t-q_0|\) and \((a_0+a_1-\delta)(z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2+z_4^2)=1\).

By the accepted-indices statement, membership means \(A=\iota(a)\), \(L=\iota(l)\), \(J=\iota(j)\). The conditions \(A[0]=L[0]=0\) say \(a e0\) and \(l e0\) (first code coordinate). By the nonzero-multiples lemma, every nonzero multiple of \(P_0\) has nonzero abscissa and ordinate, so by pair arithmetic the gadget \(Z(\iota(m),\zeta)\) is satisfiable and forces \([\zeta]=z_m\) (also for \(m=0\), where \(z_0=0\)). Then \(\operatorname N(\zeta_A) e0\) holds because \(z_a e0\), and \([q]=z_j/z_a\), so \(q_0=r(a,j)\). The absolute-value template gives \(a_0+a_1=\epsilon_l\), which is nonzero because \(z_l e0\), so its inverse witness exists. Finally \(\delta=|t-r(a,j)|\), and the four-square positivity statement turns the last equation into \(\epsilon_l-|t-r(a,j)|>0\). Conversely, for \(a,l e0\) and the strict window, all these witnesses exist.

docs.title: The exceptional values
docs.text: Double-and-add chains of raw additions, started at the literal origin and the fixed signed generator, produce the codes of the six contact values.

docs.title: Double-and-add chains
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.chain_value ZInQ.Assembly.chain_satisfiable ZInQ.Assembly.chainBuild_binDigits_value ZInQ.Assembly.chainCount_contacts

Let \(m\in\mathbb Z\), \(k\in\mathbb N\), and consider the double-and-add chain for \(k\) on the point \(p=\iota(m)\), as defined for the exceptional-values template: starting from \(\mathrm{out}=O\), \(\mathrm{base}=p\), it takes for each odd bit a fresh point \(\sigma_i\) with the call \(\langle\mathtt{raw\_add}[\mathrm{out},\mathrm{base},\sigma_i]\rangle\) and for each further bit a fresh point \(\delta_i\) with \(\langle\mathtt{raw\_add}[\mathrm{base},\mathrm{base},\delta_i]\rangle\). Then:

  1. for every assignment of rational \(5\)-tuples to the fresh points such that all raw-addition relations of the chain hold, the value of the chain (its final \(\mathrm{out}\)) is \(\iota(km)\);
  2. there is such an assignment.

The number of raw additions is the number of one bits of \(k\) plus the bit length of \(k\) minus one (\(0\) for \(k=0\)). For \(k=0,15,20,24,30,60\) this gives \(0,7,6,6,8,9\).

Proof sketch. Induction along the chain with the invariant that after \(i\) steps \(\mathrm{base}=\iota(2^im)\) and \(\mathrm{out}=\iota(k_im)\), where \(k_i=k\bmod2^i\). Both inputs of every raw addition are then canonical codes, so raw addition forces the fresh output to be \(\iota(k_im+2^im)\) or \(\iota(2^{i+1}m)\), which preserves the invariant; at the end \(k_i=k\). For 2, assign each fresh point the code forced in this way; raw addition is complete on canonical codes. Initially \(\mathrm{out}=O=\iota(0)\) is the literal code. No property of \(P_0\) beyond lying on \(E\) is used.

docs.title: Semantics of the exceptional values
docs.text:
ZInQ.Assembly.exceptions_rel_iff

For all \(N\in\mathbb Q^5\) and \(t\in\mathbb Q\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value.exceptions}}(N,t)\iff\exists\,c\in\mathcal C:\ N=\iota(c)\ \text{and}\ t=c,\)$ where \(\mathcal C=\{0,-15,-20,-24,-30,-60\}\).

Proof sketch. The polynomial is the sum of the squares of the three generator equations and of \(\kappa(\varphi)\) with \(\varphi=\bigwedge(\langle\mathtt{member}[N]\rangle,\bigvee_{c\in\mathcal C}\beta_c)\). The generator equations, outside the disjunction, force \(G=\iota(1)\), hence \(\operatorname{neg}(G)=\iota(-1)\). By the private-witness lemma the relation holds exactly when \(N\) is accepted by membership and, for some \(c\in\mathcal C\), the fresh points of the chain of \(\beta_c\) can be chosen with all its raw-addition relations, \(N\) equal to the chain value and \(t=c\). The chain of \(\beta_c\) is the chain for \(k=|c|\) on \(G\) (\(c=0\)) or on \(\operatorname{neg}(G)\) (\(c<0\)), so by the chain lemma its value is \(\iota(|c|)\) or \(\iota(-|c|)\), that is \(\iota(c)\) in both cases, and the chain is satisfiable. Hence a branch \(\beta_c\) holds exactly when \(N=\iota(c)\) and \(t=c\). Membership of \(\iota(c)\) holds by the accepted-indices statement; the witnesses of the inactive branches are arbitrary.

Assume the six-contact estimate, pole completeness and the twenty-two-prime pattern. Then for all \(N,K\in\mathbb Q^5\) and \(t\in\mathbb Q\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{value.test}}(N,K,t)\iff\exists\,n,\kappa\in\mathbb Z:\ N=\iota(n),\ K=\iota(\kappa),\ \operatorname{Test}(n,\kappa,t).\)$

Proof sketch. The template is \(\kappa(\varphi)^2\) for the conjunction \(\varphi\) listed in its definition; its calls (\(\mathtt{member}\) seven times, \(\mathtt{multiply}\), \(\mathtt{raw\_add}\) twice, \(\mathtt{pole}\)) have pairwise disjoint blocks occurring in no parameter, so by the private-witness lemma the relation holds exactly when the fresh variables can be chosen so that every conjunct holds with each call replaced by its relation.   1. Membership of \(N,K,C_1,H,U,V_0,V_1\) gives \(N=\iota(n)\), \(K=\iota(\kappa)\), \(H=\iota(h)\), \(U=\iota(s_0)\) and \(C_1,V_0,V_1\) canonical.

Since \(\operatorname{neg}(\iota(m))=\iota(-m)\), raw addition gives \(V_0=\iota(h-\kappa)\) and \(V_1=\iota(s_0-\kappa n)\). \(H[0]=0\) and \(V_0[0]=0\) give \(h e0\) and \(h e\kappa\).

Each outer recipe is a composition recipe: its polynomial is the sum of the squares (for \(\mathtt{value\_union}\), the product) of its call polynomials, which is \(\kappa\) of the conjunction (disjunction) of the call atoms. By the witness accounting and the witness-scope theorem, the call blocks lie inside the recipe's variables, are pairwise disjoint, are disjoint from the fresh ranges, and occur in no parameter. The private-witness lemma then replaces each call by its callee relation, and the fresh ranges (\(A,L,J,E_0,\dots,E_4\) for \(\mathtt{close}\), \(K\) for \(\mathtt{main}\)) become existential quantifiers. For the product recipe, the block of an inactive factor takes arbitrary values; this does not discard any fixed equation of the active factor.

docs.title: Exact precision computation and polynomial compilation
Exact precision computation and polynomial compilation
docs.text:
The ordinary-value argument needs one exact computation: from five integers \((n,\kappa,a,l,j)\) it must decide whether \(r(a,j)\) approximates \(n\) to within \(\epsilon_l\) and whether \(\epsilon_l\) is smaller than an explicit, astronomically small power of four. This chapter turns that computation into rational point-code constraints in two stages. The fixed constants are never evaluated: they enter only through their defining expressions and through capped arithmetic.

First, the computation is compiled into a natural-number polynomial. A fixed universal halting polynomial, obtained by packing finite runs of the universal interpreter into base-\(B\) integers and expressing the bit and power operations with the alpha and power formulas, is specialized at the code \(c_3\) of a wrapper around the precision machine. The result is the natural precision polynomial \(C\), with \(1\,305\,811\) natural variables, the first five being inputs; equation (C.4) states that it has a natural zero over \(\mathbf c\in\mathbb N^5\) exactly when the precision predicate accepts \(\mathbf c\).

  • The natural polynomial and the power interface

Second, the natural polynomial is translated into the rational point-code model: each natural variable becomes a code typed by the natural-code predicate and each arithmetic node a template call, so that the precision recipe has rational witnesses exactly at the codes of the natural zeros.

  • Translation to rational point codes

docs.title: The natural precision polynomial
docs.text:
This chapter proves the natural half of input \(\mathsf C\): an explicit polynomial \([\![\mathcal N]\!]\) in \(1{,}305{,}811\) variables, the first five being inputs, has a zero with natural witnesses exactly at the five-tuples accepted by the exact precision computation (equation (C.4) of the manuscript). Following the construction principle of the formalization, \(\mathcal N\) is not read from the saved file: it is defined as the output of a compiler applied to explicit programs, and the saved file construction/precision-natural-polynomial.json only cross-checks its shape.

The construction has three layers, and the chapter proves each separately.

  1. A generic compiler. Any primitive register program is compiled into a natural circuit whose natural zeros are exactly its accepting inputs. Runs are packed into base-\(B\) integers; the packing conditions are bit masks and exponentials; masks become binomial coefficients through Lucas's criterion; binomial coefficients become base-\(B\) digits of a power; and every power is one call of a fixed power template, the Matiyasevich-Robinson exponential relation of the Archive of Formal Proofs development written with the alpha sequence.
  2. Specific programs. A universal interpreter, a wrapper that inverts four Cantor pairs, and a precision program written in an ideal register language and lowered to a primitive program; each is verified against its specification, the last against the mathematical precision relation.
  3. Counts. The variable, gadget and node counts of the compiled circuits, needed by the witness accounting of the specification chapter.

The manuscript does not compile the precision machine directly. It compiles a fixed universal interpreter (\(1{,}399\) instructions, \(204\) registers) once, and specializes the resulting universal halting polynomial at the code of the wrapper. This is forced by the variable budget: the interpreter costs \(15{,}845\) power calls, whereas compiling the wrapper itself (\(146{,}780\) instructions, \(23{,}633\) registers in the manuscript's version) would cost, by the count \(2+3(m+4r+3s)\) of the packed construction, at least \(2+3(146{,}780+4\cdot23{,}633)=723{,}938\) power calls even with no decrement instruction. The precision program enters the polynomial only through one integer coefficient, the program literal \(c_3\), which is never evaluated; neither are the astronomically large constants \(D\), \(Q_0\) or \(A^{(0)}_{\rm ht}\) of the precision computation, which the program evaluates with caps.

docs.title: Semantics of the natural precision polynomial
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.natural_polynomial_semantics ZInQ.Compiler.natural_polynomial_semantics'

Let \(\mathcal N\) be the five-input natural precision circuit, with variable count \(1{,}305{,}811\) and polynomial \([\![\mathcal N]\!]\in\mathbb Z[X_0,\dots,X_{1305810}]\) (call nodes denoting literal substitution into the power template). For every \(c\in\mathbb N^5\), $\(\bigl(\exists z\in\mathbb N^{1305806},\ [\![\mathcal N]\!](c,z)=0\bigr)\iff\operatorname{accepts}(c),\)$ where \(\operatorname{accepts}\) is the precision relation: with \((n,\kappa,a,l,j)\) the signed decoding of \(c\), the early tests \(n\notin\mathcal C\), \(\kappa\ne0\), \(a,l\ge1\), \(j=na\), the admissibility of \(l,a,j\), and the strict tests \(|r(a,j)-n|<\epsilon_l\) and \(4\epsilon_l<4^{-A^{(0)}_{\rm ht}|\kappa F(n)|^{24}}\).

This is equation (C.4), the natural half of input \(\mathsf C\). Its proof has no height, restricted-converse or rational-model premise: the height constant enters only as a fixed integer expression computed with caps, and admissibility replaces the generator theorem. The witnesses are natural numbers; the rational translation is a separate statement. Admissibility is part of the relation so that the theorem needs no input about \(P_0\); under the generator theorem it follows from the early tests (admissibility of nonzero indices).

Proof sketch. By the specialization statement, \(Z_{\mathcal N}(c)\iff Z_{\mathcal H}(c_3,\operatorname{enc}_5(c))\) with \(c_3=\operatorname{code}(\mathcal W)\). By the semantics of the universal halting circuit this is \(\operatorname{halts}(c_3,\operatorname{enc}_5(c))\), which by the codes of primitive programs is "the wrapper halts on \(\operatorname{enc}_5(c)\)", which by the correctness of the wrapper is \(\operatorname{accepts}(c)\). The number \(1{,}305{,}806\) of witness coordinates is the variable count \(1{,}305{,}811\) of \(\mathcal N\) minus its five inputs.

docs.title: The alpha and power formulas
docs.text:
The alpha sequence \(U_n=\alpha_b(n)\) satisfies \(U_0=0\), \(U_1=1\), \(U_{n+2}=bU_{n+1}-U_n\). It grows for \(b\ge2\), its matrix powers have determinant one, and it is congruent in its parameter, with \(\alpha_2(n)=n\).

Natural solutions of \(x^2+y^2=1+bxy\) are adjacent pairs, by descent. Divisibility of alpha values follows divisibility of indices, with the square refinement (C.1). Modulo the companion \(v=U_{m+1}-U_{m-1}\) the sequence is periodic up to sign and reflection. Odd values are unbounded.

The alpha formula (C.2) has eight witnesses and fifteen conditions; it holds exactly when \(b>3\) and \(X=\alpha_b(N)\).

The power formula (C.3) separates the base zero and expresses \(P=Q^R\) through three alpha formulas and one congruence.

Binomial coefficients are base-\(2^{N+1}\) digits of a power, odd binomial coefficients detect bit inclusion and disjointness, and three disjointness conditions express the bitwise AND.

16 fully proved

docs.title: The alpha sequence
docs.text:
ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaZ ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaInt ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaInt_neg ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaInt_add_two

For a natural number \(b\) the alpha sequence \(U_n=\alpha_b(n)\in\mathbb Z\), \(n\in\mathbb N\), is defined by $\(U_0=0,\qquad U_1=1,\qquad U_{n+2}=b\,U_{n+1}-U_n\quad(n\ge0).\)$ It is integer-valued for every \(b\) (its values may be negative when \(b\in\{0,1\}\)). The matrix $\(M_b=\begin{pmatrix}b&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\)$ drives the recurrence: \(M_b\,(U_n,U_{n-1})^{\mathsf T}=(U_{n+1},U_n)^{\mathsf T}\) for \(n\ge1\). When an index may be negative, the sequence is extended by \(U_{-j}=-U_j\), which is consistent with the recurrence.

This is a definition. It is the sequence of the Archive of Formal Proofs development used by the manuscript; \(U_{n+1}\) is the Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind \(S_n\) (normalized by \(S_{n+2}=XS_{n+1}-S_n\), \(S_0=1\), \(S_{-1}=0\)) evaluated at \(b\). Only natural parameters \(b\) occur in this chapter, and every natural-valued use (a witness of the alpha formula) is justified by the growth lemma for \(b\ge2\).

docs.title: Growth of the alpha sequence
docs.text:
ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaZ_growth ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaZ_exponential_bounds

Let \(b\ge2\) be a natural number and \(U_n=\alpha_b(n)\). Then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\) $\(0\le U_n,\qquad U_n+1\le U_{n+1},\qquad n\le U_n .\)$ In particular the sequence is strictly increasing and \(U_n\ge1\) for \(n\ge1\). Moreover, for all natural \(c\ge1\) and \(n\), $\(c^n\le\alpha_{c+1}(n+1),\)$ and for \(b\ge3\), \(\alpha_b(n+1)\le b^n\).

The manuscript states the first group of inequalities for \(b\ge3\); the proof works for \(b\ge2\), and \(\alpha_2(n)=n\) shows that \(b=2\) is the boundary case.

Proof sketch. Joint induction on \(n\) for the pair \(0\le U_n\), \(U_n+1\le U_{n+1}\): the base is \(U_0=0\), \(U_1=1\); in the step, \(U_{n+2}-U_{n+1}=(b-2)U_{n+1}+(U_{n+1}-U_n)\ge0+1\) because \(b\ge2\) and \(U_{n+1}\ge0\). Summing the increments gives \(U_n\ge n\). For \(c^n\le\alpha_{c+1}(n+1)\) induct on \(n\) using \(\alpha_{c+1}(n+2)=(c+1)\alpha_{c+1}(n+1)-\alpha_{c+1}(n)\ge c\,\alpha_{c+1}(n+1)\), which holds because \(\alpha_{c+1}(n)\le\alpha_{c+1}(n+1)\). The upper bound \(\alpha_b(n+1)\le b^n\) is the same induction with \(\alpha_b(n+2)\le b\,\alpha_b(n+1)\).

docs.title: Matrix powers and the quadratic identity
docs.text:
ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaMat_pow ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaZ_quadratic ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaZ_addition

Let \(b\) be a natural number, \(U_n=\alpha_b(n)\) and \(M=M_b\). Then:

  1. for every \(n\ge1\), $\(M^n=\begin{pmatrix}U_{n+1}&-U_n\\U_n&-U_{n-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det M^n=1;\)$
  2. for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(U_n^2+U_{n+1}^2-b\,U_nU_{n+1}=1\); equivalently, for \(n\ge1\), \(U_n^2-bU_nU_{n-1}+U_{n-1}^2=1\);
  3. for every \(n\), \(U_n\) and \(U_{n+1}\) are coprime in \(\mathbb Z\) and are not both even;
  4. (addition formula) for all \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(U_{m+n+1}=U_{m+1}U_{n+1}-U_mU_n\).

Proof sketch. Item 1 by induction on \(n\) from \(M^{n+1}=M\cdot M^n\) and the recurrence; \(\det M=1\). The determinant reads \(U_n^2-U_{n+1}U_{n-1}=1\), and substituting \(U_{n+1}=bU_n-U_{n-1}\) gives item 2 (which can also be proved directly by induction, the left side being invariant under \((U_n,U_{n+1})\mapsto(U_{n+1},bU_{n+1}-U_n)\)). Item 3: item 2 is the Bezout relation \(U_n(U_n-bU_{n+1})+U_{n+1}\cdot U_{n+1}=1\), and reducing it modulo \(2\) excludes two even terms. Item 4 by two-step induction on \(n\), or from the lower-left entry of \(M^{m+n}=M^mM^n\).

Let \(b,b',d\) be natural numbers with \(b\equiv b'\pmod d\). Then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\) $\(\alpha_b(n)\equiv\alpha_{b'}(n)\pmod d .\)$ In particular \(\alpha_2(n)=n\) for every \(n\), and therefore \(\alpha_b(n)\equiv n\pmod d\) whenever \(b\equiv2\pmod d\).

This is congruence in the parameter, not merely between indices: it transports residues from the parameter \(w\) of the alpha formula to the parameters \(b\) (modulo \(v\)) and \(2\) (modulo \(u\)).

Proof sketch. Induct on \(n\) with the statements for \(n\) and \(n+1\) together: \(\alpha_b(n+2)=b\,\alpha_b(n+1)-\alpha_b(n)\) and each factor is congruent to its counterpart for \(b'\). For \(b=2\) the recurrence \(U_{n+2}=2U_{n+1}-U_n\) with \(U_0=0\), \(U_1=1\) has the solution \(U_n=n\). The case \(d=0\) is the trivial case \(b=b'\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaZ_pell_unordered ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaZ_pell_ordered ZInQ.AlphaPower.alphaZ_pell_converse
  1. (Unordered) Let \(b>2\) and \(x,y\in\mathbb N\) with \(x^2+y^2=1+bxy\). Then there is \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(\{x,y\}=\{\alpha_b(n),\alpha_b(n+1)\}\); in particular \(x=\alpha_b(n')\) for some \(n'\in\mathbb N\).
  2. (Ordered) Let \(b\) be any natural number and \(r<s\) natural numbers with \(s^2+r^2=1+bsr\). Then there is \(m>0\) with \(r=\alpha_b(m-1)\) and \(s=\alpha_b(m)\).
  3. Conversely, for \(b\ge2\) every pair \((\alpha_b(n),\alpha_b(n+1))\) consists of natural numbers, satisfies the equation, and has \(\alpha_b(n)<\alpha_b(n+1)\).

No ordering assumption on the pair in item 1 is needed.

Proof sketch. In item 1, \(x\ne y\), since \(2x^2=1+bx^2\) is impossible for \(b\ge2\); order the pair as \(X>Y\). Item 2 is proved by strong induction on the smaller entry \(Y=r\): if \(Y=0\) then \(X^2=1\) and \((X,Y)=(1,0)=(U_1,U_0)\). Otherwise put \(Z=bY-X\in\mathbb Z\). Vieta's relation for the quadratic in \(X\) gives \(XZ=Y^2-1\); hence \(Z\ge0\) (as \(Y\ge1\)) and \(Z<Y\) (as \(X>Y\)), and \((Y,Z)\) satisfies the same equation with \(Y>Z\). By induction \((Z,Y)=(U_{m-1},U_m)\) for some \(m>0\), and then \(X=bY-Z=U_{m+1}\). Item 1 follows from item 2 applied to the ordered pair. Item 3 is the growth lemma and the quadratic identity.
