docs.title: The ideal register language
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.Op ZInQ.Compiler.IR.Stmt ZInQ.Compiler.IR.Outcome ZInQ.Compiler.IR.BigStep ZInQ.Compiler.IR.BigStep.deterministic ZInQ.Compiler.IR.Program ZInQ.Compiler.IR.Program.WF ZInQ.Compiler.IR.Program.Accepts ZInQ.Compiler.IR.Program.Total

The ideal register language has registers indexed by \(\mathbb N\) holding natural numbers. Its statements are:

  • assignments \(x\leftarrow k\) (a natural constant), \(x\leftarrow y\), \(x\leftarrow y+z\), \(x\leftarrow y\mathbin{\dot-}z\) (truncated subtraction), \(x\leftarrow y\cdot z\), \(x\leftarrow\lfloor y/z\rfloor\) and \(x\leftarrow y\bmod z\) (with \(\lfloor y/0\rfloor=0\) and \(y\bmod0=y\)), where \(x,y,z\) are registers that may coincide;
  • sequencing \(S_1;S_2\), the conditionals \(\mathbf{if}\ y<z\ \mathbf{then}\ S_1\ \mathbf{else}\ S_2\) and \(\mathbf{if}\ y=z\ \mathbf{then}\ S_1\ \mathbf{else}\ S_2\), the loop \(\mathbf{while}\ y<z\ \mathbf{do}\ S\), and the terminal statements \(\mathbf{accept}\) and \(\mathbf{reject}\).

The big-step semantics is the inductive relation \(\langle S,\rho\rangle\Downarrow o\) between a statement, a register file and an outcome \(o\in\{\mathrm{normal}(\rho'),\mathrm{accept},\mathrm{reject}\}\), with the usual rules (assignments update one register with the exact value; a terminal outcome of \(S_1\) skips \(S_2\); a loop iterates while its test holds). A derivation exists only for terminating executions. A program is a statement \(S\) with a register bound \(\rho_S\) (all registers occurring in \(S\) are below \(\rho_S\)) and \(k\le\rho_S\) input registers; it accepts \(a\in\mathbb N^k\) if \(\langle S,\rho_0(a)\rangle\Downarrow\mathrm{accept}\) for the initial file \(\rho_0(a)\) (inputs in registers \(0,\dots,k-1\), all others \(0\)), and it is total if for every \(a\) some outcome is derivable. The language is deterministic: each statement and file have at most one outcome.

This is a definition. It is the ideal intermediate representation of the manuscript (S22): correctness is a statement about this ideal semantics, not about a budgeted simulator.

docs.title: Lowering to primitive programs
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.assignB ZInQ.Compiler.IR.ltTest ZInQ.Compiler.IR.eqTest ZInQ.Compiler.IR.code ZInQ.Compiler.IR.Stmt.len ZInQ.Compiler.IR.code_length ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cleanup ZInQ.Compiler.IR.lower ZInQ.Compiler.IR.lower_length ZInQ.Compiler.IR.lower_valid

For a program \(S\) of the ideal register language with register bound \(\rho_S\), the lowering \(\mathrm{low}(S)\) is the primitive program built as follows.

  1. Layout. Registers below \(\rho_S\) keep their meaning; register \(J=\rho_S\) is the reserved jump register (always \(0\) at block boundaries, so \(\mathrm{dec}(J,x,x)\) is an unconditional jump to \(x\)); the six registers \(J+1,\dots,J+6\) are auxiliary registers shared by all primitive blocks, each block starting and ending with them zero.
  2. Primitive blocks. Every block for an assignment to \(x\) first snapshots each source \(y\): it moves \(y\) into two fresh auxiliary registers \(a,a'\) (decrement \(y\), increment \(a\) and \(a'\), until \(y=0\)) and moves \(a\) back into \(y\), so that \(y\) is restored and \(a'\) holds its value. Only after all sources are snapshot is \(x\) cleared (a loop of decrements) and written; hence aliasing of \(x\) with \(y\) or \(z\), and \(y=z\), are safe. Then: \(x\leftarrow k\) increments \(x\) \(k\) times; \(x\leftarrow y\) and \(x\leftarrow y+z\) move the snapshots into \(x\); \(x\leftarrow y\mathbin{\dot-}z\) moves the snapshot of \(y\) into \(x\) and then, once per unit of the snapshot of \(z\), decrements \(x\) if it is positive (saturating decrement); \(x\leftarrow y\cdot z\) adds the snapshot of \(y\) into \(x\) (restoring it through a further auxiliary register) once per unit of the snapshot of \(z\), then clears the snapshot of \(y\); \(x\leftarrow\lfloor y/z\rfloor\) and \(x\leftarrow y\bmod z\) test the snapshot of \(z\) for zero (giving \(0\), respectively the snapshot of \(y\)) and otherwise move the snapshot \(r\) of \(y\) one unit at a time into a counter \(m\), keeping a quotient \(q\) and a register \(c=z-m\ge1\): each unit decrements \(c\), and when \(c\) reaches \(0\) the counter \(m\) is cleared, \(q\) is incremented and \(c\) is refilled with \(z\). This maintains \(y=r+qz+m\) with \(0\le m<z\), so at exit (\(r=0\)) \(q=\lfloor y/z\rfloor\) and \(m=y\bmod z\), and \(q\) or \(m\) is moved into \(x\). Every block ends with its auxiliary registers zero and every register below \(\rho_S\) other than \(x\) unchanged.
  3. Control. Sequencing concatenates blocks; a test \(y<z\) or \(y=z\) is a comparison loop on snapshots of \(y\) and \(z\) that branches directly to the two targets; a loop jumps back to its test.
  4. Termination. \(\mathbf{accept}\) jumps to a final cleanup stage that clears every register used by the program and then reaches the final halt; \(\mathbf{reject}\) and normal completion of \(S\) jump to a permanent self-loop \(\mathrm{dec}(J,i,i)\) at its own state \(i\).

Items 1-3 produce the open code \(\mathrm{code}(S)\) of a statement, a list of instructions with one entry state and one normal exit (the state after its last block), parameterized by its start state; item 4 closes it into the primitive program \(\mathrm{low}(S)\), valid for its register count \(r=J+7\), with all targets absolute.

This is a definition. The manuscript's lowering (S22) is described only at this level; the exact block layout is fixed by the Lean definition.

docs.title: Correctness of the lowering
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.code_forward ZInQ.Compiler.IR.code_backward ZInQ.Compiler.IR.lower_accepts_of_accepts ZInQ.Compiler.IR.accepts_of_lower_halts ZInQ.Compiler.IR.lower_halts_iff ZInQ.Compiler.IR.lower_accepts_iff ZInQ.Compiler.IR.lowering_correct

Let \(S\) be a program of the ideal register language with \(k\) inputs, register bound \(\rho_S\) and lowering \(\mathrm{low}(S)\) with \(r\) registers.

  1. (Open code) Say that a machine file \(\sigma\) simulates a file \(\rho\) if \(\sigma(i)=\rho(i)\) for \(i<\rho_S\) and \(\sigma(i)=0\) for \(i\ge\rho_S\) (in particular the jump register and the auxiliary registers are zero). Let \(S'\) be a statement of \(S\) and let \(\sigma\) simulate \(\rho\). If \(\langle S',\rho\rangle\Downarrow\mathrm{normal}(\rho')\), the run from the entry of \(\mathrm{code}(S')\) with file \(\sigma\) reaches its normal exit with a file simulating \(\rho'\); if the outcome is \(\mathrm{accept}\), it reaches the cleanup entry with every register \(i\ge\rho_S\) zero; if it is \(\mathrm{reject}\), it reaches the self-loop. Conversely, if the run from the entry with file \(\sigma\) reaches a halt instruction after \(t\) steps, then either \(\langle S',\rho\rangle\Downarrow\mathrm{accept}\); or \(\langle S',\rho\rangle\Downarrow\mathrm{normal}(\rho')\) and the run from the normal exit, with some file simulating \(\rho'\), reaches a halt instruction within \(t\) steps; or \(\langle S',\rho\rangle\Downarrow\mathrm{reject}\) and the run from the self-loop reaches a halt instruction within \(t\) steps.

For every \(a\in\mathbb N^k\):

  1. if \(\langle S,\rho_0(a)\rangle\Downarrow\mathrm{accept}\), then \(\mathrm{low}(S)\) accepts \(a\) (it reaches its final halt with every register zero);
  2. if \(\mathrm{low}(S)\) halts on \(a\) (reaches its final halt), then \(\langle S,\rho_0(a)\rangle\Downarrow\mathrm{accept}\).

Hence \(\mathrm{low}(S)\) halts on \(a\) iff it accepts \(a\) iff \(S\) accepts \(a\); for a total program that rejects \(a\), the run of \(\mathrm{low}(S)\) never halts.

Proof sketch. Blocks. Each primitive block, entered with the jump register and its auxiliary registers in the state required at block boundaries, reaches its exit after finitely many steps with the register below \(\rho_S\) updated to the exact value and every other register restored (copies restore their source; snapshots make aliased operands safe; saturating decrement is truncated subtraction; repeated addition is multiplication; division maintains \(y=r+qz+m\) with \(0\le m<z\) while it moves the dividend unit by unit). Statements. By induction on the derivation of \(\langle S',\rho\rangle\Downarrow o\), the run from the entry of the code of \(S'\) with a file simulating \(\rho\) reaches its normal exit with a file simulating \(\rho'\), the cleanup entry, or the self-loop, according to \(o\); loops by induction on completed iterations. Cleanup clears all registers and halts. (2) The run is deterministic and the final halt is reachable only through cleanup, which is entered only from the code of \(\mathbf{accept}\). By induction on the statement and, for loops, strong induction on the length of the run fragment from the entry, a fragment reaching a halt yields one of the three alternatives of (0) for that statement (the fragment is a sequence of block executions mirroring the semantics, so for a loop it contains finitely many iterations). At the top level the second and third alternatives are impossible, since the run from the self-loop never halts, so \(\langle S,\rho_0(a)\rangle\Downarrow\mathrm{accept}\).

docs.title: Signed integer routines
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.SInt ZInQ.Compiler.IR.ReprInt ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sConst ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sCopy ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sNeg ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sAbs ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sAdd ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sSub ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sMul ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sDiv ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sMod ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sLtFlag ZInQ.Compiler.IR.sEqFlag ZInQ.Compiler.IR.SContract

An integer \(z\) is represented by a pair of registers \((\sigma,\mu)\) when \(\mu=|z|\) and \(\sigma=[z<0]\); the representation is normalized: zero has \(\sigma=0\), so each integer has exactly one representation. There are statements of the ideal register language, parameterized by the registers of their operands and results and by a temporary base \(t\) (they use the registers \(t,t+1,\dots\) as temporaries), for: decoding a natural \(c\) into the representation of \(\operatorname{dec}(c)\) (\(\sigma=c\bmod2\), \(\mu=\lfloor(c+\sigma)/2\rfloor\)); an integer constant; copying; negation; absolute value; addition; subtraction; multiplication; the natural quotient \(\lfloor|z_1|/|z_2|\rfloor\) and remainder \(|z_1|\bmod|z_2|\); an assignment with natural value (such as \(|z_1|\cdot|z_2|\)) written into a signed result; and the flags \([z_1<z_2]\) and \([z_1=z_2]\). For each routine with a signed result: if the operand and result registers lie below \(t\), the two result registers are distinct, and in the starting file the operand pairs represent integers \(z_1,z_2\), the statement terminates normally, the result pair represents the corresponding integer (\(\operatorname{dec}(c)\), \(z_1\), \(-z_1\), \(|z_1|\), \(z_1+z_2\), \(z_1-z_2\), \(z_1z_2\), ...), and every register below \(t\) other than the two result registers is unchanged. Results may alias operands. For the flags: if the flag register differs from the operand registers, the statement terminates normally with the flag equal to \(1\) if the relation holds and \(0\) otherwise, and every other register unchanged.

These routines compile statements over integer variables (assignments of the operations above, conditionals on \(z_1<z_2\) or \(z_1=z_2\), which compute the flag into a temporary and branch on it, conditionals on \(|z_1|<|z_2|\) or \(|z_1|=|z_2|\), which branch on the magnitude registers, loops while \(|z_1|<|z_2|\), \(\mathbf{accept}\) and \(\mathbf{reject}\)), integer variable \(k\) being held in the pair \((o+2k,o+2k+1)\) for an offset \(o\): if every variable occurring is below \(K\) and \(o+2K\le t\), and the pairs of the variables below \(K\) represent an integer environment, the compiled statement has the outcome of the integer statement, and on normal termination the pairs represent the final environment.

Proof sketch. Each routine is a case split on the signs with natural arithmetic on the magnitudes: for addition, equal signs add magnitudes, opposite signs subtract the smaller magnitude from the larger and take the sign of the larger, and a zero result gets \(\sigma=0\); multiplication multiplies magnitudes and sets \(\sigma=\sigma_1\oplus\sigma_2\) unless the product is zero. Each case is verified by the big-step rules and arithmetic in \(\mathbb Z\); aliasing is handled by computing into temporaries first.

docs.title: Quadratic-field routines
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.FExpr ZInQ.Compiler.IR.FExpr.code ZInQ.Compiler.IR.fMul ZInQ.Compiler.IR.IExpr ZInQ.Compiler.IR.zeroFlag ZInQ.Compiler.IR.guardNonzero ZInQ.Compiler.IR.intConst ZInQ.Compiler.IR.fMul_spec ZInQ.Compiler.IR.FExpr.code_spec ZInQ.Compiler.IR.IExpr.code_spec ZInQ.Compiler.IR.zeroFlag_spec ZInQ.Compiler.IR.guardNonzero_spec ZInQ.Compiler.IR.intConst_spec

An element \(\alpha=g+hs\in\mathbb Z[s]\) is represented by two consecutive integer variables holding \(g\) and \(h\) (two signed integer pairs, four registers). There are statements over integer variables (compiled into the ideal register language by the signed integer routines), using temporaries from a base \(T\) on, that compute:

  • the value, into a result pair, of every field expression built from pairs, integer variables (as \(g+0s\)), constants of \(\mathbb Z[s]\), addition, subtraction, negation, multiplication \((g+hs)(g'+h's)=(gg'+2hh')+(gh'+hg')s\) and conjugation \(g+hs\mapsto g-hs\) (in particular multiplication by an integer);
  • the value, into a result variable, of every integer expression built from integer variables, integer constants, addition, subtraction, multiplication, negation and absolute value (in particular the norm \(\operatorname N(g+hs)=g^2-2h^2\) and the rational component \(g\));
  • an integer constant (by Horner's rule in base \(64\));
  • the flag \([\alpha=0]\), and a guard that executes \(\mathbf{reject}\) when \(\alpha=0\).

If the variables of the expression and the result lie below \(T\) (for the direct code of a field expression, all variables of the expression lie below the result pair; for a single product of two pairs, the result pair is disjoint from both operands), the statement terminates normally with the exact value in the result, and every variable below \(T\) other than the result is unchanged. Likewise the flag, in a variable distinct from \(T\) and from the pair, with \(T\) outside the pair, is computed exactly, changing only the flag and \(T\). The guard on a pair below \(T\) executes \(\mathbf{reject}\) if \(\alpha=0\), and otherwise terminates normally changing only \(T\) and \(T+1\).

Proof sketch. Compositions of the integer operations, verified componentwise and by induction on the expression; an operand that is not a variable is first evaluated into its own slot of temporaries.

docs.text:

A Jacobian triple \((X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb Z[s]^3\) is represented by three field representations in six consecutive integer variables (twelve registers). There are statements over integer variables (compiled into the ideal register language by the signed integer routines), using temporaries from a base \(T\) on, computing: the constant triples \(P^{\rm J}_0\) and \(O=(1,1,0)\); the plain Jacobian doubling; the branching addition \(\oplus\) and the doubling \(\mathrm{dbl}^\ast\) of the scalar-multiplication statement, including the cases \(Z=0\), equal abscissas (\(H=0\)) with equal or opposite ordinates, and zero ordinate; and the halving loop computing \(\mathrm{mul}(k)\) for an integer variable \(k\) (negating \(Y\) at the end when \(k<0\)). Each, started with its operand and result triples (and \(k\)) below \(T\), and, for the addition, the result triple equal to or disjoint from each operand triple, terminates normally with the exact triple of the Jacobian formulas in the result triple and every variable below \(T\) outside the result triple unchanged; the halving loop terminates because its counter halves.

Proof sketch. Straight-line compositions of the field routines implementing the displayed formulas, with branches on the zero tests of \(Z_1\), \(Z_2\), \(H\), \(\Lambda\), \(Y\); the loop is verified with the invariant of the scalar-multiplication statement, the measure being the counter.

docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.satCode ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cmulCode ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cpowCode ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cfactCode ZInQ.Compiler.IR.caddCode ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cmaxCode ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cA0Code ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cBoundCode ZInQ.Compiler.IR.divFourCode ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cA0Code_spec ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cBoundCode_spec

Fix an integer variable holding a cap \(L\) (in the precision program \(L\ge1\)). There are statements over integer variables (compiled into the ideal register language by the signed integer routines), using temporaries from a base \(T\) on, computing on natural operands the saturation \(\sigma_L(x)=\min(x,L+1)\), the saturated sum \(\sigma_L(x+y)\), the capped product \(\mathrm{cmul}_L\), the saturated maximum, the capped power \(\mathrm{cpow}_L(x,e)\) (a loop of \(e\) capped multiplications), the saturated factorial \(\sigma_L(n!)\) (a loop of \(n\) capped multiplications), the capped value \(\langle e_A\rangle_L\) of the precision height constant, the capped bound \(\beta\) of the capped precision test, and the division-by-four loop \(x\mapsto\lfloor x/4\rfloor\) repeated \(\beta\) times. Each, started with its operands, the cap and the result below \(T\) (for the division loop, \(x\ne\beta\)), terminates normally with the value prescribed by the corresponding mathematical definition in the result and every variable below \(T\) other than the result unchanged.

Proof sketch. Each statement is a direct transcription of its definition; loops are verified by their invariants (the power loop by \(\sigma_L(x^i)\) after \(i\) steps, the factorial loop by induction on the counter, the division loop by \(x_i=\lfloor x/4^i\rfloor\)), with termination by the increasing counter, which stops at the exponent, at \(n\) and at \(\beta\) respectively.

docs.title: The precision program
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionZ ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionProgram ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionProgram_wf

The precision program \(S_{\rm prec}\) is the program of the ideal register language with \(5\) inputs (the natural numbers \(c_0,\dots,c_4\) in registers \(0,\dots,4\)) that performs the steps of the exact decision program in order, using the routines: decode the five inputs into signed pairs; perform the early tests and execute \(\mathbf{reject}\) when one fails; compute the three Jacobian representatives with the point routines and reject on a zero third or second coordinate; form \(\nu_k\), \(N_k\), \(U\), \(V\), \(\theta\), \(\delta\) with the field and signed routines and reject unless the closeness inequality holds; compute \(L=\lfloor(V-1)/(4U)\rfloor\), reject if \(L=0\), compute \(M=|\kappa F(n)|\), then \(\beta\) with the capped routines, run the division-by-four loop, and execute \(\mathbf{accept}\) if its final value is at least \(1\) and \(\mathbf{reject}\) otherwise. All other registers start at \(0\); the routines take their temporaries from a common region above all named quantities.

This is a definition. The manuscript's IR S22 is not available in this repository; this program is specified from the description of S21 and S22 in Section 10, and its exact register allocation is fixed by the Lean definition.

docs.title: Correctness of the precision program
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionZ_spec ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionProgram_bigStep ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionProgram_total ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionProgram_correct ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionProgram_accepts_iff

The precision program is total, and for every \(c\in\mathbb N^5\) it accepts \(c\) if and only if \(\mathrm{decide}(c)=\mathrm{true}\), if and only if \(\operatorname{accepts}(c)\). Its outcome on an input that fails an early test is \(\mathbf{reject}\).

Proof sketch. Compose the routine contracts along the program: after each routine the registers represent exactly the quantities of the corresponding step of the decision program, every branch agrees with the corresponding test, and every loop terminates (the halving scalar loop, the bounded factorial and capped-power loops, and the division loop of at most \(L+1\) steps). Hence the derivable outcome is \(\mathbf{accept}\) exactly when the decision program returns true, and the correctness of the decision program gives the relation.

docs.title: The precision machine halts exactly on acceptance
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionMachine ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precRegs ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionMachine_halts_iff ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionMachine_accepts_iff ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionMachine_correct ZInQ.Compiler.IR.precisionMachine_valid

Let \(M_{\rm prec}=\mathrm{low}(S_{\rm prec})\), a primitive program valid for its register count \(r_{\rm prec}\), with \(5\) inputs. For every \(c\in\mathbb N^5\): $\(M_{\rm prec}\text{ halts on }c\iff M_{\rm prec}\text{ accepts }c\iff\operatorname{accepts}(c).\)$ When \(\operatorname{accepts}(c)\) fails, the run of \(M_{\rm prec}\) never halts, although the ideal program is total.

Proof sketch. Correctness of the lowering applied to the total program \(S_{\rm prec}\), followed by the correctness of the precision program. When \(\operatorname{accepts}(c)\) fails, the outcome of \(S_{\rm prec}\) on \(c\) is \(\mathbf{reject}\) and the run of \(M_{\rm prec}\) reaches the permanent self-loop of the lowering.

docs.title: Cantor pairing and its decoder
docs.text:
ZInQ.CantorDecoder.pair ZInQ.CantorDecoder.decode ZInQ.CantorDecoder.encode5 ZInQ.CantorDecoder.decode5 ZInQ.Compiler.IR.dec5

The pairing of natural numbers is $\(\operatorname{pair}(a,b)=\frac{(a+b)(a+b+1)}2+b,\)$ and the five-fold right-nested encoding is $\(\operatorname{enc}_5(c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4)=\operatorname{pair}(c_0,\operatorname{pair}(c_1,\operatorname{pair}(c_2,\operatorname{pair}(c_3,c_4)))).\)$ The decoder runs the loop on states \((s,\varrho)\) starting at \((0,x)\): while \(s<\varrho\), replace \((s,\varrho)\) by \((s+1,\varrho-(s+1))\); at exit return \((a,b)=(s-\varrho,\varrho)\). Write \(\operatorname{unpair}(x)\) for the result, and \(\operatorname{dec}_5(x)\) for the five numbers obtained by applying \(\operatorname{unpair}\) four times to successive second components (the last second component is the fifth number).

This is a definition. The loop maintains \(\varrho=x-s(s+1)/2\) and terminates because \(\varrho\) decreases.

docs.title: Unique Cantor unpairing
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cantor_pair_props ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cantor_unpair_props ZInQ.Compiler.IR.cantor_pairing_equation ZInQ.Compiler.IR.pairing_system_iff ZInQ.Compiler.IR.pairing_system_encode
  1. For all natural \(a,b\): \(2\operatorname{pair}(a,b)=(a+b)(a+b+1)+2b\), and \(\frac{(a+b)(a+b+1)}2\le\operatorname{pair}(a,b)<\frac{(a+b+1)(a+b+2)}2\) (triangular intervals). Hence \(\operatorname{pair}\) is a bijection \(\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb N\).
  2. \(\operatorname{unpair}(\operatorname{pair}(a,b))=(a,b)\) and \(\operatorname{pair}(\operatorname{unpair}(x))=x\); likewise \(\operatorname{dec}_5\circ\operatorname{enc}_5=\mathrm{id}\) and \(\operatorname{enc}_5\circ\operatorname{dec}_5=\mathrm{id}\).
  3. For natural \(a,b,t\): \(2t-(a+b)(a+b+1)-2b=0\) (in \(\mathbb Z\)) if and only if \(t=\operatorname{pair}(a,b)\).
  4. Consequently, for \(c\in\mathbb N^5\) and \(t_4=c_4\), the four pairing equations $\(2t_i=(c_i+t_{i+1})(c_i+t_{i+1}+1)+2t_{i+1}\qquad(0\le i<4)\)$ have exactly one natural solution \((t_0,t_1,t_2,t_3)\), namely \(t_i=\operatorname{pair}(c_i,t_{i+1})\), and then \(t_0=\operatorname{enc}_5(c)\).

Proof sketch. (1) \((a+b)(a+b+1)\) is even; the interval bounds follow from \(0\le b\le a+b\), and disjointness of consecutive intervals gives injectivity (equal pairs have equal \(a+b\), then equal \(b\)); surjectivity from (2). (2) The loop invariant \(\operatorname{pair}(\mathrm{loop}(s,\varrho))=s(s+1)/2+\varrho\), by strong induction on \(\varrho\); at exit \(0\le\varrho\le s\), so \(b=\varrho\) and \(a=s-b\) lie on diagonal \(s\). (3) Divide by two. (4) Solve from \(i=3\) down to \(i=0\) with (3).

Let \(M_{\rm prec}\) have \(m_{\rm prec}\) instructions and register count \(r_{\rm prec}\). The wrapper \(\mathcal W\) is the primitive program $\(\mathcal W=\Pi\ \|\ (M_{\rm prec}\text{ with every target increased by }|\Pi|),\)$ where the prefix \(\Pi\) is the open code (the lowering without its termination stage) of the following program of the ideal register language, with all its registers other than \(0,\dots,4\) (working registers, auxiliary registers and its own jump register) at indices at least \(r_{\rm prec}\): starting with the input \(x\) in register \(0\), compute \((c_0,y_1)=\operatorname{unpair}(x)\), \((c_1,y_2)=\operatorname{unpair}(y_1)\), \((c_2,y_3)=\operatorname{unpair}(y_2)\), \((c_3,c_4)=\operatorname{unpair}(y_3)\) by the decoder loop (subtract \(s+1\) from the remainder while \(s\) is below it), place \(c_i\) in register \(i\) for \(i\le4\), clear every register it used at index at least \(r_{\rm prec}\), after which the normal exit of \(\Pi\) is the first state of the relocated \(M_{\rm prec}\). Registers of \(M_{\rm prec}\) are not renamed; only its targets are relocated by \(|\Pi|\), and its final halt is the final halt of \(\mathcal W\).

This is a definition. \(\mathcal W\) is valid for \(\max(r_{\rm prec},r_\Pi)\) registers and has one input.

docs.title: Correctness of the wrapper
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.IR.wrapper_halts_iff_machine ZInQ.Compiler.IR.wrapper_halts_iff ZInQ.Compiler.IR.wrapper_halts_encode

For every \(x\in\mathbb N\), the wrapper halts on the input \(x\) (reaches its final halt from the file with \(x\) in register \(0\) and all other registers zero) if and only if \(\operatorname{accepts}(\operatorname{dec}_5(x))\). In particular, for every \(c\in\mathbb N^5\), $\(\mathcal W\text{ halts on }\operatorname{enc}_5(c)\iff\operatorname{accepts}(c).\)$

Proof sketch. The prefix terminates (each decoder loop decreases its remainder) and reaches the first relocated state with \(c_0,\dots,c_4\) in registers \(0,\dots,4\), every auxiliary register cleared, and every other register below \(r_{\rm prec}\) still zero (the prefix touches only registers \(0,\dots,4\) and registers at least \(r_{\rm prec}\)). This is the initial file of \(M_{\rm prec}\) on \((c_0,\dots,c_4)\), extended by zeros. Relocation by \(|\Pi|\) is a bijection between the runs of \(M_{\rm prec}\) and the runs of the suffix of \(\mathcal W\) that preserves the final halt; registers at least \(r_{\rm prec}\) are never read by \(M_{\rm prec}\). Hence \(\mathcal W\) halts on \(x\) iff \(M_{\rm prec}\) halts on \(\operatorname{dec}_5(x)\), iff \(\operatorname{accepts}(\operatorname{dec}_5(x))\); and \(\operatorname{dec}_5(\operatorname{enc}_5(c))=c\).

docs.title: The universal interpreter and the five-input circuit
The universal interpreter and the five-input circuit
docs.text:
Programs are numbered by \(e+1=2^w(2D+1)\), with four base-\(2^w\) digits of \(D\) per state; decoding is total. A valid primitive program has a code whose machine halts exactly when the program does.

The interpreter keeps the simulated registers in a tape list \(\operatorname{cons}(h,t)=2^h(2t+1)\) and is assembled from arithmetic and list blocks. One loop iteration executes one decoded instruction, and its all-zero halt is equivalent to virtual halting.

The shape of the explicit interpreter, including the structure of its cleanup stage, is a finite check.

Compiling the interpreter gives the universal halting circuit, with natural zeros exactly at the halting pairs. Its numbers of variables and calls follow from the shape by the counting statement of the packed construction; its node statistics, and those of the power template, are a finite check on the two explicit constructions.

The five-input circuit fixes the program input to the wrapper's code, moves the packed input to variable five, shifts the other variables by seven, and adds the four squared pairing equations. The program literal is bounded, from a finite check on the size of the wrapper, without being evaluated; the shape of the five-input circuit then follows.

19 fully proved

docs.title: The universal program numbering
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.split2 ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.decodeInstr ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.decodeMachine ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.halts ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.width ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.code

Decoding. Every \(e\in\mathbb N\) is uniquely \(e+1=2^w(2D+1)\) with \(w,D\in\mathbb N\). The machine \(\mu_e\) numbered by \(e\) is: if \(w=0\), \(\mu_e(i)=\mathrm{halt}\) for every \(i\). Otherwise, with \(\beta=2^w\) and \(d_t=\lfloor D/\beta^t\rfloor\bmod\beta\) the base-\(\beta\) digits of \(D\) (zero beyond its length), state \(i\) reads \((o,j,x,y)=(d_{4i},d_{4i+1},d_{4i+2},d_{4i+3})\) and $\(\mu_e(i)=\mathrm{inc}(j,x)\text{ if }o=1,\qquad\mu_e(i)=\mathrm{dec}(j,x,y)\text{ if }o=2,\qquad \mu_e(i)=\mathrm{halt}\text{ otherwise}.\)$ Decoding is total. The program numbered \(e\) halts on input \(n\), written \(\operatorname{halts}(e,n)\), if the run of \(\mu_e\) from state \(0\) with \(n\) in register \(0\) and all other registers zero halts.

Encoding. For a primitive program \(p=(p_0,\dots,p_{m-1})\) valid for \(r\) registers, let \(w(p)\) be the least \(w\ge2\) such that every register index and every target of \(p\) is below \(2^w\), let the fields of an instruction be \((1,j,x,0)\) for \(\mathrm{inc}(j,x)\), \((2,j,x,y)\) for \(\mathrm{dec}(j,x,y)\) and \((0,0,0,0)\) for the final halt, and put $\(D(p)=\sum_{i<m}\sum_{t<4}f_{i,t}\,2^{w(p)(4i+t)},\qquad \operatorname{code}(p)=2^{w(p)}\bigl(2D(p)+1\bigr)-1,\)$ where \(f_{i,0},\dots,f_{i,3}\) are the fields of \(p_i\).

This is a definition. The interpreter's numbering is the one specified by the universal interpreter of the manuscript; the encoding is the canonical choice of \(w\) (the manuscript only requires \(w\) large enough for all fields).

docs.title: Codes of primitive programs
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.decodeMachine_code ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.halts_code_iff ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.code_lt ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.code_ge

Let \(p\) be a primitive program with \(m\) instructions, valid for \(r\) registers. Then \(\mu_{\operatorname{code}(p)}(i)=p_i\) for every \(i<m\) and \(\mu_{\operatorname{code}(p)}(i)=\mathrm{halt}\) for \(i\ge m\). Consequently, for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), $\(\operatorname{halts}(\operatorname{code}(p),n)\iff p\text{ halts on the one input }n .\)$ Moreover \(\operatorname{code}(p)<2^{w(p)(4m+1)+1}\), and if \(m\ge2\) then \(\operatorname{code}(p)+1\ge2^{w(p)(4m-7)+1}\).

Proof sketch. \(\operatorname{code}(p)+1=2^{w}(2D+1)\) with \(2D+1\) odd, so decoding recovers \(w=w(p)\ge2\) and \(D=D(p)\). All fields are below \(2^w\), so the base-\(2^w\) digits of \(D\) are exactly the fields, and digits beyond position \(4m\) are zero. The opcode fields \(1,2,0\) decode to \(\mathrm{inc}\), \(\mathrm{dec}\), \(\mathrm{halt}\) with the same register and targets (note \(2<2^w\) as \(w\ge2\)). Hence the two machines agree, and since every target of \(p\) is below \(m\) the runs agree and halt at the same time (only at state \(m-1\)). The bounds: \(D<2^{4wm}\), and for \(m\ge2\) the instruction \(p_{m-2}\) is not a halt, so its opcode digit at position \(4(m-2)\) is at least \(1\) and \(D\ge2^{4w(m-2)}\).

docs.title: Tape lists
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.cons ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.uncons ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.listCode ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.listCode_bijective ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.listGet_listSet_self ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.listSet_listCode ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.Represents

Code finite lists of naturals by \(\operatorname{nil}=0\) and \(\operatorname{cons}(h,t)=2^h(2t+1)\). Then:

  1. \(\operatorname{cons}\) is a bijection from \(\mathbb N^2\) onto the positive naturals; for \(x>0\) the head \(h\) is the number of halvings of \(x\) until it is odd and the tail is \(t=(x/2^h-1)/2\); moreover \(t<x\) and \(h<x\);
  2. every natural number codes exactly one finite list;
  3. for a list code \(L\) and \(i\in\mathbb N\), \(\operatorname{get}(L,i)\) (the \(i\)-th entry, or \(0\) if the list is shorter) and \(\operatorname{set}(L,i,v)\) (the list with entry \(i\) replaced by \(v\), padded with zeros if it is shorter) are well defined, with \(\operatorname{get}(\operatorname{set}(L,i,v),i)=v\) and \(\operatorname{get}(\operatorname{set}(L,i,v),i')=\operatorname{get}(L,i')\) for \(i'\ne i\).

A register file \(\rho\) is represented by a list code \(L\) when \(\rho(i)=\operatorname{get}(L,i)\) for every \(i\); absent entries are zero, so a file has many representing codes.

Proof sketch. Unique factorization \(x=2^h\cdot\mathrm{odd}\) gives the bijection; \(2^h(2t+1)\ge2t+1>t\) and \(2^h>h\). Lists are coded by recursion on length, and the decoding terminates because tails decrease. The get/set equations are by induction on \(i\).

docs.title: Arithmetic blocks of the interpreter
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.runs_clear ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.compile_correct_in ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.runs_copyBlock ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.runs_addBlock ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.runs_doubleBlock ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.runs_divModBlock

The universal interpreter is assembled from primitive-program blocks, each with an entry state, exit states, argument and result registers, and private scratch registers, using a reserved jump register \(J\) (register \(2\) in the interpreter) that is zero at every block boundary. Each block clears its scratch registers before using them. For each of the following blocks, entered with \(J=0\) and arbitrary scratch values, the run reaches an exit after finitely many steps with the stated effect on its result registers and \(J=0\) again; every register other than its results and scratch registers is unchanged, and the scratch registers may be left nonzero:

  1. clear \(x\): \(x\leftarrow0\);
  2. preserving zero test of \(x\): exits to the zero or nonzero exit according to \(x\), with \(x\) unchanged (decrement and restore);
  3. copy \(x\leftarrow y\) (\(x\ne y\)): \(y\) is restored through a scratch counter;
  4. addInto \(x\leftarrow x+y\), also when \(x\) and \(y\) are the same register (the operand is snapshot before \(x\) is overwritten);
  5. ifLt \(y<z\): a comparison loop that consumes both registers and exits according to whether \(y<z\), leaving \(y=0\), \(z=z-y-1\) if \(y<z\) and \(y=y-z\), \(z=0\) otherwise (callers compare private copies);
  6. divmod with divisor \(z\ge1\): \(q\leftarrow\lfloor y/z\rfloor\), \(r\leftarrow y\bmod z\), by repeated subtraction from a private remainder maintaining \(y=qz+r\), subtracting only when \(r\ge z\) (the interpreter's divisors are at least \(2\));
  7. divmod2 of \(y\) into \((q,r)\): \(q\leftarrow q+\lfloor y/2\rfloor\), \(r\leftarrow y\bmod2\) and \(y\leftarrow0\) (halving with parity, consuming \(y\) in pairs; callers clear \(q\) first).

Proof sketch. Each block is a fixed short program; its correctness is a loop invariant (the sum of the moved register and the counter is constant for copies and additions; \(y=qz+r\) for division) and termination by a decreasing register.

docs.title: List blocks of the interpreter
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.runs_unconsBlock ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.runs_consBlock ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.runs_getStmt ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.runs_setStmt

With the conventions of the arithmetic blocks, the interpreter has blocks with the following effects, each terminating after finitely many steps:

  1. uncons \(x\mapsto(h,t)\): if \(x=\operatorname{cons}(h,t)\) then \((h,t)\), and \((0,0)\) for \(x=\operatorname{nil}\); it copies its input first and halves a positive even value until it is odd, each halving strictly decreasing that value;
  2. cons \((h,t)\mapsto\operatorname{cons}(h,t)\), copying both inputs before the final write, so that aliased arguments are safe;
  3. getList \((L,i)\mapsto\operatorname{get}(L,i)\), following \(i\) links (reading past the end gives \(0\));
  4. setList \((L,i,v)\mapsto\operatorname{set}(L,i,v)\): save the traversed prefix in reverse, replace the selected entry (padding with zeros past the end), then restore the prefix; the saved list strictly decreases during restoration.

Proof sketch. Compositions of the arithmetic blocks with loops whose measures are the halved value, the remaining index and the saved reversed prefix; the effect is computed with the tape-list equations.

docs.title: The universal interpreter
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.interpreter

The universal interpreter \(\mathcal U\) is a primitive program with \(2\) inputs (\(e\) in register \(0\), \(n\) in register \(1\)), reserved jump register \(2\), valid for \(204\) registers, assembled from the arithmetic and list blocks. It performs:

  1. Decode the number. Compute \(w\) and \(D\) with \(e+1=2^w(2D+1)\) by repeated halving of \(e+1\). If \(w=0\), go to cleanup. Otherwise set \(\beta=2^w\).
  2. Initialize. Set the tape to \(\operatorname{cons}(n,\operatorname{nil})\) (the virtual file with \(n\) in register \(0\)) and the virtual state \(\mathrm{pc}=0\).
  3. Main loop. Extract the base-\(\beta\) digits \(o,j,x,y\) of \(D\) at positions \(4\mathrm{pc},\dots,4\mathrm{pc}+3\) by repeated division. If \(o=1\): replace entry \(j\) of the tape by its successor and set \(\mathrm{pc}=x\). If \(o=2\): read \(v=\operatorname{get}(\text{tape},j)\); if \(v>0\) write \(v-1\) and set \(\mathrm{pc}=x\), else write \(v=0\) back and set \(\mathrm{pc}=y\) (the entry is always written with setList, which may pad the tape with zeros). Otherwise leave the loop (a simulated halt). Return to the start of the loop.
  4. Cleanup. Clear all \(204\) registers and reach the final halt.

Its shape, recorded in the interpreter-shape statement, is \(1{,}399\) instructions (\(1{,}022\) sub instructions, \(376\) add instructions and the final halt) over \(204\) registers. The manuscript's interpreter is pinned only through its compiled polynomial; its program is recoverable from the saved universal circuit (state and register histories carry their indices), and the Lean definition is required to reproduce it exactly, so that the counts of the compiled circuit are those of the specification.

This is a definition.

docs.title: One interpreter loop simulates one instruction
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.interpreter_step ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.exec_stepStmt

Call a configuration of \(\mathcal U\) coherent with a virtual configuration \((i,\rho)\) of \(\mu_e\) when it is at the entry of the main loop, registers hold \(w\ge1\), \(D\) and \(\beta=2^w\) of \(e\), the virtual state register holds \(\mathrm{pc}=i\), the tape register holds a list code representing \(\rho\), the jump register is zero, and every register from \(204\) on is zero; the scratch registers below \(204\) are arbitrary. From a coherent configuration:

  1. if \(\mu_e(i)=\mathrm{halt}\), the run of \(\mathcal U\) reaches the cleanup entry after finitely many steps;
  2. otherwise it returns, after at least one and finitely many steps and without passing through cleanup (every configuration on the way is at a state of the main loop, from \(165\) to \(1193\)), to a configuration coherent with the successor of \((i,\rho)\) under \(\mu_e\).

Proof sketch. Compose the block contracts: digit extraction by repeated division yields exactly \(d_{4i},\dots,d_{4i+3}\) (missing digits are zero); the opcode test admits exactly \(1\) and \(2\); getList and setList realize the read and the update of entry \(j\); copies restore their sources, the jump register stays zero, and no block writes a register from \(204\) on, so the invariant registers are preserved. Every block terminates, so one loop iteration executes exactly one decoded instruction with finite work.

docs.title: Correctness of the universal interpreter
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.interpreter_accepts_iff

For all \(e,n\in\mathbb N\): $\(\mathcal U\text{ accepts }(e,n)\iff\operatorname{halts}(e,n).\)$ That is, the interpreter reaches its final halt with all \(204\) registers zero exactly when the program numbered \(e\) halts on \(n\); the virtual final tape need not be zero.

Proof sketch. If \(w=0\), both sides hold (the decoding step goes to cleanup; \(\mu_e\) halts at once). Let \(w\ge1\). After decoding and initialization, the run is coherent with the initial virtual configuration. (\(\Leftarrow\)) If the virtual run halts after \(t\) steps, \(t\) applications of the step statement reach a configuration coherent with a halting virtual state, from which cleanup is reached; cleanup clears every register and halts. (\(\Rightarrow\)) The machine is deterministic. If the virtual run never halts, the step statement gives configurations coherent with it at arbitrarily late times, each loop iteration taking at least one step, so the interpreter never stops. Hence acceptance implies virtual halting.

docs.title: Shape of the universal interpreter
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.interpreter_shape

The universal interpreter \(\mathcal U\) satisfies the following closed decidable statements:

  1. it is valid for \(204\) registers: it has \(m=1{,}399\) instructions, its final instruction (state \(1398\)) is its only halt, every register index is below \(204\) and every target is below \(1{,}399\);
  2. it has \(s=1{,}022\) sub instructions and \(376\) add instructions;
  3. its cleanup stage is the block of states \(1194,\dots,1398\): for \(0\le j<204\) the instruction at state \(1194+j\) is \(\mathrm{dec}(j,\,1194+j,\,1195+j)\), and state \(1398\) is the final halt;
  4. the states below \(1194\) having a target at least \(1194\) are exactly \(69\), \(587\) and \(593\), and each of them is \(\mathrm{dec}(2,1194,1194)\) (an unconditional jump to the first cleanup state through the jump register \(2\)).

In the structured definition of \(\mathcal U\), state \(69\) is the exit of the decoding step on \(w=0\) and states \(587\), \(593\) are the exits of the main loop on a simulated halt; items 3 and 4 are what the correctness proof uses to say that the final halt is reached only through cleanup. The numbers are those of the manuscript's interpreter, recovered from the saved universal circuit (its state and register histories carry their indices); the Lean definition is required to reproduce them.

This is a finite computation on the explicit \(1{,}399\)-instruction program.

docs.title: The universal halting circuit
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.haltingCircuit

The universal halting circuit \(\mathcal H\) is the compiled circuit \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal U,2}\) of the packed-history construction of the universal interpreter with \(r=204\) registers and \(k=2\) inputs \(e=X_0\), \(n=X_1\): a natural circuit whose explicit variables are the inputs \(X_0,X_1\) followed by the fresh variables of the construction, whose call nodes are the power calls of the construction with their private blocks of \(79\) variables, and whose root is the encoding of the conjunction of the construction. Its node list begins with the variable nodes of \(e\) and \(n\); the program literal of the interpreter does not occur in it (the interpreter is compiled, the interpreted program is an input). Its numbers of variables, calls and nodes are recorded in the counting statement and the node-statistics check.

This is a definition.

docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.haltingCircuit_counts ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.haltingCircuit_witnessCount ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.haltingCircuit_macroCounts

The universal halting circuit \(\mathcal H\) has \(54{,}049\) explicit variables (the two inputs \(X_0,X_1\) and \(54{,}047\) witnesses), \(15{,}845\) calls of the power template with private blocks of \(79\) variables, and variable count $\(54{,}049+79\cdot15{,}845=1{,}305{,}804,\)$ so a natural zero with inputs \((e,n)\) has \(1{,}305{,}802\) witness coordinates. Its construction contains \(1{,}603\) mask macros, \(1{,}226\) bitAnd macros, \(3{,}678\) orthogonal macros, \(5{,}281\) binomial macros and \(10{,}770\) strict-inequality gadgets. Moreover \(\mathcal H\) is well scoped.

Proof sketch. The counting statement of the packed construction with \(k=2\), \(r=204\), \(m=1{,}399\), \(s=1{,}022\) (the shape check): explicit variables \(2k+9+41r+10m+31s=4+9+8364+13990+31682=54{,}049\); calls \(2+3(m+4r+3s)=2+3\cdot5281=15{,}845\); masks \(m+r=1603\); bitAnd \(r+s=1226\); orthogonal \(3(r+s)=3678\); binomial \(m+4r+3s=5281\); strict inequalities \(2+k+r+2\cdot5281=10{,}770\). Well-scopedness is item 1 of the statement on hierarchical constructions, all macro arguments of the packed construction being polynomials in earlier variables.

The node list of the universal halting circuit \(\mathcal H\) has at most \(125{,}307\) additions and at most \(98{,}361\) multiplications, \(54{,}049\) variable nodes, \(6\) constant nodes with values \(0,1,2,4,1399,-1\) in node order, and \(15{,}845\) calls. Its first two nodes are the variable nodes of \(X_0\) and \(X_1\).
  2. The node list of the power template \(\mathcal P\) has \(474\) nodes: \(82\) variable nodes, \(6\) constant nodes with values \(0,1,4,2,3,-1\) in node order, \(196\) additions, \(190\) multiplications and no calls.

Neither item involves \(c_3\) or any astronomically large constant.

Proof sketch. Item 2 is a closed computation on the \(474\) nodes of the flat power macro. Item 1 is proved without evaluating the construction. The variable nodes are the explicit variables; the constants are \(0,1,2\) (the only ones the gadgets and macros request), \(4\) and the program size \(1399\) (requested by the first item of the packed construction) and \(-1\) (requested by the encoding), first occurring in this order; the calls are counted by the compiler. For the two bounds, count the addition and multiplication nodes the construction requests, \(129{,}408\) and \(98{,}727\), and subtract the requests whose node is already present: the re-sum \(z+a\) inside every bit conjunction (\(2{,}452\) additions), the re-sum \(N+1\) in every mask binomial after the first (\(1{,}601\) additions), the product \(K\cdot F\) in every register mask after the first (\(204\) multiplications), repeats in the state equations of the halting step (\(48\) additions and \(151\) multiplications) and \(11\) repeated products of the encoding. That a node is present depends only on how it was requested earlier, so no statement about the other nodes is needed.

docs.title: Exact node statistics of the halting circuit
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.NodeCheck.HaltingAddMulCheck ZInQ.Compiler.NodeCheck.haltingAddMulCheck ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.HaltingNodeCheck ZInQ.Compiler.NodeCheck.haltingNodeCheck ZInQ.Compiler.NodeCheck.haltingNodeCheck_of_addMul ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.haltingCircuit_nodeStats

The node list of the universal halting circuit \(\mathcal H\) has exactly \(125{,}307\) additions and \(98{,}361\) multiplications, hence \(293{,}568\) nodes in all.

So the bounds of the node statistics are attained. Apart from a form of the main theorem that takes it as a hypothesis, no other statement uses the equality.

Proof sketch. A closed computation: run the construction with its hash-consing table and count the node kinds. The bounds give one inequality; the other needs every request not counted as a repeat to create a new node. The run is checked in \(89\) consecutive pieces by a builder without a table: pinned data says, for each request, whether its node already exists and where, and the builder confirms each claimed new node by comparing it with recent nodes or with sorted lists of older ones. A simulation argument shows that this builder makes the same requests and creates the same nodes as the hash-consing one.

docs.title: The five-input natural precision circuit
docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.specialize ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.precisionCircuitOf ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.precisionCircuit

Let \(c_3=\operatorname{code}(\mathcal W)\). The natural precision circuit \(\mathcal N\) is the natural circuit with \(5\) inputs obtained from the universal halting circuit \(\mathcal H\) as follows.

  1. Variables. Inputs \(X_0,\dots,X_4\) (the codes \(c_0,\dots,c_4\)); pairing variables \(X_5,\dots,X_8\) (\(t_0,\dots,t_3\)); every variable \(X_i\) of \(\mathcal H\) with \(i\ge2\) becomes \(X_{i+7}\), and every block start \(w\) of \(\mathcal H\) becomes \(w+7\). The explicit variables are listed as \(0,\dots,8\) followed by the shifted explicit witnesses of \(\mathcal H\), and the variable count is that of \(\mathcal H\) plus \(7\).
  2. Nodes. The node list of \(\mathcal H\), in order, with the variable node of \(X_0\) (\(e\)) replaced by the constant node \(c_3\), the variable node of \(X_1\) (\(n\)) replaced by the variable node of \(X_5\), every other variable node and every call block start shifted by \(7\); followed by the variable nodes of \(X_0,\dots,X_4\) and \(X_6,X_7,X_8\), the constant nodes \(1,2,-1\), and, for \(i=0,1,2,3\) with \(t_4=X_4\) and \(c_i=X_i\), the eight nodes of $\(\pi_i=2t_i+(-1)\cdot\bigl((c_i+t_{i+1})(c_i+t_{i+1}+1)+2t_{i+1}\bigr)\)$ (no hash-consing in this appended part); finally the left-nested sum of squares \(\rho^2+\pi_0^2+\pi_1^2+\pi_2^2+\pi_3^2\), where \(\rho\) is the root of \(\mathcal H\), as root.
  3. Power template. The calls refer to the power template \(\mathcal P\).

This is the pinned five-input natural polynomial of input \(\mathsf C\), defined by construction; the saved file is a cross-check of its shape. Its counts (\(54{,}056\) explicit variables, \(15{,}845\) private blocks, variable count \(1{,}305{,}811\), \(293{,}620\) nodes) are proved in the shape statement.

This is a definition.

docs.text:
ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.precisionCircuit_poly ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.precisionCircuit_natRel_iff ZInQ.Compiler.Universal.precisionCircuit_wellScoped

Let \(\theta\) be the substitution \(X_0\mapsto c_3\), \(X_1\mapsto X_5\), \(X_i\mapsto X_{i+7}\) for \(i\ge2\). Then $\([\![\mathcal N]\!]=\theta\bigl([\![\mathcal H]\!]\bigr)^2+\sum_{i=0}^3\Bigl(2X_{5+i}-(X_i+t_{i+1})(X_i+t_{i+1}+1)-2t_{i+1}\Bigr)^2,\)$ with \(t_{i+1}=X_{6+i}\) for \(i<3\) and \(t_4=X_4\). Consequently, for every \(c\in\mathbb N^5\), $\(Z_{\mathcal N}(c)\iff Z_{\mathcal H}(c_3,\operatorname{enc}_5(c)).\)$ Moreover \(\mathcal N\) is well scoped: the pairing variables \(X_5,\dots,X_8\) are disjoint from the inputs and from the shifted variables and blocks of \(\mathcal H\), the shifted blocks are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from the explicit variables, and no variable node of \(\mathcal N\) refers to a block variable. In particular no parent variable node accesses a private coordinate of a power call.

Proof sketch. Node by node, the denotation of each modified node of \(\mathcal H\) is \(\theta\) applied to the original denotation: variable nodes by definition, constants unchanged, additions and multiplications by the homomorphism property, and calls because shifting the block start by \(7\) commutes with \(\theta\) on the callee's witness variables. The appended nodes denote the four pairing polynomials and the sum of squares. For the relation: a natural zero makes every square vanish (integers), so the pairing equations hold and, by unique Cantor unpairing, \(t_0=\operatorname{enc}_5(c)\); then \(\theta([\![\mathcal H]\!])=0\) is a natural zero of \(\mathcal H\) at \((c_3,\operatorname{enc}_5(c))\) after renaming. Conversely take \(t_i\) the Cantor values and the witnesses of \(\mathcal H\) shifted by \(7\). Well-scopedness: \(\mathcal H\) is well scoped (its counting statement), its variables and blocks lie in \([2,1{,}305{,}804)\), so after the shift they lie in \([9,1{,}305{,}811)\), disjoint from the new explicit variables \(0,\dots,8\); the shift is injective, so disjointness and the absence of variable nodes inside blocks are preserved, and the appended nodes refer only to \(X_0,\dots,X_8\).

docs.title: Translation to rational point codes
docs.text:
The natural precision polynomial speaks about natural numbers; the target polynomial has rational witnesses. This chapter translates every natural-number constraint into rational point-code constraints and proves that the translation is exact: natural variables become codes typed by the natural-code predicate, additions become raw additions, multiplications become multiplication templates, constants become fixed-scalar templates, power calls become calls of the power-value recipe, and the root becomes one equality of codes. This page follows Section 10.4; the interpreter, the lowering, the wrapper and the five-input specialization of Section 10.3 are in the natural chapter, whose equation (C.4) is the input here.

Throughout, \(\iota(n)\) is the code of \([n]P_0\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_\tau\) is the rational relation of a template or recipe, and the multiplication statement M is used in its all-input form: \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}(p,q,r)\) holds exactly when \(p=\iota(a)\), \(q=\iota(b)\) and \(r=\iota(ab)\) for some integers \(a,b\). The multiplication chapter proves M from the six-contact estimate, pole completeness and the twenty-two-prime pattern; the statements below assume M explicitly. The Mordell–Weil theorem, used through the generator certificate, is proved by the two-isogeny descent and is not a hypothesis.

11 fully proved

docs.title: The typing order and the natural predicate
docs.text: The typing order does not depend on the natural predicate. Membership forces a canonical code in \(D=2E(K_0)\), raw addition on two canonical inputs forces their canonical sum, the fixed scalar templates give \([m]Q\) on \(D\), and inside \(\mathtt{multiply}\) the three root memberships are forced conjuncts of the height certificate, so every raw addition of the certificate receives canonical codes. Only once multiplication is typed on all rational inputs do the four square products and three additions of \(\mathtt{natural}\) make sense: its four untyped square roots are typed by the multiplication calls before their squares are added, and Lagrange's theorem gives exactly the codes of the natural numbers. This needs the completeness half of M. The outputs of these additions are canonical by the raw-addition contract, so no separate membership of the output is needed. The signed-encoding and exceptional templates of the assembly chapter start their addition chains at such a natural code, at the literal origin or at the fixed signed generator; the fixed generator equations are conjuncts outside the internal products of the templates that use them, and an inactive product branch is never assumed true.

docs.title: Lagrange's four-square theorem
docs.text:
ZInQ.Translation.four_squares

For every natural number \(n\) there are natural numbers \(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3\) with $\(n=a_0^2+a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2 .\)$

Proof sketch. Classical. By Euler's four-square identity the set of sums of four integer squares is closed under multiplication, so it suffices to treat primes; \(2=1+1+0+0\). For an odd prime \(p\) the \((p+1)/2\) values \(x^2\) and the \((p+1)/2\) values \(-1-y^2\) modulo \(p\) cannot be pairwise distinct, so \(x^2+y^2+1\equiv0\pmod p\) for some \(x,y\); hence some multiple \(mp\) with \(1\le m<p\) is a sum of four squares, and the least such \(m\) is \(1\) by Euler's descent. Replacing each integer \(a_i\) by \(|a_i|\) gives natural numbers.

docs.title: The natural-code predicate
docs.text:
ZInQ.Translation.MultiplicationExact ZInQ.Translation.natural_rel_iff

Assume the multiplication statement M in its all-input form: for all \(p,q,r\in\mathbb Q^5\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}(p,q,r)\iff\exists\,a,b\in\mathbb Z:\ p=\iota(a),\ q=\iota(b),\ r=\iota(ab).\)$ Then for every \(A\in\mathbb Q^5\) (an arbitrary rational \(5\)-tuple, not assumed to be a code) $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{natural}}(A)\iff A=\iota(n)\ \text{for some }n\in\mathbb N .\)$ In words: the natural-code template accepts exactly the codes of the nonnegative indices. Its four square roots are typed by the multiplication calls before their squares are added, so the three raw additions only ever receive canonical codes.

Proof sketch. The polynomial of \(\mathtt{natural}\) is the square of the compilation of a conjunction of seven calls with pairwise disjoint private blocks; the points \(\sigma_0,\dots,\sigma_3,\Sigma_0,\dots,\Sigma_3,\pi_1,\pi_2\) are fresh variables occurring in no block. By the private-block theorem, \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{natural}}(A)\) holds exactly when there are \(\sigma_i,\Sigma_i,\pi_1,\pi_2\in\mathbb Q^5\) with $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}(\sigma_i,\sigma_i,\Sigma_i)\ (i=0,\dots,3),\quad \mathrm{Add}_{\rm raw}(\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1,\pi_1),\quad\mathrm{Add}_{\rm raw}(\pi_1,\Sigma_2,\pi_2),\quad \mathrm{Add}_{\rm raw}(\pi_2,\Sigma_3,A).\)$

(\(\Rightarrow\)) By M, \(\sigma_i=\iota(a_i)=\iota(b_i)\) and \(\Sigma_i=\iota(a_ib_i)\) for integers \(a_i,b_i\). Since \(\iota\) is injective (generator certificate), \(a_i=b_i\) and \(\Sigma_i=\iota(a_i^2)\). (Injectivity can be avoided: codes are injective on points, so \([a_i]P_0=[b_i]P_0\) and \([a_ib_i]P_0=[a_i]([b_i]P_0)=[a_i]([a_i]P_0)=[a_i^2]P_0\).) The three raw additions now have canonical inputs, so by the raw-addition contract \(\pi_1=\iota(a_0^2+a_1^2)\), \(\pi_2=\iota(a_0^2+a_1^2+a_2^2)\) and \(A=\iota(a_0^2+a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2)\), and \(n=\sum_ia_i^2\in\mathbb N\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Write \(n=\sum_ia_i^2\) with \(a_i\in\mathbb N\) by Lagrange's theorem and put \(\sigma_i=\iota(a_i)\), \(\Sigma_i=\iota(a_i^2)\), \(\pi_1=\iota(a_0^2+a_1^2)\), \(\pi_2=\iota(a_0^2+a_1^2+a_2^2)\). The multiplication relations hold by M (with \(a=b=a_i\)) and the three additions by the raw-addition contract; the private-block theorem supplies the witnesses of the seven calls.

The completeness half of M is essential here; the generator certificate alone does not give this predicate.

docs.title: Natural circuits and their translation
docs.text:
A natural circuit has explicit variables, constant, variable, addition and multiplication nodes, and call nodes that substitute the power template with a private block of seventy-nine natural witnesses. Its value at an integer assignment is computed node by node; a call contributes the value of the power template, which is not required to vanish.

A model-evaluation recipe is a sum of squares of calls with pairwise disjoint private blocks, so its rational relation unfolds into a conjunction of template relations on point references, together with the generator equations and the root equality.

Induction along the source DAG gives every node point the code of the node's signed integer value. Natural guards constrain only the explicit variables, never intermediate sums or products; raw addition always receives canonical codes; globally typed multiplication types the products; the generator equations and the scalar templates supply the constants. A power call contributes the code of the power template's value at some private natural witnesses. Conversely, a natural solution provides rational witnesses for every call.

docs.title: Values and polynomial of a natural circuit
docs.text:
ZInQ.Translation.nodeVal ZInQ.Translation.circuitValue ZInQ.Translation.templateValue ZInQ.Translation.callValue ZInQ.Translation.circuitPoly ZInQ.Translation.Admissible ZInQ.Translation.circuitValue_eq_eval_poly

Let \(\mathcal N\) be a natural circuit with \(k\) inputs, in the format of the model-evaluation translation, and let \(\mathcal P\) be a natural circuit with \(3\) inputs and no call nodes (the power template). Write \(V_{\mathcal P}\) for the number of variables of \(\mathcal P\) (\(V_{\mathcal P}=82\) for the power template, so its call blocks have \(79\) variables).

Values of the power template. For \(y:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z\) the value \(\mathrm{val}^{\mathcal P}_y(j)\) of node \(j\) of \(\mathcal P\) is defined in node order by \(\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{const}\ c)=c\), \(\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{var}\ i)=y_i\), \(\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{add}\ j\ j')=\mathrm{val}(j)+\mathrm{val}(j')\) and \(\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{mul}\ j\ j')=\mathrm{val}(j)\,\mathrm{val}(j')\). Put $\(T_{\mathcal P}(y_0,\dots,y_{V_{\mathcal P}-1})=\mathrm{val}^{\mathcal P}_y(\mathrm{root}_{\mathcal P}).\)$

Values of the circuit. For \(\theta:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z\) the value \(\mathrm{val}_\theta(j)\) of node \(j\) of \(\mathcal N\) is defined in node order by the same four rules and, for a call node \(\mathrm{call}\ (a,b,c)\ w\), $\(\mathrm{val}_\theta(\mathrm{call}\ (a,b,c)\ w)=T_{\mathcal P}\bigl(\mathrm{val}_\theta(a),\mathrm{val}_\theta(b),\mathrm{val}_\theta(c),\theta_w,\theta_{w+1},\dots,\theta_{w+V_{\mathcal P}-4}\bigr).\)$ The value of the circuit is \(\mathcal N(\theta)=\mathrm{val}_\theta(\mathrm{root})\).

Polynomial. \([\![\mathcal N]\!]\) is the polynomial of the natural circuit defined in the natural chapter: the same recursion with polynomial operations, a call node denoting the substitution of the argument polynomials and the block variables \(X_{w+i}\) into the polynomial of \(\mathcal P\). Since evaluation commutes with substitution, \(\mathcal N(\theta)=[\![\mathcal N]\!](\theta)\) for every \(\theta\). For the natural precision circuit, \([\![\mathcal N]\!]\) is the natural precision polynomial \(C\) of equation (C.4); its variables are \(X_0,\dots,X_{1305810}\) and \(X_0,\dots,X_4\) are the inputs.

Admissible assignments. \(\theta\) is admissible for \(\mathcal N\) when \(\theta_v\in\mathbb N\) for every explicit variable \(v\) of kind witness and for every variable \(v\) of the block \([w,w+V_{\mathcal P}-3)\) of every call node. Inputs are not constrained by admissibility.

A call node contributes the value of the power template at its arguments and its block; it does not assert that this value vanishes. This is a definition.

docs.title: Well-formed natural circuits
docs.text:
ZInQ.Translation.WellFormedCore ZInQ.Translation.WellFormed

A natural circuit \(\mathcal N\) with \(k\) inputs, explicit variables \((i_0,\kappa_0),(i_1,\kappa_1),\dots\), nodes \(n_0,\dots,n_{K-1}\), root \(\rho\) and (if it has call nodes) power template \(\mathcal P\) with \(V_{\mathcal P}\) variables is well-formed with bound \(V\) when:

  1. the explicit variable indices are pairwise distinct, the first \(k\) entries are the inputs with indices \(0,\dots,k-1\), and no later entry is an input;
  2. every argument of an \(\mathrm{add}\), \(\mathrm{mul}\) or \(\mathrm{call}\) node \(n_j\) is a node index below \(j\), and \(\rho<K\);
  3. every \(\mathrm{var}\ i\) node refers to an explicit variable \(i\);
  4. every \(\mathrm{const}\ c\) node with \(c\notin\{0,1,-1\}\) has \(c\ge2\);
  5. the blocks \([w,w+V_{\mathcal P}-3)\) of distinct call nodes are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from the set of explicit variable indices;
  6. every explicit variable index and every block variable is below \(V\);
  7. if \(\mathcal N\) has a call node, \(\mathcal P\) has \(3\) inputs, no call nodes, and is itself well-formed with bound \(V_{\mathcal P}\), its explicit variables being \(0,\dots,V_{\mathcal P}-1\).

Condition 3 says that the parent never reads a private coordinate of a call directly; condition 4 is what the fixed-scalar templates need, since a nontrivial constant \(c\) is produced as \([c]P_0\). Under conditions 2, 3, 5 and 7, \(\mathrm{val}_\theta(j)\) depends only on the values of \(\theta\) at the explicit variables and at the blocks of the call nodes among the ancestors of \(j\), and \([\![\mathcal N]\!]\) involves only variables below \(V\).

This is a definition (a decidable predicate on a finite circuit).

docs.title: Relational form of a model-evaluation recipe
docs.text:
ZInQ.Translation.translate_rel_iff ZInQ.Translation.modelRecipe_rel_iff

Let \(\rho\) be the model-evaluation recipe obtained by translating a natural circuit with \(k\) inputs that is well-formed with some bound, in value or zero mode, with or without natural constraints on the inputs and with an optional well-formed power recipe \(\pi\) (present when the circuit has call nodes), and let \(p\) be its parameter count (\(5k\) or \(5(k+1)\)). The table of nontrivial constants of the translation is a prefix of \((4,2,3,c_3,1399)\) that contains the constants of the circuit. Call the variables of \(\rho\) that are neither parameters nor in a private block of one of its calls its free witnesses: the generator variables \(g_0,g_1,g_2\), the fresh points of the explicit witness variables and the fresh points of the constant, addition, multiplication and call nodes. For \(a\in\mathbb Q^p\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_\rho(a)\) holds if and only if there is an assignment \(x:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q\) with \(x_i=a_i\) for \(i<p\) such that:

  1. \(8x_{g_0}=1641\), \(4x_{g_1}=-15465\), \(32x_{g_2}=87483\);
  2. \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{natural}}(\mathrm{ref}(r)(x))\) for every source-variable row \((i,r,s)\) with a natural start \(s\);
  3. \(\mathrm{Rel}_{S_h}(\mathrm{ref}(-2)(x),\mathrm{ref}(r)(x))\) for every constant definition \((S_h,r,s)\);
  4. \(\mathrm{Add}_{\rm raw}(\mathrm{ref}(a)(x),\mathrm{ref}(b)(x),\mathrm{ref}(o)(x))\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}(\mathrm{ref}(a)(x),\mathrm{ref}(b)(x),\mathrm{ref}(o)(x))\) and \(\mathrm{Rel}_\pi(\mathrm{ref}(a)(x),\mathrm{ref}(b)(x),\mathrm{ref}(c)(x),\mathrm{ref}(o)(x))\) for the operations \((0,a,b,o,s)\), \((1,a,b,o,s)\) and \((2,a,b,c,o,s)\) respectively;
  5. \(\mathrm{ref}(r)(x)=\mathrm{ref}(r')(x)\) for the root equality \((r,r')\).

Under condition 1, \(\mathrm{ref}(-1)(x)=\iota(0)\), \(\mathrm{ref}(-2)(x)=\iota(1)\) and \(\mathrm{ref}(-3)(x)=\iota(-1)\). Only the values of \(x\) at the parameters and the free witnesses matter.

Proof sketch. \([\![\rho]\!]\) is the sum of the squares of its constraint polynomials, so it vanishes at \(x\) exactly when every constraint does. By the witness-scope theorem the private blocks of the calls of \(\rho\) are pairwise disjoint, disjoint from the parameters and free witnesses, and no block variable occurs in a point reference or in another constraint. Hence the existential over the witnesses of \(\rho\) splits into an existential over the free witnesses and, for each call, one over its own block; by the evaluation of a call, the latter is the callee relation at the evaluated parameter points. The generator constraints and root differences contain no block variable. The values of the three negative references are the point-reference lemma.

docs.title: Every node point is the code of the node's value
docs.text:
ZInQ.Translation.translate_sound

Assume the multiplication statement M in its all-input form. Let \(\mathcal N\) be a natural circuit with \(k\) inputs that is well-formed with some bound, with power template \(\mathcal P\) if it has call nodes, and let \(\rho\) be its translation in some mode, with or without natural constraints on the inputs, with power recipe \(\pi\) if \(\mathcal N\) has call nodes. If \(\mathcal N\) has call nodes, assume that \(\pi\) computes the power template on canonical codes: $\((\mathrm{PV})\qquad\mathrm{Rel}_\pi(\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(c),r)\iff\exists\,w\in\mathbb N^{V_{\mathcal P}-3}:\ r=\iota\bigl(T_{\mathcal P}(a,b,c,w)\bigr)\qquad(a,b,c\in\mathbb Z,\ r\in\mathbb Q^5).\)$ Let \(x:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q\) satisfy conditions 1-4 of the relational form of \(\rho\) (all conditions except the root equality), and assume that either the inputs carry natural constraints, or the input points are canonical: \(\mathrm{ref}(5i)(x)=\iota(c_i)\) with \(c_i\in\mathbb Z\) for \(i<k\).

Then there is an assignment \(\theta\), admissible for \(\mathcal N\), such that

  1. \(\mathrm{ref}(5i)(x)=\iota(\theta_i)\) for every input \(i<k\), with \(\theta_i\in\mathbb N\) when the inputs carry natural constraints and \(\theta_i=c_i\) otherwise;
  2. \(\mathrm{ref}(r_v)(x)=\iota(\theta_v)\) for every explicit variable \(v\) with point \(r_v\);
  3. \(\mathrm{ref}(\mathrm{pt}(j))(x)=\iota(\mathrm{val}_\theta(j))\) for every node \(j\).

In particular the point of the root is \(\iota(\mathcal N(\theta))\); if moreover the root equality of zero mode holds then \(\mathcal N(\theta)=0\), and in value mode the output point \(\mathrm{ref}(5k)(x)\) is \(\iota(\mathcal N(\theta))\).

Proof sketch. Inputs and explicit witnesses: a row with a natural start gives \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{natural}}(\mathrm{ref}(r_v)(x))\), hence \(\mathrm{ref}(r_v)(x)=\iota(n_v)\) with \(n_v\in\mathbb N\) by the natural-code predicate; put \(\theta_v=n_v\). Unconstrained inputs are canonical by hypothesis; put \(\theta_i=c_i\). Nodes: induction along the node list, defining \(\theta\) on the block of each call node when that node is reached.

  • \(\mathrm{var}\ i\): \(\mathrm{pt}=r_i\) and item 2 applies (well-formedness 3).
  • \(\mathrm{const}\ 0,1,-1\): the references \(-1,-2,-3\) have values \(\iota(0),\iota(1),\iota(-1)\) by the generator equations.
  • \(\mathrm{const}\ c\) with \(c\ge2\): its point is the point \(r\) of the constant definition made at the first occurrence of \(c\); the scalar template \(S_h\) has \(\mathrm{val}=c\ge1\) and \(\mathrm{Rel}_{S_h}(\iota(1),\mathrm{ref}(r)(x))\), so \(\mathrm{ref}(r)(x)=\iota(c\cdot1)\) by the semantics of the fixed-scalar templates (here \(\iota(1)\) is the code of \(P_0\in2E(K_0)\)).
  • \(\mathrm{add}\ j_1\ j_2\): by induction the operand points are \(\iota(\mathrm{val}(j_1))\) and \(\iota(\mathrm{val}(j_2))\), canonical codes, so the raw-addition contract gives \(\iota(\mathrm{val}(j_1)+\mathrm{val}(j_2))\).
  • \(\mathrm{mul}\ j_1\ j_2\): M gives \(\iota(a)=\iota(\mathrm{val}(j_1))\), \(\iota(b)=\iota(\mathrm{val}(j_2))\) and output \(\iota(ab)\); injectivity of \(\iota\) gives \(\iota(\mathrm{val}(j_1)\mathrm{val}(j_2))\).
  • \(\mathrm{call}\ (a,b,c)\ w\): the three argument points are canonical by induction, so (PV) gives \(w'\in\mathbb N^{V_{\mathcal P}-3}\) with output \(\iota(T_{\mathcal P}(\mathrm{val}(a),\mathrm{val}(b),\mathrm{val}(c),w'))\); set \(\theta\) to \(w'\) on the block of this call. By well-formedness 5 this block is used by no other call and by no explicit variable, and the values of earlier nodes do not depend on it, so the definition is consistent and keeps items 1-3 for earlier nodes.

The root equality of zero mode says that the root point equals \(\mathrm{ref}(-1)(x)=\iota(0)\), so \(\iota(\mathcal N(\theta))=\iota(0)\) and \(\mathcal N(\theta)=0\) by injectivity of \(\iota\). Raw addition only ever receives canonical codes here: this is the induction order of the manuscript's typing argument, and the natural guards constrain the explicit variables only, never intermediate sums or products, whose values may be negative.

ZInQ.Translation.translate_complete

Assume the multiplication statement M in its all-input form. Let \(\mathcal N\), \(\mathcal P\), \(\rho\) and \(\pi\) be as in the soundness statement, with (PV) for \(\pi\) if \(\mathcal N\) has call nodes. Let \(\theta\) be admissible for \(\mathcal N\), with \(\theta_i\in\mathbb N\) for every input \(i<k\) if the inputs carry natural constraints. Then the assignment \(x\) defined by

  • \(\mathrm{ref}(5i)(x)=\iota(\theta_i)\) for the inputs \(i<k\), and in value mode \(\mathrm{ref}(5k)(x)=\iota(\mathcal N(\theta))\);
  • \(x_{g_0}=1641/8\), \(x_{g_1}=-15465/4\), \(x_{g_2}=87483/32\);
  • \(\mathrm{ref}(r_v)(x)=\iota(\theta_v)\) for the fresh point \(r_v\) of every explicit witness variable \(v\);
  • \(\mathrm{ref}(\mathrm{pt}(j))(x)=\iota(\mathrm{val}_\theta(j))\) for every node \(j\) whose point is fresh (a constant node at the first occurrence of its value, an addition, multiplication or call node);
  • \(0\) elsewhere,

is well defined and satisfies conditions 1-4 of the relational form of \(\rho\), and also the root equality in value mode, and in zero mode whenever \(\mathcal N(\theta)=0\). Consequently, in zero mode with \(\mathcal N(\theta)=0\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_\rho(\iota(\theta_0),\dots,\iota(\theta_{k-1}))\) holds, and in value mode \(\mathrm{Rel}_\rho(\iota(\theta_0),\dots,\iota(\theta_{k-1}),\iota(\mathcal N(\theta)))\) holds.

Proof sketch. The fresh points of distinct explicit variables and nodes are distinct allocations, and all occurrences of one nontrivial constant share one point and one value, so \(x\) is well defined; then \(\mathrm{ref}(\mathrm{pt}(j))(x)=\iota(\mathrm{val}_\theta(j))\) for every node, including variable nodes and the constants \(0,\pm1\). Each condition holds by the completeness half of the corresponding statement: the natural rows by the natural-code predicate (\(\theta_v\in\mathbb N\) by admissibility, or by hypothesis for inputs); the constant definitions by the fixed-scalar semantics, \(\mathrm{Rel}_{S_h}(\iota(1),\iota(c))\) for \(c\ge2\); additions by the raw-addition contract; multiplications by M; calls by (PV), with the block values \((\theta_w,\dots,\theta_{w+V_{\mathcal P}-4})\in\mathbb N^{V_{\mathcal P}-3}\) supplied by admissibility. The root equality is \(\iota(\mathcal N(\theta))=\iota(0)=\mathrm{ref}(-1)(x)\) in zero mode and holds by the choice of the output point in value mode. The relational form then gives \(\mathrm{Rel}_\rho\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.Translation.translate_rel_iff_zero ZInQ.Translation.translate_rel_iff_value

Assume the multiplication statement M in its all-input form. Let \(\mathcal N\) be a natural circuit with \(k\) inputs that is well-formed with some bound, with power template \(\mathcal P\) and a well-formed power recipe \(\pi\) satisfying (PV) if it has call nodes, and let \(\rho\) be its translation, with a table of nontrivial constants that is a prefix of \((4,2,3,c_3,1399)\) containing the constants of \(\mathcal N\).

  1. Zero mode, natural inputs. For all \(E_0,\dots,E_{k-1}\in\mathbb Q^5\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_\rho(E_0,\dots,E_{k-1})\iff\exists\,\theta\ \text{admissible for }\mathcal N\text{ with } \theta_0,\dots,\theta_{k-1}\in\mathbb N,\ E_i=\iota(\theta_i)\ (i<k)\ \text{and}\ \mathcal N(\theta)=0 .\)$
  2. Value mode, unconstrained inputs. For all \(c_0,\dots,c_{k-1}\in\mathbb Z\) and \(r\in\mathbb Q^5\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_\rho(\iota(c_0),\dots,\iota(c_{k-1}),r)\iff\exists\,\theta\ \text{admissible for }\mathcal N\text{ with } \theta_i=c_i\ (i<k)\ \text{and}\ r=\iota(\mathcal N(\theta)) .\)$

In the first case the input points need not be assumed to be codes: the natural calls on the inputs type them. In the second case nothing is claimed for non-canonical inputs.

Proof sketch. By the relational form, \(\mathrm{Rel}_\rho\) is the existence of \(x\) with the prescribed parameters satisfying conditions 1-5. (\(\Rightarrow\)) The soundness statement applies (in case 1 the inputs carry natural constraints; in case 2 they are canonical by assumption) and gives \(\theta\); the root equality yields \(\mathcal N(\theta)=0\), respectively \(r=\iota(\mathcal N(\theta))\). (\(\Leftarrow\)) The completeness statement gives \(x\).

docs.title: The power-value and precision recipes
docs.text:
The two translated circuits satisfy the scope conditions: no parent variable node reads a private coordinate, the private blocks are disjoint, and every nontrivial constant is at least two.

The program literal \(c_3\) is a constant of the precision recipe. Its digits are never computed; the natural chapter bounds it by \(1399<c_3<2^{2^{24}}\) (size of the program literal), which gives the scope condition \(c_3\ge2\) here and the size chapter's literal bound.

The power-value recipe has three signed code inputs, seventy-nine private natural witnesses and an output code for the value of the power-template polynomial.

The precision parent has \(54056\) explicit variables and \(15845\) disjoint private blocks; replacing each block by its private power-value call preserves the existential assignment, and only the final root is equated to the identity. This is input C on the rational side.

With equation (C.4), the precision recipe therefore holds at codes \(\iota(c_0),\dots,\iota(c_4)\) exactly when the precision relation accepts \(c\); the assembly chapter's relation Close uses it in this form.

At each primitive formula, equality is a difference, conjunction a sum of squares and disjunction a product; the specification chapter proves that these compilations, including the globally conjoined fixed equations, give equality of polynomial values under substitution (Sums of squares and products over the rationals, Private witness blocks).

docs.title: Scope conditions of the natural precision circuit
docs.text:
ZInQ.Translation.precisionCircuit_wellFormed ZInQ.Translation.powerTemplate_wellFormed

Let \(\mathcal N\) be the natural precision circuit (the circuit of the natural precision polynomial \(C\), obtained by specializing the universal halting circuit at the program literal \(c_3\)) and \(\mathcal P\) its power template. Then \(\mathcal P\) is well-formed with bound \(82\), with explicit variables exactly \(0,1,\dots,81\) in increasing order, \(0,1,2\) the inputs, so that its call blocks have \(79\) variables; and \(\mathcal N\) is well-formed with bound \(1305811\), its \(15845\) call nodes calling \(\mathcal P\). In particular no variable node of the parent reads a private coordinate of a power call.

Proof sketch. For \(\mathcal P\): the power template has \(3\) parameters and \(79\) witnesses on the variables \(0,\dots,81\), and by its node statistics it has no call nodes and nontrivial constants \(4,2,3\), all at least \(2\). For \(\mathcal N\): by its shape it has \(5\) inputs listed first among \(54056\) distinct explicit variables, \(15845\) calls with blocks of \(79\) variables, variable count \(1305811\), and nontrivial constants \(c_3,2,4,1399\), where \(c_3>1399\ge2\) by the size of the program literal; by the specialization statement it is well scoped, so the blocks are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from the explicit variables and every variable node refers to an explicit variable. The remaining conditions (every operand of an addition, multiplication or call node is an earlier node, and the root is a node) hold for the hash-consed node lists of both constructions and are a closed decidable check, or follow from the construction.

Assume the multiplication statement M in its all-input form. Let \(T=T_{\mathcal P}\) be the polynomial function of the power template, of the \(82\) variables \(y_0,\dots,y_{81}\) (\(y_0,y_1,y_2\) its inputs). For all \(a,b,c\in\mathbb Z\) and every \(r\in\mathbb Q^5\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{power\_value}}(\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(c),r)\iff \exists\,w\in\mathbb N^{79}:\ r=\iota\bigl(T(a,b,c,w_0,\dots,w_{78})\bigr).\)$ So \(\mathtt{power\_value}\) satisfies (PV): on three canonical input codes of signed integers it relates exactly the codes of the values of the power-template polynomial at those integers and natural witnesses. The value is not required to vanish; nothing is claimed for non-canonical input tuples.

Proof sketch. \(\mathtt{power\_value}\) is the translation of \(\mathcal P\) in value mode, without natural constraints on the inputs and without a power recipe, and \(\mathcal P\) is well-formed with bound \(82\) and has no call nodes. Case 2 of the semantics of the model-evaluation translation gives: the relation holds iff \(r=\iota(\mathcal P(\theta))\) for some \(\theta\) admissible for \(\mathcal P\) with \(\theta_0,\theta_1,\theta_2=a,b,c\). Admissibility says exactly \(w=(\theta_3,\dots,\theta_{81})\in\mathbb N^{79}\), and \(\mathcal P(\theta)=T(a,b,c,w)\) depends on no other value of \(\theta\).
