docs.title: Semantics of the rational translation
docs.text:
ZInQ.Translation.precision_rel_iff ZInQ.Translation.precision_rel_iff_accepts_of

Assume the multiplication statement M in its all-input form: \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}(p,q,r)\iff\exists a,b\in\mathbb Z,\ p=\iota(a),\ q=\iota(b),\ r=\iota(ab)\) for all \(p,q,r\in\mathbb Q^5\). Let \(C\in\mathbb Z[X_0,\dots,X_{1305810}]\) be the natural precision polynomial, with inputs \(X_0,\dots,X_4\) in the order \((n,\kappa,a,l,j)\). Then for all \(E_0,\dots,E_4\in\mathbb Q^5\) (arbitrary rational \(5\)-tuples), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{precision}}(E_0,\dots,E_4)\iff \exists\,\mathbf c\in\mathbb N^5:\ E_i=\iota(c_i)\ (0\le i\le4)\ \text{and}\ \exists\,\mathbf z\in\mathbb N^{1305806}:\ C(\mathbf c,\mathbf z)=0 .\)$

Thus the precision recipe has rational witnesses exactly at the codes \(\iota(c_0),\dots,\iota(c_4)\) of natural numbers \(c_0,\dots,c_4\) at which the natural polynomial has a natural zero. Together with equation (C.4) this is input C of the assembly lemma. The multiplication statement holds under the six-contact estimate, pole completeness and the twenty-two-prime pattern by the multiplication chapter.

Proof sketch. The semantics of the power-value recipe is the (PV) property of the power recipe used by \(\mathtt{precision}\). The precision recipe is the translation of the natural precision circuit \(\mathcal N\) in zero mode with natural constraints on its five inputs, and \(\mathcal N\) is well-formed with bound \(1305811\). Case 1 of the semantics of the model-evaluation translation gives: \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{precision}}(E)\) iff \(E_i=\iota(\theta_i)\) and \(\mathcal N(\theta)=0\) for some \(\theta\) admissible for \(\mathcal N\) with \(\theta_0,\dots,\theta_4\in\mathbb N\). Every explicit variable and every block variable of \(\mathcal N\) is below \(1305811\), so \(\mathcal N(\theta)=C(\theta_0,\dots,\theta_{1305810})\). Given such \(\theta\), put \(c_i=\theta_i\) and let \(z_v=\theta_v\) when \(v\) is an explicit witness or a block variable, \(z_v=0\) otherwise; then \(\mathbf z\in\mathbb N^{1305806}\) and \(C(\mathbf c,\mathbf z)=\mathcal N(\theta)=0\). Conversely \(\theta=(\mathbf c,\mathbf z,0,0,\dots)\) is admissible. Replacing each private block of the parent by its private power-value call therefore preserves the full existential assignment, and only the final root is equated to the identity.

docs.title: Proposition D: the density of good slope primes
Proposition D: the density of good slope primes
docs.text:
Route AP replaces the twenty-two-prime pattern by long arithmetic progressions of good slope primes. Szemerédi's theorem in the primes provides them once the good slope primes are known to have positive relative upper density in the primes; this chapter proves that density statement, Proposition D of the route AP note in its weak form, following the project's research note on it. No complex multiplication enters: the description of the good slope primes uses elementary character sums only, the main term uses Dirichlet's theorem in residue classes, and the one deep-ish step, a uniform bound for the primes removed at a medium prime \(\ell\), uses a two-dimensional Selberg sieve.

Notation: \(G\) is the set of good slope primes, \(\chi\) the quadratic character of \(\mathbb F_p\), \(\varphi_p(a)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}\chi(x^3+ax)\), \(\pi(N)\) the number of primes at most \(N\), and for a set \(S\) of natural numbers \(\theta_S(N)=\sum_{n\le N,\,n\in S}\log n\) and \(\Phi_S(x)=\sum_{n\in S}(\log n)/n^x\).

23 fully proved

docs.title: The density statement for good slope primes
docs.text:
ZInQ.GoodPrimeDensity

Let \(G\) be the set of good slope primes. The density statement is the assertion that \(G\) has positive relative upper density in the primes: there is \(c>0\) such that $\(\#\bigl(G\cap[0,N]\bigr)\ge c\,\pi(N)\qquad\text{for infinitely many }N,\)$ where \(\pi(N)\) is the number of primes at most \(N\).

This is the weak form of Proposition D of the route AP note; numerically the relative density of \(G\) is about \(0.106\). Together with Szemerédi's theorem in the primes it gives long arithmetic progressions of good slope primes. It is proved in this chapter (Proposition D).

Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(\chi\) the quadratic character of \(\mathbb F_p\), and for \(a\in\mathbb F_p\) put \(\varphi_p(a)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}\chi(x^3+ax)\). Let \(\#E_a(\mathbb F_p)\) be the number of solutions of \(y^2=x^3+ax\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) plus one (the point at infinity). Then:

  1. \(\#E_a(\mathbb F_p)=p+1+\varphi_p(a)\);
  2. \(\varphi_p(k^2a)=\chi(k)\,\varphi_p(a)\) for \(k\in\mathbb F_p^ imes\), and \(\varphi_p(0)=0\);
  3. \(\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p}\chi igl((t+\alpha)(t+ eta) igr)=-1\) for \(\alpha e eta\), and \(=p-1\) for \(\alpha= eta\).

Proof sketch. (1) The equation \(y^2=c\) has \(1+\chi(c)\) solutions; sum over \(x\) with \(c=x^3+ax\). (2) Substitute \(x=kX\): \((kX)^3+k^2a\,kX=k^3(X^3+aX)\) and \(\chi(k^3)=\chi(k)\); and \(\varphi_p(0)=\sum\chi(x)^3=\sum\chi(x)=0\). (3) For \(t e- eta\) the summand is \(\chi igl((t+\alpha)/(t+ eta) igr)\), and \(t\mapsto(t+\alpha)/(t+ eta)\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb F_p\setminus\{- eta\}\) onto \(\mathbb F_p\setminus\{1\}\), so the sum is \(\sum_{w e1}\chi(w)=-1\). The Lean proofs reuse the character sums of the Selmer chapter, since \(\varphi_p(a)\) is the cubic character sum at \(-a\).

docs.title: Jacobsthal's identity
docs.text:
ZInQ.Density.jacobsthal ZInQ.Density.jac_even ZInQ.Density.sum_jac_sq

Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Every \(\varphi_p(a)\) is even, and \(\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}\varphi_p(a)^2=p(p-1)(1+\chi(-1))\). If \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) and \(r\in\mathbb F_p\) is not a square, then $\(\varphi_p(1)^2+\varphi_p(r)^2=4p .\)$

Proof sketch. Evenness: for \(x\ne0\), \(\chi(x^3+ax)=\chi(x)\chi(x^2+a)\), and the involution \(x\mapsto-x\) pairs the summands (for \(p\equiv3\pmod 4\) they cancel, for \(p\equiv1\) they agree), its fixed point \(x=0\) contributing \(0\). Second moment: by the shifted product sums, \(\sum_a\varphi_p(a)^2=\sum_{x,y}\chi(x)\chi(y)\sum_a\chi\bigl((a+x^2)(a+y^2)\bigr)=p(p-1)(1+\chi(-1))\), which is \(2p(p-1)\) for \(p\equiv1\pmod4\). Square classes: \(\varphi_p(0)=0\) and, by scaling, \(\varphi_p(a)^2\) is \(\varphi_p(1)^2\) on the \((p-1)/2\) nonzero squares and \(\varphi_p(r)^2\) on the \((p-1)/2\) non-squares; so \(\tfrac{p-1}2\bigl(\varphi_p(1)^2+\varphi_p(r)^2\bigr)=2p(p-1)\).

docs.title: Four divides the point count of \(y^2=x^3-D^2x\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Density.four_dvd_pointCount ZInQ.Density.four_dvd_pointCount_of_mod_four

Let \(p\) be an odd prime and \(D\in\mathbb F_p^\times\). Then \(4\) divides the number of points, the point at infinity included, of \(y^2=x^3-D^2x\) over \(\mathbb F_p\).

The research note states this for \(p\equiv1\pmod4\); the proof needs only that \(p\) is odd.

Proof sketch. Put \(g(x)=x(x-D)(x+D)\), with three distinct roots. Counting row by row, the point count is \(1+3+2m\) with \(m=\#X\), \(X=\{x\in\mathbb F_p^\times: g(x)\text{ a nonzero square}\}\). The involution \(\tau(x)=-D^2/x\) of \(\mathbb F_p^\times\) satisfies \(g(\tau x)=(D^2/x^2)^2g(x)\), so \(\tau(X)=X\), and an involution has \(\#X\equiv\#\mathrm{Fix}(\tau|_X)\pmod 2\). The fixed points are the solutions of \(x^2=-D^2\): none for \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), and \(\pm iD\) for \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), which lie in \(X\) together or not at all because \(g\) is odd and \(\chi(-1)=1\). So \(m\) is even and \(4\mid4+2m\).

ZInQ.Density.goodSlopePrime_iff ZInQ.Density.InClass ZInQ.Density.cp ZInQ.Density.cp_odd ZInQ.Density.exists_sq_add_sq ZInQ.Density.sq_add_sq_of_nonsquare ZInQ.Density.pointCount_pair ZInQ.Density.gcd_pointCount_eq ZInQ.Density.goodSlopePrime_of_gcd ZInQ.Density.mod_four_of_dvd_cp ZInQ.Density.d_mul_dbar ZInQ.Density.int_gcd_sub_add_two_mul ZInQ.Density.goodSlopePrime_seventeen'

Say that a prime \(p\) is in the class if \(p\equiv1\pmod8\) and \(p\bmod7\in\{3,5,6\}\) (that is, \((p/7)=-1\)), and put \(c_p=\varphi_p(1)/2\). Let \(p\) be a prime in the class. Then:

  1. \(c_p\) is odd, and \(p=c_p^2+e_p^2\) with \(e_p=\varphi_p(r_0)/2\) for any non-square \(r_0\);
  2. for every \(r\in\mathbb F_p\) with \(r^2=2\), the point counts of \(y^2=x^3-(75-53r)^2x\) and \(y^2=x^3-(75+53r)^2x\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) are \(p+1-2c_p\) and \(p+1+2c_p\), in some order;
  3. their greatest common divisor is \(4\gcd(c_p,p+1)\);
  4. \(p\) is a good slope prime if and only if \(\gcd(c_p,p+1)=1\); and an odd prime \(\ell\) dividing both \(c_p\) and \(p+1\) satisfies \(\ell\equiv1\pmod4\).

For example \(c_{17}=-1\), so \(17\) is a good slope prime.

Proof sketch. Since \(p\equiv1\pmod8\), \(2\) is a square, so some \(r\) has \(r^2=2\), and \(d=75-53r\), \(\bar d=75+53r\) satisfy \(d\bar d=7\); by quadratic reciprocity \(\chi(7)=(p/7)=-1\), so \(d\) and \(\bar d\) are nonzero and \(\chi(d)\chi(\bar d)=-1\). By scaling, \(\varphi_p(-d^2)=\chi(d)\varphi_p(-1)\) and \(\varphi_p(-1)=\chi(i)\varphi_p(1)=\varphi_p(1)\) for \(i^2=-1\), since \(i\) is a square when \(p\equiv1\pmod8\); with the point count formula this gives (2). Four divides both point counts, and \(p+1\equiv2\pmod 8\), so \(c_p\) is odd; Jacobsthal's identity gives \(p=c_p^2+e_p^2\). For \(c\) odd and \(n\equiv2\pmod4\), \(\gcd(n-2c,n+2c)=4\gcd(c,n)\), which is (3), and (4) follows from the definition of a good slope prime. If an odd \(\ell\) divides \(c_p\) and \(p+1\), then \(e_p^2=p-c_p^2\equiv-1\pmod\ell\), so \(\ell\equiv1\pmod 4\).

docs.title: The residue set and the main term
docs.text: The congruence conditions modulo \(8\), \(7\) and the small primes \(\ell\equiv1\pmod4\) define a set \(C_L\) of primes of Dirichlet density \(\delta_L\ge3/(8(L-1))\); removing the primes \(T_L\) bad at some \(\ell>L\) leaves good slope primes only.

docs.title: The residue set \(A_L\) and the primes \(C_L\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Density.deltaL_ge ZInQ.Density.QL ZInQ.Density.modSet ZInQ.Density.ML ZInQ.Density.ML_eq ZInQ.Density.crt ZInQ.Density.cond ZInQ.Density.AL ZInQ.Density.card_AL ZInQ.Density.totient_ML ZInQ.Density.deltaL ZInQ.Density.deltaL_eq ZInQ.Density.isUnit_of_mem_AL ZInQ.Density.CL ZInQ.Density.mem_CL

For \(L\ge1\) let \(Q_L\) be the set of primes \(\ell\) with \(5\le\ell\le L\) and \(\ell\equiv1\pmod4\), and \(M_L=56\prod_{\ell\in Q_L}\ell\). Let \(A_L\subseteq\mathbb Z/M_L\) be the set of residues \(a\) with \(a\equiv1\pmod8\), \(a\bmod7\in\{3,5,6\}\) and \(a\not\equiv0,-1\pmod\ell\) for every \(\ell\in Q_L\), and \(C_L\) the set of primes \(p\) with \(p\bmod M_L\in A_L\). Then every element of \(A_L\) is a unit, $\(\#A_L=3\prod_{\ell\in Q_L}(\ell-2),\qquad\varphi(M_L)=24\prod_{\ell\in Q_L}(\ell-1),\qquad \delta_L:=\frac{\#A_L}{\varphi(M_L)}=\frac18\prod_{\ell\in Q_L}\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1},\)$ and \(\delta_L\ge3/(8(L-1))\) for \(L\ge4\). Every prime \(p\in C_L\) is in the class (\(p\equiv1\pmod8\), \((p/7)=-1\)) and satisfies \(\ell\nmid p+1\) for every \(\ell\in Q_L\).

Proof sketch. The moduli \(8\), \(7\) and the \(\ell\in Q_L\) are pairwise coprime, so by the Chinese remainder theorem \(\mathbb Z/M_L\) is the product of the \(\mathbb Z/i\), and \(A_L\) is the product of the sets of allowed components, of sizes \(1\), \(3\) and \(\ell-2\); every allowed component is a unit. The totient is multiplicative. For the lower bound, every factor \((n-2)/(n-1)\) with \(5\le n\le L\) lies in \([0,1]\), so the product over \(Q_L\) is at least the product over all \(n\in[5,L]\), which telescopes to \(3/(L-1)\).

docs.text:

For a set \(S\) of natural numbers and real \(x>1\) put \(\Phi_S(x)=\sum_{n\in S}(\log n)/n^x\). For every \(L\) there is a constant \(K_L\) such that $\(\Phi_{C_L}(x)\ge\frac{\delta_L}{x-1}-K_L\qquad\text{for all }x\in(1,2].\)$

Proof sketch. This is Dirichlet's theorem in residue classes, in the form Mathlib proves it: for a unit \(a\) modulo \(M\), the series \(\sum_{n\equiv a}\Lambda(n)/n^x\) is at least \(\varphi(M)^{-1}/(x-1)-C_a\) on \((1,2]\). Sum over the \(\#A_L\) unit classes \(a\in A_L\); on primes \(\Lambda(p)=\log p\), and the contribution of proper prime powers is bounded on \((1,2]\) by its (convergent) value at exponent \(1\).

docs.title: A subset of good slope primes
docs.text:
ZInQ.Density.goodSlopePrime_of_mem_CL ZInQ.Density.BadSet ZInQ.Density.TL ZInQ.Density.badSet_eq ZInQ.Density.cp_rep ZInQ.Density.TL_subset_primes ZInQ.Density.goodSlopePrimes_subset_primes

For a prime \(\ell\) let \(\mathrm{Bad}_\ell\) be the set of primes \(p\) in the class (\(p\equiv1\pmod8\), \((p/7)=-1\)) with \(\ell\mid c_p\) and \(\ell\mid p+1\), and for \(L\ge1\) let \(T_L\) be the union of the \(\mathrm{Bad}_\ell\) over the primes \(\ell>L\) with \(\ell\equiv1\pmod4\). Then every prime of \(G^*_L=C_L\setminus T_L\) is a good slope prime.

Proof sketch. Let \(p\in C_L\setminus T_L\); it is in the class. If \(\gcd(c_p,p+1)\ne1\), take a prime \(\ell\) dividing it. Then \(\ell\) is odd (since \(c_p\) is odd), so \(\ell\equiv1\pmod4\) and hence \(\ell\ge5\). If \(\ell\le L\) then \(\ell\in Q_L\), which is impossible since \(\ell\mid p+1\); so \(\ell>L\) and \(p\in\mathrm{Bad}_\ell\subseteq T_L\), a contradiction. Hence \(\gcd(c_p,p+1)=1\), and \(p\) is a good slope prime by the description.

The primes bad at a large \(\ell\)
docs.text:

For every prime \(\ell\) and every \(N\), $\(\#\bigl(\mathrm{Bad}_\ell\cap[0,N]\bigr)\le\frac{8N}{\ell^2}+\frac{4\sqrt N}{\ell},\)$ and the left side is \(0\) when \(\ell>\sqrt N\). Consequently, for \(N\ge1\) and every finite set \(F\) of primes \(\ell\) with \(\ell^4>N\), $\(\sum_{\ell\in F}\#\bigl(\mathrm{Bad}_\ell\cap[0,N]\bigr)\le20\,N^{3/4}.\)$

The Lean statement takes for \(c_p\) any function with \(p=c_p^2+e^2\) for some \(e\), for the primes in the class; the instance is \(c_p=\varphi_p(1)/2\).

Proof sketch. By the description, \(p=c_p^2+e_p^2\), so \(p\mapsto(c_p,e_p)\) embeds \(\mathrm{Bad}_\ell\cap[0,N]\) into the lattice points \((c,e)\in[-\sqrt N,\sqrt N]^2\) with \(c\ne0\), \(\ell\mid c\) and \(\ell\mid e^2+1\) (from \(\ell\mid p+1=c^2+e^2+1\)). There are at most \(2\sqrt N/\ell\) nonzero multiples of \(\ell\) in the interval (none if \(\ell>\sqrt N\)), and \(e\) lies in at most two residue classes modulo \(\ell\), each meeting the interval in at most \(2\sqrt N/\ell+1\) points. Summing \(8N/\ell^2+4\sqrt N/\ell\) over the primes \(\ell\in F\): the second term vanishes for \(\ell>\sqrt N\), and \(\sum_{\ell>N^{1/4}}\ell^{-2}\) and \(\sum_{N^{1/4}<\ell\le\sqrt N}\ell^{-1}\) are of order \(N^{-1/4}\) and \(N^{1/4}\), giving \(20N^{3/4}\).

docs.title: The sieve bound for a medium \(\ell\)
docs.text: A prime bad at \(\ell\) is a value of \((\ell U)^2+(b+\ell V)^2\) on a box, coprime to the small primes \(q\equiv1\pmod4\). The Selberg sieve, vendored from the PrimeNumberTheoremAnd project, bounds these values; the local densities, the box count and a lower bound for the Selberg sum by elementary divisor sums supply its inputs.

docs.title: The Selberg sieve bound
docs.text:
SelbergSieve.selberg_bound_simple SelbergSieve.selbergTerms SelbergSieve.selbergBoundingSum SelbergSieve.selbergBoundingSum_pos SelbergSieve.selbergWeights SelbergSieve.selbergUbSieve SelbergSieve.selberg_bound_simple_mainSum SelbergSieve.selberg_bound_simple_errSum SelbergSieve.selberg_bound_weights SelbergSieve.selberg_bound_muPlus

Let \(\mathcal A\) be a finite set of natural numbers with nonnegative weights \(a_n\) and total mass \(X\), let \(P\) be a squarefree product of primes, let \( u\) be a multiplicative function with \(0< u(q)<1\) for the primes \(q\mid P\), and let \(y\ge1\) be the level. Put \(R_d=\sum_{n\in\mathcal A,\,d\mid n}a_n- u(d)X\), \(g(l)= u(l)\prod_{q\mid l}(1- u(q))^{-1}\) and \(S=\sum_{l\mid P,\ l^2\le y}g(l)\). Then \(S>0\) and $\(\sum_{\substack{n\in\mathcal A\ \gcd(n,P)=1}}a_n\;\le\; rac XS+\sum_{\substack{d\mid P\ d\le y}}3^{\omega(d)}|R_d| .\)$

This is Selberg's upper bound sieve. The Lean proof is the one of the PrimeNumberTheoremAnd project (https://github.com/AlexKontorovich/PrimeNumberTheoremAnd, by Arend Mellendijk), vendored unchanged except for its import lines under the Apache License 2.0, and built on Mathlib's sieve structures.

Proof sketch. Choose the Selberg weights \(\lambda_d\) (\(d\mid P\), \(d^2\le y\), \(\lambda_1=1\)) that minimize the quadratic form of the main term; then \(\mu^+(d)=\sum_{[d_1,d_2]=d}\lambda_{d_1}\lambda_{d_2}\) is an upper bound sieve, the main term equals \(X/S\) after diagonalization, \(|\lambda_d|\le1\), and \(|\mu^+(d)|\le3^{\omega(d)}\), which bounds the error term.

docs.text:

Let \(\ell,b\) be integers and \(F(U,V)=(\ell U)^2+(b+\ell V)^2\). For a prime \(q\equiv1\pmod4\) with \(q\nmid\ell\), the equation \(F(U,V)=0\) has exactly \(2q-1\) solutions in \(\mathbb F_q^2\). Consequently, for a finite set \(t\) of such primes and \(d=\prod_{q\in t}q\), the congruence \(F(U,V)\equiv0\pmod d\) has exactly \(\prod_{q\in t}(2q-1)\) solutions in \((\mathbb Z/d)^2\).

Proof sketch. \((U,V)\mapsto(\ell U,b+\ell V)\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb F_q^2\) since \(\ell\) is invertible. With \(i^2=-1\) in \(\mathbb F_q\), \(x^2+y^2=(x-iy)(x+iy)\) vanishes exactly on two lines meeting only at \(0\): \(2q-1\) points. The Chinese remainder theorem makes the count multiplicative in \(d\).

docs.title: Counting a box with a divisibility condition
docs.text:

Let \(\ell,b\) be integers, \(F(U,V)=(\ell U)^2+(b+\ell V)^2\), \(d\ge1\), and let \(\rho(d)\) be the number of solutions of \(F\equiv0\pmod d\) in \((\mathbb Z/d)^2\). For a box \(\mathcal B=[a_1,a_1+M_1)\times[a_2,a_2+M_2)\) of integer points, $\(\Bigl|\#\{(U,V)\in\mathcal B: d\mid F(U,V)\}-\rho(d)\frac{M_1M_2}{d^2}\Bigr|\le\rho(d)\,(M_1+M_2+1).\)$

Proof sketch. An interval of \(M\) consecutive integers has \(M/d+\theta\) elements in each residue class modulo \(d\), with \(|\theta|\le1\). For each of the \(\rho(d)\) residue pairs the box contains \((M_1/d+\theta_1)(M_2/d+\theta_2)\) points of the pair, which differs from \(M_1M_2/d^2\) by at most \(M_1+M_2+1\) (as \(d\ge1\)); sum over the pairs.

docs.title: A lower bound for the Selberg sum
docs.text:
ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.selbergBoundingSum_ge_tau ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.prod_factors_sum_pow_mult ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.tauDiv ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.rSum ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.rSum_ge_log ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.hDiv ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.vDiv ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.hSum ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.rDiv_eq_hDiv_mul_vDiv ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.vSum_le_four ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.log_le_hSum ZInQ.Density.GaussSieve.hSum_coprime_ge

Let a Selberg sieve have level \(w^2\) (\(w\ge1\)) and satisfy \(g(q)\ge(1-1/q)^{-2}-1\) at the primes \(q\mid P\). Then its Selberg sum satisfies $\(S\ge\sum_{\substack{m\le w\ \mathrm{rad}(m)\mid P}}\frac{\tau(m)}m,\)$ where \(\tau\) is the number of divisors. Moreover, with \(r(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\chi_4(d)\) and \(h(n)=\tau(n)/n\) if every prime factor of \(n\) is \(\equiv1\pmod4\), \(h(n)=0\) otherwise:

  1. \(\sum_{n\le w}r(n)/n\ge\frac23\log w\);
  2. \(\log w\le6\sum_{n\le w}h(n)\);
  3. for a prime \(\ell\), removing the multiples of \(\ell\) keeps at least the fraction \(1-2/\ell\): \(\sum_{n\le w,\ \ell\nmid n}h(n)\ge(1-2/\ell)\sum_{n\le w}h(n)\).

Proof sketch. Expand \(g(q)\ge\sum_{k\ge1}(k+1)q^{-k}\) multiplicatively: for \(l\mid P\) with \(l\le w\), \(g(l)\) dominates the sum of \(\tau(m)/m\) over the \(m\le w\) with radical \(l\). (1) Write \(\sum_{n\le w}r(n)/n=\sum_d(\chi_4(d)/d)H(\lfloor w/d\rfloor)\) and pair the terms \(d\equiv1,3\pmod4\) in blocks; no Euler constant is needed. (2) \(r(n)/n\) is the Dirichlet convolution of \(h\) with a nonnegative function \(v\) supported on numbers without prime factors \(\equiv1\pmod4\), whose partial sums are at most \(4\); so \(\sum r(n)/n\le4\sum h(n)\). (3) \(h(\ell m)\le2h(m)/\ell\).

Let \(\ell\) be a prime, \(b\) an integer, \(K\ge0\) and \(w\ge1\). Sift the values of \(F(U,V)=(\ell U)^2+(b+\ell V)^2\) on the box \(\mathcal B=[-K,K] imes[-K-1,K]\), each counted with its multiplicity, by the primes \(q\le w\) with \(q\equiv1\pmod4\) and \(q e\ell\), with density \( u(q)=(2q-1)/q^2\) and level \(w^2\); the total mass is \(X=(2K+1)(2K+2)\). Then the number of points of \(\mathcal B\) whose value is coprime to all these primes is at most $\( rac XS+w^8(4K+4),\)$ where \(S\) is the Selberg sum of the sieve, and \(S\ge(\log w)/10\) if \(\ell\ge5\).

Proof sketch. The Selberg sieve bound. By the local densities, \( ho(d)= u(d)d^2\) for \(d\mid P\), so the box count bounds each remainder by \(|R_d|\le d^2(4K+4)\) for \(d\mid P\); with \(3^{\omega(d)}\le d\) (the prime factors of \(d\) are at least \(5\)) the error sum is at most \(\sum_{d\le w^2}d^3(4K+4)\le w^8(4K+4)\). At a sifting prime \(g(q)=(2q-1)/(q-1)^2=(1-1/q)^{-2}-1\), so the lower bound for the Selberg sum applies: \(S\ge\sum_{m\le w,\ \mathrm{rad}(m)\mid P} au(m)/m\), which is the sum of \(h\) over \(m\le w\) prime to \(\ell\), at least \((1-2/\ell)(\log w)/6\ge(\log w)/10\) for \(\ell\ge5\).

For a prime \(\ell\) let \(\mathrm{GB}_\ell\) be the set of primes \(p=c^2+e^2\) (\(c,e\in\mathbb Z\)) with \(\ell\mid c\) and \(\ell\mid p+1\); by the description it contains \(\mathrm{Bad}_\ell\). Let \(\ell\ge5\), \(N\ge0\), \(w\ge2\) and \(K=\lfloor\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor/\ell\rfloor\). Then $\(\#\bigl(\mathrm{GB}_\ell\cap[0,N]\bigr)\le(w+1)+2\Bigl(\frac{10(2K+1)(2K+2)}{\log w}+w^8(4K+4)\Bigr).\)$

Proof sketch. For \(p\in\mathrm{GB}_\ell\cap[0,N]\), \(c=\ell U\) and \(e^2\equiv-1\pmod\ell\), so \(e\equiv b\pmod\ell\) for one of the at most two roots \(b\) of \(b^2\equiv-1\), and \(e=b+\ell V\) (after choosing the sign of \(e\) and \(b\in[0,\ell)\)) with \((U,V)\) in the box \([-K,K]\times[-K-1,K]\); distinct primes give distinct points. A prime \(p>w\) is coprime to every sifting prime, so all but at most \(w+1\) of these primes are counted by the sifted sum of the sieve for the primes bad at \(\ell\); apply its bound, with \(S\ge(\log w)/10\), for each root \(b\).

docs.title: The uniform bound for the primes bad at a medium \(\ell\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Density.UniformBadBound

The uniform bad-prime bound is the assertion that there are constants \(A>0\) and \(N_1\) such that for every \(N\ge N_1\) and every prime \(\ell\equiv1\pmod4\) with \(5\le\ell\) and \(\ell^4\le N\), $\(\#\bigl(\mathrm{Bad}_\ell\cap[0,N]\bigr)\le\frac{A\,N}{\ell^2\log N}.\)$

It is Proposition 4.2 of the research note, isolated as a statement so that Theorem D can be proved from it before the sieve; it is proved in the uniform bound holds.

docs.title: The uniform bound holds
docs.text:
ZInQ.Density.uniformBadBound_holds ZInQ.Density.uniformBadBound ZInQ.Density.uniformGaussBadBound ZInQ.Density.gaussBad_final_ineq

The uniform bad-prime bound holds. More precisely, there is \(N_1\) such that for every \(N\ge N_1\) and every prime \(\ell\equiv1\pmod4\) with \(5\le\ell\) and \(\ell^4\le N\), $\(\#\bigl(\mathrm{GB}_\ell\cap[0,N]\bigr)\le\frac{14402\,N}{\ell^2\log N},\)$ and \(\mathrm{Bad}_\ell\subseteq\mathrm{GB}_\ell\).

The research note proves the bound with \(A_1=16003\) and \(N_1=e^{1920}\); the Lean proof has \(A=14402\) and a threshold \(N_1\) that is not explicit.

Proof sketch. Put \(u=N^{1/40}\) and \(w=\lfloor u\rfloor\), and apply the count of \(\mathrm{GB}_\ell\). Since \(\sqrt N=u^{20}\), \(K\le u^{20}/\ell\), and \(\ell^4\le N\) gives \(\ell\le u^{10}\). The main term \(20(2K+1)(2K+2)/\log w\) is then at most a constant times \(N/(\ell^2\log N)\) (as \(\log N=40\log u\) and \(\log w\ge\log(u-1)\)), while the error terms \(w+1\) and \(2w^8(4K+4)\) are of order \(u^{28}\), which is at most \(N/(\ell^2\log N)\) once \(400\log u\le u^2\) and \(u\ge4\). An elementary real inequality collects the constants into \(14402\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.Density.abel_bound ZInQ.Density.thetaS ZInQ.Density.phiTerm ZInQ.Density.PhiS ZInQ.Density.abel_summation ZInQ.Density.abel_partial_sum_le ZInQ.Density.sum_one_div_rpow_le ZInQ.Density.thetaS_le_log4 ZInQ.Density.thetaS_le_log_mul_card ZInQ.Density.thetaS_le_of_eventually ZInQ.Density.summable_phiTerm

For a set \(S\) of natural numbers put \(\theta_S(N)=\sum_{n\le N,\ n\in S}\log n\) and, for \(x>1\), \(\Phi_S(x)=\sum_{n\in S}(\log n)/n^x\). Let \(\kappa\ge0\) and \(B\) be reals with \(\theta_S(N)\le\kappa N+B\) for every \(N\). Then for every \(x\in(1,2]\) the series \(\Phi_S(x)\) converges and $\(\Phi_S(x)\le\kappa\,\frac x{x-1}+B .\)$

Proof sketch. Discrete partial summation writes \(\sum_{n\le M}\mathbf 1_S(n)\log n\cdot n^{-x}\) as \(\theta_S(M)M^{-x}+\sum_{n<M}\theta_S(n)\bigl(n^{-x}-(n+1)^{-x}\bigr)\). Insert the bound on \(\theta_S\); the constant \(B\) telescopes to at most \(B\), and \(\sum_n n\bigl(n^{-x}-(n+1)^{-x}\bigr)\) is at most \(\sum_{n\le M}n^{-x}\le x/(x-1)\), by Bernoulli's inequality. The partial sums are bounded and the terms nonnegative.

docs.title: Dirichlet density gives relative upper density
docs.text:
ZInQ.Density.primesRelUpperDensityPos_of_dirichlet

Let \(S\) be a set of natural numbers, and let \(\eta>0\) and \(K\) be reals with $\(\Phi_S(x)\ge\frac\eta{x-1}-K\qquad\text{for all }x\in(1,2].\)$ Then \(S\) has positive relative upper density in the primes: there is \(c>0\) with \(\#(S\cap[0,N])\ge c\,\pi(N)\) for infinitely many \(N\).

This is Proposition 5.3 of the research note (a positive lower Dirichlet density in the von Mangoldt normalisation gives a positive upper relative density).

Proof sketch. Suppose not. Then for every \(c>0\) eventually \(\#(S\cap[0,N])<c\,\pi(N)\), and with Chebyshev's bound \(\pi(N)\le(\log4+\varepsilon)N/\log N\) this gives \(\theta_S(N)\le\#(S\cap[0,N])\log N\le\kappa N\) for large \(N\) with \(\kappa\) as small as we like, hence \(\theta_S(N)\le\kappa N+B\) for all \(N\). Abel summation gives \(\Phi_S(x)\le\kappa x/(x-1)+B\), which contradicts the lower bound as \(x\to1^+\) once \(2\kappa<\eta\).

Assume the uniform bad-prime bound. Then the good slope primes have positive relative upper density in the primes.

The proof goes through Theorem D of the research note: for a suitable \(L\), the set \(G^*_L=C_L\setminus T_L\) of good slope primes satisfies \(\Phi_{G^*_L}(x)\ge\eta_L/(x-1)-K\) on \((1,2]\) with \(\eta_L>0\), a positive lower Dirichlet density. The Lean proof applies this to the larger set of all good slope primes directly.

Proof sketch. Let \(A,N_1\) be the constants of the uniform bound and choose \(L\ge5\) with \(\log L\ge16A\log4\). For \(N\ge\max(N_1,2)\), the uniform bound for the primes \(L<\ell\le N^{1/4}\), summed with the prime tail, and the lattice count for the primes \(\ell>N^{1/4}\) give \(\#(T_L\cap[0,N])\le\alpha_LN/\log N+20N^{3/4}\) with \(\alpha_L=3A\log4/(L\log L)\le\delta_L/2\). With \(\varepsilon=\delta_L/4\), eventually \(\theta_{T_L}(N)\le(\alpha_L+\varepsilon)N\), so Abel summation gives \(\Phi_{T_L}(x)\le(\alpha_L+\varepsilon)x/(x-1)+B\). Since \(C_L\setminus T_L\) consists of good slope primes, \(\Phi_G\ge\Phi_{C_L}-\Phi_{T_L}\), and the main term gives \(\Phi_G(x)\ge(\delta_L-\alpha_L-\varepsilon)/(x-1)-K'\) with \(\delta_L-\alpha_L-\varepsilon\ge\delta_L/4>0\). Dirichlet density gives relative upper density.

docs.title: Szemerédi's theorem in the primes (Green–Tao)
docs.text:
Route AP replaces the twenty-two-prime pattern by long arithmetic progressions of good slope primes. They come from two theorems: the good slope primes have positive relative density (Proposition D), and every set of primes of positive relative upper density contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length (Green and Tao, Theorem 1.2). This chapter proves the second in Lean. It is the only part of the formalization that rests on code not written in this project: the Lean proof of the Green–Tao theorem for the set of all primes by Vasily Ilin, from the repository Vilin97/Autoformalization (directory green-tao/), distributed under the Apache License 2.0 and vendored in this repository with its license and a notice of the changes made to port it. The chapter extends that proof to dense sets of primes without changing any vendored file.

Notation: \(\lambda_{\alpha,W,b}\) is the W-tricked prime weight on \(\mathbb Z/N\) and \(\lambda^A_{\alpha,W,b}\) its restriction to a set \(A\); \(\Lambda_k(f)\) is the normalized count of \(k\)-term progressions in \(\mathbb Z/N\) weighted by \(f\).

10 fully proved

docs.title: Szemerédi's theorem in the primes
docs.text:
ZInQ.GreenTaoDense ZInQ.ContainsArbitraryAPs ZInQ.PrimesRelUpperDensityPos

A set \(A\) of natural numbers contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length if for every \(k\) there are natural numbers \(a\) and \(b\ge1\) with \(a+bj\in A\) for every \(j<k\). A set \(A\) has positive relative upper density in the primes if there is a real \(c>0\) such that $\(c\,\pi(N)\le\#\bigl(A\cap[0,N]\bigr)\)$ for infinitely many \(N\), where \(\pi\) is the prime counting function; for a set of primes this says \(\limsup_{N\to\infty}\#(A\cap[1,N])/\pi(N)>0\).

Szemerédi's theorem in the primes, in its dense form, is the assertion that every set of primes of positive relative upper density contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length.

This is Theorem 1.2 of Green and Tao, with "infinitely many progressions" weakened to "one". Green and Tao prove it in outline; Tao and Ziegler give a complete proof. Route AP needs it for the good slope primes above \(\max S_b\). It was first a hypothesis of the route AP variants of the main theorem; it is proved in this chapter (Szemerédi's theorem in the primes holds).

docs.title: The Green–Tao theorem
docs.text:
ZInQ.greenTao_primes Submission.green_tao

The set of primes contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length: for every \(k\) there are natural numbers \(a\) and \(b\ge1\) such that \(a+bj\) is prime for every \(j<k\).

This is Theorem 1.1 of Green and Tao. Its Lean proof is not written in this project: it is Vasily Ilin's proof from the repository Vilin97/Autoformalization (directory green-tao/, commit 0dc67d87416c19690dd641a178ada32cca95c651), produced under Ilin's direction as a submission to the green_tao target of the lean-eval benchmark and distributed under the Apache License 2.0. It is vendored in this repository with its license and a notice, and ported to the project's Lean and Mathlib versions with proof edits only; its statement is unchanged, and it is the statement here, since the two definitions of "contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length" agree word for word.

Proof sketch. The vendored proof follows Green and Tao. After the W-trick (restricting to a reduced residue class \(b\) modulo \(W=\prod_{p\le w}p\) and weighting the primes \(Wn+b\) by \(\log(Wn+b)\)), the weighted primes in a cyclic group \(\mathbb Z/N\) of prime order are bounded by a Selberg-sieve majorant \(\nu\) that satisfies the linear forms condition. The relative Szemerédi theorem (transference: a weight \(0\le f\le\nu\) of positive mean has a dense model) and the dense Szemerédi theorem, from the hypergraph removal lemma, give a positive count of \(k\)-term progressions weighted by \(f\); the diagonal progressions are negligible, so some progression with nonzero difference has positive weight at every term, and a short-interval lift turns it into a progression of primes. Lengths \(k\le2\) come from the progression \(2,3\).

docs.title: From density to windows
docs.text: The density hypothesis counts all of \([0,N]\) at infinitely many \(N\); the W-trick samples a window \((X/4,X]\) at a scale tied to the cyclic modulus. A dyadic decomposition and Chebyshev's lower bound put a fixed share of the mass into some window of ratio \(2\), and Bertrand's postulate chooses a prime modulus whose sampled window contains most of it.

docs.title: The window lemma
docs.text:
ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.frequently_window ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.frequently_window_of ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.card_filter_range_le_add_Ioc ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.card_filter_range_le_sum_windows ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.isLittleO_sqrt_mul_log ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.eventually_window_error

Let \(A\) be a set of natural numbers of positive relative upper density in the primes, with \(c\,\pi(N)\le\#(A\cap[0,N])\) for infinitely many \(N\), where \(c>0\). Put \(c_1=c\log2/24\). Then for infinitely many \(Z\), $\(\#\bigl(A\cap(\lfloor Z/2\rfloor,Z]\bigr)\ge\frac{c_1Z}{\log Z}.\)$ In particular some \(c_1>0\) has this property.

The set \(A\) need not consist of primes. The point is that the density hypothesis, which counts all of \([0,N]\), yields mass in a window of ratio \(2\), which is what the sampling of the W-trick sees.

Proof sketch. Let \(N\) be large with \(c\,\pi(N)\le\#(A\cap[0,N])\), and let \(J\) be the largest integer with \(2^J\le\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\). Cut \([0,N]\) into the tail \([0,\lfloor N/2^J\rfloor]\) and the windows \((\lfloor N/2^{j+1}\rfloor,\lfloor N/2^j\rfloor]\) for \(j<J\). The tail has at most \(2\sqrt N+1\) elements. Every window has \(Z_j=\lfloor N/2^j\rfloor\ge\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\), so \(\log Z_j\ge\frac13\log N\) for large \(N\), and \(Z_j\) tends to infinity with \(N\). If every window had fewer than \(c_1Z_j/\log Z_j\) elements of \(A\), the windows together would hold fewer than \(\sum_j 3c_1Z_j/\log N\le6c_1N/\log N=\frac c4\log2\cdot N/\log N\) elements. Chebyshev's lower bound \(\pi(N)\log N\ge N\log2-\log(N+1)\) then gives \(c\,\pi(N)>\#(A\cap[0,N])\) once the error terms \((2\sqrt N+2)\log N+c\log(N+1)\) are below \(\frac34c\log2\cdot N\), which holds for large \(N\) because \(\sqrt x\log x=o(x)\). So for every large such \(N\) some window, with \(Z_j\ge\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\), is good. Only the lower bound for \(\pi\) is used.

docs.title: Choosing the prime modulus
docs.text:
ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.exists_prime_modulus_of_frequently_window ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.exists_prime_scale_near ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.card_window_le_card_quarter

Let \(A\) be a set of natural numbers and \(c_1>0\) such that \(\#(A\cap(\lfloor Z/2\rfloor,Z])\ge c_1Z/\log Z\) for infinitely many \(Z\). Then for every \(W>0\) and every bound \(Q_0\) there is a prime \(q\ge Q_0\) such that \(X=W\lfloor q/8\rfloor\) satisfies \(X\ge Q_0\) and $\(\#\bigl(A\cap(\lfloor X/4\rfloor,X]\bigr)\ge\frac{c_1}{6}\cdot\frac{X}{\log X}.\)$

The scale \(X=W\lfloor q/8\rfloor\) and the window \((X/4,X]\) are those that the W-trick of the Green–Tao proof samples in the cyclic group of order \(q\).

Proof sketch. Bertrand. For any \(Z\) put \(m=\lfloor Z/W\rfloor+1\); Bertrand's postulate gives a prime \(q\) with \(8m<q\le16m\), so \(m\le\lfloor q/8\rfloor\le2m\), hence \(q>8\lfloor Z/W\rfloor\) and \(Z\le W\lfloor q/8\rfloor\le2Z+2W\). Window transfer. For \(Z\le X\le2Z+2W\), the window \((\lfloor Z/2\rfloor,Z]\) lies in \((\lfloor X/4\rfloor,X]\) up to the at most \(W/2+1\) integers of \((\lfloor Z/2\rfloor,\lfloor X/4\rfloor]\). Now take a good \(Z\) so large that \(\log Z\le c_1Z/(2(W+1))\) and \(Z\ge Q_0W+2W+Q_0+3\). Then \(q\ge Q_0\), \(X\ge Z\ge Q_0\), \(X\le3Z\), and \(c_1Z/\log Z\ge2(W+1)\), so \(A\) has at least \(\frac12c_1Z/\log Z\ge\frac{c_1}6X/\log X\) elements in \((\lfloor X/4\rfloor,X]\), using \(X\le3Z\) and \(\log Z\le\log X\).

docs.title: The weight of a set of primes
docs.text: The weight of \(A\) is the prime weight times the indicator of \(A\). It lies below the prime weight, so majorization and the height bound carry over; positivity now means membership in \(A\), and the residue pigeonhole runs over the elements of \(A\) only.

docs.title: The W-tricked weight of a set of primes
docs.text:
ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.wTrickedSetWeight ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.wTrickedSetWeight_nonneg ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.wTrickedSetWeight_le ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.wTrickedSetWeight_pos_iff

Let \(N\ge1\), let \(\alpha\) be real and \(W,b\) natural numbers, and for \(n\in\mathbb Z/N\) let \(\bar n\) be its representative in \([0,N)\). The W-tricked prime weight of the Green–Tao proof is $\(\lambda_{\alpha,W,b}(n)=\begin{cases}\alpha\,\dfrac{\varphi(W)}{W}\log(W\bar n+b)&\text{if } \lfloor N/64\rfloor\le\bar n\le\lfloor N/4\rfloor\text{ and }W\bar n+b\text{ is prime},\\[1ex] 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\)$ For a set \(A\) of natural numbers, the W-tricked weight of \(A\) is \(\lambda^A_{\alpha,W,b}(n)=\lambda_{\alpha,W,b}(n)\) if \(W\bar n+b\in A\) and \(0\) otherwise. If \(\alpha\ge0\), then \(0\le\lambda^A_{\alpha,W,b}\le\lambda_{\alpha,W,b}\); if \(\alpha>0\) and \(W>0\), then \(\lambda^A_{\alpha,W,b}(n)>0\) exactly when \(\lfloor N/64\rfloor\le\bar n\le\lfloor N/4\rfloor\) and \(W\bar n+b\) is a prime in \(A\).

The bound \(\lambda^A\le\lambda\) is what lets the weight of \(A\) inherit, unchanged, the majorization of the prime weight by the Selberg-sieve majorant and its pointwise height bound.

docs.title: Extraction of a progression in the set
docs.text:
ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.containsAP_of_wTrickedSetWeight_offDiagMass_pos

Let \(A\) be a set of natural numbers, \(k\ge2\), \(N\ge1\), \(\alpha>0\), \(W>0\) and \(b\) natural. If the off-diagonal mass of the weight of \(A\) is positive, $\(\sum_{a\in\mathbb Z/N}\ \sum_{d\in\mathbb Z/N,\ d\ne0}\ \prod_{j<k}\lambda^A_{\alpha,W,b}(a+jd)>0,\)$ then \(A\) contains a \(k\)-term arithmetic progression: there are natural numbers \(a'\) and \(d'>0\) with \(a'+jd'\in A\) for every \(j<k\).

Proof sketch. Some \(a\) and \(d\ne0\) have \(\lambda^A(a+jd)>0\) for every \(j<k\). By the positivity criterion of the weight, every representative \(\overline{a+jd}\) lies in \([\lfloor N/64\rfloor,\lfloor N/4\rfloor]\), an interval of less than half the length of \(\mathbb Z/N\), and \(W\overline{a+jd}+b\in A\). The short-interval lift of the vendored proof turns a cyclic progression inside such an interval into an integer progression with positive difference in \(\{n:Wn+b\in A\}\), and the affine map \(n\mapsto Wn+b\) carries it into \(A\). This is the vendored extraction for the primes, with the positivity criterion of the weight of \(A\) in place of that of the prime weight.

docs.title: The residue pigeonhole for a set of primes
docs.text:
ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.exists_reducedResidue_setWeight_mean_lower_bound ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.quarterIntervalSetClass ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.wTrickedSetWeight_untrickPrimeZMod ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.setClass_log_mass_div_card_le_mean ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.card_mul_log_cutoff_le_setClass_log_mass

Let \(A\) be a set of natural numbers, \(w\) and \(N\ge1\) natural numbers, \(\alpha\ge0\), \(W=\prod_{p\le w}p\) and \(X=W\lfloor N/8\rfloor\), and suppose \(w\le\lfloor X/4\rfloor\). Let \(S\) be the set of primes \(p\in A\) with \(\lfloor X/4\rfloor<p\le X\). Then there is a residue \(0\le b<W\) coprime to \(W\) such that the mean of the W-tricked weight of \(A\) over \(\mathbb Z/N\) satisfies $\(\frac1N\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z/N}\lambda^A_{\alpha,W,b}(n)\ \ge\ \frac{\alpha}{W}\cdot\frac{\#S\cdot\log(\lfloor X/4\rfloor+1)}{N}.\)$

Proof sketch. Every \(p\in S\) exceeds \(w\), so it is coprime to \(W\); pigeonholing \(S\) over the \(\varphi(W)\) reduced classes gives a class \(b\) with \(\#S\le\varphi(W)\,\#S_b\), where \(S_b\) is the set of \(p\in S\) with \(p\equiv b\pmod W\). Each \(p\in S_b\) is \(W\bar n+b\) for the residue \(n\) of \((p-b)/W\), which lies in \([\lfloor N/64\rfloor,\lfloor N/4\rfloor]\), and these \(n\) are distinct; at each, \(\lambda^A(n)=\alpha\frac{\varphi(W)}W\log p\ge\alpha\frac{\varphi(W)}W\log(\lfloor X/4\rfloor+1)\). Summing over \(S_b\) and dividing by \(N\) gives the bound. This is the vendored density selection with the primes of \((\lfloor X/4\rfloor,X]\) replaced by the elements of \(A\) among them; the original pigeonhole is already stated for an arbitrary finite set of primes above \(w\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.hasPrimeModulusSubweightCounts ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.HasPrimeModulusSubweightCounts ZInQ.GreenTaoDense.hasPrimeModulusSubweightCounts_of_orderedRemoval_of_linearForms

For \(k\ge3\) let \(\alpha_k>0\) be the scale of the W-tricked prime weight in the Green–Tao proof (the constant fixed there from \(k\) and the normalizer of the smooth sieve cutoff, small enough that the weight lies below the sieve majorant). For \(f:\mathbb Z/N o\mathbb R\) write \(\mathbb E f= rac1N\sum_nf(n)\) and \(\Lambda_k(f)=\mathbb E_{a,d\in\mathbb Z/N}\prod_{j<k}f(a+jd)\).

For every \(k\ge3\) and every \(\delta>0\) there are a natural number \(w\) and a real \(c>0\) such that, with \(W=\prod_{p\le w}p\), for every sufficiently large \(M\) with \(N=M+1\) prime, every residue \(0\le b<W\) coprime to \(W\) and every \(f:\mathbb Z/N o\mathbb R\) with $\(0\le f\le\lambda_{\alpha_k,W,b}\qquad ext{and}\qquad\mathbb Ef\ge\delta,\)$ the count satisfies \(\Lambda_k(f)\ge c\).

The Green–Tao proof for the set of all primes shows this only for the prime weight itself, at one prime modulus beyond each bound, and for one fixed density. The proof never uses more: the change is in the quantifiers.

Proof sketch. Write \(k=r+2\). The dense Szemerédi theorem, from the ordered hypergraph removal of the vendored proof, gives for density \(\delta/2\) a count \(\Lambda_k(g)\ge c_0>0\) for every \(g:\mathbb Z/N o[0,1]\) with \(\mathbb Eg\ge\delta/2\), uniformly in \(N\). The parameter package of the relative counting step, chosen for the reserves \(\delta/2\) and \(c_0/2\), and the linear forms condition of the Selberg-sieve majorant \( u_b\), uniform over the reduced classes \(b\), fix \(w\) and a threshold. For \(N=M+1\) prime and large, \(N\) is coprime to \((r+1)!\), the prime weight lies below \( u_b\) for every \(b<W\) at once, and so does every \(f\le\lambda\). The relative Szemerédi theorem, which holds for every \(0\le f\le u\), then gives \(\Lambda_k(f)\ge c_0-c_0/2=c\). The deep inputs, the hypergraph removal lemma and the linear forms estimate for the majorant, are those of the vendored proof, used unchanged.

Let \(A\) be a set of primes and \(c_1>0\) such that \(\#(A\cap(\lfloor Z/2\rfloor,Z])\ge c_1Z/\log Z\) for infinitely many \(Z\). Then for every \(k\) the set \(A\) contains a \(k\)-term arithmetic progression: there are natural numbers \(a\) and \(d>0\) with \(a+jd\in A\) for every \(j<k\).

Proof sketch. For \(k\le2\) truncate a progression of length \(3\); so let \(k\ge3\) and \(\alpha=\alpha_k\). Put \(c_2=c_1/6\) and \(\delta=\alpha c_2/32\), fixed before \(w\). Transference for every large prime modulus gives \(w\), \(c>0\) and a threshold; put \(W=\prod_{p\le w}p\). The modulus selection gives a prime \(q=M+1\) beyond the transference threshold, the threshold of the height bound \((2\alpha\log q)^k<qc\) and \(2W+4w+16\), such that \(A\) has at least \(c_2X/\log X\) elements in \((\lfloor X/4\rfloor,X]\), \(X=W\lfloor q/8\rfloor\); these are primes, so they form the set \(S\) of the residue pigeonhole. The pigeonhole gives a reduced class \(b\) with \(\mathbb E\lambda^A\ge\frac\alpha W\#S\log(\lfloor X/4\rfloor+1)/q\), and the vendored Chebyshev arithmetic, with the constant \(\log2/4\) replaced by \(c_2\), bounds this below by \(\alpha c_2/32=\delta\). Since \(0\le\lambda^A\le\lambda\), transference gives \(\Lambda_k(\lambda^A)\ge c\). The weight is at most \(2\alpha\log q\), so the diagonal progressions (\(d=0\)) carry less than the count, and the off-diagonal mass is positive. Extraction gives the progression in \(A\).

docs.title: Szemerédi's theorem in the primes holds
docs.text:
ZInQ.greenTaoDense

Every set of primes of positive relative upper density contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length.

This is Theorem 1.2 of Green and Tao (in the weakened form of Szemerédi's theorem in the primes), proved here by extending the vendored Lean proof of the Green–Tao theorem from the set of all primes to dense subsets. No vendored file is changed: the steps that use a property of the set of all primes are redone for the subset in new files, those adapted from vendored proofs under the vendored proof's Apache License.

Proof sketch. Let \(A\) be a set of primes of positive relative upper density and \(k\) a length. The window lemma gives \(c_1>0\) with \(\#(A\cap(\lfloor Z/2\rfloor,Z])\ge c_1Z/\log Z\) for infinitely many \(Z\). Transference holds for every large prime modulus and every weight below the W-tricked prime weight, so the theorem on progressions in a set with mass in dyadic windows applies and gives a \(k\)-term progression in \(A\) with positive difference.

The proof for all primes uses three properties that a dense set lacks: Chebyshev's lower bound in the fixed window \((X/4,X]\) at every large scale, a modulus chosen freely after the density, and the progression \(2,3\) for the small lengths. They are replaced by the window lemma, the Bertrand modulus selection with transference at every large prime modulus, and truncation of a progression of length \(3\).

docs.title: The main theorem and its hypotheses
The main theorem and its hypotheses
docs.text:
Throughout, \(K_0=\mathbb Q(s)\) with \(s^2=2\), \(d=75-53s\), and \(E:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(K_0\). For a reduced fraction \(a/b\) with \(b>0\), \(h(a/b)=\log\max(|a|,b)\). In the rank hypotheses and the articles that state them, \(d\) instead denotes a positive integer and \(C_d\) the congruent number curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb Q\); the row-5b chapter writes \(n\) and \(C_n\) for these.

The target is the manuscript's Theorem 1.1, in the exact form frozen by the upstream project.

The main theorem proves the target from five hypotheses, none of them proved here: the minimal height hypothesis below (the one instance of the manuscript's Theorem 4.1 that the proof uses; not a published theorem, its proof combines refereed theorems and exact computations with new arguments, the manuscript's and this project's, reviewed only by AI models), and four statements about L-series of elliptic curves over \(\mathbb Q\), from which the certified rank hypothesis CR₃ below follows. Three of the four are textbook theorems: the positive-rank half of Gross–Zagier, the functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), with conductor \(32d^2\) and root number \(-1\), stated on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), and Hecke's continuation of \(L(C_d,s)\) to an entire function for every \(d\ne0\). No original source of Hecke's continuation was read, and the original source of the conductor and the functional equation has not been read in full. The fourth is a consequence of Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in one reading of its genus sums, reading A: for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), if \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes to order at least \(2\) at \(s=1\), two genus sums of class numbers are even. No refereed text found by the project's literature search, which AI agents carried out, states reading A explicitly; Tian–Yuan–Zhang's introductory theorem with the same parity criteria, read literally, is false; and their proof passes through their Proposition 3.4, whose proof is only sketched in the arXiv version; the journal's proof was not assessed on this point. A new argument written for this project, Proposition N, reviewed twice by AI models and never by a human, derives reading A from unambiguous results of that version; its derivation from a restatement of those results is proved here, but no proof checks that the restatement matches the paper, and only AI models have compared it with the paper, and it is supporting evidence, not a hypothesis of the main theorem. The rest of this chapter follows the manuscript's inputs and ends with the other forms of the theorem: from the minimal height hypothesis, CR₃ and the manuscript's prime pattern; from the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃ alone; and from other forms of the rank hypothesis, among them those through which the proof passes.

The manuscript proves it from six inputs. Three of them depend on deep arithmetic whose conclusions are nonetheless elementary statements. The six-contact height estimate bounds the height of a rational number by its odd contact support.

The proof uses the estimate at a single prime set and radius, \(S=S_{\rm mul}\) and \(R=D\), and the main theorem assumes only this instance.

The trust statement for H follows the manuscript's proof of the six-contact estimate up to its last step, with some steps replaced or re-sourced and several checked by no referee. Combining three of the manuscript's bounds, it gives a bound on the height of the Hauptmodul value \(J(u)=-57600F(u)^2/G(u)^6\), where \(F(u)=u(u+15)(u+20)(u+24)(u+30)(u+60)\) and \(G(u)=7u^2+300u+3600\) (the manuscript does not display that bound). This bound, at \(R=D\), is the \(j\)-form of the height hypothesis; it is not proved here and is not a published theorem. The manuscript's last step returns from \(J(u)\) to \(u\). That return is replaced here by a proved inequality, so the \(j\)-form at \(S=S_{\rm mul}\) implies the minimal height hypothesis; the target holds under the \(j\)-form together with CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk or with the three statements about L-series below.

  • The height hypothesis in its \(j\)-form

Pole completeness asserts the rational solubility of one explicit polynomial for all suitably prepared inputs. The polynomial here is the Route K one, whose curves are congruent number curves, and pole completeness is no longer assumed: the Route K chapter proves it from a narrower hypothesis, CR₃, which turns an explicit 2-Selmer certificate of a congruent number curve into a rational point.

CR₃ follows from a form stated with the 2-Selmer group itself, CR₃^Sel, because the explicit system is that Selmer group (Proposition 0). CR₃^Sel in turn follows from a hypothesis in the terms of Smith's row-5b determinant, CR₃^5b, and CR₃^5b from one in Tian, Yuan and Zhang's terms, CR₃^TYZ (the row-5b chapter); by Rédei's formula, CR₃^TYZ is equivalent to its form CR₃^TYZ_Cl with their class numbers (the Rédei chapter). Each of CR₃^Sel, CR₃^5b, CR₃^TYZ and CR₃^TYZ_Cl concludes that every Selmer class comes from a rational point; CR₃ itself concludes only that \(C_d\) has a rational point \((x,y)\) with \(x\ne0\) and \(x/a\) a square, for the one given \(a\). CR₃^Sel, CR₃^TYZ and CR₃^TYZ_Cl also have forms that conclude only that the curve has positive rank. These imply narrower hypotheses still, which ask for positive rank only on the two curves of a slot choice (the positive-rank chapter).

The generator argument uses the Mordell–Weil theorem for \(E\) over \(K_0\). It was a hypothesis until the two-isogeny descent of the model chapter proved it.

The multiplication certificate needs twenty-two simultaneous prime values of linear forms with prescribed reduction behaviour, and the size bounds need every unit class modulo the catalogue modulus to contain twenty-two primes below the explicit cutoff \(2^{W^8}\).

The multiplication proof uses the prime pattern only to write every integer as a sum of three slopes with controlled contact primes, the slope representation. A second pattern in primes, with two slopes and twelve linear forms, also gives it, so it can replace the twenty-two-prime pattern.

Neither pattern is needed any more. Route AP proves the completeness of the multiplication template, for the same polynomial, from long arithmetic progressions of good slope primes; these come from Szemerédi's theorem in the primes, proved from the Green–Tao theorem (the Green–Tao chapter), and from the positive density of the good slope primes, Proposition D.

The catalogue bound is no longer an assumption of substance: the progressions chapter proves it from an effective Dirichlet theorem. Under the remaining hypotheses (the minimal form of the height estimate, the certified rank hypothesis CR₃ and the twenty-two-prime pattern) the target holds; this is the form of the theorem closest to the manuscript's inputs. It also holds with pole completeness in place of CR₃, or with the two-slope pattern in place of the twenty-two-prime pattern.

With route AP the prime pattern drops out, and the target holds under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃ alone, or under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^Sel or CR₃^5b.

Under the minimal height hypothesis the target also holds with CR₃ replaced by CR₃^TYZ or CR₃^TYZ_Cl, by any of the positive-rank forms, by positive rank on the two curves of a slot choice (for every input of the descent, or only for the inputs of admissible numbers), or by any of the equivalent forms that ask for infinitely many rational points instead of positive rank.

The positive-rank form of CR₃^TYZ_Cl, CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk, follows from three statements about L-series: two standard theorems (the functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) with root number \(-1\), whose original source has not been read in full, stated on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), and the positive-rank half of Gross–Zagier) and Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b, which follows from the main theorem's other two L-series statements, Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A and Hecke's continuation (the literature section of the positive-rank chapter). The target holds under the minimal height hypothesis or its \(j\)-form together with those three statements, and under the \(j\)-form and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk; the first of these forms is the step through which the main theorem is proved.

19 fully proved

docs.title: The main theorem
docs.text:
ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_tyzThm35ReadingA_heckeContinuation_functionalEquation5_grossZagier

Assume the minimal height hypothesis and four statements about L-series of elliptic curves: the Gross–Zagier statement, the functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), Hecke's continuation of \(L(C_d,s)\), and Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A. Then the target statement holds: some integer polynomial in \(292{,}890{,}231{,}905\) variables, of degree below \(2\uparrow\uparrow7\) and with coefficients below \(2\uparrow\uparrow8\), has rational zero projection to its first variable exactly \(\mathbb Z\).

Here \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb Q\), for a natural number \(d\). For a Weierstrass curve \(E\) over \(\mathbb Q\), \(L(E,s)\) is its L-series, the Dirichlet series whose coefficients are those of the Euler product \(\prod_p f_p(p^{-s})^{-1}\), where \(f_p\) is the local polynomial of a minimal model of \(E\) over \(\mathbb Q_p\); its value at \(s\) is the sum of the series where it converges absolutely, and \(0\) elsewhere. An entire continuation of \(L(E,s)\) is a function \(F:\mathbb C o\mathbb C\), complex differentiable everywhere, with \(F(s)=L(E,s)\) whenever \(\operatorname{Re}s>3/2\); two entire continuations of the same \(L(E,s)\) are equal (entire continuations). The order of vanishing of an entire function at a point is its order there as an analytic function, a value in \(\{0,1,2,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}\). \(T^{ m Cl}_{5a}(d)\) and \(T^{ m Cl}_{5b}(d)\) in \(\mathbb Z/2\) are the first genus sum and the genus sum of class numbers of row 5b. The five hypotheses are:

  • the minimal height hypothesis: for every \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), \(h(u)\le H_6(D)\,M_{S_{ m mul}}(u)^{24}\), with the notation of the minimal height hypothesis;
  • the Gross–Zagier statement: for every Weierstrass curve \(E\) over \(\mathbb Q\) with nonzero discriminant and every entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(E,s)\) whose order of vanishing at \(s=1\) is exactly \(1\), \(E(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order;
  • the functional equation on the strip: for every squarefree natural number \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), every entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\) and every complex \(s\) with \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), $\(\Lambda(2-s)=-\Lambda(s),\qquad \Lambda(s)=(32d^2)^{s/2}(2\pi)^{-s}\,\Gamma(s)\,F(s),\)$ where \((32d^2)^{s/2}=e^{(s/2)\log(32d^2)}\) and \((2\pi)^{-s}=e^{-s\log2\pi}\) (conductor \(32d^2\), root number \(-1\));
  • Hecke's continuation: for every natural number \(d e0\), \(L(C_d,s)\) has an entire continuation;
  • Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A: for every squarefree natural number \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) and every entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\) whose order of vanishing at \(s=1\) is at least \(2\), \(T^{ m Cl}_{5a}(d)=0\) and \(T^{ m Cl}_{5b}(d)=0\) in \(\mathbb Z/2\).

None of the five is proved here. The Gross–Zagier statement is a textbook theorem: Gross–Zagier (1986) with an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field (Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein 1990, or Friedberg–Hoffstein 1995) and modularity (Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor 2001); Kolyvagin's conclusion that the rank is exactly one is not used. The functional equation and Hecke's continuation are textbook theorems: \(C_d\) has complex multiplication by \(\mathbb Z[i]\), so \(L(C_d,s)\) is the L-function of a Hecke character of \(\mathbb Q(i)\) (Hecke, Deuring), which is entire, with conductor \(32d^2\) for odd squarefree \(d\) and root number \(-1\) for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) (Birch–Stephens). The functional equation is stated only on the strip, where \(\Gamma(s)\) and \(\Gamma(2-s)\) are both finite, and it is used only at \(s=1\). No original source of Hecke's continuation was read, and the original source of the conductor and the functional equation has not been read in full. The minimal height hypothesis is the one instance of the manuscript's six-contact height estimate (its Theorem 4.1) that the proof uses; the proof of that estimate combines refereed theorems and exact computations with new arguments, the manuscript's and this project's, reviewed only by AI models, and it is not a published theorem.

Tian–Yuan–Zhang. The last hypothesis is a consequence of Theorem 3.5(2) of Tian, Yuan and Zhang (arXiv:1411.4728v1; Asian J. Math. 21 (2017)) for \(n=d\equiv5\pmod8\), under one reading of their genus sums, reading A: the decompositions of \(n\) are the set partitions of its primes, each counted once, with a trivial factor allowed (reading A). It is needed only when their invariant \(\mathcal L(n)\) is \(0\): they define \(\mathcal L(n)\) from \(L(C_n,1)\) or \(L'(C_n,1)\) and set it to \(0\) exactly when the order of vanishing at \(s=1\) is at least \(2\). Their printed hypothesis is a condition on their genus point \(P(n)\), followed by an "i.e." that restates it as the evenness of \(2^{- ho(n)}\mathcal L(n)\) and is not proved in the paper; when \(\mathcal L(n)=0\) the condition on \(P(n)\) follows from the first assertion of their Theorem 3.5 and their Lemma 3.18, so the "i.e." is not needed. No refereed text found by the project's literature search, which AI agents carried out, states reading A explicitly; the one statement found is in an unrefereed preprint (Smith). Their introductory theorem with the same parity criteria (Theorem 1.2 of the arXiv version, Theorem 1.4 of the journal version) requires every factor to exceed \(1\), and read that way it is false in both versions: \(d=26565\) and \(d=33117\) are counterexamples (exact class-group computations and explicit points giving rank at least \(3\), not checked here). Their proof of Theorem 3.5(2) passes through their Proposition 3.4, whose proof is only a sketch in the arXiv version; the journal's proof was not assessed on this point, and the comparison of the two versions was made by AI agents and not checked by a human. A new argument written for this project (Proposition N), reviewed twice by AI models and never by a human, derives reading A from unambiguous results of the arXiv version without that proposition. Its derivation of reading A from a restatement of those results is proved here, but no proof checks that the restatement matches the paper, and only AI models have compared it with the paper; it is supporting evidence, not a hypothesis of this theorem.

The target also holds under other hypotheses. Hecke's continuation and reading A imply Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b (proof below), so the form of the main theorem from the \(j\)-form and the L-series statements with the minimal height hypothesis, row 5b, the functional equation and the Gross–Zagier statement assumes less. The four L-series statements imply the certified rank hypothesis CR₃, so the main theorem from two hypotheses, under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃, assumes less again; CR₃ is not a statement of the literature. The main theorem from three hypotheses assumes the minimal height hypothesis, CR₃ and the manuscript's twenty-two-prime pattern.

Proof sketch. Let \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) be squarefree with \(T^{ m Cl}_{5b}(d)=1\). Then \(d e0\), so Hecke's continuation gives an entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\). If its order of vanishing at \(s=1\) were at least \(2\), reading A would give \(T^{ m Cl}_{5b}(d)=0\); so the order is at most \(1\). This is Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b (row 5b from reading A and Hecke's continuation), and the main theorem from the \(j\)-form and the L-series statements, in its form with the minimal height hypothesis, row 5b, the functional equation and the Gross–Zagier statement, gives the target.

That form is proved as follows. Taking \(s=1\), which lies in the strip, the functional equation gives \(\Lambda(1)=-\Lambda(1)\), so \(\Lambda(1)=0\); since \(\Gamma(1)=1\) and the two powers are nonzero, every entire continuation of \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes at \(s=1\) (vanishing at the centre). With row 5b the order of vanishing is exactly \(1\) (analytic rank one). The discriminant of \(C_d\) is \(64d^6 e0\), so the Gross–Zagier statement gives a point of infinite order on \(C_d\). This is the positive-rank class-number hypothesis CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk (its derivation), and the form of the main theorem from the positive-rank forms with the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk applies. Its proof passes to CR₃: when \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\), a point of infinite order puts a rational point in every 2-Selmer class (RK9, with Mordell–Weil for \(C_d\)), so CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk gives CR₃^TYZ_Cl; Rédei's formula turns it into CR₃^TYZ; Theorem 3.6 gives CR₃^5b; Corollary 4.4 gives CR₃^Sel; Proposition 0 gives CR₃. Finally the main theorem from two hypotheses applies to the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃: route AP gives the completeness of the multiplication template, and CR₃ gives pole completeness.

docs.title: The six-contact height estimate
docs.text:
ZInQ.SixContactEstimate

Let \(\mathcal C=\{0,-15,-20,-24,-30,-60\}\). For a finite set \(S\) of primes containing every prime at most \(324\) and \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), let \(M_S(u)\) be the product of the primes \(p\notin S\) for which \(v_p(u-c)\) is positive and odd for some \(c\in\mathcal C\). Put \(F_0=324!\), \(D=F_0\,3^{256F_0^4}\), \(G_0=116064000000\), \(E_0=10(DG_0)^2\), \(Q_R=R^{RE_0}\), \(B_{\rm cm}=D^2\,3^{21000D^2}+1\), \(C_{\rm cm}=2B_{\rm cm}+4096(1028+5D+84000D^2)\) and \(H_6(S;R)=2\cdot10^{13}\max(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_R^{17})\).

The six-contact estimate is the assertion that for every such \(S\), every real \(R\ge\max(D,\max S,10^{12})\) and every \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), $\(h(u)\le H_6(S;R)\,M_S(u)^{24}.\)$

Its proof needs Shimura curves, modularity and Arakelov geometry; here it is a hypothesis of the main theorem.

docs.title: The minimal height hypothesis
docs.text:
ZInQ.SixContactMin

Let \(\mathcal C\), \(h\), \(M_S\), \(D\), \(E_0\) and \(C_{\rm cm}\) be as in the six-contact height estimate, and put $\(H_6(D)=2\cdot10^{13}\max\bigl(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_D^{17}\bigr),\qquad Q_D=D^{DE_0}.\)$ Let \(S_{\rm mul}=S_{\rm ht}\cup\mathcal H\cup\{p\text{ prime}:p\mid c_*\}\) be the prime set of the multiplication certificate: \(S_{\rm ht}\) is the set of primes at most \(324\), \(\mathcal H\) is the prime catalogue (the first twenty-two primes greater than \(324\) in each unit class modulo \(W=4P_s\)), and \(c_*=4M_0\), where \(M_0\) is the least formal multiple of \(N_s\).

The minimal height hypothesis is the assertion that for every \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), $\(h(u)\le H_6(D)\,M_{S_{\rm mul}}(u)^{24}.\)$

This is the instance \(S=S_{\rm mul}\), \(R=D\) of the six-contact estimate, and it is the only form of that estimate the proof of the main theorem uses: the precision bound of the value relation needs it at \(S_{\rm ht}\subseteq S_{\rm mul}\), where \(M_{S_{\rm mul}}(u)\) divides \(M_{S_{\rm ht}}(u)\), and the finite box of multiplication soundness needs it at \(S_{\rm mul}\). The constant \(H_6(D)\) is the precision constant \(A^{(0)}_{\rm ht}\). Here it is a hypothesis of the main theorem.

Every prime of \(S_{\rm mul}\) is at most \(D\). Consequently the six-contact height estimate implies the minimal height hypothesis: for every \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), \(h(u)\le H_6(D)\,M_{S_{\rm mul}}(u)^{24}\).

Proof sketch. Every \(p\in S_{\rm mul}\) satisfies \(p\le R=\max(D,H_{\max},c_*,10^{12})\), and \(R=D\) because the catalogue bound holds; so \(\max S_{\rm mul}\le D\). Also \(D\ge324!>10^{12}\). The set \(S_{\rm mul}\) is a finite set of primes containing every prime at most \(324\), and \(R=D\) satisfies \(R\ge\max(D,\max S_{\rm mul},10^{12})\), so the six-contact estimate applies with \(S=S_{\rm mul}\) and \(R=D\). Its constant \(H_6(S_{\rm mul};D)\) is \(H_6(D)\), and its conclusion is the minimal height hypothesis.

For \(B\in\mathbb Q\) and witnesses \(b_0,\ldots,b_5,e,z,r_1,r_2,w\in\mathbb Q\) put \(m=(1-2b_0)(1+b_1)(1+2b_2)(1+4b_3)(1+6b_4)(1+12b_5)\), \(A=mB\), \(H=A(A-B^2)\), \(T_1=A(A-e)(A+e)\), \(T_2=A(Az^2-eH)(Az^2+eH)\) and $\(Q_{\rm pole}=B\Bigl(\sum_{i=0}^5(b_i^2-b_i)^2+(eHzw-1)^2+(r_1^2-T_1)^2+(r_2^2-T_2)^2\Bigr).\)$ Write \(\Phi(B)\) when \(Q_{\rm pole}\) has a rational zero with input \(B\). For \(B\ne0\) a zero puts \((A,r_1)\) on the congruent number curve \(y^2=x(x-e)(x+e)\) and \((Az^2,zr_2)\) on \(y^2=x(x-eH)(x+eH)\).

Pole completeness is the assertion that every rational \(B\) with square reduced denominator, \(0<B<1/2\) and \(v_p(B)\ge4\) for every \(p\in S_0=\{2,3,5,7,13\}\) satisfies \(\Phi(B)\).

This is the pole polynomial of Route K, with the curves \(y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+\ell)\); the manuscript's \(Q_{\rm pole}\) has the factors \(A+3e\) and \(Az^2+3eH\) (the curves \(y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+3\ell)\)) and derives pole completeness from its restricted converse theorem by a simultaneous descent. Here pole completeness is no longer a hypothesis of the main theorem: it is proved from the certified rank hypothesis CR₃ (pole completeness from the certified rank hypothesis), and also from positive rank on the two congruent number curves of a slot choice, CR₃^DL,Rk (pole completeness from CR₃^DL,Rk).

docs.title: The certified rank hypothesis
docs.text:
ZInQ.CertifiedRank

For an integer \(d\) let \(C_d\) be the congruent number curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\). The certified rank hypothesis CR₃ is the following assertion. Let \(d\) be a squarefree positive integer with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), and let \(a\) be a squarefree integer dividing \(d\) with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\). Suppose that the Selmer system \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) of the configuration of \(d\) has exactly \(8\) solutions and that one of them has first coordinate the class of \(a\), that is \(a_0=[a<0]\), \(a_1=0\) and \(u_p=[p\mid a]\) for the primes \(p\mid d\). Then \(C_d\) has a rational point \((x,y)\) with \(x e0\) and \(x/a\) a square in \(\mathbb Q\).

CR₃ is a statement about Legendre symbols and rational points only; no Selmer group enters it. It rests on the following theorems. Proposition 0 is proved (Proposition 0), so CR₃ follows from its Selmer form (CR₃ from its Selmer form). So are the elementary steps of route (i), namely the rule of row 5b (Theorem 4.3) with Corollary 4.4, the identity of the row-5b determinant with the genus sum (Theorem 3.6) and Rédei's formula, and so is the last step below, from positive rank to every Selmer class (RK9, with Mordell–Weil for \(C_d\)). The analytic and rank theorems are not proved here.

  • Proposition 0 (descent-alt §4.1; its place-2 rows for \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) are rechecked in slot-k §2.1) identifies the solutions of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) with the 2-Selmer group \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\), so the hypotheses say that \(\dim\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)=3\) and that \(a\) is a first Kummer coordinate of \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\).
  • Positive rank, by route (i). For \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) with \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\) and a first coordinate with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\), the shape CR₃ assumes, an elementary computation (the row-5b determinant of Smith's Monsky matrices, reproved in tyz-5b §§2–4) shows that the genus sum \(T_{5b}(d)\) of Tian, Yuan and Zhang is odd. Their Theorem 3.5 and the argument of the proof of their Theorem 3.5(2), as completed in nt-tyz §4 by Proposition N, then give that \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes to order exactly one at \(s=1\). Gross–Zagier, applied over an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field \(K\) that satisfies the Heegner hypothesis and has \(L(C_d^K,1) e0\) (Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein), then gives \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\ge1\); \(C_d\) is modular because it has complex multiplication by \(\mathbb Z[i]\). Tian–Yuan–Zhang and Gross–Zagier are published. The form of TYZ used is the one their proof gives, which rests on their Proposition 3.4, whose proof is a sketch; Proposition N replaces that step by a direct parity count, and it is not refereed.
  • Route (ii), an alternative that is not needed: Kriz's 2-converse theorem (Theorems 10.13 and 10.17(2), an unrefereed preprint) with the corank lemma (the Cassels–Tate pairing on \(Ш(C_d)/Ш(C_d)_{ m div}\) is nondegenerate and alternating, so \(\dim(Ш/Ш_{ m div})[2]\) is even; no finiteness of \(Ш\) is assumed) gives \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)=1\) and \(Ш(C_d)[2]=0\).
  • Then \(\dim C_d(\mathbb Q)/2C_d(\mathbb Q)=2+\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is at least \(3=\dim\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\), so the Kummer map is onto \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) (RK9) and the class \(a\) comes from a point \(P\), which may be taken of infinite order (replace \(P\) by \(P+2Q\)). The torsion classes are \(1,-1,d,-d\), which \(a\) is not since \(|a|\equiv7\) and \(d\equiv5\pmod8\). A point of infinite order has \(x otin\{0,\pm d\}\), so its first Kummer coordinate is the class of \(x\): \(x\in a\mathbb Q^{*2}\).

The congruences \(d\equiv5\), \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\) are exactly what the descent lemma produces, so CR₃ is as narrow as the proof allows short of naming the configurations of the slot construction. A form that names them, with positive rank as its conclusion, is CR₃^DL,Rk; it follows from the positive-rank forms CR₃^Rk and CR₃^TYZ,Rk, and the main theorem also holds under it and under the positive-rank forms of the hypothesis (the positive-rank chapter). CR₃ is not proved here; it is a hypothesis of the main theorem from three hypotheses and of the main theorem from two hypotheses, while the main theorem derives it from four statements about L-series. It implies pole completeness for the pole polynomial with the curves \(x+\ell\).

docs.title: The twenty-two-prime pattern
docs.text:
ZInQ.FixedPrimePattern

Let \(P_s\) be the product of the primes at most \(324\) and \(W=4P_s\). Let \(\mathcal H\) consist of the first twenty-two primes greater than \(324\) in each unit residue class modulo \(W\), and \(\mathcal K=\{dh: d\mid P_s^4,\ d>0,\ h\in\mathcal H\}\). Call a prime \(p\) good if it splits in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\), both reductions of \(E\) at the places above \(p\) are good, and their orders \(d_1,d_2\) satisfy \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=4\) and \(p\nmid d_1d_2\).

The pattern assertion is that for every \(A\in\mathbb Z\) and every real \(B_0\) there are integers \(u_1,u_2,v\) with \(v\ne0\) such that, with \(u_3=Av-u_1-u_2\), each of the twenty-two values $\(v,\qquad u_j-bv\quad(1\le j\le3,\ b\in\{0,-15,-20,-24,-30,-60,1\})\)$ equals \(\epsilon kp\) with \(\epsilon=\pm1\), \(k\in\mathcal K\) and \(p>B_0\) a good prime.

The manuscript proves it with the Green–Tao asymptotic for linear equations in primes. Here it is a hypothesis of the three-hypothesis form of the main theorem only, and it is no longer needed: route AP changes the completeness proof of the multiplication template, not the polynomial, so that it needs only arithmetic progressions of good slope primes (the statement 22P_AP), and these follow from Szemerédi's theorem in the primes and Proposition D, both proved (the main theorem from two hypotheses).

docs.title: The catalogue bound
docs.text:
ZInQ.CatalogueBound8 ZInQ.CatalogueBound

With \(W=4P_s\) as in the prime pattern, every unit residue class modulo \(W\) contains at least twenty-two primes \(p\) with \(324<p<2^{W^8}\).

The manuscript deduces the same statement with the smaller cutoff \(2^{W^3}\) from the explicit progression estimate of Bennett, Martin, O'Bryant and Rechnitzer. Here the cutoff is \(2^{W^8}\), the range of the effective Dirichlet theorem of the progressions chapter, which proves the statement; the size bounds use it only through this cutoff.

docs.title: The two-slope prime pattern
docs.text:
ZInQ.TwoSlopePattern ZInQ.GoodSlopePrime

Let \(\mathcal C=\{0,-15,-20,-24,-30,-60\}\), let \(\mathcal H\) be the prime catalogue of the twenty-two-prime pattern (the first twenty-two primes greater than \(324\) in each unit residue class modulo \(W=4P_s\)), and \(E:y^2=x^3-(75-53\sqrt2)^2x\). Call a prime \(p\) a good slope prime if there is \(r\in\mathbb Z/p\) with \(r^2=2\), \(75-53r e0\) and \(75+53r e0\) in \(\mathbb Z/p\), and the numbers \(d_1,d_2\) of points, the point at infinity included, of \(y^2=x^3-(75-53r)^2x\) and \(y^2=x^3-(75+53r)^2x\) over \(\mathbb Z/p\) satisfy \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=4\). For odd \(p\) this says that \(p\) splits in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\), that both reductions of \(E\) at the places above \(p\) are good, and that their orders satisfy \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=4\): the good primes of the twenty-two-prime pattern without the condition \(p mid d_1d_2\).

The two-slope pattern is the assertion that for every \(A\in\mathbb Z\) there are integers \(u,v\) with \(v e0\) such that

  1. for each \(c\in\mathcal C\), the absolute values of the twelve numbers \(u-cv\) and \(u-(A+10-c)v\) are good slope primes greater than \(324\) and outside \(\mathcal H\);
  2. each of \(v\), \(u-v\) and \(u-(A+9)v\) has \(q\)-adic valuation at most \(4\) at every prime \(q\le324\) and at most \(1\) at every \(q\in\mathcal H\).

(The three numbers in 2 are nonzero: \(u=v\) would make \(u+15v=16v\) prime, and \(u=(A+9)v\) would make \(u-(A+25)v=-16v\) prime.) In other words, a homothetic copy \(u-v\cdot(\mathcal C\cup(A+10-\mathcal C))\) of a twelve-point set lies in the good slope primes, with the common difference \(v\) and the numerators of \(t-1\) controlled at the old primes. The proof uses it through the three slopes \(u/v\), \(A+10-u/v\) and \(-10\), which sum to \(A\).

This is a different linear pattern in primes from the twenty-two-prime pattern, not a consequence of it. Its expected proof is the argument of Proposition 6.2 with two variables and twelve linear forms: the Green–Tao–Ziegler theory of linear equations in primes (the Green–Tao asymptotic, the Möbius–nilsequences theorem and the inverse theorem for the Gowers norms), as for the twenty-two-prime pattern. It is not proved here; the main theorem holds with it in place of the twenty-two-prime pattern.

Assume the minimal height hypothesis, the certified rank hypothesis CR₃ and the twenty-two-prime pattern. Then the target statement holds: some integer polynomial in \(292{,}890{,}231{,}905\) variables, of degree below \(2\uparrow\uparrow7\) and with coefficients below \(2\uparrow\uparrow8\), has rational zero projection to its first variable exactly \(\mathbb Z\).

The minimal height hypothesis is the one instance \(S=S_{\rm mul}\), \(R=D\) of the six-contact height estimate that the proof uses, so the theorem holds in particular under the six-contact estimate itself (the six-contact estimate implies its minimal form). CR₃ enters only through pole completeness, which it implies for the Route K pole polynomial (pole completeness from the certified rank hypothesis); so the theorem also holds under pole completeness in place of CR₃. The twenty-two-prime pattern enters only through the slope representation; since the two-slope pattern also gives the slope representation, the theorem holds under the two-slope pattern in place of the twenty-two-prime pattern. The manuscript's fourth input, the catalogue bound, is replaced by a theorem with a larger cutoff (the catalogue bound holds): every unit class modulo \(W\) contains twenty-two primes \(p\) with \(324<p<2^{W^8}\), by an effective Dirichlet theorem, where the manuscript has the cutoff \(2^{W^3}\). The bound on the addition and multiplication nodes of the universal halting circuit, and the circuit's exact node statistics, are finite checks proved in the compiler chapter; the theorem holds as well with either one added as a hypothesis.

The twenty-two-prime pattern is not needed at all: route AP proves the completeness of the multiplication template from long progressions of good slope primes, which Szemerédi's theorem in the primes and Proposition D supply, so the target holds under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃ alone (the main theorem from two hypotheses). The present form, which keeps the manuscript's prime pattern, uses none of that material. The main theorem replaces CR₃ by four statements about L-series from which CR₃ follows, and does without the pattern.

Assume the minimal height hypothesis and the certified rank hypothesis CR₃. Then the target statement holds: some integer polynomial in \(292{,}890{,}231{,}905\) variables, of degree below \(2\uparrow\uparrow7\) and with coefficients below \(2\uparrow\uparrow8\), has rational zero projection to its first variable exactly \(\mathbb Z\).

The polynomial is the same as in the main theorem from three hypotheses; only the proof of the completeness of its multiplication template changes. The twenty-two-prime pattern is not assumed: route AP proves completeness from long arithmetic progressions of good slope primes (the statement 22P_AP), and 22P_AP follows from Szemerédi's theorem in the primes and Proposition D, both proved. On the way the theorem holds under each set of hypotheses (i) the minimal height hypothesis, CR₃ and 22P_AP; (ii) the minimal height hypothesis, CR₃, Szemerédi's theorem in the primes and the positive relative upper density of the good slope primes; (iii) the minimal height hypothesis, CR₃ and that density statement alone.

Proof sketch. Under 22P_AP, Proposition AP writes every integer as a sum of three slopes satisfying the weakened condition 2′, and the completeness of the multiplication template under the weakened slope representation (with Lemma P absorbing a pole at an old prime) replaces the completeness step of the assembly lemma; pole completeness comes from CR₃ (pole completeness from the certified rank hypothesis). This gives (i). The dense form of Green–Tao and the density statement give 22P_AP, which gives (ii); Szemerédi's theorem in the primes is proved, which gives (iii); Proposition D proves the density statement, which gives the theorem.

Assume the minimal height hypothesis and the Selmer form CR₃^Sel of the certified rank hypothesis. Then the target statement holds.

CR₃^Sel speaks of the 2-Selmer group of the congruent number curve, defined by local solubility of its 2-coverings, instead of the explicit linear system in Legendre symbols, and asks that every Selmer class come from a rational point. The theorem also holds under the minimal height hypothesis, CR₃^Sel and the twenty-two-prime pattern; under the minimal height hypothesis, CR₃^Sel, Szemerédi's theorem in the primes and the positive relative upper density of the good slope primes; and under the minimal height hypothesis, CR₃^Sel and that density statement.
