docs.text:
ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankTYZ ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankTYZCl

Assume the minimal height hypothesis and the Tian–Yuan–Zhang form CR₃^TYZ of the certified rank hypothesis. Then the target statement holds. The theorem also holds under the minimal height hypothesis and the class-number form CR₃^TYZ_Cl.

CR₃^TYZ asks, for every squarefree positive \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) with \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\) and odd genus sum \(T_{5b}(d)\) of row 5b, that every 2-Selmer class of \(C_d\) come from a rational point. Here \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\). It differs from the row-5b form CR₃^5b only in that the condition \(\det M_{5b}=1\) is replaced by \(T_{5b}(d)=1\). CR₃^TYZ_Cl is the same assertion with the genus sum \(T^{\mathrm{Cl}}_{5b}(d)=\sum_\pi\prod_{B\in\pi}\#2\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d_B}))\bmod 2\) of Tian, Yuan and Zhang's genus class numbers in place of \(T_{5b}(d)\), the sum running, as for \(T_{5b}(d)\), over the set partitions \(\pi\) of the primes of \(d\) with one block \(d_B\equiv7\), one block \(d_B\equiv3\) and all others \(d_B\equiv1\pmod8\).

Proof sketch. By Theorem 3.6, \(\det M_{5b}=T_{5b}(d)\) for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), so CR₃^TYZ implies CR₃^5b; CR₃^5b implies CR₃^Sel by Corollary 4.4; then apply the main theorem from the Selmer form of the rank hypothesis in its form with the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^Sel alone. For the second form, Rédei's formula, which is proved, gives \(T^{\mathrm{Cl}}_{5b}(d)=T_{5b}(d)\) for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), so CR₃^TYZ_Cl is equivalent to CR₃^TYZ, and the first form applies.

docs.text:
ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankRk ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankTYZRk ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankTYZClRk

Assume the minimal height hypothesis and the positive-rank form CR₃^Rk of the certified rank hypothesis. Then the target statement holds. The theorem also holds under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^TYZ,Rk, and under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk.

Here \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\). Each of these hypotheses concludes only that \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order, which is what the published theorems give:

  • CR₃^Rk: for squarefree positive \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), if \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\) and some \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\), then \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order;
  • CR₃^TYZ,Rk: for squarefree positive \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) with odd genus sum \(T_{5b}(d)\) of row 5b, \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order;
  • CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk: the same with the genus sum of class numbers \(T^{\mathrm{Cl}}_{5b}(d)\) odd.

No condition on the Selmer group enters the last two. Since CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk implies CR₃^TYZ,Rk and CR₃^TYZ,Rk implies CR₃^Rk, the form with CR₃^Rk assumes the least of the three.

Proof sketch. Mordell–Weil for the congruent number curves holds, so each positive-rank form gives the matching form whose conclusion is that every 2-Selmer class of \(C_d\) comes from a rational point: a point of infinite order and a Selmer group of order \(8\) give every Selmer class (RK9). Thus CR₃^Rk gives CR₃^Sel, and the main theorem from the Selmer form of the rank hypothesis applies in its form with the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^Sel alone. Likewise CR₃^TYZ,Rk gives CR₃^TYZ and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk gives CR₃^TYZ_Cl, and the main theorem from the Tian–Yuan–Zhang forms applies in its two forms.

docs.title: The main theorem from positive rank on the two curves of a slot choice
docs.text:
ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankDLRk ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankDLAdmRk

Assume the minimal height hypothesis and the hypothesis CR₃^DL,Rk. Then the target statement holds.

CR₃^DL,Rk is the following assertion. Let \(\beta,\theta\) be integers and \(p_0\) a prime dividing \(\beta\) such that \(\beta\) is odd and squarefree with \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\); \(\theta>0\) is squarefree with \(\theta\equiv1\pmod8\); \(\beta\) and \(\theta\) are coprime; \([\beta/\ell]=0\) for every prime \(\ell\mid\theta\); and \([\theta/p]=0\) for every prime \(p\mid\beta\). Then there are slot data \(q_0\), \(r_p\) (\(p\in P(\beta)\setminus\{p_0\}\)) and \(r_\ell\) (\(\ell\in P(\theta)\)) for \(\beta,\theta,p_0\), satisfying the slot conditions, such that, with $\(d_1=|\beta|\,q_0\prod_pr_p\prod_\ell r_\ell,\)$ both \(C_{d_1}(\mathbb Q)\) and \(C_{d_1\theta}(\mathbb Q)\) have a point of infinite order. Here \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\). These are the two curves at which the proof of pole completeness uses the rank hypothesis. CR₃^DL,Rk follows from CR₃^Rk and from CR₃^TYZ,Rk, so this form assumes no more than the main theorem from the positive-rank forms.

The theorem also holds under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk, which asks only that for every admissible \(B\) there be a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) with \(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\) odd and \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), a prime \(p_0\mid\beta\) and slot data whose two curves have points of infinite order; CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk follows from CR₃^DL,Rk.

Proof sketch. The proof does not pass through CR₃.

  1. CR₃^DL,Rk implies pole completeness. For an admissible input, the multiplier lemma and the properties (θ1)–(θ4) give slot inputs \(\beta,\theta,p_0\), and CR₃^DL,Rk gives slot data whose two curves have positive rank. On each curve the Selmer certificate of the realization gives, by Proposition 0, a Selmer group of order \(8\) containing a class \((\beta,b)\); with the point of infinite order and Mordell–Weil, RK9 makes that class come from a rational point \((x,y)\) with \(x/\beta\) a square, and the two points give a zero of the pole polynomial. Under CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk, which supplies for each admissible input a multiplier, a prime \(p_0\) and slot data whose two curves have points of infinite order, the same argument at those curves gives pole completeness directly.
  2. Szemerédi's theorem in the primes and Proposition D give 22P_AP, and Proposition AP turns 22P_AP into the slope representation under field 2′.
  3. The bound on the addition and multiplication nodes of the universal halting circuit holds.
  4. The assembly lemma under field 2′, applied to the minimal height hypothesis and steps 1–3, gives the target.

docs.text:
ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankInf ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankTYZInf ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankTYZClInf ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_certifiedRankDLInf

Assume the minimal height hypothesis and the hypothesis CR₃^Inf. Then the target statement holds, as in the main theorem from three hypotheses. The theorem also holds under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^TYZ,Inf, under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Inf, and under the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^DL,Inf.

Each of these hypotheses concludes only that certain equations \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) have infinitely many rational solutions, a statement that mentions no group law:

  • CR₃^Inf: for squarefree positive \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), if \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\) and some \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\), then \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions;
  • CR₃^TYZ,Inf: for squarefree positive \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) with odd genus sum \(T_{5b}(d)\) of row 5b, \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions;
  • CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Inf: the same with the genus sum of class numbers \(T^{\mathrm{Cl}}_{5b}(d)\) odd;
  • CR₃^DL,Inf: for all \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfying the hypotheses of the realization, some choice of slot data gives \(d_1\) such that both \(y^2=x^3-d_1^2x\) and \(y^2=x^3-(d_1|\theta|)^2x\) have infinitely many rational solutions.

Here \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\), whose 2-Selmer group enters the premises of CR₃^Inf.

Proof sketch. Each hypothesis is equivalent to its positive-rank form: CR₃^Inf to CR₃^Rk, CR₃^TYZ,Inf to CR₃^TYZ,Rk, CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Inf to CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk, and CR₃^DL,Inf to CR₃^DL,Rk. The first three cases then follow from the main theorem from the positive-rank forms, and the last from the main theorem from positive rank on the two curves of a slot choice.

docs.title: The main theorem from the \(j\)-form and the L-series statements
docs.text:
ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_sixContactMin_tyzRow5b_functionalEquation5_grossZagier ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_jHeightBound_certifiedRankTYZClRk ZInQ.exists_bounded_integer_polynomial_defining_integers_of_jHeightBound_tyzRow5b_functionalEquation5_grossZagier

The target statement holds under each of the following three sets of hypotheses:

  1. the minimal height hypothesis, Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b, the functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), and the Gross–Zagier statement;
  2. the \(j\)-form of the height hypothesis at \(S=S_{\rm mul}\) and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk;
  3. the \(j\)-form of the height hypothesis at \(S=S_{\rm mul}\), Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b, the functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), and the Gross–Zagier statement.

Here \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\), and an entire continuation of the L-series \(L(E,s)\) of a Weierstrass curve \(E\) over \(\mathbb Q\) is a function \(F:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\), complex differentiable everywhere, with \(F(s)=L(E,s)\) for \(\operatorname{Re}s>3/2\). The hypotheses are:

  • Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b: for every squarefree natural number \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) whose genus sum of class numbers \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)\) is \(1\) in \(\mathbb Z/2\), \(L(C_d,s)\) has an entire continuation whose order of vanishing at \(s=1\) is at most \(1\);
  • the functional equation on the strip: for every squarefree natural number \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), every entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\) and every complex \(s\) with \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), \(\Lambda(2-s)=-\Lambda(s)\), where \(\Lambda(s)=(32d^2)^{s/2}(2\pi)^{-s}\Gamma(s)F(s)\) (conductor \(32d^2\), root number \(-1\));
  • the Gross–Zagier statement: for every elliptic curve \(E\) over \(\mathbb Q\) (a Weierstrass equation with nonzero discriminant) and every entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(E,s)\) with order of vanishing exactly \(1\) at \(s=1\), \(E(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order;
  • CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk: for every squarefree natural number \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) with \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=1\), \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order;
  • the \(j\)-form at \(S_{\rm mul}\): for every \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), $\(h(J(u))\le(40\cdot10^4\cdot2^{24}+22)\,\max\bigl(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_D^{17}\bigr)\,M_{S_{\rm mul}}(u)^{24},\)$ where \(J\) is the Hauptmodul value, and \(\mathcal C\), \(h\), \(C_{\rm cm}\), \(Q_D\), \(S_{\rm mul}\) and \(M_S(u)\) are as in the minimal height hypothesis and the \(j\)-form of the height hypothesis.

The functional equation (Hecke and Deuring, with root number \(-1\) for \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) by Birch–Stephens) and Gross–Zagier (with an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field and modularity) follow from textbook theorems; no original source of Hecke's continuation was read, and the original source of the conductor and the functional equation has not been read in full. Row 5b is Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) for \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) in reading A, in contrapositive form and for the row \((7,3)\) only, with Hecke's continuation for the existence of the continuation (row 5b from reading A and Hecke's continuation). The main theorem replaces row 5b by reading A and Hecke's continuation, from which row 5b follows, and its proof goes through the first form here. No refereed text found by the project's literature search, which AI agents carried out, states reading A explicitly; the one statement found is in an unrefereed preprint. Tian, Yuan and Zhang's introductory theorem with the same parity criteria (Theorem 1.2 of the arXiv version, Theorem 1.4 of the journal version) requires every factor to exceed \(1\), and read that way it is false in both versions; their proof of Theorem 3.5(2) passes through a proposition whose proof is only a sketch in the arXiv version, and the journal's proof was not assessed on this point. The comparison of the two versions was made by AI agents, not checked by a human, and Tian's expository accounts were not read. A proof written for this project (Proposition N), with two automated reviews and no human review, derives reading A from their unambiguous statements. The \(j\)-form is the bound that the project's trust statement for the manuscript's proof of the six-contact estimate gives before its last step. That statement follows the manuscript's argument, replaces some of its steps with arguments written for this project and one with an argument from another version of the manuscript, and combines three of its bounds into one that the manuscript does not display; many of its steps, including all of the manuscript's new arguments, have had only automated reviews. It is not a published theorem. None of these hypotheses is proved here.

Proof sketch. Taking \(s=1\) in the functional equation gives vanishing at the centre: every entire continuation of \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes at \(1\). For squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) with \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=1\), row 5b gives an entire continuation of order at most \(1\) at \(s=1\), and since it vanishes there its order is exactly \(1\). As \(d\ne0\), \(C_d\) is an elliptic curve, so the Gross–Zagier statement gives a point of infinite order: this is CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk. The \(j\)-form at \(S_{\rm mul}\) implies the minimal height hypothesis, through \(12h(u)\le h(J(u))+450\) for \(u\notin\mathcal C\); since \(\max(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_D^{17})\,M_{S_{\rm mul}}(u)^{24}\ge1\), the constant \(450\) is absorbed, and \((40\cdot10^4\cdot2^{24}+22+450)/12\le2\cdot10^{13}\) gives the bound \(H_6(D)\,M_{S_{\rm mul}}(u)^{24}\). In each of the three cases this yields the minimal height hypothesis and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk, and the third form of the main theorem from the positive-rank forms applies.

docs.title: The height hypothesis in its j-form
The height hypothesis in its \(j\)-form
docs.text:
The proof of the six-contact estimate passes through the Hauptmodul value $\(J(u)=-57600\,\frac{F(u)^2}{G(u)^6},\qquad F(u)=u(u+15)(u+20)(u+24)(u+30)(u+60),\quad G(u)=7u^2+300u+3600.\)$ For \(j=J(u)\), the manuscript bounds \(h(j)\) through the projective height \(h([z_m])\) of the even theta constants of an abelian surface \(A\) and the Faltings height \(h_F(A)\). Combining three of its bounds, \(h(j)\le40h([z_m])+22\), \(h([z_m])\le10^4\cdot2^{24}\max(1,h_F(A))\) and \(\max(1,h_F(A))\le\max(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_R^{17})M_S(u)^{24}\), gives, for \(S\) and \(R\) as in the six-contact estimate, $\(h(J(u))\le(40\cdot10^4\cdot2^{24}+22)\max(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_R^{17})\,M_S(u)^{24}.\)$ The manuscript does not display this combined bound; it returns from \(J(u)\) to \(u\) by the rational-root theorem. This section proves the return as a different inequality, \(12h(u)\le h(J(u))+450\) for \(u\notin\mathcal C\), from two explicit polynomial identities that bound the cancellation in \(J(u)\); it replaces the manuscript's rational-root step.

The \(j\)-form of the height hypothesis is the bound on \(h(J(u))\) above at \(R=D\), stated for every \(S\). It is not proved here and it is not a published theorem. It is what the argument of the six-contact estimate gives before its last step, in the form of the trust statement for H: the manuscript's steps, with the integral model and the CM case replaced, the finiteness of a twist proved by an argument from another version of the manuscript, the theta expression for \(j\) given other published sources together with computations, and several steps checked by no referee. That argument supports the \(j\)-form at \(S=S_{\rm mul}\), the set the main theorems use. At \(S=S_{\rm mul}\) the \(j\)-form implies the minimal height hypothesis (the \(j\)-form implies the minimal height hypothesis).

Notation (\(\mathcal C\), \(M_S\), \(D\), \(E_0\), \(Q_R\), \(C_{\rm cm}\)) is as in the six-contact height estimate, and \(h(a/b)=\log\max(|a|,b)\) for a reduced fraction \(a/b\) with \(b>0\).

6 fully proved

docs.text:

Let \(\mathcal C\), \(D\), \(E_0\), \(Q_R=R^{RE_0}\) and \(C_{\rm cm}\) be as in the six-contact height estimate, for a reduced fraction \(a/b\) with \(b>0\) let \(h(a/b)=\log\max(|a|,b)\), and let \(J\) be the Hauptmodul value. For real \(R\) put $\(X(R)=\max\bigl(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_R^{17}\bigr).\)$ For a finite set \(S\) of natural numbers and \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), \(M_S(u)\) is the product of the primes \(p\notin S\) for which \(v_p(u-c)\) is positive and odd for some \(c\in\mathcal C\) (as in the six-contact estimate, now for any such \(S\)).

For a finite set \(S\) of natural numbers, the \(j\)-form of the height hypothesis at \(S\) is the assertion that for every \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), $\(h(J(u))\le(40\cdot10^4\cdot2^{24}+22)\,X(D)\,M_S(u)^{24}.\)$

The main theorems use it at \(S=S_{\rm mul}\).

The constant comes from combining three bounds of the manuscript's proof of the six-contact estimate, for \(j=J(u)\), the projective height \(h([z_m])\) of the even theta constants of an abelian surface \(A\) and its Faltings height \(h_F(A)\): \(h(j)\le40h([z_m])+22\), \(h([z_m])\le10^4\cdot2^{24}\max(1,h_F(A))\) and \(\max(1,h_F(A))\le X(R)\,M_S(u)^{24}\), using \(\max(1,h_F(A))\ge1\); the \(j\)-form takes this at \(R=D\). The manuscript does not display the combination. It proves the bound on \(\max(1,h_F(A))\) only for \(S\) containing every prime at most \(324\) and \(R\ge\max(D,\max S,10^{12})\). So the combination gives the \(j\)-form at \(R=D\) only for such \(S\) with \(\max S\le D\), among them \(S=S_{\rm mul}\) (every prime of \(S_{\rm mul}\) is at most \(D\)), the only set the main theorems use.

The \(j\)-form is not a published theorem; it rests on the steps of the trust statement for H before the last one, some of which replace or re-source the manuscript's steps and some of which no referee has checked. At \(S=S_{\rm mul}\) it implies the minimal height hypothesis (proved here). Here it is a hypothesis of two variants of the main theorem (the main theorem from the \(j\)-form and the L-series statements).

docs.text: Two polynomial identities express \(3a^7\) and \(2^{10}3^85^6\,b^7\) as combinations of the binary forms \(F_h(a,b)\) and \(G_h(a,b)\). Let \(F_h\) and \(G_h\) be the binary forms of the Hauptmodul value. For all integers \(a,b\), $\(3a^7=(-200a-4800b)F_h(a,b)+(29a^5+3700a^4b+164400a^3b^2+2880000a^2b^3+17280000ab^4)\,G_h(a,b),\)$ $\(104976000000\,b^7=(-1001a-37650b)F_h(a,b)+(143a^5+20557a^4b+1026600a^3b^2+20691900a^2b^3+133110000ab^4+29160000b^5)\,G_h(a,b),\)$ where \(104976000000=2^{10}3^85^6\). Put $\(C_0=(57600\cdot3^7)(57600\cdot104976000000^7)=57600^2\cdot3^7\cdot(2^{10}3^85^6)^7.\)$ If \(a,b\) are coprime integers and an integer \(c\) divides both \(57600F_h(a,b)^2\) and \(G_h(a,b)^6\), then \(c\mid C_0\).

Proof sketch. The two identities are polynomial identities, checked by expanding. For all integers \(x,y\), $\(57600(x+y)^7=57600x^2\,(x^5+7x^4y+21x^3y^2+35x^2y^3+35xy^4+21y^5)+y^6\cdot57600(7x+y).\)$ With \(x=AF_h(a,b)\) and \(y=BG_h(a,b)\), the first term is a multiple of \(57600F_h(a,b)^2\) and the second a multiple of \(G_h(a,b)^6\), so \(c\) divides \(57600(AF_h(a,b)+BG_h(a,b))^7\) for all integers \(A,B\). Raising the two identities to the seventh power gives \(c\mid57600\cdot3^7a^{49}\) and \(c\mid57600\cdot104976000000^7b^{49}\). Since \(a,b\) are coprime, so are \(a^{49},b^{49}\), and there are integers \(s,t\) with \(sa^{49}+tb^{49}=1\). Then $\(C_0=(57600\cdot104976000000^7s)(57600\cdot3^7a^{49})+(57600\cdot3^7t)(57600\cdot104976000000^7b^{49}),\)$ a combination of two multiples of \(c\), so \(c\mid C_0\).

Let \(F_h\) and \(G_h\) be the binary forms of the Hauptmodul value. If \(a,b,m\) are integers with \(|a|\le m\) and \(|b|\le m\), then \(|a^ib^j|\le m^{i+j}\) for all natural numbers \(i,j\). Let \(a,b,m\) be integers with \(|a|\le m\), \(|b|\le m\), \(m>0\), and \(m=|a|\) or \(m=|b|\). Then $\(m^{12}\le10^{48}\max\bigl(57600F_h(a,b)^2,\ G_h(a,b)^6\bigr).\)$

Proof sketch. Suppose not. Then \(57600\cdot10^{48}F_h^2<m^{12}\) and \(10^{48}G_h^6<m^{12}\), so taking square and sixth roots, \(240\cdot10^{24}|F_h|<m^6\) and \(10^8|G_h|<m^2\); hence \(240\cdot10^{24}\,m|F_h|<m^7\) and \(10^8\,m^5|G_h|<m^7\). Since \(|a^ib^j|\le m^{i+j}\), each cofactor in the two identities of the cancellation bound is at most the sum of the absolute values of its coefficients times the matching power of \(m\).

If \(m=|a|\), the first identity and the triangle inequality give $\(3m^7\le5000\,m|F_h|+20328129\,m^5|G_h|<\Bigl(\frac{5000}{240\cdot10^{24}}+\frac{20328129}{10^8}\Bigr)m^7<3m^7,\)$ a contradiction. If \(m=|b|\), the second identity gives $\(104976000000\,m^7\le38651\,m|F_h|+184009200\,m^5|G_h|<\Bigl(\frac{38651}{240\cdot10^{24}}+\frac{184009200}{10^8}\Bigr)m^7,\)$ again a contradiction.

Let \(\mathcal C\) be as in the six-contact height estimate, for a reduced fraction \(a/b\) with \(b>0\) let \(h(a/b)=\log\max(|a|,b)\), and let \(J\) be the Hauptmodul value. For every \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), $\(12\,h(u)\le h(J(u))+450.\)$

This replaces the manuscript's rational-root bound \(h(u)<h(J(u))+74\), a different inequality.

Proof sketch. Write \(u=a/b\) in lowest terms with \(b>0\), and \(F_h=F_h(a,b)\), \(G_h=G_h(a,b)\). Then \(F(u)=F_h/b^6\) and \(G(u)=G_h/b^2\), and \(G_h>0\) since \(7G_h=(7a+150b)^2+2700b^2\). So \(J(u)=n/d\) with \(n=-57600F_h^2\) and \(d=G_h^6>0\). Writing \(J(u)\) in lowest terms as \( u/\delta\) with \(\delta>0\), there is an integer \(c\) with \(n=c u\) and \(d=c\delta\); \(c>0\) because \(d,\delta>0\). Then \(c\) divides both \(57600F_h^2\) and \(G_h^6\), so \(c\mid C_0\) by the cancellation bound, and \(c\le C_0\). Hence $\(\max(57600F_h^2,\,G_h^6)=c\,H,\qquad H=\max(| u|,\delta)\ge1.\)$ Put \(m=\max(|a|,b)>0\). The lower bound gives $\(m^{12}\le10^{48}cH\le10^{48}C_0H\le10^{139}H.\)$ Since \(h(u)=\log m\) and \(h(J(u))=\log H\), taking logarithms gives \(12h(u)\le139\log10+h(J(u))\). Finally \(e>2.7\) and \(2.7^3>10\) give \(\log10<3\), so \(139\log10<417\le450\).

docs.title: The minimal height hypothesis from the \(j\)-form
The \(j\)-form implies the minimal height hypothesis
docs.text:
ZInQ.JHeight.heightH6_eq ZInQ.JHeight.sixContactMin_of_jHeightBound

Let \(\mathcal C\), \(h\) and \(X(R)=\max(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_R^{17})\) be as in the \(j\)-form of the height hypothesis. For every real \(R\), \(H_6(S;R)=2\cdot10^{13}X(R)\) for every \(S\), by the definition of \(H_6(S;R)\) in the six-contact estimate (it does not depend on \(S\)); write \(H_6(R)\) for it. If the \(j\)-form holds at \(S=S_{\rm mul}\), then the minimal height hypothesis holds: for every \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), $\(h(u)\le H_6(D)\,M_{S_{\rm mul}}(u)^{24}.\)$

Proof sketch. Let \(u\notin\mathcal C\), write \(M=M_{S_{\rm mul}}(u)\) and \(K=40\cdot10^4\cdot2^{24}+22\). From the height of \(J(u)\) to the height of \(u\), \(12h(u)\le h(J(u))+450\), and the \(j\)-form gives \(h(J(u))\le K\,X(D)\,M^{24}\). Here \(X(D)\ge1\), and \(M\ge1\) because it is a product of primes, so \(Y=X(D)M^{24}\ge1\). Then $\(h(u)\le\frac{KY+450}{12}\le2\cdot10^{13}\,Y=H_6(D)\,M^{24},\)$ since \(K+450<2.4\cdot10^{14}\) and \(Y\ge1\).

docs.title: The elliptic model of integer indices
The elliptic model of integer indices
docs.text:
The polynomial never manipulates an integer index directly. It represents the index \(n\) by the five rational coordinates of the point \([n]P_0\) on an elliptic curve over \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\), and this chapter proves that the representation is faithful: the canonical codes form exactly the infinite cyclic group \(2E(K_0)=\mathbb ZP_0\) (input \(\mathsf G\) of the assembly lemma), the membership polynomial recognizes exactly those codes among arbitrary rational inputs, and raw addition computes the group law on canonical codes. Beyond the classical background (two-isogeny descent, reduction modulo primes, heights and division polynomials), the one input beyond the manuscript's elementary arguments is the Mordell-Weil theorem for \(E/K_0\), which is proved from the descent index with Mathlib's height theory, so it is not a hypothesis; every finite check is isolated as its own statement.

6 fully proved

docs.title: Point codes
docs.text: Let \(K_0=\mathbb Q(s)\) with \(s^2=2\), \(d=75-53s\), \(E:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) and \(P_0=\bigl(\frac{1641-1160s}{8},\frac{-123720+87483s}{32}\bigr)\). A point is coded by five rationals: \((1,0,0,0,0)\) for the identity and \((0,x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1)\) for an affine point with \(x=x_0+x_1s\), \(y=y_0+y_1s\); \(\iota(n)\) is the code of \([n]P_0\). The integer index and the coordinates play distinct roles throughout.

docs.title: Point codes
docs.text:
ZInQ.pointCode ZInQ.iota

The code of a point of \(E(K_0)\) is the element of \(\mathbb Q^5\) $\(\operatorname{code}(O)=(1,0,0,0,0),\qquad \operatorname{code}(x,y)=(0,x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1)\quad\text{where }x=x_0+x_1s,\ y=y_0+y_1s,\)$ with \(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1\in\mathbb Q\) the components of the coordinates. For \(n\in\mathbb Z\), $\(\iota(n)=\operatorname{code}([n]P_0)\in\mathbb Q^5 .\)$ A canonical code is the code of a point of \(E(K_0)\); a code of a point of \(2E(K_0)\) is a code of a point of the carrier \(D=2E(K_0)\).

The integer index \(n\) and the five rational coordinates of \(\iota(n)\) play different roles: the index is what the later chapters compute with, the coordinates are what the polynomial sees. Since \(P_0\) has infinite order, distinct indices have distinct codes.

docs.title: The generator certificate
docs.text: By rank one, \(R=(1+s,2s)\) on \(C:y^2=x^3-(3-s)^2x\) is \([m]S+T\) with \(S\) a generator modulo torsion and \(m\) odd. If \(|m|\ge3\), the generator has \(x\)-height below \(\log9\), and the finite search shows that every such nontorsion point is \(\pm(R+T')\) with \(T'\) two-torsion, so has the same canonical height as \(R\), contradicting \(\widehat h(R)=m^2\widehat h(S)>0\). Hence \(2C(K_0)\) is generated by \(2R\), and the change of variables sends \(2R\) to \(P_0\).

docs.title: The generator certificate
docs.text:
ZInQ.generator_certificate ZInQ.carrierD_eq_zmultiples ZInQ.indexEquivCarrier ZInQ.iota_injective

The point \(P_0\) has infinite order and $\(2E(K_0)=\mathbb ZP_0 .\)$ Consequently \(n\mapsto[n]P_0\) is an isomorphism \(\mathbb Z\to2E(K_0)=D\), the carrier \(D\) is torsion-free, and \(n\mapsto\iota(n)\) is injective.

This is Proposition 3.1. The manuscript assumes the Mordell–Weil theorem to pass from the descent index and the torsion bound to rank one; here Mordell–Weil is itself proved from the descent, so the statement has no hypothesis. That \(P_0\) has infinite order already follows from the torsion theorem.

Proof sketch. Work on \(C\) through the isomorphism \(\theta\). By the rank-one theorem, \(C(K_0)=\mathbb ZS\oplus C(K_0)[2]\) with \(S\) of infinite order; write \(R=[m]S+T\) with \(T\in C(K_0)[2]\). Then \(m\) is odd, in particular \(m\ne0\). Suppose \(|m|\ge3\). Then \(h_x(S)<\log9\), so by the search box \(x(S)\) lies in the candidate set of the finite search, and \(f(x(S))=y(S)^2\) is a square; hence \(x(S)\) is one of the seven survivors. The survivors \(0,\pm\delta\) are abscissas of two-torsion points, excluded because \(S\) has infinite order. The other four are the abscissas of \(R+T'\) for \(T'\in C(K_0)[2]\), so \(S=\pm(R+T')\) for some \(T'\) (equal abscissas force equal or opposite points), and the basic properties give \(\widehat h(S)=\widehat h(R)\). But \(\widehat h(R)=\widehat h([m]S)=m^2\widehat h(S)=m^2\widehat h(R)\) with \(m^2\ge9\) and \(\widehat h(R)>0\), a contradiction. So \(m=\pm1\), \(C(K_0)=\mathbb ZR\oplus C(K_0)[2]\) and \(2C(K_0)=\mathbb Z\,[2]R\), with \([2]R\) of infinite order. Applying \(\theta^{-1}\), which sends \([2]R\) to \(P_0\) by the certificate for \(R\), gives \(2E(K_0)=\mathbb ZP_0\) with \(P_0\) of infinite order. Injectivity of \(\iota\) follows from injectivity of codes.

docs.title: Membership and raw addition
docs.text:
Membership in \(2E(K_0)\), apart from the identity, is expressed by choosing a preimage with nonzero ordinate and its tangent slope. It is an all-input statement, and with the generator certificate it shows that accepted inputs are exactly the codes \(\iota(n)\), each with a unique index. The template itself is defined in the specification chapter (the membership template).

Raw addition has the narrower contract \(\operatorname{Add}_{\rm raw}(\iota(a),\iota(b),R)\iff R=\iota(a+b)\); its five branches are the cases of the chord-and-tangent law, and it is correct on all canonical codes. The template is defined in the specification chapter (the raw addition template).

Later chapters supply canonical codes to raw addition: multiplication first imposes membership of its three root inputs, and in the natural predicate the four untyped tuples are typed by multiplication calls before their squares are added, after which Lagrange's four-square theorem gives exactly \(\iota(\mathbb N)\). That step uses multiplication completeness (see the multiplication template); the generator certificate alone does not supply the natural predicate.

docs.title: Polynomial membership in the doubled group
docs.text:
ZInQ.rel_member_iff

For every \(p\in\mathbb Q^5\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{member}}(p)\iff p=\operatorname{code}(Q)\ \text{for some }Q\in2E(K_0),\)$ where \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{member}}(p)\) means that the polynomial of the membership template vanishes at \(p\) and some rational values of its seven witnesses \(X=(X_0,X_1)\), \(Y=(Y_0,Y_1)\), \(H=(H_0,H_1)\), \(u\). This is an all-input statement: \(p\) is an arbitrary rational \(5\)-tuple, not assumed to be a code.

Explicitly, apart from the identity branch \(p=(1,0,0,0,0)\), the template asks for \(X,Y,H\in K_0\) and \(u\in\mathbb Q\) with $\(p_0=0,\quad Y^2=X^3-d^2X,\quad u\operatorname N(Y)=1,\quad 2YH=3X^2-d^2,\quad x=H^2-2X,\quad y=H(X-x)-Y,\)$ where \(x=p_1+p_2s\), \(y=p_3+p_4s\), each field equation being two rational equations (the template writes the last as \(y=H(X-(H^2-2X))-Y\), equivalent given the abscissa equation).

Proof sketch. The template polynomial is the square of the compilation of its formula, so it vanishes exactly when one branch holds. If the identity branch holds, \(p=\operatorname{code}(O)\) and \(O\in2E(K_0)\). If the doubling branch holds, \((X,Y)\in E(K_0)\), \(Y\ne0\) because \(u\operatorname N(Y)=1\), \(H=(3X^2-d^2)/(2Y)\) is the tangent slope, and \((x,y)\) is given by the doubling formula, so \(p=\operatorname{code}([2](X,Y))\). Conversely let \(Q=[2]T\). If \(Q=O\), the identity branch holds with arbitrary witnesses. Otherwise \(T=(X,Y)\) is affine with \(Y\ne0\), since a point with \(Y=0\) has \([2]T=O\): every nonidentity double has a preimage with nonzero ordinate. Take \(H\) the tangent slope and \(u=\operatorname N(Y)^{-1}\); the doubling branch holds with \(p=\operatorname{code}(Q)\).

For every \(p\in\mathbb Q^5\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{member}}(p)\iff\exists n\in\mathbb Z:\ p=\iota(n),\)$ and the integer \(n\) is then unique. In words, the canonical point codes form exactly the infinite cyclic group \(2E(K_0)=\mathbb ZP_0\), and the membership polynomial types arbitrary inputs.

docs.title: Raw addition on canonical codes
docs.text:
ZInQ.rel_rawAdd_iff

For all \(P,Q\in E(K_0)\) and every \(r\in\mathbb Q^5\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{raw\_add}} igl(\operatorname{code}(P),\operatorname{code}(Q),r igr)\iff r=\operatorname{code}(P+Q),\)$ where \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{raw\_add}}(p,q,r)\) means that the polynomial of the raw addition template vanishes at \((p,q,r)\) and some rational values of its six witnesses (two slope pairs \(m_g,m_d\) and two inverse witnesses \(u_g,u_d\)). No assumption beyond \(P,Q\in E(K_0)\) is needed; two-torsion inputs are included.

Write \(x,y\) for the abscissa and ordinate encoded by \(p\), \(x',y'\) for those of \(q\), and \(x_r,y_r\) for those of \(r\). The five branches of the template are: (1) \(p=O\) and \(q=r\); (2) \(p_0=0\), \(q=O\) and \(p=r\); (3) \(p_0=q_0=0\), \(x=x'\), \(y=-y'\) and \(r=O\); (4) \(p_0=q_0=0\), \(u_g\operatorname N(x'-x)=1\), \((x'-x)m_g=y'-y\), \(r_0=0\), \(x_r=m_g^2-x-x'\), \(y_r=m_g(x-x_r)-y\); (5) \(p_0=q_0=0\), \(x=x'\), \(y=y'\), \(u_d\operatorname N(y)=1\), \(2ym_d=3x^2-d^2\), \(r_0=0\), \(x_r=m_d^2-x-x'\), \(y_r=m_d(x-x_r)-y\). Here \(O=(1,0,0,0,0)\).

Proof sketch. The template polynomial is the square of the compilation of its formula, so it vanishes exactly when one branch holds, the witnesses of the other branches being arbitrary. Cases. \(P=O\): branches 2-5 need \(p_0=0\), and branch 1 holds exactly when \(r=\operatorname{code}(Q)=\operatorname{code}(P+Q)\). \(P\) affine, \(Q=O\): branch 1 needs \(p_0=1\), branches 3-5 need \(q_0=0\), and branch 2 holds exactly when \(r=\operatorname{code}(P)\). Both affine: if \(x e x'\), branches 3 and 5 fail, branch 4 is satisfiable (\(\operatorname N(x'-x) e0\)), it forces \(m_g\) to be the chord slope, and then \(r\) is the code of the chord sum. If \(x=x'\) then \(y'=\pm y\) by the curve equation, and branch 4 fails. If \(y=-y'\), branch 3 holds with \(r=\operatorname{code}(O)=\operatorname{code}(P+Q)\), and branch 5 would need \(y=y'\) and \(\operatorname N(y) e0\), i.e. \(y=0\) and \(y e0\). If \(y=y' e0\), branch 3 fails and branch 5 forces the tangent slope and \(r=\operatorname{code}([2]P)\). In each case the forced \(r\) is the code given by the group law of \(E\), and conversely that \(r\) with the forced witnesses satisfies the branch.

docs.title: Descent, torsion and rank
docs.text:
The classical two-isogeny descent for curves \(y^2=x^3+bx\) supplies the Kummer map, its multiplicativity, the identification of its kernel with the image of an isogeny, and the factorization of doubling through the isogeny and its dual.

docs.title: Two-isogenies and the Kummer map
docs.text:
ZInQ.Descent.SqClass ZInQ.Descent.sqc ZInQ.Descent.kummer ZInQ.Descent.phi ZInQ.Descent.rescale

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic different from \(2\) and \(b\in K^ imes\), and let \(E_b:y^2=x^3+bx\) (an elliptic curve: its discriminant is \(-64b^3 e0\)). Write \(K^ imes/K^{ imes2}\) multiplicatively.

  • The Kummer map (the \(x\)-squareclass map) \(\alpha_b:E_b(K) o K^ imes/K^{ imes2}\) is $\(\alpha_b(O)=1,\qquad \alpha_b igl((0,0) igr)=b\,K^{ imes2},\qquad \alpha_b igl((x,y) igr)=x\,K^{ imes2}\ \ (x e0).\)$
  • The two-isogeny \(\varphi_b:E_b o E_{-4b}\) is $\(\varphi_b(O)=\varphi_b igl((0,0) igr)=O,\qquad \varphi_b igl((x,y) igr)=\Bigl( rac{y^2}{x^2},\ rac{y(b-x^2)}{x^2}\Bigr)\ \ (x e0).\)$ Its values lie on \(E_{-4b}:Y^2=X^3-4bX\), by the identity \(y^2(b-x^2)^2x^2=y^6-4bx^4y^2\) for \(y^2=x^3+bx\).
  • The rescaling \(\lambda_b:E_{16b} o E_b\) is \(\lambda_b(O)=O\), \(\lambda_b((x,y))=(x/4,\,y/8)\); it is a group isomorphism (the change of coordinates \((x,y)\mapsto(u^2x,u^3y)\) with \(u=1/2\)), with inverse \((x,y)\mapsto(4x,8y)\).

In this chapter \(b=-d^2\) gives \(E=E_{-d^2}\), \(E'=E_{4d^2}:y^2=x^3+4d^2x\), the isogeny \(\varphi=\varphi_{-d^2}:E o E'\) and the dual isogeny \(\hat\varphi=\lambda_{-d^2}\circ\varphi_{4d^2}:E' o E_{-16d^2} o E\); and \(b=-\delta^2\) gives the curve \(C=E_{-\delta^2}\).

docs.title: The Kummer map is a homomorphism
docs.text:
ZInQ.Descent.kummer_add ZInQ.Descent.kummerHom ZInQ.Descent.mul_addX_eq ZInQ.Descent.kummer_two_nsmul

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic different from \(2\) and \(b\in K^ imes\). The Kummer map \(\alpha_b:E_b(K) o K^ imes/K^{ imes2}\) is a group homomorphism. In particular \(\alpha_b(2P)=1\) for every \(P\in E_b(K)\).

Along the way: let \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\) be affine points of \(E_b(K)\) that are not negatives of each other, let \(\lambda\) be the slope of the chord (or tangent) through them, and let \(x_3=\lambda^2-x_1-x_2\) be the abscissa of their sum. Then \(x_1x_2x_3=(y_1-\lambda x_1)^2\).

Proof sketch. (Silverman, Proposition X.4.9; Silverman-Tate, Section III.5.) Since \(\alpha_b(-P)=\alpha_b(P)\) and squareclasses have exponent two, it suffices to show \(\alpha_b(P_1)\alpha_b(P_2)\alpha_b(P_3)=1\) whenever \(P_1+P_2+P_3=O\). If one of the points is \(O\) this is \(\alpha_b(-P)=\alpha_b(P)\). Otherwise the three points are the intersections, with multiplicity, of a line \(y=\lambda x+ u\) with \(E_b\), so \(x^3+bx-(\lambda x+ u)^2=(x-x_1)(x-x_2)(x-x_3)\) and \(x_1x_2x_3= u^2\). If no \(x_i\) is \(0\) this gives the claim (\( u e0\)). If some \(P_i=(0,0)\), then \( u=0\), the other two abscissas are the roots of \(x^2-\lambda^2x+b\), and their product is \(b=\alpha_b((0,0))\) modulo squares. The case analysis matches the chord, tangent and vertical cases of the addition law; in the formula for \(x(P+Q)\) via the slope, the identity follows from the factorization of the cubic above, with \( u=y_1-\lambda x_1\). Finally \(\alpha_b(2P)=\alpha_b(P)^2=1\), since square classes have exponent two.

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic different from \(2\) and \(b\in K^ imes\). For every \(P\in E_b(K)\), $\(\lambda_b\Bigl(\varphi_{-4b} igl(\varphi_b(P) igr)\Bigr)=[2]P .\)$ In particular, for \(b=-d^2\) over \(K_0\), \(\hat\varphi\circ\varphi=[2]\) on \(E(K_0)\). Let \(\epsilon=1+s\), \(\delta=3-s\) and \(C=E_{-\delta^2}:y^2=x^3-\delta^2x\) over \(K_0\). Then \(\epsilon^4=17+12s\), \(\epsilon^6=99+70s\), \(\delta=\epsilon^4d\), and the map $\(\theta:E(K_0)\to C(K_0),\qquad \theta(O)=O,\quad \theta(x,y)=(\epsilon^4x,\ \epsilon^6y)\)$ is an isomorphism of groups, with inverse \((x,y)\mapsto(\epsilon^{-4}x,\epsilon^{-6}y)\). It maps \(E(K_0)[2]\) onto \(C(K_0)[2]=\{O,(0,0),(\delta,0),(-\delta,0)\}\) and satisfies \(\alpha_{-\delta^2}(\theta(P))=\alpha_{-d^2}(P)\) for every \(P\in E(K_0)\).

For \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\), multiplying by \(\epsilon^{12}\) gives \((\epsilon^6y)^2=(\epsilon^4x)^3-\epsilon^8d^2(\epsilon^4x)\) and \(\epsilon^8d^2=\delta^2\); the converse is the same computation, \(\epsilon\) being a unit. The map preserves the group law because chord and tangent slopes are multiplied by \(\epsilon^2\) (for the tangent slope use \(3(\epsilon^4x)^2-\delta^2=\epsilon^8(3x^2-d^2)\)), so the sum formulas \(x_3=\lambda^2-x_1-x_2\), \(y_3=\lambda(x_1-x_3)-y_1\) scale by \(\epsilon^4\) and \(\epsilon^6\); vertical pairs go to vertical pairs. Two-torsion points have \(y=0\) and abscissas \(0,\pm d\), sent to \(0,\pm\delta\). Abscissas are multiplied by the square \(\epsilon^4\), and \((0,0)\) has class \(-d^2\) on \(E\) and \(-\delta^2\) on \(C\), both equal to \(-1\) modulo squares.

docs.title: The first descent image has order eight
docs.text:
ZInQ.kummer_range_E ZInQ.card_kummer_range_E ZInQ.descentGroup_eq

Let \(\alpha=\alpha_{-d^2}:E(K_0) o K_0^ imes/K_0^{ imes2}\) be the Kummer map of \(E\). Its image is the subgroup generated by the classes of \(-1\), \(\epsilon=1+s\) and \(d\); this subgroup has order \(8\), its elements being the classes of \(\pm1,\pm\epsilon,\pm d,\pm\epsilon d\), which are pairwise distinct. The two-torsion points give $\(\alpha(O)=1,\quad\alpha((0,0))=-d^2\equiv-1,\quad\alpha((d,0))=d,\quad\alpha((-d,0))=-d,\)$ and the point \((\epsilon^{-4}(1+s),\,\epsilon^{-6}\cdot2s)\in E(K_0)\), the preimage of \(R=(1+s,2s)\in C(K_0)\) under the change of variables, has class \(\epsilon\).

Proof sketch. Upper bound. Let \((x,y)\in E(K_0)\) with \(x e0\) and let \(\pi\) be a prime of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) not associate to \(d\); put \(m=v_\pi(x)\). If \(y=0\) then \(x=\pm d\) and \(m=0\). Otherwise \(2v_\pi(y)=v_\pi(x^3-d^2x)\), where the two terms have valuations \(3m\) and \(m+2v_\pi(d)=m\); if \(m e0\) these differ, so \(2v_\pi(y)=\min(3m,m)\), which is odd when \(m\) is odd. Hence every \(v_\pi(x)\) with \(\pi ot\sim d\) is even, and by unique factorization \(x=u\,d^{e}z^2\) with \(u\) a unit, \(e\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\in K_0^ imes\); the unit classes are those of \(\pm1,\pm\epsilon\). The class of \((0,0)\) is \(-d^2\equiv-1\). Distinctness. \(v_d\) is odd on \(\pm d,\pm\epsilon d\) and even on \(\pm1,\pm\epsilon\); \(d\) is totally positive, so within each half the four sign vectors \((+,+),(-,-),(+,-),(-,+)\) separate the classes, and squares are totally positive. Lower bound. The listed two-torsion values give \(-1\) and \(d\). The point \(R\) lies on \(C\) and the change of variables maps \(E\) isomorphically onto \(C\) scaling abscissas by \(\epsilon^4\), so its preimage lies on \(E\) with abscissa \(\epsilon^{-4}(1+s)\equiv\epsilon\). Since \(\alpha\) is a homomorphism, its image contains the subgroup generated by \(-1,\epsilon,d\), hence equals it.

docs.text:
ZInQ.kummer_E'_trivial

Let \(E'=E_{4d^2}:y^2=x^3+4d^2x\) over \(K_0\) and \(\alpha'=\alpha_{4d^2}\) its Kummer map. Then \(\alpha'(Q)=1\) for every \(Q\in E'(K_0)\).

Proof sketch. \(\alpha'(O)=1\) and \(\alpha'((0,0))=4d^2\) is a square. Let \(Q=(x,y)\) with \(x e0\). Total positivity. In each real embedding \(\sigma(y)^2=\sigma(x)(\sigma(x)^2+4\sigma(d)^2)\) with the second factor positive, so \(\sigma(x)>0\); also \(y e0\), since \(x^2=-4d^2\) has no solution in the real field \(K_0\). Even valuations. Let \(m=v_\pi(x)\). If \(\pi\) is associate to neither \(s\) nor \(d\), \(v_\pi(4d^2)=0\) and, as for the first image, odd \(m\) is impossible. At \(\pi=s\), \(v_s(4d^2)=4\); the terms \(x^3\) and \(4d^2x\) have valuations \(3m\) and \(m+4\), equal only for \(m=2\), so for odd \(m\) the valuation \(2v_s(y)\) would be \(\min(3m,m+4)\), odd. At \(\pi=d\), \(v_d(4d^2)=2\); the valuations \(3m\) and \(m+2\) are equal only for \(m=1\), so odd \(m e1\) is excluded as before. If \(m=1\), write \(x=dw\) with \(v_d(w)=0\); then \(y^2=d^3w(w^2+4)\) forces \(v_d(w^2+4)\) odd, in particular \(w^2\equiv-4\) modulo \(d\), so \((w/2)^2\) would be \(-1\) in the residue field \(\mathbb F_7\), which is impossible. Conclusion. By unique factorization \(x=uz^2\) with \(u\) a unit; \(u=x/z^2\) is totally positive, hence a square, so \(\alpha'(Q)=1\).

\(2E(K_0)\) is the kernel of the Kummer map \(\alpha:E(K_0)\to K_0^\times/K_0^{\times2}\), and $\([E(K_0):2E(K_0)]=8 .\)$ More precisely \(\alpha\) induces an isomorphism of \(E(K_0)/2E(K_0)\) onto the subgroup of \(K_0^\times/K_0^{\times2}\) generated by \(-1,\epsilon,d\), which is elementary abelian of order \(8\).

Proof sketch. The manuscript uses the exact two-isogeny sequence $\(0\to E'(K_0)[\hat\varphi]/\varphi(E(K_0)[2])\to E'(K_0)/\varphi(E(K_0))\to E(K_0)/2E(K_0) \to E(K_0)/\hat\varphi(E'(K_0))\to0,\)$ whose outer terms are the two Kummer images; the first term vanishes because the nonkernel two-torsion points \((\pm d,0)\) map to the generator \((0,0)\) of the dual kernel. A direct route with the same inputs: since the second descent image is trivial, the kernel theorem for \(\varphi=\varphi_{-d^2}\) gives \(\varphi(E(K_0))=E'(K_0)\). The kernel theorem for \(\varphi_{4d^2}:E'\to E_{-16d^2}\), transported by the rescaling \(\lambda_{-d^2}\) (which multiplies abscissas by \(1/4\), a square, and sends the class \(-16d^2\) of \((0,0)\) to \(-d^2\)), gives \(\ker\alpha=\hat\varphi(E'(K_0))\). Since \(\hat\varphi\circ\varphi=[2]\), $\(2E(K_0)=\hat\varphi\bigl(\varphi(E(K_0))\bigr)=\hat\varphi(E'(K_0))=\ker\alpha .\)$ As \(\alpha\) is a homomorphism, \(E(K_0)/2E(K_0)\cong\alpha(E(K_0))\), of order \(8\) by the first descent image.

docs.title: Torsion and rank
docs.text:
Reduction at the primes \((17,s-6)\) and \((23,s-5)\), with \(20\) and \(24\) points, shows that the torsion is exactly the full two-torsion; in particular \(P_0\) has infinite order, so its nonzero multiples are affine with nonzero coordinates. The Mordell-Weil theorem then gives rank one, and real signs of squareclasses show that \(R\) is an odd multiple of a generator modulo torsion.

The Mordell-Weil theorem for \(E/K_0\), first a hypothesis of the main theorem, is a consequence of the descent index and the classical descent theorem with heights.

docs.title: Reduction is injective on prime-to-\(p\) torsion
docs.text:
ZInQ.red_add ZInQ.eq_zero_of_red_eq_zero

Let \(p\) be an odd prime and \(r\in\mathbb Z\) with \(r^2\equiv2\pmod p\). Then \(\rho:\mathbb Z[s]\to\mathbb F_p\), \(a+bs\mapsto a+br\bmod p\), is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel the prime \(\mathfrak p=(p,s-r)\); it extends to the local ring \(\mathbb Z[s]_{\mathfrak p}\subset K_0\). Let \(A\in\mathbb Z[s]\) with \(\rho(A)\ne0\), let \(W:y^2=x^3+Ax\) over \(K_0\) and \(\widetilde W:y^2=x^3+\rho(A)x\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) (an elliptic curve, since \(p\) is odd and \(\rho(A)\ne0\)). Define \(\operatorname{red}:W(K_0)\to\widetilde W(\mathbb F_p)\) by \(\operatorname{red}(O)=O\), \(\operatorname{red}(x,y)=(\rho(x),\rho(y))\) if \(x\in\mathbb Z[s]_{\mathfrak p}\), and \(\operatorname{red}(x,y)=O\) otherwise. Then:

  1. \(\operatorname{red}\) is a group homomorphism;
  2. if \(T\in W(K_0)\) has finite order prime to \(p\) and \(\operatorname{red}(T)=O\), then \(T=O\). Hence \(\operatorname{red}\) is injective on every finite subgroup of \(W(K_0)\) of order prime to \(p\), and the order of such a subgroup divides \(\#\widetilde W(\mathbb F_p)\).

(If \(x\in\mathbb Z[s]_{\mathfrak p}\) then \(y\in\mathbb Z[s]_{\mathfrak p}\) too, because \(y^2=x^3+Ax\) is integral there.)

Proof sketch. This is reduction modulo a prime of good reduction (Silverman, Proposition VII.2.1 and Proposition VII.3.1(b)), applied after embedding \(K_0\) in its completion at \(\mathfrak p\), which is \(\mathbb Q_p\) because \(\mathfrak p\) has residue degree one. Part 1 holds because the group law is given by polynomial formulas in projective coordinates that reduce to those of \(\widetilde W\). For part 2, the kernel of reduction is the group of points with \(v_{\mathfrak p}(x)<0\); on it \(z=-x/y\) defines an isomorphism with the formal group \(\widehat W(\mathfrak p)\), which has no nontrivial torsion of order prime to \(p\) because multiplication by an integer prime to \(p\) is invertible on it.

Consequently, for every nonzero \(m\in\mathbb Z\) the point \([m]P_0\) is affine, its abscissa and ordinate are nonzero, and \(z([m]P_0)=-x/y\) and \(w([m]P_0)=1/x\) are nonzero elements of \(K_0\). For \(m e0\), \([m]P_0\) is not torsion either, so it is neither \(O\) nor a point with \(y=0\); and \(x=0\) forces \(y^2=0\) on \(E\). Hence \(x,y e0\), so \(z=-x/y e0\) and \(w=1/x e0\). Assume that \(E(K_0)\) is finitely generated (the Mordell-Weil hypothesis). Then there is a point \(S\in C(K_0)\) of infinite order such that every \(P\in C(K_0)\) is uniquely \(P=[m]S+T\) with \(m\in\mathbb Z\) and \(T\in C(K_0)[2]\): $\(C(K_0)=\mathbb ZS\oplus C(K_0)[2]\cong\mathbb Z\times(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2 .\)$ The same holds for \(E(K_0)\) with \(\theta^{-1}(S)\) and \(E(K_0)[2]\).

Proof sketch. \(C(K_0)\cong E(K_0)\) via \(\theta\), so \(C(K_0)\) is finitely generated with torsion subgroup \(C(K_0)[2]\cong(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2\) and \([C(K_0):2C(K_0)]=8\). By the structure theorem, \(C(K_0)\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2\), whose quotient by twice itself has order \(2^{r+2}\); so \(r=1\). Concretely, \(C(K_0)/C(K_0)[2]\) is torsion-free, finitely generated and of rank one, hence infinite cyclic; any \(S\) mapping to a generator works, and the sum is direct because \(\mathbb ZS\) is torsion-free.

docs.title: The free index of \(R\) is odd
docs.text:
ZInQ.odd_free_index

Let \(S\in C(K_0)\) be as in the rank-one theorem and write \(R=(1+s,2s)=[m]S+T\) with \(m\in\mathbb Z\) and \(T\in C(K_0)[2]\). Then \(m\) is odd.

Proof sketch. Let \(\alpha_C=\alpha_{-\delta^2}\), a homomorphism. The sign vector of a nonzero element is constant on its squareclass, since squares are totally positive. The class \(\alpha_C(R)=1+s\) has sign vector \((+,-)\). The two-torsion classes are \(\alpha_C(O)=1\), \(\alpha_C((0,0))=-\delta^2\equiv-1\), \(\alpha_C((\delta,0))=\delta\) and \(\alpha_C((-\delta,0))=-\delta\), all with equal signs because \(\delta=3-s\) is totally positive. If \(m\) were even, \(\alpha_C(R)=\alpha_C(S)^m\alpha_C(T)\equiv\alpha_C(T)\) would have equal signs. So \(m\) is odd.

docs.title: Mordell-Weil for \(E/K_0\) from the descent
docs.text:
ZInQ.mordellWeilE

The group \(E(K_0)\) is finitely generated; that is, the Mordell-Weil hypothesis for the generator curve holds.

This is not part of the manuscript's argument, which cites the Mordell-Weil theorem. It shows that, given the descent index already proved in this chapter, the hypothesis can be discharged by the classical descent theorem.

Proof sketch. (Silverman, Theorem VIII.3.1 and Section VIII.6.) Let \(h\) be the naive height \(h(P)=\sum_v\log\max(1,|x(P)|_v)\) on \(E(K_0)\), \(h(O)=0\), the sum over the places of the number field \(K_0\) with their usual normalization. Then \(h\ge0\); there is a constant \(c\) with \(|h(P+Q)+h(P-Q)-2h(P)-2h(Q)|\le c\) for all \(P,Q\) (the approximate parallelogram law); and for every bound \(B\) only finitely many \(P\) have \(h(P)\le B\) (Northcott's property for \(K_0\), since each \(x\)-coordinate determines at most two points). The descent theorem says that an abelian group with such a height and finite \(G/2G\) is finitely generated: elements of height below an explicit bound, together with representatives of \(G/2G\), generate. Here \([E(K_0):2E(K_0)]=8\) is finite by the descent index.

docs.title: The field, the curve and division polynomials
The field, the curve and division polynomials
docs.text:
Everything takes place over \(K_0=\mathbb Q(s)\), \(s^2=2\), written in the basis \(1,s\), so that each field equation is two rational equations. A field element is nonzero exactly when its norm is, which is how one rational witness expresses every nonvanishing condition; the pair arithmetic and the inverse witnesses are set up in the specification chapter (pair arithmetic, inverse witnesses).

The handful of explicit identities and sign facts used throughout (the square of \(d\), powers of \(\epsilon=1+s\), \(\delta=\epsilon^4d\), norms, total positivity of \(d\) and \(\delta\)) are collected in one closed statement.

The curve is \(E:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) with \(d=75-53s\), and the base point is \(P_0\); that its coordinates satisfy the curve equation is a closed identity in \(K_0\).

Codes are injective, negation flips the two ordinate coordinates, and the code of a sum of multiples of \(P_0\) is the code of the summed index.

13 fully proved

docs.title: The field \(K_0=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.K0 ZInQ.sqrt2 ZInQ.epsilon ZInQ.delta ZInQ.Zs

Let \(K_0=\mathbb Q(s)\) with \(s^2=2\). Every element of \(K_0\) is uniquely \(u+vs\) with \(u,v\in\mathbb Q\), its components; addition is componentwise and $\((a+bs)(c+es)=(ac+2be)+(ae+bc)s .\)$ The conjugate of \(z=u+vs\) is \(\bar z=u-vs\), the norm is \(\operatorname N(z)=z\bar z=u^2-2v^2\in\mathbb Q\) and the trace is \(\operatorname{Tr}(z)=2u\). The two real embeddings are \(\sigma_+(u+vs)=u+v\sqrt2\) and \(\sigma_-(u+vs)=u-v\sqrt2\); \(\operatorname N(z)=\sigma_+(z)\sigma_-(z)\). An element is totally positive if both embeddings are positive, and its sign vector is the pair of signs of \(\sigma_+(z),\sigma_-(z)\).

The subring \(\mathbb Z[s]=\{u+vs:u,v\in\mathbb Z\}\) has fraction field \(K_0\). Two fixed elements recur throughout the chapter: $\(\epsilon=1+s,\qquad \delta=3-s .\)$

The field is \(\mathbb Q\) adjoined a square root of \(2\); \(2\) is not a rational square, so \(K_0\) is a field of degree two over \(\mathbb Q\).

docs.title: Explicit identities in \(K_0\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.k0_identities ZInQ.K0.totallyPositive_iff ZInQ.k0_signs

With \(s^2=2\), \(\epsilon=1+s\), \(\delta=3-s\) and \(d=75-53s\), the following closed statements hold in \(K_0\) and in \(\mathbb Z\):

  1. \(d^2=11243-7950s\) and \(\operatorname N(d)=75^2-2\cdot53^2=7\);
  2. \(\epsilon(s-1)=1\), \(\epsilon^2=3+2s\), \(\epsilon^4=17+12s\), \(\epsilon^6=99+70s\) and \(\operatorname N(\epsilon)=-1\);
  3. \(d\,\epsilon^4=\delta\), that is \((75-53s)(17+12s)=3-s\); \(\delta^2=11-6s\); \(\operatorname N(\delta)=7\); \(\operatorname N(s)=-2\);
  4. \(75>0\) and \(75^2>2\cdot53^2\); \(3>0\) and \(3^2>2\cdot1^2\); \(1^2<2\cdot1^2\); \(2\le2^2\);
  5. \(2^6\cdot7^4=392^2=153664\), \(7^2<392\) and \(676=26^2\).

An element \(u+vs\) with \(u,v\in\mathbb Q\) is totally positive exactly when \(u>0\) and \(u^2>2v^2\). So item 4 says that \(d\) and \(\delta\) are totally positive, that \(\epsilon\) has sign vector \((+,-)\) (as \(\sigma_-(\epsilon)=1-\sqrt2<0<\sigma_+(\epsilon)\)), and that \(\sigma_\pm(\delta)=3\mp\sqrt2\) lies in \([1,5]\) (both bounds amount to \(\sqrt2\le2\)).

All items are equalities of explicit elements of \(K_0\) (two rational components each) or comparisons of explicit integers: a finite computation.

Proof sketch. Expand with \(s^2=2\) and compare components; evaluate the integers. For the positivity criterion: \(u\pm v\sqrt2>0\) for both signs is \(u>|v|\sqrt2\), i.e. \(u>0\) and \(u^2>2v^2\).

docs.title: The generator curve \(E\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.genCurve ZInQ.genCurve_two_torsion

Put \(d=75-53s\in\mathbb Z[s]\), so that $\(d^2=11243-7950s,\qquad A:=-d^2=-11243+7950s,\qquad \operatorname N(d)=75^2-2\cdot53^2=7 .\)$ The curve \(E\) over \(K_0\) is the short Weierstrass curve $\(E:\ y^2=x^3-d^2x=x^3+Ax .\)$ Its discriminant \(-64A^3=64d^6\) is nonzero, so \(E\) is an elliptic curve. Its group of \(K_0\)-rational points, with the usual chord-and-tangent law and identity \(O\), is written \(E(K_0)\). Since \(x^3-d^2x=x(x-d)(x+d)\), the points of order dividing two are $\(E(K_0)[2]=\{O,\ (0,0),\ (d,0),\ (-d,0)\}.\)$

The group law is the standard one for \(y^2=x^3+Ax\): \(-(x,y)=(x,-y)\); if \(x_1\ne x_2\) the sum of \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\) has \(\lambda=(y_2-y_1)/(x_2-x_1)\); if the points are equal with \(y_1\ne0\), \(\lambda=(3x_1^2+A)/(2y_1)\); in both cases \(x_3=\lambda^2-x_1-x_2\) and \(y_3=\lambda(x_1-x_3)-y_1\); and \((x,y)+(x,-y)=O\).

docs.title: The coordinates of \(P_0\) satisfy the curve equation
docs.text:
ZInQ.genP0_equation

Let \(x_0=\frac{1641-1160s}{8}\) and \(y_0=\frac{-123720+87483s}{32}\) in \(K_0\). Then $\(y_0^2=x_0^3-d^2x_0\qquad(d^2=11243-7950s),\)$ and \(y_0\ne0\).

This is a closed identity between explicit elements of \(K_0\): after expanding with \(s^2=2\), both components of \(y_0^2-x_0^3+d^2x_0\) are explicit rationals, and the claim is that both vanish. It is a finite computation.

Proof sketch. Expand both sides with the product rule of \(K_0\) and compare the two rational components. Alternatively, it follows from the certificate for \(R\): the point \(2R\) of \(C\) is sent by the inverse change of variables to \((x_0,y_0)\), and the change of variables preserves the curve equations; that route needs no separate arithmetic, but the direct expansion is shorter.

docs.title: Elementary properties of codes
docs.text:
ZInQ.pointCode_injective ZInQ.iota_add
  1. The map \(\operatorname{code}:E(K_0)\to\mathbb Q^5\) is injective. The first coordinate of a code is \(1\) exactly for \(O\) and \(0\) for every affine point.
  2. For every point \(Q\), \(\operatorname{code}(-Q)\) is \(\operatorname{code}(Q)\) with its last two coordinates negated. In particular \(\iota(0)=(1,0,0,0,0)\) and, for every \(n\in\mathbb Z\), \(\iota(-n)\) is \(\iota(n)\) with its last two coordinates negated.
  3. \(\iota(1)=\bigl(0,\tfrac{1641}{8},-145,-\tfrac{15465}{4},\tfrac{87483}{32}\bigr)\).
  4. For all \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\), \(\iota(a)\) and \(\iota(b)\) are codes of the points \([a]P_0\) and \([b]P_0\), whose sum \([a+b]P_0\) has code \(\iota(a+b)\).

Proof sketch. (1) The components of an element of \(K_0\) determine it, so the code determines \(x\) and \(y\); the first coordinate separates \(O\) from affine points. (2) \(-(x,y)=(x,-y)\) and \(-O=O\). (3) Read off the coordinates of \(P_0\): \(1160/8=145\) and \(123720/32=15465/4\). (4) \([a]P_0+[b]P_0=[a+b]P_0\) in the group \(E(K_0)\).

docs.title: Division polynomials
docs.text: Fixed multiples \([n]Q\), for fixed integers \(n\) that may have millions of digits, are expressed by the normalized division polynomials of the specification (their definition). The specification chapter states their classical multiplication formulas as a proposition (the multiplication-by-n formulas) and derives from it the semantics of the fixed-scalar templates (fixed-scalar semantics). Here the proposition is proved as a background theorem, and it gives the fixed point codes \(\iota(n)\). The recursion is only ever used symbolically. The proof goes through Jacobian coordinates: the triples \((\phi_n,\omega_n,\psi_n)\) satisfy exact doubling and adding identities, first at the generic point of the curve, where no division polynomial vanishes, and an induction on \(n\) shows that these triples represent the multiples \([n]P\).

docs.title: Division polynomials compute multiples
docs.text:
ZInQ.mulByN_formulas

The multiplication-by-\(n\) formulas hold for \(E\) over \(K_0\): for every affine point \(P=(x,y)\in E(K_0)\) and every integer \(n e0\),

  1. \([n]P=O\) if and only if \(\psi_n(P)=0\);
  2. if \([n]P e O\), then $\(x([n]P)=x- rac{\psi_{n+1}(P)\,\psi_{n-1}(P)}{\psi_n(P)^2},\qquad y([n]P)= rac{\psi_{2n}(P)}{2\,\psi_n(P)^4},\)$

where \(\psi_k\) are the normalized division polynomials of \(y^2=x^3+Ax\) with \(A=-d^2=-11243+7950s\). More generally the same holds for \(y^2=x^3+Ax\) over any field of characteristic zero with \(A e0\).

Proof sketch. This is the classical theorem (Sutherland, Lecture 5, Lemmas 5.20 and 5.24 and Theorem 5.21; Silverman, Exercise 3.7). A route through Jacobian coordinates avoids divisors and handles the identity uniformly. Represent points of \(E\) by nonzero triples \((X,Y,Z)\) with \(Y^2=X^3+AXZ^4\), up to the weighted scaling \(u\cdot(X,Y,Z)=(u^2X,u^3Y,uZ)\) with \(u e0\): the triple represents the affine point \((X/Z^2,Y/Z^3)\) if \(Z e0\) and \(O\) if \(Z=0\). The Jacobian doubling formula sends a representative of \(Q\) to a representative of \([2]Q\), for every \(Q\), and the Jacobian addition formula sends representatives of two distinct points \(Q_1 e Q_2\) to a representative of \(Q_1+Q_2\) (including the cases where one of them is \(O\) or \(Q_1=-Q_2\)).

Fix an affine \(P=(x,y)\), put \(\phi_n=x\psi_n^2-\psi_{n+1}\psi_{n-1}\) and \(\omega_n=\psi_{2n}/(2\psi_n)\) (a polynomial in \(x,y\)), and write \(J_n(P)=(\phi_n(P),\omega_n(P),\psi_n(P))\). The doubling and adding identities \(\mathrm{dbl}(J_k)=J_{2k}\) and \(\mathrm{add}(J_{k+1},J_k)=(-1)\cdot J_{2k+1}\) (\(k\ge1\)) hold at every point of the curve: at the generic point of \(y^2=x^3+Ax\), in the function field, no \(\psi_n\) with \(n e0\) vanishes, so there the abscissas of the multiples can be computed by strong induction from the recurrences of \(\psi\) (the duplication formula for \(n=2m\), the chord through \([m+1]P\) and \([m]P\) for \(n=2m+1\)), which gives the identities in the coordinate ring; evaluating at \(P\) gives them at \(P\). Claim: for every \(n\ge1\), \(J_n(P)\) is a representative of \([n]P\) (in particular a nonzero triple). Strong induction on \(n\):

  • \(n=1\): \(\phi_1=x\), \(\omega_1=y\), \(\psi_1=1\).
  • \(n=2k\), \(k\ge1\): \(J_k(P)\) represents \([k]P\), so its double represents \([2k]P\), and the double of \(J_k\) is \(J_{2k}\).
  • \(n=2k+1\), \(k\ge1\): \(J_{k+1}(P)\) and \(J_k(P)\) represent \([k+1]P\) and \([k]P\), which are distinct because their difference is \(P e O\); so their sum \(\mathrm{add}(J_{k+1},J_k)(P)=(-1)\cdot J_{2k+1}(P)\) represents \([2k+1]P\), and so does \(J_{2k+1}(P)\).

Reading off the third coordinate gives part 1 for \(n\ge1\). If \(\psi_n(P) e0\), then \([n]P=(\phi_n/\psi_n^2,\ \omega_n/\psi_n^3)\) evaluated at \(P\), and \(\phi_n/\psi_n^2=x-\psi_{n+1}\psi_{n-1}/\psi_n^2\), \(\omega_n/\psi_n^3=2\psi_n\omega_n/(2\psi_n^4)=\psi_{2n}/(2\psi_n^4)\): part 2. Negative \(n\) follow from \(\psi_{-n}=-\psi_n\) (so \(\psi_{-n\pm1}=-\psi_{n\mp1}\) and \(\psi_{-2n}=-\psi_{2n}\)) and \([-n]P=-[n]P=(x([n]P),-y([n]P))\).

These are the fixed point codes of the specification: for any fixed \(n\) they are explicit elements of \(\mathbb Q^5\), but \(n\) may be astronomically large, and the statement is used only symbolically.

The negative indices follow from \([-n]P_0=-[n]P_0\) and the code of a negative.

docs.title: Arithmetic of \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]\)
docs.text: The descent uses unique factorization in \(\mathbb Z[s]\), its units \(\pm(1+s)^k\), and the two special primes: \((s)\) above \(2\) and \((d)=(\delta)\) above \(7\).

docs.title: \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]\) is a principal ideal domain
docs.text:
ZInQ.Zs.isPrincipalIdealRing ZInQ.Zs.uniqueFactorizationMonoid

The ring \(\mathbb Z[s]\) is a principal ideal domain (the ring of integers of \(K_0\) has class number one). Consequently it is a unique factorization domain with fraction field \(K_0\): every \(x\in K_0^\times\) is \(x=u\prod_\pi\pi^{v_\pi(x)}\) with \(u\in\mathbb Z[s]^\times\), \(\pi\) running over a set of representatives of the prime elements up to units, and integers \(v_\pi(x)\), almost all zero, uniquely determined by \(x\). The valuations satisfy \(v_\pi(xy)=v_\pi(x)+v_\pi(y)\) and \(v_\pi(x+y)\ge\min(v_\pi(x),v_\pi(y))\), with equality when the two valuations differ.

Proof sketch. The manuscript's route: \(K_0\) has discriminant \(8\) and the Minkowski bound is \(\frac{2!}{2^2}\sqrt8=\sqrt2<2\), so every ideal class contains an integral ideal of norm \(1\), i.e. the unit ideal. An elementary route better suited to formalization: \(\mathbb Z[s]\) is Euclidean for \(|\operatorname N|\). Given \(a,b\in\mathbb Z[s]\), \(b\ne0\), write \(a/b=u+vs\) and let \(q=\lfloor u\rceil+\lfloor v\rceil s\) with nearest integers; then \(|\operatorname N(a/b-q)|\le\max(\tfrac14,\tfrac24)<1\), so \(a=qb+\rho\) with \(|\operatorname N(\rho)|<|\operatorname N(b)|\). Unique factorization and the valuation rules follow from the principal ideal property in the usual way.

ZInQ.Zs_unit_sqClass ZInQ.isSquare_of_totallyPositive_unit
  1. \(\mathbb Z[s]^\times=\{\pm\epsilon^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}\) with \(\epsilon=1+s\), and \(\epsilon^{-1}=s-1\), \(\operatorname N(\epsilon)=-1\).
  2. The unit squareclasses \(\mathbb Z[s]^\times/(\mathbb Z[s]^\times)^2\) are exactly the four classes of \(1,-1,\epsilon,-\epsilon\), whose sign vectors are \((+,+)\), \((-,-)\), \((+,-)\) and \((-,+)\) respectively.
  3. Every totally positive unit is the square of a unit.

Proof sketch. (1) \((1+s)(s-1)=1\). If \(u\) is a unit, replace it by \(\pm u\) so that \(\sigma_+(u)>0\), and choose \(k\) with \(1\le\sigma_+(u\epsilon^{-k})<1+\sqrt2\). A unit \(w=a+bs\) with \(1\le\sigma_+(w)<1+\sqrt2\) has \(|\sigma_-(w)|=1/\sigma_+(w)\le1\), so \(2a=\sigma_+(w)+\sigma_-(w)\in[0,2+\sqrt2)\) and \(2b\sqrt2=\sigma_+(w)-\sigma_-(w)\in[0,2+\sqrt2)\). Hence \(a,b\in\{0,1\}\); of \(0,1,s,1+s\) only \(1\) and \(1+s\) are units, and \(\sigma_+(1+s)=1+\sqrt2\) is excluded, so \(w=1\) and \(u=\pm\epsilon^k\). (2) By (1) the quotient is generated by \(-1\) and \(\epsilon\); \(\sigma_+(\epsilon)=1+\sqrt2>0>1-\sqrt2=\sigma_-(\epsilon)\), so the four sign vectors differ, and squares of units are totally positive, so the four classes are distinct. (3) A totally positive unit has sign vector \((+,+)\), so lies in the class of \(1\).

docs.title: Residue computations modulo seven
docs.text:
ZInQ.residues_mod_seven ZInQ.not_isSquare_neg_one_zmod_seven

The following closed statements about integers modulo \(7\) hold:

  1. \(3^2\equiv2\pmod 7\);
  2. \(75-53\cdot3=-84\equiv0\pmod7\), and \(3-3=0\);
  3. for every \(t\in\mathbb Z/7\mathbb Z\), \(t^2\ne-1\) (the squares modulo \(7\) are \(0,1,2,4\)).

They say that \(s\mapsto3\) defines a ring homomorphism \(\mathbb Z[s]\to\mathbb F_7\) killing \(d\) and \(\delta\), and that \(-1\) is not a square in \(\mathbb F_7\). This is a finite computation.

Proof sketch. Direct evaluation; the third item is a check of the seven residues.

docs.title: The primes \((s)\) and \((d)\) of \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.prime_sqrt2Z ZInQ.prime_genDZ ZInQ.vS_formula_withTop
  1. \(s\) is a prime element of \(\mathbb Z[s]\), \(2=s^2\), and \(\mathbb Z[s]/(s)\cong\mathbb F_2\) via \(a_0+a_1s\mapsto a_0\bmod2\). For \(c_0,c_1\in\mathbb Q\) not both zero, $\(v_s(c_0+c_1s)=\min\bigl(2v_2(c_0),\ 2v_2(c_1)+1\bigr),\)$ with \(v_2\) the \(2\)-adic valuation on \(\mathbb Q\) and \(v_2(0)=+\infty\).
  2. \(d=75-53s\) is a prime element with \(\operatorname N(d)=7\), and \(\mathbb Z[s]/(d)\cong\mathbb F_7\) via \(a_0+a_1s\mapsto a_0+3a_1\bmod7\). In this residue field \(-1\) is not a square.
  3. \(\delta=3-s=\epsilon^4d\) with \(\epsilon^4=17+12s\), so \(\delta\) and \(d\) are associates and \(v_d=v_\delta\). Moreover \(v_s(d)=v_s(\delta)=v_s(\epsilon)=0\), \(v_d(s)=v_d(2)=0\), and \(d\) is totally positive (\(\sigma_\pm(d)=75\mp53\sqrt2>0\)), as is \(\delta\).

Proof sketch. An element whose norm is \(\pm\) a rational prime is irreducible, hence prime in the principal ideal domain \(\mathbb Z[s]\); \(\operatorname N(s)=-2\), \(\operatorname N(d)=7\). The residue maps are ring homomorphisms by the residue computations modulo seven (and \(s^2=2\equiv0\) modulo \(2\)), surjective, with kernels \((s)\) and \((d)\) since the quotients have \(|\operatorname N|\) elements. For the formula in (1), \(v_s\) of a rational \(c\) is \(2v_2(c)\) and of \(cs\) is \(2v_2(c)+1\); the two values have different parity, so the valuation of the sum is their minimum. (3) is the identity \((75-53s)(17+12s)=3-s\), and \(75^2=5625>5618=2\cdot53^2\).

docs.title: A dyadic valuation computation
docs.text:
ZInQ.vS_sq_add_one ZInQ.val_s_sq_add_delta_sq
  1. Let \(A,B\in\mathbb Q\) with \(v_2(A)=0\) and \(v_2(B)\ge0\) (so \(A+Bs\) is a unit at the prime \((s)\)). Then \(v_s\bigl((A+Bs)^2+1\bigr)=2\) if \(v_2(B)\ge1\), and \(=3\) if \(v_2(B)=0\).
  2. Consequently, for \(a,b\in\mathbb Z[s]\) with \(s\nmid a\) and \(s\nmid b\), $\(v_s\bigl(a^2+\delta^2b^2\bigr)\in\{2,3\}.\)$

Proof sketch. (1) \((A+Bs)^2+1=(A^2+2B^2+1)+2ABs\). A \(2\)-adic unit has \(A^2\equiv1\pmod 8\). If \(B\) is even, the rational part is \(\equiv2\pmod8\), of \(2\)-adic valuation \(1\), while \(v_2(2AB)\ge2\); by the valuation formula at \((s)\) the valuation is \(\min(2,\ge5)=2\). If \(B\) is a \(2\)-adic unit, the rational part is \(\equiv4\pmod8\) (valuation \(2\)) and \(v_2(2AB)=1\), giving \(\min(4,3)=3\). (2) \(\delta b\) is prime to \(s\) since \(v_s(\delta)=0\). Put \(w=a/(\delta b)=a\,\overline{\delta b}/\operatorname N(\delta b)\); here \(\operatorname N(\delta b)\) is odd and \(a\,\overline{\delta b}\in\mathbb Z[s]\) is prime to \(s\), so its rational component is odd. Hence \(w=A+Bs\) as in (1), and \(a^2+\delta^2b^2=(\delta b)^2(w^2+1)\) with \(v_s((\delta b)^2)=0\).

For \(x\in K_0\) let \(h(x)\) be the absolute logarithmic Weil height, $\(h(x)=\frac1{[K_0:\mathbb Q]}\sum_{v}n_v\log\max(1,|x|_v) =\frac12\sum_v n_v\log\max(1,|x|_v),\)$ the sum over the places \(v\) of \(K_0\) (the two real places and the finite places), with \(|\cdot|_v\) extending the usual absolute value of \(\mathbb Q\) and local degrees \(n_v\). For a point \(T\in C(K_0)\) put $\(h_x(T)=h(x(T))\ \ (T\ne O),\qquad h_x(O)=0 .\)$ For \(x\in\mathbb Q\) this is the height \(\log\max(|a|,b)\) of a reduced fraction \(a/b\).

docs.title: The height of a fraction in \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.hK0_div ZInQ.hK0_div_of_isCoprime ZInQ.hK0_ratCast

Let \(a,b\in\mathbb Z[s]\) with \(b\ne0\), and let \(g\) be a greatest common divisor of \(a\) and \(b\) in \(\mathbb Z[s]\). Then $\(h(a/b)=\frac12\Bigl(\log\max(|\sigma_+a|,|\sigma_+b|)+\log\max(|\sigma_-a|,|\sigma_-b|) -\log|\operatorname N(g)|\Bigr).\)$ In particular, for coprime \(a,b\), \(\exp(2h(a/b))=\max(|\sigma_+a|,|\sigma_+b|)\cdot\max(|\sigma_-a|,|\sigma_-b|)\); for a rational \(p/q\) in lowest terms with \(q>0\), \(h(p/q)=\log\max(|p|,q)\); and \(h\ge0\).

Proof sketch. Write \(a=ga'\), \(b=gb'\) with \(a',b'\) coprime; the right side is unchanged because \(\prod_\sigma|\sigma g|=|\operatorname N(g)|\). For coprime \(a',b'\) and \(x=a'/b'\), \(\sum_v n_v\log\max(1,|x|_v)=\sum_v n_v\log\max(|a'|_v,|b'|_v)-\sum_vn_v\log|b'|_v\); the last sum vanishes by the product formula, and at every finite place \(\max(|a'|_v,|b'|_v)=1\) by coprimality, leaving the two real places. Integers \(p,q\) coprime in \(\mathbb Z\) are coprime in \(\mathbb Z[s]\), and then both real places give \(\max(|p|,q)\).

Put $\(F_2(a,b)=(a^2+\delta^2b^2)^2,\qquad G_2(a,b)=4ab(a^2-\delta^2b^2).\)$ Let \(T=(x,y)\in C(K_0)\) with \(y e0\), and let \(a,b\in\mathbb Z[s]\) with \(b e0\) and \(x=a/b\). Then \(G_2(a,b) e0\), \([2]T e O\) and $\(x([2]T)= rac{F_2(a,b)}{G_2(a,b)} .\)$ If instead \(y=0\), then \([2]T=O\).

With the tangent slope \(\lambda=(3x^2-\delta^2)/(2y)\), \(x([2]T)=\lambda^2-2x= rac{(3x^2-\delta^2)^2-8x(x^3-\delta^2x)}{4y^2}= rac{(x^2+\delta^2)^2}{4x(x^2-\delta^2)}\), using \(y^2=x(x^2-\delta^2)\); homogenize with \(x=a/b\). Since \(y e0\), \(x otin\{0,\delta,-\delta\}\), so \(a e0\) and \(a^2 e\delta^2b^2\), hence \(G_2(a,b) e0\). A point with \(y=0\) equals its own negative.

docs.title: Archimedean bounds for the duplication forms
docs.text:
ZInQ.duplication_archimedean

Let \(\Delta\) be a real number with \(1\le\Delta\le5\), let \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), \(M=\max(|a|,|b|)\), \(F=(a^2+\Delta^2b^2)^2\) and \(G=4ab(a^2-\Delta^2b^2)\). Then $\(M^4\le\max(|F|,|G|)\le676\,M^4 .\)$ Since \(\sigma_\pm(\delta)=3\mp\sqrt2\in[1,5]\), at either real embedding of \(K_0\) the values of the duplication forms satisfy \(\max(|\sigma a|,|\sigma b|)^4\le\max(|\sigma F_2(a,b)|,|\sigma G_2(a,b)|)\le676\max(|\sigma a|,|\sigma b|)^4\).

Proof sketch. \(a^2+\Delta^2b^2\ge a^2+b^2\ge M^2\) gives the lower bound from \(F\) alone. \(a^2+\Delta^2b^2\le26M^2\) gives \(F\le676M^4\), and \(|G|\le4|a||b|(a^2+\Delta^2b^2)\le104M^4\). The constant \(676=26^2\).

docs.title: The common divisor of the duplication forms
docs.text:
ZInQ.duplication_common_divisor

Let \(a,b\in\mathbb Z[s]\) be coprime and let \(g\) be a greatest common divisor of \(F_2(a,b)\) and \(G_2(a,b)\) (assume they are not both zero). Then \(v_\pi(g)=0\) for every prime \(\pi\) associate to neither \(s\) nor \(\delta\), \(v_s(g)\le6\) and \(v_\delta(g)\le4\). Consequently $\(|\operatorname N(g)|\le2^6\cdot7^4=392^2 .\)$

Proof sketch. It suffices to bound \(v_\pi(F_2(a,b))\) whenever \(\pi\) divides both forms. Primes \(\pi mid2\delta\). If \(\pi\mid a\) then \(\pi\mid a^2+\delta^2b^2\) forces \(\pi\mid b\); similarly \(\pi\mid b\) forces \(\pi\mid a\); and \(\pi\mid a^2-\delta^2b^2\) together with \(\pi\mid a^2+\delta^2b^2\) gives \(\pi\mid2a^2\). All contradict coprimality. At \(\delta\). If \(\delta mid a\), \(F_2\equiv a^4 ot\equiv0\). If \(\delta\mid a\), then \(\delta mid b\) and with \(a=\delta a'\), \(F_2=\delta^4(a'^2+b^2)^2\); since \(-1\) is not a square modulo \(\delta\) (residue field \(\mathbb F_7\)), \(\delta mid a'^2+b^2\), so \(v_\delta(F_2)=4\). At \(s\). If exactly one of \(a,b\) is divisible by \(s\), \(a^2+\delta^2b^2\) is prime to \(s\) and \(v_s(F_2)=0\). If neither is, the dyadic valuation computation gives \(v_s(a^2+\delta^2b^2)\in\{2,3\}\), so \(v_s(F_2)\le6\). Finally \(|\operatorname N(s)|=2\), \(|\operatorname N(\delta)|=7\) and \(2^6\cdot7^4=153664=392^2\).

docs.title: Height bounds for doubling on \(C\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.hx_two_smul_bounds

For every \(T\in C(K_0)\), $\(4h_x(T)-\log392\ \le\ h_x([2]T)\ \le\ 4h_x(T)+\log676 .\)$

Proof sketch. If \(T=O\) both sides are trivial. If \(T=(x,0)\), then \([2]T=O\) and \(x\in\{0,\pm\delta\}\) with \(h(0)=0\) and \(h(\pm\delta)=\tfrac12\log7\) (since \(\operatorname N(\delta)=7\) and both embeddings of \(\delta\) exceed \(1\)); then \(4h_x(T)-\log392\le2\log7-\log392<0\) and the upper bound is trivial. Otherwise write \(x(T)=a/b\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb Z[s]\) coprime, so \(h_x(T)=\frac12\sum_\sigma\log M_\sigma\) with \(M_\sigma=\max(|\sigma a|,|\sigma b|)\). By the duplication forms \(x([2]T)=F_2(a,b)/G_2(a,b)\), and by the height of a fraction with \(g=\gcd(F_2,G_2)\), $\(h_x([2]T)=\tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_\sigma\log\max(|\sigma F_2|,|\sigma G_2|)-\log|\operatorname N(g)|\Bigr).\)$ The archimedean bounds give \(4\log M_\sigma\le\log\max(|\sigma F_2|,|\sigma G_2|)\le\log676+4\log M_\sigma\), and \(0\le\log|\operatorname N(g)|\le2\log392\) by the common-divisor lemma. Combining yields both inequalities.

docs.title: The canonical height
docs.text: The canonical height is the limit of \(4^{-m}h_x([2^m]T)\); it differs from \(h_x\) by bounded amounts and is a quadratic form.

docs.title: The canonical height on \(C(K_0)\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.canonHeight

For \(T\in C(K_0)\) the canonical height \(\widehat h(T)\) is defined by $\(2\,\widehat h(T)=\lim_{m\to\infty}4^{-m}\,h_x\bigl([2^m]T\bigr).\)$ Formally, \(\widehat h(T)\) is half the limit of the real sequence \(4^{-m}h_x([2^m]T)\); that the sequence converges for every \(T\) is proved, from the duplication height bounds, with the basic properties of \(\widehat h\). The factor \(2\) is the manuscript's normalization, under which \(2\widehat h\) is comparable with \(h_x\).

docs.title: Basic properties of the canonical height
docs.text:
ZInQ.canonHeight_tendsto ZInQ.two_canonHeight_le ZInQ.hx_le_two_canonHeight ZInQ.canonHeight_two_smul ZInQ.canonHeight_add_twoTorsion

For every \(T\in C(K_0)\) the limit defining \(\widehat h(T)\) exists, and:

  1. \[2\widehat h(T)\le h_x(T)+\frac{\log676}{3}\qquad\text{and}\qquad h_x(T)\le2\widehat h(T)+\frac{\log392}{3};\]
  2. \(\widehat h([2]T)=4\widehat h(T)\);
  3. \(\widehat h(-T)=\widehat h(T)\), and \(\widehat h(T+T')=\widehat h(T)\) for every \(T'\in C(K_0)[2]\);
  4. \(\widehat h(T)\ge0\).

Proof sketch. Put \(c_m=4^{-m}h_x([2^m]T)\). The duplication height bounds give \(-4^{-m-1}\log392\le c_{m+1}-c_m\le4^{-m-1}\log676\), so \((c_m)\) is Cauchy, and summing the geometric series from \(m=0\) gives \(-\frac{\log392}3\le\lim c_m-h_x(T)\le\frac{\log676}3\), which is (1). (2) is a shift of the index. (3): \(x(-P)=x(P)\) and \([2^m](-T)=-[2^m]T\); and \([2](T+T')=[2]T\), so by (2) \(\widehat h(T+T')=\widehat h([2]T)/4=\widehat h(T)\). (4) holds since \(h_x\ge0\).

docs.title: The canonical height is quadratic
docs.text:
ZInQ.canonHeight_parallelogram ZInQ.canonHeight_zsmul

For all \(P,Q\in C(K_0)\) and \(m\in\mathbb Z\), $\(\widehat h(P+Q)+\widehat h(P-Q)=2\widehat h(P)+2\widehat h(Q),\qquad \widehat h([m]P)=m^2\,\widehat h(P).\)$

Proof sketch. (Silverman, Theorem VIII.9.3; Néron-Tate.) The naive height satisfies the approximate parallelogram law: there is a constant \(c\) with \(|h_x(P+Q)+h_x(P-Q)-2h_x(P)-2h_x(Q)|\le c\) for all \(P,Q\) (Silverman, Theorem VIII.6.2). Apply it to \([2^n]P,[2^n]Q\), divide by \(4^n\) and let \(n\to\infty\): since \([2^n](P\pm Q)=[2^n]P\pm[2^n]Q\), the error \(c/4^n\) tends to \(0\) and the exact parallelogram law follows. Taking \(Q=P\) gives \(\widehat h(O)=0\) and the case \(m=2\); induction on \(m\ge1\) with \(\widehat h((m+1)P)=2\widehat h(mP)+2\widehat h(P)-\widehat h((m-1)P)\) gives \(m^2\widehat h(P)\), and \(\widehat h(-P)=\widehat h(P)\) gives negative \(m\). The constant \(c\) is not needed explicitly.

If \(R\) were \([m]S+T\) with \(|m|\ge3\), the generator \(S\) would have \(h_x(S)<\log9\), by \(h_x(2R)=\log41\) and one explicit integer comparison.

A point of such small height has its abscissa in an explicit finite set: \(14{,}008\) roots of \(7{,}004\) primitive quadratics and \(111\) rationals. An exact square test leaves only the two-torsion abscissas and the four translates of \(R\).

docs.title: The height of \(2R\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.hx_two_R

\(h_x([2]R)=h\bigl(\tfrac{57-28s}{8}\bigr)=\log41\).

The proof reduces to three closed integer facts, a finite computation: $\(57^2-2\cdot28^2=41^2\ (=1681),\qquad 49^2>2\cdot28^2\ (2401>1568),\qquad 57\text{ is odd}.\)$

Proof sketch. By the certificate for \(R\), \(x([2]R)=a/b\) with \(a=57-28s\) and \(b=8=s^6\). The only prime dividing \(b\) is \(s\), and \(s\nmid a\) because \(57\) is odd, so \(a,b\) are coprime. Both embeddings of \(a\) exceed \(8\): \(57+28\sqrt2>8\) trivially, and \(57-28\sqrt2>8\) because \(49>28\sqrt2\), i.e. \(49^2>2\cdot28^2\). By the height of a fraction, \(h=\tfrac12\log(\sigma_+(a)\sigma_-(a))=\tfrac12\log\operatorname N(a)=\tfrac12\log41^2\).

The following inequalities between natural numbers hold: $\(41^3\cdot676\cdot392^{36}<9^{108},\qquad 392<41^3 .\)$ Equivalently \(\frac{\log(41^3\cdot676)}{108}+\frac{\log392}{3}<\log9\) and \(\log41>\frac{\log392}{3}\). This is a finite computation: the two sides of the first inequality have \(102\) and \(104\) decimal digits.

Proof sketch. Evaluate both sides; \(41^3=68921\). The logarithmic forms follow by monotonicity of \(\log\) after multiplying the first by \(108\) and the second by \(3\).

  1. \(\widehat h(R)>0\); more precisely \(8\widehat h(R)=2\widehat h([2]R)\ge\log41-\frac{\log392}{3}>0\).
  2. If \(R=[m]S+T\) with \(S\in C(K_0)\), \(T\in C(K_0)[2]\) and \(m\in\mathbb Z\), \(|m|\ge3\), then $\(h_x(S)\le\frac{\log(41^3\cdot676)}{108}+\frac{\log392}{3}<\log9 .\)$

By the basic properties and the height of \(2R\), \(2\widehat h([2]R)\ge h_x([2]R)-\frac{\log392}3=\log41-\frac{\log392}3\), positive by the comparison \(392<41^3\), and \(\widehat h([2]R)=4\widehat h(R)\); this is (1). For (2), \(2\widehat h([2]R)\le h_x([2]R)+\frac{\log676}{3}=\log41+\frac{\log676}{3}\), so \(2\widehat h(R)\le\frac{3\log41+\log676}{12}=\frac{\log(41^3\cdot676)}{12}\). Since \(T\) is two-torsion and \(\widehat h\) is quadratic, \(\widehat h(R)=\widehat h([m]S)=m^2\widehat h(S)\ge9\widehat h(S)\), so \(2\widehat h(S)\le\frac{\log(41^3\cdot676)}{108}\). Then \(h_x(S)\le2\widehat h(S)+\frac{\log392}{3}\), and the final strict inequality is the comparison \(41^3\cdot676\cdot392^{36}<9^{108}\).

docs.title: The search box for small heights
docs.text:
ZInQ.search_box

Let \(x\in K_0\) with \(h(x)<\log9\).

  1. If \(x\in\mathbb Q\), then \(x=p/q\) with \(p,q\in\mathbb Z\) coprime, \(|p|\le9\) and \(1\le q\le9\) (in fact \(|p|,q\le8\)).
  2. If \(x\notin\mathbb Q\), then there are integers \(a,b,c,k\) with $\(1\le a\le81,\quad|b|\le162,\quad|c|\le81,\quad\gcd(a,b,c)=1,\quad b^2-4ac=2k^2,\quad 1\le k\le162,\)$ such that \(x=\frac{-b+ks}{2a}\) or \(x=\frac{-b-ks}{2a}\); then \(aX^2+bX+c\) is the primitive minimal polynomial of \(x\) and both its roots lie in \(K_0\).

Proof sketch. (1) \(h(p/q)=\log\max(|p|,q)<\log9\). (2) Write \(x=u+vs\) with \(v\ne0\) and \(x=\alpha/\beta\) with \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Z[s]\) coprime. The integer polynomial \(f(X)=\operatorname N(\beta X-\alpha)=\operatorname N(\beta)X^2-\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha\bar\beta)X+\operatorname N(\alpha)\) has the real roots \(r_\pm=\sigma_\pm(x)\), and \(|\operatorname N(\beta)|\max(1,|r_+|)\max(1,|r_-|)=\prod_\sigma\max(|\sigma\alpha|,|\sigma\beta|)=e^{2h(x)}<81\). Divide \(f\) by its content and fix the sign to get \(aX^2+bX+c\) with \(a\ge1\) and \(a\max(1,|r_+|)\max(1,|r_-|)<81\). Then \(a<81\), \(|b|=a|r_++r_-|<162\) and \(|c|=a|r_+r_-|<81\). The discriminant is \(a^2(r_+-r_-)^2=8a^2v^2=2k^2\) with \(k=2a|v|>0\); as \(2k^2\in\mathbb Z\) and \(k\in\mathbb Q\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\), and \(2k^2<162^2+4\cdot81^2=2\cdot162^2\) gives \(k<162\). Finally \(2au=-b\) and \(2av=\pm k\).
