docs.title: An exact square test in \(K_0\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.SqTest ZInQ.isSquare_iff_sqTest

For \(u,v\in\mathbb Q\) say that \(\mathrm{Sq}(u,v)\) holds if there are a sign \(\eta\in\{1,-1\}\) and rationals \(t,y_0\) with $\(t^2=u^2-2v^2,\qquad y_0^2=\frac{u+\eta t}{2},\)$ such that either \(y_0\ne0\) and \(\bigl(y_0+\tfrac{v}{2y_0}s\bigr)^2=u+vs\), or \(y_0=0\), \(v=0\) and \(u/2=y_1^2\) for some \(y_1\in\mathbb Q\). Then $\(u+vs\ \text{is a square in }K_0\iff\mathrm{Sq}(u,v),\)$ including the case \(u+vs=0\). Since a rational number has a rational square root exactly when its reduced numerator and denominator are perfect squares (and it is nonnegative), \(\mathrm{Sq}\) is decidable by finitely many integer square-root extractions.

Proof sketch. (\(\Leftarrow\)) In the first case the square is exhibited; in the second \((y_1s)^2=2y_1^2=u=u+vs\). (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(u+vs=(y_0+y_1s)^2\), then \(u=y_0^2+2y_1^2\), \(v=2y_0y_1\) and \(u^2-2v^2=(y_0^2-2y_1^2)^2\). Take \(t=|y_0^2-2y_1^2|\) and \(\eta\) with \(\eta t=y_0^2-2y_1^2\); then \((u+\eta t)/2=y_0^2\). If \(y_0\ne0\), \(y_1=v/(2y_0)\); if \(y_0=0\), then \(v=0\) and \(u=2y_1^2\).

ZInQ.smallHeight_search

Let \(f(x)=x^3-\delta^2x\) with \(\delta^2=11-6s\). Let \(\mathcal Q\) be the set of integer triples \((a,b,c)\) with \(1\le a\le81\), \(|b|\le162\), \(|c|\le81\), \(\gcd(a,b,c)=1\) and \(b^2-4ac=2k^2\) for an integer \(1\le k\le162\); let \(\mathcal X_2\) be the set of the numbers \(x=\frac{-b\pm ks}{2a}\in K_0\) for \((a,b,c)\in\mathcal Q\) and both signs; and let \(\mathcal X_1\) be the set of rationals \(p/q\) with \(\gcd(p,q)=1\), \(|p|\le9\), \(1\le q\le9\). Then:

  1. \(|\mathcal Q|=7004\), the roots counted with their sign number \(14008\), and \(|\mathcal X_1|=111\);
  2. for \(x\in\mathcal X_1\cup\mathcal X_2\), \(f(x)\) is a square in \(K_0\) if and only if $\(x\in\Bigl\{0,\ \delta,\ -\delta,\ 1+s,\ 23-17s,\ 2+4s,\ \tfrac{5-4s}{2}\Bigr\}.\)$

Each membership test is the exact square test applied to the two rational components of \(f(x)\). This is a finite computation over explicit finite sets.

Proof sketch. Enumerate the box: for each \((a,b,c)\) check primitivity and whether \((b^2-4ac)/2\) is a positive perfect square \(k^2\) with \(k\le162\); for each resulting \(x\) and each rational candidate compute the components of \(f(x)\) exactly and run the square test. An independent replay of exactly this computation gives the stated counts and survivors.

docs.title: Multiplication and the finite false-triple guard
Multiplication and the finite false-triple guard
docs.text:
The multiplication template is the arithmetic core of the construction: it must accept a triple of rational \(5\)-tuples exactly when they are the codes \(\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(ab)\) of integer multiples of the generator \(P_0\) of \(2E(K_0)\). Its \(35{,}134\) witnesses consist of three rational constants fixing \(P_0\), four fixed scalar multiples by \(c_*=4M_0\), one height certificate of \(27\) slope certificates with six test groups each, and one inverse of a finite guard product. This chapter proves input M of the assembly lemma.

The proof is asymmetric. Soundness (accepted triples are true) works on arbitrary rational inputs and uses the six-contact height estimate H: at every odd contact prime of every slope outside \(S_{\rm mul}\), the certificate forces \(n_1n_2\equiv n_3\) modulo \(p^{25}\), so H bounds a false triple to the box \([-T,T]^3\) with \(T=(48A_{\rm ht})^{13}\), where the guard excludes it. Completeness (true triples are accepted) uses the twenty-two-prime pattern 22P to choose slopes with controlled contact primes and pole completeness PC to supply the pole witnesses. Both directions use the generator certificate \(2E(K_0)=\mathbb ZP_0\), whose Mordell-Weil input is proved by the two-isogeny descent. The astronomically large constants \(c_*\), \(\ell_0\), \(A_{\rm ht}\) and \(T\) appear only symbolically; the finite computations of the chapter are a few small closed identities and inequalities.

3 fully proved

docs.title: The pole obstruction
docs.text: Write \(\Phi(B)\) for the rational solubility of the pole polynomial \(Q_{\rm pole}\) with input \(B\). For \(B\ne0\) the witnesses give a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) and points \((A,r_1)\in C_e\), \((Az^2,zr_2)\in C_{eH}\) on the congruent number curves \(C_\ell:y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+\ell)\) (the manuscript has \(x+3\ell\)), and a parity argument on the valuation of the abscissa shows that \(\Phi(B)\) is impossible when \(v_p(B)\) is negative and odd at a prime \(p\notin\{2,3,5,7,13\}\). This elementary direction is what soundness uses; the converse, pole completeness, is used only for completeness, and the Route K chapter proves it from the certified rank hypothesis.

docs.title: Parity of the abscissa on \(y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+\ell)\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.abscissa_val_even

Let \(p\) be a prime, \(\ell\in\mathbb Q^ imes\) with \(v_p(\ell)\) even, and \(x,y\in\mathbb Q\) with \(x e0\) and $\(y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+\ell).\)$ Then \(v_p(x)\) is even.

Proof sketch. If \(v_p(x)=v_p(\ell)\) there is nothing to prove. Otherwise \(v_p(x-\ell)=v_p(x+\ell)=\min(v_p(x),v_p(\ell))\), by the equality case of the ultrametric inequality, at every prime \(p\); in particular both factors are nonzero, so the right side is nonzero, \(y e0\), and $\(2v_p(y)=v_p(x)+2\min igl(v_p(x),v_p(\ell) igr).\)$ Hence \(v_p(x)\) is even. (This is the manuscript's square-scaling step: after scaling \(\ell\) to a unit, the cubic has valuation \(v_p(x)\) if \(v_p(x)>0\) and \(3v_p(x)\) if \(v_p(x)<0\).) The manuscript's curve \(y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+3\ell)\) needs \(p e3\) at this step; the Route K curve needs no condition on \(p\).

docs.title: The one-sided pole obstruction
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.pole_obstruction

Let \(S_0=\{2,3,5,7,13\}\) and let \(\Phi(B)\) be the rational solubility of the pole polynomial \(Q_{ m pole}\) with input \(B\), as in pole completeness (that article is linked for the definition of \(\Phi\) only; the hypothesis PC is not assumed). If \(B\in\mathbb Q\), \(B e0\) and \(\Phi(B)\), then for every prime \(p otin S_0\) it is not the case that \(v_p(B)\) is negative and odd.

This is Lemma 5.1, for the Route K pole polynomial, whose curves are \(y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+\ell)\) instead of the manuscript's \(y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+3\ell)\); the statement and \(S_0\) are unchanged. It uses no hypothesis: it is the elementary direction of the pole predicate, and the multiplication soundness argument uses it at the odd contact primes.

Proof sketch. Take a rational zero \((b_0,\dots,b_5,e,z,r_1,r_2,w)\) of \(Q_{ m pole}\) with input \(B e0\). Since \(B e0\) the sum of squares in \(Q_{ m pole}\) vanishes, so every summand does: \(b_i^2=b_i\), hence \(b_i\in\{0,1\}\); \(eHzw=1\), hence \(e,H,z e0\); \(r_1^2=T_1\) and \(r_2^2=T_2\). The multiplier \(m\) is a product of factors in \(\{\pm1\},\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{1,5\},\{1,7\},\{1,13\}\), so it is a signed divisor of \(2730=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\) and \(v_p(m)=0\) for \(p otin S_0\).

Suppose \(k=v_p(B)<0\) is odd. Then \(v_p(A)=v_p(mB)=k\); since \(2k<k\), \(v_p(A-B^2)=2k\), so \(v_p(H)=3k\). The equations say that \((A,r_1)\) lies on \(C_e:y^2=x(x-e)(x+e)\) and, multiplying \(r_2^2=T_2\) by \(z^2\), that \((Az^2,zr_2)\) lies on \(C_{eH}\): \((zr_2)^2=z^2T_2=Az^2(Az^2-eH)(Az^2+eH)\). Both abscissas are nonzero (\(m e0\) because \(1-2b_0=\pm1\) and the other factors are positive, and \(z e0\)), and both parameters \(e,eH\) are nonzero. The valuations of \(e\) and \(eH\) differ by the odd number \(3k\), so exactly one of them is even. If \(v_p(e)\) is even, the parity lemma applied to \((A,r_1)\) makes \(v_p(A)=k\) even; if \(v_p(eH)\) is even, it makes \(v_p(Az^2)=k+2v_p(z)\) even. Both contradict \(k\) odd.

docs.title: Correctness of the multiplication template
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.multiplication_exact ZInQ.Mult.multiplication_exact_unique ZInQ.Mult.multiplication_existsUnique

Assume the minimal height hypothesis, pole completeness and the slope representation. For all \(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3\in\mathbb Q^5\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)\iff\exists\,a,b\in\mathbb Z:\quad (Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)=\bigl(\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(ab)\bigr),\)$ where \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)\) means that the polynomial of the multiplication template, which has \(15\) parameters and \(35{,}134\) witnesses, vanishes at \((Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)\) and some \(w\in\mathbb Q^{35134}\). The inputs are arbitrary rational \(5\)-tuples, not assumed to be codes; when the relation holds, \(a\) and \(b\) are unique.

This is input M of the assembly lemma. The two directions use different hypotheses:

  • soundness (\(\Rightarrow\)) uses the six-contact estimate H in its minimal form (through the finite-box deduction) and the generator certificate, but not pole completeness and not the slope representation;
  • completeness (\(\Leftarrow\)) uses pole completeness PC and the slope representation, which the prime pattern 22P gives (to build the slope certificates of a true triple), and the generator certificate (through the fixed-scalar and guard semantics), but not the six-contact estimate.

Neither direction uses the catalogue bound. The Mordell–Weil input of the generator certificate is proved by the two-isogeny descent, so it is not a hypothesis. No constant of the template (\(c_*\), \(\ell_0\), \(T\)) is evaluated. The template's three parameter points, written \(P_0,P_1,P_2\) in the specification, are written \(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3\) in this chapter, since \(P_0\) denotes the generator.

Proof sketch. Combine soundness of the multiplication template with completeness of the multiplication template. Uniqueness of \(a,b\) is injectivity of \(\iota\) (the generator certificate).

docs.title: The certificate and its semantics
docs.text:
This section fixes the constants of the multiplication certificate and translates each of its templates into a mathematical predicate. All statements here are exact equivalences for the constructed templates, proved from the semantics of the expression language; the arithmetic happens in the soundness and completeness sections.

11 fully proved

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: The certificate uses the prescribed constants \(c_*=4M_0\), \(\ell_0=12P_s^{2916}H_{\rm cat}^{732}\), \(R\), \(A_{\rm ht}\) and \(T\) of the specification. The sound direction works outside \(S_{\rm mul}=S_{\rm ht}\cup\mathcal H\cup\operatorname{supp}(c_*)\); the complete direction clears denominators at the old primes \(S_b=S_{\rm ht}\cup\mathcal H\) with the exponents \(B_p\), \(C_p=14B_p\), \(D_p=51C_p\), \(E_p=52C_p+v_p(12)+4\).   1. \(M_0\ge1\), so \(c_*=4M_0\ge4\), and \(\ell_0\ge1\).
  2. \(S_{ m mul}\) is a finite set of primes containing every prime \(p\le324\); every \(p\in S_{ m mul}\) satisfies \(p\le R\); and \(R\ge D\), \(R\ge10^{12}\). Hence the six-contact estimate applies with \(S=S_{ m mul}\) and this \(R\), and its constant is \(H_6(S_{ m mul};R)=A_{ m ht}\) (as real numbers, \(Q=R^{RE_0}\) being an integer power). Under the minimal height hypothesis, \(h(u)\le A_{ m ht}M_{S_{ m mul}}(u)^{24}\) for every \(u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\mathcal C\), since \(H_6(D)\le H_6(S_{ m mul};R)\).
  3. \(A_{ m ht}\ge2\cdot10^{13}\); in particular \(48A_{ m ht}\ge1\) and \(T=(48A_{ m ht})^{13}>4\).
  4. The catalogue primes exceed \(324\) and are pairwise distinct, so \(H_{ m cat}\) is squarefree with set of prime factors \(\mathcal H\). Consequently \(v_p(\ell_0)=E_p\) for \(p\in S_b\) and \(v_p(\ell_0)=0\) for every prime \(p otin S_b\).
  5. Every prime \(p otin S_{ m mul}\) satisfies \(p>324\), \(p mid c_*\), \(p mid\ell_0\) and \(p otin S_0=\{2,3,5,7,13\}\).

No constant is evaluated: every item follows from the defining expressions.

Proof sketch. (1) The search defining \(M_0\) succeeds at an index at most \(N_s^{10}\) (the successful formal multiple of the size chapter, with \(N_s\ge1\)), so \(M_0\ge1\). (2) Primes of \(S_{ m ht}\) are at most \(324\le10^{12}\le R\); catalogue primes are at most \(H_{\max}\le R\) by the definition of the catalogue maximum; a prime dividing \(c_*\ge1\) is at most \(c_*\le R\). \(S_{ m mul}\) is finite because the catalogue is finite and \(c_* e0\). The six-contact constant at \(R\) is \(2\cdot10^{13}\max(1,C_{ m cm},Q_R^{17})\) with \(Q_R=R^{RE_0}\), literally \(A_{ m ht}\); it is increasing in \(R\ge1\), and \(R\ge D\). (3) is immediate from the maximum with \(1\). (4) Distinct residue classes, or distinct positions in one class, give distinct primes. Then \(v_p(\ell_0)=v_p(12)+2916\) for \(p\le324\) and \(v_p(\ell_0)=732\) for \(p\in\mathcal H\), which equal \(E_p\) by the clearing arithmetic (\(C_p=56\), resp. \(C_p=14\) and \(v_p(12)=0\)). (5) \(S_{ m mul}\) contains all primes at most \(324\) and all prime divisors of \(c_*\) and of \(\ell_0\).

docs.title: The local templates and the twelve tests
docs.text:
The templates \(\mathtt{raw\_z}\), \(\mathtt{raw\_inverse\_x}\) and \(\mathtt{log25}\) compute \(z=-x/y\), \(1/x\) and the truncated logarithm \(L\) on codes of \(2E(K_0)\).

For indices \(n_1,n_2,n_3\), a test group chooses \(H=[h]P_0\) and \(U_i=[z_i]P_0\) and sets \(V_0=H-[c_*]P_0\), \(V_i=U_i-[c_*n_i]P_0\). Its twelve tests are the four inverse abscissas at \(H,U_i\), their conjugate counterparts at \(V_0,V_i\), three differences of \(L\)-ratios and one product test. Identity inverse abscissas are zero, and the two guarded denominators are nonzero once \(H\) and \(V_0\) are not the identity.

docs.title: Semantics of the local-parameter, inverse-abscissa and logarithm templates
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.rawZ_rel_iff_of ZInQ.Mult.rawZ_not_rel ZInQ.Mult.rawInverseX_rel_iff_of ZInQ.Mult.rawInverseX_not_rel ZInQ.Mult.log25_rel_iff ZInQ.Mult.rawZ_rel_iota ZInQ.Mult.rawInverseX_rel_iota

Let \(Q\in E(K_0)\) with code \(p=\operatorname{code}(Q)\), and let \(\zeta,v,\lambda\) be rational pairs, \([u]=u_0+u_1s\).

  1. If \(Q=O\) or \(y(Q) e0\), then \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{raw\_z}}(p,\zeta)\iff[\zeta]=z(Q)\), where \(z(O)=0\) and \(z(Q)=-x(Q)/y(Q)\). If \(Q\) is affine with \(y(Q)=0\), the relation fails for every \(\zeta\).
  2. If \(Q=O\) or \(x(Q) e0\), then \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{raw\_inverse\_x}}(p,v)\iff[v]=1/x(Q)\), with value \(0\) at \(O\). If \(Q\) is affine with \(x(Q)=0\), the relation fails for every \(v\).
  3. For all pairs \(\zeta,\lambda\): \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{log25}}(\zeta,\lambda)\iff[\lambda]=L([\zeta])\).

In particular, for \(Q\in\mathbb ZP_0\) (assuming the generator certificate, so that a nonidentity multiple of \(P_0\) has \(x,y e0\)) the three templates compute \(z(Q)\), \(1/x(Q)\) and \(L(z(Q))\).

Proof sketch. Each template polynomial is the square of the compilation of its formula (\(Z(p,\zeta)\) with one fresh variable, \(I\!X(p,v)\), and the pair equation \(L(\zeta)\doteq\lambda\)), so it vanishes exactly when the formula holds. The pair-arithmetic theorem describes \(Z(p,\zeta)\) and \(I\!X(p,v)\) exactly: the identity branch applies iff \(p=O\), and the affine branch requires \([y(p)] e0\), resp. \([x(p)][v]=1\). For (3), pair arithmetic represents the field operations, so the two components of \(L(\zeta)-\lambda\) vanish iff \([\lambda]=L([\zeta])\).

Let \(h,z_1,z_2,z_3,c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3\in\mathbb Z\) with \(h e0\) and \(h e c_0\). Put $\(A_i= rac{\Lambda(U_i)}{\Lambda(H)},\qquad B_i= rac{\Lambda(V_i)}{\Lambda(V_0)}\qquad(i=1,2,3).\)$ With \(\sigma\) the conjugation of \(K_0\), the twelve test values \( au(h,z;c)=( au_1,\dots, au_{12})\in K_0^{12}\) are $\( egin{aligned} & au_1= ho(H),\quad au_{1+i}= ho(U_i),\quad au_5=\sigma ho(V_0),\quad au_{5+i}=\sigma ho(V_i),\ & au_{8+i}=A_i-\sigma B_i\quad(i=1,2,3),\qquad au_{12}=A_1A_2-A_3 . \end{aligned}\)$ That is: four inverse abscissas at \(H,U_i\), their four conjugate counterparts at \(V_0,V_i\), three differences of the corresponding \(L\)-ratios, and the product of the first two unprimed ratios minus the third. For all \(c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3\in\mathbb Z\) and all rational pairs \(D_1,\dots,D_{12}\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{test\_group}} igl(\iota(c_0),\iota(c_1),\iota(c_2),\iota(c_3),D_1,\dots,D_{12} igr) \iff\exists\,h,z_1,z_2,z_3\in\mathbb Z:\ h e0,\ h e c_0,\ [D_j]= au_j(h,z;c)\ (1\le j\le12).\)$ (The template's output pairs \(D_0,\dots,D_{11}\) are \(D_1,\dots,D_{12}\) here.) The four inputs must be canonical codes, as they are in every use: the raw addition contract is only valid on canonical codes.

Proof sketch. By the evaluation of calls and the lifting of private blocks, the relation holds iff there are values of the \(162\) witnesses satisfying every conjunct. (\(\Rightarrow\)) The membership calls make each \(F_i\) a code \(\iota(f_i)\) (accepted inputs have unique indices). Since \(\operatorname{neg}(\iota(c_i))=\iota(-c_i)\) is canonical, raw addition gives \(V_i=\iota(f_i-c_i)\). The atoms \(\operatorname{fin}(F_0)\) and \(\operatorname{fin}(V_0)\) say \(f_0 e0\) and \(f_0 e c_0\). By the local-template semantics the three calls on each of the eight points give \(\zeta_i=z(\Pi_i)\), \(\lambda_i=L(\zeta_i)\) and \( ho_i=1/x(\Pi_i)\); the inverse atoms give \(\lambda_0,\lambda_4 e0\); the ratio equations give \(q_{\sigma,i}=\lambda_{4\sigma+i}/\lambda_{4\sigma}\); and the final pair equations say \([D_j]= au_j\). Take \(h=f_0\), \(z_i=f_i\). (\(\Leftarrow\)) Put \(F_0=\iota(h)\), \(F_i=\iota(z_i)\), \(V_0=\iota(h-c_0)\), \(V_i=\iota(z_i-c_i)\), choose the member and raw-addition blocks by completeness of those templates, \(\zeta,\lambda, ho\) as computed, the inverse witnesses \(1/N(\lambda_0)\) and \(1/N(\lambda_4)\), which exist by the nonvanishing lemma, and the ratios.

For \(t,\ell\in\mathbb Q\) and \(c=(c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3)\in\mathbb Z^4\), the slope predicate \(\mathrm{Slope}(t,\ell;c)\) holds when all of the following hold:

  1. \(t otin\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\) and \(\ell e0\);
  2. there are \(\eta\in\{1,-1\}\) and \(q\in\mathbb Q\) such that, with $\(R_0= rac{\eta F(t)}{(t-1)^8},\qquad a=1-R_0q^2,\qquad R=\ell^2a^2R_0,\)$ one has \(a e0\);
  3. there are, for \(g=1,\dots,6\), integers \(h_g,z_{g,1},z_{g,2},z_{g,3}\) with \(h_g e0\) and \(h_g e c_0\) such that, with the test values \(D_{gj}= au_j(h_g,z_g;c)\in K_0\) and the normalized values $\(C_{gj}= rac{D_{gj}}{R_0^{k_j}(t-1)^{k_j+1}}\qquad(k_j=1 ext{ for }j\le8,\ k_j=25 ext{ for }j\ge9),\)$ the elements \(W_g=\prod_{j=1}^{12} igl(1+RC_{gj}^2 igr)\) of \(K_0\) and \(\Theta=\operatorname{Tr}\sum_{g=1}^6W_g^{-1}\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy \(W_g e0\) for every \(g\), \(\Theta e0\), and $\(\Phi igl(R/\Theta^2 igr).\)$

Here \(F(t)=t(t+15)(t+20)(t+24)(t+30)(t+60)\), \(\Phi\) is the rational solubility of the pole polynomial, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(u+vs)=2u\). Since \(F(t) e0\), \(\ell e0\) and \(a e0\), the pole input \(R/\Theta^2\) is nonzero, so the prefactor \(B\) of \(Q_{ m pole}\) cannot make the pole constraint vacuous. docs.title: The height certificate and the multiplication template
docs.text:
The height certificate imposes membership on the three inputs, writes each abscissa as \((a_{i0}+a_{i1}s)/b_i\), expresses each of the nine rational quantities as a sum of three slopes, and imposes the slope predicate on all \(27\) slopes. The multiplication template conjoins it with the four fixed scalar graphs, which supply the shift points \(\iota(c_*),\iota(c_*n_i)\), and with the inverse of the finite guard.

The guard is a product, over the false triples \((a,b,c)\in[-T,T]^3\), of denominator-cleared squared distances to \((\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(c))\); its semantics is proved in the specification chapter (semantics of the guard template). By injectivity of codes it passes every true triple and rejects every false triple in the box.

docs.title: Semantics of the height certificate template
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.heightCertificate_rel_iff ZInQ.Mult.HeightCert

For all \(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3\in\mathbb Q^5\), \(\ell\in\mathbb Q\) and \(c\in\mathbb Z^4\), the relation \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{height\_certificate}}(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3,\ell,\iota(c_0),\iota(c_1),\iota(c_2),\iota(c_3))\) holds if and only if:

  1. there are \(n_1,n_2,n_3\in\mathbb Z\) with \(Y_i=\iota(n_i)\); write \(x([n_i]P_0)=x_{i0}+x_{i1}s\) with \(x_{i0},x_{i1}\in\mathbb Q\), where \(x_{i0}=x_{i1}=0\) if \(n_i=0\) (these are the coordinates \((Y_i)_1,(Y_i)_2\));
  2. there are \(a_{i0},a_{i1},b_i\in\mathbb Q\) (\(i=1,2,3\)) with \(b_i\ne0\) and \(b_ix_{ij}=a_{ij}\);
  3. for each of the nine quantities \((Q_1,\dots,Q_9)=(a_{10},a_{11},b_1,a_{20},a_{21},b_2,a_{30},a_{31},b_3)\) there are rationals \(t_{k,1},t_{k,2},t_{k,3}\) with \(t_{k,1}+t_{k,2}+t_{k,3}=Q_k\) and \(\mathrm{Slope}(t_{k,l},\ell;c)\) for \(l=1,2,3\).

Thus the certificate first forces all three inputs to be members of \(2E(K_0)\): membership is a conjunct inside the certificate, not a precondition, so even untyped rational inputs, if accepted, have unique indices.

Proof sketch. Unfold the conjunction of the \(35{,}106\)-witness template. The three membership calls give \(Y_i=\iota(n_i)\) by membership and the generator certificate. The atoms \(b_iu_i\doteq1\), \(b_i(Y_i)_1\doteq a_{i0}\), \(b_i(Y_i)_2\doteq a_{i1}\) are item 2. Each of the nine sum atoms and twenty-seven slope calls gives item 3 through the slope semantics, the four shift points being the canonical codes \(\iota(c_k)\). The converse chooses the same witnesses.

ZInQ.Mult.multiply_rel_iff_unguarded ZInQ.Mult.multiply_rel_iff ZInQ.Mult.multiply_rel_iff_cert

For all \(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3\in\mathbb Q^5\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)\) holds if and only if there are \(n_1,n_2,n_3\in\mathbb Z\) with \(Y_i=\iota(n_i)\) such that $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{height\_certificate}}\bigl(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3,\ell_0,\iota(c_*),\iota(c_*n_1),\iota(c_*n_2),\iota(c_*n_3)\bigr) \quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply.guard}}(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3).\)$ The part without the guard is the unguarded certificate.

docs.title: The guard passes true triples and rejects false triples in the box
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.guard_true_triple ZInQ.Mult.guard_false_triple ZInQ.Mult.guard_rel_iff ZInQ.Mult.guardPoly_zero_set
  1. For all \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply.guard}}(\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(ab))\).
  2. For all \(n_1,n_2,n_3\in\mathbb Z\) with \(|n_i|\le T\) and \(n_1n_2\ne n_3\), \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply.guard}}(\iota(n_1),\iota(n_2),\iota(n_3))\) fails.

That is: a false accepted triple in the box would make its own guard factor zero, while at a true triple every factor is positive by injectivity of codes, so the inverse exists. The cutoff \(T\) is used symbolically.

Proof sketch. By the guard semantics, the guard holds exactly when the input triple is not \((\iota(a'),\iota(b'),\iota(c'))\) for a false triple \((a',b',c')\in[-T,T]^3\). (1) If \((\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(ab))=(\iota(a'),\iota(b'),\iota(c'))\), injectivity of \(\iota\) gives \(a=a'\), \(b=b'\), \(ab=c'\), so \(a'b'=c'\) and the triple is not false. (2) The triple itself is such a false triple.

docs.title: Completeness: true triples are accepted
docs.text:
Completeness says that the multiplication template accepts \((\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(ab))\) for all integers \(a,b\). It uses the slope representation, a consequence of the twenty-two-prime pattern 22P, to choose the slopes, pole completeness PC to supply the pole witnesses, and the generator certificate (hence Mordell-Weil) through the fixed-scalar and guard semantics. It does not use the six-contact estimate.

12 fully proved

docs.title: Slopes from the prime pattern
docs.text:
Each of the nine integral homogeneous quantities of a true triple is written as a sum of three slopes \(u_j/v\) whose twenty-two linear forms take values \(\pm kp\) with \(k\) in the fixed catalogue multipliers and \(p\) a large good prime. Each slope then has bounded valuations at the old primes \(S_b\) and at most six odd contact primes outside \(S_b\), each of exact valuation one and good.

The rest of the proof uses only the conclusion with no lower bound on the contact primes: every integer is a sum of three good slopes. The two-slope pattern gives this too, with the slopes \(u/v\), \(A+10-u/v\) and the constant \(-10\).

Neither pattern is needed: route AP weakens the condition at the old primes so that a slope may have a pole there when \(F(t)>0\), absorbs such a pole in the slope certificate, and obtains the weakened representation from long progressions of good slope primes.

docs.title: Slopes of an integer from the prime pattern
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.pattern_slopes

Assume the twenty-two-prime pattern. For every \(A\in\mathbb Z\) and every real \(B_0\) there are \(t_1,t_2,t_3\in\mathbb Q\) with \(t_1+t_2+t_3=A\) such that each \(t=t_j\) satisfies:

  1. \(t otin\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\);
  2. for every \(p\in S_b\): \(|v_p(t-1)|\le B_p\) and \(|v_p(F(t)/(t-1)^8)|\le8B_p\), in particular both are at most \(C_p=14B_p\);
  3. every odd contact prime \(p otin S_b\) of \(t\) satisfies \(p>B_0\), is a good slope prime (it splits in \(K_0\), both reductions of \(E\) above it are good, and their orders \(d_1,d_2\) satisfy \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=4\); the good primes of the pattern hypothesis satisfy moreover \(p mid d_1d_2\), which is not needed here), and has \(v_p(t-c)=1\) for every \(c\in\mathcal C\) with \(v_p(t-c)>0\) (there is only one such \(c\), because \(p>324\) divides no difference of two elements of \(\mathcal C\));
  4. \(t\) has at most six odd contact primes outside \(S_b\).

This is the application of Proposition 6.2 to one of the nine integral homogeneous quantities of a true triple; the selected prime values need not be distinct.

Proof sketch. Apply the pattern with \(A\) and \(B_0'=\max(B_0,H_{\max})\): there are integers \(u_1,u_2,v\), \(v e0\), with \(u_3=Av-u_1-u_2\), such that \(v\) and every \(u_j-bv\) (\(b\in\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\)) equal \(\epsilon kp\) with \(\epsilon=\pm1\), \(k=dh'\) (\(d\mid P_s^4\), \(h'\in\mathcal H\)) and \(p>B_0'\) a good pattern prime. Put \(t_j=u_j/v\); then \(\sum_jt_j=A\) and \(t_j-b=(u_j-bv)/v e0\), which is (1). For \(q\in S_b\), \(q e p\) because \(p>H_{\max}\), and \(v_q(k)\le B_q\): if \(q\le324\), \(v_q(d)\le4\) and \(q mid h'\); if \(q\in\mathcal H\), \(q mid d\) and \(v_q(h')\le1\). So every pattern value has \(q\)-adic valuation in \([0,B_q]\), and \(t-1=(u_j-v)/v\), \(F(t)/(t-1)^8=v^2\prod_{c\in\mathcal C}(u_j-cv)/(u_j-v)^8\) give (2). For a prime \(q otin S_b\) with \(v_q(t_j-c)>0\), \(q\) divides \(u_j-cv=\epsilon kp\) and not \(k\), so \(q=p\) is the prime of that value; hence at most one such prime for each of the six \(c\), which is (4). Moreover \(v_q(u_j-cv)=1\) and \(v_q(v)\in\{0,1\}\), so \(v_q(t_j-c)>0\) forces \(v_q(t_j-c)=1\); and \(q=p>B_0'\ge B_0\) is a good pattern prime, hence a good slope prime, which is (3).

docs.title: The slope representation
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.SlopeRepresentation ZInQ.Mult.GoodSlope

For a real \(B_0\), say that \(t\in\mathbb Q\) satisfies conditions 1-4 for \(B_0\) if:

  1. \(t otin\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\);
  2. for every \(p\in S_b\): \(|v_p(t-1)|\le B_p\) and \(|v_p(F(t)/(t-1)^8)|\le8B_p\);
  3. every odd contact prime \(p otin S_b\) of \(t\) satisfies \(p>B_0\), is a good slope prime (there is \(r\in\mathbb Z/p\) with \(r^2=2\) and \(75\mp53r e0\) such that the point counts \(d_1,d_2\) of \(y^2=x^3-(75\mp53r)^2x\) over \(\mathbb Z/p\) satisfy \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=4\); for odd \(p\): \(p\) splits in \(K_0\) and both reductions of \(E\) above \(p\) are good with orders of gcd \(4\)), and \(v_p(t-c)=1\) for every \(c\in\mathcal C\) with \(v_p(t-c)>0\);
  4. \(t\) has at most six odd contact primes outside \(S_b\).

A good slope is a \(t\) satisfying conditions 1-4 for \(B_0=0\); as primes are positive, these are the conditions for any \(B_0\le0\), and the conditions for any \(B_0\) imply them.

The slope representation is the assertion that every integer \(A\) is a sum \(t_1+t_2+t_3=A\) of three good slopes.

These are the conditions of the slopes from the prime pattern. The slope representation is all that the completeness of the multiplication template uses of a prime pattern; both the twenty-two-prime pattern and the two-slope pattern give it.

docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.slopeRepresentation_of_fixedPrimePattern

Assume the twenty-two-prime pattern. Then the slope representation holds: every integer is a sum of three good slopes.

Proof sketch. For \(A\in\mathbb Z\), the slopes of an integer from the prime pattern with \(B_0=0\) give \(t_1+t_2+t_3=A\) with each \(t_j\) satisfying conditions 1-4 for \(B_0=0\); these are exactly the conditions of a good slope.

docs.title: The two-slope pattern gives the slope representation
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.slopeRepresentation_of_twoSlopePattern

Assume the two-slope pattern. Then the slope representation holds: every integer \(A\) is the sum of the three good slopes $\( rac uv+\Bigl(A+10- rac uv\Bigr)+(-10)=A,\)$ with \(u,v\) given by the pattern for \(A\).

Proof sketch. The twelve numbers \(u-cv\) and \(u-(A+10-c)v\) (\(c\in\mathcal C\)) are, up to sign, good slope primes greater than \(324\) outside \(\mathcal H\), hence outside \(S_b\); and \(v\), \(u-v\), \(u-(A+9)v\) have valuation at most \(B_q\) at every \(q\in S_b\).

The slope \(t=u/v\). Here \(t-c=(u-cv)/v\). If \(u=v\) then \(u+15v=16v\) would be prime, so \(u-v e0\), and \(t otin\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\). At \(q\in S_b\) every \(u-cv\) is a \(q\)-adic unit, so \(v_q(t-1)=v_q(u-v)-v_q(v)\) and \(v_q(F(t)/(t-1)^8)=2v_q(v)-8v_q(u-v)\) lie in \([-B_q,B_q]\) and \([-8B_q,8B_q]\). An odd contact prime \(q otin S_b\) of \(t\) divides some \(u-cv\), so it is the prime \(|u-cv|\), a good slope prime; then \(v_q(u-c'v)\le1\) for all \(c'\), and \(v_q(t-c')>0\) forces \(v_q(v)=0\) and \(v_q(t-c')=1\). There are at most six such primes, one for each \(c\).

The slope \(A+10-u/v=u_2/v\), with \(u_2=(A+10)v-u\). Now \(u_2-cv=-(u-(A+10-c)v)\) and \(u_2-v=-(u-(A+9)v)\), and the same argument applies with the other six primes.

The slope \(-10\). Its contact values \(-10-c\) are \(-10,5,10,14,20,50\), whose prime factors are at most \(7\), so it has no odd contact prime outside \(S_b\). Further \(-10-1=-11\) and \(F(-10)=-7\cdot10^6=-2^6\cdot5^6\cdot7\), so at \(q\le324\) the two valuations of condition 2 are at most \(1\le4\) and \(13\le32\) in absolute value, and at \(q\in\mathcal H\) they vanish.

docs.title: The witnesses of a test group
docs.text:
Each odd contact prime of a slope gets its own private test group. At such a prime, with reduced group orders \(d_1,d_2\), \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=4\), the shift \(h\) is chosen with \(h\equiv0\pmod{\operatorname{lcm}(M_0,d_1)}\) and \(h\equiv c_*\pmod{d_2}\), and \(U_i=[n_i]H\). Then \(H,U_i\) lie in the formal group at one place and \(V_0,V_i\) at the conjugate place, and the four \(L\)-tests are congruent to \(n_i-n_i\) and \(n_1n_2-n_3=0\) modulo \(p^{28}\). Groups not assigned to a prime use \(h=2c_*\); the manuscript leaves them unspecified.

Because every shift is a multiple of \(M_0\), all eight points of every group lie in the small formal subgroup at the old primes, so every test is integral there.

docs.title: Choice of the shift at a selected prime
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.shift_choice ZInQ.Mult.shift_choice'

Let \(M\ge1\) and \(d_1,d_2\ge1\) be integers with \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=4\). Then there is an integer \(h>4M\) with $\(h\equiv0\pmod{\operatorname{lcm}(M,d_1)},\qquad h\equiv4M\pmod{d_2}.\)$ In the application \(M=M_0\), \(4M=c_*\), and \(d_1,d_2\) are the orders of the two reduced curve groups at a selected prime; then \(h\ne0\), \(h\ne c_*\), \(M_0\mid h\), \(d_1\mid h\) and \(d_2\mid h-c_*\).

Proof sketch. The two congruences are compatible iff \(\gcd(\operatorname{lcm}(M,d_1),d_2)\mid4M\). Since \(\operatorname{lcm}(M,d_1)\mid Md_1\), \(\gcd(\operatorname{lcm}(M,d_1),d_2)\mid\gcd(Md_1,d_2)\mid\gcd(Md_1,Md_2)=M\gcd(d_1,d_2)=4M\). By the Chinese remainder theorem the solutions form a residue class modulo \(\operatorname{lcm}(\operatorname{lcm}(M,d_1),d_2)\), which contains integers larger than \(4M\).

docs.title: Precision of the tests at a selected prime
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.tests_precision_selected

Let \(p>324\) be a prime with good reduction at a split pair of places: \(p\) is odd, \(r\in\mathbb Z\) satisfies \(r^2\equiv2\pmod p\), \(75\mp53r ot\equiv0\pmod p\), and $\(d_1=\#\widetilde E_r(\mathbb F_p),\qquad d_2=\#\widetilde E_{-r}(\mathbb F_p),\qquad \widetilde E_{\pm r}:y^2=x^3-(75\mp53r)^2x,\)$ counting the point at infinity. Let \(\mathfrak p_1=(p,s-r)\) and \(\mathfrak p_2=(p,s+r)=\sigma\mathfrak p_1\). Let \(h\in\mathbb Z\) with \(h e0\), \(h e c_*\), \(d_1\mid h\) and \(d_2\mid h-c_*\), let \(n_1,n_2\in\mathbb Z\), \(n_3=n_1n_2\), and \( au= au igl(h,(n_1h,n_2h,n_3h);\,c_*,c_*n_1,c_*n_2,c_*n_3 igr)\). Then $\(v_{\mathfrak p_1}( au_j)\ge1\quad(1\le j\le8),\qquad v_{\mathfrak p_1}( au_j)\ge28\quad(9\le j\le12).\)$

Proof sketch. Reduction modulo \(\mathfrak p_1\) is a homomorphism \(E(K_0) o\widetilde E_r(\mathbb F_p)\), a group of order \(d_1\), so the reduction of \([h]P_0\) is \([h/d_1] igl([d_1]\overline{P_0} igr)=O\); by the definition of reduction, \(H=[h]P_0\) lies in \(E_1(K_{\mathfrak p_1})\). Likewise \(V_0=[h-c_*]P_0\in E_1(K_{\mathfrak p_2})\). Then \(U_i=[n_i]H\in E_1(K_{\mathfrak p_1})\) and \(V_i=[n_i(h-c_*)]P_0=[n_i]V_0\in E_1(K_{\mathfrak p_2})\). For a point \(Q e O\) of \(E_1\), \(v(1/x(Q))=2v(z(Q))\ge2\); with \(v_{\mathfrak p_1}(\sigma y)=v_{\mathfrak p_2}(y)\) this gives the first eight bounds. Since \(\lambda_{\mathfrak p_1}\) is a homomorphism, \(\lambda_{\mathfrak p_1}(U_i)=n_i\lambda_{\mathfrak p_1}(H)\) with \(\lambda_{\mathfrak p_1}(H) e0\), and the truncation error at \(p>324\) gives \(A_i=n_i(1+\epsilon_i)/(1+\epsilon_0)\) with \(v(\epsilon)\ge28\), so \(v_{\mathfrak p_1}(A_i-n_i)\ge28\). In the same way \(v_{\mathfrak p_2}(B_i-n_i)\ge28\), that is \(v_{\mathfrak p_1}(\sigma B_i-n_i)\ge28\). Hence \( au_{8+i}=A_i-\sigma B_i\) and \( au_{12}=A_1A_2-A_3\equiv n_1n_2-n_3=0\) have valuation at least \(28\).

docs.title: Integrality of the tests at the old primes
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.tests_integral_old

Let \(n_1,n_2,n_3\in\mathbb Z\) and \(h\in\mathbb Z\) with \(M_0\mid h\), \(h e0\) and \(h e c_*\), and let \( au= au igl(h,(n_1h,n_2h,n_3h);\,c_*,c_*n_1,c_*n_2,c_*n_3 igr)\). Then $\(v_{\mathfrak p}( au_j)\ge0\qquad(1\le j\le12)\)$ for every prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) above a prime of \(S_b\).

This is the manuscript's "the small formal subgroup in the definition of \(M_0\) gives \(v_p(D_{gj})\ge0\) at \(S_b\)", with the step expanded.

Proof sketch. Put \(Q_0=[M_0]P_0\). By the definition of \(M_0\) (which is \(\ge1\)), \(1/x(Q_0)=(a+bs)/c\) with \(N_s^4\mid a,b\) and \(\gcd(c,N_s)=1\); the primes dividing \(N_s=P_sH_{ m cat}\) are exactly those of \(S_b\). Hence at every prime \(\mathfrak p\) above \(p\in S_b\), \(v_{\mathfrak p}(1/x(Q_0))\ge4\) (at odd \(p\), \(v_{\mathfrak p}(a),v_{\mathfrak p}(b)\ge4\) and \(v_{\mathfrak p}(c)=0\); at \((s)\), \(v_s(a),v_s(b)\ge8\)), so \(Q_0\in E_1(K_{\mathfrak p})\) with \(v_{\mathfrak p}(z(Q_0))\ge2\). Since \(c_*=4M_0\), the points \(H=[h/M_0]Q_0\), \(U_i=[n_i]H\), \(V_0=[(h-c_*)/M_0]Q_0\) and \(V_i=[n_i]V_0\) are multiples of \(Q_0\) (note \(z_i-c_*n_i=n_i(h-c_*)\)). By the formal group, each lies in \(E_1(K_{\mathfrak p})\) with \(v(z)\ge2\), hence \(v(1/x)=2v(z)\ge4\), at every prime above \(p\), including the conjugate one; this gives \( au_1,\dots, au_8\). For the ratios, \(H,V_0 e O\); by the unit form of the truncated logarithm, \(A_i= igl(z(U_i)/z(H) igr)\cdot u\) with \(u\) a unit (or \(A_i=0\) if \(U_i=O\)), and \(v(z([n_i]H))\ge v(z(H))\), so \(A_i\) is integral; likewise \(B_i\) at the conjugate prime, so \(\sigma B_i\) is integral at \(\mathfrak p\). Hence \( au_9,\dots, au_{12}\) are integral.

docs.title: The pole input
docs.text: Weak approximation chooses \(q\) small at \(S_b\), integral at the selected primes, and close to a real root of \(1-R_0q^2\) without equality, with \(\eta\) chosen to make \(R_0>0\). In both real embeddings every \(W_g\) is at least \(1\), so \(\Theta\in(0,12]\) and the pole input \(R/\Theta^2\) is positive and, for \(a\) small, below \(1/2\). At \(S_b\) the clearing exponents of \(\ell_0\) give \(v_p(R/\Theta^2)\ge103C_p+8\ge4\); at a selected prime the trace residues give valuation one; elsewhere the valuation is even. These are exactly the hypotheses of pole completeness, including all nonzero guards.

docs.title: Weak approximation for the parameter \(q\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.weak_approx_q

Let \(S\) and \(S'\) be disjoint finite sets of primes, \(e_p\in\mathbb N\) for \(p\in S\), \(x_0\in\mathbb R\), \(\delta>0\), and \(X\subset\mathbb R\) finite. Then there is \(q\in\mathbb Q\setminus X\) with $\(v_p(q)\ge e_p\ (p\in S),\qquad v_p(q)\ge0\ (p\in S'),\qquad |q-x_0|<\delta .\)$

In the completeness argument \(S=S_b\) with \(e_p=C_p\), \(S'\) is the set of selected odd contact primes of the slope, \(x_0=R_0^{-1/2}\) is a real root of \(1-R_0q^2\), and \(X=\{\pm x_0\}\), so that \(a=1-R_0q^2\) is nonzero and arbitrarily small, and is a unit at \(S_b\) and at the selected primes.

Proof sketch. Put \(M=\prod_{p\in S}p^{e_p}\) and choose a prime \(\ell\notin S\cup S'\). The numbers \(Mn/\ell^k\) (\(n\in\mathbb Z\), \(k\in\mathbb N\)) are dense in \(\mathbb R\), and each satisfies the valuation conditions because \(\ell\notin S\cup S'\). Infinitely many of them lie in \((x_0-\delta,x_0+\delta)\); choose one outside the finite set \(X\).

docs.title: Positivity and smallness of the pole input
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.pole_input_small

Let \(R_0\in\mathbb Q\) with \(R_0>0\), \(\ell\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\}\), and fix \(C_{gj}\in K_0\) (\(1\le g\le6\), \(1\le j\le12\)). There is a real \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every \(a\in\mathbb Q\) with \(0<|a|<\varepsilon\), putting \(R=\ell^2a^2R_0\), \(W_g=\prod_{j=1}^{12}(1+RC_{gj}^2)\) and \(\Theta=\operatorname{Tr}\sum_gW_g^{-1}\):

  1. both real embeddings of every \(W_g\) are at least \(1\); in particular \(W_g\ne0\);
  2. \(0<\Theta\le12\);
  3. \(0<R/\Theta^2<1/2\).

This makes precise the manuscript's "as \(a\to0\), \(W_g\to1\), \(\Theta\to12\), and \(R/\Theta^2\to0\) through positive values". The \(C_{gj}\) do not depend on \(q\), so \(\varepsilon\) can be fixed before \(q\) is chosen.

Proof sketch. \(R>0\), and \(\sigma_\pm(1+RC^2)=1+R\,\sigma_\pm(C)^2\ge1\), so \(\sigma_\pm(W_g)\ge1\) and \(\sigma_\pm(W_g^{-1})\in(0,1]\). Since \(\operatorname{Tr}=\sigma_++\sigma_-\), \(\Theta\) is a sum of twelve numbers in \((0,1]\). Let \(K\) be the maximum of \(1\) and all \(\sigma_\pm(C_{gj})^2\). Then \(\sigma_\pm(W_g)\le(1+RK)^{12}\), so \(\Theta\ge12(1+RK)^{-12}\) and \(R/\Theta^2\le R(1+RK)^{24}/144\). If \(RK\le1\) this is at most \(2^{24}R/144\), which is below \(1/2\) when \(R<72\cdot2^{-24}\). Choose \(\varepsilon\) with \(\ell^2\varepsilon^2R_0<\min(1/K,\,72\cdot2^{-24})\).

docs.title: Valuations of the pole input of a completed slope
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.pole_input_valuations ZInQ.Mult.poleInput

Let \(t\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy conditions 1-4 of the slope representation (for some \(B_0\)), and let \(P(t)\) be its set of odd contact primes outside \(S_b\). Let \(\eta\in\{1,-1\}\), \(R_0=\eta F(t)/(t-1)^8\), and let \(q\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy \(v_p(q)\ge C_p\) for \(p\in S_b\) and \(v_p(q)\ge0\) for \(p\in P(t)\), with \(a=1-R_0q^2 e0\); put \(R=\ell_0^2a^2R_0\). Let \(D_{gj}\in K_0\) (\(1\le g\le6\), \(1\le j\le12\)) satisfy

  • (i) \(v_{\mathfrak p}(D_{gj})\ge0\) for all \(g,j\) and every prime \(\mathfrak p\) above a prime of \(S_b\);
  • (ii) for each \(p\in P(t)\) there are \(g\) and a prime \(\mathfrak p\) above \(p\) with \(v_{\mathfrak p}(D_{gj})\ge k_j\) for all \(j\);

and form \(C_{gj},W_g,\Theta\) as in the slope predicate, assuming \(W_g e0\) and \(\Theta e0\). Then \(B=R/\Theta^2\) satisfies:

  1. \(v_p(B)\ge103C_p+8\ge4\) for every \(p\in S_b\), in particular for every \(p\in S_0\);
  2. \(v_p(B)=1\) for every \(p\in P(t)\);
  3. \(v_p(B)\) is even for every other prime \(p otin S_b\).

Consequently the reduced denominator of \(B\) is a perfect square.

Proof sketch. (1) Let \(p\in S_b\). By condition 2, \(|v_p(R_0)|\le C_p\) and \(|v_p(t-1)|\le C_p\), so \(v_p(R_0q^2)\ge C_p>0\) and \(a\) is a \(p\)-adic unit; with \(v_p(\ell_0)=E_p\), \(v_p(R)=2E_p+v_p(R_0)\). Measuring valuations above \(p\) on the scale of \(v_p\), (i) gives \(v(C_{gj})\ge-25C_p-26C_p=-D_p\), so \(v(RC_{gj}^2)\ge2E_p-C_p-2D_p>v_p(12)\) by the clearing inequalities. Hence \(W_g^{-1}-1\) has valuation \(>v_p(12)\) at every place above \(p\), and so does \(\Theta-12=\operatorname{Tr}\sum_g(W_g^{-1}-1)\); thus \(v_p(\Theta)=v_p(12)\) and \(v_p(B)=2E_p+v_p(R_0)-2v_p(12)\ge2E_p-C_p-2v_p(12)=103C_p+8\). (2) Let \(p\in P(t)\). By condition 3 and the contact valuations, \(v_p(R_0)=1\) and \(v_p(t-1)=0\); \(v_p(q)\ge0\) makes \(a\) a unit, and \(v_p(\ell_0)=0\), so \(v_p(R)=1\). At each place \(\mathfrak q\) above \(p\), \(v_{\mathfrak q}(1+RC^2)=\min(0,1+2v_{\mathfrak q}(C))\), so \(W_g^{-1}\) is \(\mathfrak q\)-integral with residue \(1\) if all \(v_{\mathfrak q}(C_{gj})\ge0\) and residue \(0\) otherwise. Fix a place \(\mathfrak p\) above \(p\); the twelve summands \(W_g^{-1},\sigma(W_g^{-1})\) of \(\Theta\) are then \(\mathfrak p\)-integral with residues \(0\) or \(1\) (the residue of \(\sigma(W_g^{-1})\) at \(\mathfrak p\) being that of \(W_g^{-1}\) at \(\sigma\mathfrak p\)), and by (ii) the assigned group and place, where all \(v(C_{gj})=v(D_{gj})-k_j\ge0\), contributes residue \(1\). The sum of the residues lies in \(\{1,\dots,12\}\) and \(p>324\), so \(v_p(\Theta)=0\) and \(v_p(B)=1\). (3) For \(p otin S_b\), \(p otin P(t)\): if \(v_p(t)<0\) then \(v_p(R_0)=6v_p(t)-8v_p(t)\) is even; otherwise at most one of the seven values \(t-c\), \(t-1\) has positive valuation, and that valuation is even (for \(t-c\)) or enters multiplied by \(8\) (for \(t-1\)). So \(v_p(R_0)\) is even, \(v_p(R)=2v_p(\ell_0a)+v_p(R_0)\) is even, and so is \(v_p(B)=v_p(R)-2v_p(\Theta)\). Every negative valuation of \(B\) is therefore even.

docs.title: Completeness of the slope certificate for a true triple
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.slope_complete

Assume pole completeness. Let \(n_1,n_2\in\mathbb Z\), \(n_3=n_1n_2\) and \(c=(c_*,c_*n_1,c_*n_2,c_*n_3)\). If \(t\in\mathbb Q\) satisfies conditions 1-4 of the slope representation (for some \(B_0\)), then $\(\mathrm{Slope}(t,\ell_0;c).\)$

This is where pole completeness is used: it supplies the eleven pole witnesses once the pole input is shown to satisfy its hypotheses, including all nonzero guards.

Proof sketch. Condition 1 gives \(t otin\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\), and \(\ell_0 e0\). Choose \(\eta\) with \(R_0=\eta F(t)/(t-1)^8>0\). Let \(p_1,\dots,p_m\) (\(m\le6\)) be the odd contact primes of \(t\) outside \(S_b\); each \(p_g\) is a good slope prime with orders \(d_1,d_2\), \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=4\), and \(p_g>324\). For \(g\le m\) the shift choice gives \(h_g>c_*\) with \(M_0\mid h_g\), \(d_1\mid h_g\) and \(d_2\mid h_g-c_*\); for \(g>m\) put \(h_g=2c_*\). Put \(z_{g,i}=n_ih_g\) and \(D_{gj}= au_j(h_g,z_g;c)\). Each \(h_g e0,c_*\). Assume pole completeness and the slope representation. For all \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\), $\(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}\bigl(\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(ab)\bigr).\)$

docs.title: Local conventions: the formal group and the truncated logarithm
Local conventions: the formal group and the truncated logarithm
docs.text:
The multiplication certificate reads arithmetic information off points of \(2E(K_0)\) at finite places. This section fixes the local conventions of the manuscript and proves the local facts that both directions of the multiplication statement use. Throughout, \(E:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) with \(d=75-53s\), a point of \(E(K_0)\) is regarded as a point over every completion \(K_{\mathfrak p}\) of \(K_0\), \(z=-x/y\) and \(w=1/x\) with \(z(O)=w(O)=0\), and \(E_1(K_{\mathfrak p})\) is the set of points with \(v_{\mathfrak p}(x)<0\) together with \(O\). For a point \(P\) of \(E(K_0)\) with \(x(P)\ne0\), \(P\in E_1(K_{\mathfrak p})\) exactly when \(v_{\mathfrak p}(1/x(P))\ge1\); this is how the inverse-abscissa tests detect the formal group.

14 fully proved

docs.title: Primes of \(K_0\)
docs.text: An odd prime \(p\) is unramified in \(K_0\); it splits into two conjugate primes when \(2\) is a square modulo \(p\) and is inert otherwise. Conjugation exchanges the valuations at conjugate primes, which is how the conjugated tests of a test group refer to the other place above \(p\).

docs.title: The primes of \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]\) above an odd prime
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.primeR_split ZInQ.Mult.primeP_inert ZInQ.Mult.vp_ratCast ZInQ.Mult.vp_star ZInQ.Mult.vp_trace_ge

Let \(p\) be an odd prime and \(\sigma\) the conjugation \(s\mapsto-s\) of \(K_0\).

  1. If \(2\) is a square modulo \(p\), choose \(r\in\mathbb Z\) with \(r^2\equiv2\pmod p\). Then \(\mathfrak p_r=(p,s-r)\) and \(\mathfrak p_{-r}=(p,s+r)\) are distinct prime ideals of \(\mathbb Z[s]\), \(a+bs\mapsto(a+br)\bmod p\) induces \(\mathbb Z[s]/\mathfrak p_r\cong\mathbb F_p\), \(p\mathbb Z[s]=\mathfrak p_r\mathfrak p_{-r}\) and \(\sigma(\mathfrak p_r)=\mathfrak p_{-r}\). Otherwise \(p\mathbb Z[s]\) is prime, with residue field of \(p^2\) elements, and \(\sigma(p\mathbb Z[s])=p\mathbb Z[s]\). In both cases these are all the prime ideals of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) containing \(p\).
  2. For a prime \(\mathfrak p\ni p\) let \(v_{\mathfrak p}\) be the normalized valuation of \(K_0\) (\(v_{\mathfrak p}(K_0^\times)=\mathbb Z\), \(v_{\mathfrak p}(0)=+\infty\)). Then \(p\) is unramified: \(v_{\mathfrak p}(q)=v_p(q)\) for every \(q\in\mathbb Q\).
  3. \(v_{\sigma\mathfrak p}(y)=v_{\mathfrak p}(\sigma y)\) for every \(y\in K_0\).
  4. For \(y\in K_0\) and \(m\in\mathbb Z\), if \(v_{\mathfrak p}(y)\ge m\) and \(v_{\sigma\mathfrak p}(y)\ge m\), then \(v_p(\operatorname{Tr}y)\ge m\), where \(\operatorname{Tr}y=y+\sigma y\in\mathbb Q\).

At the prime \(2\) the corresponding facts are those of the prime \((s)\).

Proof sketch. (1) is Dedekind-Kummer for \(\mathbb Z[s]=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2-2)\), whose discriminant \(8\) is prime to \(p\): \(X^2-2\) is separable modulo \(p\) and factors as \((X-r)(X+r)\) or is irreducible. (2) \(p\mathbb Z[s]\) is a product of distinct primes, so \(v_{\mathfrak p}(p)=1\). (3) \(\sigma\) is a ring automorphism of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) mapping \(\mathfrak p\) to \(\sigma\mathfrak p\). (4) \(\operatorname{Tr}y=y+\sigma y\) and \(v_{\mathfrak p}(\sigma y)=v_{\sigma\mathfrak p}(y)\ge m\); the ultrametric inequality gives \(v_{\mathfrak p}(\operatorname{Tr}y)\ge m\), and \(v_{\mathfrak p}=v_p\) on \(\mathbb Q\).

docs.title: The formal group and its logarithm
docs.text:
For the integral equation \(y^2=x^3+Ax\) over a discretely valued field, the points with \(v(x)<0\) form a subgroup on which \(z\) is injective, with \(v(w)=2v(z)\), filtered by the subgroups \(v(z)\ge k\), so multiplication by an integer never lowers \(v(z)\); this part has an elementary chord-and-tangent proof. Over a complete field, \(z\) turns the group law into a formal group law, whose formal logarithm converges on \(v(z)>0\), is a homomorphism, and is an isometry where \(v(z)>e/(p-1)\); at an odd unramified prime this is the whole formal group. These are classical (Silverman IV and VII.2); here they are background statements, the formal group law and the logarithm being the deepest inputs of the chapter. The manuscript's remark that identifying the formal neighbourhood with the reduction kernel of a minimal model needs Silverman VII.2.1-2.2 is not used: every argument below works with the integral equation of \(E\) itself.

For \(E\) the invariant differential is \(dz/\sqrt{1+4d^2z^4}\), so the logarithm is an explicit binomial series, and the polynomial \(L\) of the truncated logarithm template is \(16575\) times its truncation in degree \(25\).

docs.title: The formal neighbourhood of \(y^2=x^3+Ax\) and its filtration
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.formal_val_x_y ZInQ.Mult.formalFilt ZInQ.Mult.mem_formalNbhd_iff ZInQ.Mult.zCoord_injOn ZInQ.Mult.zsmul_mem_formalFilt

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic \(0\) with a discrete valuation \(v\) normalized by \(v(K^ imes)=\mathbb Z\) (for instance \(K_0\) with \(v_{\mathfrak p}\), or a completion of \(K_0\)). Let \(A\in K^ imes\) with \(v(A)\ge0\), and \(W:y^2=x^3+Ax\) over \(K\). Put $\(W_1(K)=\{O\}\cup\{(x,y)\in W(K):v(x)<0\},\)$ and for \(P=(x,y)\in W_1(K)\) put \(z(P)=-x/y\), \(w(P)=1/x\) and \(\omega(P)=-1/y\), with \(z(O)=w(O)=\omega(O)=0\). Then:

  1. for every affine \(P=(x,y)\in W_1(K)\) there is an integer \(N\ge1\) with \(v(x)=-2N\) and \(v(y)=-3N\); hence \(y e0\), \(v(z(P))=N\), \(v(w(P))=2N=2v(z(P))\) and \(v(\omega(P))=3N\);
  2. for every integer \(k\ge1\) the set \(W_k(K)=\{P\in W_1(K):v(z(P))\ge k\}\) (containing \(O\)) is a subgroup of \(W(K)\); in particular \(W_1(K)\) is a subgroup;
  3. \(z\) is injective on \(W_1(K)\);
  4. for every \(P\in W_1(K)\) and \(n\in\mathbb Z\), \([n]P\in W_1(K)\) and \(v(z([n]P))\ge v(z(P))\).

In part 1, \(w=1/x\) is the manuscript's parameter; it differs from the auxiliary variable \(\omega=-1/y\) of Silverman, which is used only inside the proof. This is the elementary part of Silverman VII.2.2 (there stated for a minimal equation over a complete field; only the integrality of \(A\) is used). The formal group law itself is a separate statement.

Proof sketch. (1) If \(v(x)<0\) then \(v(Ax)\ge v(x)>3v(x)\), so \(2v(y)=v(x^3+Ax)=3v(x)\); thus \(v(x)\) is even, \(v(x)=-2N\) with \(N\ge1\), and \(v(y)=-3N\).

Coordinates. For affine \(P\in W_1(K)\), \(x=z/\omega\) and \(y=-1/\omega\), and dividing the equation by \(-y^3\) gives $\(\omega=z^3+Az\omega^2 . ag{\)*\(}\)$ Conversely a pair \((z,\omega)\) with \(\omega e0\) satisfying \((*)\) is the image of the affine point \((z/\omega,-1/\omega)\). If \(v(z)\ge1\), \(v(\omega)\ge1\) and \((z,\omega)\) satisfies \((*)\), then \(v(Az\omega^2)>v(\omega)\), so \(v(\omega)=3v(z)\); in particular \(\omega=0\) iff \(z=0\). The map \((x,y)\mapsto(z,\omega)\) is the projective change of coordinates \([X:Y:Z]\mapsto[-X:-Z:Y]\), which sends \(O=[0:1:0]\) to \((0,0)\) and lines to lines.

(2)-(3) Negation is \((x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)\), i.e. \((z,\omega)\mapsto(-z,-\omega)\), which preserves \(v(z)\). Let \(P_1,P_2\in W_k(K)\) be affine with coordinates \((z_i,\omega_i)\), so \(v(z_i)\ge k\) and \(v(\omega_i)=3v(z_i)\ge3k\). Subtracting the two instances of \((*)\) gives the identity $\((\omega_2-\omega_1) igl(1-Az_1(\omega_1+\omega_2) igr)=(z_2-z_1) igl(z_1^2+z_1z_2+z_2^2+A\omega_2^2 igr),\)$ whose left factor \(u=1-Az_1(\omega_1+\omega_2)\) is a unit. Hence \(z_1=z_2\) forces \(\omega_1=\omega_2\), i.e. \(P_1=P_2\); this is (3). Put $\(\lambda= rac{z_1^2+z_1z_2+z_2^2+A\omega_2^2}{1-Az_1(\omega_1+\omega_2)},\qquad u=\omega_1-\lambda z_1 .\)$ If \(P_1 e P_2\), \(\omega=\lambda z+ u\) is the line through them; if \(P_1=P_2\) the same formula gives the tangent, by implicit differentiation of \((*)\): \(\omega'(1-2Az\omega)=3z^2+A\omega^2\). In both cases \(v(\lambda)\ge2k\) and \(v( u)\ge3k\). Substituting \(\omega=\lambda z+ u\) in \((*)\) gives the cubic $\((1+A\lambda^2)z^3+2A\lambda u z^2+(A u^2-\lambda)z- u=0,\)$ whose leading coefficient is a unit and whose roots, with multiplicity, are \(z_1\), \(z_2\) and the \(z\)-coordinate \(z_3\) of the third intersection point \(Q\) of the line with \(W\); by the chord construction of the group law, \(P_1+P_2=-Q\). By Vieta, $\(z_3=-z_1-z_2- rac{2A\lambda u}{1+A\lambda^2},\qquad v(z_3)\ge k .\)$ If \(z_3=0\) then \(\omega_3= u\) and \((*)\) gives \( u=0\), so \(Q=O\) and \(P_1+P_2=O\in W_k(K)\). Otherwise \(\omega_3=\lambda z_3+ u\) satisfies \(v(\omega_3)\ge3k\ge1\), hence \(v(\omega_3)=3v(z_3)\) and \(\omega_3 e0\), so \(Q=(z_3/\omega_3,-1/\omega_3)\) is affine with \(v(x(Q))=-2v(z_3)\le-2k\), and \(P_1+P_2=-Q\in W_k(K)\) with \(z(P_1+P_2)=-z_3\). Sums involving \(O\) are trivial. (Alternatively, \(z(P_1+P_2)=-z_3\) can be verified directly from the Weierstrass addition formulas: the \((x,y)\)-line \(y=\ell x+m\) is \(\omega=\lambda z+ u\) with \(\lambda=-\ell/m\), \( u=-1/m\) when \(m e0\), and the case \(m=0\) is the line through \(O\).)

(4) By (2) with \(k=v(z(P))\) (or \(P=O\)), \(W_k(K)\) is a subgroup containing \(P\), hence \([n]P\).

docs.title: The chord estimate in a formal neighbourhood
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.chord_add_five ZInQ.Mult.formal_third_point_five

Let \(K\) be a field with a discrete valuation \(v\), let \(A\in K\) with \(v(A)\ge0\), and let \(k\ge1\). For affine points \(P_1,P_2\in W_k(K)\) of \(y^2=x^3+Ax\) with \(P_1+P_2\) affine, write \(z=-x/y\) and \(\omega=-1/y\). Then \(P_1+P_2\) has \(v(z(P_1+P_2))\ge k\) and \(v(\omega(P_1+P_2))\ge3k\), and there is a line \(\omega=\lambda z+ u\) in the \((z,\omega)\)-plane passing through \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) with \(v(\lambda)\ge2k\), \(v( u)\ge3k\) and $\(z(P_1+P_2)=z(P_1)+z(P_2)+ rac{2A\lambda u}{1+A\lambda^2},\qquad v igl(z(P_1+P_2)-z(P_1)-z(P_2) igr)\ge5k .\)$ If \(P_1 e P_2\) then \(z(P_1) e z(P_2)\), since \(z\) is injective on \(W_1(K)\), so this line is the line through the two points. In particular \(W_k(K)\) is closed under addition and \(z\) is additive modulo valuation \(5k\).

Proof sketch. This is the chord computation behind the canonical article on formal neighbourhoods. In the coordinates \((z,\omega)\) the curve is \(\omega=z^3+Az\omega^2\). The slope of the chord satisfies \(\lambda(z_2-z_1)=\omega_2-\omega_1\); expanding with the curve equation and \(v(z_i)\ge k\), \(v(\omega_i)\ge3k\) gives \(v(\lambda)\ge2k\), and then \( u=\omega_1-\lambda z_1\) has \(v( u)\ge3k\). Substituting the line into the curve equation gives a cubic in \(z\) whose three roots are \(z_1,z_2\) and \(z_3\); by Vieta \(z_1+z_2+z_3=-2A\lambda u/(1+A\lambda^2)\), and \(z(P_1+P_2)=-z_3\) because negation changes the sign of \(z\). The valuation bound follows from \(v(1+A\lambda^2)=0\). For \(P_1=P_2\) the same computation applies to the tangent line, whose slope \(\lambda\) is obtained by differentiating the curve equation; the bounds on \(\lambda\) and \( u\) are proved in the same way.

docs.title: The formal group law of \(y^2=x^3+Ax\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.omegaSeries_hasSum ZInQ.Mult.formalAdd ZInQ.Mult.formalGroupLaw_exists ZInQ.Mult.hasSum_formalAdd

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic \(0\), complete with respect to a discrete valuation \(v\) normalized by \(v(K^\times)=\mathbb Z\), with valuation ring \(\mathcal O\) and maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\). Let \(A\in\mathcal O\setminus\{0\}\), \(W:y^2=x^3+Ax\), and let \(W_1(K)\) and \(z\) be as in the formal neighbourhood statement. Then:

  1. there is a unique power series \(\omega(T)\in\mathcal O[[T]]\) with \(\omega(T)=T^3+AT\,\omega(T)^2\); it has the form \(T^3(1+\cdots)\), and \(\omega(P)=\omega(z(P))\) (that is, \(-1/y=\omega(-x/y)\)) for every affine \(P=(x,y)\in W_1(K)\);
  2. there is a commutative formal group law \(F(T_1,T_2)=T_1+T_2+(\text{terms of degree}\ge2)\) in \(\mathcal O[[T_1,T_2]]\), with formal inverse \(i(T)=-T\), such that $\(z(P+Q)=F\bigl(z(P),z(Q)\bigr)\qquad(P,Q\in W_1(K)),\)$ the series converging because \(z(P),z(Q)\in\mathfrak m\).

This is Silverman IV.1.1-IV.1.2 and VII.2.2; the manuscript uses it through the formal logarithm.

Proof sketch. (1) The coefficients of \(\omega\) are determined recursively by \((*)\) \(\omega=T^3+AT\omega^2\), since the coefficient of \(T^n\) on the right involves only lower coefficients of \(\omega\); they lie in \(\mathbb Z[A]\subset\mathcal O\) (Silverman IV.1.1). For an affine \(P\in W_1(K)\), both \(\omega(P)\) and \(\omega(z(P))\) are solutions \(\omega_0\) of \(\omega_0=z^3+Az\omega_0^2\) with \(v(\omega_0)\ge1\), where \(z=z(P)\); the map \(\omega_0\mapsto z^3+Az\omega_0^2\) is a contraction of \(\mathfrak m\) (its difference quotient \(Az(\omega_0+\omega_0')\) has positive valuation), so the solution is unique. (2) Replace the elements \(z_i,\omega_i\) in the chord construction of the formal neighbourhood statement by the power series \(T_i,\omega(T_i)\): the slope \(\lambda(T_1,T_2)\), the intercept \(\nu=\omega(T_1)-\lambda T_1\) and $\(F(T_1,T_2)=T_1+T_2+\frac{2A\lambda\nu}{1+A\lambda^2}\)$ are power series in \(\mathcal O[[T_1,T_2]]\) (Silverman IV.1.2; the difference quotient defining \(\lambda\) is a polynomial expression in \(T_1,T_2\) and the coefficients of \(\omega\), and \(1+A\lambda^2\) is invertible). Evaluating at \((z(P),z(Q))\) and using (1) recovers \(-z_3=z(P+Q)\). The formal group law axioms for \(F\) (associativity and commutativity as identities of power series) are Silverman IV.1.2, deduced there from the group law of \(W\); \(i(T)=-T\) because negation is \(z\mapsto-z\).

docs.title: The formal logarithm
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.formalLog ZInQ.Mult.ellLog ZInQ.Mult.formalLog_formalAdd ZInQ.Mult.ellLog_add ZInQ.Mult.summable_log

In the setting of the formal group law \(F\) of \(W:y^2=x^3+Ax\) over the complete field \(K\), let \(p>0\) be the residue characteristic and \(e=v(p)\ge1\). There is a power series $\(\log(T)=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{b_{r-1}}{r}\,T^r\in K[[T]],\qquad b_i\in\mathcal O,\ b_0=1,\)$ such that:

  1. \(\log(F(T_1,T_2))=\log(T_1)+\log(T_2)\) in \(K[[T_1,T_2]]\), and \(\frac{d}{dT}\log(T)\,dT\) is the expansion in \(z\) of the invariant differential \(dx/(2y)\);
  2. for \(t\in K\) with \(v(t)>0\) the series \(\log(t)\) converges, and \(\lambda(P)=\log(z(P))\) defines a group homomorphism \(\lambda:W_1(K)\to(K,+)\); in particular \(\lambda([n]P)=n\lambda(P)\) for \(P\in W_1(K)\) and \(n\in\mathbb Z\).

This is the formal logarithm of Silverman IV.5; the manuscript states that it converges on \(v(z)>0\). Its isometry range is a separate statement.

Proof sketch. (1) is Silverman IV.4.2, IV.5.2 and IV.5.5: the normalized invariant differential of \(F\) is \(\omega_F(T)\,dT\) with \(\omega_F\in\mathcal O[[T]]\), \(\omega_F(0)=1\); its formal integral is \(\log\), whose degree-\(r\) coefficient is \(b_{r-1}/r\); invariance of \(\omega_F\) under translation gives \(\log\circ F=\log+\log\). The invariant differential of \(W\) is \(dx/(2y)\), and its expansion in \(z\) is the invariant differential of \(F\) (Silverman IV.1, IV.5.1). (2) Convergence: \(v(b_{r-1}t^r/r)\ge rv(t)-e\log_pr\to\infty\) (Silverman IV.6.3), and in a complete nonarchimedean field a series whose terms tend to \(0\) converges. Evaluating the identity of (1) at \((z(P),z(Q))\) and using \(z(P+Q)=F(z(P),z(Q))\) gives \(\lambda(P+Q)=\lambda(P)+\lambda(Q)\); evaluation of convergent power series in two variables at elements of \(\mathfrak m\) is a ring homomorphism.

docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.evalLog_isometry ZInQ.Mult.ellLog_injOn ZInQ.Mult.val_z_zsmul_eq

In the setting of the formal logarithm of \(W:y^2=x^3+Ax\) over \(K\), with residue characteristic \(p\) and \(e=v(p)\):

  1. if \(t\in K\) and \(v(t)>e/(p-1)\), then \(v(\log(t)-t)>v(t)\), so \(v(\log(t))=v(t)\);
  2. consequently, on the subgroup of \(P\in W_1(K)\) with \(v(z(P))>e/(p-1)\) (together with \(O\)), \(\lambda\) is injective, \(v(\lambda(P))=v(z(P))\), and for \(n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}\), $\(v igl(z([n]P) igr)=v igl(z(P) igr)+v(n).\)$

In particular, if \(p\) is odd and \(e=1\), then \(e/(p-1)<1\), so (2) holds on all of \(W_1(K)\): \(W_1(K)\) is torsion-free and \(\lambda\) is injective on it.

This is the manuscript's statement that the logarithm "is an isometry with inverse exponential on \(v(z)>e/(p-1)\)" (Silverman IV.6.3-IV.6.4), with its reason: the degree-\(r\) coefficient has denominator dividing \(r\), so each relative error has valuation at least \((r-1)v(z)-e\,v_p(r)>0\).

Proof sketch. (1) For \(r\ge2\) the term \(b_{r-1}t^r/r\) has valuation relative to \(t\) at least \((r-1)v(t)-e\,v_p(r)\). Since \(p^{v_p(r)}\le r\) and \(p^m\ge1+m(p-1)\), one has \(v_p(r)\le(r-1)/(p-1)\), so this is at least \((r-1) igl(v(t)-e/(p-1) igr)>0\); the relative errors also tend to infinity with \(r\), so the tail \(\log(t)-t\) has valuation \(>v(t)\). (2) Let \(k\) be the least integer \(>e/(p-1)\); by the filtration, \(W_k(K)\) is a subgroup and the set in question. For \(P\in W_k(K)\setminus\{O\}\), (1) gives \(v(\lambda(P))=v(z(P))<\infty\), so \(\lambda(P) e0\); as \(\lambda\) is a homomorphism, it is injective on \(W_k(K)\). For \(n e0\), \([n]P\in W_k(K)\), \([n]P e O\) by injectivity (\(\lambda([n]P)=n\lambda(P) e0\)), and \(v(z([n]P))=v(\lambda([n]P))=v(n\lambda(P))=v(n)+v(z(P))\).

docs.title: The formal logarithm of \(E\) is a binomial series
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.uSeries_eq ZInQ.Mult.invDiffSeries_ode ZInQ.Mult.coeff_formalLog_genE

For the generator curve \(E:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) (\(A=-d^2\), \(d=75-53s\)), with \(z=-x/y\):

  1. the abscissa reciprocal \(u=1/x\) is the unique power series \(u(z)=z^2+O(z^3)\) with \(z^2(1-d^2u^2)=u\), and \(1+2d^2z^2u(z)=\sqrt{1+4d^2z^4}\) (the square root with constant term \(1\)); in particular \(u(z)=z^2\) times a unit of \(\mathbb Z[s][[z]]\);
  2. the invariant differential is $\(\frac{dx}{2y}=\frac{dz}{\sqrt{1+4d^2z^4}},\qquad (1+4d^2z^4)^{-1/2}=\sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^j\binom{2j}{j}d^{2j}z^{4j};\)$
  3. hence the formal logarithm of \(E\) is $\(\log(T)=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{(-1)^j\binom{2j}{j}\,d^{2j}}{4j+1}\,T^{4j+1}.\)$

These are identities of formal power series with coefficients in \(K_0\); they hold over every completion of \(K_0\).

Proof sketch. From \(y^2=x^3+Ax\), \(z^2=x^2/y^2=x/(x^2+A)=u/(1+Au^2)\), so \(Az^2u^2-u+z^2=0\), whose power-series root with \(u(0)=0\) satisfies \(1-2Az^2u=\sqrt{1-4Az^4}\) and \(u=z^2(1+Az^4+\cdots)\). Since \(x=1/u\) and \(y=-x/z\), \(dx/(2y)=z\,du/(2u)\). Differentiating the quadratic gives \(du\,(1-2Az^2u)=2z(1+Au^2)\,dz\), and with \(z^2(1+Au^2)=u\) this yields \(dx/(2y)=dz/\sqrt{1-4Az^4}\). With \(A=-d^2\) and \(\binom{-1/2}{j}4^j=(-1)^j\binom{2j}{j}\) the binomial series gives (2), and termwise integration with constant term \(0\) gives (3), the formal logarithm being the formal integral of the invariant differential normalized by \(\log(T)=T+\cdots\).

docs.title: The truncated logarithm
docs.text: At every finite place, \(L(z)\) is \(16575z\) times a unit as soon as \(v(z)\ge1\). At a prime \(p>324\) the truncation is much finer: \(L(z)/16575=\log(z)(1+\epsilon_z)\) with \(v(\epsilon_z)\ge28\), because every omitted term has relative valuation at least \(r-1-v_p(r)\ge28\).

docs.title: The truncated logarithm is \(16575z\) times a unit
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.truncLog_eq_mul_unit ZInQ.Mult.log25_eq_mul_unit ZInQ.Mult.log25_ne_zero

Let \(\mathfrak p\) be any nonzero prime of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) (including \((s)\)), with normalized valuation \(v_{\mathfrak p}\) on \(K_0\). For every \(z\in K_0\) with \(v_{\mathfrak p}(z)\ge1\), $\(L(z)=16575\,z\,(1+\eta),\qquad v_{\mathfrak p}(\eta)\ge2 .\)$ In particular \(L(z)\ne0\) whenever \(z\ne0\) and \(v_{\mathfrak p}(z)\ge1\) for some \(\mathfrak p\). The same holds, with the same proof, for \(z\) in the completion of \(K_0\) at \(\mathfrak p\).

Proof sketch. \(\eta=\sum_{j=1}^{6}(c_j/16575)\,d^{2j}z^{4j}\) with the integer coefficients \(c_j\) of \(L\). Here \(v_{\mathfrak p}(c_j)\ge0\), \(v_{\mathfrak p}(d)\ge0\) since \(d\in\mathbb Z[s]\), and \(v_{\mathfrak p}(16575)\le2\): it is \(0\) at \((s)\) and at every prime above a rational prime not dividing \(16575=3\cdot5^2\cdot13\cdot17\), and \(v_p(16575)\le2\) at the primes above \(p\in\{3,5,13,17\}\), which are unramified. Hence each term has valuation at least \(4j-2\ge2\).

docs.title: The truncation error at a large prime
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.log25_truncation_error

Let \(p>324\) be a prime, \(\mathfrak p\) a prime of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) above \(p\), \(K_{\mathfrak p}\) the completion of \(K_0\) at \(\mathfrak p\) with valuation \(v\) (\(v(p)=1\)), and \(\lambda\) the formal logarithm of \(E\) over \(K_{\mathfrak p}\). For every \(P\in E_1(K_{\mathfrak p})\) with \(P\ne O\):

  1. \(v(\lambda(P))=v(z(P))\ge1\);
  2. \(L(z(P))=16575\,\lambda(P)\,(1+\epsilon)\) with \(\epsilon\in K_{\mathfrak p}\) and \(v(\epsilon)\ge28\).

For \(P=O\) both sides of (2) vanish.

Proof sketch. Put \(t=z(P)\), so \(v(t)\ge1\), and \(\lambda(P)=\log(t)\) is the binomial series. By the coefficient identity, \(\log(t)-L(t)/16575=\sum_{j\ge7}(-1)^j\binom{2j}{j}d^{2j}t^{4j+1}/(4j+1)\). With \(r=4j+1\ge29\), each term relative to \(t\) has valuation at least \((r-1)v(t)-v_p(r)\ge r-1-v_p(r)\ge28\): if \(p\nmid r\) this is \(r-1\ge28\), and if \(p\mid r\) then \(r\ge p\ge331\) and \(v_p(r)\le\log_{331}r<r-29\). So \(\log(t)-L(t)/16575=t\delta\) with \(v(\delta)\ge28\). The terms \(1\le j\le6\) of \(\log(t)/t-1\) have valuation at least \(4j\ge4\) because \(4j+1\le25<p\), and the tail has valuation at least \(28\); hence \(\log(t)=t\cdot(\text{unit})\), which is (1). Then \(L(t)/16575=\log(t)(1+\epsilon)\) with \(\epsilon=-t\delta/\log(t)\) and \(v(\epsilon)=v(\delta)\ge28\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.genP0_val_s ZInQ.Mult.genP0_mem_formalFilt_three

Let \(v_s\) be the valuation of \(K_0\) at the prime \((s)\), normalized by \(v_s(s)=1\) (so \(v_s(2)=2\)). Then $\(v_s\bigl(x(P_0)\bigr)=-6,\qquad v_s\bigl(y(P_0)\bigr)=-9,\qquad v_s\bigl(z(P_0)\bigr)=3 .\)$ Hence, for the formal neighbourhood of \(E\) over \(K_0\) at the valuation \(v_s\), \(P_0\in E_3\subset E_1\), and every multiple \([n]P_0\) (\(n\in\mathbb Z\)) lies in \(E_1\) with \(v_s(z([n]P_0))\ge3\). The filtration depends only on the valuations of the coordinates, so the same holds in the completion \(K_{(s)}\).

The numerical input is the separate finite check of the \(2\)-adic valuations of the coordinate numerators.

Proof sketch. \(x(P_0)=(1641-1160s)/8\). By the valuation formula at \((s)\), \(v_s(1641-1160s)=\min(2v_2(1641),2v_2(1160)+1)=\min(0,7)=0\) (using \(v_2(1641)=0\), \(v_2(1160)=3\)) and \(v_s(8)=6\). Similarly \(y(P_0)=(-123720+87483s)/32\) with \(v_s(-123720+87483s)=\min(2v_2(123720),2v_2(87483)+1)=\min(2\cdot3,0+1)=1\) and \(v_s(32)=10\), so \(v_s(y)=-9\). Then \(v_s(z)=v_s(x)-v_s(y)=3\). The statements about multiples follow from the subgroup property of \(E_3\) and from \(v_s(z([n]P))\ge v_s(z(P))\) in the formal group.

ZInQ.Mult.ellLog_ratio

Assume the Mordell-Weil hypothesis for \(E/K_0\). Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(\mathfrak p\) a prime of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) above \(p\), and \(\lambda\) the formal logarithm of \(E\) over the completion \(K_{\mathfrak p}\). Let \(h,u\in\mathbb Z\) with \(h e0\) such that \([h]P_0\) and \([u]P_0\) lie in \(E_1(K_{\mathfrak p})\). Then $\(\lambda([h]P_0) e0\qquad ext{and}\qquad\lambda([u]P_0)= rac uh\,\lambda([h]P_0).\)$

These are the manuscript's full-log ratios: the ratio of two full logarithms of multiples of \(P_0\) in the formal group is a rational number, the ratio of the indices.

Proof sketch. Put \(H=[h]P_0\) and \(U=[u]P_0\). Since \(P_0\) has infinite order, \(H e O\). As \(p\) is odd and unramified, the isometry range of the logarithm is all of \(E_1(K_{\mathfrak p})\), so \(\lambda\) is injective on it and \(\lambda(H) e0\). Both \([u]H\) and \([h]U\) equal \([uh]P_0\) and lie in the subgroup \(E_1(K_{\mathfrak p})\), and \(\lambda\) is a homomorphism, so \(u\lambda(H)=\lambda([u]H)=\lambda([h]U)=h\lambda(U)\).

docs.title: Soundness: accepted triples are true
docs.text:
Soundness says that every rational triple accepted by the multiplication template consists of codes \(\iota(n_1),\iota(n_2),\iota(n_3)\) with \(n_3=n_1n_2\). It uses the generator certificate (hence Mordell-Weil) to give the inputs indices, the pole obstruction at single primes, and the six-contact height estimate H. It does not use pole completeness or the prime pattern.

docs.title: The congruence at odd contact primes
docs.text:
Fix an accepted slope \(t\) and a prime \(p\notin S_{\rm mul}\) at which some \(v_p(t-c)\), \(c\in\mathcal C\), is positive and odd. Then \(v_p(R_0)=v_p(t-c)\) is odd and \(v_p(R)\) is odd and no larger.

Each factor \(1+RC_{gj}^2\) then has valuation \(\min(0,\text{odd})\) at both places above \(p\), so every summand of the trace \(\Theta\) is integral, and the pole obstruction applied to \(R/\Theta^2\) forces one group and one place at which the first eight tests have valuation at least \(1\) and the last four at least \(25\). The manuscript's argument is written as if \(p\) split; it works verbatim for inert \(p\), where the conjugated tests refer to the same place.

At that place the first tests put \(H,U_i\) in the formal group at \(\mathfrak p\) and \(V_0,V_i\) in the formal group at the conjugate place. The full-log ratios are the rational numbers \(z_i/h\) and \((z_i-c_*n_i)/(h-c_*)\); one of \(h,h-c_*\) is a unit at \(p\), which makes its truncated ratio integral; the difference test transfers integrality to the other ratio, and only then do the relative errors of valuation \(28\) become absolute congruences. Subtracting the two congruences and dividing by \(c_*\), which is prime to \(p\), gives \(n_i\equiv A_i\), and the product test gives the congruence.

ZInQ.Mult.contact_valuations

Let \(t\in\mathbb Q\setminus(\mathcal C\cup\{1\})\), \(\eta\in\{1,-1\}\) and \(q\in\mathbb Q\), and put \(R_0=\eta F(t)/(t-1)^8\), \(a=1-R_0q^2\) and \(R=\ell_0^2a^2R_0\) with \(a e0\). Let \(p otin S_b\) be a prime and \(c\in\mathcal C\) with \(k=v_p(t-c)\) positive and odd. Then:

  1. \(v_p(t-c')=0\) for every \(c'\in\mathcal C\setminus\{c\}\) and \(v_p(t-1)=0\); hence \(v_p(R_0)=v_p(F(t))=k\);
  2. \(r=v_p(R)\) is odd and \(r\le k\).

The manuscript records only that the factor valuations below are minima of zero and an odd integer; the case \(v_p(a)<0\), where \(r=3k+4v_p(q)<k\) and \(r\) may be negative, is part of the statement.

Proof sketch. Since \(p otin S_b\), \(p>324\) and \(v_p(\ell_0)=0\). As \(v_p(t-c)>0\), \(t\) is \(p\)-integral and \(t\equiv c\pmod p\); for \(c' e c\), \(t-c'\equiv c-c' ot\equiv0\) because \(0<|c-c'|\le60<p\), and \(t-1\equiv c-1 ot\equiv0\) because \(0<|c-1|\le61<p\). This gives (1). Then \(v_p(R_0q^2)=k+2v_p(q)\) is odd, hence nonzero (if \(q=0\), \(a=1\)). If it is positive, \(v_p(a)=0\); if it is negative, \(v_p(a)=k+2v_p(q)<0\). So \(v_p(a)\le0\) and \(r=2v_p(a)+k\) is odd and at most \(k\).

docs.title: The trace forces one common group and place
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.common_group

Let \(t,\eta,q,R_0,a,R\) be as in the slope predicate with \(\ell=\ell_0\) (so \(t otin\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\) and \(a e0\)), let \(D_{gj}\in K_0\) (\(1\le g\le6\), \(1\le j\le12\)) be arbitrary, and let \(C_{gj}\), \(W_g\) and \(\Theta\) be formed from them as in the slope predicate, with \(W_g e0\), \(\Theta e0\) and \(\Phi(R/\Theta^2)\). Let \(p otin S_b\) be an odd contact prime of \(t\). Then there are a group \(g\) and a prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) above \(p\) such that $\(v_{\mathfrak p}(D_{gj})\ge1\quad(1\le j\le8),\qquad v_{\mathfrak p}(D_{gj})\ge25\quad(9\le j\le12).\)$

The pole obstruction is used here, at the prime \(p otin S_0\); this is the only place where the sound direction uses the pole predicate, and it does not use pole completeness.

Proof sketch. Let \(k=v_p(t-c)\) and \(r=v_p(R)\); by the contact valuations \(k\) is odd, \(v_p(R_0)=k\), \(v_p(t-1)=0\), and \(r\) is odd with \(r\le k\). Fix a prime \(\mathfrak p_0\) above \(p\) and let \(\mathfrak q\) range over \(\{\mathfrak p_0,\sigma\mathfrak p_0\}\). For each factor, \(v_{\mathfrak q}(RC_{gj}^2)=r+2v_{\mathfrak q}(C_{gj})\) is odd (or \(C_{gj}=0\)), hence \(v_{\mathfrak q}(1+RC_{gj}^2)=\min(0,r+2v_{\mathfrak q}(C_{gj}))\): no cancellation occurs. So \(v_{\mathfrak q}(W_g^{-1})=\sum_j\max(0,-r-2v_{\mathfrak q}(C_{gj}))\ge0\). Since \(\Theta=\sum_g(W_g^{-1}+\sigma W_g^{-1})\) and \(v_{\mathfrak p_0}(\sigma y)=v_{\sigma\mathfrak p_0}(y)\), $\(v_p(\Theta)\ge m:=\min_{g,\mathfrak q}v_{\mathfrak q}(W_g^{-1})\ge0 .\)$ The pole input \(B=R/\Theta^2\) is nonzero with \(\Phi(B)\), and \(v_p(B)=r-2v_p(\Theta)\) is odd, so by the pole obstruction it is positive: \(v_p(\Theta)\le(r-1)/2\). In particular \(r\ge1\) and some pair \((g,\mathfrak q)\) has \(s:=v_{\mathfrak q}(W_g^{-1})\le(r-1)/2\). For each \(j\), either \(r+2v_{\mathfrak q}(C_{gj})>0\), so \(v_{\mathfrak q}(C_{gj})\ge-(r-1)/2\), or the deficit \(-(r+2v_{\mathfrak q}(C_{gj}))\) is at most \(s\le(r-1)/2\); in both cases \(v_{\mathfrak q}(C_{gj})\ge-(3r-1)/4\). Then \(v_{\mathfrak q}(D_{gj})=v_{\mathfrak q}(C_{gj})+k_jk\ge k_jk-(3k-1)/4\), which is \((k+1)/4>0\) for \(k_j=1\) and \((97k+1)/4\ge24.5\) for \(k_j=25\); integrality gives the bounds \(1\) and \(25\). Take \(\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\).

docs.title: From the local tests to the congruence
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.tests_to_congruence

Let \(p>324\) be a prime, \(\mathfrak p\) a prime of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) above \(p\), and \(c\in\mathbb Z\) with \(p mid c\). Let \(n_1,n_2,n_3\in\mathbb Z\) and \(h,z_1,z_2,z_3\in\mathbb Z\) with \(h e0\), \(h e c\), and let \( au= au(h,z;\,c,cn_1,cn_2,cn_3)\) be the twelve test values. If $\(v_{\mathfrak p}( au_j)\ge1\quad(1\le j\le8)\qquad ext{and}\qquad v_{\mathfrak p}( au_j)\ge25\quad(9\le j\le12),\)$ then \(p^{25}\mid n_1n_2-n_3\).

In the certificate \(c=c_*\), and \(p mid c_*\) holds for every \(p otin S_{ m mul}\).

Proof sketch. Let \(\mathfrak q=\sigma\mathfrak p\) (possibly \(\mathfrak q=\mathfrak p\) if \(p\) is inert), \(v=v_{\mathfrak p}\), and let \(\lambda_{\mathfrak p},\lambda_{\mathfrak q}\) be the formal logarithms over the two completions. With \(H=[h]P_0\), \(U_i=[z_i]P_0\), \(V_0=[h-c]P_0\), \(V_i=[z_i-cn_i]P_0\):

  1. The points lie in the formal groups. \(v_{\mathfrak p}( ho(Q))\ge1\) means \(Q=O\) or \(v_{\mathfrak p}(x(Q))<0\). Tests \(1\)-\(4\) put \(H,U_i\) in \(E_1(K_{\mathfrak p})\); since \(v_{\mathfrak p}(\sigma y)=v_{\mathfrak q}(y)\), tests \(5\)-\(8\) put \(V_0,V_i\) in \(E_1(K_{\mathfrak q})\).
  2. Full-log ratios. By the full-logarithm ratio lemma, \(\lambda_{\mathfrak p}(U_i)=\alpha_i\lambda_{\mathfrak p}(H)\) and \(\lambda_{\mathfrak q}(V_i)= eta_i\lambda_{\mathfrak q}(V_0)\) with the rational numbers \(\alpha_i=z_i/h\) and \( eta_i=(z_i-cn_i)/(h-c)\).
  3. Truncated ratios. By the truncation error at \(p>324\), \(A_i=\alpha_i\,u_i\) in \(K_{\mathfrak p}\) and \(B_i= eta_i\,u_i'\) in \(K_{\mathfrak q}\) with units \(u_i,u_i'\) congruent to \(1\) modulo valuation \(28\) (when \(U_i=O\) or \(V_i=O\) the ratio is \(0\) and the claims below are trivial).
  4. Integrality. Since \(p mid c\), one of \(h,h-c\) is a \(p\)-adic unit. If \(p mid h\), then \(\alpha_i\) is \(p\)-integral, so \(A_i\) is \(\mathfrak p\)-integral with \(v_{\mathfrak p}(A_i-\alpha_i)\ge28\); tests \(9\)-\(11\) give \(v_{\mathfrak p}(\sigma B_i)\ge0\), that is \(v_{\mathfrak q}(B_i)\ge0\), so \( eta_i=B_iu_i'^{-1}\) is \(p\)-integral and \(v_{\mathfrak q}(B_i- eta_i)\ge28\). If \(p\mid h\), argue symmetrically from \( eta_i\). Only now do the relative errors give absolute congruences: in both cases \(\alpha_i, eta_i\) are \(p\)-integral, \(A_i\equiv\alpha_i\) modulo valuation \(28\) at \(\mathfrak p\), and \(\sigma B_i\equiv eta_i\) modulo valuation \(28\) at \(\mathfrak p\) (as \( eta_i\) is rational).
  5. The congruence. With test \(8+i\): \(v_{\mathfrak p}(A_i- eta_i)\ge25\). Hence \(z_i-hA_i=h(\alpha_i-A_i)\) and \(z_i-cn_i-(h-c)A_i=(h-c)( eta_i-A_i)\) have valuation at least \(25\), and so does their difference \(c(n_i-A_i)\); as \(p mid c\), \(v_{\mathfrak p}(n_i-A_i)\ge25\). Finally \(n_1n_2-n_3=(n_1-A_1)n_2+A_1(n_2-A_2)+(A_1A_2-A_3)+(A_3-n_3)\) with \(A_1\) integral and test \(12\) gives \(v_p(n_1n_2-n_3)\ge25\).

docs.title: The finite-box deduction
docs.text:
For a false triple, \(f=n_1n_2-n_3\ne0\) is divisible by \(M_{S_{\rm mul}}(t)^{25}\) for each of the \(27\) slopes, so the six-contact estimate bounds every slope height by \(A_{\rm ht}|f|^{24/25}\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.slope_height_le

Assume the minimal height hypothesis. Let \(n_1,n_2,n_3\in\mathbb Z\) with \(f=n_1n_2-n_3 e0\), put \(c=(c_*,c_*n_1,c_*n_2,c_*n_3)\), and let \(t\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy \(\mathrm{Slope}(t,\ell_0;c)\). Then $\(M_{S_{ m mul}}(t)^{25}\mid f\qquad ext{and}\qquad h(t)\le A_{ m ht}\,|f|^{24/25}.\)$

This is where the sound direction uses the six-contact estimate, in its minimal form: the instance \(S=S_{ m mul}\), \(R=D\), whose constant \(H_6(D)\) is at most \(A_{ m ht}=H_6(S_{ m mul};R)\) for the fixed \(R=\max(D,H_{\max},c_*,10^{12})\ge D\).

Proof sketch. \(M_{S_{ m mul}}(t)\) is a product of distinct primes \(p otin S_{ m mul}\), each an odd contact prime of \(t\), so \(p^{25}\mid f\) by the local congruence; the prime powers are pairwise coprime, so \(M_{S_{ m mul}}(t)^{25}\mid f\), and since \(f e0\), \(M_{S_{ m mul}}(t)^{24}\le|f|^{24/25}\). The slope predicate gives \(t otin\mathcal C\). The minimal height hypothesis and the properties of the constants (\(H_6(D)\le H_6(S_{ m mul};R)=A_{ m ht}\), as \(H_6\) is increasing in \(R\ge1\)) give \(h(t)\le A_{ m ht}M_{S_{ m mul}}(t)^{24}\le A_{ m ht}|f|^{24/25}\).

docs.title: Sum and quotient bounds for rational heights
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.rational_height_bounds

For a rational number \(x=a/b\) in lowest terms with \(b>0\) let \(h(x)=\log\max(|a|,b)\). For all \(x_1,x_2,x_3,x,y\in\mathbb Q\) with \(y\ne0\): $\(h(x_1+x_2+x_3)\le h(x_1)+h(x_2)+h(x_3)+\log3,\qquad h(x/y)\le h(x)+h(y),\)$ and \(h(-x)=h(x)\ge0\), \(h(1/y)=h(y)\).

Proof sketch. Write \(x_i=a_i/b_i\) in lowest terms. The sum is \(\bigl(\sum_ia_i\prod_{j\ne i}b_j\bigr)/(b_1b_2b_3)\); after reduction its numerator has absolute value at most \(3\prod_i\max(|a_i|,b_i)\) and its denominator at most \(\prod_ib_i\le\prod_i\max(|a_i|,b_i)\). For the quotient, \(x/y=(a d)/(b c)\) for \(y=c/d\), and reduction only decreases numerator and denominator, whose absolute values are at most \(\max(|a|,b)\max(|c|,d)\). Inversion swaps numerator and denominator up to sign.

docs.title: Height bounds in \(K_0\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.field_height_bounds

Let \(h\) be the absolute logarithmic height on \(K_0\) and \(\epsilon=1+s\). For all \(x,y\in K_0\) and \(x_0,x_1\in\mathbb Q\):

  1. \(h(xy)\le h(x)+h(y)\) and \(h(x+y)\le h(x)+h(y)+\log2\);
  2. \(h(s)=\tfrac12\log2\) and \(h(\epsilon)=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)\); hence \(h(\epsilon^4x)\le h(x)+2\log(1+\sqrt2)\);
  3. \(h(x_0+x_1s)\le h(x_0)+h(x_1)+\tfrac32\log2\), where on \(\mathbb Q\) the height \(h\) is the rational height \(\log\max(|a|,b)\).

These are the "fixed coordinate change" estimates of the finite-box deduction.

Proof sketch. Place by place, \(\max(1,|xy|_v)\le\max(1,|x|_v)\max(1,|y|_v)\), and \(\max(1,|x+y|_v)\) is at most \(\max(1,|x|_v)\max(1,|y|_v)\) at finite places and twice that at the two real places; dividing \(\sum_vn_v\log(\cdot)\) by \([K_0:\mathbb Q]=2\) gives (1). For \(s\), both real embeddings have absolute value \(\sqrt2\) and \(|s|_v\le1\) at finite places. \(\epsilon\) is a unit with embeddings \(1+\sqrt2>1\) and \(|1-\sqrt2|<1\), so \(h(\epsilon)=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)\) and \(h(\epsilon^4x)\le4h(\epsilon)+h(x)\). (3) follows from (1), (2) and the agreement of \(h\) with the rational height on \(\mathbb Q\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.box_inequality

Let \(A\ge1\) be real and \(N\ge0\) an integer with $\(N^2<24A\,N^{48/25}+10 .\)$ Then \(N<(48A)^{13}\).

Proof sketch. If \(N\le4\), then \(N<48\le(48A)^{13}\). Let \(N\ge5\) and suppose \(N^{2/25}\ge48A\). Then \(24AN^{48/25}\le\tfrac12N^{2/25}N^{48/25}=\tfrac12N^2\), so \(N^2<\tfrac12N^2+10\) and \(N^2<20\), contradicting \(N\ge5\). Hence \(N^{2/25}<48A\), so \(N<(48A)^{25/2}\le(48A)^{13}\) because \(48A\ge1\).
