docs.title: Soundness of the multiplication template
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.multiply_sound

Assume the minimal height hypothesis. For all \(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3\in\mathbb Q^5\), if \(\mathrm{Rel}_{\mathtt{multiply}}(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)\), then there are \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\) with \((Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)=(\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(ab))\).

This direction is sound on arbitrary rational inputs. It uses the generator certificate and the six-contact estimate in its minimal form, but neither pole completeness nor the prime pattern.

Proof sketch. By the unfolding of the template, \(Y_i=\iota(n_i)\) for some integers \(n_i\), the unguarded certificate accepts \((\iota(n_1),\iota(n_2),\iota(n_3))\) with the shift points \(\iota(c_*),\iota(c_*n_i)\), and the guard holds. If \(n_1n_2\ne n_3\), the finite-box deduction gives \(|n_i|<T\) for all \(i\), so the triple is a false triple in \([-T,T]^3\) and the guard fails, a contradiction. Hence \(n_3=n_1n_2\); take \(a=n_1\), \(b=n_2\).

docs.title: Primes in arithmetic progressions
docs.text:
The size bounds need every unit class modulo \(W=4\prod_{p\le324}p\) to contain twenty-two primes above \(324\) below an explicit cutoff. The manuscript takes this from the explicit progression estimate of Bennett, Martin, O'Bryant and Rechnitzer. This chapter proves it instead from an effective form of Dirichlet's theorem with crude but explicit constants: for \(q\ge2^{16}\), every unit class modulo \(q\) has twenty-two primes in \((q^2,2^{q^8})\). The proof is the classical one, made quantitative; every constant is explicit, and the value of an \(L\)-function at \(s=1\) is reached as a limit from the right.

Notation: \(\chi\) is a Dirichlet character modulo \(q\), \(\chi_0\) the principal one, \(M=\log q+3\) and \(S_\chi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\chi(n)\Lambda(n)/n\).

2 fully proved

docs.title: \(L\)-values near \(s=1\)
docs.text:
Summation by parts bounds \(L(\sigma,\chi)\), its derivative and its partial sums for real \(\sigma\ge1\), and the classical product inequality gives \(|L(1,\chi)|\ge1/(256M^7)\) when \(\chi^2\ne\chi_0\).

  • Character sums and \(L\)-values near \(s=1\)

docs.title: Real characters
docs.text:
When \(\chi^2=\chi_0\), the value \(L(1,\chi)\) is tied to a quadratic field: \(\chi\) is a Legendre symbol \((d/\cdot)\) away from \(2q\), the Dedekind zeta function of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\) factors as \(\zeta(s)L(s,\chi)\) up to finitely many local factors, and the class number formula with crude bounds on the discriminant, the roots of unity and the regulator gives \(|L(1,\chi)|\ge1/(40q^{3/2})\). The splitting law and the field need only that \(d\) is not a square.

docs.title: The count
docs.text:
Mertens' first theorem (with constant \(3\)), the identity relating \(L(1,\chi)S_\chi(x)\) to \(\sum_{n\le x}\chi(n)\log n/n\), and orthogonality give at least twenty-two primes of each unit class in \((q^8,q^8e^{5qB}]\), where \(B=(M^2+6q)/c\) and \(c\) is a lower bound for \(|L(1,\chi)|\) at all nonprincipal \(\chi\); here \(\log(e^{5qB})\) is of order \(q^{11/2}\).

docs.title: The theorem and its instance
docs.text: At \(q=W\) this is the catalogue bound with cutoff \(2^{W^8}\), the fourth hypothesis of the main theorem.

docs.title: An effective Dirichlet theorem
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.effective_dirichlet

Let \(q\ge2^{16}\) be an integer and \(a\) an integer coprime to \(q\). Then at least \(22\) primes \(p\equiv a\pmod q\) satisfy $\(q^2<p<2^{q^8} .\)$

Proof sketch. Put \(M=\log q+3\) and \(c=\min\bigl(1/(256M^7),1/(40q^{3/2})\bigr)\). By the lower bound at every nonprincipal character, \(|L(1,\chi)|\ge c\) for all \(\chi\ne\chi_0\), so the twenty-two primes statement gives \(22\) primes \(p\equiv a\pmod q\) with \(q^8<p\le q^8e^{5qB}\), where \(B=(M^2+6q)/c\). It remains to show \(q^8e^{5qB}<2^{q^8}\). From \(\log t\le t-1\) at \(t=\sqrt q\), \(\log q\le2\sqrt q-2\), so \(M\le3\sqrt q\) and \(M^2+6q\le15q\). Then \(1/c=\max(256M^7,40q^{3/2})\le256\cdot3^7q^{7/2}\le2^{20}q^{7/2}\), so \(B\le15\cdot2^{20}q^{9/2}\) and \(8\log q+5qB\le8q+2^{27}q^{11/2}\le2^{28}q^{11/2}\). Since \(q\ge2^{16}\), \(q^{5/2}\ge2^{40}\) and \(q^8\log2\ge q^8/2\ge2^{39}q^{11/2}\). Hence \(\log(q^8e^{5qB})<q^8\log2\), and every such prime satisfies \(q^2<q^8<p<2^{q^8}\).

The bound is far from sharp: the proof gives such primes below \(\exp(Cq^{11/2})\) for an explicit \(C\), and the exponent \(8\) leaves room for cruder constants.

docs.title: The catalogue bound holds
docs.text:
ZInQ.catalogueBound8

The catalogue bound holds: with \(P_s=\prod_{p\le324}p\) and \(W=4P_s\), for every integer \(r\) with \(0\le r<W\) and \(\gcd(r,W)=1\), at least \(22\) primes \(p\) satisfy $\(324<p<2^{W^8}\qquad\text{and}\qquad p\equiv r\pmod W .\)$

This replaces the explicit progression estimate of Bennett, Martin, O'Bryant and Rechnitzer that the manuscript uses at the cutoff \(2^{W^3}\); the larger cutoff \(2^{W^8}\) is the range of the effective Dirichlet theorem.

Proof sketch. By the small explicit bounds, \(W>10^5>2^{16}\). The effective Dirichlet theorem at \(q=W\) and \(a=r\) gives \(22\) primes \(p\equiv r\pmod W\) with \(W^2<p<2^{W^8}\), and \(W^2>324\). Since \(0\le r<W\), the congruence \(p\equiv r\pmod W\) says that \(p\) leaves the remainder \(r\) on division by \(W\). The constant \(W\) is never evaluated beyond these bounds.

docs.title: Counting primes in a residue class
Counting primes in a residue class
docs.text:
The count follows the classical proof of Dirichlet's theorem with explicit constants. Mertens' first theorem controls \(\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)/n\) to within \(3\), and the principal character inherits this up to the primes dividing \(q\).

For a nonprincipal \(\chi\), the identity \(\log n=\sum_{d\mid n}\Lambda(d)\) relates \(L(1,\chi)\sum_{n\le x}\chi(n)\Lambda(n)/n\) to the bounded sum \(\sum_{n\le x}\chi(n)\log n/n\), so the twisted sum is at most \((M^2+6q)/|L(1,\chi)|\); the lower bounds for \(|L(1,\chi)|\) of the preceding sections combine into one bound for all nonprincipal characters.

Orthogonality isolates one residue class; above \(y=q^8\), prime powers with exponent at least \(2\) add less than \(1/5\) and each prime adds at most \(\log y/y\). So the interval \((q^8,q^8e^{5qB}]\) holds twenty-two primes of the class when every twisted sum is at most \(B\).

7 fully proved

Let \(\Lambda\) be the von Mangoldt function and \(\psi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)\). For every real \(x\ge0\), \(\psi(x)\le3x\). For every real \(x\ge1\), $\(\log x-2\le\sum_{n\le x}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n}\le\log x+3,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{n\le x}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n}-\log x\Bigr|\le3 .\)$

Proof sketch. Chebyshev's bound \(\psi(x)\le\log4\cdot x+2\sqrt x\log x\) for \(x\ge1\), with \(\log x\le2\sqrt x/e\) (from \(\log t\le t-1\) at \(t=\sqrt x/e\)) and \(4/e\le1.5\), gives \(\psi(x)\le(\log4+1.5)x\le3x\); for \(x<2\), \(\psi(x)=0\). Let \(N=\lfloor x\rfloor\ge1\). Since \(\log n=\sum_{d\mid n}\Lambda(d)\), $\(\log N!=\sum_{d\le N}\Lambda(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac Nd\Bigr\rfloor =N\sum_{d\le N}\frac{\Lambda(d)}d-\sum_{d\le N}\Lambda(d)\Bigl\{\frac Nd\Bigr\},\)$ and the last sum lies in \([0,\psi(N)]\). With \(N\log N-N\le\log N!\le N\log N\) and \(\psi(N)\le3N\), this gives \(\log N-1\le\sum_{d\le N}\Lambda(d)/d\le\log N+3\). Finally \(\log N\le\log x\le\log N+1\), since \(x/N<2\).

Let \(q\ge1\) and let \(1\le y\le x\) be real. Then $\(\sum_{\substack{y<n\le x\\ \gcd(n,q)=1}}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n}\ge\log\frac xy-6-\log q ;\)$ the left side is \(S_{\chi_0}(x)-S_{\chi_0}(y)\) for the principal character \(\chi_0\) modulo \(q\). Moreover, for every integer \(N\ge0\), \(\sum_{n\le N,\ \gcd(n,q)>1}\Lambda(n)/n\le\log q\).

Proof sketch. By Mertens' first theorem, \(\sum_{y<n\le x}\Lambda(n)/n\ge(\log x-2)-(\log y+3)\ge\log(x/y)-6\). The terms with \(\gcd(n,q)>1\) and \(\Lambda(n)\ne0\) are the powers \(p^k\) of the primes \(p\mid q\), and all of them together contribute at most \(\sum_{p\mid q}\sum_{k\ge1}\log p/p^k=\sum_{p\mid q}\log p/(p-1)\le\sum_{p\mid q}\log p\le\log q\).

Let \(q\ge1\), let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\), put \(M=\log q+3\), and for real \(x\) let $\(S_\chi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\frac{\chi(n)\Lambda(n)}{n},\qquad T_\chi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\frac{\chi(n)\log n}{n}.\)$ Then for every real \(x\ge1\), $\(|L(1,\chi)|\,|S_\chi(x)|\le|T_\chi(x)|+\frac{2q\,\psi(x)}{x}\le M^2+6q ,\)$ and hence, as \(L(1,\chi)\ne0\), \(|S_\chi(x)|\le(M^2+6q)/|L(1,\chi)|\).

Proof sketch. Write \(\log n=\sum_{d\mid n}\Lambda(d)\) and \(n=dm\), using \(\chi(dm)=\chi(d)\chi(m)\): $\(T_\chi(x)=\sum_{d\le x}\frac{\chi(d)\Lambda(d)}{d}\sum_{m\le x/d}\frac{\chi(m)}{m} =L(1,\chi)S_\chi(x)+\sum_{d\le x}\frac{\chi(d)\Lambda(d)}{d}R\Bigl(\frac xd\Bigr),\)$ where \(R(y)=\sum_{m\le y}\chi(m)/m-L(1,\chi)\) satisfies \(|R(y)|\le2q/y\) for \(y\ge1\). So \(|L(1,\chi)||S_\chi(x)|\le|T_\chi(x)|+(2q/x)\sum_{d\le x}\Lambda(d)=|T_\chi(x)|+2q\psi(x)/x\), and \(|T_\chi(x)|\le M^2\) while \(\psi(x)\le3x\).

Let \(q\ge1\), put \(M=\log q+3\), and let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\). Then $\(|L(1,\chi)|\ge\min\Bigl(\frac1{256\,M^7},\ \frac1{40\,q^{3/2}}\Bigr).\)$

Proof sketch. If \(\chi^2\ne\chi_0\), the lower bound at complex characters gives \(|L(1,\chi)|\ge1/(256M^7)\). If \(\chi^2=\chi_0\), the lower bound at real characters gives \(|L(1,\chi)|\ge1/(40q^{3/2})\). In both cases \(|L(1,\chi)|\) is at least the minimum.

Let \(q\ge1\) and let \(a\) be a unit modulo \(q\), with inverse \(a^{-1}\) modulo \(q\). For real \(x\) put $\(S_a(x)=\sum_{\substack{n\le x\\ n\equiv a\ (\mathrm{mod}\ q)}}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n},\qquad S_\chi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\frac{\chi(n)\Lambda(n)}{n}\)$ for each Dirichlet character \(\chi\) modulo \(q\). Then $\(S_a(x)=\frac1{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\chi\bmod q}\chi(a^{-1})\,S_\chi(x),\)$ the sum running over the \(\varphi(q)\) Dirichlet characters modulo \(q\), where \(\chi(a^{-1})=\chi(a)^{-1}=\overline{\chi(a)}\). Consequently, for all real \(x,y\), $\(S_a(x)-S_a(y)=\frac1{\varphi(q)}\,\mathrm{Re}\sum_{\chi\bmod q}\chi(a^{-1}) \bigl(S_\chi(x)-S_\chi(y)\bigr).\)$

Proof sketch. Exchange the sums and apply the orthogonality relation \(\sum_\chi\chi(a^{-1})\chi(n)=\varphi(q)\) if \(n\equiv a\pmod q\) and \(0\) otherwise. Subtract the identities at \(x\) and \(y\); the left side is real, so it equals the real part of the right side.

docs.title: Higher prime powers contribute little
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.sum_nonprime_vonMangoldt_div_le_two ZInQ.Progressions.sum_Ioc_nonprime_vonMangoldt_div_le ZInQ.Progressions.sum_vonMangoldt_mul_le_sum_primePow ZInQ.Progressions.sum_Icc_log_div_mul_pred_le'

For every integer \(N\ge0\), $\(\sum_{\substack{n\le N\\ n\text{ not prime}}}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n}\le2 ,\)$ that is, the prime powers \(p^k\) with \(k\ge2\) contribute at most \(2\) to \(\sum_{n\le N}\Lambda(n)/n\). Moreover, for all integers \(Y\ge1\) and \(M\ge0\), with \(s=\lfloor\sqrt Y\rfloor\), $\(\sum_{\substack{Y<n\le M\\ n\text{ not prime}}}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n} \le\frac{\log s+2+2\log4}{s}.\)$

Proof sketch. A sum of \(\Lambda(n)h(n)\) with \(h\ge0\) is at most the double sum of \(\log p\cdot h(p^k)\) over primes \(p\) and exponents \(k\) that cover its prime powers. The telescoping bound \(\sum_{s<n\le N}\log n/(n(n-1))\le(\log s+2)/s-(\log N+2)/N\) for \(1\le s\le N\) holds term by term. For the first bound, the sum is at most \(\sum_p\sum_{k\ge2}\log p/p^k\le\sum_p\log p/(p(p-1))\le\sum_{m\ge2}\log m/(m(m-1))\le2\), by the telescoping bound at \(s=1\). For the second, a prime \(p\le s\) contributes at most \(2\log p/Y\), since its powers above \(Y\) form a geometric series with ratio \(1/p\le1/2\) starting below \(1/Y\); these primes give at most \(2\theta(s)/Y\le2\log4\cdot s/Y\le2\log4/s\). A prime \(p>s\) contributes at most \(\log p/(p(p-1))\), and these primes give at most \(\sum_{n>s}\log n/(n(n-1))\le(\log s+2)/s\).

Let \(q\ge3\) and \(B\ge1\) be such that \(\bigl|\sum_{n\le t}\chi(n)\Lambda(n)/n\bigr|\le B\) for every nonprincipal Dirichlet character \(\chi\) modulo \(q\) and every real \(t\ge1\). Let \(a\ge0\) be an integer coprime to \(q\). Then at least \(22\) primes \(p\equiv a\pmod q\) satisfy $\(q^8<p\le q^8e^{5qB}.\)$ In particular, if \(c>0\) and \(|L(1,\chi)|\ge c\) for every nonprincipal character \(\chi\) modulo \(q\), then this holds with \(B=((\log q+3)^2+6q)/c\).

Proof sketch. Let \(S_a(t)=\sum_{n\le t,\ n\equiv a}\Lambda(n)/n\), \(y=q^8\) and \(x=q^8e^{5qB}\), so \(\log(x/y)=5qB\). Detecting the class by characters, the principal character contributes at least \(\log(x/y)-6-\log q\) to \(\varphi(q)(S_a(x)-S_a(y))\), and each of the other \(\varphi(q)-1\) characters at most \(2B\) in absolute value. So $\(S_a(x)-S_a(y)\ge\frac{\log(x/y)-6-\log q-2B(\varphi(q)-1)}{\varphi(q)}\ge1,\)$ using \(\varphi(q)\le q\), \(\log q\le q-1\), \(B\ge1\) and \(q\ge3\). On the other hand, each prime \(p>y\) contributes \(\log p/p\le\log y/y\le16/6561\) (as \(y\ge3^8=6561\) and \(\log t/t\) decreases for \(t\ge3\)), and the prime powers \(p^k\) with \(k\ge2\) above \(y\) contribute at most \((\log s+2+2\log4)/s\le16/81\) with \(s=\lfloor\sqrt y\rfloor=q^4\ge81\). If at most \(21\) primes \(p\equiv a\) lay in \((y,x]\), then \(S_a(x)-S_a(y)\le21\cdot16/6561+16/81<1\). For the last claim, the twisted sum bound gives \(|S_\chi(t)|\le((\log q+3)^2+6q)/c\), which is at least \(1\) since \(c\le|L(1,\chi)|\le\log q+3\) for some nonprincipal \(\chi\) (one exists as \(q\ge3\)).

docs.title: Ideal counts in quadratic fields
docs.text:
The Dedekind zeta function is the Dirichlet series of the number \(a_K(n)\) of ideals of norm \(n\). These counts are multiplicative. In a quadratic field, at a prime power \(p^k\) they are the partial sums of the powers of a sign \(\varepsilon_p\in\{-1,0,1\}\), and if \(\mathcal O_K\) contains a square root of a non-square integer \(d\), then for odd \(p\nmid d\) that sign is the Legendre symbol \((d/p)\). Comparing Euler products then factors \(\zeta_K\) as \(\zeta\) times an \(L\)-function, up to finitely many local factors.

5 fully proved

Let \(K\) be a number field with ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\). For \(n\ge0\) let \(a_K(n)\) be the number of ideals \(I\subseteq\mathcal O_K\) of absolute norm \(N(I)=|\mathcal O_K/I|=n\). This number is finite, and the Dedekind zeta function is the Dirichlet series $\(\zeta_K(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_K(n)\,n^{-s},\)$ absolutely convergent for \(\mathrm{Re}\,s>1\).

Proof sketch. There are finitely many ideals of norm at most \(n\), because \(\mathcal O_K\) has finite quotients. The Dirichlet series is the definition of \(\zeta_K\). Absolute convergence for \(\mathrm{Re}\,s>1\) follows from the asymptotic count of ideals of norm at most \(t\), which is \(O(t)\) (it is \(\kappa_Kt+o(t)\), the input to the class number formula), by partial summation.

docs.title: Ideal counts are multiplicative

Let \(K\) be a number field. For coprime natural numbers \(m,n\), $\(a_K(mn)=a_K(m)\,a_K(n),\)$ and \(a_K(1)=1\).

Proof sketch. The only ideal of norm \(1\) is \(\mathcal O_K\). The map \((J,J')\mapsto JJ'\) sends pairs of ideals of norms \(m\) and \(n\) to ideals of norm \(mn\), since the norm is multiplicative. It is a bijection, with inverse \(I\mapsto(I+m\mathcal O_K,\,I+n\mathcal O_K)\): since \((m)+(n)=\mathcal O_K\), one has \((I+(m))(I+(n))=I\) when \(mn\in I\), and \(JJ'+(m)=J\) when \(m\in J\) and \(J'+(m)=\mathcal O_K\). The norm of \(I+(m)\) divides both \(m^{[K:\mathbb Q]}\) and \(mn\), hence divides \(m\); likewise for \(n\), and the product of the two norms is \(mn\), so they are exactly \(m\) and \(n\). No prime factorization is used.

Let \(K\) be a number field of degree \(2\) and \(p\) a prime. Put \(\varepsilon_p=a_K(p)-1\). Then \(\varepsilon_p\in\{-1,0,1\}\), and for every \(k\ge0\) $\(a_K(p^k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\varepsilon_p^{\,j} ;\)$ conversely, \(\varepsilon_p\) is the only integer with this property. Equivalently, for every complex \(s\) with \(\mathrm{Re}\,s>0\), $\(\sum_{k\ge0}a_K(p^k)p^{-ks}=(1-p^{-s})^{-1}(1-\varepsilon_pp^{-s})^{-1}.\)$

Proof sketch. The ideals of norm \(p^k\) are the products \(\prod_i\mathfrak p_i^{a_i}\) of the primes \(\mathfrak p_i\) above \(p\) with \(\sum_ia_if_i=k\), where \(f_i\) is the residue degree: unique factorization gives a bijection with these exponent vectors. Write \(p\mathcal O_K=\prod_i\mathfrak p_i^{e_i}\); then \(\sum_ie_if_i=2\). Three cases remain. Split: two primes of norm \(p\), so \(a_K(p^k)=k+1\) and \(\varepsilon_p=1\). Inert: one prime of norm \(p^2\), so \(a_K(p^k)\) is \(1\) for even \(k\) and \(0\) for odd \(k\), and \(\varepsilon_p=-1\). Ramified: one prime of norm \(p\), so \(a_K(p^k)=1\) and \(\varepsilon_p=0\). In each case the formula holds; the case \(k=1\) shows that \(\varepsilon_p\) is determined. Since \(|\varepsilon_p|\le1\) and \(|p^{-s}|<1\), the Euler factor is the Cauchy product of two geometric series.

docs.title: The splitting law in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.localEps_eq_legendreSym ZInQ.Progressions.idealCount_prime_eq_legendreSym ZInQ.Progressions.idealCount_prime_pow_eq_legendreSym ZInQ.Progressions.IdealCount.idealCount_prime_eq_card_ringHom ZInQ.Progressions.IdealCount.card_ringHom_eq_card_sqrt

Let \(K\) be a number field of degree \(2\) and \(d\) an integer that is not a square, such that \(\mathcal O_K\) contains an element \(\alpha\) with \(\alpha^2=d\); for instance \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\) and \(\alpha=\sqrt d\). Let \(p\) be an odd prime with \(p\nmid d\). Then the local sign \(\varepsilon_p=a_K(p)-1\) is the Legendre symbol: $\(\varepsilon_p=\Bigl(\frac dp\Bigr),\)$ so \(a_K(p)=1+(d/p)\) and \(a_K(p^k)=\sum_{j=0}^k(d/p)^j\) for every \(k\ge0\).

The hypothesis that \(d\) is not a square cannot be dropped: in \(K=\mathbb Q(i)\) with \(\alpha=1\), \(d=1\) and \(p=3\), the prime \(3\) is inert, so \(\varepsilon_3=-1\ne(1/3)\).

Proof sketch. Ideals of norm \(p\) are the kernels of ring homomorphisms \(\mathcal O_K\to\mathbb Z/p\), and distinct homomorphisms have distinct kernels, so \(a_K(p)\) is the number of such homomorphisms. With \(t\) the trace from \(\mathcal O_K\) to \(\mathbb Z\), every \(x\in\mathcal O_K\) satisfies \(2dx=d\,t(x)+t(\alpha x)\,\alpha\), as one checks in the basis \(1,\alpha\) of \(K\), using \(t(\alpha)=0\). Since \(2d\) is invertible modulo \(p\), a homomorphism \(\varphi\) is determined by \(r=\varphi(\alpha)\), which satisfies \(r^2=d\); conversely, for each \(r\) with \(r^2=d\), the map \(x\mapsto(d\,t(x)+t(\alpha x)r)/(2d)\) is a ring homomorphism, by two trace identities obtained by comparing coefficients in the basis \(1,\alpha\). Hence \(a_K(p)=\#\{r\in\mathbb Z/p:r^2=d\}=1+(d/p)\). No Kummer–Dedekind theorem and no index computation are needed. The formula for \(a_K(p^k)\) then follows from the prime-power formula.

Let \(K\) be a number field of degree \(2\), with \(\varepsilon_p=a_K(p)-1\), let \(q\ge1\), and let \(\chi\) be a Dirichlet character modulo \(q\) with \(\varepsilon_p=\chi(p)\) for every prime \(p mid2q\). Then for every real \(s>1\), $\(\zeta_K(s)=\zeta(s)\,L(s,\chi)\prod_{p\mid2q} rac{1-\chi(p)p^{-s}}{1-\varepsilon_pp^{-s}},\)$ the product running over the primes dividing \(2q\), and \(L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)n^{-s}\). More generally, for any finite set \(P\) of primes with \(\varepsilon_p=\chi(p)\) for every prime \(p otin P\), the same identity holds for every complex \(s\) with \(\mathrm{Re}\,s>1\), with the product over \(p\in P\).

The hypothesis on \(\varepsilon_p\) holds in the following situation: \(d\) is an integer that is not a square, \(\mathcal O_K\) contains an element \(\alpha\) with \(\alpha^2=d\) (for instance \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\)), no prime \(p mid2q\) divides \(d\), and \(\chi(p)= igl( rac dp igr)\) for every prime \(p mid2q\).

Proof sketch. For \(\mathrm{Re}\,s>1\) all three Dirichlet series converge absolutely and have Euler products: the coefficients \(a_K\) are multiplicative with the local factors \((1-p^{-s})^{-1}(1-\varepsilon_pp^{-s})^{-1}\), and \(\zeta(s)L(s,\chi)\) has the local factors \((1-p^{-s})^{-1}(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1}\). For \(p otin P\) the local factors agree. The quotient of the two Euler products is therefore the finite product over \(p\in P\). In the situation of the last paragraph, a prime \(p mid2q\) is odd and does not divide \(d\), so \(\varepsilon_p=(d/p)=\chi(p)\) by the splitting law. (Here \(\chi(p)=0\) for \(p\mid q\), so only \(p=2 mid q\) contributes a nontrivial numerator.) The hypothesis \(q\ge1\) matters: for \(q=0\) every prime divides \(2q\) but the product would be empty.

Character sums and \(L\)-values near \(s=1\)

Throughout, \(q\ge1\), \(\chi\) is a Dirichlet character modulo \(q\), \(\chi_0\) the principal one, and \(M=\log q+3\). For \(\chi\ne\chi_0\) the \(L\)-function \(L(s,\chi)\) is entire and equals \(\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)n^{-s}\) for \(\mathrm{Re}\,s>1\). Every bound below is explicit, and the value at \(s=1\) is always reached as a limit from the right, never through a conditionally convergent series.

Let \(q\ge1\) and let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\). For every real \(x\), $\(\Bigl|\sum_{1\le n\le x}\chi(n)\Bigr|\le q .\)$ More generally \(\bigl|\sum_{a\le n<b}\chi(n)\bigr|\le q\) and \(\bigl|\sum_{a<n\le b}\chi(n)\bigr|\le q\) for all integers \(a,b\ge0\) (the sums are empty when \(b\le a\)). The sum of \(\chi\) over any \(q\) consecutive integers \(a\le n<a+q\) is \(0\).

Proof sketch. The values of \(\chi\) on any \(q\) consecutive integers run once through its values on \(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z\), whose sum is \(0\) because \(\chi\) is nonprincipal. Removing complete blocks of \(q\) consecutive integers from the interval leaves fewer than \(q\) terms, each of absolute value at most \(1\).

Let \(q\ge1\) and let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\). For all integers \(N,K\ge0\) and real \(\sigma\):

  1. if \(\sigma\ge0\), then \(\bigl|\sum_{N<n\le K}\chi(n)n^{-\sigma}\bigr|\le q\,(N+1)^{-\sigma}\); if \(\sigma\ge1\) and \(N\ge1\), this is at most \(2q/N\);
  2. if \(\sigma\ge1\) and \(N\ge2\), then \(\bigl|\sum_{N<n\le K}\chi(n)\log n\cdot n^{-\sigma}\bigr|\le q\log(N+1)\,(N+1)^{-\sigma}\); if moreover \(N\ge3\), this is at most \(2q\log N/N\).

For real \(\sigma>1\) the same bounds hold for the infinite tails: with \(L(\sigma,\chi)\) the value of the \(L\)-function and \(N\ge0\), $\(\Bigl|L(\sigma,\chi)-\sum_{1\le n\le N}\frac{\chi(n)}{n^{\sigma}}\Bigr|\le q\,(N+1)^{-\sigma},\)$ which is at most \(2q/N\) for \(N\ge1\); and for \(N\ge2\), $\(\Bigl|\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\chi(n)\log n}{n^{\sigma}} -\sum_{1\le n\le N}\frac{\chi(n)\log n}{n^{\sigma}}\Bigr|\le q\log(N+1)\,(N+1)^{-\sigma},\)$ which is at most \(2q\log N/N\) for \(N\ge3\).

Proof sketch. Summation by parts: if every partial sum \(\sum_{N<n\le m}c_n\) has absolute value at most \(B\) and \(f\ge0\) is nonincreasing on \(n\ge N+1\), then \(\bigl|\sum_{N<n\le K}c_nf(n)\bigr|\le B\,f(N+1)\). Take \(c_n=\chi(n)\), so \(B=q\) by the bound on character sums, and \(f(n)=n^{-\sigma}\), respectively \(f(n)=\log n\cdot n^{-\sigma}\), which is nonincreasing for \(n\ge3\) because \(\log t/t\) decreases on \([e,\infty)\) and \(t^{1-\sigma}\) is nonincreasing. Then \(q(N+1)^{-\sigma}\le q/(N+1)\le2q/N\), and \(q\log(N+1)(N+1)^{-\sigma}\le q\log(N+1)/(N+1)\le q\log N/N\le2q\log N/N\) for \(N\ge3\). For \(\sigma>1\) both series converge absolutely (the first to \(L(\sigma,\chi)\)), and a bound on every finite tail \(\sum_{N<n\le K}\) passes to the limit \(K\to\infty\).

Let \(q\ge1\), let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\), and let \(L(s,\chi)\) be its \(L\)-function, the entire continuation of \(\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)n^{-s}\). Put \(M=\log q+3\). For every real \(\sigma\ge1\), $\(|L(\sigma,\chi)|\le M ;\)$ in particular \(|L(1,\chi)|\le M\).

Proof sketch. For \(\sigma>1\) the series converges absolutely to \(L(\sigma,\chi)\). Split it at \(N=q\): the first \(q\) terms contribute at most \(\sum_{n\le q}1/n\le1+\log q\), and by the tail bound the rest has absolute value at most \(q(q+1)^{-\sigma}\le1\), so \(|L(\sigma,\chi)|\le\log q+3\). The value at \(\sigma=1\) follows by continuity of \(L(s,\chi)\) as \(\sigma\to1^+\): a closed bound on \(L(\sigma,\chi)\) for all \(\sigma>1\) passes to \(\sigma=1\).

Let \(q\ge1\), let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\), and put \(M=\log q+3\). For every real \(x\), $\(\Bigl|\sum_{1\le n\le x}\frac{\chi(n)\log n}{n}\Bigr|\le M^2 .\)$ (For \(x<1\) the sum is empty.)

Proof sketch. Since \(\chi\) is nonprincipal, \(q\ge2\). Let \(N=\lfloor x\rfloor\). For every real \(\sigma\ge1\) and every \(K\), \(\sum_{n\le K}|\chi(n)\log n\cdot n^{-\sigma}|\le\log K\,(1+\log K)\), from \(\sum_{n\le K}1/n\le1+\log K\). So the terms with \(n\le\min(N,q)\) contribute at most \(\log q\,(1+\log q)\). If \(N>q\), the tail bound at \(N=q\), \(\sigma=1\) bounds the terms with \(q<n\le N\) by \(q\log(q+1)/(q+1)\le\log q+1\). The total is at most \(\log^2q+2\log q+1\le(\log q+3)^2\). This is a statement about finite sums; no limit is involved.

Let \(q\ge1\), let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\), and put \(M=\log q+3\). For every real \(\sigma>1\), the complex derivative of the \(L\)-function satisfies $\(|L'(\sigma,\chi)|\le M^2 ,\)$ and \(L'(\sigma,\chi)=-\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)\log n\cdot n^{-\sigma}\).

Proof sketch. For \(\sigma>1\) the series may be differentiated term by term, which gives the formula for \(L'(\sigma,\chi)\). Since \(\chi\) is nonprincipal, \(q\ge2\). Split the series at \(N=q\): the terms with \(n\le q\) contribute at most \(\sum_{n\le q}\log n/n\le\log q\,(1+\log q)\), and by the tail bound the rest has absolute value at most \(q\log(q+1)(q+1)^{-\sigma}\le\log q+1\). The total is at most \(\log^2q+2\log q+1\le(\log q+3)^2\).

Let \(q\ge1\), let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\), and put \(M=\log q+3\). For every real \(\sigma\ge1\), $\(|L(\sigma,\chi)-L(1,\chi)|\le(\sigma-1)M^2 .\)$

Proof sketch. The function \(t\mapsto L(t,\chi)\) on \([1,\sigma]\) is the restriction of an entire function, so it is continuous on \([1,\sigma]\) and differentiable with derivative \(L'(t,\chi)\), of absolute value at most \(M^2\) for \(1<t\le\sigma\). The mean value inequality for vector-valued functions on a segment, which allows one exceptional endpoint, gives the bound.

Let \(q\ge1\) and let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\). For every integer \(N\ge0\), $\(\Bigl|\sum_{1\le n\le N}\frac{\chi(n)}{n}-L(1,\chi)\Bigr|\le\frac{q}{N+1},\)$ and hence, for every real \(x>0\), $\(\Bigl|\sum_{1\le n\le x}\frac{\chi(n)}{n}-L(1,\chi)\Bigr|\le\frac{2q}{x}.\)$

Proof sketch. For real \(\sigma>1\) the series for \(L(\sigma,\chi)\) converges absolutely, and by the tail bound \(|L(\sigma,\chi)-\sum_{n\le N}\chi(n)n^{-\sigma}|\le q(N+1)^{-\sigma}\le q/(N+1)\). Let \(\sigma\to1^+\): the left side tends to \(|L(1,\chi)-\sum_{n\le N}\chi(n)/n|\) by continuity of \(L(s,\chi)\) and of each term, so this is at most \(q/(N+1)\). The value at \(1\) is reached as a limit; no conditionally convergent series is summed. For \(x\ge1\) take \(N=\lfloor x\rfloor\), so \(q/(N+1)\le q/x\le2q/x\). For \(0<x<1\) the sum is empty and \(|L(1,\chi)|\le q\le2q/x\), the case \(N=0\).

Let \(\chi_0\) be the principal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\), for any modulus \(q\). For every real \(x>0\), the Dirichlet series \(L(s,\chi_0)=\sum_{n\ge1}\chi_0(n)n^{-s}\) satisfies $\(|L(1+x,\chi_0)|\le1+\frac1x .\)$

Proof sketch. For real \(s=1+x>1\), \(L(s,\chi_0)=\sum_{n\ge1}\chi_0(n)n^{-s}\) with \(0\le\chi_0(n)\le1\), so \(|L(s,\chi_0)|\le\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\le1+\int_1^\infty t^{-s}\,dt =1+1/x\), comparing each term \(n^{-s}\), \(n\ge2\), with \(\int_{n-1}^nt^{-s}\,dt\).

docs.title: A lower bound for \(|L(1,\chi)|\) at complex characters
docs.text:

Let \(q\ge1\) and let \(\chi\) be a Dirichlet character modulo \(q\) with \(\chi^2\ne\chi_0\) (so \(\chi\) takes a nonreal value). Put \(M=\log q+3\). Then $\(|L(1,\chi)|\ge\frac1{256\,M^7}.\)$

Proof sketch. For every real \(x>0\) the Euler product gives the classical inequality $\(|L(1+x,\chi_0)|^3\,|L(1+x,\chi)|^4\,|L(1+x,\chi^2)|\ge1,\)$ from \(3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta\ge0\). Take \(0<x\le1\). Then \(|L(1+x,\chi_0)|\le1+1/x\le2/x\), \(|L(1+x,\chi^2)|\le M\) since \(\chi^2\) is nonprincipal, and \(|L(1+x,\chi)|\le|L(1,\chi)|+xM^2\) by the variation bound. If \(|L(1,\chi)|\le xM^2\), then \(|L(1+x,\chi)|\le2xM^2\) and \(1\le(8/x^3)(16x^4M^8)M=128\,xM^9\). With \(x=1/(256M^9)\le1\) this is false, so \(|L(1,\chi)|>xM^2=1/(256M^7)\).

docs.title: Quadratic fields
docs.text:
For an integer \(d\) that is not the square of a rational number (for instance a squarefree \(d\ne1\)), the field \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\) is a number field of degree \(2\). The residue of its Dedekind zeta function at \(s=1\) is given by the class number formula, and this section bounds each ingredient of that formula so as to bound the residue from below by \(\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}2/(6\sqrt{|d|})\).

The basis \(1,\sqrt d\) bounds the discriminant; the real embeddings decide the signature; roots of unity have order at most \(6\).

An imaginary quadratic field has unit rank \(0\) and regulator \(1\); in a real quadratic field every unit above \(1\) is at least the golden ratio.

With the class number at least \(1\) this bounds the residue.

7 fully proved

docs.title: The quadratic field \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.instNumberField ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.instCharZero ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.finrank ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.not_isSquare_of_squarefree ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.fact_not_isSquare ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.sqrtInt ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.sqrtInt_sq

For an integer \(d\), let \(K_d=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-d)\) be the \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra with basis \(1,\sqrt d\) and \((\sqrt d)^2=d\). If \(d\) is not the square of a rational number, then \(K_d\) is a number field of degree \([K_d:\mathbb Q]=2\), and \(\sqrt d\) is an algebraic integer of \(K_d\) with square \(d\). Every squarefree integer \(d e1\) satisfies this hypothesis.

Proof sketch. If \(d\) is not a rational square, \(X^2-d\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), so the algebra is a field; it has characteristic \(0\) and dimension \(2\) over \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\sqrt d\) is a root of the monic integer polynomial \(X^2-d\). A squarefree \(d e1\) is not the square of a rational number (\(d e0\), and \(d=a^2/b^2\) in lowest terms forces \(b=1\) and \(d=a^2\), so \(d=1\)).

docs.title: The discriminant of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.abs_discr_le ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.exists_four_mul_eq_sq_mul_discr ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.discr_basis

Let \(d\) be an integer that is not the square of a rational number, and let \(D_K\) be the discriminant of the ring of integers of \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\). Then $\(|D_K|\le4|d| .\)$

Proof sketch. The trace of \(x+y\sqrt d\) is \(2x\), so the basis \(1,\sqrt d\) has discriminant \(\det\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2d\end{pmatrix}=4d\). Since \(\sqrt d\) is integral, the matrix expressing \(1,\sqrt d\) in an integral basis of \(\mathcal O_K\) has integer entries, so \(4d=m^2D_K\) with \(m\) its determinant, a nonzero integer. Hence \(|D_K|\le4|d|\). The ring of integers is never computed. (In fact, for squarefree \(d\), \(D_K=d\) if \(d\equiv1\pmod4\) and \(4d\) otherwise.)

docs.text:

Let \(d\) be an integer that is not the square of a rational number and \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\), with \(r_1\) real and \(r_2\) complex places. If \(d<0\), then \(r_1=0\) and \(r_2=1\), and \(K\) is totally complex; if \(d>0\), then \(r_1=2\) and \(r_2=0\), and \(K\) is totally real.

Proof sketch. Every embedding of \(K\) into \(\mathbb C\) sends \(x+y\sqrt d\) to \(x+y\beta\) with \(\beta^2=d\). The embeddings are real exactly when \(d>0\); when \(d<0\) none is real, and the two complex conjugate embeddings form one complex place. In both cases \(r_1+2r_2=2\).

docs.title: Roots of unity in a quadratic field
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.torsionOrder_le_six ZInQ.Progressions.torsionOrder_le_six_of_finrank_eq_two ZInQ.Progressions.le_six_of_totient_le_two

Let \(K\) be a number field of degree \(2\), for example \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\) with \(d\) an integer that is not the square of a rational number. The group of roots of unity of \(K\) has order \(w_K\le6\).

Proof sketch. The roots of unity of \(K\) form a finite cyclic group, so \(K\) contains a primitive root of unity \(\zeta\) of order \(w_K\). Then \(\mathbb Q(\zeta)\subseteq K\) has degree \(\varphi(w_K)\le2\). By induction over prime powers and coprime products, \(\varphi(n)\le2\) forces \(n\mid12\), and then \(n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}\), so \(w_K\le6\).

Let \(d<0\) be an integer (so \(d\) is not the square of a rational number) and \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\). Then the regulator of \(K\) is \(R_K=1\).

Proof sketch. By the signature, \(r_1+r_2-1=0\). So the unit group of \(\mathcal O_K\) has rank \(0\), and the regulator is the determinant of an empty matrix, which is \(1\).

docs.title: The regulator of a real quadratic field
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.regulator_ge_of_pos ZInQ.Progressions.Qsqrt.unit_quadratic ZInQ.Progressions.golden_le_of_quadratic ZInQ.Progressions.log_golden_le_abs_log

Let \(d>0\) be an integer that is not the square of a rational number and \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\). The regulator of \(K\) satisfies $\(R_K\ge\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.\)$

Proof sketch. By the signature, the unit rank is \(1\), and \(R_K=|\log|\sigma(\varepsilon_0)||\) for a fundamental unit \(\varepsilon_0\) and a real embedding \(\sigma\), with \(|\sigma(\varepsilon_0)|\ne1\) because \(R_K>0\). For a unit \(u\), the trace \(t=u+u'\) and the norm \(n=uu'\) are rational integers, with \(n=\pm1\), so \(y=\sigma(u)\) satisfies \(y^2-ty+n=0\). Suppose \(|y|>1\). If \(n=-1\), then \(|t|=|y-1/y|>0\), so \(|t|\ge1\); since \(t\mapsto t-1/t\) is increasing and equals \(1\) at \(\phi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\), \(|y|\ge\phi\). If \(n=1\), then \(|t|=|y+1/y|>2\), so \(|t|\ge3\) and \(|y|\ge(3+\sqrt5)/2=\phi^2>\phi\). If \(|y|<1\), the same argument applies to \(1/y\). In all cases \(|\log|y||\ge\log\phi\).

docs.title: A lower bound for the residue of \(\zeta_K\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.dedekindZeta_residue_ge ZInQ.Progressions.log_golden_pos ZInQ.Progressions.log_golden_lt_one

Let \(d\) be an integer that is not the square of a rational number, \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\), and let $\(\kappa_K=\frac{2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2}h_KR_K}{w_K\sqrt{|D_K|}}\)$ be the residue at \(s=1\) of the Dedekind zeta function \(\zeta_K(s)\) (the class number formula), where \(h_K\) is the class number, \(R_K\) the regulator, \(w_K\) the number of roots of unity and \(D_K\) the discriminant. Then $\(\kappa_K\ge\frac{\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}}{6\sqrt{|d|}} .\)$

Proof sketch. Note \(0<\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}2<1\). Use \(h_K\ge1\), \(w_K\le6\) and \(\sqrt{|D_K|}\le2\sqrt{|d|}\), so the denominator is at most \(12\sqrt{|d|}\). If \(d<0\), then \(r_1=0\), \(r_2=1\) and \(R_K=1\), so the numerator is at least \(2\pi>2\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}2\) and \(\kappa_K\ge\pi/(6\sqrt{|d|})\). If \(d>0\), then \(r_1=2\), \(r_2=0\) and \(R_K\ge\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}2\), so the numerator is at least \(4\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}2\) and \(\kappa_K\ge\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}2/(3\sqrt d)\). Both are at least the claimed bound.

docs.title: Real characters
docs.text:
A real nonprincipal character \(\chi\) agrees, on primes not dividing \(2q\), with the Legendre symbol \((d/\cdot)\) of a squarefree \(d\ne1\) with \(|d|\) dividing \(q\). Through the factorization of the Dedekind zeta function of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\), the value \(L(1,\chi)\) is the residue \(\kappa_K\) times finitely many local factors, each at least \((p-1)/(p+1)\); the residue bound of the quadratic fields section then gives \(|L(1,\chi)|\ge1/(40q^{3/2})\).

2 fully proved

docs.title: Real characters are Legendre symbols away from \(2q\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.exists_legendre_of_real_char ZInQ.Progressions.exists_legendre_of_real_char_dvd

Let \(q\ge1\) and let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\) with \(\chi^2=\chi_0\). Then there is a squarefree integer \(d e1\) such that \(|d|\) divides \(q\), \(8\) divides \(q\) if \(d\) is even, and $\(\chi(p)=\Bigl( rac dp\Bigr)\qquad ext{for every prime }p mid2q .\)$ In particular \(|d|\le q\) and every prime factor of \(d\) divides \(q\).

Proof sketch. A real character is \(1\) at the square of every unit. Hensel lifting shows which units are squares: modulo \(p^k\) with \(p\) odd, the squares of units are the residues that are squares modulo \(p\); modulo \(2^k\), every \(n\equiv1\pmod8\) is a square. So modulo \(p^k\), \(p\) odd, \(\chi\) is \(1\) at the quadratic residues and constant at the nonresidues, hence \(\chi(\ell)=(p^*/\ell)\) for primes \(\ell mid2p\) or \(\chi\) is trivial, with \(p^*=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}p\) (by reciprocity, \((\ell/p)=(p^*/\ell)\)). Modulo \(2^k\), \(\chi(\ell)\) depends only on \(\ell mod8\) and is fixed by \(\chi(3),\chi(5)\in\{\pm1\}\); the four cases give \(d=1,-1,2,-2\), and \(\chi(5)=-1\) forces \(k\ge3\). For coprime moduli, split \(\chi\) by the Chinese remainder theorem; the integers \(d\) of the two components multiply, by multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol. Induction over the factorization of \(q\) gives a squarefree \(d\) with \(|d|\mid q\), \(2\mid d\Rightarrow8\mid q\) and \(\chi(p)=(d/p)\) for primes \(p mid2q\). If \(d=1\), then \(\chi(p)=1\) for every prime \(p mid2q\); since every unit class modulo \(q\) contains such primes (Dirichlet's theorem, without bounds), \(\chi\) would be principal. So \(d e1\).

docs.title: A lower bound for \(L(1,\chi)\) at real characters
docs.text:
ZInQ.Progressions.norm_LFunction_one_ge_of_sq_eq_one ZInQ.Progressions.log_golden_div_le_norm_LFunction_one

Let \(q\ge1\) and let \(\chi\) be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo \(q\) with \(\chi^2=\chi_0\). Then $\(|L(1,\chi)|\ge rac1{40\,q^{3/2}} .\)$

Proof sketch. Take \(d\) from the classification of real characters: \(d e1\) is squarefree, \(|d|\) divides \(q\), and \(\chi(p)=(d/p)\) for every prime \(p mid2q\). Then \(d\) is not the square of a rational number; let \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)\), with \(\alpha=\sqrt d\in\mathcal O_K\) and \(\varepsilon_p=a_K(p)-1\in\{-1,0,1\}\). Since \(|d|\) divides \(q\), no prime \(p mid2q\) divides \(d\), so the factorization of \(\zeta_K\) applies: for real \(s>1\), $\(\zeta_K(s)=\zeta(s)\,L(s,\chi)\prod_{p\mid2q} rac{1-\chi(p)p^{-s}}{1-\varepsilon_pp^{-s}},\)$ where \(L(s,\chi)\), the sum of the Dirichlet series, is the value of the \(L\)-function. Multiply by \(s-1\) and let \(s o1^+\): \((s-1)\zeta_K(s) o\kappa_K\) by the class number formula, \((s-1)\zeta(s) o1\), \(L(s,\chi) o L(1,\chi)\) by continuity, and the finite product is continuous at \(s=1\) (its denominators do not vanish since \(|\varepsilon_p|\le1<p\)). Hence $\(\kappa_K=L(1,\chi)\prod_{p\mid2q} rac{1-\chi(p)/p}{1-\varepsilon_p/p}.\)$ Each factor has absolute value at most \((1+1/p)/(1-1/p)=(p+1)/(p-1)\), and \(\prod_{p\mid2q}(p+1)/(p-1)\le3\prod_{p\mid q,\ p ext{ odd}}p\le3q\), since \((p+1)/(p-1)\le p\) for \(p\ge3\) and the factor at \(p=2\) is \(3\). So \(|L(1,\chi)|\ge\kappa_K/(3q)\). The residue bound with \(|d|\le q\) gives \(\kappa_K\ge\log rac{1+\sqrt5}2/(6\sqrt q)\), and \(\log rac{1+\sqrt5}2>0.48>18/40\), so \(|L(1,\chi)|\ge1/(40q^{3/2})\).

Sources
  • Davenport, Chapter 6
  • Marcus, Chapter 7
  • Apostol, Chapter 6

docs.title: The rank hypothesis as positive rank
The rank hypothesis as positive rank
docs.text:
The forms CR₃^Sel, CR₃^5b, CR₃^TYZ and CR₃^TYZ_Cl of the certified rank hypothesis met so far conclude that every 2-Selmer class of \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) comes from a rational point, and CR₃ itself that one given class does. The theorems behind them (Tian–Yuan–Zhang as completed by Proposition N, which is not refereed, and Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary field; Kriz's 2-converse with the corank lemma is an alternative that is not needed) give a rank statement (\(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\ge1\)), not a statement about Selmer classes. This chapter proves the step between the two, RK9, by the complete 2-descent. The descent map \(\delta_d\) has kernel \(2C_d(\mathbb Q)\) and image in \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\), and \(C_d(\mathbb Q)[2]\) has order \(4\). So when \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is finitely generated, a point of infinite order gives \(|C_d(\mathbb Q)/2C_d(\mathbb Q)|\ge8\), and when \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has order \(8\) the image is all of it. So CR₃^Sel, CR₃^TYZ and CR₃^TYZ_Cl have positive-rank forms that ask only for a point of infinite order on \(C_d\). With Mordell–Weil for every \(C_d\), proved in its own section, the positive-rank forms imply the original ones, and the positive-rank form of CR₃^Sel implies CR₃. A section derives CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk from three statements about L-series of elliptic curves. The proof of pole completeness applies the hypothesis at only two curves, those of a slot choice, and a further section states the positive-rank hypothesis for exactly those curves. A last section restates the positive-rank hypotheses with the conclusion that the equation \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions, which mentions no group law.

Throughout, \(C_d\) is the curve \(E_{-d^2}\), \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) is the Selmer group of the Proposition 0 chapter, and \(u\equiv v\) means that \(u/v\) is a nonzero square. The Mordell–Weil section writes \(C_n\) for a positive integer \(n\), as the row-5b chapter does; elsewhere in this chapter the letter is \(d\).

9 fully proved

docs.title: The complete 2-descent
docs.text:
The Kummer maps at the roots \(0\) and \(d\) of \(x^3-d^2x\) make up the descent map \(\delta_d\). Over \(\mathbb Q\) its kernel is \(2C_d(\mathbb Q)\), its image lies in the 2-Selmer group, and RK9 follows by counting.

  • The complete 2-descent on a congruent number curve

docs.title: Mordell–Weil for the congruent number curves
docs.text:
RK9 needs \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) to be finitely generated. The two-isogeny descent and the descent theorem with the naive height prove it for every \(d\ne0\).

  • Mordell–Weil by two-isogeny descent

docs.title: The hypotheses in positive-rank form
docs.text: Three positive-rank hypotheses: CR₃^Rk keeps the premises of CR₃^Sel, CR₃^TYZ,Rk asks, for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod 8\), only for an odd genus sum of Rédei's bits, and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk for an odd genus sum of class numbers, as in Tian, Yuan and Zhang's own statement. CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk implies CR₃^TYZ,Rk by Rédei's formula, and CR₃^TYZ,Rk implies CR₃^Rk by Corollary 4.4 and Theorem 3.6.

docs.title: The certified rank hypothesis in positive-rank form
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.CertifiedRankRk

The hypothesis CR₃^Rk is the following assertion. Let \(d\) be a squarefree positive integer with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\). Suppose that the 2-Selmer group \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has exactly \(8\) elements and contains a pair \((a,b)\) with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\). Then \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order.

The premises are those of CR₃^Sel; only the conclusion changes, from "every Selmer class comes from a rational point" to \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\ge1\), which is what the theorems below conclude. It rests on:

  • for this 2-adic shape, Tian–Yuan–Zhang (Theorem 3.5 and the argument of the proof of Theorem 3.5(2), as completed in nt-tyz §4 by Proposition N, which is not refereed), which gives that \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes to order exactly one at \(s=1\), and Gross–Zagier over an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field (Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein), which gives \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\ge1\). Their hypothesis, an odd genus sum of class numbers, follows from the premises of CR₃^Rk by Corollary 4.4, Theorem 3.6 and Rédei's formula;
  • as an alternative that is not needed, Kriz's 2-converse theorem (Theorem 10.13, a preprint whose publication status was not checked) for \(C_d\) at \(p=2\), whose standing assumption holds since \(d\ge21\) (by Proposition 0, as in CR₃^Sel), together with the corank lemma (the Cassels–Tate pairing on \(Ш/Ш_{\rm div}\) is nondegenerate and alternating, so \(\dim(Ш/Ш_{\rm div})[2]\) is even, with no finiteness of \(Ш\) assumed), giving \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)=1\).

Neither rank theorem is proved here, so CR₃^Rk is a hypothesis. With Mordell–Weil for \(C_d\) it implies CR₃^Sel, by RK9.

docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.CertifiedRankTYZRk

The hypothesis CR₃^TYZ,Rk is the following assertion. Let \(d\) be a squarefree positive integer with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) whose genus sum of row 5b, built from Rédei's bits, is odd: \(T_{5b}(d)=1\). Then \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order.

No condition on \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) enters. It rests on Tian–Yuan–Zhang (Theorem 3.5 and the argument of the proof of Theorem 3.5(2), as completed in nt-tyz §4, Proposition N), which gives that \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes to order exactly one at \(s=1\), followed by Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field, which gives \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\ge1\). Rédei's formula identifies \(T_{5b}(d)\) with Tian, Yuan and Zhang's genus sum of class numbers. The deep theorems are not proved here, so CR₃^TYZ,Rk is a hypothesis. It is the Tian–Yuan–Zhang form CR₃^TYZ with the premise \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\) dropped and the conclusion replaced by positive rank.

docs.title: The class-number hypothesis in positive-rank form
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.CertifiedRankTYZClRk

The hypothesis CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk is the following assertion. Let \(d\) be a squarefree positive integer with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) whose genus sum of class numbers $\(T^{\mathrm{Cl}}_{5b}(d)=\sum_\pi\prod_{B\in\pi}\#\bigl(2\,\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d_B}))\bigr)\pmod 2\)$ is \(1\). Here \(\pi\) runs over the set partitions of the primes of \(d\) with exactly one block with \(d_B\equiv7\), exactly one with \(d_B\equiv3\), and all other blocks with \(d_B\equiv1\pmod8\); \(d_B\) is the product of the primes in \(B\), and \(2\,\mathrm{Cl}(K)\) is the subgroup of squares of the class group of the ring of integers of \(K\). Then \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order.

This is Tian–Yuan–Zhang with their own genus class numbers (Theorem 3.5, first assertion, with Theorem 3.3, Proposition 3.2, Lemmas 2.8, 3.16, 3.18, 3.21 and Proposition 2.3), as completed by Proposition N (nt-tyz §4; an unpublished argument written for this project, with two automated reviews and no human review): if \(T^{\mathrm{Cl}}_{5b}(d)\) is odd then their invariant \(\mathcal L(d)\) is nonzero, and since the root number is \(-1\), \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes to order exactly one at \(s=1\); followed by Gross–Zagier over an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field (Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein), which gives \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\ge1\). No Rédei formula and no condition on \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) enter. It follows from three statements about \(L(C_d,s)\) and \(L(E,s)\): Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b, which rests on the unrefereed Proposition N, the vanishing of \(L(C_d,s)\) at \(s=1\), and the Gross–Zagier statement (Row 5b, vanishing at the centre and Gross–Zagier give CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk). The vanishing in turn follows from the textbook functional equation, with root number \(-1\), on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\) (the functional equation gives vanishing at the centre). Those statements are themselves hypotheses, so CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk is not proved here.

The hypothesis CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk implies CR₃^TYZ,Rk: if every squarefree positive \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) with \(T^{\mathrm{Cl}}_{5b}(d)=1\) has a point of infinite order on \(C_d\), then so does every squarefree positive \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) with \(T_{5b}(d)=1\).

Along the way: the 4-rank statement and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk together give CR₃^TYZ,Rk.

Then \(d\) is odd, so the two genus sums agree, \(T^{\mathrm{Cl}}_{5b}(d)=T_{5b}(d)=1\), and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk gives a point of infinite order on \(C_d\). The 4-rank statement holds by Rédei's theorem, which gives the implication without assumption.

docs.title: The two curves of a slot choice
docs.text:
Pole completeness applies the hypothesis at the two curves \(C_{d_1}\) and \(C_{d_2}\) of a slot choice; this section states the positive-rank hypothesis for exactly those curves and derives pole completeness from it.

  • The rank hypothesis on the two curves of a slot choice

docs.title: The hypotheses as infinitely many rational points
docs.text:
The positive-rank forms mention the group law on \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\). For \(d\ne0\), with Mordell–Weil, a point of infinite order exists exactly when \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions, so each of CR₃^Rk, CR₃^TYZ,Rk, CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk and CR₃^DL,Rk is equivalent to a form with that conclusion, which mentions no group law.

  • The rank hypotheses as infinitely many rational points

docs.title: The rank hypotheses as infinitely many rational points
The rank hypotheses as infinitely many rational points
docs.text:
The positive-rank hypotheses CR₃^Rk, CR₃^TYZ,Rk, CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk and CR₃^DL,Rk conclude that a curve \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has a rational point of infinite order, so their statements involve the group law on \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\). This section restates each of them with the conclusion that the equation \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions, a statement that mentions no group law. For \(d\ne0\) the two conclusions are equivalent: a point of infinite order has infinitely many distinct multiples, and conversely, by Mordell–Weil, a finitely generated group of points all of finite order is finite. Hence each new form is equivalent to its positive-rank form, with the same premises, and the main theorem holds under the minimal height hypothesis and any of them.

Throughout, \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\), as in the rest of the positive-rank chapter.

7 fully proved

docs.title: Infinitely many points and infinite order
Infinitely many rational solutions of \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.InfinitelyManyPoints

For a natural number \(d\), the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational points when the set $\(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Q^2 : y^2=x^3-d^2x\}\)$ of its affine rational solutions is infinite.

The statement involves only rational solutions of one equation: no group law, no point at infinity and no condition on \(d\).

Remark (classical meaning). For a squarefree positive integer \(d\), the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) having infinitely many rational points is the classical statement that \(d\) is a congruent number. This is a remark about what the condition means classically; it is not proved here, and no article uses it.

Let \(d\ne0\) be a natural number and \(C_d\) the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb Q\). Then \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) contains a point of infinite order if and only if \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions \((x,y)\in\mathbb Q^2\).

Along the way, for \(d\ne0\):

  • every rational solution \((x,y)\) of \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) is a nonsingular point of \(C_d\);
  • the map that sends one extra element to the point at infinity \(O\) and each rational solution \((x,y)\) to the affine point \((x,y)\) is a bijection from the set of rational solutions with one extra element adjoined onto \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\);
  • hence \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions if and only if \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is infinite.

Proof sketch. The discriminant of \(C_d\) is a nonzero multiple of \(d^6\), hence nonzero, so every solution of the equation is a nonsingular point. The points of \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) are \(O\) and the affine points, which are exactly the rational solutions; so the map above is a bijection, and the solution set is infinite exactly when \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is. If \(P\) has infinite order, the multiples \(nP\) (\(n\ge0\)) are pairwise distinct, so \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is infinite. Conversely, suppose every point has finite order. By Mordell–Weil, \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is finitely generated, and a finitely generated abelian group in which every element has finite order is finite; so \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is finite, and there are only finitely many solutions.

docs.text: The four hypotheses keep the premises of CR₃^Rk, CR₃^TYZ,Rk, CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk and CR₃^DL,Rk.

docs.title: The certified rank hypothesis in infinitely-many-points form
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.CertifiedRankInf

The hypothesis CR₃^Inf is the following assertion. Let \(d\) be a squarefree positive integer with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\). Suppose that the 2-Selmer group \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has exactly \(8\) elements and contains a pair \((a,b)\) with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\). Then \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions \((x,y)\in\mathbb Q^2\).

The premises are those of CR₃^Rk; only the conclusion changes, from "a point of infinite order on \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\)" to "infinitely many rational solutions", which mentions no group law. The two hypotheses are equivalent, so CR₃^Inf rests on the same theorems: Tian–Yuan–Zhang as completed by Proposition N, which is not refereed, and Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary field. None of them is proved here, so CR₃^Inf is a hypothesis.

Remark (classical meaning). For the squarefree \(d\) here, infinitely many rational solutions is the classical statement that \(d\) is a congruent number. This is not part of the hypothesis and is not used.

The premises are those of CR₃^TYZ,Rk; only the conclusion changes, from a point of infinite order to infinitely many rational solutions, which mentions no group law. The two hypotheses are equivalent, so CR₃^TYZ,Inf rests on Tian–Yuan–Zhang as completed by Proposition N, which is not refereed, and Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary field, as CR₃^TYZ,Rk does. It is a hypothesis, not proved here.

docs.title: The class-number hypothesis in infinitely-many-points form
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.CertifiedRankTYZClInf

The hypothesis CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Inf is the following assertion. Let \(d\) be a squarefree positive integer with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) whose genus sum of class numbers $\(T^{\mathrm{Cl}}_{5b}(d)=\sum_\pi\prod_{B\in\pi}\#\bigl(2\,\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d_B}))\bigr)\pmod 2\)$ is \(1\). Here \(\pi\) runs over the set partitions of the primes of \(d\) with exactly one block with \(d_B\equiv7\), exactly one with \(d_B\equiv3\), and all other blocks with \(d_B\equiv1\pmod8\); \(d_B\) is the product of the primes in \(B\), and \(2\,\mathrm{Cl}(K)\) is the subgroup of squares of the class group of the ring of integers of \(K\). Then \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions \((x,y)\in\mathbb Q^2\).

The premises are those of CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk; only the conclusion changes, from a point of infinite order to infinitely many rational solutions, which mentions no group law. The two hypotheses are equivalent, so CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Inf rests on Tian–Yuan–Zhang with their own genus class numbers, as completed by Proposition N, which is not refereed, followed by Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary field. No Rédei formula and no condition on \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) enter. It is a hypothesis, not proved here.

Remark (classical meaning). For the squarefree \(d\) here, infinitely many rational solutions is the classical statement that \(d\) is a congruent number. This is not part of the hypothesis and is not used.

docs.title: The infinitely-many-points hypothesis on the two curves of a slot choice
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.CertifiedRankDLInf

The hypothesis CR₃^DL,Inf is the following assertion. Let \(\beta,\theta\) be integers and \(p_0\) a natural number such that:

  • \(\beta\) is odd and squarefree with \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), and \(p_0\) is a prime dividing \(\beta\);
  • \(\theta>0\) is squarefree with \(\theta\equiv1\pmod8\);
  • \(\beta\) and \(\theta\) are coprime;
  • \([\beta/\ell]=0\) for every prime \(\ell\mid\theta\), and \([\theta/p]=0\) for every prime \(p\mid\beta\).

Then there are slot data \(q_0\), \(r_p\) (\(p\in P(\beta)\setminus\{p_0\}\)) and \(r_\ell\) (\(\ell\in P(\theta)\)) for \(\beta,\theta,p_0\), satisfying the slot conditions, such that, with $\(d_1=|\beta|\,q_0\prod_{p}r_p\prod_{\ell}r_\ell ,\)$ both \(y^2=x^3-d_1^2x\) and \(y^2=x^3-(d_1|\theta|)^2x\) have infinitely many rational solutions \((x,y)\in\mathbb Q^2\).

The premises are those of CR₃^DL,Rk; only the conclusion changes, from points of infinite order on the two curves to infinitely many rational solutions of their equations, which mentions no group law. The assertion still depends on the slot conditions, so a change to the slot construction changes what it asserts. The two hypotheses are equivalent. Since CR₃^DL,Rk follows from CR₃^Rk and from CR₃^TYZ,Rk, the equivalences make CR₃^DL,Inf follow from CR₃^Inf and from CR₃^TYZ,Inf, so it rests on the same theorems: Tian–Yuan–Zhang as completed by Proposition N, which is not refereed, and Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary field. It is a hypothesis, not proved here.

docs.text: Each equivalence holds pointwise, since every curve in these hypotheses has \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), so \(d\ne0\). The main theorem in each of the four forms is the main theorem from the infinitely-many-points forms.

docs.title: The infinitely-many-points forms are equivalent to the positive-rank forms
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.certifiedRankInf_iff_certifiedRankRk ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.certifiedRankTYZInf_iff_certifiedRankTYZRk ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.certifiedRankTYZClInf_iff_certifiedRankTYZClRk ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.certifiedRankDLInf_iff_certifiedRankDLRk

The hypotheses CR₃^Inf and CR₃^Rk are equivalent. Likewise CR₃^TYZ,Inf is equivalent to CR₃^TYZ,Rk, CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Inf to CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk, and CR₃^DL,Inf to CR₃^DL,Rk.

Proof sketch. In each pair the two hypotheses have the same premises and differ only in the conclusion, so it suffices to compare the conclusions for each fixed value of the data. For CR₃^Inf, CR₃^TYZ,Inf and CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Inf, fix \(d\) with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\); then \(d\ne0\), and by the equivalence of infinite order and infinitely many points, \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order exactly when \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has infinitely many rational solutions. For CR₃^DL,Inf, fix \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfying the premises and a choice of slot data. By the realization, \(d_1\equiv5\pmod8\), and \(d_1|\theta|\equiv5\pmod8\) as well (as in CR₃^DL,Rk from CR₃^Rk), so both are nonzero and the same equivalence applies to each of the two curves.

docs.title: CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk from three literature statements
docs.text:
The positive-rank class-number hypothesis CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk follows from three statements about the L-series \(L(C_d,s)\) of the curves \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) and the L-series \(L(E,s)\) of elliptic curves \(E\) over \(\mathbb Q\). Two of them are textbook theorems: the functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) with root number \(-1\), stated on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\) for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), and the positive-rank half of Gross–Zagier for every elliptic curve over \(\mathbb Q\). The third is Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b: when the genus sum of class numbers \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)\) is odd, the order of vanishing of \(L(C_d,s)\) at \(s=1\) is at most one. Row 5b follows from their Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A, which no refereed text found by a literature search carried out by AI agents states explicitly (AI agents compared the journal version of their paper with the arXiv version; Tian's expository articles were not read). The bound on the order follows from reading A, which Proposition N, an unpublished argument reviewed only by AI models and never by a human, derives from their unambiguous statements; the existence of the continuation is Hecke's.

The order of vanishing is read off an entire continuation of the L-series from the half-plane \(\operatorname{Re}s>3/2\), and such a continuation is unique. The functional equation gives vanishing at the centre; with row 5b this gives an entire continuation with a simple zero at \(s=1\), and Gross–Zagier then gives a point of infinite order on \(C_d\). Row 5b in turn follows from Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A (both genus sums are even when the order of vanishing is at least two) together with Hecke's continuation of \(L(C_d,s)\).

The L-series in these statements is defined from local polynomials of minimal equations over the completions of \(\mathbb Q\). A subsection computes \(L(C_d,s)\) for odd squarefree \(d\), which includes every squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\): the equation \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) is minimal at every prime, the local factor at a prime \(p\nmid2d\) is \(1-a_pT+pT^2\) with \(a_p=p+1-\#C_d(\mathbb F_p)\) and the factor at \(p\mid2d\) is \(1\), so \(L(C_d,s)\) is the Dirichlet series of the formal standard Euler product. That computation is proved; it shows that the L-series in the functional equation, row 5b and reading A, for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), is the standard one, and proves none of the literature statements. It says nothing about \(L(C_d,s)\) for even or non-squarefree \(d\), which Hecke's continuation also covers, nor about the other curves in Gross–Zagier.

None of the literature statements is proved here; the reductions between them are.

Throughout, \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb Q\) for a natural number \(d\), and the order of vanishing of an entire function at a point is its order as an analytic function, a value in \(\{0,1,2,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}\).

12 fully proved

docs.title: Entire continuations of the L-series of an elliptic curve
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.IsLContinuation ZInQ.Literature.IsLContinuation.eq

Let \(E\) be a Weierstrass equation over \(\mathbb Q\). For each prime \(p\) let \(f_p(T)\) be the local polynomial of a minimal model of \(E\) over \(\mathbb Q_p\): \(1-a_pT+pT^2\) with \(a_p=p+1-\#\tilde E(\mathbb F_p)\) (the points of the reduction, the point at infinity included) if the reduction is good, \(1-T\) if it is split multiplicative, \(1+T\) if it is nonsplit multiplicative, and \(1\) if it is additive. The L-series of \(E\) is the Dirichlet series $\(L(E,s)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nn^{-s},\)$ whose coefficients \(a_n\) are those of the formal Euler product \(\prod_pf_p(p^{-s})^{-1}\); its value at \(s\) is the sum of the series where the series converges absolutely, and \(0\) elsewhere. The recipe applies to every Weierstrass equation over \(\mathbb Q\); the case that matters is an elliptic curve, where the discriminant is nonzero.

A function \(F:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) is an entire continuation of \(L(E,s)\) if \(F\) is complex differentiable on all of \(\mathbb C\) and \(F(s)=L(E,s)\) for every complex \(s\) with \(\operatorname{Re}s>3/2\).

Two entire continuations of the same \(L(E,s)\) are equal everywhere.

When \(E\) is an elliptic curve, the series converges absolutely on the half-plane \(\operatorname{Re}s>3/2\), by Hasse's bound on \(a_p\) (a standard fact, not proved here), so there \(L(E,s)\) is the sum of the series. By the uniqueness, a statement about the order of vanishing of an entire continuation at \(s=1\) does not depend on which continuation is chosen.

Proof sketch (of the uniqueness). Let \(F\) and \(G\) be entire continuations of \(L(E,s)\). The half-plane \(\operatorname{Re}s>3/2\) is open and contains \(2\), so \(F\) and \(G\) agree on a neighbourhood of \(2\). Both are complex differentiable on \(\mathbb C\), hence analytic on the connected set \(\mathbb C\), and the identity theorem gives \(F=G\).

docs.title: Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.TYZRow5b

Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b is the following assertion. For every natural number \(d\) with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), \(d\) squarefree and genus sum of class numbers \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=1\) in \(\mathbb Z/2\), there is an entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\) whose order of vanishing at \(s=1\) is at most \(1\).

The assertion includes the existence of the continuation. It is Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) for \(n\equiv5\pmod8\) in reading A (the reading in which \(d_1=1\) is admitted), in contrapositive form and for the row \((7,3)\) only, with Hecke's continuation for the existence. In their terms the conclusion is \(\mathcal L(n)\ne0\), which they identify with order of vanishing at most one (for order one their definition of \(\mathcal L(n)\) uses a regulator, and so rests on the rank part of the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture in analytic rank one, which they cite from Coates–Wiles, Rubin, Gross–Zagier and Kolyvagin). No refereed text found by the project's literature search, which AI agents carried out, prints this form (their journal version was compared with the arXiv version by AI agents, and Tian's expository articles were not read); the only printed statement found is Smith's, which is unrefereed. The bound on the order follows from Proposition N, an unpublished argument from unambiguous statements of Tian, Yuan and Zhang that has not been refereed or checked by a human reader. The existence of the continuation is Hecke's, which Proposition N does not supply. It is not proved here except from two other hypotheses, reading A and Hecke's continuation.

docs.title: The functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) on the strip \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.completedL ZInQ.Literature.FunctionalEquation5

For a natural number \(N\), a function \(F:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) and a complex number \(s\), the completed function is $\(\Lambda_N(s)=N^{s/2}\,(2\pi)^{-s}\,\Gamma(s)\,F(s),\)$ where \(\Gamma\) is the gamma function, given the value \(0\) at its poles \(0,-1,-2,\dots\); \((2\pi)^{-s}=e^{-s\log2\pi}\); \(N^{s/2}=e^{(s/2)\log N}\) if \(N>0\); and \(0^{s/2}\) is \(0\) for \(s\ne0\) and \(1\) for \(s=0\). Below, only \(N=32d^2\) with \(d>0\) is used, and only at points \(s\) and \(2-s\) with \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\).

The functional equation on the critical strip is the following assertion. For every natural number \(d\) with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) and \(d\) squarefree, every entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\), and every complex number \(s\) with \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\), $\(\Lambda_{32d^2}(2-s)=-\Lambda_{32d^2}(s).\)$

For every \(s\) in the strip, neither \(s\) nor \(2-s\) is a pole of \(\Gamma\), so there \(\Gamma(s)\) and \(\Gamma(2-s)\) are the true values. The textbook functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\), which is the L-function of a Hecke character of \(\mathbb Q(i)\) since \(C_d\) has complex multiplication by \(\mathbb Z[i]\) (Hecke, Deuring), has conductor \(32d^2\) for odd squarefree \(d\) and root number \(-1\) for \(d\equiv5,6,7\pmod8\) (Birch–Stephens); restricted to the strip it gives this statement. The root number \(-1\) for these \(d\) is also printed by Tian, Yuan and Zhang, but no original source of the conductor and of the functional equation has been read in full. Only \(s=1\) is used. The identity is not asserted off the strip; with the value \(0\) at the poles of \(\Gamma\) it would fail at \(s=0\), where it would say \(L(C_d,2)=0\). It is a hypothesis, not proved here.

docs.title: Gross–Zagier: a simple zero gives a point of infinite order
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.GrossZagier

The Gross–Zagier statement is the following assertion. Let \(E\) be a Weierstrass equation over \(\mathbb Q\) with nonzero discriminant, that is, an elliptic curve over \(\mathbb Q\) (the equation need not be minimal), and let \(F\) be an entire continuation of \(L(E,s)\). If the order of vanishing of \(F\) at \(s=1\) is exactly \(1\), then \(E(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order.

This is the positive-rank half of the theorem of Gross and Zagier (1986), which gives a Heegner point of infinite order over an imaginary quadratic field \(K\) when \(L'(E/K,1)\ne0\). It is applied with an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field \(K\) that satisfies the Heegner hypothesis and has \(L(E^K,1)\ne0\) (Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein 1990, through Waldspurger's formula, or Friedberg–Hoffstein 1995), and with the modularity of \(E\) (Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor 2001; Shimura 1971 for curves with complex multiplication). Since the order of vanishing of \(L(E,s)\) at \(s=1\) is odd, the root number of \(E\) is \(-1\), so the Heegner point lies in \(E(\mathbb Q)\) up to torsion and gives a point of infinite order there. Kolyvagin's conclusion that the rank is exactly one is not used. The exact theorem numbers, and the level and discriminant hypotheses of these results, have not been checked here. It is a hypothesis, not proved here.

docs.text: Root number \(-1\) makes the completed L-function vanish at the centre \(s=1\); with row 5b this makes the order of vanishing exactly one.

docs.title: Vanishing at the centre for \(d\equiv5\pmod8\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.RootNumberVanishing

Vanishing at the centre is the following assertion. For every natural number \(d\) with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) and \(d\) squarefree, and every entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\), $\(F(1)=0.\)$

This is what root number \(-1\) gives at the centre of the functional equation: there \(\Lambda(1)=-\Lambda(1)\), and \(\Gamma(1)\ne0\). The functional equation gives vanishing at the centre derives it from the functional equation on the critical strip. As stated here it is a hypothesis, not proved here.

docs.title: The functional equation gives vanishing at the centre
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.rootNumberVanishing_of_functionalEquation

The functional equation of \(L(C_d,s)\) on the critical strip implies vanishing at the centre: if for every squarefree natural number \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), every entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\) and every \(s\) with \(0<\operatorname{Re}s<2\) one has \(\Lambda_{32d^2}(2-s)=-\Lambda_{32d^2}(s)\), then \(F(1)=0\) for every such \(d\) and \(F\).

Proof sketch. Let \(d\) and \(F\) be given and take \(s=1\), which lies in the strip. Since \(2-1=1\), the functional equation reads \(\Lambda_{32d^2}(1)=-\Lambda_{32d^2}(1)\), so \(\Lambda_{32d^2}(1)=0\). Since \(\Gamma(1)=1\), this says \((32d^2)^{1/2}(2\pi)^{-1}F(1)=0\). As \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), \(d e0\), so \(32d^2 e0\); also \(2\pi e0\). A nonzero base raised to a nonzero exponent is nonzero, so both powers are nonzero and \(F(1)=0\).

docs.title: Analytic rank one for the curves of row 5b
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.analyticOrder_eq_one

Assume Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b and vanishing at the centre. Let \(d\) be a natural number with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), \(d\) squarefree and \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=1\). Then \(L(C_d,s)\) has an entire continuation whose order of vanishing at \(s=1\) is exactly \(1\).

Proof sketch. Row 5b gives an entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\) whose order of vanishing at \(1\) is at most \(1\). Since \(F\) is entire it is analytic at \(1\), and \(F(1)=0\) by vanishing at the centre, so its order of vanishing at \(1\) is not \(0\). An order at most \(1\) and not \(0\) is \(1\).

Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b, vanishing at the centre and the Gross–Zagier statement together imply the class-number hypothesis in positive-rank form CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk: for every natural number \(d\) with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), \(d\) squarefree and \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=1\), the curve \(C_d\) has a rational point of infinite order.

The hypothesis taken here is vanishing at the centre. Combined with the functional equation gives vanishing at the centre, the functional equation on the critical strip may be assumed in its place; that combination is the one used by the main theorem from the \(j\)-form and the L-series statements.

Proof sketch. Let \(d\) be as above. Analytic rank one gives an entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\) whose order of vanishing at \(s=1\) is exactly \(1\). Since \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), \(d\ne0\), so \(-d^2\ne0\) and the discriminant \(-64(-d^2)^3=64d^6\) of \(C_d\) is nonzero: \(C_d\) is an elliptic curve. The Gross–Zagier statement applied to \(C_d\) and \(F\) gives a point of infinite order in \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\).

docs.title: Row 5b from Tian–Yuan–Zhang's own statement
docs.text: Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) for \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) concerns two genus sums, \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5a}\) and \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}\). Only the second is needed for row 5b.

docs.title: The first genus sum \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5a}\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.Admissible5aNat ZInQ.Literature.T5aCl

Let \(d\) be a natural number. For a set \(B\) of primes of \(d\) write \(d_B=\prod_{p\in B}p\). A set partition \(\pi\) of the primes of \(d\) is admissible for row 5a if exactly one block \(B\) of \(\pi\) has \(d_B\equiv5\pmod8\) and every block \(B\) of \(\pi\) has \(d_B\equiv5\) or \(d_B\equiv1\pmod8\). The first genus sum of class numbers is $\(T^{\rm Cl}_{5a}(d)=\sum_{\pi}\prod_{B\in\pi}g(d_B)\pmod 2,\)$ the sum over the set partitions \(\pi\) of the primes of \(d\) that are admissible for row 5a, where \(g\) is the genus class number.

This is the set-partition form of Tian–Yuan–Zhang's first sum for \(n\equiv5\pmod8\), including the one-block partition. No identity with their printed sum is proved here.

docs.title: Hecke's continuation of \(L(C_d,s)\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.HeckeContinuation

Hecke's continuation is the following assertion. For every natural number \(d\ne0\), \(L(C_d,s)\) has an entire continuation.

The curve \(C_d\) has complex multiplication by \(\mathbb Z[i]\), so \(L(C_d,s)\) is the L-function of a Hecke character of \(\mathbb Q(i)\) (Deuring, Hecke), and that L-function is entire. This is standard, but no original source for it has been read. It is a hypothesis, not proved here.

docs.title: Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.TYZThm35ReadingA

Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A is the following assertion. For every natural number \(d\) with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) and \(d\) squarefree, and every entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\) whose order of vanishing at \(s=1\) is at least \(2\), both genus sums are even: $\(T^{\rm Cl}_{5a}(d)=0\quad\text{and}\quad T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/2.\)$

This is a consequence of Theorem 3.5(2) of Tian, Yuan and Zhang for \(n=d\equiv5\pmod8\), under one reading of their genus sums, reading A: the decompositions of \(n\) are the set partitions of its primes, each counted once, with a trivial factor \(d_1=1\) allowed. In that reading their two sums are \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5a}(n)\) and \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5a}(n)+T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(n)\), so their evenness is the conclusion above. Only the case \(\mathcal L(n)=0\) of their theorem is needed: they define the invariant \(\mathcal L(n)\) from \(L(C_n,1)\) or \(L'(C_n,1)\) and set it to \(0\) exactly when the order of vanishing at \(s=1\) is at least \(2\). Their printed hypothesis is a condition on their genus point \(P(n)\), followed by an "i.e." that restates it as the evenness of \(2^{-\rho(n)}\mathcal L(n)\) and is not proved in the paper. When \(\mathcal L(n)=0\), the condition on \(P(n)\) follows directly from the first assertion of their Theorem 3.5 and their Lemma 3.18, so the "i.e." is not needed.

No refereed text found by the project's literature search, which AI agents carried out, states reading A explicitly; the one statement found is in an unrefereed preprint (Smith). Their introductory theorem with the same parity criteria (Theorem 1.2 of the arXiv version, Theorem 1.4 of the journal version) requires every factor to exceed \(1\); read that way it is false in both versions, with counterexamples \(d=26565\) and \(d=33117\), and it is not cited. Their proof of Theorem 3.5(2) passes through their Proposition 3.4, whose proof is only a sketch in the arXiv version; the journal's proof was not assessed on this point, and the comparison of the two versions was made by AI agents, not checked by a human. Proposition N, a new argument written for this project, reviewed twice by AI models and never by a human, derives reading A from unambiguous results of the paper without Proposition 3.4; it is supporting evidence, not a hypothesis. Reading A is a hypothesis, not proved here.

docs.title: Row 5b from reading A and Hecke's continuation
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.tyzRow5b_of_readingA

Tian–Yuan–Zhang's Theorem 3.5(2) in reading A and Hecke's continuation together imply Tian–Yuan–Zhang's row 5b.

Proof sketch. Let \(d\) be a squarefree natural number with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) and \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=1\). Then \(d\ne0\), so Hecke's continuation gives an entire continuation \(F\) of \(L(C_d,s)\); take it. If its order of vanishing at \(s=1\) were not at most \(1\), it would be at least \(2\), and reading A would give \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=0\), contradicting \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=1\). Only the row-5b half of reading A is used.
