docs.title: The L-series of the congruent number curves, computed
The L-series of the congruent number curves, computed
docs.text:
Most literature statements of this section are about the L-series \(L(C_d,s)\), defined by the recipe of entire continuations: an Euler product over the finite places of \(\mathbb Q\) of local polynomials, each read off a minimal equation of \(C_d\) over the completion, where the minimal equation is one chosen once and for all. This subsection computes that recipe for odd squarefree \(d\), which includes every squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\). Nothing here is assumed; every statement is proved.

Two general facts come first. Over a discrete valuation ring, an integral equation whose discriminant is not divisible by the twelfth power of the maximal ideal is minimal, and two minimal equations with nonzero discriminant differ by a change of variables with \(u\) a unit, which reduces to a change of variables over the residue field. So the local polynomial at a place of good reduction, or of additive reduction with nonzero discriminant, can be computed from any minimal equation, not only from the chosen one.

For \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) the discriminant is \((2d)^6\) and \(c_4=48d^2\). For odd squarefree \(d\) no prime has its twelfth power dividing \((2d)^6\), so the equation is minimal at every prime; the reduction is good at the primes \(p mid2d\) and additive at the primes \(p\mid2d\). The local polynomial is therefore \(1-a_pT+pT^2\) with \(a_p=p+1-\#C_d(\mathbb F_p)\) (the point at infinity included) at \(p mid2d\), and \(1\) at \(p\mid2d\). Since only one place lies over each prime, the Dirichlet coefficient of \(L(C_d,s)\) at \(p^k\) is the coefficient of \(T^k\) in the inverse of that polynomial. At a prime \(p mid2d\) the coefficient is \(p\) minus the number of affine solutions of \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb F_p\); at a prime \(p\mid2d\) it is \(0\). The coefficients are multiplicative, so \(L(C_d,s)\) is the Dirichlet series whose coefficients are those of the formal Euler product \(\prod_{p mid2d}(1-a_pp^{-s}+p^{1-2s})^{-1}\).

The computation proves none of the literature statements of this section (the functional equation, Gross–Zagier, row 5b, reading A and Hecke's continuation): it shows only that \(L(C_d,s)\), for the squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) that the functional equation, row 5b and reading A concern, is the standard L-series. It says nothing about \(L(C_d,s)\) for even or non-squarefree \(d\), which Hecke's continuation also covers, nor about \(L(E,s)\) for the other elliptic curves in Gross–Zagier. Neither the continuation of \(L(C_d,s)\), nor Hasse's bound, nor the conductor is proved here.

Throughout, \(d\) is a natural number, \(p\) a prime, and \(v\) a finite place of \(\mathbb Q\) with prime \(p_v\), completion \(\mathbb Q_v\), valuation ring \(\mathcal O_v\), maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m_v\) and residue field \(\kappa_v\). The number of elements of an infinite set is taken to be \(0\); only finite residue fields occur.

13 fully proved

docs.title: Minimal equations over a discrete valuation ring
Minimal Weierstrass equations over a discrete valuation ring
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.isMinimal_baseChange_of_notMem ZInQ.Literature.vK_u_eq_one ZInQ.Literature.exists_reduction_variableChange

Let \(R\) be a discrete valuation ring with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\), residue field \(\kappa\) and fraction field \(K\), and let \(v:K o\mathbb Z\cup\{\infty\}\) be its normalized valuation, so that \(v(x)\ge0\) exactly when \(x\in R\). For a field \(F\), a change of variables \(C=(u,r,s,t)\) over \(F\) (\(u\in F^ imes\), \(r,s,t\in F\)) takes a Weierstrass equation \(W\) over \(F\) to the equation \(C\cdot W\) obtained by the substitution \(x=u^2x'+r\), \(y=u^3y'+su^2x'+t\); then \(\Delta(C\cdot W)=u^{-12}\Delta(W)\) and \(c_4(C\cdot W)=u^{-4}c_4(W)\). Below \(F=K\) unless stated. The equation \(W\) is integral if its coefficients lie in \(R\), and minimal if it is integral and \(v(\Delta(C\cdot W))\ge v(\Delta(W))\) for every change of variables \(C\) over \(K\) with \(C\cdot W\) integral. The reduction \( ilde W\) of a minimal \(W\) is the equation over \(\kappa\) obtained by reducing its coefficients modulo \(\mathfrak m\).

  1. If \(W\) is a Weierstrass equation with coefficients in \(R\) and \(\Delta(W) otin\mathfrak m^{12}\), then \(W\), as an equation over \(K\), is minimal.
  2. Let \(W\) be a Weierstrass equation over \(K\) with \(\Delta(W) e0\) and \(C=(u,r,s,t)\) a change of variables over \(K\). If \(W\) and \(C\cdot W\) are both minimal, then \(v(u)=0\).
  3. Let \(W\) be a Weierstrass equation over \(K\) and \(C=(u,r,s,t)\) a change of variables over \(K\) such that \(W\) and \(C\cdot W\) are both minimal and \(v(u)=0\). Then there is a change of variables \(C'\) over \(\kappa\) with \(\widetilde{C\cdot W}=C'\cdot ilde W\).

Proof sketch. (1) \(W\) is integral. Let \(C\cdot W\) be integral. If \(v(u)\le0\), then \(v(\Delta(C\cdot W))=v(\Delta(W))-12v(u)\ge v(\Delta(W))\). If \(v(u)>0\), then \(u\in\mathfrak m\) and \(\delta=\Delta(C\cdot W)\in R\), so \(\Delta(W)=u^{12}\delta\in\mathfrak m^{12}\), which is excluded.

(2) Minimality of \(W\) applied to \(C\), and of \(C\cdot W\) applied to \(C^{-1}\), gives \(v(\Delta(W))=v(\Delta(C\cdot W))=v(\Delta(W))-12v(u)\). Since \(\Delta(W) e0\) its valuation is finite, so \(12v(u)=0\) and \(v(u)=0\).

(3) \(u\) is a unit of \(R\). Between two integral equations, a change of variables whose \(u\) is a unit of \(R\) has \(r,s,t\in R\) as well (a standard fact), so it is a change of variables over \(R\) between the two equations with coefficients in \(R\). Reducing \(u,r,s,t\) modulo \(\mathfrak m\) gives \(C'\), and reduction commutes with the substitution.

docs.title: Point counts under changes of variables and field isomorphisms
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.equation_variableChange_iff ZInQ.Literature.solutionsVariableChangeEquiv ZInQ.Literature.pointEquivOption ZInQ.Literature.natCard_point_variableChange ZInQ.Literature.natCard_point_map_ringEquiv

Let \(F\) be a field, \(E\) a Weierstrass equation over \(F\) and \(C=(u,r,s,t)\) a change of variables over \(F\), with \(C\cdot E\) as in minimal Weierstrass equations. The points of \(E\) over \(F\) are the point at infinity and the nonsingular solutions \((x,y)\in F^2\) of \(E\). The number of elements of an infinite set is taken to be \(0\).

  1. For \(x,y\in F\), \((x,y)\) is a solution of \(C\cdot E\) if and only if \((u^2x+r,\ u^3y+su^2x+t)\) is a solution of \(E\).
  2. The map \((x,y)\mapsto(u^2x+r,\ u^3y+su^2x+t)\) is a bijection from the solutions of \(C\cdot E\) in \(F^2\) to those of \(E\), with inverse \((x,y)\mapsto igl((x-r)/u^2,\ (y-s(x-r)-t)/u^3 igr)\).
  3. If \(\Delta(E) e0\), the points of \(E\) over \(F\) are in bijection with the solutions of \(E\) in \(F^2\) together with one extra element (the point at infinity): every solution is nonsingular.
  4. If \(\Delta(E) e0\), then \(C\cdot E\) and \(E\) have the same number of points over \(F\).
  5. If \(\Delta(E) e0\) and \(f:F o F'\) is an isomorphism of fields, then the equation \(E^f\) over \(F'\) obtained by applying \(f\) to the coefficients has the same number of points over \(F'\) as \(E\) has over \(F\).

Proof sketch. (1) Substitute the coefficients of \(C\cdot E\) and clear the powers of \(u e0\); the two equations differ by the factor \(u^6\). (2) The two maps are mutually inverse by direct computation, and each preserves the equations by (1). (3) An equation with nonzero discriminant is nonsingular at every solution. (4) By (3) for \(E\) and for \(C\cdot E\) (whose discriminant \(u^{-12}\Delta(E)\) is nonzero), and the bijection (2). (5) \(f imes f\) maps the solutions of \(E\) bijectively to those of \(E^f\), and (3) adds the point at infinity on both sides.

docs.title: The local polynomial from any minimal equation
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.vK_minimal_Δ ZInQ.Literature.vK_minimal_c₄ ZInQ.Literature.localPolynomial_of_hasAdditiveReduction ZInQ.Literature.natCard_point_reduction_minimal ZInQ.Literature.localPolynomial_of_hasGoodReduction

Let \(R\), \(\mathfrak m\), \(\kappa\), \(K\) and \(v\) be as in minimal Weierstrass equations, and let \(q\) be the number of elements of \(\kappa\) (\(0\) if \(\kappa\) is infinite). A minimal equation \(W\) has good reduction if \(v(\Delta(W))=0\), multiplicative reduction if \(v(\Delta(W))>0\) and \(v(c_4(W))=0\) (split or nonsplit according as the slopes of the tangents at the node lie in \(\kappa\) or not), and additive reduction if \(v(\Delta(W))>0\) and \(v(c_4(W))>0\).

Every Weierstrass equation \(W\) over \(K\) has a minimal equation of the form \(C_0\cdot W\); fix one, \(W^{\min}\), chosen once and for all. The local polynomial of \(W\) is $$f_W(T)= egin{cases}1-aT+qT^2,\quad a=q+1-# ilde W^{\min}(\kappa), & ext{if \(W^{\min}\) has good reduction},\ 1-T & ext{if \(W^{\min}\) has split multiplicative reduction},\ 1+T & ext{if \(W^{\min}\) has nonsplit multiplicative reduction},\ 1 & ext{otherwise},\end{cases}$$ where \(\# ilde W^{\min}(\kappa)\) is the number of points of the reduction over \(\kappa\), the point at infinity included.

Now let \(W\) be a Weierstrass equation over \(K\) that is itself minimal.

  1. If \(\Delta(W) e0\), then \(v(\Delta(W^{\min}))=v(\Delta(W))\) and \(v(c_4(W^{\min}))=v(c_4(W))\).
  2. If \(\Delta(W) e0\) and \(W\) has additive reduction, then \(f_W(T)=1\).
  3. If \(W\) has good reduction, then \(\# ilde W^{\min}(\kappa)=\# ilde W(\kappa)\) and $\(f_W(T)=1- igl(q+1-\# ilde W(\kappa) igr)T+qT^2 .\)$

So at a place of good reduction, or of additive reduction with nonzero discriminant, the local polynomial can be read off any minimal equation, not only the chosen one.

Proof sketch. (1) \(W^{\min}=C_0\cdot W\) with \(W\) and \(C_0\cdot W\) both minimal, so by minimal Weierstrass equations (2) the \(u\) of \(C_0\) has \(v(u)=0\); since \(\Delta\) and \(c_4\) are multiplied by \(u^{-12}\) and \(u^{-4}\), their valuations do not change. (2) By (1), \(v(\Delta(W^{\min}))>0\) and \(v(c_4(W^{\min}))>0\), so \(W^{\min}\) has neither good nor multiplicative (split or nonsplit) reduction, and \(f_W=1\). (3) Good reduction gives \(\Delta(W) e0\), so by (1) \(W^{\min}\) has good reduction as well. By minimal Weierstrass equations (2) and (3) there is a change of variables \(C'\) over \(\kappa\) with \( ilde W^{\min}=C'\cdot ilde W\). The reduction \( ilde W\) has nonzero discriminant, since \(W\) has good reduction, so by point counts (4) the two reductions have the same number of points, and the first case of the definition gives the formula.

docs.title: The curve and the completions of \(\mathbb Q\)
The model \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over a ring
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.cdModel ZInQ.Literature.cdModel_Δ ZInQ.Literature.cdModel_c₄ ZInQ.Literature.cdModel_map ZInQ.Literature.cdModel_eq_shortCurve

For a commutative ring \(S\) and a natural number \(d\), the model \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(S\) is the Weierstrass equation with coefficients $\(a_1=a_2=a_3=a_6=0,\qquad a_4=-d^2\)$ in \(S\). Its invariants are $\(\Delta=(2d)^6=64d^6,\qquad c_4=48d^2,\)$ the integers \((2d)^6\) and \(48d^2\) read in \(S\). For a ring homomorphism \(S\to S'\), applying it to the coefficients gives the model \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(S'\). Over a field \(F\) the model is the short Weierstrass curve \(y^2=x^3+Ax\) with \(A=-d^2\); over \(\mathbb Q\) it is the curve \(C_d\).

Proof sketch (of the basic facts). Substitute \(a_1=a_2=a_3=a_6=0\), \(a_4=-d^2\) into the formulas for \(b_2,b_4,b_6,b_8\): \(b_2=b_6=0\), \(b_4=-2d^2\), \(b_8=-d^4\), so \(c_4=b_2^2-24b_4=48d^2\) and \(\Delta=-8b_4^3=64d^6\). A ring homomorphism fixes \(0\) and maps \(-d^2\) to \(-d^2\).

docs.title: The places of \(\mathbb Q\) and their completions
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.factNatGenerator ZInQ.Literature.natGenerator_injective ZInQ.Literature.exists_natGenerator_eq ZInQ.Literature.northcott_natCard_residueField ZInQ.Literature.ePadic ZInQ.Literature.isUnit_intCast_iff ZInQ.Literature.irreducible_natGenerator ZInQ.Literature.maximalIdeal_eq_span ZInQ.Literature.intCast_mem_maximalIdeal_pow_iff ZInQ.Literature.natCast_mem_maximalIdeal_iff ZInQ.Literature.residueEquiv ZInQ.Literature.natCard_residueField

A finite place \(v\) of \(\mathbb Q\) is a nonzero prime ideal of the ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q\). Write \(p_v\) for the positive generator of \(v\), \(\mathbb Q_v\) for the completion of \(\mathbb Q\) at \(v\), \(\mathcal O_v\) for its valuation ring, \(\mathfrak m_v\) for the maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O_v\) and \(\kappa_v=\mathcal O_v/\mathfrak m_v\) for the residue field.

  1. \(p_v\) is a prime number. Every prime \(p\) is \(p_v\) for some finite place \(v\), and distinct finite places have distinct primes.
  2. For every natural number \(b\), only finitely many finite places \(v\) have \(\#\kappa_v\le b\).
  3. There is a ring isomorphism \(\mathcal O_v\cong\mathbb Z_{p_v}\) onto the \(p_v\)-adic integers.
  4. For an integer \(n\): \(n\) is a unit of \(\mathcal O_v\) if and only if \(p_v\nmid n\); and for every \(k\ge0\), \(n\in\mathfrak m_v^k\) if and only if \(p_v^k\mid n\). For a natural number \(n\), \(n\in\mathfrak m_v\) if and only if \(p_v\mid n\).
  5. \(p_v\) is irreducible in \(\mathcal O_v\) and generates \(\mathfrak m_v\).
  6. There is a ring isomorphism \(\kappa_v\cong\mathbb Z/p_v\mathbb Z\), and \(\#\kappa_v=p_v\).

Proof sketch. (1) The finite places correspond bijectively to the primes by \(v\mapsto p_v\). (3) is the standard identification of the completion of \(\mathbb Q\) at \(p\) with \(\mathbb Q_p\), restricted to the valuation rings. Transport (4)–(6) along it: in \(\mathbb Z_p\) an integer is a unit exactly when its \(p\)-adic absolute value is \(1\), that is when \(p\nmid n\); \(p\) is irreducible, so it is a uniformizer and \(\mathfrak m^k=(p^k)\); an integer lies in \(p^k\mathbb Z_p\) exactly when \(p^k\) divides it; and \(\mathbb Z_p/p\mathbb Z_p\cong\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\), which has \(p\) elements. (2) By (6) \(\#\kappa_v=p_v\), and by (1) only finitely many places have \(p_v\le b\).

For a finite place \(v\) of \(\mathbb Q\) and a natural number \(d\), let \(C_{d,v}\) be the curve \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb Q\) with its coefficients read in the completion \(\mathbb Q_v\) (notation of the places of \(\mathbb Q\)). Its basic facts:

  1. \(C_{d,v}\) is the model \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb Q_v\), and it is the model \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathcal O_v\) with its coefficients read in \(\mathbb Q_v\). In particular it is integral.
  2. \(\Delta(C_{d,v})\) is the image in \(\mathbb Q_v\) of the element \((2d)^6\) of \(\mathcal O_v\), and \(c_4(C_{d,v})\) is the image of \(48d^2\).
  3. If \(d e0\), then \(\Delta(C_{d,v}) e0\).
  4. If \(C_{d,v}\) is minimal over \(\mathcal O_v\), its reduction is the model \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\kappa_v\).

Proof sketch (of the basic facts). (1) The model over a field is the short curve with \(A=-d^2\), and mapping the model over \(\mathbb Q\), or over \(\mathcal O_v\), into \(\mathbb Q_v\) gives the model over \(\mathbb Q_v\). (2) The discriminant and \(c_4\) commute with mapping the coefficients, and the model over \(\mathcal O_v\) has \(\Delta=(2d)^6\) and \(c_4=48d^2\). (3) \(\mathbb Q_v\) has characteristic \(0\), so \(2d e0\) there. (4) A minimal equation is reduced through its equation with coefficients in \(\mathcal O_v\), which here is the model over \(\mathcal O_v\) (the map \(\mathcal O_v o\mathbb Q_v\) is injective), and reducing the model over \(\mathcal O_v\) gives the model over \(\kappa_v\).

docs.title: Minimality and reduction type of \(C_d\) at each prime
docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.not_dvd_two_mul_pow_six ZInQ.Literature.isMinimal_cdLocal ZInQ.Literature.hasGoodReduction_cdLocal ZInQ.Literature.hasAdditiveReduction_cdLocal ZInQ.Literature.natCard_point_reduction_cdLocal

Let \(v\) be a finite place of \(\mathbb Q\) with prime \(p=p_v\), and \(C_{d,v}\) the curve \(C_d\) over \(\mathbb Q_v\). Reduction types are those of the local polynomial.

  1. For every prime number \(\ell\) and every odd squarefree \(d\), \(\ell^{12} mid(2d)^6\).
  2. If \(d\) is odd and squarefree, then \(C_{d,v}\) is minimal over \(\mathcal O_v\), for every \(v\).
  3. For every natural number \(d\) with \(p mid2d\), \(C_{d,v}\) is minimal and has good reduction.
  4. If \(d\) is odd and squarefree and \(p\mid2d\), then \(C_{d,v}\) is minimal and has additive reduction.
  5. For every natural number \(d\) with \(p mid2d\), if \(C_{d,v}\) is minimal (which holds by (3)), then the reduction of \(C_{d,v}\) has as many points over \(\kappa_v\) as the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) has over \(\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\), the point at infinity included in both counts.

Proof sketch. (1) If \(\ell^{12}\mid(2d)^6\), then \((\ell^2)^6\mid(2d)^6\), so \(\ell^2\mid2d\). Since \(d\) is odd and squarefree, \(2d\) is squarefree, so \(\ell\) would be a unit, which it is not.

(2) By the curve over \(\mathbb Q_v\) (1) and (2), \(C_{d,v}\) comes from the model over \(\mathcal O_v\), whose discriminant is \((2d)^6\). By the places of \(\mathbb Q\) (4), \((2d)^6\in\mathfrak m_v^{12}\) exactly when \(p^{12}\mid(2d)^6\), which (1) with \(\ell=p\) excludes. So minimal Weierstrass equations (1) applies.

(3) \(p mid2d\) gives \(2d otin\mathfrak m_v\), so \((2d)^6 otin\mathfrak m_v\) as \(\mathfrak m_v\) is prime, and a fortiori \((2d)^6 otin\mathfrak m_v^{12}\): the equation is minimal as in (2). Its discriminant is a unit of \(\mathcal O_v\), so its valuation is \(0\): good reduction.

(4) Minimal by (2). From \(p\mid2d\), the discriminant \((2d)^6\) lies in \(\mathfrak m_v\), and so does \(c_4=48d^2=2d\cdot24d\); both have positive valuation, which is additive reduction.

(5) By the curve over \(\mathbb Q_v\) (4) the reduction is the model over \(\kappa_v\); its discriminant, the reduction of \((2d)^6\), is nonzero since \((2d)^6 otin\mathfrak m_v\). Transport along the isomorphism \(\kappa_v\cong\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\) of the places of \(\mathbb Q\) (6), which maps the model to the model, and apply point counts (5).

docs.title: The Euler polynomial of \(C_d\) at \(p\)
docs.text:

For natural numbers \(d\) and \(p\), the Euler polynomial of \(C_d\) at \(p\) is the polynomial with integer coefficients $\(P_{d,p}(T)=\begin{cases}1 & \text{if } p\mid2d,\\ 1-\bigl(p+1-N_d(p)\bigr)T+pT^2 & \text{if } p\nmid2d,\end{cases}\)$ where \(N_d(p)\) is the number of points of the model \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\): the point at infinity and the nonsingular solutions. Only prime \(p\) is used below; for a prime \(p\nmid2d\), \(N_d(p)=\#C_d(\mathbb F_p)\) is the number of points of \(C_d\) over \(\mathbb F_p\), the point at infinity included. In every case the constant coefficient of \(P_{d,p}\) is \(1\).

Let \(v\) be a finite place of \(\mathbb Q\) with prime \(p=p_v\), \(C_{d,v}\) the curve \(C_d\) over \(\mathbb Q_v\), and \(f_{C_{d,v}}\) its local polynomial over \(\mathcal O_v\) (read off the minimal equation chosen once and for all).

  1. For every natural number \(d\) with \(p mid2d\), $\(f_{C_{d,v}}(T)=1- igl(p+1-\#C_d(\mathbb F_p) igr)T+pT^2,\)$ where \(\#C_d(\mathbb F_p)\) is the number of points of \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb F_p\), the point at infinity included.
  2. If \(d\) is odd and squarefree and \(p\mid2d\), then \(f_{C_{d,v}}(T)=1\).
  3. If \(d\) is odd and squarefree, then \(f_{C_{d,v}}=P_{d,p}\), the Euler polynomial of \(C_d\) at \(p\), for every \(v\).

Proof sketch. (1) By minimality and reduction type (3), \(C_{d,v}\) is minimal with good reduction, so the local polynomial (3) gives \(1-(q+1-\# ilde C_{d,v}(\kappa_v))T+qT^2\). Here \(q=\#\kappa_v=p\) by the places of \(\mathbb Q\) (6), and the reduction has \(\#C_d(\mathbb F_p)\) points by minimality and reduction type (5). (2) By minimality and reduction type (4), \(C_{d,v}\) is minimal with additive reduction; \(d\) is odd, so \(d e0\) and \(\Delta(C_{d,v}) e0\) (the curve over \(\mathbb Q_v\) (3)); the local polynomial (2) gives \(1\). (3) Split on whether \(p\mid2d\): (2) and (1) give the two cases of the definition of \(P_{d,p}\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.LFunction_cd_apply_prime_pow

For a Weierstrass equation \(E\) over \(\mathbb Q\), write \(a_n(E)\) for the coefficients of the Dirichlet series \(L(E,s)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n(E)n^{-s}\) of entire continuations. They are the coefficients of the Euler product over the finite places \(v\) of \(\mathbb Q\) in which the factor at \(v\) is the series whose coefficient at \(q_v^k\) is the coefficient of \(T^k\) in \(f_v(T)^{-1}\), and whose other coefficients are \(0\); here \(q_v=\#\kappa_v\) and \(f_v\) is the local polynomial of \(E\) over \(\mathcal O_v\) (notation of the places of \(\mathbb Q\)). For each \(n\) the coefficient at \(n\) of the finite partial products is eventually constant, and \(a_n(E)\) is that value.

Let \(d\) be an odd squarefree natural number, \(p\) a prime and \(k\ge0\). Then $\(a_{p^k}(C_d)= ext{the coefficient of }T^k ext{ in }P_{d,p}(T)^{-1},\)$ where \(P_{d,p}\) is the Euler polynomial of \(C_d\) at \(p\) (its constant coefficient is \(1\), so it is invertible as a power series).

Proof sketch. By the places of \(\mathbb Q\) (1) there is a finite place \(v\) with \(p_v=p\). Every factor has coefficient \(1\) at \(1\), since the inverse series \(f_w(T)^{-1}\) is formed with constant coefficient \(1\). For a place \(w e v\), \(q_w=p_w e p\) (the places of \(\mathbb Q\) (1) and (6)), and no divisor \(m e1\) of \(p^k\) is a power of \(p_w\), so the factor at \(w\) vanishes at every such \(m\). The partial products converge because for each bound only finitely many places have \(q_w\) below it (the places of \(\mathbb Q\) (2)); take a finite set of places containing \(v\) on which the coefficient at \(p^k\) has stabilized. The product of the factors at the other places of the set has coefficient \(1\) at \(1\) and \(0\) at every divisor \(m e1\) of \(p^k\), so the Dirichlet convolution with it leaves the coefficient at \(p^k\) of the factor at \(v\) unchanged. That coefficient is the coefficient of \(T^k\) in \(f_v(T)^{-1}\) (as \(q_v=p\)), and \(f_v=P_{d,p}\) by the local polynomial of \(C_d\) (3).

docs.text:

With \(a_n(C_d)\) the coefficients of \(L(C_d,s)\) as in the coefficients at prime powers, and \(p\) a prime:

  1. If \(d\) is odd and squarefree, then $\(a_p(C_d)= egin{cases}0 & ext{if } p\mid2d,\ p+1-\#C_d(\mathbb F_p) & ext{if } p mid2d,\end{cases}\)$ where \(\#C_d(\mathbb F_p)\) is the number of points of \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) over \(\mathbb F_p\), the point at infinity included.
  2. If \(d\) is odd and squarefree and \(p\mid2d\), then \(a_p(C_d)=0\).
  3. For every natural number \(d\) with \(p mid2d\), $\(\#C_d(\mathbb F_p)=\#\{(x,y)\in\mathbb F_p^2:\ y^2=x^3-d^2x\}+1 .\)$
  4. If \(d\) is odd and squarefree and \(p mid2d\), then $\(a_p(C_d)=p-\#\{(x,y)\in\mathbb F_p^2:\ y^2=x^3-d^2x\}.\)$

The point-count formula (4) holds only at the primes \(p mid2d\); at the primes \(p\mid2d\) the coefficient is \(0\) by (2).

Proof sketch. (1) Take \(k=1\) in the coefficients at prime powers. For a polynomial \(P\) with \(P(0)=1\), the coefficient of \(T\) in \(P^{-1}\) is minus the coefficient of \(T\) in \(P\) (compare the coefficients of \(T\) in \(P\cdot P^{-1}=1\)). The coefficient of \(T\) in the Euler polynomial \(P_{d,p}\) is \(0\) if \(p\mid2d\) and \(-(p+1-\#C_d(\mathbb F_p))\) otherwise. (2) is the first case of (1). (3) Since \(p mid2d\), both \(2\) and \(d\) are nonzero in \(\mathbb F_p\), so \(-d^2 e0\) and the discriminant \(-64(-d^2)^3\) of \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\) is nonzero; by point counts (3) the points are the affine solutions and the point at infinity. (4) Combine (1) and (3).

docs.text:

With \(a_n(E)\) the coefficients of \(L(E,s)\) as in the coefficients at prime powers:

  1. For every Weierstrass equation \(E\) over \(\mathbb Q\), the function \(n\mapsto a_n(E)\) is multiplicative: \(a_1(E)=1\) and \(a_{mn}(E)=a_m(E)a_n(E)\) for coprime \(m\) and \(n\).
  2. If \(d\) is odd and squarefree and \(n\ne0\), then $\(a_n(C_d)=\prod_{p^k\parallel n}\bigl(\text{the coefficient of }T^k\text{ in }P_{d,p}(T)^{-1}\bigr),\)$ the product over the primes \(p\) dividing \(n\), with \(p^k\) the exact power of \(p\) dividing \(n\), and \(P_{d,p}\) the Euler polynomial of \(C_d\) at \(p\).

Proof sketch. (1) The factor at a place \(v\) has coefficient \(1\) at \(1\) (the constant coefficient of \(f_v(T)^{-1}\) is \(1\)) and is supported on the powers of \(q_v=p_v\), a prime, so it is multiplicative; an Euler product of multiplicative factors is multiplicative. (2) Write \(n\) as the product of its prime powers; by (1) \(a_n(C_d)\) is the product of the \(a_{p^k}(C_d)\), each given by the coefficients at prime powers.

docs.text:
ZInQ.Literature.cdCoeff ZInQ.Literature.LSeries_cd_eq ZInQ.Literature.LSeries_cd_eq_of_mod_eight

For natural numbers \(d\) and \(n\) put \(c_d(0)=0\) and, for \(n e0\), $\(c_d(n)=\prod_{p^k\parallel n} igl( ext{the coefficient of }T^k ext{ in }P_{d,p}(T)^{-1} igr),\)$ with \(P_{d,p}\) the Euler polynomial of \(C_d\) at \(p\). The local factor \(P_{d,p}(T)^{-1}\) is \(1\) at the primes \(p\mid2d\) and \((1-a_pT+pT^2)^{-1}\) with \(a_p=p+1-\#C_d(\mathbb F_p)\) at the primes \(p mid2d\); \(c_d\) is built from these factors as the coefficients of the formal Euler product \(\prod_{p mid2d}(1-a_pp^{-s}+p^{1-2s})^{-1}\) are, multiplicatively, with the coefficient of \(T^k\) in the factor at \(p\) placed at \(p^k\).

  1. If \(d\) is odd and squarefree, then for every complex number \(s\) $\(L(C_d,s)=\sum_{n\ge1}c_d(n)\,n^{-s},\)$ both sides read as in entire continuations: the sum of the series where it converges absolutely, and \(0\) elsewhere.
  2. The same holds for every squarefree \(d\) with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\).

This is an identity of series values, not of continuations. The literature statements use an entire continuation, which is required to agree with these series only on \(\operatorname{Re}s>3/2\); for \(\operatorname{Re}s\le3/2\), which contains the point \(s=1\) where the functional equation is used, nothing about the continuation is computed here.

For squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), \(L(C_d,s)\) is the L-series in the functional equation, in the vanishing at the centre, in row 5b and in reading A. Hecke's continuation is stated for every \(d e0\) and Gross–Zagier for every elliptic curve over \(\mathbb Q\); their L-series is not computed here beyond odd squarefree \(d\).

Proof sketch. (1) The two Dirichlet series have the same coefficient at every \(n e0\), by every coefficient (2), so they agree at every \(s\). (2) \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) makes \(d\) odd; apply (1).

docs.title: Mordell–Weil by two-isogeny descent
docs.text:
For a positive integer \(n\) let \(C_n:y^2=x^3-n^2x\) and \(C'_n:y^2=x^3+4n^2x\) over \(\mathbb Q\). When \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\) has order \(8\), a point of infinite order on \(C_n\) yields every 2-Selmer class of \(C_n\), but only once \(C_n(\mathbb Q)\) is known to be finitely generated. This section proves that by the classical route. The two-isogeny descent shows that \(2C_n(\mathbb Q)\) has finite index, and the descent theorem with the naive height turns the finite index into finite generation, as for the generator curve in Mordell–Weil for \(E/K_0\) from the descent.

The descent uses the Kummer map \(\alpha_b\), the two-isogeny \(\varphi_b:E_b\to E_{-4b}\) and the rescaling \(\lambda_b:E_{16b}\to E_b\) of the descent chapter, for the curves \(E_b:y^2=x^3+bx\); here \(C_n=E_{-n^2}\) and \(C'_n=E_{4n^2}\). Over the number field \(K_0\) the index \([E(K_0):2E(K_0)]\) was computed exactly. Here only its finiteness is needed, and it follows from the finiteness of the two Kummer images over \(\mathbb Q\).

This section writes \(n\) for the positive integer of the curve; the rest of the positive-rank chapter, following the Proposition 0 chapter, writes \(d\) and \(C_d\) for the same curves, and the statement of finite generation is also given in that form.

9 fully proved

docs.title: Two-torsion
docs.text: \(C_n\) has full rational two-torsion, of order four. The two-torsion lemma of the 2-descent proves the same count over any field in which \(2\ne0\), as a separate statement.

docs.title: The two-torsion of \(C_n(\mathbb Q)\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.twoTorsion_card ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwTwoTorsion_iff ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwIsElliptic ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwTwoTorsion_nonsingular ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwTwoTorsionPt

Let \(n\) be a positive integer and \(C_n:y^2=x^3-n^2x\) over \(\mathbb Q\). Then \(C_n\) is an elliptic curve, and for each \(e\in\{0,n,-n\}\) the point \((e,0)\) is a nonsingular point of \(C_n\). A point \(P\in C_n(\mathbb Q)\) satisfies \(2P=O\) if and only if $\(P\in\{O,\ (0,0),\ (n,0),\ (-n,0)\}.\)$ In particular exactly \(4\) points \(P\in C_n(\mathbb Q)\) satisfy \(2P=O\).

Proof sketch. \(C_n\) is the curve \(E_b:y^2=x^3+bx\) with \(b=-n^2\ne0\); its discriminant \(-64b^3=64n^6\) is nonzero, so \(C_n\) is elliptic. Each \(e\in\{0,\pm n\}\) is a root of \(x^3-n^2x=x(x-n)(x+n)\), so \((e,0)\) lies on \(C_n\), and points of an elliptic curve are nonsingular. Clearly \(2O=O\). For an affine point \(P=(x,y)\) we have \(-P=(x,-y)\), so \(2P=O\) if and only if \(y=0\); then \(x(x-n)(x+n)=0\), that is \(x\in\{0,n,-n\}\), and conversely. The four points are distinct: \(O\) is not affine, and \(0,n,-n\) are distinct because \(n\ne0\).

docs.text: The finite-index argument needs \(\varphi_b\) to be additive. Collinear points with nonzero abscissas go to collinear points whose abscissas sum to the square of the new slope, and on \(E_{-4b}\) this forces the images to add up. The point at infinity, the point \((0,0)\) and the degenerate sums are treated separately.

Let \(K\) be a field and \(b,\ell, u\in K\) with \( u e0\). Put $\(L= rac b u-\ell,\qquad N=- u- rac{b\ell^2}{ u}.\)$

  1. (The image line.) If \(x e0\), \(y=\ell x+ u\) and \(y^2=x^3+bx\), then \(X=y^2/x^2\) and \(Y=y(b-x^2)/x^2\), the formulas of the two-isogeny \(\varphi_b\) at \((x,y)\), satisfy \(Y=LX+N\).
  2. (The abscissa sum.) If \(x_1,x_2,x_3\in K\) are nonzero and $\(x_1+x_2+x_3=\ell^2,\qquad x_1x_2+x_1x_3+x_2x_3=b-2\ell u,\qquad x_1x_2x_3= u^2,\)$ then $\(\sum_{i=1}^3 rac{(\ell x_i+ u)^2}{x_i^2}=L^2 .\)$
  3. (Tangency.) If in 1 also \(2y\ell=3x^2+b\), then \(2LY=3X^2-4b\).

No assumption on the characteristic of \(K\) or on \(b\) is needed.

Proof sketch. Each identity becomes polynomial after clearing the nonzero denominators \(x\) (or \(x_1,x_2,x_3\)) and \( u\). In 1, substitute \(y=\ell x+ u\): the difference of the two sides is a multiple of \(y^2-x^3-bx\). In 2, use the first two relations to eliminate \(x_3=\ell^2-x_1-x_2\) and \(b=x_1x_2+(x_1+x_2)x_3+2\ell u\); the difference is then a polynomial multiple of \(x_1x_2x_3- u^2\). In 3, use the tangency condition to eliminate \(b=2y\ell-3x^2\); the difference is a polynomial multiple of the curve equation.

  • (Chords.) If \(P_1=(x_1,y_1)\) and \(P_2=(x_2,y_2)\) in \(E_b(K)\) have \(x_1,x_2 e0\), \(x_1 e x_2\), \(x_1x_2 e b\), and \(P_1+P_2\) has nonzero abscissa, then \(\varphi_b(P_1+P_2)=\varphi_b(P_1)+\varphi_b(P_2)\).
  • (Doubling.) If \(P=(x,y)\) has \(x e0\), \(y e0\) and \(2P\) has nonzero abscissa, then \(\varphi_b(2P)=2\varphi_b(P)\). Equivalently, \(\varphi_b(2R)=2\varphi_b(R)\) whenever \(R otin\{O,T\}\) and \(2R otin\{O,T\}\).

Proof sketch. (Silverman–Tate, Section III.4.) Chords. Let \(y=\ell x+ u\) be the chord through \(P_1,P_2\). Then \(P_1+P_2=(x_3,-(\ell x_3+ u))\) with \(x_1+x_2+x_3=\ell^2\). The factorization of \(x^3+bx-(\ell x+ u)^2\) gives \(x_1x_2x_3= u^2\), so \( u e0\). Subtracting the curve equations of \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) and dividing by \(x_1-x_2\) gives \(x_1x_2+x_1x_3+x_2x_3=b-2\ell u\). By the image-line identity, \(\varphi_b(P_1)\), \(\varphi_b(P_2)\) and \(\varphi_b(-(P_1+P_2))\) lie on \(Y=LX+N\), so \(\varphi_b(P_1+P_2)=(X_3,-(LX_3+N))\). By the abscissa-sum identity, \(X_1+X_2+X_3=L^2\). Finally \(X_1 e X_2\): by the curve equations, \(X_1=X_2\) would give \(x_1x_2(x_1-x_2)(x_1x_2-b)=0\). Addition along a line on \(E_{-4b}\) gives the claim.

Doubling. Take the tangent slope \(\ell\), with \(2y\ell=3x^2+b\), and the same relations with \(x_1=x_2=x\). From \(x(2P)\cdot(2y)^2=(x^2-b)^2\) and \(x(2P) e0\) we get \(b e x^2\), so the image ordinate \(y(b-x^2)/x^2\) is nonzero. The tangency identity and doubling along a line on \(E_{-4b}\) give the claim. For \(R=(x,y) otin\{O,T\}\) we have \(x e0\); \(2R e O\) forces \(y e0\), and \(2R e T\) forces \(x(2R) e0\).

docs.title: The two-isogeny is a homomorphism
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwPhi_add ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwPhiHom ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwPhiHom_apply ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwPhi_neg ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwAdd_tZero_some ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwTZero_add_tZero ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwNeg_tZero ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwPhi_tZero ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwPhi_add_tZero

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic different from \(2\) and \(b\in K^ imes\). The two-isogeny \(\varphi_b:E_b(K) o E_{-4b}(K)\) is a group homomorphism: $\(\varphi_b(P+Q)=\varphi_b(P)+\varphi_b(Q)\qquad(P,Q\in E_b(K)).\)$

Along the way, with \(T=(0,0)\):

  • \(\varphi_b(-P)=-\varphi_b(P)\) for every \(P\);
  • \(T+T=O\), hence \(-T=T\), and \(\varphi_b(T)=O\);
  • for an affine point \((x,y)\) with \(x e0\), \((b/x,\,-by/x^2)\) lies on \(E_b\) and \((x,y)+T=(b/x,\,-by/x^2)\); and \(\varphi_b(P+T)=\varphi_b(P)\) for every \(P\).

Proof sketch. (Silverman–Tate, Section III.4.) The first three items are direct computations; for example, \(\varphi_b(b/x,-by/x^2)\) has coordinates \(y^2/x^2\) and \(y(b-x^2)/x^2\).

Additivity. If \(P\) or \(Q\) is \(O\) or \(T\), use \(\varphi_b(P+T)=\varphi_b(P)\) and \(\varphi_b(T)=O\). If \(P+Q=O\), use \(\varphi_b(-P)=-\varphi_b(P)\). If \(P+Q=T\), then \(Q=-P+T\) and \(\varphi_b(Q)=-\varphi_b(P)\). Otherwise \(P=(x_1,y_1)\) and \(Q=(x_2,y_2)\) with \(x_1,x_2 e0\). If \(x_1=x_2\), then \(Q=P\) (the doubling case) or \(Q=-P\) (excluded). If \(x_1x_2=b\), then \(P+T\) has abscissa \(b/x_1=x_2\), so \(Q=\pm(P+T)\). If \(Q=P+T\), then \(\varphi_b(P+Q)=\varphi_b(2P+T)=\varphi_b(2P)=2\varphi_b(P)=\varphi_b(P)+\varphi_b(Q)\); the doubling hypotheses hold because \(P+Q otin\{O,T\}\). If \(Q=-(P+T)\), then \(P+Q=T\), which is excluded. In the remaining case \(P+Q e T\) has nonzero abscissa, and the chord case applies.

docs.title: The index of \(2C_n(\mathbb Q)\)
docs.text: Over any field of characteristic different from \(2\), the dual isogeny factors doubling, so \(2E_b(K)\) has finite index once both Kummer images are finite. Over \(\mathbb Q\) the Kummer image of \(E_c\) lies in the classes of the signed divisors of \(c\), by a count of \(p\)-adic valuations. Applied to \(C_n\) and \(C'_n\), this gives the weak Mordell–Weil theorem.

docs.title: The index of \(2E_b(K)\) from the two Kummer images
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwFiniteIndex_two_of_kummer ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwKer_kummer_finiteIndex ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwPhiHat ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwPhiHat_phi ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwKer_kummer_eq_range ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.mwKer_kummer'_le_comap

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic different from \(2\) and \(b\in K^\times\), and let $\(\hat\varphi=\lambda_b\circ\varphi_{-4b}:E_{-4b}(K)\to E_{16b}(K)\to E_b(K)\)$ be the dual isogeny. If the Kummer images \(\alpha_b(E_b(K))\) and \(\alpha_{-4b}(E_{-4b}(K))\) are finite, then \(2E_b(K)\) has finite index in \(E_b(K)\).

Along the way:

  • for \(c\in K^\times\), if \(\alpha_c(E_c(K))\) is finite, then \(\ker\alpha_c\) has finite index in \(E_c(K)\);
  • \(\hat\varphi\) is a group homomorphism, and \(\hat\varphi(\varphi_b(P))=2P\) for every \(P\in E_b(K)\);
  • \(\ker\alpha_b=\hat\varphi\bigl(E_{-4b}(K)\bigr)\);
  • \(\hat\varphi(Q)\in2E_b(K)\) for every \(Q\in\ker\alpha_{-4b}\).

Proof sketch. (Silverman–Tate, Section III.5; Silverman, Proposition X.4.9.) Since \(\alpha_c\) is a homomorphism, \(E_c(K)/\ker\alpha_c\cong\alpha_c(E_c(K))\), which proves the first item. \(\hat\varphi\) is the composite of the homomorphism \(\varphi_{-4b}\) and the group isomorphism \(\lambda_b\), and \(\hat\varphi\circ\varphi_b=[2]\) is the doubling factorization.

For the kernel, write \(P=\lambda_b(P')\) with \(P'\in E_{16b}(K)\). The map \(\lambda_b\) divides abscissas by the square \(4\) and sends \((0,0)\), of class \(16b\), to \((0,0)\), of class \(b\); so \(\alpha_b(P)=\alpha_{16b}(P')\). By the kernel theorem for \(\varphi_{-4b}:E_{-4b}\to E_{16b}\), \(\alpha_{16b}(P')=1\) if and only if \(P'\in\varphi_{-4b}(E_{-4b}(K))\), that is, if and only if \(P\in\hat\varphi(E_{-4b}(K))\). If \(\alpha_{-4b}(Q)=1\), the kernel theorem for \(\varphi_b\) gives \(Q=\varphi_b(P)\), so \(\hat\varphi(Q)=2P\).

Finally, \(\alpha_b(2P)=\alpha_b(P)^2=1\), so \(2E_b(K)\subseteq\ker\alpha_b\) and $\([E_b(K):2E_b(K)]=[\ker\alpha_b:2E_b(K)]\,[E_b(K):\ker\alpha_b].\)$ The second factor is finite by the first item. For the first, \(\ker\alpha_b=\hat\varphi(E_{-4b}(K))\), so \([\ker\alpha_b:2E_b(K)]=[E_{-4b}(K):\hat\varphi^{-1}(2E_b(K))]\). The group \(\hat\varphi^{-1}(2E_b(K))\) contains \(\ker\alpha_{-4b}\), which has finite index by the first item.

docs.text:

Let \(c\) be a nonzero integer. Then the Kummer image \(\alpha_c(E_c(\mathbb Q))\subseteq\mathbb Q^ imes/\mathbb Q^{ imes2}\) of \(E_c:y^2=x^3+cx\) is finite.

Along the way:

  • if \(x,y\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy \(y^2=x^3+cx\) and \(x e0\), then \(v_p(x)\) is even for every prime \(p mid c\);
  • if \(B\) is a positive integer and \(q\in\mathbb Q^ imes\) has \(v_p(q)\) even for every prime \(p mid B\), then \(q\equiv m\) modulo squares for some integer \(m\) with \(|m|\) dividing \(B\).

Proof sketch. (Silverman–Tate, Section III.5.)

Valuations. Let \(p mid c\), so \(v_p(cx)=v_p(x)\). If \(y=0\) then \(x^2=-c\), so \(2v_p(x)=v_p(c)=0\). Otherwise \(2v_p(y)=v_p(x^3+cx)\). If \(v_p(x)<0\), the term \(x^3\) dominates: \(2v_p(y)=3v_p(x)\), so \(v_p(x)\) is even. If \(v_p(x)>0\), the term \(cx\) dominates: \(2v_p(y)=v_p(x)\).

Signed divisors. Write \(q=r/s\) in lowest terms with \(s>0\), let \(N=rs=qs^2\), and write \(|N|=t^2a\) with \(a\) squarefree. Put \(m=\operatorname{sign}(N)\,a\), so \(q\equiv N\equiv m\) modulo squares. Every prime \(p\mid a\) divides \(B\): otherwise \(v_p(N)=v_p(q)+2v_p(s)\) is even, so \(v_p(a)=v_p(N)-2v_p(t)\ge1\) is even, hence \(p^2\mid a\), against squarefreeness. As \(a\) is squarefree, \(|m|=a\) divides \(B\).

Finiteness. The image lies in the classes of the integers \(m\) with \(|m|\) dividing \(|c|\), a finite set. Indeed \(\alpha_c(O)=1\) (take \(m=1\)) and \(\alpha_c((0,y))=c\) (take \(m=c\)). For \(x e0\), \(\alpha_c((x,y))\) is the class of \(x\), which by the two lemmas, with \(B=|c|\), is the class of such an \(m\).

docs.title: The weak Mordell–Weil theorem for \(C_n\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.finiteIndex_two_points

Let \(n\) be a positive integer. Then \(2C_n(\mathbb Q)\) has finite index in \(C_n(\mathbb Q)\).

Proof sketch. \(C_n=E_{-n^2}\), and the isogenous curve is \(E_{-4\cdot(-n^2)}=E_{4n^2}=C'_n:y^2=x^3+4n^2x\). Since \(n\ne0\), the curves \(C_n\), \(C'_n\) and \(E_{16\cdot(-n^2)}=E_{-16n^2}\) are elliptic over \(\mathbb Q\). The Kummer images \(\alpha_{-n^2}(C_n(\mathbb Q))\) and \(\alpha_{4n^2}(C'_n(\mathbb Q))\) are finite, by the finiteness of the Kummer image over \(\mathbb Q\) for the nonzero integers \(c=-n^2\) and \(c=4n^2\). The index theorem with \(b=-n^2\) then shows that \(2C_n(\mathbb Q)\) has finite index.

docs.title: Finite generation
docs.text: The naive height on \(\mathbb Q\) completes the descent.

docs.title: Mordell–Weil for the congruent number curves
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.fg_points ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.fg_points_all

Let \(n\) be a positive integer. The group \(C_n(\mathbb Q)\) of rational points of \(C_n:y^2=x^3-n^2x\) is finitely generated.

In the form used by the positive-rank chapter: for every natural number \(d\ne0\), the group \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is finitely generated.

Proof sketch. (Silverman, Theorem VIII.3.1 and Section VIII.6; Silverman–Tate, Chapter III.) \(C_n\) is an elliptic curve over \(\mathbb Q\). Let \(h\) be the naive height: \(h(O)=0\), and \(h((x,y))=\sum_v\log\max(1,|x|_v)\) over the places of \(\mathbb Q\), which is \(\log\max(|r|,|s|)\) for \(x=r/s\) in lowest terms. Then:

  • \(h\ge0\);
  • there is a constant \(c\) with \(|h(P+Q)+h(P-Q)-2h(P)-2h(Q)|\le c\) for all \(P,Q\) (the approximate parallelogram law);
  • for every bound \(B\) only finitely many \(P\) have \(h(P)\le B\) (Northcott's property for \(\mathbb Q\), since each abscissa determines at most two points).

The descent theorem says that an abelian group \(G\) with such a height, in which \(2G\) has finite index, is finitely generated. By the weak Mordell–Weil theorem, \(2C_n(\mathbb Q)\) has finite index in \(C_n(\mathbb Q)\). The second form is the first with \(n=d\).

docs.title: The rank hypothesis on the two curves of a slot choice
The rank hypothesis on the two curves of a slot choice
docs.text:
Pole completeness uses the rank hypothesis at two curves only. For an admissible input \(B\), a multiplier \(m\), a prime \(p_0\mid\beta\) and slot data for \(\beta,\theta,p_0\), these are \(C_{d_1}\) and \(C_{d_1|\theta|}=C_{d_2}\), with \(d_1=|\beta|\,q_0\prod r_p\prod r_\ell\) as in the realization. Both carry Selmer certificates for \(\beta\), so through Proposition 0 their 2-Selmer groups have order \(8\) and contain a class with first coordinate \(\beta\). This section states the positive-rank hypothesis for exactly these curves, CR₃^DL,Rk: for every triple \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfying the hypotheses of the realization, some slot choice gives two curves with rational points of infinite order. CR₃^DL,Rk follows from the positive-rank forms CR₃^Rk and CR₃^TYZ,Rk of the positive-rank chapter, and it implies pole completeness: on a certified curve, a point of infinite order makes every Selmer class come from a rational point, and this gives the points with abscissas in \(\beta\mathbb Q^{*2}\) that the pole polynomial needs. The same holds for CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk, which asks only that for every admissible \(B\) some multiplier, prime \(p_0\) and slot choice give two curves with points of infinite order.

Throughout, \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\), as in the rest of the positive-rank chapter.

9 fully proved

docs.title: Certificates and the 2-Selmer group
docs.text: Through Proposition 0, a Selmer certificate for \((d,a)\) says that \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has order \(8\) and contains a class with first coordinate \(a\).

docs.title: The 2-Selmer group of a certified curve
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.sel_of_selmerCertified

Let \(d\) be a squarefree natural number with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), and let \(a\) be a squarefree integer dividing \(d\) such that \((d,a)\) carries a Selmer certificate: the system \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) has exactly \(8\) solutions, and one of them has first coordinate the class of \(a\). Then \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\), and \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) for some integer \(b\).

Proof sketch. By Proposition 0, unknowns \(\sigma\) solve \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) if and only if \((a(\sigma),b(\sigma))\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\), and every element of \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has this form. So \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) is the image of the solution set under \(\sigma\mapsto(a(\sigma),b(\sigma))\). This map is injective for odd \(d\), so \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\). Let \(\sigma\) be the solution whose first coordinate is the class of \(a\), that is \(a_0=[a<0]\), \(a_1=0\) and \(u_p=[p\mid a]\). Since \(a\) is a squarefree divisor of \(d\), \(a(\sigma)=(-1)^{[a<0]}\prod_{p\mid a}p=a\), so \((a,b(\sigma))\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\). These are steps 1 and 2 of the proof of CR₃ from its Selmer form, at a single certificate.

docs.title: The positive-rank hypothesis on the two curves of a slot choice
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.CertifiedRankDLRk

The hypothesis CR₃^DL,Rk is the following assertion. Let \(\beta,\theta\) be integers and \(p_0\) a natural number such that:

  • \(\beta\) is odd and squarefree with \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), and \(p_0\) is a prime dividing \(\beta\);
  • \(\theta>0\) is squarefree with \(\theta\equiv1\pmod8\);
  • \(\beta\) and \(\theta\) are coprime;
  • \([\beta/\ell]=0\) for every prime \(\ell\mid\theta\), and \([\theta/p]=0\) for every prime \(p\mid\beta\).

Then there are slot data \(q_0\), \(r_p\) (\(p\in P(\beta)\setminus\{p_0\}\)) and \(r_\ell\) (\(\ell\in P(\theta)\)) for \(\beta,\theta,p_0\), satisfying the slot conditions, such that, with $\(d_1=|\beta|\,q_0\prod_{p}r_p\prod_{\ell}r_\ell ,\)$ both \(C_{d_1}(\mathbb Q)\) and \(C_{d_1|\theta|}(\mathbb Q)\) contain a point of infinite order. Here \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\).

The hypotheses on \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) are those of the realization, which the multiplier lemma and (θ1)–(θ4) give for an admissible input. By the realization, \(d_1\) and \(d_1|\theta|=d_1\theta=d_2\) are squarefree and \(\equiv5\pmod8\), \(\beta\) divides both, and both \((d_1,\beta)\) and \((d_2,\beta)\) carry Selmer certificates. So these are the two curves at which the proof of pole completeness applies the rank hypothesis, and both have 2-Selmer groups of order \(8\). The slot data are existential: points of infinite order on the two curves of any one slot choice suffice. The assertion depends on the slot conditions, so a change to the slot construction changes what it asserts.

CR₃^DL,Rk is not proved here; it is a hypothesis. It follows from CR₃^Rk and from CR₃^TYZ,Rk, so it rests on the same theorems: Tian–Yuan–Zhang as completed by Proposition N, which is not refereed, and Gross–Zagier with an auxiliary field.

docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.CertifiedRankDLAdmRk

The hypothesis CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk is the following assertion. For every admissible \(B\) there are:

  • a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) such that \(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\) is odd with \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\);
  • a prime \(p_0\) dividing \(\beta\);
  • slot data \(q_0\), \(r_p\) (\(p\in P(\beta)\setminus\{p_0\}\)) and \(r_\ell\) (\(\ell\in P(\theta)\)) for \(\beta\), \(\theta=\mathrm{sqf}(m(m-B))\) and \(p_0\), satisfying the slot conditions;

such that, with \(d_1=|\beta|\,q_0\prod_pr_p\prod_\ell r_\ell\), both \(C_{d_1}(\mathbb Q)\) and \(C_{d_1|\theta|}(\mathbb Q)\) contain a point of infinite order. Here \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\).

These are the data that the multiplier lemma and the existence of the slots produce for an admissible input. So CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk asks for the points only at the inputs that admissible numbers produce, while CR₃^DL,Rk asks for them at every triple \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfying the hypotheses of the realization. Like CR₃^DL,Rk, it depends on the slot conditions and on the definitions of admissibility, \(\beta\) and \(\theta\).

CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk is not proved here; it is a hypothesis, implied by CR₃^DL,Rk.

Proof sketch. Let \(B\) be admissible. By the multiplier lemma in its combined form with the existence of the slots, of which only the multiplier part is used here, there is a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) with \(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\) odd and \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), and \(\beta\) has a prime factor \(p_0\). docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.certifiedRankDLRk_of_certifiedRankRk ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.slots_d₂_facts

The hypothesis CR₃^Rk implies CR₃^DL,Rk.

Along the way: let \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfy the hypotheses of CR₃^DL,Rk, let \(q_0\), \(r_p\), \(r_\ell\) be any slot data for \(\beta,\theta,p_0\), and let \(d_1=|\beta|\,q_0\prod_pr_p\prod_\ell r_\ell\). Then \(d_1|\theta|\) is squarefree, \(d_1|\theta|\equiv5\pmod8\), \(\beta\) divides \(d_1|\theta|\), and \((d_1|\theta|,\beta)\) carries a Selmer certificate.

Proof sketch. Along the way. By the realization, \(d_2=d_1\theta=d_1|\theta|\) is squarefree and \((d_2,\beta)\) carries a Selmer certificate. Also \(d_1\equiv5\) and \(\theta\equiv1\pmod8\), so \(d_1|\theta|\equiv5\pmod8\); and \(\beta\mid d_1\), so \(\beta\mid d_1|\theta|\).

The implication. Let \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfy the hypotheses of CR₃^DL,Rk. Then \(\beta\) is odd, \(\theta\) is odd (because \(\theta\equiv1\pmod8\)), they are coprime and \(p_0\in P(\beta)\), so slot data exist; take any. By the realization, \(d_1\) is squarefree with \(d_1\equiv5\pmod8\), \(\beta\mid d_1\), and \((d_1,\beta)\) carries a Selmer certificate; the statement along the way gives the same for \(d_1|\theta|\). Since \(\beta\) is squarefree, the lemma on the 2-Selmer group of a certified curve, with \(a=\beta\), gives on each of the two curves \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2|=8\) and a class \((\beta,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2\), with \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\). CR₃^Rk then gives a point of infinite order on each curve.

The hypothesis CR₃^TYZ,Rk implies CR₃^DL,Rk.

For a single curve: assume CR₃^TYZ,Rk, let \(d\) be a squarefree natural number with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), and let \(a\) be a squarefree integer dividing \(d\) with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\) such that \((d,a)\) carries a Selmer certificate. Then \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order.

Proof sketch. One curve. The lemma on the 2-Selmer group of a certified curve gives \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\) and some \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\). Since \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\), Corollary 4.4 gives \(\det M_{5b}=1\). By Theorem 3.6, \(\det M_{5b}=T_{5b}(d)\), so \(T_{5b}(d)=1\), and CR₃^TYZ,Rk gives the point.

The two curves. Let \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfy the hypotheses of CR₃^DL,Rk. Then \(\beta,\theta\) are odd and coprime and \(p_0\in P(\beta)\), so slot data exist; take any. By the realization, \(d_1\) is squarefree with \(d_1\equiv5\pmod8\), \(\beta\mid d_1\), and \((d_1,\beta)\) carries a Selmer certificate; by the facts proved along the way to CR₃^DL,Rk from CR₃^Rk, the same holds for \(d_1|\theta|\). Since \(\beta\) is squarefree with \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), the one-curve statement with \(a=\beta\) applies to both curves.

docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.exists_point_of_selmerCertified_of_infinite_order

Let \(d\) be a squarefree natural number with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), and let \(a\) be a squarefree integer dividing \(d\) with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\) such that \((d,a)\) carries a Selmer certificate. If \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has a point of infinite order, then there are \(x,y\in\mathbb Q\) with \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\), \(x e0\) and \(x/a\) a square in \(\mathbb Q\).

The conclusion is that of the certified rank hypothesis CR₃ at \((d,a)\): on a certified curve, positive rank gives the point that CR₃ asks for.

Proof sketch. The lemma on the 2-Selmer group of a certified curve gives \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\) and some \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\). Since \(d e0\), the group \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is finitely generated by Mordell–Weil for the congruent number curves. It has a point of infinite order and \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\), so by RK9 every Selmer class comes from a rational point; in particular the x-form of the 2-covering \(D_{a,b}\) holds over \(\mathbb Q\). Here \(b e0\), since \(b\) is squarefree. The squarefree \(a\) with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\) is not a square, so the first alternative of the x-form is excluded, and there is \(x\) with \(x/a\), \((x-d)/b\) and \((x+d)/(ab)\) squares. As in steps 3–5 of the proof of CR₃ from its Selmer form, \(x e0\), and \(y=abr_1r_2r_3\) gives the point.

Assume CR₃^DL,Rk. Then pole completeness holds: every admissible \(B\) satisfies \(\Phi(B)\).

For a single input: let \(B\) be admissible, \(m\) a signed divisor of \(2730\), \(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\) and \(\theta=\mathrm{sqf}(m(m-B))\), and let \(p_0\) be a natural number such that \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfy the hypotheses of CR₃^DL,Rk. If for some slot data \(q_0\), \(r_p\), \(r_\ell\) for \(\beta,\theta,p_0\), with \(d_1=|\beta|\,q_0\prod_pr_p\prod_\ell r_\ell\), both \(C_{d_1}(\mathbb Q)\) and \(C_{d_1|\theta|}(\mathbb Q)\) have points of infinite order, then \(\Phi(B)\) holds.

Proof sketch. One input. By the realization, \(d_1\) is squarefree with \(d_1\equiv5\pmod8\), \(\beta\mid d_1\), and \((d_1,\beta)\) carries a Selmer certificate; by the facts proved along the way to CR₃^DL,Rk from CR₃^Rk, the same holds for \(d_1|\theta|\). Also \(\beta\) is squarefree with \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\). The lemma on a point of infinite order on a certified curve, with \(a=\beta\), gives a point \((x_1,y_1)\) on \(C_{d_1}\) and a point \((x_2,y_2)\) on \(C_{d_1|\theta|}\), with \(x_i\ne0\) and \(x_i/\beta\) squares. Since \(0<B<1/2\), the integer \(m\) is not \(B\). Take \(N=d_1\ne0\). Then \(C_{N\theta}\) is \(C_{d_1|\theta|}\), since \((d_1|\theta|)^2=(d_1\theta)^2\), and the lemma on points and pole solubility gives \(\Phi(B)\).

Pole completeness. By the reformulation through admissible inputs, it suffices to treat an admissible \(B\). The multiplier lemma in its combined form with the existence of the slots, of which only the multiplier part is used here, gives a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) with \(\beta\) odd and \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), and a prime factor \(p_0\) of \(\beta\). By the descent lemma's facts about admissible inputs, which rest on (θ1)–(θ4), the triple \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfies the hypotheses of CR₃^DL,Rk. CR₃^DL,Rk gives slot data whose two curves have points of infinite order, and the first part gives \(\Phi(B)\). Unlike the proof from CR₃, the slot data come from the hypothesis, not from the descent lemma; of the descent lemma only the facts about admissible inputs are used.

docs.title: The complete 2-descent on a congruent number curve
The complete 2-descent on a congruent number curve
docs.text:
For a field \(K\) with \(2\ne0\) and \(d\in K^\times\), the curve \(C_d:y^2=x(x-d)(x+d)\) has full rational two-torsion. Its complete 2-descent map \(\delta_d\) sends a point to the pair of Kummer classes at the roots \(0\) and \(d\): \((x,y)\mapsto(x,x-d)\) in \((K^\times/K^{\times2})^2\), with the usual values at the torsion points (Silverman, Proposition X.1.4). At the root \(0\) the formulas are those of the Kummer map \(\alpha_b\) of the two-isogeny descent. The Kummer map \(\kappa_{b,e}\) at a general root \(e\) is a homomorphism by the chord argument. Over \(\mathbb Q\) the descent map has kernel exactly \(2C_d(\mathbb Q)\), by an explicit halving formula. Read in square classes, it agrees with the Kummer map of the coverings, so over \(\mathbb Q\) the pairs \(s(P)\) of squarefree representatives \(r(c)\) of its values lie in \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\). A count in finitely generated abelian groups then gives RK9: positive rank and a Selmer group of order \(8\) make every Selmer class come from a rational point.

Over a general field \(K\), \(d\) is a nonzero element of \(K\) and \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) is the curve \(E_{-d^2}\); over \(\mathbb Q\), \(d\) is a positive integer, and \(C_d\) and \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) are those of the Proposition 0 chapter. Throughout, \(u\equiv v\) means that \(u/v\) is a nonzero square.

12 fully proved

Let \(K\) be a field, \(b,e\in K\), and \(E_b:y^2=x^3+bx\). Write \(K^ imes/K^{ imes2}\) multiplicatively, and let the class of \(0\) be \(1\). The Kummer map at \(e\) is the map \(\kappa_{b,e}:E_b(K) o K^ imes/K^{ imes2}\) given by $\(\kappa_{b,e}(O)=1,\qquad \kappa_{b,e} igl((x,y) igr)= egin{cases}3e^2+b, & x=e,\ x-e, & x e e,\end{cases}\)$ with the values read modulo squares.

Suppose that \(e\) is a root of the cubic, \(e^3+be=0\). Then \((e,0)\) satisfies the equation of \(E_b\), and every point \((x,y)\in E_b(K)\) with \(x=e\) has \(y=0\). If moreover \(2 e0\) and \(b e0\), then \((e,0)\) is a point \(T_e\in E_b(K)\), every point \((x,y)\in E_b(K)\) with \(x=e\) equals \(T_e\), and \(\kappa_{b,e}(T_e)\) is the class of \(3e^2+b\).

Proof sketch. The equation at \((e,0)\) reads \(0=e^3+be\). A point \((e,y)\) on \(E_b\) has \(y^2=e^3+be=0\), so \(y=0\), and the point is \(T_e\). The value at \(T_e\) is the first case of the definition.

docs.text:

Let \(K\) be a field with \(2 e0\), let \(b\in K^ imes\), and let \(e\in K\) be a root of \(x^3+bx\). Then for all \(P,Q\in E_b(K)\) $\(\kappa_{b,e}(P+Q)=\kappa_{b,e}(P)\,\kappa_{b,e}(Q),\)$ so \(\kappa_{b,e}\) is a group homomorphism \(E_b(K) o K^ imes/K^{ imes2}\).

Along the way:

  • \(\kappa_{b,e}(-P)=\kappa_{b,e}(P)\) for every \(P\) (for any field and any \(b,e\));
  • the root is simple: \(3e^2+b e0\);
  • for \((x,y)\in E_b(K)\) with \(x e e\), the point \((x,y)+T_e\) has abscissa \(e+(3e^2+b)/(x-e)\);
  • \(\kappa_{b,e}(P+T_e)=\kappa_{b,e}(P)\cdot(3e^2+b)\) for every \(P\);
  • (here \(b=0\) is allowed) if \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\) are points of \(E_b(K)\) whose sum is affine, \(\ell\) is the slope of the chord or tangent through them and \(x_3\) is the abscissa of the sum, then \((x_1-e)(x_2-e)(x_3-e)= igl(y_1-\ell(x_1-e) igr)^2\).

Proof sketch. (Silverman, Proposition X.1.4.) \(\kappa_{b,e}(-P)=\kappa_{b,e}(P)\) because negation keeps the abscissa. Write \(\kappa=\kappa_{b,e}\).

  1. Simple root. If \(3e^2+b=0\), then \(e(e^2+b)=0\); \(e=0\) gives \(b=0\), and \(e^2=-b\) gives \(2b=0\), so \(b=0\) either way.
  2. Translation by \(T_e\). For \(x e e\) the chord through \((x,y)\) and \((e,0)\) gives the abscissa \(e+(3e^2+b)/(x-e)\), which is not \(e\) by step 1, so \(\kappa(P+T_e)\) is the class of \((3e^2+b)/(x-e)\), that is of \((3e^2+b)(x-e)\). For \(P=O\) the claim is \(\kappa(T_e)=3e^2+b\). For \(P=T_e\), \(P+T_e=O\) and \((3e^2+b)^2\) is a square.
  3. Chord identity. Expand the addition formulas, using the curve equations at the two points and \(e^3+be=0\), in the chord case and in the tangent case.
  4. General case. If \(P\) or \(Q\) is \(O\) there is nothing to prove; if one of them is \(T_e\), use step 2. If \(Q=-P\), both sides are \(1\). If \(P+Q=T_e\), write \(Q=-P+T_e\); step 2 and \(\kappa(-P)=\kappa(P)\) give \(\kappa(P)\kappa(Q)=\kappa(P)^2(3e^2+b)=\kappa(T_e)\). Otherwise the three abscissas differ from \(e\), so \( u=y_1-\ell(x_1-e) e0\) by step 3, and \(x_3-e=(x_1-e)(x_2-e) igl( u/((x_1-e)(x_2-e)) igr)^2\).

Let \(K\) be a field with \(2\ne0\) and \(d\in K^\times\). Then \(\delta_d(P+Q)=\delta_d(P)\,\delta_d(Q)\) for all \(P,Q\in C_d(K)\), so \(\delta_d\) is a group homomorphism \(C_d(K)\to(K^\times/K^{\times2})^2\). Then \(\delta_d(2P)=\delta_d(P)^2=1\), since every square class has order dividing \(2\).

Let \(K\) be a field with \(2 e0\) and \(d\in K^ imes\), and let \(k(P)=(k_1(P),k_2(P))\in K imes K\) be the Kummer map of the coverings of \(C_d\): \((1,1)\) at \(O\); \((-1,-d)\), \((d,2)\), \((-d,-2d)\) at \((0,0)\), \((d,0)\), \((-d,0)\); and \((x,x-d)\) at every other point \((x,y)\). At every other point both maps give \((x,x-d)\). The values \(-1,-d,d,2,-2d\) are nonzero since \(2 e0\) and \(d e0\), and \(x\), \(x-d\) are nonzero off the torsion abscissas.

docs.title: The halving lemma
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.exists_two_nsmul_eq_of_squares ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.halve_identities ZInQ.RouteK.Rank.some_eq_or_eq_neg

Let \(K\) be a field with \(2\ne0\) and \(d\in K^\times\), and let \((x,y)\in C_d(K)\). If \(x=r_1^2\), \(x-d=r_2^2\) and \(x+d=r_3^2\) for some \(r_1,r_2,r_3\in K\), then \((x,y)=2Q\) for some \(Q\in C_d(K)\).

Along the way, over any field and for any \(d\): two affine points of \(C_d(K)\) with the same abscissa are equal or opposite; and for \(r_1,r_2,r_3\in K\) with \(r_1^2+D=r_3^2\), where \(D=r_1^2-r_2^2\), and for \(x'=r_1^2+r_1r_2+r_1r_3+r_2r_3\) and \(y'=(r_1+r_2)(r_1+r_3)(r_2+r_3)\): \(y'^2=x'^3-D^2x'\) and \((3x'^2-D^2)^2=(r_1^2+2x')(2y')^2\).

Proof sketch. Take \(x',y'\) as in the statement. Here \(d=r_1^2-r_2^2\) and \(r_1^2+d=r_3^2\), so the two polynomial identities hold with \(D=d\). The first puts \(Q=(x',y')\) on \(C_d\). Next, \(y'\ne0\): \(r_1+r_2=0\) would give \(d=r_1^2-r_2^2=0\), \(r_1+r_3=0\) would give \(d=r_3^2-r_1^2=0\), and \(r_2+r_3=0\) would give \(2d=r_3^2-r_2^2=0\). So \(Q\) is not \(2\)-torsion, \(2Q\) is affine, and by the second identity its abscissa \(\lambda^2-2x'\), with \(\lambda=(3x'^2-d^2)/(2y')\), equals \(r_1^2=x\). Two points with the same abscissa have the same \(y^2\), so they are equal or opposite. Hence \((x,y)=2Q\) or \((x,y)=2(-Q)\).

Let \(K\) be a field with \(2 e0\) and \(d\in K^ imes\). The points \(P\in C_d(K)\) with \(2P=O\) are exactly \(O\), \((0,0)\), \((d,0)\) and \((-d,0)\), and these are four distinct points; so \(C_d(K)[2]\) has exactly \(4\) elements.

Proof sketch. The numbers \(0\), \(d\), \(-d\) are roots of \(x^3-d^2x\). An affine point satisfies \(2(x,y)=O\) exactly when \(y=0\), which on \(C_d\) means \(x(x-d)(x+d)=0\), and a point whose abscissa is a root is the corresponding torsion point \(T_e\). The three affine points are distinct because \(d e0\) and \(d e-d\) (as \(2d e0\)), and none of them is \(O\).

Every nonzero integer, and every nonzero rational number, has the square class of a squarefree integer (signs allowed); so every class in \(\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times2}\) is the class of a squarefree integer. For a square class \(c\) fix such an integer \(r(c)\), its squarefree representative. Then \(r(c)\) is squarefree and nonzero, its square class is \(c\), and \(c\mapsto r(c)\) is injective. If \(c\) is the class of a rational \(q\ne0\), then \(r(c)\equiv q\), that is \(r(c)=qs^2\) for some nonzero \(s\in\mathbb Q\).

Proof sketch. Write \(|n|=b^2a\) with \(a\) squarefree and \(b>0\); then \(n=\operatorname{sign}(n)\,a\cdot b^2\), and \(\operatorname{sign}(n)\,a\) is squarefree. A nonzero rational \(q\) with numerator \(u\) and denominator \(v\) is \((uv)\cdot(1/v)^2\), so it has the class of the nonzero integer \(uv\). Injectivity holds because \(r(c)\) determines its class \(c\).

Let \(d\) be a positive integer. For \(P\in C_d(\mathbb Q)\), $\(\delta_d(P)=1\iff P=2Q ext{ for some }Q\in C_d(\mathbb Q).\)$ So the kernel of the homomorphism \(\delta_d\) on \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is \(2C_d(\mathbb Q)\). Along the way: \(2 e0\) and \(d e0\) in \(\mathbb Q\), and \(2\) is not a square in \(\mathbb Q\).

Proof sketch. (⇐) is the last part of the homomorphism theorem. (⇒) Take \(P=O\) to \(Q=O\). At \((0,0)\) the first coordinate is the class of \(-d^2<0\), not a square. At \((d,0)\) the second is the class of \(2d^2\), not a square since \(2\) is not a rational square (a squarefree integer that is a rational square is \(1\)). At any other point \((x,y)\), \(x\) and \(x-d\) are squares, \(x=r_1^2\) and \(x-d=r_2^2\). Then \(x+d e0\), since otherwise \(x=-d<0\). Also \(r_1r_2 e0\), as \(x(x-d) e0\). Put \(r_3=y/(r_1r_2)\); then \(r_3^2=y^2/(x(x-d))=x+d\), and the halving lemma gives \(Q\).

Let \(d\) be a positive integer. For \(P\in C_d(\mathbb Q)\) with \(\delta_d(P)=(\alpha,\beta)\), let \(s(P)=(r(\alpha),r(\beta))\in\mathbb Z^2\) be the pair of squarefree representatives. Then the x-form of the covering \(D_{s(P)}\) holds over \(\mathbb Q\), and \(s(P)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\). For \(P,Q\in C_d(\mathbb Q)\) (and any natural number \(d\)), \(s(P)=s(Q)\) if and only if \(\delta_d(P)=\delta_d(Q)\).

Along the way: if \(f:K\to L\) is a homomorphism of fields and the x-form of \(D_{a,b}\) for \(d\) holds over \(K\), then the x-form of \(D_{f(a),f(b)}\) for \(f(d)\) holds over \(L\). In particular, for a natural number \(d\) and integers \(a,b\), the x-form of \(D_{a,b}\) over \(\mathbb Q\) gives the x-form of \(D_{a,b}\) over every field of characteristic zero.

Proof sketch. By the comparison with the Kummer map of the coverings, \(r(\alpha)\equiv k_1(P)\) and \(r(\beta)\equiv k_2(P)\), and \(k_1(P)\), \(k_2(P)\) are nonzero. So by the Kummer-map lemma over \(\mathbb Q\) the x-form of \(D_{s(P)}\) holds over \(\mathbb Q\). A field homomorphism sends squares to squares, so the x-form is carried to \(\mathbb R\) and to every \(\mathbb Q_p\). Both representatives are squarefree, so \(s(P)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\). The last claim holds because \(r\) is injective.

Let \(A\) be a finitely generated abelian group whose \(2\)-torsion \(A[2]\) has exactly \(4\) elements and which has an element of infinite order, and suppose that \(A/2A\) is finite. Then \(A/2A\) has at least \(8\) elements.

Along the way: for a finite abelian group \(T\), \(\#(T/2T)=\#T[2]\); \(2z=0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb Z/2\); and \(\mathbb Z^n\) has no nonzero element \(v\) with \(2v=0\).

Proof sketch. By the structure theorem \(A\cong\mathbb Z^n\times T\) with \(T\) finite, and \(n\ge1\) because \(A\) has an element of infinite order. The map \(\rho:A\to\mathbb Z/2\times T/2T\), \((v,t)\mapsto(v_0\bmod2,\ t\bmod2T)\), is onto and kills \(2A\), so \(\#(A/2A)\ge2\,\#(T/2T)\). For finite \(T\), doubling has kernel and cokernel of the same size, so \(\#(T/2T)=\#T[2]\). Since \(\mathbb Z^n\) is torsion-free, \(A[2]\) injects into \(T[2]\). Hence \(\#(A/2A)\ge2\cdot4=8\).

Let \(d\) be a positive integer. Suppose that \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is finitely generated, that it has a point of infinite order, and that \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has exactly \(8\) elements. Then for every \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) the x-form of the covering \(D_{a,b}\) holds over \(\mathbb Q\).

Along the way: the pair of squarefree representatives \((\alpha,\beta)\mapsto(r(\alpha),r(\beta))\) is injective on \((\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times2})^2\), and \(C_d(\mathbb Q)/2C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has as many elements as the set of pairs \(s(P)\), \(P\in C_d(\mathbb Q)\).

Proof sketch. Since the kernel of \(\delta_d\) is \(2C_d(\mathbb Q)\), \(C_d(\mathbb Q)/2C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is in bijection with the image of \(\delta_d\), and through the injective pair of representatives with the set \(S=\{s(P)\}\). The image theorem gives \(S\subseteq\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\). The Selmer group has \(8\) elements, so \(S\) is finite, and it is nonempty since it contains \(s(O)\); hence \(C_d(\mathbb Q)/2C_d(\mathbb Q)\) is finite. Over \(\mathbb Q\) the \(2\)-torsion of \(C_d\) has exactly \(4\) elements, so the counting theorem gives \(\#S\ge8=\#\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\), and \(S=\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\). Every element of \(S\) is some \(s(P)\), and the x-form of its covering holds over \(\mathbb Q\).

docs.title: The row-5b determinant
docs.text:
The certified rank hypothesis CR₃ rests, through Proposition 0, on the Selmer form CR₃^Sel: for squarefree \(n\equiv5\pmod8\) with \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)|=8\) and a Selmer class with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\), every 2-Selmer class of \(C_n\) comes from a rational point. The route to CR₃^Sel used here goes through Tian, Yuan and Zhang (as completed by Proposition N, which is not refereed), whose criterion for analytic rank one is a genus sum \(T_{5b}(n)\) of 4-ranks of class groups; row 5b of Smith's Table 2 writes that sum as the determinant of an explicit matrix \(M_{5b}\) in Legendre symbols. This chapter proves the elementary step between the Selmer group and that determinant (tyz-5b §4), and the identity of the determinant with the genus sum (tyz-5b §§2–3). By the first, on a Selmer-minimal curve, \(\det M_{5b}\) is the parity of the number of primes \(\equiv3\pmod4\) dividing the first coordinate of a non-torsion Selmer class. So CR₃^Sel follows from CR₃^5b, the same hypothesis with the 2-adic condition replaced by \(\det M_{5b}=1\); CR₃^5b is a hypothesis, not proved here. By the second, \(T_{5b}(n)=\det M_{5b}\) for squarefree \(n\equiv5\pmod8\), with Rédei's \(g\) in Legendre symbols (Smith's row 5b, proved below by forest expansions of both sides), so CR₃^5b follows from CR₃^TYZ, the same hypothesis with the genus sum \(T_{5b}(n)\) in place of the determinant. By Rédei's formula the genus sum is the same with the class numbers of Tian, Yuan and Zhang; that form of the hypothesis is in the Rédei chapter.

Throughout, \(C_n\) is the congruent number curve \(y^2=x^3-n^2x\), and the Selmer system and the configuration of \(n\) are those of the Route K chapter; the Selmer group is that of the Proposition 0 chapter. The Rédei chapter and the positive-rank chapter, outside its Mordell–Weil section, write \(d\) and \(C_d\) for the same number and curve.

11 fully proved

Let \(n>0\) be odd and squarefree with prime set \(P\). For \(p e q\) in \(P\) put \(a_{pq}=(q/p)_+\in\mathbb F_2\), which is \(0\) if \(q\) is a square modulo \(p\) and \(1\) otherwise, and put \(y_p=(-1/p)_+=[p\equiv3\pmod4]\) and \(z_p=(2/p)_+=[p\equiv\pm3\pmod8]\). Smith's matrix \(L\) (Smith's \(A\)) is the \(P imes P\) matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\) with \(L_{pq}=a_{pq}\) for \(p e q\) and \(L_{pp}=\sum_{q e p}a_{pq}\), so its rows sum to zero. With \(D_z\) the diagonal matrix of the \(z_p\), define the \((P\sqcup P)\)-square matrix \(M_1\) and its bordering \(M_{5b}\): $\(M_1= egin{pmatrix}L+L^{\mathsf T}&L^{\mathsf T}\ L&D_z\end{pmatrix},\qquad M_{5b}= egin{pmatrix}L+L^{\mathsf T}&L^{\mathsf T}&0\ L&D_z&y\ 0&y^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix},\)$ that is, \(M_{5b}\) is \(M_1\) bordered by the column \((0,y)\), the row \((0,y)^{\mathsf T}\) and a zero corner. The same matrices are defined for any configuration, with \([q/p]\), \(\lambda\), \(\mu\) in place of \(a_{pq}\), \(y\), \(z\), and for \(n\) they are those of the configuration of \(n\): \(a_{pq}=[q/p]\), \(y=\lambda\), \(z=\mu\).

\(M_1\) is symmetric, and by quadratic reciprocity \(a_{pq}+a_{qp}=y_py_q\) for \(p e q\), so \(L+L^{\mathsf T}\) has entries \(y_py_q\) off the diagonal and \(0\) on it.

These are the matrices of row 5b of Smith's Table 2; row 5b says that for \(n\equiv5\pmod8\) the determinant of \(M_{5b}\) is the genus sum \(T_{5b}(n)\) of Tian, Yuan and Zhang (Theorem 3.6 for Rédei's \(g\) in Legendre symbols, and with their class numbers through the agreement of the two genus sums, by Rédei's formula).

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a configuration on \(S\) of product class \(c(\mathcal C)=5\), and let \(M_1\) be its matrix. For \(e,f\in\mathbb F_2\) let \(\tau_{e,f}\) be the tuple with \(a_0=b_0=e\), \(a_1=0\), \(b_1=f\), \(u=f\mathbf 1\), \(v=e\mathbf 1\) (for a number \(n\), the class of \((-1,-n)^e(n,2)^f\)). Let \(H\) be the set of solutions of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C)\) with \(b_1=0\) and \(a_0=\lambda\cdot u\). Then:

  1. adding \(\tau_{e,f}\) coordinatewise maps solutions to solutions, and every solution is uniquely \(h+\tau_{e,f}\) with \(h\in H\), namely with \((e,f)=(a_0+\lambda\cdot u,\,b_1)\);
  2. the map \(h\mapsto(u+v,\,u)\) is a bijection from \(H\) onto \(\ker M_1\), with inverse \((s,t)\mapsto(u,v)=(t,s+t)\), \(a_0=b_0=\lambda\cdot t\), \(a_1=b_1=0\);
  3. consequently \(\Sigma(\mathcal C)\) has exactly \(4\,|\ker M_1|\) solutions.

Proof sketch. For class \(5\), \(\sum_x\lambda_x=0\), \(\sum_x\mu_x=1\), and the rows (D) read \(a_1=0\), \(b_1=\mu\cdot u\), \(\lambda\cdot v=\lambda\cdot u\). Monsky's matrix \(K\) kills constant vectors, so adding \(\tau_{e,f}\) preserves every row, and it changes \((a_0+\lambda\cdot u,\,b_1)\) by \((e,f)\); this gives 1. By reciprocity \((Ls)_x=(Ks)_x\) and \((L^{\mathsf T}t)_x=(Kt)_x+\lambda_x(\lambda\cdot t+t_x)\), so \(M_1(s,t)=0\) reads \(Kt+\lambda*(s+t)=(\lambda\cdot s+\lambda\cdot t)\lambda\) and \(Ks+\mu*t=0\); summing the rows gives \(\lambda\cdot s=0\) and \(\mu\cdot t=0\). With these, the rows E1, E2, (R) and (D) for the tuple built from \((s,t)\) are the two kernel equations, and conversely; the two maps are inverse on \(H\) because \(a_1=0\) and \(a_0=b_0\) on solutions. Part 3 counts \(4\cdot|H|\).

Let \(n>0\) be squarefree with \(n\equiv5\pmod8\). To a tuple \((a_0,a_1,b_0,b_1,u,v)\) over the primes of \(n\) attach the pair \(a=(-1)^{a_0}2^{a_1}\prod_pp^{u_p}\), \(b=(-1)^{b_0}2^{b_1}\prod_pp^{v_p}\). Then \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\) is exactly the set of pairs of the solutions of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_n)\), and $\(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)|=4\,|\ker M_1|,\qquad\text{that is}\qquad \dim\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)=2+\operatorname{corank}M_1 .\)$ Moreover the tuples whose pair lies in \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\) and which have \(b_1=0\) (\(b\) odd) and \(a_0=y\cdot u\) (\(a\equiv1\pmod4\)) form a subspace \(H\), and \((u,v)\mapsto(u+v,\,u)\) is a bijection from \(H\) onto \(\ker M_1\); here \(u+v\) and \(u\) are the indicator vectors of the primes dividing \(ab\) and \(a\).

Proof sketch. By Proposition 0 a tuple solves \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_n)\) exactly when its pair lies in \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\), every Selmer class is such a pair, and distinct tuples give distinct pairs. The configuration of \(n\) has product class \(5\), and its matrix \(M_1\) is that of \(n\); the statement is the class-5 statement for the configuration of \(n\).

Let \(M\) be a symmetric square matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\) of corank one, whose kernel is \(\{0,k\}\) with \(k\ne0\). Then for every vector \(v\), $\(\det\begin{pmatrix}M&v\\ v^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}=v\cdot k .\)$

Proof sketch. If \(v\cdot k=0\), the vector \((k,0)\) is a nonzero kernel vector of the bordered matrix, whose determinant is therefore \(0\). If \(v\cdot k=1\), let \((w,t)\) be in the kernel: \(Mw+tv=0\) and \(v\cdot w=0\). Pairing the first equation with \(k\) and using \(k^{\mathsf T}M=(Mk)^{\mathsf T}=0\) gives \(t(v\cdot k)=t=0\); then \(Mw=0\), so \(w\in\{0,k\}\), and \(v\cdot w=0\ne v\cdot k\) forces \(w=0\). The kernel is trivial, so the determinant is the nonzero element \(1\) of \(\mathbb F_2\). (The note's proof uses \(\operatorname{adj}M=kk^{\mathsf T}\) instead.)

Let \(n>0\) be squarefree with \(n\equiv5\pmod8\) and \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)|=8\). Let \((a_0,a_1,b_0,b_1,u,v)\) be a tuple over the primes of \(n\) whose pair \((a,b)\) lies in \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\) and which is not one of the four torsion tuples \(\tau_{e,f}\) (the classes of \((-1,-n)^e(n,2)^f\)). Then $\(\det M_{5b}=y\cdot u=\sum_{p\mid a}y_p ,\)$ the parity of the number of primes \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) dividing \(a\).

Proof sketch. By Proposition 0 the tuple solves \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_n)\), which has \(8\) solutions, so by Lemma 4.1 \(|\ker M_1|=2\). Subtracting from the tuple its torsion part \(\tau_{e,f}\) with \((e,f)=(a_0+y\cdot u,\,b_1)\) gives an element \(h\) of \(H\), and \(k=(u_h+v_h,\,u_h)\) is a nonzero element of \(\ker M_1\) (it is nonzero because the tuple is not torsion), so \(\ker M_1=\{0,k\}\). \(M_1\) is symmetric and \(M_{5b}\) is \(M_1\) bordered by \((0,y)\), so Lemma 4.2 gives \(\det M_{5b}=(0,y)\cdot k=y\cdot u_h\). Finally \(u_h=u+f\mathbf 1\) and \(y\cdot\mathbf 1=0\) since \(n\equiv1\pmod4\), so \(y\cdot u_h=y\cdot u\). The proof does this for any configuration of class \(5\) whose system has \(8\) solutions, and specializes to the configuration of \(n\).

Let \(n>0\) be squarefree with \(n\equiv5\pmod8\) and \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)|=8\). If some \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\) has \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\), then \(\det M_{5b}=1\).

Proof sketch. Write \((a,b)\) as the pair of a solution of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_n)\) (Proposition 0). For class \(5\) the solution has \(a_1=0\), so \(|a|=\prod_pp^{u_p}\), and its class modulo \(4\) gives \(y\cdot u=[\,|a|\equiv3\pmod4\,]=1\). The solution is not torsion: the torsion first coordinates have absolute value \(1\) or \(n\), both \(\equiv1\pmod4\). Theorem 4.3 gives \(\det M_{5b}=y\cdot u=1\).

The note states the corollary for a first coordinate with odd part \(\equiv3\pmod4\); the statement here takes the shape \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\) of the hypothesis CR₃^Sel, a special case.

docs.title: The certified rank hypothesis in row-5b form
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.CertifiedRank5b

The hypothesis CR₃^5b is the following assertion. Let \(n>0\) be squarefree with \(n\equiv5\pmod8\). If \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)|=8\) and the determinant of Smith's row-5b matrix \(M_{5b}\), built from the Legendre symbols of the primes of \(n\), is \(1\), then for every \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\) the 2-covering \(D_{a,b}\) of \(C_n\) has a rational point; that is, every 2-Selmer class of \(C_n\) comes from a rational point.

CR₃^5b is not proved here; it is a hypothesis, used only through CR₃^Sel, which it implies. It follows from the hypothesis CR₃^TYZ in the terms of Tian, Yuan and Zhang (CR₃^TYZ implies CR₃^5b). It rests on the following. The first and the last are theorems here, the middle two are not:

  • Row 5b of Smith's table (elementary, reproved in tyz-5b §§2–3 by a forest expansion of determinants and Rédei's formulas for the 4-ranks of class groups; here Theorem 3.6 and Rédei's formula through the agreement of the two genus sums): for squarefree \(n\equiv5\pmod8\), \(\det M_{5b}\) equals the genus sum \(T_{5b}(n)=\sum_{d_0\equiv7,\,d_1\equiv3\,(8)}g(d_0)g(d_1)\mathcal L_1(n/d_0d_1)\) modulo \(2\), where \(g(d)\) is the parity of \(\#2\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d}))\) and \(\mathcal L_1(m)\) is the sum, over the set partitions of the primes of \(m\) into blocks \(B\) with \(d_B\equiv1\pmod8\) (\(d_B\) the product of the primes in \(B\)), of \(\prod_B g(d_B)\).
  • Tian–Yuan–Zhang, Theorem 3.5 and the argument of the proof of their Theorem 3.5(2) (§3.3), as completed in nt-tyz §4 (Proposition N): if \(T_{5b}(n)\) is odd, then their invariant \(\mathcal L(n)\) is nonzero, so \(L(C_n,s)\) vanishes to order exactly one at \(s=1\) (the root number is \(-1\) for \(n\equiv5\pmod8\)). The form used is the one their proof gives; it rests on their Proposition 3.4, whose proof is a sketch, and nt-tyz §4 proves it directly. Their statement groups this sum with another (tyz-5b §1.2).
  • Gross–Zagier, over an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field \(K\) that satisfies the Heegner hypothesis and has \(L(C_n^K,1)\ne0\) (Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein): then \(\operatorname{rank}C_n(\mathbb Q)\ge1\).
  • Then \(\dim C_n(\mathbb Q)/2C_n(\mathbb Q)=2+\operatorname{rank}C_n(\mathbb Q)\ge3=\dim\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\), so the Kummer map is onto \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\) and every Selmer class comes from a rational point (RK9, with Mordell–Weil for \(C_n\)).

Compared with CR₃^Sel, only the 2-adic condition changes: "some Selmer class has \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\)" becomes "\(\det M_{5b}=1\)", which it implies. So CR₃^5b is logically stronger than CR₃^Sel, but it is stated in the terms of Smith's table, one step closer to Tian, Yuan and Zhang's own statement.
