docs.title: The certified rank hypothesis in Tian–Yuan–Zhang form
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.CertifiedRankTYZ

The hypothesis CR₃^TYZ is the following assertion. Let \(n\) be squarefree with \(n\equiv5\pmod8\). If \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)|=8\) and the genus sum \(T_{5b}(n)\) is \(1\), then for every \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\) the 2-covering \(D_{a,b}\) of \(C_n\) has a rational point; that is, every 2-Selmer class of \(C_n\) comes from a rational point.

CR₃^TYZ is not proved here; it is a hypothesis. It rests on the following. The second and the last are theorems here, the other two are not:

  • Tian–Yuan–Zhang, Theorem 3.5 (first assertion) and the argument of the proof of their Theorem 3.5(2) (§3.3), as completed in nt-tyz §4 (Proposition N): for squarefree \(n\equiv5\pmod8\), if \(\sum_{d_0\equiv7,\,d_1\equiv3\,(8)}g(d_0)g(d_1)\mathcal L_1(n/d_0d_1)\) is odd, then \(L(C_n,s)\) vanishes to order exactly one at \(s=1\) (the root number is \(-1\)). Here \(g(d)\) is the parity of \(\#2\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d}))\) and \(\mathcal L_1(m)\) is the sum of \(\prod g\) over the partitions of the primes of \(m\) into blocks \(\equiv1\pmod8\). Their Theorem 1.2 is not cited in its literal form.
  • Rédei's formula: for odd squarefree \(n\) and every nonempty set \(B\) of primes of \(n\) with \(d_B\equiv7,3\) or \(1\pmod8\), \(g_n(B)\) is the parity of \(\#2\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d_B}))\). So \(T_{5b}(n)\) is the genus sum of the previous item. This is a theorem here: Rédei's formula.
  • Gross–Zagier, over an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field \(K\) that satisfies the Heegner hypothesis and has \(L(C_n^K,1)\ne0\) (Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein), for the curve \(C_n\), which is modular because it has complex multiplication by \(\mathbb Z[i]\): analytic rank one gives \(\operatorname{rank}C_n(\mathbb Q)\ge1\).
  • Then, as \(C_n(\mathbb Q)[2]\) has order \(4\), \(\dim C_n(\mathbb Q)/2C_n(\mathbb Q)\ge3=\dim\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\), so the Kummer map is onto \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_n)\) and every Selmer class comes from a rational point. This is a theorem here: Positive rank and a Selmer group of order eight give every Selmer class (RK9), with Mordell–Weil for the congruent number curves.

CR₃^TYZ differs from the row-5b form only in its last condition: \(\det M_{5b}=1\) becomes \(T_{5b}(n)=1\). By Theorem 3.6 the two conditions coincide for these \(n\), so CR₃^TYZ implies CR₃^5b (CR₃^TYZ implies CR₃^5b). The form of the hypothesis with the class numbers \(\#2\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d_B}))\) in place of \(g_n(B)\) is in the Rédei chapter.

docs.title: Forests and minors over \(\mathbb F_2\)
docs.text:
Over \(\mathbb F_2\) a determinant is a permanent, and the minors of the Laplacian of a family of bits count forests. This section proves the counting statements that the identity \(T_{5b}(n)=\det M_{5b}\) of row 5b rests on. No arithmetic enters: \(V\) is any finite set (for an odd number \(n\), the set of its primes), the bits \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb F_2\) are arbitrary, and the Laplacian \(L_U\) of the bits on \(U\subseteq V\) is defined here; for the bits of \(n\), \(L_V\) is Smith's matrix \(L\).

There are three main results. The forest lemma, the case over \(\mathbb F_2\) of the all-minors matrix-tree theorem, writes a minor of \(L_U\) as a sum over forests. The second expands the determinant of the symmetric block matrix \(P(c,d)=\begin{pmatrix}D_d&L^{\mathsf T}\\L&D_c\end{pmatrix}\) as a forest sum. The third relates the forests on \(V\) to the set partitions of \(V\) whose blocks are unions of trees.

15 fully proved

docs.title: Minors over \(\mathbb F_2\)
docs.text: A minor with rows \(R\) and columns \(C\) is a sum over the bijections \(R\to C\), with no signs; for \(R=C\) it is the principal minor. Two identities, for a rank-one change of a matrix and for a bordered matrix, serve for the determinants of Smith's matrices.

Let \(V\) be a finite set and \(M\) a \(V\times V\) matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\). For \(R,C\subseteq V\) put $\(\operatorname{per}M[R,C]=\sum_{\sigma}\prod_{i\in R}M_{i\sigma(i)},\)$ the sum over the bijections \(\sigma:R\to C\). This is the minor of \(M\) with rows \(R\) and columns \(C\) used below; it needs no signs and no ordering of \(R\) and \(C\). Then:

  1. (principal minors) for \(S\subseteq V\), \(\det M[S,S]=\operatorname{per}M[S,S]\); in particular \(\det M=\operatorname{per}M[V,V]\);
  2. if \(|R|\ne|C|\), then \(\operatorname{per}M[R,C]=0\);
  3. \(\operatorname{per}M[R,C]\) depends only on the rows of \(M\) indexed by \(R\);
  4. (transpose) \(\operatorname{per}M^{\mathsf T}[A,C]=\operatorname{per}M[C,A]\) for \(A,C\subseteq V\).

Proof sketch. (1) In the Leibniz expansion of \(\det M[S,S]\) every sign \(\pm1\) is \(1\) in \(\mathbb F_2\), and the permutations of \(S\) are exactly the bijections \(S\to S\); the case \(S=V\) is \(\det M\). (2) There are no bijections. (3) The products only involve rows in \(R\). (4) Inverting a bijection \(A\to C\) gives a bijection \(C\to A\), and this matches the two sums term by term: with \(c=\sigma(a)\), \(\prod_{a\in A}M^{\mathsf T}_{a\sigma(a)}=\prod_{c\in C}M_{c\sigma^{-1}(c)}\).

Let \(V\) be a finite set, \(M\) a \(V\times V\) matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\), \(R,C\subseteq V\), and let \(\operatorname{per}M[R,C]\) be the minor of \(M\) with rows \(R\) and columns \(C\), the sum over the bijections \(R\to C\). Then:

  1. (row expansion) for \(i\in R\), \(\operatorname{per}M[R,C]=\sum_{v\in C}M_{iv}\operatorname{per}M[R\setminus\{i\},C\setminus\{v\}]\);
  2. (linearity in a row) for \(i\in R\) and finitely many row vectors \(r_u\), the minor of the matrix \(M\) with row \(i\) replaced by \(\sum_u r_u\) is the sum over \(u\) of the minors of \(M\) with row \(i\) replaced by \(r_u\); in particular this holds for a sum \(r+s\) of two rows;
  3. (equal rows) if \(i\ne k\) lie in \(R\) and rows \(i\) and \(k\) of \(M\) are equal, then \(\operatorname{per}M[R,C]=0\).

Proof sketch. (1) Group the bijections by \(v=\sigma(i)\): removing \(i\) leaves a bijection \(R\setminus\{i\}\to C\setminus\{v\}\), and each such bijection extends uniquely by \(i\mapsto v\); a bijection is onto \(C\), so every \(v\in C\) occurs. (2) By (1), whose terms are linear in row \(i\), while the smaller minors in (1) do not involve row \(i\), since a minor depends only on the rows it uses. (3) Composing with the transposition of \(i\) and \(k\) is an involution of the bijections \(R\to C\); it has no fixed point, since \(\sigma(i)\ne\sigma(k)\), and it keeps each product, since rows \(i\) and \(k\) agree. So the terms cancel in pairs.

Let \(K\) be a field, \(I\) a finite index set, \(A\) an \(I\times I\) matrix over \(K\) and \(u,w\in K^I\). Write \(A^{(j\leftarrow u)}\) for \(A\) with column \(j\) replaced by \(u\). Then $\(\det(A+uw^{\mathsf T})=\det A+\sum_{j\in I}w_j\det A^{(j\leftarrow u)}.\)$ If moreover \(Ax=u\) for some \(x\in K^I\), then $\(\det(A+uw^{\mathsf T})=\det A\,(1+w\cdot x).\)$ No invertibility is assumed. The determinant is additive in a column over finite sums: if column \(j\) of \(A\) is replaced by \(\sum_{u\in T}f_u\), the determinant is \(\sum_{u\in T}\det A^{(j\leftarrow f_u)}\).

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), where \(-t=t\), \(s-t=s+t\) and \(t^2=t\):

  • for an \(I\times I\) matrix \(A\) and \(v\in\mathbb F_2^I\), the bordered matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}A&v\\v^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}\), indexed by \(I\) and one more index, has determinant \(\det(A+vv^{\mathsf T})+\det A\);
  • for a symmetric \(I\times I\) matrix \(B\) and \(v\in\mathbb F_2^I\), \(\sum_{i,j}v_iv_jB_{ij}=\sum_iv_iB_{ii}\).

Proof sketch. Transpose: row \(i\) of \(A^{\mathsf T}+wu^{\mathsf T}\) is row \(i\) of \(A^{\mathsf T}\) plus \(w_iu^{\mathsf T}\). By multilinearity in the rows, the determinant is the sum, over the sets \(s\) of rows, of the determinant of the matrix whose rows in \(s\) are those of \(A^{\mathsf T}\) and whose other rows are \(w_iu^{\mathsf T}\). If two rows lie outside \(s\) the term vanishes: the two rows are multiples of \(u^{\mathsf T}\), so one of them is zero or a multiple of the other. What remains is \(s=I\), giving \(\det A\), and \(s=I\setminus\{j\}\), giving \(w_j\det A^{(j\leftarrow u)}\). If \(Ax=u\), then \(u=\sum_kx_k(\text{column }k)\); by linearity in column \(j\), and since the terms with \(k\ne j\) have two equal columns, \(\det A^{(j\leftarrow u)}=x_j\det A\), which gives the second formula. For the bordered matrix, the matrix with corner \(1\) in place of \(0\) has determinant \(\det(A-vv^{\mathsf T})= \det(A+vv^{\mathsf T})\), by the Schur complement of the corner. Its last row is the last row of the bordered matrix plus \((0,\dots,0,1)\), so by linearity in the last row it is also the bordered determinant plus the determinant of a block triangular matrix with diagonal blocks \(A\) and \(1\), that is, plus \(\det A\). For the quadratic form, the terms \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) with \(i\ne j\) are equal by symmetry and cancel, and \(v_i^2=v_i\).

docs.title: Forests and the forest lemma
docs.text: Expanding the diagonal entries of the Laplacian turns a minor into a sum over maps. A map with a cycle has an even number of compatible bijections and drops out, and each forest contributes once exactly when the deleted columns meet every tree once.

docs.title: The Laplacian of a family of bits
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.lapl

Let \(V\) be a finite set and \(a=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in V}\) a family of bits \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb F_2\). For \(U\subseteq V\) the Laplacian of \(a\) on \(U\) is the \(V imes V\) matrix \(L_U\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) with $\((L_U)_{ij}=a_{ij}\quad(i e j),\qquad (L_U)_{ii}=\sum_{k\in U,\,k e i}a_{ik}.\)$ Only the diagonal depends on \(U\): the diagonal entry in row \(i\) is the sum of the bits of that row over the columns in \(U\) other than \(i\), also when \(i otin U\). The bits \(a_{ii}\) are never used. We write \(L=L_V\).

For the bits \(a_{pq}\) of an odd squarefree number, \(L_V\) is Smith's matrix \(L\): the two definitions agree entry by entry.

docs.text:

Let \(V\) be a finite set with \(N\) elements and \(f:V\to V\) a map.

  • The root of \(i\in V\) is \(r_f(i)=f^N(i)\), and \(f\) is acyclic if every root is a fixed point of \(f\).
  • For \(U,R\subseteq V\), \(f\) moves \(R\) in \(U\) if it is the identity outside \(R\) and, for \(i\in R\), \(f(i)\in U\) and \(f(i)\ne i\).
  • For \(U,F\subseteq V\), a forest on \(U\) rooted at \(F\) is an acyclic map that moves \(U\setminus F\) in \(U\). Its tree at \(\rho\in F\) is \(T_\rho=\{v\in U:r_f(v)=\rho\}\), and a set \(W\) is a transversal of it if, for every \(\rho\in F\), exactly one element of \(W\) has root \(\rho\).
  • Given bits \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb F_2\) (\(i,j\in V\)), the weight of \(f\) on \(R\subseteq V\) is \(\mathrm{wt}_R(f)=\prod_{i\in R}a_{if(i)}\); for a forest on \(U\) rooted at \(F\) we write \(\mathrm{wt}(f)=\mathrm{wt}_{U\setminus F}(f)\).
  • The roots of \(g\) in \(U\) are its fixed points in \(U\), and a forest on \(U\) is a forest on \(U\) rooted at some \(F\subseteq U\).

These notions satisfy the following.

  1. In an acyclic map every periodic point is fixed, and a map that is not acyclic has a periodic point that is not fixed. So \(f\) is acyclic exactly when it has no cycle of length at least \(2\).
  2. A fixed point is its own root. If \(f\) is acyclic, \(f(x)\) and every \(f^k(x)\) have the same root as \(x\).
  3. Let \(f\) move \(U\setminus F\) in \(U\). Then a point \(x\) with \(f(x)\ne x\) lies in \(U\setminus F\), a point outside \(U\setminus F\) is its own root, and the iterates and the root of a point of \(U\) stay in \(U\). If moreover \(f\) is acyclic, the root of every point of \(U\) lies in \(F\).
  4. A map is a forest on \(U\) if and only if it is the identity outside \(U\), maps \(U\) into \(U\) and is acyclic. A forest on \(U\) rooted at \(F\subseteq U\) has exactly \(F\) as its roots in \(U\); so every forest on \(U\) is rooted at exactly one \(F\subseteq U\), namely its set of roots in \(U\).
  5. Hence, for every \(\mathbb F_2\)-valued function \(H\) of a set and a map, $\(\sum_{F\subseteq U}\ \sum_{f}H(F,f)=\sum_{g}H\bigl(R_U(g),g\bigr),\)$ where \(f\) runs over the forests on \(U\) rooted at \(F\), \(g\) over the forests on \(U\), and \(R_U(g)\) is the set of roots of \(g\) in \(U\).

docs.title: Expanding the diagonal of a Laplacian
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.pmin_lapl_eq_sum_maps ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.compat ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.mem_compat

Let \(a\) be bits on a finite set \(V\), let \(U\subseteq V\) with Laplacian \(L_U\), and let \(R,C\subseteq V\) with \(C\subseteq U\). For a map \(f:V\to V\) let \(\mathrm{compat}_{R,C}(f)\) be the set of bijections \(\sigma:R\to C\) with \(\sigma(i)\in\{i,f(i)\}\) for every \(i\in R\). Then $\(\operatorname{per}L_U[R,C]=\sum_f\mathrm{wt}_R(f)\cdot\#\mathrm{compat}_{R,C}(f),\)$ the sum over the maps \(f\) that move \(R\) in \(U\), with the counts read in \(\mathbb F_2\).

Proof sketch. Fix a bijection \(\sigma:R\to C\) and expand \(\prod_{i\in R}(L_U)_{i\sigma(i)}\). If \(\sigma(i)\ne i\), the factor is the single bit \(a_{i\sigma(i)}\), and \(\sigma(i)\in C\subseteq U\); it is the choice \(f(i)=\sigma(i)\). If \(\sigma(i)=i\), the factor is \(\sum_{j\in U,\,j\ne i}a_{ij}\), and each term is a choice \(f(i)=j\). Extending by the identity outside \(R\), the product becomes \(\sum\mathrm{wt}_R(f)\) over the maps \(f\) that move \(R\) in \(U\) and satisfy \(\sigma(i)\in\{i,f(i)\}\) for all \(i\in R\). Summing over \(\sigma\) and exchanging the two sums gives the claim.

docs.title: Maps with a cycle contribute an even number
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.card_compat_even

Let \(U,F\) be subsets of a finite set \(V\), and let \(f\) be a map that moves \(U\setminus F\) in \(U\) and is not acyclic. Then for every \(C\subseteq V\) the number of bijections \(\sigma:U\setminus F\to C\) with \(\sigma(i)\in\{i,f(i)\}\) for all \(i\in U\setminus F\) is even.

Proof sketch. Since \(f\) is not acyclic, some point \(x\) is periodic and not fixed; let \(Z\) be its forward orbit. No point of \(Z\) is fixed, so \(Z\subseteq U\setminus F\); \(f\) maps \(Z\) onto itself and is injective on \(Z\). Let \(\sigma\) be compatible. If \(\sigma(j)=f(j)\) for some \(j\in Z\), then \(\sigma(f(j))\ne f(j)\) by injectivity of \(\sigma\), since \(f(j)\ne j\); so \(\sigma(f(j))=f(f(j))\), and going around the orbit, \(\sigma=f\) on all of \(Z\). Hence either \(\sigma(x)=x\) and \(\sigma\) is the identity on \(Z\), or \(\sigma(x)=f(x)\) and \(\sigma=f\) on \(Z\). Switching \(\sigma\) on \(Z\) between the identity and \(f\), and keeping it elsewhere, gives again a compatible bijection onto \(C\), because both maps send \(Z\) onto \(Z\). This switch is an involution of the compatible bijections without fixed points, since it changes \(\sigma(x)\). So their number is even.

docs.title: The map \(\sigma_W\) and the transversal criterion
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.sigmaW_mem_iff ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.sigmaW ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.merge

Let \(U,F,W\) be subsets of a finite set \(V\) and let \(f\) be a forest on \(U\) rooted at \(F\). Call a point reached from \(W\) if it is \(f^k(w)\) for some \(w\in W\) and \(k\ge0\), and let \(\sigma_W\) be the map equal to \(f\) at the points of \(U\setminus F\) reached from \(W\) and equal to the identity elsewhere. Call a bijection \(\sigma:U\setminus F\to U\setminus W\) compatible with \(f\) if \(\sigma(i)\in\{i,f(i)\}\) for all \(i\in U\setminus F\).

If \(F,W\subseteq U\) and \(|F|=|W|\), then \(\sigma_W\) is a compatible bijection if and only if \(W\) is a transversal of \(f\).

Along the way: consider the conditions (A) no point of \(U\setminus F\) reached from \(W\) is sent by \(f\) into \(W\), and (B) two points of \(U\setminus F\) reached from \(W\) with the same image under \(f\) are equal. If (A) and (B) hold, then no two different points of \(W\) have the same root.

Proof sketch. Since \(|U\setminus F|=|U\setminus W|\), \(\sigma_W\) is a compatible bijection if and only if (A) and (B) hold. Suppose (A) and (B), and let \(w\ne w'\) in \(W\) have the same root. Take \(f^a(w)=f^b(w')\) with \(a+b\) minimal and look at the points just before the meeting point: either one of them violates (A) or (B), or one of them lies outside \(U\setminus F\), is fixed by \(f\), and contradicts the minimality. So the root map is injective on \(W\). It sends \(W\) into \(F\), and \(|W|=|F|\), so every tree contains exactly one point of \(W\). Conversely, let \(W\) be a transversal. If \(f^k(w)\in U\setminus F\) and \(f^{k+1}(w)\in W\), then \(f^{k+1}(w)\) and \(w\) have the same root, so \(f^{k+1}(w)=w\); then \(w\) is periodic, hence fixed, and so is \(f^k(w)\), a contradiction; this gives (A). If \(f^a(w)\) and \(f^b(w')\) in \(U\setminus F\) have the same image, then \(w\) and \(w'\) have the same root, so \(w=w'\); if \(a<b\), then \(f^{a+1}(w)\) is periodic, hence fixed, and so is \(f^b(w)\), a contradiction; so \(a=b\), which gives (B).

docs.title: A forest has at most one compatible bijection
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.card_compat_acyc ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.eq_sigmaW

Let \(U,F,W\) be subsets of a finite set \(V\), let \(f\) be a forest on \(U\) rooted at \(F\), and let \(\sigma_W\) and the bijections compatible with \(f\) be as in the transversal criterion.

  1. Every compatible bijection equals \(\sigma_W\).
  2. If \(F,W\subseteq U\) and \(|F|=|W|\), the number of compatible bijections is \(1\) if \(W\) is a transversal of \(f\) and \(0\) otherwise.

Proof sketch. (1) Let \(\sigma\) be compatible. By induction on \(k\), if \(f^k(w)\in U\setminus F\) with \(w\in W\), then \(\sigma(f^k(w))=f(f^k(w))\). For \(k=0\), \(\sigma(w)\) lies in \(U\setminus W\), so \(\sigma(w)\ne w\). For the step, \(f^k(w)\) is in \(U\setminus F\) too (otherwise \(f\) fixes it), and \(f^{k+1}(w)=\sigma(f^k(w))\) is already the image of another point, so \(\sigma\) cannot fix it. In the other direction, let \(i\in U\setminus F\) have \(\sigma(i)=f(i)\) without being reached from \(W\). Then \(i\notin W\), so \(i=\sigma(j)\) for some \(j\); \(\sigma(j)=j\) is impossible, since then \(j=i\) and \(\sigma(i)=i\), so \(\sigma(j)=f(j)=i\), and \(j\) is not reached from \(W\) either. Repeating this \(N=|V|\) times gives a point whose \(N\)-th iterate is \(i\); then \(i\) is a root, hence fixed by \(f\), which contradicts \(i\in U\setminus F\). So \(\sigma=f\) exactly at the points of \(U\setminus F\) reached from \(W\), that is, \(\sigma=\sigma_W\).

(2) By (1) there is at most one compatible bijection, \(\sigma_W\), and by the transversal criterion \(\sigma_W\) is one exactly when \(W\) is a transversal.

docs.title: The forest lemma (Lemma 2.1)
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.pmin_lapl_eq_forests

Let \(a\) be bits on a finite set \(V\), let \(U\subseteq V\) with Laplacian \(L_U\), and let \(F,W\subseteq U\) with \(|F|=|W|\). Then $\(\operatorname{per}L_U[U\setminus F,\,U\setminus W]=\sum_f\mathrm{wt}(f),\)$ the sum over the forests \(f\) on \(U\) rooted at \(F\) of which \(W\) is a transversal, that is, in which every tree contains exactly one element of \(W\). This is the case over \(\mathbb F_2\) of the all-minors matrix-tree theorem.

Proof sketch. Since \(U\setminus W\subseteq U\), the diagonal expansion writes the minor as \(\sum_f\mathrm{wt}(f)\cdot\#\mathrm{compat}(f)\) over the maps \(f\) that move \(U\setminus F\) in \(U\), where \(\mathrm{compat}(f)\) is the set of bijections \(\sigma:U\setminus F\to U\setminus W\) with \(\sigma(i)\in\{i,f(i)\}\). The maps that are not acyclic have an even number of compatible bijections and drop out. The acyclic ones are the forests on \(U\) rooted at \(F\), and for a forest the number of compatible bijections is \(1\) if \(W\) is a transversal and \(0\) otherwise.

docs.title: A determinant as a forest sum
docs.text: Expanding the two diagonal blocks of \(P(c,d)\) leaves, for each choice of deleted rows and columns, the product of a minor of \(L\) with its transpose, which over \(\mathbb F_2\) is the minor itself; the forest lemma turns it into forests weighted by their roots and trees.

docs.title: Minors of anti-diagonal block matrices and of diagonal shifts
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.pmin_fromBlocks_anti ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.glue ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.pmin_add_diagonal

Minors over \(\mathbb F_2\) are the permanent minors \(\operatorname{per}M[R,C]\), sums over the bijections \(R o C\).

  1. (Anti-diagonal blocks.) Let \(M,N\) be \(V imes V\) matrices over \(\mathbb F_2\) and \(A,C\subseteq V\). On the rows and columns \(A\sqcup C\) of \(V\sqcup V\), $\(\operatorname{per} egin{pmatrix}0&M\N&0\end{pmatrix}[A\sqcup C,A\sqcup C] =\operatorname{per}M[A,C]\cdot\operatorname{per}N[C,A].\)$
  2. (Diagonal shift.) Let \(Q\) be a square matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\) indexed by a finite set \(X\), and \(e\in\mathbb F_2^X\) with diagonal matrix \(D_e\). Then $\(\operatorname{per}(Q+D_e)[X,X]=\sum_{S\subseteq X}e^S\operatorname{per}Q[X\setminus S,X\setminus S], \qquad e^S=\prod_{x\in S}e_x.\)$

Proof sketch. (1) A pair of bijections \( u:A o C\) and \( au:C o A\) glues to the bijection of \(A\sqcup C\) that sends \(a\) in the first copy to \( u(a)\) in the second and \(c\) in the second copy to \( au(c)\) in the first, and its product is the product of the two. Every bijection of \(A\sqcup C\) with a nonzero product sends each copy into the other, since the diagonal blocks vanish, and so arises from exactly one such pair. (2) Write each entry as \((D_e)_{x\sigma(x)}+Q_{x\sigma(x)}\) and expand \(\prod_x(Q+D_e)_{x\sigma(x)}\) over the sets \(S\) of points where the diagonal term is taken. The term vanishes unless \(\sigma\) fixes \(S\) pointwise, and then it is \(e^S\prod_{x otin S}Q_{x\sigma(x)}\). Exchange the sums: the bijections of \(X\) that fix \(S\) pointwise are the bijections of \(X\setminus S\).

docs.title: The determinant of \(P(c,d)\) as a forest sum
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.det_Pmat ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.Pmat ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.card_eq_of_isTransv ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.sum_transv ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.sum_powerset_sum

Let \(a\) be bits on a finite set \(V\), \(L=L_V\) their Laplacian, and \(c,d\in\mathbb F_2^V\), with diagonal matrices \(D_c\), \(D_d\). Let \(P(c,d)\) be the symmetric \((V\sqcup V)\)-square matrix $\(P(c,d)=\begin{pmatrix}D_d&L^{\mathsf T}\\L&D_c\end{pmatrix}.\)$ Then $\(\det P(c,d)=\sum_{F\subseteq V}c^F\sum_f\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{\rho\in F}d(T_\rho),\)$ the inner sum over the forests \(f\) on \(V\) rooted at \(F\), where \(c^F=\prod_{\rho\in F}c_\rho\), \(T_\rho\) is the tree of \(f\) at \(\rho\), and \(d(T)=\sum_{v\in T}d_v\).

Proof sketch. By the permanent form of principal minors, \(\det P(c,d)\) is the permanent of \(P(c,d)\) on all of \(V\sqcup V\). Write \(P(c,d)=Q+D\) with \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&L^{\mathsf T}\\L&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(D\) diagonal with diagonal \(e=(d,c)\). The expansion of a diagonal shift gives \(\operatorname{per}(Q+D)=\sum_Se^S\operatorname{per}Q[S^c,S^c]\), over the subsets \(S\) of \(V\sqcup V\). Write \(S=W\sqcup F\), so that \(e^S=d^Wc^F\) and \(S^c=(V\setminus W)\sqcup(V\setminus F)\). By the anti-diagonal block rule, $\(\operatorname{per}Q[S^c,S^c]=\operatorname{per}L^{\mathsf T}[V\setminus W,V\setminus F]\cdot \operatorname{per}L[V\setminus F,V\setminus W]=\operatorname{per}L[V\setminus F,V\setminus W]^2 =\operatorname{per}L[V\setminus F,V\setminus W],\)$ using the transpose rule and \(t^2=t\) in \(\mathbb F_2\). If \(|F|\ne|W|\), this minor is \(0\), and \(W\) is a transversal of no forest rooted at \(F\), since a transversal has one point in each of the \(|F|\) trees. If \(|F|=|W|\), the forest lemma for \(U=V\) makes it the sum of \(\mathrm{wt}(f)\) over the forests \(f\) rooted at \(F\) of which \(W\) is a transversal. Exchanging the sums, a forest rooted at \(F\) carries \(c^F\mathrm{wt}(f)\sum_Wd^W\) over its transversals \(W\). A transversal is a choice of one point in each tree, so \(\sum_Wd^W=\prod_{\rho\in F}d(T_\rho)\).

docs.title: Forests and set partitions
docs.text: A family of forests on the blocks of a set partition is a forest on the whole set that preserves the blocks. The compatible partitions with prescribed numbers of roots per block are counted by pairings of the roots.

docs.title: Gluing forests along a set partition
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.prod_sum_allF ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.restrict ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.iterate_agree ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.root_agree ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.restrict_mem_allF ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.ofPartFun ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.part_ofPartFun ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.parts_eq_image_part ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.finpartition_ext_part ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.mem_part_univ ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.part_mem_univ ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.part_eq_part_of_mem

Let \(\pi\) be a set partition of a finite set \(V\), and write \(\pi(i)\) for the block containing \(i\). For a map \(f:V\to V\) and \(B\subseteq V\) let \(f|_B\) be the map equal to \(f\) on \(B\) and to the identity off \(B\). For each block \(B\) and each map \(g\) let \(h_B(g)\in\mathbb F_2\). Then $\(\prod_{B\in\pi}\ \sum_{g}h_B(g)=\sum_f\ \prod_{B\in\pi}h_B(f|_B),\)$ where in the factor of \(B\), \(g\) runs over the forests on \(B\), and \(f\) runs over the forests on \(V\) with \(f(i)\in\pi(i)\) for every \(i\), that is, those that map every block into itself.

Along the way:

  1. if a map \(g\) sends \(B\) into \(B\) and \(f\) agrees with \(g\) on \(B\), then on \(B\) the iterates of \(f\) agree with those of \(g\) and stay in \(B\); in particular \(f\) and \(g\) have the same roots at the points of \(B\), and these roots lie in \(B\);
  2. if \(f\) is a forest on \(V\) that maps \(B\) into itself, then \(f|_B\) is a forest on \(B\);
  3. every point lies in its block, every \(\pi(i)\) is a block, the blocks are exactly the sets \(\pi(i)\), and \(j\in\pi(i)\) implies \(\pi(j)=\pi(i)\); a set partition is determined by its blocks \(\pi(i)\), \(i\in V\);
  4. a function \(b\) from \(V\) to the subsets of \(V\) with \(i\in b(i)\) for all \(i\), and \(b(j)=b(i)\) whenever \(j\in b(i)\), is the block function of a set partition, the one whose blocks are the sets \(b(i)\).

Proof sketch. Expanding the product of sums gives a sum over the families \((g_B)_{B\in\pi}\) of forests on the blocks. Glue such a family into the map \(f\) with \(f(j)=g_{\pi(j)}(j)\). It maps each block into itself, and it is acyclic: on a block \(B\) it agrees with \(g_B\), which maps \(B\) into itself, so by (1) the root of a point of \(B\) is its root under \(g_B\), a point of \(B\) fixed by \(g_B\) and hence by \(f\). Conversely, a forest \(f\) on \(V\) that maps each block into itself has the restrictions \(f|_B\), which are forests on the blocks by (2). Gluing the restrictions returns \(f\), and restricting a glued family returns the family, since each \(g_B\) is the identity off \(B\). This bijection matches the terms.

docs.title: Pairings are odd in number exactly on sets of even size
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.card_fpfi ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.fpfi ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.mem_fpfi ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.fpfi_invol ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.card_fpfi_pair

A pairing of a finite set \(X\) is a fixed-point-free involution of \(X\): a map \(s:X\to X\) with \(s(x)\ne x\) and \(s(s(x))=x\) for all \(x\in X\), that is, a partition of \(X\) into pairs. The number of pairings of \(X\) is odd if \(|X|\) is even and even if \(|X|\) is odd. For distinct \(x,y\in X\), the pairings \(s\) of \(X\) with \(s(x)=y\) correspond bijectively to the pairings of \(X\setminus\{x,y\}\).

Proof sketch. The bijection removes the pair \(\{x,y\}\) from a pairing with \(s(x)=y\), and puts it back in a pairing of \(X\setminus\{x,y\}\). The parity statement is by strong induction on \(|X|\). The empty set has one pairing and a point has none. For \(|X|\ge2\) choose distinct \(x,y\in X\) and conjugate pairings by the transposition \(\tau\) of \(x\) and \(y\), \(s\mapsto\tau s\tau\). This is an involution of the pairings of \(X\), and its fixed points are exactly the pairings with \(s(x)=y\). The other pairings cancel in pairs, so the number of pairings of \(X\) has the parity of the number of pairings of \(X\setminus\{x,y\}\), a set of size \(|X|-2\), and induction applies.

docs.title: Set partitions compatible with a forest

Let \(f\) be a forest on a finite set \(V\), with root map \(r\) and set of roots \(R\) (its fixed points); every root \(r(i)\) lies in \(R\), and each element of \(R\) is its own root. A set partition \(\pi\) of \(V\) is compatible with \(f\) if \(f(i)\) lies in the block \(\pi(i)\) of \(i\) for every \(i\). In a compatible partition, \(\pi(f^k(i))=\pi(i)\) for all \(k\), so \(\pi(r(i))=\pi(i)\): a point lies in a block if and only if its root does.

Let \( ho_7 e ho_3\) be roots of \(f\). Then the set partitions \(\pi\) compatible with \(f\) such that \( ho_7\) is the only root in its block, \( ho_3\) is the only root in its block, and the block of every other root contains exactly two roots, are as many as the pairings of \(R\setminus\{ ho_7, ho_3\}\).

Proof sketch. Extend a pairing \(s\) of \(R\setminus\{ ho_7, ho_3\}\) by the identity and put \(b_s(i)=\{j\in V:r(j)=r(i) ext{ or }r(j)=s(r(i))\}\). Then \(i\in b_s(i)\), and \(j\in b_s(i)\) implies \(b_s(j)=b_s(i)\) because \(s\) is an involution, so \(b_s\) is the block function of a set partition \(\pi_s\). It is compatible with \(f\), since \(r(f(i))=r(i)\). The roots in the block of \( ho_7\) are just \( ho_7\), since \(s\) fixes \( ho_7\), and likewise for \( ho_3\); the roots in the block of any other root \( ho\) are \( ho\) and \(s( ho) e ho\). The map \(s\mapsto\pi_s\) is injective, since \(s( ho)\) is the root other than \( ho\) in the block of \( ho\). It is onto: given such a partition \(\pi\), let \(s( ho)\) be the other root in the block of \( ho\), for \( ho\in R\setminus\{ ho_7, ho_3\}\). Then \(s( ho) otin\{ ho_7, ho_3\}\), as otherwise \( ho\) would be a second root in their block, and \(s(s( ho))= ho\), so \(s\) is a pairing. Finally \(\pi=\pi_s\), because the block of \(i\) in either partition consists of the points whose root lies in the block of \(r(i)\), and the roots in that block are \(r(i)\) and \(s(r(i))\); a set partition is determined by its blocks.

docs.title: Row 5b of Smith's table
docs.text:
Row 5b of Smith's Table 2 says that for squarefree \(n\equiv5\pmod8\) the determinant of \(M_{5b}\) is the genus sum \(T_{5b}(n)\) of Tian, Yuan and Zhang (Theorem 3.6). Here Rédei's \(g\) is defined from the bits through the cofactors \(\kappa_\rho(B)\) of the Laplacian of a block, so both sides depend only on the bits \(a_{pq}\), \(y_p\), \(z_p\) of the primes of \(n\). That this \(g\) is the parity of a class number is Rédei's formula; it is not needed in this section.

Most statements are about bits \(a_{ij}\), \(y_i\), \(z_i\) on an abstract finite set \(V\); for the primes of \(n\), \(V\) is the set of primes, and the odd number is still written \(n\), as in the rest of the chapter. The proof writes both sides of Theorem 3.6 as the same sum over the forests on \(V\). The determinant goes through a rank-one update and the matrix \(P(c,d)\) of the forests section. The genus sum goes block by block, through Lemma 2.2 and the cofactor forms (2.1) and (2.2) of \(g\), glued along the partition. Only reciprocity \(a_{pq}+a_{qp}=y_py_q\) and \(y(V)=0\) are used, and \(y(V)=0\) holds since \(n\) is squarefree and \(n\equiv1\pmod4\). The partition forms of Propositions 3.3–3.5 are proved as well, but the proof of Theorem 3.6 does not pass through them.

16 fully proved

ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.redeiG ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.kappa ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.Recip ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.gBit

Let \(V\) be a finite set with bits \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb F_2\) (\(i,j\in V\)) and \(y_i,z_i\in\mathbb F_2\) (\(i\in V\)). For \(S\subseteq V\) write \(y(S)=\sum_{i\in S}y_i\) and \(z(S)=\sum_{i\in S}z_i\). The bits satisfy reciprocity if \(a_{ij}+a_{ji}=y_iy_j\) for all \(i\ne j\) in \(V\).

For \(B\subseteq V\) let \(L_B\) be the Laplacian of the bits \(a\) on \(B\), and for \(\rho\in V\) put $\(\kappa_\rho(B)=\det L_B[B\setminus\{\rho\},\,B\setminus\{\rho\}],\)$ the principal minor of \(L_B\) on the rows and columns of \(B\setminus\{\rho\}\); for \(B=\{\rho\}\) it is the empty determinant \(1\). Rédei's \(g\) of \(B\) is $\(g(B)=\begin{cases}\sum_{\rho\in B}y_\rho\,\kappa_\rho(B)&\text{if }y(B)=1,\\ \sum_{\rho\in B}z_\rho\,\kappa_\rho(B)&\text{if }y(B)=0.\end{cases}\)$

For a natural number \(n\) with set of primes \(P\) and \(B\subseteq P\), \(g_n(B)\) is \(g(B)\) for the bits of the primes of \(n\) of Smith's matrices: \(a_{pq}=(q/p)_+\), \(y_p=(-1/p)_+\) and \(z_p=(2/p)_+\).

The definition does not assume reciprocity. Under reciprocity and \(y(B)=1\) the cofactors \(\kappa_\rho(B)\), \(\rho\in B\), are all equal (Lemma 2.2), and since \(\sum_{\rho\in B}y_\rho=1\) the first case is their common value \(\kappa(B)\); this is Rédei's form \(g(B)=\kappa(B)\). For odd squarefree \(n\) and a nonempty \(B\) with \(d_B=\prod_{p\in B}p\equiv7,3\) or \(1\pmod8\), Rédei's formula identifies \(g_n(B)\) with the parity of the order of the subgroup of squares \(2\mathrm{Cl}\) of the class group of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d_B})\).

docs.text:

Let \(a\) be bits on a finite set \(V\), let \(B\subseteq V\), and let \(c_v=\sum_{u\in B}(L_B)_{uv}\) be the column sums of \(L_B\) over the rows of \(B\). For a forest \(\varphi\) and a root \(i\) of \(\varphi\), \(T_i(\varphi)\) is the tree of \(i\).

Cofactors as forest counts. For \( ho\in V\), \(\kappa_ ho(B)=\operatorname{per}L_B[B\setminus\{ ho\},B\setminus\{ ho\}]\). For \( ho\in B\), \(\kappa_ ho(B)=\sum_f\mathrm{wt}(f)\), the sum over the forests \(f\) on \(B\) rooted at \(\{ ho\}\), that is, the spanning arborescences of \(B\) with root \( ho\).

Under reciprocity, the column sums are \(c_v=y_v\,(1+y(B))\) for every \(v\in B\). Moreover:

  1. Under reciprocity, if \(y(B)=1\), then \(\kappa_i(B)=\kappa_j(B)\) for all \(i,j\in B\).
  2. For \(i,j\in B\), \(\operatorname{per}L_B[B\setminus\{i\},B\setminus\{j\}]=\kappa_i(B)\).
  3. (The \(\kappa\)-difference.) For \(i e j\) in \(B\), $\(\kappa_i(B)+\kappa_j(B)=\sum_\varphi\mathrm{wt}(\varphi)\sum_{v\in T_i(\varphi)}c_v,\)$ the sum over the forests \(\varphi\) on \(B\) rooted at \(\{i,j\}\).

Along the way: for \(i e j\) in \(B\), \(v\in B\) with \(v e j\) and a forest \(\varphi\) on \(B\) rooted at \(\{i,j\}\), the set \(\{j,v\}\) is a transversal of \(\varphi\) if and only if \(v\) lies in the tree of \(i\).

Proof sketch. Forest counts. The principal minor is a permanent over \(\mathbb F_2\). For \( ho\in B\), apply the forest lemma with \(U=B\) and \(F=W=\{ ho\}\): a forest rooted at \(\{ ho\}\) has the single tree \(B\), so \(\{ ho\}\) is always a transversal. Column sums. The diagonal entry of column \(v\) is \(\sum_{u\in B,u e v}a_{vu}\), so \(c_v=\sum_{u\in B,u e v}(a_{vu}+a_{uv})=\sum_{u\in B,u e v}y_vy_u=y_v(y(B)+y_v)=y_v(1+y(B))\), using \(y_v^2=y_v\). (2) The forest lemma with \(F=\{i\}\) and \(W=\{j\}\); again \(j\) lies in the single tree. (3) Put \(R=B\setminus\{j\}\), so that \(\kappa_j(B)=\operatorname{per}L_B[R,R]\). Replace row \(i\) by the sum of all rows of \(R\). By linearity in that row the minor changes by the minors with row \(i\) replaced by another row of \(R\), and these vanish because they have two equal rows. The sum of the rows of \(R\) is \(c+(L_B)_{j,\cdot}\), so by linearity \(\kappa_j(B)\) is the minor with row \(i\) replaced by \((L_B)_{j,\cdot}\) plus the minor with row \(i\) replaced by \(c\). Expanding the first along that row and comparing with the expansion of (2) along row \(j\) gives \(\kappa_i(B)\). Expanding the second along the row \(c\) gives \(\sum_{v\in R}c_v\operatorname{per}L_B[B\setminus\{i,j\},B\setminus\{j,v\}]\). By the forest lemma with \(F=\{i,j\}\) and \(W=\{j,v\}\), and the transversal criterion above, each of these minors is the sum of \(\mathrm{wt}(\varphi)\) over the forests \(\varphi\) rooted at \(\{i,j\}\) with \(v\) in the tree of \(i\). Exchanging the sums, and noting that \(j\) is never in the tree of \(i\), gives the right side of (3). (1) If \(y(B)=1\), every \(c_v\) with \(v\in B\) vanishes by the column sums, and (3) gives \(\kappa_i(B)=\kappa_j(B)\).

Let \(a,y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\) and \(B\subseteq V\).

  • If \(y(B)=1\), then \(\sum_{\rho\in B}y_\rho\,\kappa_\rho(B)=g(B)\).
  • If the bits satisfy reciprocity and \(y(B)=1\), then \(g(B)=\kappa_\rho(B)\) for every \(\rho\in B\), and (2.1) \(\sum_{\rho\in B}z_\rho\,\kappa_\rho(B)=z(B)\,g(B)\).
  • (2.2) If \(y(B)=0\), then \(\sum_{\rho\in B}z_\rho\,\kappa_\rho(B)=g(B)\).

Proof sketch. The first and the last statements are the definition of \(g\). Assume reciprocity and \(y(B)=1\). By Lemma 2.2 all \(\kappa_r(B)\), \(r\in B\), equal \(\kappa_\rho(B)\) for a fixed \(\rho\in B\), so \(g(B)=\sum_ry_r\kappa_r(B)=y(B)\,\kappa_\rho(B)=\kappa_\rho(B)\). Then \(\sum_rz_r\kappa_r(B)=z(B)\,\kappa_\rho(B)=z(B)\,g(B)\); here \(B\) is not empty because \(y(B)=1\).

docs.text:

Let \(a,y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\). A set \(B\subseteq V\) has class \(1\), \(5\), \(7\) or \(3\) according as \((y(B),z(B))\) is \((0,0)\), \((0,1)\), \((1,0)\) or \((1,1)\). The genus sum of row 5b of the bits is $\(T_{5b}=\sum_\pi\prod_{B\in\pi}g(B),\)$ the sum over the set partitions \(\pi\) of \(V\) (into nonempty blocks) with exactly one block of class \(7\), exactly one block of class \(3\) and no block of class \(5\), so that all other blocks have class \(1\).

For a natural number \(n\) with set of primes \(P\) and \(B\subseteq P\) put \(d_B=\prod_{p\in B}p\). The genus sum of \(n\) is $\(T_{5b}(n)=\sum_\pi\prod_{B\in\pi}g_n(B),\)$ the sum over the set partitions \(\pi\) of \(P\) with exactly one block with \(d_B\equiv7\pmod8\), exactly one block with \(d_B\equiv3\pmod8\), and every block with \(d_B\equiv7\), \(3\) or \(1\pmod8\). In Smith's notation, \(T_{5b}(n)=\sum_{d_0\equiv7,\,d_1\equiv3\,(8)}g_n(d_0)g_n(d_1)\mathcal L_1(n/d_0d_1)\), where \(g_n(d_0)\) is \(g_n(B)\) for the block \(B\) with \(d_B=d_0\) and \(\mathcal L_1(m)\) is the sum of \(\prod g_n\) over the partitions of the primes of \(m\) into blocks \(\equiv1\pmod8\).

docs.text: A rank-one update reduces \(\det M_1\) to \(\det P(z,y)\), and \(\det M_{5b}\) to the determinants of \(P(z[k\mapsto1],y)\) and \(P(z[k\mapsto0],y)\), \(k\in V\). Let \(a,y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\) and \(L=L_V\) their Laplacian on \(V\); its rows sum to zero. Define the \((V\sqcup V)\)-square matrix \(M_1\) and its bordering \(M_{5b}\) from the bits as in Smith's matrices: $\(M_1=\begin{pmatrix}L+L^{\mathsf T}&L^{\mathsf T}\\ L&D_z\end{pmatrix},\qquad M_{5b}=\begin{pmatrix}M_1&(0,y)\\ (0,y)^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}.\)$ For the bits of a natural number \(n\) these are Smith's \(M_1\) and \(M_{5b}\). Let \(P(c,d)=\begin{pmatrix}D_d&L^{\mathsf T}\\ L&D_c\end{pmatrix}\) for \(c,d\in\mathbb F_2^V\), the matrix whose determinant is a sum over forests, write \(z[k\mapsto t]\) for \(z\) with the entry at \(k\) replaced by \(t\), \(z^S\) for \(\prod_{\rho\in S}z_\rho\), and \(\mathbf 1\) for the all-ones vector on \(V\).

  1. For all \(c,d\in\mathbb F_2^V\), \(P(c,d)\,(\mathbf 1,0)=(d,0)\), and the diagonal entry of the adjugate of \(P(c,d)\) at the lower copy \(k'\) of \(k\in V\) is \(\operatorname{adj}P(c,d)_{k'k'}=\det P(c[k\mapsto1],d)+\det P(c[k\mapsto0],d)\).
  2. Under reciprocity, \(M_1=P(z,y)+ww^{\mathsf T}\) with \(w=(y,0)\), and $\(\det M_1=(1+y(V))\det P(z,y).\)$
  3. Under reciprocity, $\(\det M_{5b}=(1+y(V))\sum_{k\in V}y_k\bigl(\det P(z[k\mapsto1],y)+\det P(z[k\mapsto0],y)\bigr)\)$ and $\(\det M_{5b}=(1+y(V))\sum_{F\subseteq V}\Bigl(\sum_{k\in F}y_kz^{F\setminus k}\Bigr) \sum_f\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{\rho\in F}y(T_\rho),\)$ the inner sum over the forests \(f\) on \(V\) rooted at \(F\), with \(T_\rho\) the tree of \(\rho\).

Proof sketch. (1) The rows of \(L\) sum to zero, so \(P(c,d)(\mathbf 1,0)=(d,0)\). Row \(k'\) of \(P(c[k\mapsto1],d)\) is row \(k'\) of \(P(c[k\mapsto0],d)\) plus the unit vector at \(k'\); by linearity in that row, the difference of the two determinants is the determinant with row \(k'\) replaced by the unit vector, which is \(\operatorname{adj}P_{k'k'}\) and does not depend on \(c_k\). (2) By reciprocity \(L+L^{\mathsf T}\) has entries \(y_iy_j\) off the diagonal and \(0\) on it, while \((ww^{\mathsf T})_{ii}=y_i^2=y_i\) cancels the diagonal of \(D_y\); so \(M_1=P(z,y)+ww^{\mathsf T}\). With \(x=(\mathbf 1,0)\) we have \(P(z,y)x=w\), and the rank-one update with a preimage gives \(\det M_1=\det P(z,y)\,(1+w\cdot x)=(1+y(V))\det P(z,y)\). (3) Put \(P=P(z,y)\) and \(v=(0,y)\). The bordered determinant is \(\det M_{5b}=\det(M_1+vv^{\mathsf T})+\det M_1\). Since \(v\cdot x=0\), also \((P+vv^{\mathsf T})x=w\), so \(\det(M_1+vv^{\mathsf T})=(1+y(V))\det(P+vv^{\mathsf T})\). Expanding \(\det(P+vv^{\mathsf T})\) by the rank-one formula, the term \(\det P\) cancels against \(\det M_1\), and \(\det M_{5b}=(1+y(V))\sum_jv_j\det P^{(j\leftarrow v)}\), with \(P^{(j\leftarrow v)}\) the matrix \(P\) with column \(j\) replaced by \(v\). Expanding that column gives \(\sum_{i,j}v_iv_j\operatorname{adj}(P)_{ij}\). The adjugate of the symmetric matrix \(P\) is symmetric, so over \(\mathbb F_2\) this is \(\sum_iv_i\operatorname{adj}(P)_{ii}=\sum_ky_k\operatorname{adj}(P)_{k'k'}\), and (1) gives the first formula. For the second, insert the forest expansion of \(\det P(z[k\mapsto t],y)\) and use \(\prod_{\rho\in F}z[k\mapsto1]_\rho+\prod_{\rho\in F}z[k\mapsto0]_\rho=[k\in F]\,z^{F\setminus k}\).

Let \(a,y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\) that satisfy reciprocity, and let \(B\subseteq V\). Let \(w_7(B)\), \(w_3(B)\) and \(w_1(B)\) be \(g(B)\) if \(B\) has class \(7\), \(3\), respectively \(1\), and \(0\) otherwise. For a forest \(f\) on \(B\) with root set \(S\subseteq B\) put $\(Y(f)=\prod_{\rho\in S}y(T_\rho),\)$ the product of the sums of \(y\) over its trees \(T_\rho=\{v\in B:\text{the root of }v\text{ is }\rho\}\), and let \(\mathrm{wt}(f)=\mathrm{wt}_{B\setminus S}(f)\). Then $\(w_7(B)=\sum_{f\text{ with one root }\rho}(y_\rho+z_\rho)\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\,Y(f),\qquad w_3(B)=\sum_{f\text{ with one root }\rho}z_\rho\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\,Y(f),\)$ $\(w_1(B)=\sum_{f\text{ with two roots }i,j}z_iz_j\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\,Y(f),\)$ the sums over the forests \(f\) on \(B\) with exactly one, respectively exactly two, roots in \(B\).

Along the way: grouping the forests on \(B\) by their root sets, a sum over the forests with \(k\) roots of \(e(S)\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\,Y(f)\) is \(\sum_{S\subseteq B,|S|=k}e(S)\sum_{f\text{ rooted at }S}\mathrm{wt}(f)\,Y(f)\); a forest with the single root \(\rho\) has \(Y(f)=y(B)\); and for any \(e_\rho\in\mathbb F_2\), \(\sum_{\rho\in B}e_\rho\,y(B)\,\kappa_\rho(B)=\sum_{f\text{ with one root }\rho}e_\rho\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\,Y(f)\).

Proof sketch. Classes 7 and 3. By the forest count of the cofactors in Lemma 2.2, \(\kappa_\rho(B)\) is the sum of \(\mathrm{wt}(f)\) over the forests on \(B\) with the single root \(\rho\), and for these \(Y(f)=y(B)\). So the right sides are \(\sum_\rho(y_\rho+z_\rho)\,y(B)\,\kappa_\rho(B)\) and \(\sum_\rho z_\rho\,y(B)\,\kappa_\rho(B)\). If \(y(B)=0\), both sides vanish. If \(y(B)=1\), (2.1) turns them into \((1+z(B))\,g(B)\) and \(z(B)\,g(B)\), which are \(w_7(B)\) and \(w_3(B)\).

Class 1. By (2.2) and a check of the two values of \(y(B)\), \(w_1(B)=(1+y(B))(1+z(B))\sum_\rho z_\rho\kappa_\rho(B)\). Since \(z_\rho(1+z_\rho)=0\), \((1+z(B))\sum_\rho z_\rho\kappa_\rho(B)\) is the sum over the ordered pairs \(\rho\ne j\) in \(B\) of \(z_\rho z_j\kappa_\rho(B)\), that is, the sum over the two-element sets \(\{i,j\}\subseteq B\) of \(z_iz_j(\kappa_i(B)+\kappa_j(B))\). By Lemma 2.2(3) this is \(z_iz_j\sum_\varphi\mathrm{wt}(\varphi)\sum_{v\in T_i}c_v\) over the forests \(\varphi\) rooted at \(\{i,j\}\), and by the column sums of Lemma 2.2, \(\sum_{v\in T_i}c_v=y(T_i)(1+y(B))\). As \(B\) is the union of the two trees, \(y(B)=y(T_i)+y(T_j)\), hence \((1+y(B))\,y(T_i)(1+y(B))=y(T_i)(1+y(T_i)+y(T_j))=y(T_i)\,y(T_j)=Y(\varphi)\). Grouping the forests with two roots by their root sets gives the formula for \(w_1(B)\).

Let \(a,y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\), and let \(w_7,w_3,w_1\) be the block weights: \(w_c(B)\) is \(g(B)\) if \(B\) has class \(c\) and \(0\) otherwise.

  1. (The genus sum.) For blocks \(B_7\ne B_3\) let \(m_{B_7,B_3}\) be \(w_7\) on \(B_7\), \(w_3\) on \(B_3\) and \(w_1\) on every other set. Then $\(T_{5b}=\sum_\pi\ \sum_{B_7\in\pi}\ \sum_{B_3\in\pi,\,B_3\ne B_7}\ \prod_{B\in\pi}m_{B_7,B_3}(B),\)$ the outer sum over all set partitions \(\pi\) of \(V\). If a product \(\prod_{B\in\pi}m_{B_7,B_3}(B)\) is nonzero, then \(B_7\) has class \(7\), \(B_3\) has class \(3\) and every other block of \(\pi\) has class \(1\).
  2. (One block of class \(7\), the others of class \(3\).) For a block \(B_7\) let \(m'_{B_7}\) be \(w_7\) on \(B_7\) and \(w_3\) on every other set. For every set partition \(\pi\) of \(V\), the sum \(\sum_{B_7\in\pi}\prod_{B\in\pi}m'_{B_7}(B)\) is \(\prod_{B\in\pi}g(B)\) if \(\pi\) has exactly one block of class \(7\) and all other blocks of class \(3\), and \(0\) otherwise.

Proof sketch. A factor \(w_c(B)\) vanishes unless \(B\) has class \(c\). So a nonzero marked product forces the classes of the marked blocks and of the others. (1) In a partition counted by \(T_{5b}\) the blocks of classes \(7\) and \(3\) are unique, so its marked sum has exactly one nonzero term, \(\prod_Bg(B)\); for any other partition every marked product vanishes. (2) If \(\pi\) has exactly one block of class \(7\) and the others of class \(3\), the only marked choice with nonzero product is that block, and the product is \(\prod_Bg(B)\). Otherwise a nonzero marked product would make \(B_7\) a block of class \(7\) and all other blocks of class \(3\), which is excluded.

Let \(y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\), \(f\) a forest on \(V\) with root set \(R\), and write \(z^S=\prod_{ ho\in S}z_ ho\). For blocks \(B_7,B_3\) and a block \(B\), the root factor \(e_B(S)\) of a set \(S\) is \(y_ ho+z_ ho\) if \(B=B_7\) and \(S=\{ ho\}\); \(z_ ho\) if \(B=B_3 e B_7\) and \(S=\{ ho\}\); \(z^S\) if \(B otin\{B_7,B_3\}\) and \(|S|=2\); and \(0\) in all other cases.

For a set partition \(\pi\) of \(V\) compatible with \(f\), $\(\sum_{B_7\in\pi}\ \sum_{B_3\in\pi,\,B_3 e B_7}\ \prod_{B\in\pi}e_B(B\cap R) =\sum_{ ho_7\in R}\ \sum_{ ho_3\in R,\, ho_3 e ho_7}[\pi\in A( ho_7, ho_3)]\, (y_{ ho_7}+z_{ ho_7})\,z^{R\setminus ho_7},\)$ where \(A( ho_7, ho_3)\) is the set of compatible partitions in which \( ho_7\) and \( ho_3\) are each the only root of their block and the block of every other root contains exactly two roots.

Along the way: for any set partition \(\pi\) of \(V\), any \(S\subseteq V\) and any \(\varphi:V o\mathbb F_2\), \(\prod_{B\in\pi}\prod_{i\in B\cap S}\varphi(i)=\prod_{i\in S}\varphi(i)\).

Proof sketch. The last identity holds because the sets \(B\cap S\), \(B\in\pi\), are disjoint with union \(S\). For the main identity, every block of a compatible partition contains a root, and the block of a root determines it. A marked product \(\prod_Be_B(B\cap R)\) is nonzero only if \(B_7\) and \(B_3\) each contain exactly one root, \( ho_7\) and \( ho_3\), and every other block exactly two; then \(\pi\in A( ho_7, ho_3)\), \(B_7\) and \(B_3\) are the blocks of \( ho_7\) and \( ho_3\), and the product is \((y_{ ho_7}+z_{ ho_7})\,z_{ ho_3}\prod z^{B\cap R}\) over the other blocks, which is \((y_{ ho_7}+z_{ ho_7})\,z^{R\setminus ho_7}\) by the last identity. So the pairs of distinct blocks with nonzero product correspond to the pairs of distinct roots \(( ho_7, ho_3)\) with \(\pi\in A( ho_7, ho_3)\), with the same terms.

Let \(a,y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\) that satisfy reciprocity, with \(y(V)=0\). Then $\(T_{5b}=\sum_f\Bigl(\sum_{k\in R}y_kz^{R\setminus k}\Bigr)\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{ ho\in R}y(T_ ho),\)$ the sum over the forests \(f\) on \(V\), with \(R\) the root set of \(f\), \(z^S=\prod_{ ho\in S}z_ ho\) and \(T_ ho\) the tree of \( ho\).

Along the way, for a forest \(f\) on \(V\) with root set \(R\): if \(y(V)=0\) and every tree has \(y(T_ ho)=1\), then \(|R|\) is even; and if \(|R|\) is even, then summing over the set partitions \(\pi\) compatible with \(f\) and over the marked blocks \(B_7 e B_3\) of \(\pi\) the product of the root factors \(\prod_{B\in\pi}e_B(B\cap R)\) gives \(\sum_{k\in R}y_kz^{R\setminus k}\), for any bits \(y,z\). For any \(B\subseteq V\), the roots of the restriction \(f|_B\) (the points of \(B\) fixed by \(f\)) are the roots of \(f\) in \(B\).

Proof sketch. Start from the marked form of \(T_{5b}\), with \(w_7\) on \(B_7\), \(w_3\) on \(B_3\) and \(w_1\) on the other blocks. Write each block weight as a forest sum on its block, with one root for \(w_7,w_3\) and two roots for \(w_1\), and glue along \(\pi\): each marked product becomes a sum over the forests \(f\) on \(V\) compatible with \(\pi\). For such \(f\) the roots of \(f|_B\) are the roots of \(f\) in \(B\), its trees are those of \(f\), and the products over the blocks of the factors indexed by \(B\cap R\) multiply to products over \(R\); so the glued term is \( igl(\prod_Be_B(B\cap R) igr)\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{ ho\in R}y(T_ ho)\). Exchange the sums and fix \(f\) with \(\prod_ ho y(T_ ho) e0\). Then every tree has \(y(T_ ho)=1\), and since \(V\) is the union of the trees, \(|R|\equiv y(V)=0\pmod2\). For a compatible partition the marked sum of the root factors is a sum over pairs of roots \( ho_7 e ho_3\): the term is \((y_{ ho_7}+z_{ ho_7})z^{R\setminus ho_7}\) if \( ho_7\) and \( ho_3\) are the only roots of their blocks and every other block holds exactly two roots, and \(0\) otherwise. For fixed \(( ho_7, ho_3)\) these partitions are as many as the pairings of \(R\setminus\{ ho_7, ho_3\}\), an odd number since \(|R|-2\) is even. Summing over the \(|R|-1\) choices of \( ho_3\), again an odd number, leaves \(\sum_{ ho_7\in R}(y_{ ho_7}+z_{ ho_7})z^{R\setminus ho_7}\), which is \(\sum_ky_kz^{R\setminus k}+|R|\,z^R=\sum_ky_kz^{R\setminus k}\).

Let \(n\) be odd with set of primes \(P\) and bits \(a_{pq}\), \(y_p\), \(z_p\), and let \(B\subseteq P\). Then \(d_B=\prod_{p\in B}p\) is odd, \(y_p=\lambda(p)\) and \(z_p=\mu(p)\) for every \(p\in P\), and $\(y(B)=\lambda(d_B),\qquad z(B)=\mu(d_B),\)$ where \(\lambda(c)=[c\equiv3\pmod4]\) and \(\mu(c)=[c\equiv3,5\pmod8]\). Consequently \(d_B\equiv7\pmod8\) if and only if \(B\) has class \(7\), \(d_B\equiv3\pmod8\) if and only if \(B\) has class \(3\), and \(d_B\equiv7,3\) or \(1\pmod8\) if and only if \(B\) does not have class \(5\). So a set partition of \(P\) is counted by \(T_{5b}(n)\) if and only if it is counted by the genus sum \(T_{5b}\) of the bits of \(n\), and $\(T_{5b}(n)=T_{5b}\quad\text{for the bits }a_{pq},\,y_p,\,z_p\text{ of }n.\)$

Proof sketch. For a prime \(p\mid n\), \(y_p=(-1/p)_+=\lambda(p)\) and \(z_p=(2/p)_+=\mu(p)\). The maps \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are additive on the odd classes modulo \(8\), and \(d_B\) is a product of odd primes, so \(y(B)=\lambda(d_B)\) and \(z(B)=\mu(d_B)\). An odd class modulo \(8\) is determined by its values of \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), which gives the three equivalences, checked on the four odd classes. So the conditions defining \(T_{5b}(n)\) and \(T_{5b}\) select the same set partitions, and the products \(\prod_Bg_n(B)\) are the same by definition.

Let \(n\) be squarefree with \(n\equiv5\pmod8\). Then $\(\det M_{5b}=T_{5b}(n).\)$ More generally, for bits \(a,y,z\) on a finite set \(V\) that satisfy reciprocity and \(y(V)=0\), the determinant of the matrix \(M_{5b}\) built from the bits is the genus sum \(T_{5b}\) of the bits.

Along the way: the bits of an odd number satisfy reciprocity, and for squarefree \(n\equiv5\pmod8\) with set of primes \(P\), \(y(P)=0\).

Proof sketch. Let the bits satisfy reciprocity and \(y(V)=0\). In the forest form of \(\det M_{5b}\) the factor \(1+y(V)\) is \(1\), and grouping the forests by their root sets turns it into \(\sum_f\bigl(\sum_{k\in R}y_kz^{R\setminus k}\bigr)\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{\rho\in R}y(T_\rho)\) over all forests \(f\) on \(V\), with \(R\) the root set of \(f\). This is the forest form of the genus sum, so \(\det M_{5b}=T_{5b}\).

For \(n\), the bits of the primes of \(n\) satisfy reciprocity, \(a_{pq}+a_{qp}=y_py_q\), by quadratic reciprocity. Since \(n\) is squarefree, it is the product of its primes, so \(y(P)=\lambda(n)=\lambda(5)=0\). The matrix \(M_{5b}\) of the bits is Smith's \(M_{5b}\), and the genus sum of the bits is \(T_{5b}(n)\).

Let \(f\) be a forest on a finite set \(V\) with root set \(R\), and let \(E\subseteq R\). The set partitions compatible with \(f\) in which every root in \(E\) is the only root of its block and every block containing a root outside \(E\) contains exactly two roots are as many as the fixed-point-free involutions of \(R\setminus E\). For \(E=R\) there is exactly one.

For \(k=1\) or \(2\), a set partition compatible with \(f\) has exactly \(k\) roots in every block if and only if it is one of the partitions of the count with \(E=R\), respectively \(E=\emptyset\). So the number of compatible partitions with exactly \(k\) roots in every block is the number for \(E=R\), respectively \(E=\emptyset\).

Proof sketch. A fixed-point-free involution \(s\) of \(R\setminus E\), extended by the identity on \(E\), gives the partition whose block at a root \(\rho\) is the set of points whose root is \(\rho\) or \(s(\rho)\); this is a bijection onto the partitions described. For \(E=R\) the only involution of the empty set gives the partition into the trees of \(f\). Since every block of a compatible partition contains a root, "every block has exactly \(k\) roots" is the condition of the count with \(E=R\) for \(k=1\) and with \(E=\emptyset\) for \(k=2\).

Let \(a,y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\) that satisfy reciprocity. Then $\(\det P(z,y)=\sum_{\pi}\prod_{B\in\pi}g(B)=\sum_f z^R\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{\rho\in R}y(T_\rho),\)$ the first sum over the set partitions \(\pi\) of \(V\) into blocks of class \(3\), the second over the forests \(f\) on \(V\), with \(R\) the root set of \(f\). If \(y(V)=0\), then \(\det M_1\) is the same sum over the partitions into blocks of class \(3\); if \(y(V)=1\), then \(\det M_1=0\).

The forest sum behind it: for every \(k\), $\(\sum_\pi\prod_{B\in\pi}\ \sum_{h\text{ with }k\text{ roots}}z^{S(h)}\,\mathrm{wt}(h)\,Y(h) =\sum_fN_k(f)\,z^R\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{\rho\in R}y(T_\rho),\)$ where \(h\) runs over the forests on the block \(B\) with exactly \(k\) roots, \(S(h)\) is the root set of \(h\), \(Y(h)\) is the product of the sums of \(y\) over its trees, and \(N_k(f)\) is the number of set partitions compatible with \(f\) in which every block contains exactly \(k\) roots.

Proof sketch. For the forest sum, glue along \(\pi\): the product over the blocks of the forest sums is a sum over the forests \(f\) on \(V\) compatible with \(\pi\), and for such \(f\) the product of the block terms of the restrictions \(f|_B\) is \(z^R\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{\rho\in R}y(T_\rho)\) if every block holds exactly \(k\) roots and \(0\) otherwise. Exchanging the sums gives the coefficient \(N_k(f)\).

Now take \(k=1\). For a set partition \(\pi\), \(\prod_{B\in\pi}w_3(B)\) is \(\prod_Bg(B)\) if all blocks have class \(3\) and \(0\) otherwise, and each \(w_3(B)\) is the sum over the forests on \(B\) with one root \(\rho\) of \(z_\rho\,\mathrm{wt}(h)\,Y(h)\). So the class-3 partition sum is \(\sum_fN_1(f)\,z^R\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_\rho y(T_\rho)\), and \(N_1(f)=1\), since exactly one partition compatible with \(f\) has one root in every block, the partition into the trees of \(f\). Grouping the forests by their root sets, the forest expansion of \(\det P(z,y)\) is the same sum. Finally \(\det M_1=(1+y(V))\det P(z,y)\).

Let \(a,y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\) that satisfy reciprocity and \(y(V)=0\). Then $\(\det M_{5b}=\sum_\pi\prod_{B\in\pi}g(B),\)$ the sum over the set partitions \(\pi\) of \(V\) with exactly one block of class \(7\) and all other blocks of class \(3\).

Along the way, with \(m'_{B_7}\) equal to \(w_7\) on \(B_7\) and \(w_3\) on every other block: under reciprocity each marked product \(\prod_{B\in\pi}m'_{B_7}(B)\) is a sum over the forests on \(V\) compatible with \(\pi\), as in the proof below. For a forest \(f\) on \(V\) with root set \(R\) and a set partition \(\pi\) compatible with \(f\), the marked sum of the root factors (for each block, \(y_\rho+z_\rho\) on \(B_7\) and \(z_\rho\) on the others when the block contains the single root \(\rho\), and \(0\) when it contains another number of roots) is \(\sum_{\rho_7\in R}(y_{\rho_7}+z_{\rho_7})z^{R\setminus\rho_7}\) if every block of \(\pi\) contains exactly one root, and \(0\) otherwise.

Proof sketch. The partition sum is the marked sum \(\sum_\pi\sum_{B_7\in\pi}\prod_{B\in\pi}m'_{B_7}(B)\) over all set partitions. Write \(w_7\) and \(w_3\) as forest sums with one root per block and glue along \(\pi\); each marked product becomes a sum over the forests \(f\) compatible with \(\pi\) of the product of the root factors times \(\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{\rho\in R}y(T_\rho)\). Exchanging the sums, the coefficient of \(f\) is the sum, over the compatible partitions with exactly one root per block, of \(\sum_{\rho_7\in R}(y_{\rho_7}+z_{\rho_7})z^{R\setminus\rho_7}\). Exactly one compatible partition has one root in every block, the partition into the trees of \(f\). If \(\prod_\rho y(T_\rho)\ne0\), then \(|R|\) is even because \(y(V)=0\), so \(\sum_\rho z_\rho z^{R\setminus\rho}=|R|\,z^R\) vanishes and the coefficient is \(\sum_{k\in R}y_kz^{R\setminus k}\). This is the coefficient of \(f\) in the forest form of \(\det M_{5b}\), where \(1+y(V)=1\), after grouping the forests by their root sets.

docs.title: From class-1 blocks to class-3 blocks (Proposition 3.5)
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.sum_class1_eq_sum_class3 ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.Sec3.sum_class1_eq_forest

Let \(a,y,z\) be bits on a finite set \(V\) that satisfy reciprocity and \(y(V)=0\). Then $\(\sum_{\pi\text{ into blocks of class }1}\ \prod_{B\in\pi}g(B)\;=\;\sum_{\pi\text{ into blocks of class }3}\ \prod_{B\in\pi}g(B),\)$ both sums over set partitions of \(V\).

Along the way, under reciprocity alone, $\(\sum_{\pi\text{ into blocks of class }1}\ \prod_{B\in\pi}g(B)=\sum_f\,p(R)\,z^R\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_{\rho\in R}y(T_\rho),\)$ the sum over the forests \(f\) on \(V\) with root set \(R\), where \(p(R)\) is the number of fixed-point-free involutions of \(R\).

Proof sketch. Write \(w_1(B)\) as the sum over the forests on \(B\) with two roots \(i,j\) of \(z_iz_j\,\mathrm{wt}(h)\,Y(h)\), and glue along the partition. As in Proposition 3.3, the class-1 partition sum becomes \(\sum_fN_2(f)\,z^R\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_\rho y(T_\rho)\), with \(N_2(f)\) the number of compatible partitions in which every block holds exactly two roots; by the count with \(E=\emptyset\), \(N_2(f)=p(R)\). By Proposition 3.3 the class-3 partition sum is \(\sum_fz^R\,\mathrm{wt}(f)\prod_\rho y(T_\rho)\). Compare the coefficients forest by forest. If \(\prod_\rho y(T_\rho)\ne0\), every tree has \(y(T_\rho)=1\), so \(|R|\equiv y(V)=0\pmod2\), and the number of pairings of a set of even size is odd; so \(p(R)\) is odd and the coefficients agree in \(\mathbb F_2\).

docs.title: Rédei's formula for the 4-rank of class groups
Rédei's formula for the 4-rank of class groups
docs.text:
For a set \(B\) of primes of an odd number \(d\), the genus sum \(T_{5b}(d)\) of the row-5b chapter uses Rédei's \(g_d(B)\), a determinant in the residue bits of the primes. Tian, Yuan and Zhang state their criterion for analytic rank one with the genus class numbers \(g(d_B)=|\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d_B}))^2|\) instead, where \(d_B=\prod_{p\in B}p\). This chapter proves Rédei's formula, \(g(d_B)\equiv g_d(B)\pmod2\) for every block of a genus sum. So the certified rank hypothesis stated with Tian, Yuan and Zhang's own class numbers is equivalent to the one stated with Rédei's \(g\).

The proof is genus theory in the ring of integers of \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\), \(n\) odd and squarefree, with Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions in place of the Hasse–Minkowski theorem:

  • the classes of the ramified primes fill \(\mathrm{Cl}[2]\);
  • the genus characters \(\chi_q([\mathfrak a])=[N\mathfrak a/q]\), one for each prime \(q\mid n\), together take at least \(2^{t-1}\) values;
  • counting then gives the principal genus theorem \(\mathrm{Cl}^2=\bigcap_q\ker\chi_q\), and Rédei's theorem: \(g(n)\) is odd if and only if the kernel of the Rédei matrix is spanned by the exponent vector of \((\sqrt{-n})\);
  • linear algebra over \(\mathbb F_2\) turns that kernel condition into \(g_d(B)=1\).

Throughout, \(n\ge1\) is an integer and \(K=\mathbb Q(\omega)\) with \(\omega^2=-n\). We write \(\mathcal O\) for its ring of integers, \(\sigma\) for its nontrivial automorphism and \(\mathrm{Cl}\) for the class group of \(\mathcal O\). \(N\) is the absolute norm of elements and ideals, and \([a/p]\in\mathbb F_2\) is the residue bit. The set \(T_n\) of ramified primes, \(t=|T_n|\), and the prime ideals \(\mathfrak p_p\) are defined in the ramified primes.

On notation: the letter \(n\) is reserved for the field \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\), while \(d\) is the odd number whose primes carry the bits \(a_{pq}\), \(y_p\), \(z_p\), and \(g_d(B)\) is Rédei's \(g\) of a set \(B\) of its primes. The row-5b chapter writes \(n\) and \(C_n\) for that number; here, as in the Selmer chapter, the congruent number curve is \(C_d\).

8 fully proved

docs.title: The genus class number and Rédei's formula
The genus class number
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.gCl ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.QNeg ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.QNeg.factNotIsSquare ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.QNeg.numberField

For a natural number \(n\) let \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) be the quadratic algebra \(\mathbb Q[\omega]/(\omega^2+n)\). For \(n\ge1\) the number \(-n\) is not a square in \(\mathbb Q\), so \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) is a field, and a number field. For \(n\ge1\) let \(\mathrm{Cl}\) be the class group of the ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\). The genus class number of \(n\) is $\(g(n)=\bigl|\mathrm{Cl}^2\bigr|,\)$ the order of the subgroup of squares \(\mathrm{Cl}^2=\{c^2:c\in\mathrm{Cl}\}\) of the class group.

This is the number \(g(n)=\#2\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n}))\) of Tian, Yuan and Zhang, who write the class group additively; it is the order of the subgroup of squares, not of the 2-torsion. A finite commutative group has a subgroup of squares of odd order exactly when that subgroup has no element of order \(2\) (when the subgroup of squares has odd order), so \(g(n)\) is odd exactly when no element of order \(2\) of \(\mathrm{Cl}\) is a square, that is, when \(\mathrm{Cl}[2]\cap\mathrm{Cl}^2=1\).

docs.title: The statement of Rédei's formula
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.RedeiFormula

Rédei's formula is the following assertion. Let \(d\) be odd and squarefree, and let \(B\) be a nonempty set of primes of \(d\) whose product \(d_B=\prod_{p\in B}p\) satisfies \(d_B\equiv7\), \(3\) or \(1\pmod8\). Then $\(g(d_B)\equiv g_d(B)\pmod 2,\)$ where \(g(d_B)\) is the genus class number of \(d_B\), the order of the subgroup of squares of the class group of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d_B})\), and \(g_d(B)\in\mathbb F_2\) is Rédei's \(g\) of \(B\) for the bits \(a_{pq}\), \(y_p\), \(z_p\) of the primes of \(d\): $\(g_d(B)=\sum_{\rho\in B}y_\rho\,\kappa_\rho(B)\ \text{ if }y(B)=1,\qquad g_d(B)=\sum_{\rho\in B}z_\rho\,\kappa_\rho(B)\ \text{ if }y(B)=0.\)$

The blocks allowed include every block that occurs in the genus sum \(T_{5b}(d)\): the blocks of a set partition are nonempty, and the partitions counted by the genus sum have only blocks with \(d_B\equiv7\), \(3\) or \(1\pmod8\). Blocks with \(d_B\equiv5\pmod8\) never occur. The empty set is excluded because \(g(1)=1\) (the class group of \(\mathbb Q(i)\) is classically trivial), while Rédei's \(g\) of the empty set is \(0\).

docs.title: Rédei's formula
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.redeiFormula

Rédei's formula holds. Let \(d\) be odd and squarefree, and let \(B\) be a nonempty set of primes of \(d\) with \(d_B=\prod_{p\in B}p\equiv7\), \(3\) or \(1\pmod8\). Then $\(g(d_B)\equiv g_d(B)\pmod 2:\)$ the parity of the order of the subgroup of squares of the class group of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d_B})\) is Rédei's \(g\) of \(B\), computed from the residue bits of the primes of \(d\).

Proof sketch. Rédei's theorem on the 4-rank proves the 4-rank statement: for odd squarefree \(n>1\), \(g(n)\) is odd if and only if the kernel of the Rédei matrix of \(n\) is \(\{0,e_n\}\). From the 4-rank statement, \(g(d_B)\equiv g_d(B)\pmod2\) follows for every odd \(d\) and every nonempty set \(B\) of primes of \(d\). The number \(d_B\) is odd, squarefree and greater than \(1\), and its primes are the elements of \(B\). The Rédei matrix of \(d_B\) is the Laplacian \(L_B\) of the bits of \(d\), bordered by the column \(z_B\) exactly when \(y(B)=0\). Its kernel is \(\{0,e_{d_B}\}\) if and only if the kernel of \((L_B\mid z_B)\) is trivial, and that holds if and only if \(g_d(B)=1\). The argument uses neither the squarefreeness of \(d\) nor the congruence of \(d_B\) modulo \(8\).

docs.title: The Rédei matrix
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.redeiEntry

Let \(n\) be a natural number and \(T_n\) its set of ramified primes: the primes of \(n\), together with \(2\) unless \(n\equiv3\pmod4\). The Rédei matrix \(R\) of \(n\) is the matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\) with rows indexed by the primes \(q\mid n\) and columns by \(T_n\), with entries $\(R_{q2}=[2/q],\qquad R_{qq}=\Bigl[ rac{n/q}{q}\Bigr]\quad(q e2),\qquad R_{qp}=[p/q]\quad(p e q,\ p e2),\)$ where \([a/q]\in\mathbb F_2\) is the residue bit. A vector \(e\in\mathbb F_2^{T_n}\) is killed by \(R\) when \(\sum_{p\in T_n}R_{qp}e_p=0\) for every prime \(q\mid n\).

For odd squarefree \(n\), \(R\) is the matrix of the genus characters on the ambiguous classes: \(\chi_q(\psi(e))=\sum_{p\in T_n}R_{qp}e_p\) (the genus characters on the ambiguous classes).

docs.title: Consequences for the certified rank hypothesis
docs.text:
By Rédei's formula, the genus sum of class numbers equals the genus sum of Rédei bits, so the class-number form CR₃^TYZ_Cl of the certified rank hypothesis is equivalent to CR₃^TYZ.

The same comparison of genus sums shows that the positive-rank form of CR₃^TYZ_Cl implies the positive-rank form of CR₃^TYZ; that implication is stated in the positive-rank chapter (CR₃^TYZ_Cl,Rk implies CR₃^TYZ,Rk).

docs.title: The genus sum of class numbers
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.T5bCl ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.neZero_dProd

For a natural number \(d\) and a set \(B\) of primes of \(d\), the product \(d_B=\prod_{p\in B}p\) is a positive integer, so its genus class number \(g(d_B)\) is defined. The genus sum of class numbers of row 5b is $\(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=\sum_{\pi}\prod_{B\in\pi}g(d_B)\pmod 2,\)$ the sum over the set partitions \(\pi\) of the primes of \(d\) with exactly one block \(B\) having \(d_B\equiv7\pmod8\), exactly one having \(d_B\equiv3\pmod8\), and every block having \(d_B\equiv7\), \(3\) or \(1\pmod8\). These are the set partitions of the genus sum \(T_{5b}(d)\); the sum \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)\) has Tian, Yuan and Zhang's genus class numbers \(g(d_B)\) in place of Rédei's \(g_d(B)\).

docs.title: The certified rank hypothesis with class numbers
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.CertifiedRankTYZCl

The hypothesis CR₃^TYZ_Cl is the following assertion. Let \(d\) be squarefree with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\). If \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\) and the genus sum of class numbers \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)\) is \(1\), then for every \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) the 2-covering \(D_{a,b}\) of \(C_d\) has a rational point; that is, every 2-Selmer class of \(C_d\) comes from a rational point.

CR₃^TYZ_Cl is not proved here; it is a hypothesis, stated in Tian, Yuan and Zhang's own terms, with their genus class numbers \(g(d_B)\), so that no Rédei formula enters its justification. It rests on the following:

  • Tian–Yuan–Zhang, Theorem 3.5 and the argument of the proof of their Theorem 3.5(2) (§3.3), as completed in nt-tyz §4 (Proposition N): for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), if the genus sum \(\sum_{d_0\equiv7,\,d_1\equiv3\,(8)}g(d_0)g(d_1)\mathcal L_1(d/d_0d_1)\), which is \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)\) modulo \(2\), is odd, then \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes to order exactly one at \(s=1\). Here \(\mathcal L_1(m)\) is the sum, over the set partitions of the primes of \(m\) into blocks \(B\) with \(d_B\equiv1\pmod8\), of \(\prod_B g(d_B)\).
  • Gross–Zagier, over an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field satisfying the Heegner hypothesis with \(L(C_d^K,1)\ne0\): analytic rank one gives \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\ge1\).
  • The step from positive rank to every Selmer class: when \(|\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)|=8\) and \(C_d\) has a rational point of infinite order, every 2-Selmer class of \(C_d\) comes from a rational point. This step is proved (positive rank and a Selmer group of order eight give every Selmer class), with Mordell–Weil for the congruent number curves.

By Rédei's formula, CR₃^TYZ_Cl is equivalent to the hypothesis CR₃^TYZ stated with Rédei's \(g\) (CR₃ with class numbers is CR₃^TYZ).

docs.title: The genus sum of class numbers is the genus sum of Rédei bits
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.T5bCl_eq_T5b' ZInQ.RouteK.Rank5b.T5bCl_eq_T5b

Let \(d\) be odd and squarefree. Then $\(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=T_{5b}(d):\)$ the genus sum of row 5b with the genus class numbers \(g(d_B)\) equals the genus sum with Rédei's \(g_d(B)\). Along the way, the same identity is proved for every odd squarefree \(d\) from Rédei's formula taken as an assumption.

Proof sketch. Both sums run over the same set partitions of the primes of \(d\). Every block \(B\) of such a partition is nonempty and has \(d_B\equiv7\), \(3\) or \(1\pmod8\), so Rédei's formula, taken as an assumption, gives \(g(d_B)\equiv g_d(B)\pmod2\) factor by factor, and the two sums agree term by term. By Rédei's formula, its hypothesis holds, so \(T^{\rm Cl}_{5b}(d)=T_{5b}(d)\) for every odd squarefree \(d\).

From the Rédei matrix to Rédei's bits
docs.text:
For an odd number \(d\) and a nonempty set \(B\) of its primes, the Rédei matrix of \(d_B\) is the Laplacian \(L_B\) of the bits \(a_{qp}=[p/q]\) of \(d\), bordered by the column \(z_B\) exactly when \(y(B)=0\). Its kernel is \(\{0,e_{d_B}\}\) exactly when \(g_d(B)=1\). docs.title: Rédei's bit as a kernel condition
The kernel of \((L_B\mid z_B)\) through a square matrix
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.redeiK_kernel_iff_updateCol ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.redeiK_lapl_rowSum ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.redeiK_sum_updateCol ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.redeiK_zmod2_cases

Let \(V\) be a finite set with bits \(a_{ij},y_i,z_i\in\mathbb F_2\) on \(V\) satisfying reciprocity, as in Rédei's \(g\) from the bits. Let \(B\subseteq V\), \(\rho\in B\), \(y(B)=\sum_{i\in B}y_i\), and let \(L_B\) be the Laplacian of \(a\) on \(B\). Say that the kernel of \((L_B\mid z_B)\) is trivial if the following holds: for every \(e:V\to\mathbb F_2\) vanishing off \(B\) and every \(e_2\in\mathbb F_2\) with \(e_2=0\) when \(y(B)=1\), if $\(\sum_{p\in B}(L_B)_{qp}e_p+e_2z_q=0\quad\text{for every }q\in B,\)$ then \(e_2=0\) and \(e\) is constant on \(B\) (identically \(0\) or identically \(1\) there). So the column \(z_B\) counts only when \(y(B)=0\).

Let \(w=y\) if \(y(B)=1\) and \(w=z\) otherwise, and let \(N\) be \(L_B\) with its column \(\rho\) replaced by \(w\). Then the kernel of \((L_B\mid z_B)\) is trivial if and only if every \(F:V\to\mathbb F_2\) vanishing off \(B\) with \(\sum_{p\in B}N_{qp}F_p=0\) for all \(q\in B\) vanishes on \(B\).

Along the way, without reciprocity:

  • the rows of \(L_B\) sum to zero over \(B\): \(\sum_{p\in B}(L_B)_{qp}=0\) for \(q\in B\);
  • splitting off the column \(\rho\): \(\sum_{p\in B}N_{qp}F_p=\sum_{p\in B}(L_B)_{qp}F'_p+w_qF_\rho\), where \(F'\) is \(F\) with \(F'_\rho=0\);
  • every element of \(\mathbb F_2\) is \(0\) or \(1\).

Proof sketch. (⇒) Let \(F\) vanish off \(B\) with \(\sum_pN_{qp}F_p=0\) on \(B\). Put \(e=F\) with \(e_\rho=0\), and \(e_2=F_\rho\), so that \(L_Be+F_\rho w=0\) on \(B\).

  • If \(y(B)=1\), sum over \(q\in B\). Under reciprocity the column sums of \(L_B\) over \(B\) are \(y_v(1+y(B))=0\), while \(\sum_{q\in B}w_q=y(B)=1\), so \(F_\rho=0\).
  • In either case the triviality of the kernel applies (with \(w=z\) when \(y(B)=0\)). It gives \(e_2=0\) and \(e\) constant on \(B\), and \(e_\rho=0\), so \(F=0\) on \(B\).

(⇐) Given \((e,e_2)\), replace \(e\) by \(e-e_\rho\) on \(B\); this does not change \(L_Be\) on \(B\), since the rows of \(L_B\) sum to zero. Set its value at \(\rho\) to \(e_2\) and call the result \(F\). Then \(\sum_pN_{qp}F_p=0\) on \(B\) (when \(y(B)=1\) because \(e_2=0\), when \(y(B)=0\) because \(w=z\)), so \(F=0\) on \(B\): \(e_2=0\), and \(e=e_\rho\) is constant on \(B\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.kernel_trivial_iff_redeiG ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.redeiK_det_updateCol ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.redeiK_ker_iff_det

Let \(V\) be a finite set with bits \(a_{ij},y_i,z_i\in\mathbb F_2\) satisfying reciprocity, and let \(B\subseteq V\) be nonempty. Then the kernel of \((L_B\mid z_B)\) is trivial (the column \(z_B\) counting only when \(y(B)=0\)) if and only if \(g(B)=1\), where $\(g(B)=\sum_{\rho\in B}y_\rho\,\kappa_\rho(B)\ \text{ if }y(B)=1,\qquad g(B)=\sum_{\rho\in B}z_\rho\,\kappa_\rho(B)\ \text{ if }y(B)=0,\)$ and \(\kappa_\rho(B)=\det L_B[B\setminus\rho,B\setminus\rho]\).

Along the way, without reciprocity:

  • for \(\rho\in B\) and any \(w:V\to\mathbb F_2\), the matrix \(L_B\) with column \(\rho\) replaced by \(w\) has determinant \(\sum_{v\in B}w_v\,\kappa_v(B)\) on \(B\times B\);
  • a square matrix \(N\) on \(B\) has trivial kernel, in the sense that every \(F:V\to\mathbb F_2\) vanishing off \(B\) with \(\sum_{p\in B}N_{qp}F_p=0\) for all \(q\in B\) vanishes on \(B\), if and only if its determinant on \(B\times B\) is nonzero.

Proof sketch. Fix \(\rho\in B\), let \(w=y\) if \(y(B)=1\) and \(w=z\) otherwise, and let \(N\) be \(L_B\) with column \(\rho\) replaced by \(w\). By the kernel through a square matrix, the kernel of \((L_B\mid z_B)\) is trivial if and only if \(N\) has trivial kernel on \(B\), that is, \(\det N\ne0\). Expanding \(\det N\) along column \(\rho\), the minor of \(L_B\) with row \(v\) and column \(\rho\) deleted is \(\kappa_v(B)\) (Lemma 2.2(2)), so \(\det N=\sum_{v\in B}w_v\kappa_v(B)\), which is \(g(B)\) by its definition. In \(\mathbb F_2\), nonzero means \(1\).

Let \(d\) be a natural number, \(B\) a set of primes of \(d\) and \(d_B=\prod_{p\in B}p\). Then:

  • the primes of \(d_B\) are exactly the elements of \(B\), and \(d_B\) is squarefree;
  • if \(B\) is nonempty, then \(d_B>1\);
  • for \(q\in B\), \(d_B/q=\prod_{k\in B,\,k\ne q}k\);
  • every element of \(B\) lies in \(T_{d_B}\), and every element of \(T_{d_B}\) is \(2\) or an element of \(B\).

If \(d\) is odd, then moreover:

  • the primes of \(d\) are different from \(2\), so \(2\) is not a prime of \(d_B\) and \(d_B\) is odd;
  • \(2\in T_{d_B}\) if and only if \(d_B\not\equiv3\pmod4\);
  • \(y(B)=\sum_{q\in B}y_q=1\) if and only if \(d_B\equiv3\pmod4\).

Proof sketch. \(d_B\) is a product of distinct primes, so its primes are the elements of \(B\) and it is squarefree; the statements about \(T_{d_B}\) follow from its definition. For odd \(d\), \(y(B)\) is \(\lambda(d_B)=[d_B\equiv3\pmod4]\), by the multiplicativity of \(\lambda\) on odd residues modulo \(8\).

Let \(d\) be odd, \(B\) a set of primes of \(d\), \(R\) the Rédei matrix of \(d_B\), and \(L_B\) the Laplacian on \(B\) of the bits \(a_{qp}=[p/q]\) of \(d\). For \(q\in B\) and every function \(F\) from the natural numbers to \(\mathbb F_2\), $\(\sum_{p\in T_{d_B}}R_{qp}F(p)=\sum_{p\in B}(L_B)_{qp}F(p)+ egin{cases}0,&d_B\equiv3\pmod4,\ z_qF(2),& ext{otherwise.}\end{cases}\)$ More precisely, for \(q\in B\) and every prime \(p\) of \(d\), the entry given by the formula of the Rédei matrix of \(d_B\), namely \([p/q]\) for \(p e q\) and \([(d_B/q)/q]\) for \(p=q\), equals \((L_B)_{qp}\).

Proof sketch. The off-diagonal entries are \([p/q]=a_{qp}=(L_B)_{qp}\). On the diagonal, \(d_B/q=\prod_{k\in B,\,k e q}k\), and the other primes of \(B\) are prime to \(q\), so by the multiplicativity of the residue bit \([(d_B/q)/q]=\sum_{k\in B,\,k e q}[k/q]=(L_B)_{qq}\). The set \(T_{d_B}\) is \(B\) if \(d_B\equiv3\pmod4\) and \(B\cup\{2\}\) otherwise, with \(2 otin B\); the column at \(2\) has entries \([2/q]=z_q\).

docs.title: The two kernel conditions agree
docs.text:

Let \(d\) be odd and \(B\) a set of primes of \(d\). Let \(e_{d_B}\in\mathbb F_2^{T_{d_B}}\) be \(1\) at the primes of \(d_B\) and \(0\) at \(2\). Then every vector of \(\mathbb F_2^{T_{d_B}}\) killed by the Rédei matrix of \(d_B\) is \(0\) or \(e_{d_B}\) if and only if the kernel of \((L_B\mid z_B)\) is trivial for the bits \(a,y,z\) of \(d\).

Proof sketch. A vector on \(T_{d_B}\) corresponds to its restriction \(e\) to \(B\), together with its value \(e_2\) at \(2\) when \(2\in T_{d_B}\) (and \(e_2=0\) otherwise). Then:

  • \(2\notin T_{d_B}\) exactly when \(d_B\equiv3\pmod4\), that is, when \(y(B)=1\);
  • the two linear systems agree, by the formula for the Rédei matrix of \(d_B\) in the bits;
  • \(e_{d_B}\) corresponds to \(e=1\) on \(B\) with \(e_2=0\), and \(0\) to \(e=0\) with \(e_2=0\).

docs.title: Rédei's formula from the 4-rank statement
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.redeiFormula_of_oddGClStatement ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.gCl_dProd_eq_gBit

The 4-rank statement implies Rédei's formula. More precisely, assume the 4-rank statement. Then for every odd \(d\) and every nonempty set \(B\) of primes of \(d\), $\(g(d_B)\equiv g_d(B)\pmod2;\)$ neither the squarefreeness of \(d\) nor a condition on \(d_B\) modulo \(8\) is needed.

Proof sketch. The number \(d_B\) is odd, squarefree and greater than \(1\). By the 4-rank statement, \(g(d_B)\) is odd if and only if every vector killed by the Rédei matrix of \(d_B\) is \(0\) or \(e_{d_B}\). That holds if and only if the kernel of \((L_B\mid z_B)\) is trivial for the bits of \(d\). These bits satisfy reciprocity because \(d\) is odd, so the kernel is trivial if and only if \(g_d(B)=1\). Compare parities.
