docs.title: The field ℚ(√(-n)) and its primes
The field \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and its primes
docs.text:
As in the rest of the chapter, \(n\ge1\) is an integer and \(K=\mathbb Q(\omega)\) with \(\omega^2=-n\); \(\mathcal O\) is its ring of integers, \(\sigma\) its nontrivial automorphism and \(N\) the norm of elements and of ideals. This section collects what the genus theory of the next section needs about \(K\):

  • its conjugation and norms;
  • the rational integers in \(\mathcal O\);
  • the splitting of a rational prime into split, inert and ramified primes;
  • the set \(T_n\) of primes of the discriminant and the prime ideals \(\mathfrak p_p\) over them, with \((\omega)=\prod_{p\mid n}\mathfrak p_p\);
  • the identity \(I\cdot\sigma(I)=(N(I))\) for ideals \(I\) of \(\mathcal O\).

The hypotheses vary from fact to fact: the field, its primes and \(I\cdot\sigma(I)=(N(I))\) need only \(n\ge1\); that the primes of \(n\) ramify needs \(n\) squarefree; the description of \(\mathfrak p_p\) for every \(p\in T_n\) and of \((\omega)\) needs \(n\) odd and squarefree. Ramification is decided by norms of ideals and residue fields, so no integral basis of \(\mathcal O\) is needed.

9 fully proved

docs.title: The conjugation of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.conj_apply ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.card_gal ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.omega_sq ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.conj_omega ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.conj_unique ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.conj_conj ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.conj_mul_self ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.eq_one_or_eq_conj ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.exists_conj_ne_one ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.algebraMap_smul

Let \(n\ge1\) and let \(K=\mathbb Q(\omega)=\mathbb Q[\omega]/(\omega^2+n)\), so that \(\omega^2=-n\). Then \(K\) has exactly two automorphisms over \(\mathbb Q\), and a nontrivial one exists. Every nontrivial automorphism \(\sigma\) satisfies \(\sigma(\omega)=-\omega\) and is the conjugation $\(\sigma(a+b\omega)=a-b\omega\qquad(a,b\in\mathbb Q).\)$ Hence the nontrivial automorphism \(\sigma\) is unique, \(\sigma\circ\sigma=1\), and every automorphism of \(K\) is \(1\) or \(\sigma\). The automorphisms of \(K\) act on its ring of integers \(\mathcal O\) compatibly with the inclusion \(\mathcal O\subset K\).

Proof sketch. \(K/\mathbb Q\) is Galois of degree \(2\), so it has two automorphisms, and one of them is not the identity. Let \(\sigma\ne1\). The image \(z=\sigma(\omega)\) is again a root of \(X^2+n\), so it has trace \(0\) and norm \(n\); writing \(z=a+b\omega\), this gives \(a=0\) and \(b^2=1\). If \(b=1\), then \(\sigma\) fixes the generator \(\omega\), so \(\sigma=1\). Hence \(b=-1\), that is, \(\sigma(\omega)=-\omega\), and writing \(x=a+b\omega\) gives \(\sigma(x)=a-b\omega\). So any two nontrivial automorphisms agree, and applying the conjugation twice gives the identity.

Let \(n\ge1\), \(K=\mathbb Q(\omega)\) with \(\omega^2=-n\), \(\mathcal O\) its ring of integers and \(\sigma\) its nontrivial automorphism.

  • \(\omega\) lies in \(\mathcal O\), with \(\omega^2=-n\) and \(\sigma(\omega)=-\omega\) there. Put \(\theta=(1+\omega)/2=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\omega\). If \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), then \(\theta\) lies in \(\mathcal O\), and \(2\theta=1+\omega\).
  • The norm of \(K/\mathbb Q\) is \(N(a+b\omega)=a^2+nb^2\). For every \(x\in K\), \(N(x)=x\,\sigma(x)\) and \(N(x)\ge0\).
  • \(\mathcal O\) has rank \(2\) over \(\mathbb Z\). For \(x\in\mathcal O\), the norm \(N(x)\) is an integer, the norm of \(x\) over \(\mathbb Z\); it satisfies \(N(x)\ge0\) and \(N(x)=x\,\sigma(x)\) in \(\mathcal O\). Moreover \(N(m)=m^2\) for \(m\in\mathbb Z\), \(N(\omega)=n\) and \(N(1+\omega)=1+n\).

Proof sketch. \(\omega\) is a root of \(X^2+n\), and \(\sigma(\omega)=-\omega\) in \(\mathcal O\) because it holds in \(K\). For \(n+1=4m\), \(\theta\) is a root of \(X^2-X+m\). The norm is the determinant of multiplication by \(x=a+b\omega\) on the basis \(1,\omega\), which is \(a^2+nb^2\ge0\). It equals \((a+b\omega)(a-b\omega)=x\,\sigma(x)\) because \(\sigma\) is the conjugation. For \(x\in\mathcal O\) the norm of \(K/\mathbb Q\) is the norm of \(\mathcal O/\mathbb Z\), so it is an integer; since \(\mathcal O\) has rank \([K:\mathbb Q]=2\) over \(\mathbb Z\), \(N(m)=m^2\). The values \(N(\omega)=n\) and \(N(1+\omega)=1+n\) are the formula \(a^2+nb^2\).

docs.text:

Let \(n\ge1\) and let \(\mathcal O\) be the ring of integers of \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\). Then \(\mathcal O\cap\mathbb Q=\mathbb Z\): a rational number that lies in \(\mathcal O\) is an integer. The map \(\mathbb Z\to\mathcal O\) is injective, and:

  • for integers \(a,b\), \(a\) divides \(b\) in \(\mathcal O\) if and only if \(a\) divides \(b\) in \(\mathbb Z\), and likewise for natural numbers;
  • an integer \(m\) is a unit of \(\mathcal O\) if and only if \(m=\pm1\), and a unit of \(\mathcal O\) that is a rational number is \(\pm1\);
  • for natural numbers \(a,b\), \(a\mathcal O=b\mathcal O\) if and only if \(a=b\).

Proof sketch. A rational number that is integral over \(\mathbb Z\) is an integer, because \(\mathbb Z\) is integrally closed. If \(b=ay\) in \(\mathcal O\) with \(a\ne0\), then \(y=b/a\) is a rational number in \(\mathcal O\), hence an integer; if \(a=0\), then \(b=0\) by injectivity. An integer \(m\) is a unit exactly when \(m\mid1\) in \(\mathcal O\), that is, in \(\mathbb Z\). Finally \(a\mathcal O=b\mathcal O\) means \(a\mid b\) and \(b\mid a\) in \(\mathcal O\), hence in \(\mathbb N\), so \(a=b\).

docs.title: Primes
docs.text: A prime of \(\mathcal O\) over \(p\) is split, inert or ramified according to its norm and to whether \(\sigma\) fixes it. The ramified ones lie over the primes of \(T_n\), and for odd squarefree \(n\) every prime of \(T_n\) ramifies.

Let \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal O\) the ring of integers of \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and \(\sigma\) the nontrivial automorphism. An ideal \(P\) of \(\mathcal O\) lies over \(p\) if \(P\cap\mathbb Z=p\mathbb Z\). Let \(p\) be a prime and \(P\) a maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O\) lying over \(p\). Then one of the following holds:

  • split: \(\sigma P e P\), \(P\cdot\sigma P=p\mathcal O\) and \(N(P)=p\);
  • inert: \(\sigma P=P\), \(P=p\mathcal O\) and \(N(P)=p^2\);
  • ramified: \(\sigma P=P\), \(P^2=p\mathcal O\) and \(N(P)=p\).

Along the way, with \( au\) any automorphism of \(K\) acting on the ideals of \(\mathcal O\):

  • \(N(m\mathcal O)=m^2\) for every natural number \(m\), and \(m e0\) in \(\mathcal O\) for \(m e0\);
  • an ideal \(P\) over \(p\) contains \(p\), so \(p\mathcal O\subseteq P\) and \(p\mathcal O\subseteq au P\); an integer lies in \(P\) if and only if \(p\) divides it; and for \(p\) prime, \(P e0\);
  • \(p\mathbb Z\) is a prime ideal of \(\mathbb Z\), a prime ideal of \(\mathcal O\) containing \(p\) lies over \(p\), and every nonzero prime ideal of \(\mathcal O\) lies over some prime;
  • \( au\) fixes every integer and every ideal \(m\mathcal O\), and sends nonzero ideals to nonzero ideals and maximal ideals to maximal ideals;
  • a maximal ideal \(P\) with \(P^k\subseteq au P\) for some \(k\) satisfies \( au P=P\);
  • if \(I\) divides \(J\) and \(N(I)=N(J) e0\), then \(I=J\).

Proof sketch. Since \(p\mathcal O\subseteq P\), write \(p\mathcal O=PM\). Then \(N(P)N(M)=N(p\mathcal O)=p^2\), and \(N(P) e1\) because \(P e\mathcal O\).

  • If \(N(P)=p^2\), then \(N(M)=1\), so \(M=\mathcal O\) and \(P=p\mathcal O\). As \(p\mathcal O\subseteq\sigma P\), the maximal ideal \(P\) is contained in \(\sigma P\), so \(\sigma P=P\): inert.
  • If \(N(P)=p\), then \(N(M)=p\) is prime, so \(M\) is a prime ideal; it contains \(p\), so it lies over \(p\). The automorphisms act transitively on the primes over \(p\), so \(M= au P\) with \( au=1\) or \( au=\sigma\).
  • If \(M=P\), then \(P^2=p\mathcal O\subseteq\sigma P\), so \(\sigma P=P\): ramified.
  • If \(M=\sigma P\), the case \(\sigma P=P\) is ramified and the case \(\sigma P e P\) is split.

Only norms of ideals and the transitivity of the Galois action are used, not ramification indices.

Let \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal O\) the ring of integers of \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\), \(p\) a prime and \(P\) a maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O\) lying over \(p\) with \(P^2=p\mathcal O\). Then \(p\mid n\), or \(p=2\) and \(n\equiv1\pmod4\).

Along the way:

  • an ideal \(P\) with \(P^2=p\mathcal O\) has \(N(P)=p\);
  • if \(P\) is maximal and \(N(P)=p\) is prime, every element of \(\mathcal O\) is congruent modulo \(P\) to an integer;
  • if moreover \(\tau P=P\) for an automorphism \(\tau\) of \(K\), then \(x-\tau(x)\in P\) for every \(x\in\mathcal O\);
  • for \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), the element \(\theta=(1+\omega)/2\) of \(\mathcal O\) satisfies \(\sigma(\theta)=1-\theta\), where \(\sigma\) is the nontrivial automorphism.

Proof sketch. \(P^2=p\mathcal O\subseteq\sigma P\), so \(\sigma P=P\); and \(N(P)^2=N(p\mathcal O)=p^2\), so \(N(P)=p\). Then \(\mathcal O/P\) has \(p\) elements, so \(\mathbb Z\to\mathcal O/P\) is onto: every \(x\) is congruent to an integer \(m\) modulo \(P\), and so is \(\sigma(x)\), since \(\sigma\) fixes \(m\) and \(P\). Hence \(x-\sigma(x)\in P\).

  • With \(x=\omega\): \(2\omega\in P\), so \(-4n=(2\omega)^2\in P\cap\mathbb Z=p\mathbb Z\) and \(p\mid4n\). If \(p\nmid n\), then \(p=2\) and \(n\) is odd.
  • If \(p=2\nmid n\) and \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), take \(x=\theta\): \(\theta-(1-\theta)=2\theta-1=\omega\in P\). Then \(-n=\omega^2\in P\cap\mathbb Z=2\mathbb Z\), a contradiction. So \(n\equiv1\pmod4\).

For a natural number \(n\), let \(T_n\) be the set of prime factors of \(n\) (empty for \(n=0\)) if \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), and that set together with \(2\) otherwise; write \(t=|T_n|\). Every element of \(T_n\) is prime, and every prime factor of \(n\) lies in \(T_n\). Motivation: for odd squarefree \(n\), \(T_n\) is the set of primes dividing the discriminant of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\), and these are exactly the primes that ramify there.

Now let \(n\ge1\) and let \(\mathcal O\) be the ring of integers of \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\). Every prime \(p\) has a maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O\) lying over it, since \(\mathcal O\) is integral over \(\mathbb Z\). For a prime \(p\), \(\mathfrak p_p\) denotes a fixed choice of a maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O\) lying over \(p\); for \(p\) not prime, \(\mathfrak p_p=\mathcal O\). Thus for every prime \(p\) the ideal \(\mathfrak p_p\) is maximal and lies over \(p\), and \(\mathfrak p_p\ne0\) for every natural number \(p\).

Let \(n\) be odd and squarefree and \(p\in T_n\). Then \(\mathfrak p_p\) is maximal, \(\mathfrak p_p^2=p\mathcal O\) and \(N(\mathfrak p_p)=p\). Moreover \(\mathfrak p_p\) is the only prime ideal of \(\mathcal O\) lying over \(p\), and every automorphism of \(K\) fixes \(\mathfrak p_p\).

These rest on the following, for \(n\ge1\):

  • if \(n\) is squarefree and \(p\) is a prime dividing \(n\), every maximal ideal \(P\) over \(p\) has \(P^2=p\mathcal O\);
  • if \(n\equiv1\pmod4\), every maximal ideal \(P\) over \(2\) has \(P^2=2\mathcal O\);
  • if \(P\) is a maximal ideal over a prime \(p\) with \(P^2 e p\mathcal O\), then for \(x\in\mathcal O\), \(x^2\in p\mathcal O\) implies \(x\in p\mathcal O\).

Proof sketch. For the last item, \(P\) is split or inert. If it is split, \(x\) lies in the prime ideals \(P\) and \(\sigma P\), which both contain \(p\mathcal O\); they are distinct maximal ideals, so coprime, and \(x\in P\cap\sigma P=P\cdot\sigma P=p\mathcal O\). If it is inert, \(p\mathcal O=P\) is prime.

  • For \(p\mid n\): \(\omega^2=-n\in p\mathcal O\). If \(P^2 e p\mathcal O\), then \(\omega=py\), and taking norms gives \(n=p^2N(y)\), contradicting squarefreeness.
  • For \(n=4c+1\): \((1+\omega)^2=2(\omega-2c)\in2\mathcal O\). If \(P^2 e2\mathcal O\), then \(1+\omega=2y\), and taking norms gives \(1+n=4N(y)\), but \(1+n=4c+2\).

An element \(p\in T_n\) divides \(n\), or is \(2\) with \(n ot\equiv3\pmod4\), that is, with \(n\equiv1\pmod4\) as \(n\) is odd. So \(\mathfrak p_p^2=p\mathcal O\), and then \(N(\mathfrak p_p)=p\). A prime ideal \(Q\) over \(p\) contains \(p\mathcal O=\mathfrak p_p^2\), so it contains the maximal ideal \(\mathfrak p_p\) and equals it. For an automorphism \( au\), \(\mathfrak p_p^2=p\mathcal O\subseteq au\mathfrak p_p\), so \( au\mathfrak p_p=\mathfrak p_p\).

docs.title: The ideal \((\sqrt{-n})\) is the product of the ramified odd primes
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.span_omega ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.omegaO_mem_ramIdeal

Let \(n\) be odd and squarefree. Then $\((\omega)=\prod_{p\mid n}\mathfrak p_p\)$ in \(\mathcal O\), the product over the primes \(p\) dividing \(n\). This rests on the following, for every \(n\ge1\): if \(p\) is a prime dividing \(n\), then \(\omega\in\mathfrak p_p\).

Proof sketch. For a prime \(p\mid n\), \(\omega^2=-n\) lies in \(\mathfrak p_p\), which contains \(p\), and \(\mathfrak p_p\) is prime, so \(\omega\in\mathfrak p_p\); that is, \(\mathfrak p_p\) divides \((\omega)\). For distinct primes \(p,q\mid n\) the maximal ideals \(\mathfrak p_p\) and \(\mathfrak p_q\) are distinct (if they were equal, \(q\in\mathfrak p_p\) would give \(p\mid q\)), so they are pairwise coprime, and their product divides \((\omega)\). The norms agree: \(\prod_{p\mid n}N(\mathfrak p_p)=\prod_{p\mid n}p=n=N(\omega)\ne0\), as \(n\) is squarefree. An ideal dividing an ideal of the same nonzero norm equals it.

Let \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal O\) the ring of integers of \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and \(\sigma\) the nontrivial automorphism. Every ideal \(I\) of \(\mathcal O\) satisfies $\(I\cdot\sigma(I)=\bigl(N(I)\bigr),\)$ the principal ideal generated by the natural number \(N(I)\). Consequently \(N(\tau I)=N(I)\) for every automorphism \(\tau\) of \(K\) and every ideal \(I\).

Proof sketch. Induction on the factorization of \(I\) into prime ideals. For \(I=0\) both sides are \(0\), and for \(I=\mathcal O\) both are \(\mathcal O\). For a nonzero prime \(P\), lying over a prime \(p\), the trichotomy gives \(P\cdot\sigma P=p\mathcal O=(N(P))\) when \(P\) is split or ramified, and \(P\cdot\sigma P=P^2=p^2\mathcal O=(N(P))\) when it is inert. Both sides are multiplicative in \(I\). For the norms, the case \(\tau=1\) is clear, and \(N(I)=0\) means \(I=0=\tau I\). Otherwise \(\tau=\sigma\) and \(N(I)N(\sigma I)=N(N(I)\mathcal O)=N(I)^2\), and \(N(I)\ne0\) can be cancelled.

docs.text:
Let \(n>1\) be odd and squarefree, \(t=|T_n|\), and let \(\chi:\mathrm{Cl}\to\mathbb F_2^{\{q\mid n\}}\) be the genus map, \(c\mapsto(\chi_q(c))_q\). Counting gives $\([\mathrm{Cl}:\mathrm{Cl}^2]=|\mathrm{Cl}[2]|\le2^{t-1}\le|\mathrm{im}\,\chi|=[\mathrm{Cl}:\ker\chi]\le[\mathrm{Cl}:\mathrm{Cl}^2],\)$ so the principal genus theorem \(\mathrm{Cl}^2=\bigcap_q\ker\chi_q\) holds and \(|\mathrm{Cl}[2]|=2^{t-1}\). Since \(g(n)=|\mathrm{Cl}^2|\) is odd exactly when \(\mathrm{Cl}[2]\cap\mathrm{Cl}^2=1\), Rédei's theorem follows: \(g(n)\) is odd if and only if the kernel of the Rédei matrix is \(\{0,e_n\}\), where \(e_n\) is the exponent vector of \((\sqrt{-n})\).

6 fully proved

docs.title: When the subgroup of squares has odd order
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.odd_card_range_sq_iff ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.card_ker_sq_mul_card_range_sq

Let \(G\) be a finite commutative group, \(G^2=\{x^2:x\in G\}\) its subgroup of squares and \(G[2]=\{x\in G:x^2=1\}\) its 2-torsion. Then \(|G^2|\) is odd if and only if \(G[2]\cap G^2=1\).

Moreover every commutative group \(G\) satisfies \(|G[2]|\cdot|G^2|=|G|\), where an infinite group is given order \(0\).

Proof sketch. If \(|G^2|\) is odd, an element of \(G[2]\cap G^2\) has order dividing \(2\) and, as an element of \(G^2\), dividing \(|G^2|\), so it is trivial. If \(|G^2|\) is even, Cauchy's theorem gives an element of order \(2\) in \(G^2\), and it lies in \(G[2]\cap G^2\). The identity is the first isomorphism theorem for the homomorphism \(x\mapsto x^2\), whose kernel is \(G[2]\) and whose image is \(G^2\).

For \(n\ge1\) the genus map of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) is the homomorphism $\(\chi:\mathrm{Cl}\to\mathbb F_2^{\{q\mid n\}},\qquad c\mapsto(\chi_q(c))_q,\)$ indexed by the primes \(q\mid n\). Let \(n>1\) be odd and squarefree and \(t=|T_n|\). Then the image of the genus map has at least \(2^{t-1}\) elements.

Along the way:

  • every \(n>1\) has a prime factor;
  • for odd \(n\) with \(r\) prime factors, \(t=r\) if \(n\equiv3\pmod4\) and \(t=r+1\) otherwise;
  • for a nonempty finite set \(I\), the hyperplane \(\{e\in\mathbb F_2^I:\sum_ie_i=0\}\), the kernel of the sum map \(\mathbb F_2^I\to\mathbb F_2\), has \(2^{|I|-1}\) elements.

Proof sketch. Let \(r\ge1\) be the number of primes of \(n\).

  • If \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), then \(t=r\). The genus characters take every value with \(\sum_q\varepsilon_q=0\), so the image of \(\chi\) contains the sum-zero hyperplane, which has \(2^{r-1}\) elements.
  • Otherwise \(t=r+1\), since \(2\) is not a prime of \(n\). The genus characters take every value, so the image of \(\chi\) is all of \(\mathbb F_2^r\), which has \(2^r=2^{t-1}\) elements.

docs.title: The principal genus theorem
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.range_sq_eq_ker_chi ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.range_sq_eq_ker_genusMap_and_card ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.range_sq_le_ker_genusMap ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.mem_ker_genusMap ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.fourRank_sq_eq_one ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.fourRank_eq_of_mul_eq

Let \(n>1\) be odd and squarefree, \(\mathrm{Cl}\) the class group of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and \(t=|T_n|\). Then the subgroup of squares is the intersection of the kernels of the genus characters, $\(\mathrm{Cl}^2=\bigcap_{q\mid n}\ker\chi_q,\)$ which is the kernel of the genus map, and \(|\mathrm{Cl}[2]|=2^{t-1}\).

Along the way:

  • for every \(n\ge1\), a class lies in the kernel of the genus map exactly when \(\chi_q\) vanishes on it for every prime \(q\mid n\), and \(\mathrm{Cl}^2\) lies in that kernel, since every element of \(\mathbb F_2\) has \(2x=0\);
  • natural numbers with \(a\le b\), \(c\le d\), \(b,c>0\) and \(ac=bd\) satisfy \(a=b\) and \(c=d\).

Proof sketch. The genus characters take values in \(\mathbb F_2\), so \(\mathrm{Cl}^2\subseteq\ker\chi\). Count: $\(|\mathrm{Cl}^2|\cdot|\mathrm{Cl}[2]|=|\mathrm{Cl}|=|\ker\chi|\cdot|\mathrm{im}\,\chi|.\)$ Here \(|\mathrm{Cl}^2|\le|\ker\chi|\), and \(|\mathrm{Cl}[2]|\le2^{t-1}\le|\mathrm{im}\,\chi|\) by the bound on the 2-torsion and the number of genera. The arithmetic fact above gives \(|\mathrm{Cl}^2|=|\ker\chi|\), hence \(\mathrm{Cl}^2=\ker\chi\), and \(|\mathrm{Cl}[2]|=|\mathrm{im}\,\chi|\), hence \(|\mathrm{Cl}[2]|=2^{t-1}\). This is the classical count of genera, with the principal genus theorem obtained by counting.

Let \(n>1\) be odd and squarefree, \(\mathrm{Cl}\) the class group of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and \(t=|T_n|\). Then \(|\mathrm{Cl}[2]|=2^{t-1}\), and the kernel of the ambiguous class map \(\psi:\mathbb F_2^{T_n}\to\mathrm{Cl}\) has exactly two elements.

Proof sketch. The first claim is part of the principal genus theorem. The image of \(\psi\) is \(\mathrm{Cl}[2]\), so \(|\ker\psi|\cdot2^{t-1}=|\mathbb F_2^{T_n}|=2^t\). Since \(n>1\) has a prime factor, which lies in \(T_n\), \(t\ge1\), and \(|\ker\psi|=2\).

docs.title: The 4-rank statement
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.OddGClStatement

The 4-rank statement is the following assertion. For every odd squarefree \(n>1\), the genus class number \(g(n)\) is odd if and only if every \(e\in\mathbb F_2^{T_n}\) with $\(\sum_{p\in T_n}R_{qp}\,e_p=0\quad\text{for every prime }q\mid n\)$ is \(0\) or \(e_n\). Here \(R\) is the Rédei matrix of \(n\), and \(e_n\in\mathbb F_2^{T_n}\) is \(1\) at the primes of \(n\) and \(0\) at \(2\); it is the exponent vector of the ideal \((\sqrt{-n})\).

The hypothesis \(n>1\) is needed. For \(n=1\) the class group of \(\mathbb Q(i)\) is trivial (a classical fact), so \(g(1)=1\) is odd. But \(T_1=\{2\}\), the Rédei matrix has no rows and \(e_1=0\), so the nonzero vector at \(2\) is killed by it.

The 4-rank statement holds: for every odd squarefree \(n>1\), the genus class number \(g(n)=|\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n}))^2|\) is odd if and only if every vector \(e\in\mathbb F_2^{T_n}\) killed by the Rédei matrix of \(n\) is \(0\) or \(e_n\). Here \(e_n\) is \(1\) at the primes of \(n\) and \(0\) at \(2\), and it is nonzero for \(n>1\).

Proof sketch. By the principal genus theorem and the values of the genus characters on the ambiguous classes, \(\psi(e)\in\mathrm{Cl}^2\) if and only if \(\sum_pR_{qp}e_p=0\) for every prime \(q\mid n\). Also \(\psi(e_n)=1\), the image of \(\psi\) is \(\mathrm{Cl}[2]\), and \(g(n)=|\mathrm{Cl}^2|\) is odd if and only if \(\mathrm{Cl}[2]\cap\mathrm{Cl}^2=1\).

  • If \(g(n)\) is odd and \(e\) is killed by \(R\), then \(\psi(e)\in\mathrm{Cl}[2]\cap\mathrm{Cl}^2=1\). So \(e\in\ker\psi\), which has two elements and contains \(0\) and \(e_n\ne0\); hence \(e\in\{0,e_n\}\).
  • Conversely, an element of \(\mathrm{Cl}[2]\cap\mathrm{Cl}^2\) is \(\psi(m)\) with \(m\) killed by \(R\). So \(m\in\{0,e_n\}\), and \(\psi(m)=1\).

docs.title: Ambiguous classes and genus characters
docs.text:
This section is the genus theory of \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\), in the notation of the chapter: \(\mathcal O\), \(\sigma\), \(N\), \(\mathrm{Cl}\), the set \(T_n\) with \(t=|T_n|\), the prime ideals \(\mathfrak p_p\) and the residue bits \([a/q]\). The main results assume \(n\) odd and squarefree; each article states its own hypotheses, and some auxiliary facts hold for every \(n\ge1\).

  • For \(n\) odd and squarefree, the ambiguous class map \(\psi:\mathbb F_2^{T_n}\to\mathrm{Cl}\) sends \(e\) to \(\prod_p[\mathfrak p_p]^{e_p}\). By Hilbert 90 for ideals its image is \(\mathrm{Cl}[2]\), and its kernel contains the exponent vector \(e_n\) of \((\sqrt{-n})\), so \(|\mathrm{Cl}[2]|\le2^{t-1}\) for \(n>1\).
  • For each prime \(q\mid n\), the genus character \(\chi_q\) sends the class of a nonzero ideal \(I\) with \(q\nmid N(I)\) to \([N(I)/q]\). It is well defined because norms of elements are squares modulo \(q\), and on the ambiguous classes it is given by the Rédei matrix.
  • Through the slot lemma, Dirichlet's theorem shows that the genus characters take every family of values \((\varepsilon_q)_{q\mid n}\), subject only to \(\sum_q\varepsilon_q=0\) when \(n\equiv3\pmod4\).
13 fully proved

Let \(n\ge1\) and let \(\mathrm{Cl}\) be the class group of the ring of integers \(\mathcal O\) of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\). For \(p\in T_n\), let \(c_p=[\mathfrak p_p]\) if \([\mathfrak p_p]^2=1\), and \(c_p=1\) otherwise; so \(c_p^2=1\) in every case. The ambiguous class map is $\(\psi:\mathbb F_2^{T_n}\to\mathrm{Cl},\qquad \psi(e)=\prod_{p\in T_n}c_p^{\,e_p},\)$ where each exponent \(e_p\in\mathbb F_2\) is read as \(0\) or \(1\). Let \(n\) be odd and squarefree, \(\sigma\) the nontrivial automorphism of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and \(I\) a nonzero ideal of \(\mathcal O\) with \(\sigma I=I\). Then \([I]\) lies in the image of \(\psi\).

Along the way:

  • for \(n\) odd and squarefree, every nonzero ideal \(J\ne\mathcal O\) with \(\sigma J=J\) is divisible by a nonzero ideal \(Q\ne\mathcal O\) with \(\sigma Q=Q\) whose class lies in the image of \(\psi\);
  • for every \(n\) with \(n\equiv1\pmod4\), \(2\in T_n\).

Proof sketch. For the divisor: take a maximal ideal \(P\supseteq J\); it is nonzero, so it lies over a prime \(p\).

  • If \(P\) is split, then \(J=\sigma J\subseteq\sigma P\), so \(J\subseteq P\cap\sigma P=P\cdot\sigma P=p\mathcal O\). Take \(Q=p\mathcal O\), which is \(\sigma\)-stable and principal, of class \(1\).
  • If \(P\) is inert, take \(Q=P=p\mathcal O\), again of class \(1\).
  • If \(P\) is ramified, then \(p\mid n\), or \(p=2\) and \(n\equiv1\pmod4\); in both cases \(p\in T_n\), so \(P=\mathfrak p_p\) is the only prime over \(p\). Take \(Q=P\), which is \(\sigma\)-stable, with class \([\mathfrak p_p]=\psi(\delta_p)\).

Then argue by strong induction on \(N(I)\). If \(I=\mathcal O\), its class is \(1\). Otherwise \(I=QJ\) with \(Q\) as above; cancelling \(Q=\sigma Q\) in \(Q\,\sigma J=QJ\) gives \(\sigma J=J\), and \(N(J)<N(I)\) since \(N(Q)\ge2\). So \([I]=[Q][J]\) lies in the image of \(\psi\).

Let \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal O\) the ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and \(q\) a prime. Every ideal class of \(\mathcal O\) contains a nonzero ideal \(I\) with \(q mid N(I)\). Along the way, an ideal \(I\) with \(I+q\mathcal O=\mathcal O\) satisfies \(q mid N(I)\).

Proof sketch. Let \(c\) be the class, and take a nonzero ideal \(J\) in \(c^{-1}\). Since \(\mathcal O\) is a Dedekind domain and \(J\cdot q\mathcal O\subseteq J\) is nonzero, there is \(a\in J\) with \(J\cdot q\mathcal O+(a)=J\). As \(a\in J\), write \((a)=JM\). Then \(J(q\mathcal O+M)=J=J\mathcal O\), and cancelling \(J\) gives \(M+q\mathcal O=\mathcal O\). Also \(M e0\), since otherwise \(q\mathcal O=\mathcal O\) and \(q\) would divide \(1\) in \(\mathcal O\), hence in \(\mathbb Z\). From \([J][M]=[(a)]=1\), \([M]=c\). Finally, if \(q\) divided \(N(M)\), some maximal ideal over \(q\) would divide \(M\); it would contain both \(M\) and \(q\), hence \(M+q\mathcal O=\mathcal O\), which is impossible for a maximal ideal.

docs.title: Norms are squares modulo the primes of \(n\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.isSquare_normZ_mod ZInQ.RouteK.Redei.legBit_absNorm_span

Let \(n\ge1\) be squarefree, \(\mathcal O\) the ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and \(q\) a prime dividing \(n\). For every \(x\in\mathcal O\), the norm \(N(x)\) is a square modulo \(q\). Hence \([N((x))/q]=0\) for every principal ideal \((x)\) of \(\mathcal O\).

Proof sketch. As \(n\) is squarefree and \(q\mid n\), the ideal \(\mathfrak p_q\) over \(q\) is ramified: \(\mathfrak p_q^2=q\mathcal O\), so \(N(\mathfrak p_q)=q\) and \(\sigma\mathfrak p_q=\mathfrak p_q\). So \(x\equiv m\pmod{\mathfrak p_q}\) for an integer \(m\), and \(x-\sigma(x)\in\mathfrak p_q\). Then $\(N(x)-m^2=x\bigl(\sigma(x)-x\bigr)+(x-m)(x+m)\in\mathfrak p_q\cap\mathbb Z=q\mathbb Z.\)$ The ideal norm of \((x)\) is \(|N(x)|=N(x)\), since norms are nonnegative, so its residue bit is \(0\). No coordinates on \(\mathcal O\) are needed.

Let \(n\ge1\) be squarefree, \(\mathcal O\) the ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) and \(q\) a prime dividing \(n\). If \(I\) and \(J\) are nonzero ideals of \(\mathcal O\) in the same ideal class, with \(q mid N(I)\) and \(q mid N(J)\), then $\([N(I)/q]=[N(J)/q].\)$ Along the way, for every \(n\ge1\), every prime \(q\) and ideals \(I,J\) of \(\mathcal O\) with \(q mid N(I)\) and \(q mid N(J)\): \(q mid N(IJ)\) and \([N(IJ)/q]=[N(I)/q]+[N(J)/q]\). (A natural number not divisible by \(q\) is nonzero modulo \(q\).)

Proof sketch. Take a nonzero ideal \(M\) in the inverse class of \([I]\) with \(q mid N(M)\). For every nonzero \(L\) in the class of \(I\) with \(q mid N(L)\), the ideal \(LM=(\alpha)\) is principal, so \([N(L)/q]+[N(M)/q]=[N(LM)/q]=[N((\alpha))/q]=0\), because norms are squares modulo \(q\) and the residue bit is additive on integers prime to \(q\). In \(\mathbb F_2\), \(a+b=0\) means \(a=b\), so \([N(L)/q]=[N(M)/q]\). Apply this to \(L=I\) and \(L=J\).

Let \(n\ge1\), \(\mathrm{Cl}\) the class group of the ring of integers \(\mathcal O\) of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\), and \(q\) a prime dividing \(n\). For each class \(c\in\mathrm{Cl}\) fix a nonzero ideal \(I_c\in c\) with \(q\nmid N(I_c)\); one exists by the choice of representatives prime to \(q\). If \(n\) is squarefree, the genus character \(\chi_q:\mathrm{Cl}\to\mathbb F_2\) is $\(\chi_q(c)=[N(I_c)/q];\)$ if \(n\) is not squarefree, \(\chi_q=0\).

For squarefree \(n\) the value does not depend on the choice: \(\chi_q([I])=[N(I)/q]\) for every nonzero ideal \(I\) of \(\mathcal O\) with \(q\nmid N(I)\). And \(\chi_q\) is a homomorphism, \(\chi_q(cd)=\chi_q(c)+\chi_q(d)\), because for representatives \(I\in c\) and \(J\in d\) prime to \(q\), \(IJ\in cd\) is prime to \(q\) and \([N(IJ)/q]=[N(I)/q]+[N(J)/q]\).

Let \(n\) be odd and squarefree, \(q\) a prime dividing \(n\) and \(R\) the Rédei matrix of \(n\). For every \(e\in\mathbb F_2^{T_n}\), $\(\chi_q igl(\psi(e) igr)=\chi_q\Bigl(\prod_{p\in T_n}[\mathfrak p_p]^{e_p}\Bigr)=\sum_{p\in T_n}R_{qp}\,e_p .\)$ In particular \(\chi_q([\mathfrak p_p])=R_{qp}\) for every \(p\in T_n\), and \(\chi_q([\mathfrak p_q])= igl[(n/q)/q igr]\).

Proof sketch. As \(n\) is odd, \(q e2\), and \(N(\mathfrak p_p)=p\) for every \(p\in T_n\).

  • For \(p=2\): \(q mid2\), so \(\chi_q([\mathfrak p_2])=[2/q]=R_{q2}\).
  • For \(p e q\) odd: \(q mid p\), so \(\chi_q([\mathfrak p_p])=[p/q]=R_{qp}\).
  • For \(p=q\): the ideal \(J=\prod_{p\mid n,\,p e q}\mathfrak p_p\) satisfies \(\mathfrak p_qJ=(\omega)\), which is principal, and \(N(J)=\prod_{p\mid n,\,p e q}p=n/q\) is prime to \(q\). Hence \(\chi_q([\mathfrak p_q])=-\chi_q([J])=[(n/q)/q]=R_{qq}\), as \(-a=a\) in \(\mathbb F_2\).

The formula for \(\prod_p[\mathfrak p_p]^{e_p}\) follows because \(\chi_q\) is a homomorphism, and it is the formula for \(\psi(e)\) because \(c_p=[\mathfrak p_p]\) for odd squarefree \(n\).

docs.title: Split primes
docs.text:

Let \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal O\) the ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\), and \(p\) an odd prime with \(p\nmid n\) such that \(-n\) is a square modulo \(p\). Then \(\mathcal O\) has a nonzero ideal of norm \(p\).

Proof sketch. Take a maximal ideal \(P\) over \(p\); it is nonzero. If \(P\) is split, \(N(P)=p\). It is not ramified, since a ramified prime divides \(n\) or is \(2\). It is not inert either: if \(P=p\mathcal O\) and \(m^2\equiv-n\pmod p\), then \((m+\omega)(m-\omega)=m^2+n\in P\). As \(P\) is prime and \(\sigma\)-stable, and \(\sigma\) exchanges the two factors, both lie in \(P\), so their sum \(2m\in P\cap\mathbb Z=p\mathbb Z\). As \(p\) is odd, \(p\mid m\), and then \(p\mid(m^2+n)-m^2=n\), a contradiction.

Let \(n\) be odd and squarefree, and let \(\varepsilon\) assign a bit \(\varepsilon_q\in\mathbb F_2\) to each prime \(q\mid n\), with \(\sum_q\varepsilon_q=0\) if \(n\equiv3\pmod4\). Then there is an ideal class \(c\) of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-n})\) with \(\chi_q(c)=\varepsilon_q\) for every prime \(q\mid n\).

Along the way:

  • \(\prod_i(-1)^{f_i}=(-1)^{\sum_if_i}\) for finitely many bits \(f_i\in\mathbb F_2\);
  • for an integer \(a\) and finitely many nonzero natural numbers \(m_i\), the Jacobi symbol satisfies \(\bigl(a/\prod_im_i\bigr)=\prod_i(a/m_i)\);
  • the primes dividing an odd number are different from \(2\).

Proof sketch. The primes \(q\mid n\) are odd. By the slot lemma there is a prime \(\ell\nmid n\) with \([\ell/q]=\varepsilon_q\) for every \(q\mid n\), and with \(\ell\equiv1\pmod8\) if \(\sum_q\varepsilon_q=0\) and \(\ell\equiv3\pmod8\) otherwise; so \(\ell\) is odd. As \(n=\prod_{q\mid n}q\), multiplicativity gives \((\ell/n)=\prod_q(\ell/q)=(-1)^{\sum_q\varepsilon_q}\). Then \((-n/\ell)=\chi_4(\ell)\,(n/\ell)\), and Jacobi reciprocity gives \((-n/\ell)=1\):

  • if \(\sum_q\varepsilon_q=0\), then \(\ell\equiv1\pmod4\), so \(\chi_4(\ell)=1\) and \((n/\ell)=(\ell/n)=1\);
  • otherwise \(n\equiv1\pmod4\) by the hypothesis on \(\varepsilon\), and \(\ell\equiv3\pmod4\), so \(\chi_4(\ell)=-1\) and \((n/\ell)=(\ell/n)=-1\).

So \(-n\) is a square modulo \(\ell\), and \(\mathcal O\) has a nonzero ideal \(P\) of norm \(\ell\). As \(q\nmid\ell\) for every \(q\mid n\), its class has \(\chi_q([P])=[\ell/q]=\varepsilon_q\).

docs.title: Route AP: progressions of good primes in place of the prime pattern
Route AP: progressions of good primes in place of the prime pattern
docs.text:
The completeness of the multiplication template needs every integer to be a sum of three good slopes, the slope representation. The manuscript obtains it from the twenty-two-prime pattern of Proposition 6.2, whose proof uses the Green–Tao–Ziegler theory of linear equations in primes. Route AP replaces the twenty-two-prime pattern by the statement 22P_AP, that the good slope primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, through a change in the completeness proof only: the polynomial is unchanged, and so are the slope predicate and soundness. Since 22P_AP follows from Szemerédi's theorem in the primes and the positive density of the good slope primes, both proved here, the twenty-two-prime pattern is no longer a hypothesis of the main theorem.

The obstacle is the common difference: a progression of many primes has a difference divisible by every small prime to a high power, so its slopes have poles at the old primes \(S_b\), which condition 2 of the slope representation forbids. Lemma P shows that such a pole is harmless: the parameter \(q\) of the slope certificate, chosen \(\ell\)-adically close to a square root of \(R_0^{-1}\), absorbs it.

17 fully proved

Let \(\ell\) be a prime and \(t\in\mathbb Q\), written \(t=u/v\) in lowest terms with \(v>0\). Then \(t\) satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma P at \(\ell\) if

  1. \(e=v_\ell(v)\ge1\), that is, \(t\) has a pole at \(\ell\);
  2. \(e\ge3\) if \(\ell=2\);
  3. none of the seven numbers \(u-cv\), \(c\in\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\), is divisible by \(\ell\).

The contact numerator of \((u,v)\) is \(F(u,v)=\prod_{c\in\mathcal C}(u-cv)\), so that \(F(u/v)=F(u,v)/v^6\).

The research note also asks for \(F(t)>0\); that condition only fixes the sign \(\eta=1\) of the slope predicate, and it is kept in field 2′ of the slope conditions rather than here.

Let \(\ell\) be a prime and let \(t=u/v\) satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma P at \(\ell\), with \(e=v_\ell(v)\), and put \(R_0=F(t)/(t-1)^8\). Then:

  1. \(v_\ell(R_0)=2e\), \(v_\ell(t-1)=-e\), and \(R_0\) is a square in \(\mathbb Q_\ell\);
  2. for every integer \(N\) the set of \(x\in\mathbb Q_\ell\) with \(|1-R_0x^2|_\ell\le\ell^{-N}\) is non-empty and open in \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); more precisely there are \(m\in\mathbb Z\) and \(k,M\in\mathbb N\) such that every rational \(q\) with \(|q-m/\ell^k|_\ell\le\ell^{-M}\) satisfies \(|1-R_0q^2|_\ell\le\ell^{-N}\), that is \(v_\ell(1-R_0q^2)\ge N\) (or \(1-R_0q^2=0\)). In particular such a rational \(q\) exists.

Proof sketch. (1) With \(F(u,v)\) the contact numerator, \(R_0=F(u,v)\,v^2/(u-v)^8\). The numbers \(u-cv\) and \(u-v\) are \(\ell\)-units, so \(v_\ell(R_0)=2e\) and \(v_\ell(t-1)=v_\ell(u-v)-v_\ell(v)=-e\). Since \(v\mid F(u,v)-u^6\), the unit \(X=F(u,v)\) is congruent to \(u^6\) modulo \(\ell^e\); Hensel's lemma for \(Y^2-X\) at \(Y=u^3\) applies because \(|u^6-X|_\ell\le\ell^{-e}<|2u^3|_\ell^2\) (for \(\ell=2\) this needs \(e\ge3\)). So \(X=y^2\) in \(\mathbb Z_\ell\), and \(R_0=z^2\) with \(z=vy/(u-v)^4\). (2) Put \(w=z^{-1}\), so that \(R_0w^2=1\). If \(|x-w|_\ell\le|w|_\ell\min(1,\ell^{-N})\), then \(1-R_0x^2=R_0(w-x)(w+x)\) has absolute value at most \(\ell^{-N}\), by the ultrametric inequality. The set is the preimage of a closed ball, which is open in \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); and the rationals \(m/\ell^k\) are dense in \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), which gives the rational ball.

The note's hypothesis \(F(t)>0\) is not needed for these statements; it only fixes \(\eta=1\).

Let \(p\) be a prime, \(\eta\in\{1,-1\}\), \(\ell\in\mathbb Q\) nonzero with \(v_p(\ell)\ge0\), and \(t\in\mathbb Q\setminus(\mathcal C\cup\{1\})\) with \(R_0=\eta F(t)/(t-1)^8\). Suppose that for some \(e\in\mathbb N\) $\(v_p(R_0)=2e,\qquad v_p(t-1)=-e .\)$ Let \(q\in\mathbb Q\) with \(a=1-R_0q^2\ne0\) and $\(v_p(a)\ge23e+v_p(12)+2,\)$ and let \(D_{gj}\in K_0\) (\(1\le g\le6\), \(1\le j\le12\)) be integral at every prime of \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]\) above \(p\). Form \(R=\ell^2a^2R_0\), \(C_{gj}\), \(W_g\) and \(\Theta\) as in the slope predicate, and assume \(\Theta\ne0\). Then the pole input \(B=R/\Theta^2\) has \(v_p(B)\ge4\).

Proof sketch. Measure valuations above \(p\) on the scale of \(v_p\). Then \(v(C_{gj})\ge-2ek_j+e(k_j+1)=-e(k_j-1)\), and \(v(R)=2v_p(\ell)+2v_p(a)+2e\), so \(v(RC_{gj}^2)\ge2v_p(a)+2e-2e(k_j-1)\ge2v_p(a)-46e>v_p(12)\) for \(k_j\in\{1,25\}\). Each factor \(1+RC_{gj}^2\), hence each \(W_g\) and \(W_g^{-1}\), is \(\equiv1\) to valuation \(>v_p(12)\) at every place above \(p\), so \(\Theta-12=\operatorname{Tr}\sum_g(W_g^{-1}-1)\) has valuation \(>v_p(12)\) and \(v_p(\Theta)=v_p(12)\). Finally \(v_p(B)=v(R)-2v_p(12)\ge2v_p(a)-2v_p(12)\ge4\). This is the manuscript's real-place argument (\(a\to0\)) transported to \(\mathbb Q_p\).

docs.title: Weak approximation with residue targets
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.weak_approx_targets ZInQ.Mult.padicNorm_le_zpow_iff_ap ZInQ.Mult.exists_crt_idempotent_ap ZInQ.Mult.padicNorm_div_pow_mul_le_ap

Let \(S\) and \(S'\) be disjoint finite sets of primes. For \(p\in S\) let \(m_p\in\mathbb Z\) and \(k_p,n_p\in\mathbb N\). Let \(x_0\in\mathbb R\), \(\delta>0\) and \(X\subset\mathbb R\) finite. Then there is a nonzero \(q\in\mathbb Q\) with \(q\notin X\), \(|q-x_0|<\delta\), $\(\Bigl|q-\frac{m_p}{p^{k_p}}\Bigr|_p\le p^{-n_p}\quad(p\in S),\qquad v_p(q)\ge0\quad(p\in S').\)$

This generalizes the weak approximation used by the original completeness proof, where every target is \(0\): route AP needs \(q\) close to a \(p\)-adic square root of \(R_0^{-1}\) at the old primes where a slope has a pole.

Proof sketch. Let \(K=\sum_{p\in S}(n_p+k_p)\). By the Chinese remainder theorem choose integers \(E_p\equiv1\pmod{p^K}\) with \(E_p\equiv0\pmod{p'^K}\) for the other \(p'\in S\), and put \(y=\sum_{p\in S}(m_p/p^{k_p})E_p\); then \(|y-m_p/p^{k_p}|_p\le p^{-n_p}\) and \(y\) is integral at \(S'\). Weak approximation for the parameter \(q\), applied to the target \(x_0-y\) with valuations \(\ge K\) on \(S\), \(\ge0\) on \(S'\), and the excluded set \(\{-y\}\cup(X-y)\), gives \(q'\); take \(q=y+q'\).

Let \(t\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy conditions 1, 2′, 3, 4 (for some \(B_0\)), and let \(P(t)\) be its set of odd contact primes outside \(S_b\). Let \(\eta\in\{1,-1\}\), \(R_0=\eta F(t)/(t-1)^8\), let \(\ell e0\) with \(v_p(\ell)=E_p\) for \(p\in S_b\) and \(v_p(\ell)=0\) for every other prime, and let \(q\in\mathbb Q\) with \(a=1-R_0q^2 e0\) such that

  • for every \(p\in S_b\), either the bounds of condition 2 hold at \(p\) and \(v_p(q)\ge C_p\), or there is \(e\in\mathbb N\) with \(v_p(F(t)/(t-1)^8)=2e\), \(v_p(t-1)=-e\) and \(v_p(a)\ge23e+v_p(12)+2\);
  • \(v_p(q)\ge0\) for every \(p\in P(t)\).

Let \(D_{gj}\in K_0\) satisfy (i) and (ii) of the valuations of the pole input of a completed slope (integral above \(S_b\); for each \(p\in P(t)\) some group and place with \(v_{\mathfrak p}(D_{gj})\ge k_j\)), and assume \(W_g e0\) and \(\Theta e0\). Then \(B=R/\Theta^2\) satisfies:

  1. \(v_p(B)\ge4\) for every \(p\in S_b\), in particular for every \(p\in S_0\);
  2. \(v_p(B)=1\) for every \(p\in P(t)\);
  3. \(v_p(B)\) is even for every other prime \(p otin S_b\);

and the reduced denominator of \(B\) is a perfect square.

The only change from the original lemma is part 1: \(v_p(B)\ge4\) replaces \(v_p(B)\ge103C_p+8\), which is all that pole completeness and the square denominator need.

Proof sketch. At \(p\in S_b\) with the first alternative, the original argument applies verbatim. With the second alternative, Lemma P(3) gives \(v_p(B)\ge4\); its integrality hypothesis is (i), and \(v_p(\ell)=E_p\ge0\). At \(p\in P(t)\), conditions 1 and 3 alone give \(v_p(F(t)/(t-1)^8)=1\) and \(v_p(t-1)=0\), and the original argument applies. At the other primes the parity argument is unchanged, since \(a\) enters \(R\) squared.

Assume pole completeness. Let \(n_1,n_2\in\mathbb Z\), \(n_3=n_1n_2\) and \(c=(c_*,c_*n_1,c_*n_2,c_*n_3)\). If \(t\in\mathbb Q\) satisfies conditions 1, 2′, 3, 4 (for some \(B_0\)), then $\(\mathrm{Slope}(t,\ell_0;c).\)$

Proof sketch. As for the completeness of the slope certificate for a true triple, except for the choice of \(q\). Choose \(\eta\) with \(R_0=\eta F(t)/(t-1)^8>0\), the shifts \(h_g\) at the selected odd contact primes, the test values \(D_{gj}\) and \(\varepsilon\) from the positivity lemma, exactly as before. Let \(S_{ m pole}\subseteq S_b\) be the old primes at which field 2′ uses its second alternative; there \(F(t)>0\), so \(\eta=1\). For \(p\in S_{ m pole}\) Lemma P(2) with \(N=23e_p+v_p(12)+2\), \(e_p=v_p( ext{denominator of }t)\), gives a rational ball \(|q-m_p/p^{k_p}|_p\le p^{-n_p}\) on which \(v_p(1-R_0q^2)\ge N\). Weak approximation with residue targets chooses a nonzero \(q otin\{\pm R_0^{-1/2}\}\) in these balls, with \(v_p(q)\ge C_p\) at the other primes of \(S_b\) (target \(0\)), \(v_p(q)\ge0\) at the selected primes, and \(q\) so close to \(R_0^{-1/2}\) that \(0<|a|<\varepsilon\). Then \(W_g e0\), \(\Theta e0\) and \(0<B<1/2\); the tests are integral above \(S_b\) because every shift is a multiple of \(M_0\); and the valuations of the pole input under field 2′ give \(v_p(B)\ge4\) on \(S_0\) and a square reduced denominator, with Lemma P(1) supplying \(v_p(R_0)=2e_p\) and \(v_p(t-1)=-e_p\) at \(S_{ m pole}\). docs.title: Proposition AP
docs.text: A progression of good slope primes long enough to contain the fourteen numerators of the slopes \(u/v\) and \(A+10-u/v\) gives, with the constant slope \(-10\), a representation of \(A\).

docs.title: The statement 22P_AP: long progressions of good slope primes
docs.text:
ZInQ.GoodPrimeAP

The statement 22P_AP is the assertion that for every \(K\in\mathbb N\) there are integers \(x\ge1\) and \(v\ge1\) such that each of the \(K+1\) numbers $\(x,\ x+v,\ x+2v,\ \dots,\ x+Kv\)$ is a good slope prime larger than every prime of \(S_b=S_{\rm ht}\cup\mathcal H\).

It mentions neither an integer to be represented, nor the catalogue multipliers, nor valuations at the old primes, except through the lower bound \(\max S_b\); and it places no condition on the common difference \(v\). It replaces the twenty-two-prime pattern as the arithmetic input of the completeness of the multiplication template. It was introduced as a hypothesis and is now proved: it follows from Szemerédi's theorem in the primes and the positive density of the good slope primes (22P_AP from Green–Tao and Proposition D), both proved here.

docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.goodSlopeAP_of_progression ZInQ.Mult.contactPoly_pos_of_pos ZInQ.Mult.contactPoly_pos_of_lt ZInQ.Mult.mem_patternShifts_bounds

Let \(u,v\in\mathbb Z\) with \(v>0\). Suppose that for each \(b\in\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\) the number \(|u-bv|\) is a prime larger than every prime of \(S_b\), that for each \(b\in\mathcal C\) it is a good slope prime, and that \(F(u/v)>0\). Then \(t=u/v\) satisfies conditions 1, 2′, 3, 4 for \(B_0=0\).

In addition, \(F(t)>0\) whenever \(t>0\) or \(t<-60\).

Proof sketch. A prime dividing \(u\) and \(v\) would divide the seven numbers \(u-bv\), which are distinct primes, so \(u/v\) is in lowest terms; the numbers are nonzero, so \(t\notin\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\). Let \(p\in S_b\) and \(e=v_p(v)\); all seven numbers are \(p\)-units. If \(e\le B_p\) then \(v_p(t-1)=-e\) and \(v_p(F(t)/(t-1)^8)=2e\) satisfy the bounds of condition 2 (when \(e=0\) both vanish). Otherwise \(e\ge B_p+1\ge2\), and \(e\ge5\) at \(p=2\), so \(t\) satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma P at \(p\), and \(F(t)>0\) is assumed: field 2′ holds. Conditions 3 and 4 are the argument of the two-slope pattern: an odd contact prime of \(t\) outside \(S_b\) divides some \(u-cv\), so it is that good slope prime, with contact valuation \(1\), and there are at most six of them. The sign statement holds because the six factors \(t-c\) of \(F(t)\) are all positive, or all negative.

docs.title: Proposition AP: progressions of good slope primes give the slope representation
docs.text:
ZInQ.Mult.slopeRepresentationAP_of_goodPrimeAP

Assume 22P_AP. Then the slope representation under field 2′ holds: every integer \(A\) is a sum of three rationals satisfying conditions 1, 2′, 3, 4 for \(B_0=0\).

Proof sketch. Put \(A'=A+10\), \(T=\mathcal C\cup\{1\}\) and \(S_A^+=T\cup(A'-T)\), so that \(\max S_A^+=\max(1,A'+60)\) and \(\min S_A^+=\min(-60,A'-1)\). Take a progression \(x+jv\) (\(0\le j\le K_A\), \(K_A=\max S_A^+-\min S_A^+\)) of good slope primes above \(\max S_b\) and put \(u=x+(\max S_A^+)v\). For \(c'\in S_A^+\) the number \(u-c'v=x+(\max S_A^+-c')v\) is a term of the progression. Put \(t_1=u/v\), \(t_2=A'-u/v=(A'v-u)/v\) and \(t_3=-10\), so \(t_1+t_2+t_3=A\). Then \(t_1>\max S_A^+\ge1\) and \(t_2=A'-\max S_A^+-x/v<-60\), so \(F(t_1),F(t_2)>0\). The numerators of \(t_1\) are \(u-bv\) and those of \(t_2\) are \(-(u-(A'-b)v)\) (\(b\in T\)), all terms of the progression, so both slopes satisfy field 2′ by the lemma on slopes with prime numerators. The constant \(-10\) is a good slope (as in the two-slope pattern), hence satisfies field 2′.

Only fourteen terms of the progression are used. Field 2′ cannot be avoided: a progression of \(K+1\) primes larger than \(K+1\) has its difference divisible by every prime at most \(K+1\), and \(K_A\) grows with \(|A|\).

docs.title: 22P_AP from Green–Tao
docs.text: The good slope primes have positive relative density (Proposition D), and every such set of primes contains arbitrarily long progressions (Szemerédi's theorem in the primes).

docs.title: 22P_AP from Green–Tao and Proposition D
docs.text:
ZInQ.goodPrimeAP_of_greenTaoDense

Assume Szemerédi's theorem in the primes (every set of primes of positive relative upper density contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length) and that the good slope primes have positive relative upper density in the primes. Then 22P_AP holds.

Both assumptions are theorems here (Szemerédi's theorem in the primes, Proposition D), so 22P_AP holds unconditionally.

Proof sketch. Let \(M=\max S_b\) and \(G'\) the set of good slope primes larger than \(M\). The good slope primes up to \(N\) number at most \(|G'\cap[0,N]|+M+1\). If \(\delta\pi(N)\) is at most the number of good slope primes up to \(N\) for infinitely many \(N\), then, since \(\pi(N)\to\infty\), \(M+1\le(\delta/2)\pi(N)\) for all large \(N\), and \((\delta/2)\pi(N)\le|G'\cap[0,N]|\) for infinitely many \(N\). So \(G'\) is a set of primes of positive relative upper density, and Szemerédi's theorem in the primes gives, for every \(K\), a progression \(a+bj\) (\(j\le K\), \(b\ge1\)) in \(G'\); its first term is a prime, so \(a\ge1\).

docs.title: Pole completeness from certified rank (Route K)
Pole completeness from certified rank (Route K)
docs.text:
The manuscript's pole polynomial puts two points on curves \(y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+3\ell)\), and the manuscript derives pole completeness from its restricted converse theorem, whose proof uses Kato's Euler system, Waldspurger's formula, Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein and Nekovář's Selmer complexes. Route K changes the polynomial to the congruent number curves \(C_\ell:y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+\ell)\); the elementary direction, Lemma 5.1, is unchanged (the one-sided pole obstruction). This chapter proves pole completeness for the new polynomial from one narrow hypothesis on congruent number curves, the certified rank hypothesis CR₃, by an explicit descent: for every admissible input \(B\) it produces two curves \(C_n\) and \(C_{n\theta}\) whose 2-Selmer groups, written as an \(\mathbb F_2\)-linear system in Legendre symbols, have dimension \(3\) and contain the class \(\beta\). CR₃ turns these certificates into rational points, and two such points give a zero of the pole polynomial.

Throughout, \(C_d\) is the curve \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\); it depends only on \(d^2\).

18 fully proved

docs.title: Configurations and the Selmer system
docs.text:
An odd squarefree \(d>0\) is recorded by its primes, their classes modulo \(8\) and their Legendre symbols; Proposition 0 writes the 2-Selmer group of \(C_d\) as the solutions of a linear system in these data. The system makes sense for any configuration, realized by a number or not.

Two operations shrink a configuration and carry its solutions bijectively onto those of the smaller one, keeping \(a_0,a_1,b_0,b_1\): removing a glue prime with a single partner, and gluing a set of primes into one virtual prime through glue primes. At the end of the reduction stands a configuration of two primes, whose system is computed directly.

docs.title: Configurations
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Config ZInQ.RouteK.oddClasses ZInQ.RouteK.lam8 ZInQ.RouteK.mu8 ZInQ.RouteK.Config.lam ZInQ.RouteK.Config.mu ZInQ.RouteK.Config.prodClass ZInQ.RouteK.Config.bit_symm_of_cls_one

For an odd class \(c\) modulo \(8\) put \(\lambda(c)=[c\equiv3\pmod4]\) and \(\mu(c)=[c\equiv3,5\pmod8]\), as elements of \(\mathbb F_2\).

A configuration \(\mathcal C\) on a finite set \(S\) of symbols (the "primes" of \(\mathcal C\)) consists of a class \(c_x\in\{1,3,5,7\}\subset\mathbb Z/8\) for every \(x\in S\) and a bit \([y/x]\in\mathbb F_2\) for every pair \(x\ne y\) of elements of \(S\), subject to reciprocity: $\([x/y]+[y/x]=\lambda_x\lambda_y\qquad(x\ne y),\)$ where \(\lambda_x=\lambda(c_x)\) and \(\mu_x=\mu(c_x)\). Bits \([x/x]\) on the diagonal play no role. The product class of \(\mathcal C\) is \(c(\mathcal C)=\prod_{x\in S}c_x\) modulo \(8\); it is again odd. A symbol \(r\) with \(c_r=1\) is a glue prime; for it \(\lambda_r=\mu_r=0\), so reciprocity makes its bits symmetric, \([r/x]=[x/r]\).

The model is an odd squarefree \(d>0\): its primes with their classes modulo \(8\) and their Legendre symbols form a configuration, by quadratic reciprocity (the configuration of an odd number). Configurations that no number realizes occur only as intermediate steps of the descent.

docs.title: The Selmer system of a configuration
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Config.IsSol ZInQ.RouteK.Config.sols ZInQ.RouteK.Unknowns ZInQ.RouteK.Unknowns.first ZInQ.RouteK.Config.monsky ZInQ.RouteK.Config.E1 ZInQ.RouteK.Config.E2 ZInQ.RouteK.twoAdicRows ZInQ.RouteK.Config.D ZInQ.RouteK.dot

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a configuration on \(S\). The Selmer system \(\Sigma(\mathcal C)\) has the unknowns \(a_0,a_1,b_0,b_1\in\mathbb F_2\) and \(u,v\in\mathbb F_2^S\). Write \((Ku)_x=\sum_{y\ne x}[y/x](u_y+u_x)\) (Monsky's matrix) and \(\lambda\cdot u=\sum_x\lambda_xu_x\), and likewise \(\mu\cdot u\), \(\lambda\cdot v\). The equations are $\(\begin{aligned} (\mathrm{E1}_x)\quad&(Ku)_x+\lambda_xv_x=a_0\lambda_x+a_1\mu_x&&(x\in S),\\ (\mathrm{E2}_x)\quad&\mu_xu_x+(Kv)_x+\lambda_xv_x=b_0\lambda_x+b_1\mu_x&&(x\in S),\\ (\mathrm R)\quad&a_0=b_0, \end{aligned}\)$ and the two rows (D) for the product class \(c=c(\mathcal C)\):

\(c\) rows (D) \(1\) \(a_1=0\), \(\mu\cdot u=0\), \(\lambda\cdot v=\lambda\cdot u\) \(3\) \(a_1=0\), \(b_0=\lambda\cdot v\), \(b_1=\mu\cdot u\) \(5\) \(a_1=0\), \(b_1=\mu\cdot u\), \(\lambda\cdot v=\lambda\cdot u\) \(7\) \(a_1=0\), \(\mu\cdot u=0\), \(b_0=\lambda\cdot v\)

Its solutions form a finite set (an \(\mathbb F_2\)-subspace); "dimension \(3\)" means exactly \(8\) solutions. The first coordinate of a solution is \((a_0,a_1,u)\), standing for the class \(a=(-1)^{a_0}2^{a_1}\prod_xx^{u_x}\); the solution stands for the pair of classes \((a,b)\) with \(b=(-1)^{b_0}2^{b_1}\prod_xx^{v_x}\).

Every solution has \(a_1=0\), and the system depends only on the classes and the off-diagonal bits of \(\mathcal C\).

For the configuration of an odd squarefree \(d>0\), Proposition 0 (descent-alt §4.1) identifies the solutions of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\), through \((a,b)\), with the 2-Selmer group of \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\): the rows E1, E2 are the local conditions at the primes of \(d\), (R) the real place and (D) the place \(2\). Proposition 0 is formalized in its own chapter (Proposition 0); the descent of this chapter does not use it, and it connects the system to rational points only through the certified rank hypothesis and its Selmer form.

docs.text:

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a configuration on \(S\), let \(r\in S\) be a glue prime (\(c_r=1\)), and let \(y\in S\setminus\{r\}\) be its partner: \([r/y]=1\) and \([r/z]=0\) for every \(z\notin\{r,y\}\). Let \(\mathcal C\setminus r\) be the restriction of \(\mathcal C\) to \(S\setminus\{r\}\). Then a tuple \((a_0,a_1,b_0,b_1,u,v)\) solves \(\Sigma(\mathcal C)\) if and only if \(u_r=u_y\), \(v_r=v_y\) and its restriction to \(S\setminus\{r\}\) solves \(\Sigma(\mathcal C\setminus r)\). Consequently forgetting \(u_r,v_r\) is a bijection from the solutions of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C)\) onto those of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C\setminus r)\); it keeps \(a_0,a_1,b_0,b_1\), and its inverse sets \(u_r=u_y\), \(v_r=v_y\). In particular the two systems have the same number of solutions.

The same holds for a family: if \(S=S_0\sqcup R\) where every \(r\in R\) is a glue prime with a partner \(y(r)\in S_0\) and \([r/z]=0\) for every \(z\notin\{r,y(r)\}\) (other elements of \(R\) included), then restriction to \(S_0\) is a bijection from the solutions of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C)\) onto those of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C|_{S_0})\), inverted by \(u_r=u_{y(r)}\), \(v_r=v_{y(r)}\).

Proof sketch. Since \(c_r=1\), \(\lambda_r=\mu_r=0\) and \([z/r]=[r/z]\), so \(\mathrm{E1}_r\) reads \([y/r](u_y+u_r)=u_y+u_r=0\) and \(\mathrm{E2}_r\) reads \(v_y+v_r=0\). The unknowns \(u_r,v_r\) occur elsewhere only in \(\mathrm{E1}_y\), \(\mathrm{E2}_y\), through the terms \([r/y](u_r+u_y)\) and \([r/y](v_r+v_y)\), which vanish once \(\mathrm{E1}_r\), \(\mathrm{E2}_r\) hold; every other row is the corresponding row of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C\setminus r)\). The product class does not change because \(c_r=1\), and \(r\) contributes nothing to \(\lambda\cdot u\), \(\mu\cdot u\), \(\lambda\cdot v\), so the rows (D) and (R) agree. The single-prime statement is the family statement with \(R=\{r\}\), after reindexing.

docs.title: The gluing lemma
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Config.Gluing.bijOn ZInQ.RouteK.Config.Gluing ZInQ.RouteK.Config.glue ZInQ.RouteK.Config.glueMap ZInQ.RouteK.Config.glueLift ZInQ.RouteK.Config.Gluing.solsEquiv ZInQ.RouteK.Config.Gluing.solsEquiv_symm_apply ZInQ.RouteK.Config.Gluing.card_sols ZInQ.RouteK.Config.glue_prodClass

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a configuration on \(S=S'\sqcup\{g\}\sqcup G\sqcup R\), where \(R=\{r_\ell:\ell\in G\}\) consists of glue primes (\(c_{r_\ell}=1\)) with $\([r_\ell/\ell]=[r_\ell/g]=1,\qquad[r_\ell/z]=0\text{ for every other }z\in S .\)$ Put \(X=G\cup\{g\}\). Let \(\mathcal C^*\) be the configuration on \(S'\sqcup\{g^*\}\) that agrees with \(\mathcal C\) on \(S'\) and has $\(c_{g^*}=c_g\prod_{\ell\in G}c_\ell,\qquad[y/g^*]=\sum_{x\in X}[y/x],\qquad [g^*/y]=\sum_{x\in X}[x/y]\qquad(y\in S');\)$ it satisfies reciprocity because \(\lambda\) is additive on odd classes, and \(c(\mathcal C^*)=c(\mathcal C)\). Then the map \(\Phi\) that keeps \(a_0,a_1,b_0,b_1\) and \(u|_{S'}\), \(v|_{S'}\) and sends \(u_g,v_g\) to \(u_{g^*},v_{g^*}\) is a bijection from the solutions of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C)\) onto those of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C^*)\). Its inverse sets \(u_x=u_{g^*}\), \(v_x=v_{g^*}\) for \(x\in X\) and, for \(\ell\in G\), $\(\begin{aligned} u_{r_\ell}&=\sum_{y\in S'}[y/\ell](u_y+u_{g^*})+u_{g^*}+\lambda_\ell(v_{g^*}+a_0),&&(2.1)\\ v_{r_\ell}&=\sum_{y\in S'}[y/\ell](v_y+v_{g^*})+v_{g^*}+\mu_\ell u_{g^*}+\lambda_\ell(v_{g^*}+b_0)+b_1\mu_\ell.&&(2.2) \end{aligned}\)$ In particular the two systems have the same number of solutions.

Proof sketch. (1) For \(\ell\in G\) the row \(\mathrm{E1}_{r_\ell}\) reads \((u_\ell+u_{r_\ell})+(u_g+u_{r_\ell})=0\), so \(u_\ell=u_g\); likewise \(\mathrm{E2}_{r_\ell}\) gives \(v_\ell=v_g\). (2) At \(y\in S'\) no glue prime is linked to \(y\), and with \(u\) constant on \(X\) the terms from \(X\) in \((Ku)_y\) add up to \([g^*/y](u_g+u_y)\); so \(\mathrm{E1}_y\), \(\mathrm{E2}_y\) are the rows of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C^*)\). (3) The unknown \(u_{r_\ell}\) occurs only in \(\mathrm{E1}_{r_\ell}\), \(\mathrm{E1}_\ell\) and \(\mathrm{E1}_g\); the row \(\mathrm{E1}_\ell\) determines it, which is (2.1) (all solutions have \(a_1=0\)), and the sum \(\mathrm{E1}_g+\sum_\ell\mathrm{E1}_\ell\), in which the glue unknowns and the terms between two elements of \(X\) cancel, is the row \(\mathrm{E1}_{g^*}\). The \(\mathrm{E2}\) rows behave the same way and give (2.2). (4) The product class is unchanged because \(c_{r_\ell}=1\), and \(\lambda\cdot u=\lambda|_{S'}\cdot u|_{S'}+\lambda_{g^*}u_{g^*}\), and likewise for \(\mu\cdot u\) and \(\lambda\cdot v\), so (D) and (R) agree. Hence \(\Phi\) maps solutions to solutions; the formulas of the inverse map solutions back, and the two maps are mutually inverse by step 1, (2.1) and (2.2).

Let \(\mathcal C_0\) be a configuration on two symbols \(\{p^*,q_0\}\) with \(c_{p^*}=7\) and \(c_{q_0}=3\), and put \(x=[q_0/p^*]\) (so \([p^*/q_0]=x+1\)). Then the solutions of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_0)\) are exactly the tuples with \(a_0,u_{p^*},u_{q_0}\) free and, with \(w=u_{p^*}+u_{q_0}\), $\(v_{p^*}=a_0+xw,\quad v_{q_0}=a_0+(x+1)w,\quad a_1=0,\quad b_0=a_0,\quad b_1=u_{q_0}.\)$ So \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_0)\) has exactly \(8\) solutions (dimension \(3\)), and for each \(a_0\in\mathbb F_2\) it has the solution $\(\sigma_0:\quad u=(u_{p^*},u_{q_0})=(1,0),\quad v_{p^*}=a_0+x,\quad v_{q_0}=a_0+x+1,\quad a_1=0,\quad b_0=a_0,\quad b_1=0,\)$ whose first coordinate \((a_0,0,\mathbf 1_{p^*})\) is the class \((-1)^{a_0}p^*\).

Proof sketch. Here \(\lambda=(1,1)\), \(\mu=(0,1)\) and \(c(\mathcal C_0)=21\equiv5\). Then \((Ku)_{p^*}=xw\) and \((Ku)_{q_0}=(x+1)w\), and the rows are \(xw+v_{p^*}=a_0\), \((x+1)w+v_{q_0}=a_0\), \(x(v_{p^*}+v_{q_0})+v_{p^*}=b_0\), \(u_{q_0}+(x+1)(v_{p^*}+v_{q_0})+v_{q_0}=b_0+b_1\), \(a_0=b_0\), and the rows (D) for \(c=5\): \(a_1=0\), \(b_1=u_{q_0}\), \(v_{p^*}+v_{q_0}=w\). The \(\mathrm E1\) rows give \(v_{p^*}\) and \(v_{q_0}\), hence \(v_{p^*}+v_{q_0}=w\); substituting, the \(\mathrm E2\) rows follow from (R) and \(b_1=u_{q_0}\). The equivalence is a finite check over the nine bits \(x,a_0,a_1,b_0,b_1,u_{p^*},u_{q_0},v_{p^*},v_{q_0}\), done by the kernel.

For a prime \(p\) and an integer \(a\), the residue bit \([a/p]\in\mathbb F_2\) is \(0\) if \(a\) is a square modulo \(p\) and \(1\) otherwise; for \(a\) prime to \(p\) it is the bit of the Legendre symbol, \((a/p)=(-1)^{[a/p]}\), and for \(p\mid a\) it is \(0\) (this value is never used). Put \(\lambda_p=[-1/p]\) and \(\mu_p=[2/p]\). For an integer \(\beta\) put \(s(\beta)=[\beta<0]\in\mathbb F_2\), and let \(P(\beta)\) be the set of primes dividing \(\beta\).

docs.title: Quadratic reciprocity in residue bits
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.legBit_reciprocity ZInQ.RouteK.lamBit_eq ZInQ.RouteK.muBit_eq ZInQ.RouteK.legBit_mul ZInQ.RouteK.legBit_prod ZInQ.RouteK.legBit_eq_zero_iff ZInQ.RouteK.legBit_symm_of_one_mod_four ZInQ.RouteK.legBit_symm_of_three_mod_four ZInQ.RouteK.legBit_eq_iff_legendreSym ZInQ.RouteK.natCast_zmod_ne_zero_of_prime_ne

Let \(p\ne q\) be odd primes. Then $\([q/p]+[p/q]=\lambda_p\lambda_q,\qquad\lambda_p=[p\equiv3\pmod4],\qquad \mu_p=[p\equiv3,5\pmod8],\)$ and \([ab/p]=[a/p]+[b/p]\) for integers \(a,b\) prime to \(p\) (so the bit of a finite product of integers prime to \(p\) is the sum of their bits). For \(a\) prime to \(p\), \([a/p]=0\) if and only if \((a/p)=1\); more generally, for \(b\in\mathbb F_2\), \([a/p]=b\) if and only if \((a/p)=(-1)^b\). A prime \(q\ne p\) is prime to \(p\).

These are quadratic reciprocity, its two supplementary laws and the multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol, rewritten in \(\mathbb F_2\). In particular, for a prime \(r\equiv1\pmod4\) the bits are symmetric, \([y/r]=[r/y]\), and for \(q\equiv3\pmod4\), \([y/q]=[q/y]+\lambda_y\).

Proof sketch. Quadratic reciprocity gives \((q/p)(p/q)=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}2\frac{q-1}2}\), the first supplement \((-1/p)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\) and the second \((2/p)=1\) exactly when \(p\equiv\pm1\pmod8\). Taking the bits of these \(\pm1\) identities turns products into sums.

Let \((f_k)_{k\in K}\) be a finite family of distinct odd primes. Its configuration has the symbols \(K\), the classes \(c_k=f_k\bmod 8\) and the bits \([f_a/f_b]\) (the residue bit of \(f_a\) modulo \(f_b\)); reciprocity is quadratic reciprocity in residue bits. For an odd positive integer \(d\), the configuration \(\mathcal C_d\) of \(d\) is that of the primes dividing \(d\).

For an integer \(a\), the class of \(a\) in the coordinates of \(d\) is \((s(a),0,u)\) with \(u_p=[p\mid a]\) for the primes \(p\mid d\); when \(a\) is a squarefree odd divisor of \(d\) it is the first coordinate of \(a=(-1)^{s(a)}\prod_{p\mid a}p\).

A Selmer certificate for \((d,a)\), with \(d\) odd and positive, is the statement that \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) has exactly \(8\) solutions and that one of them has first coordinate the class of \(a\). Through Proposition 0 it says that \(\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)=3\) and that \(a\) is a first Kummer coordinate of \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\), a certificate of Selmer type in the sense of slot-k §1.2.

docs.title: The inputs \(\beta\) and \(\theta\)
docs.text: An admissible input \(B\) and a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) determine the squarefree parts \(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\) and \(\theta=\mathrm{sqf}(m(m-B))\). The multiplier is chosen so that \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), and \(\theta\) then has four local properties.

docs.title: Admissible inputs, the squarefree part, \(\beta\) and \(\theta\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.sqf ZInQ.RouteK.betaOf ZInQ.RouteK.thetaOf ZInQ.RouteK.Admissible ZInQ.RouteK.sqfInt ZInQ.RouteK.sqfNat ZInQ.RouteK.sqf_spec ZInQ.RouteK.sqf_eq_of_eq_mul_sq ZInQ.RouteK.poleCompleteness_iff_admissible

A rational \(B\) is admissible if its reduced denominator is a square, \(0<B<1/2\), and \(v_p(B)\ge4\) for every \(p\in S_0=\{2,3,5,7,13\}\). These are the hypotheses of pole completeness, which therefore says that every admissible \(B\) satisfies \(\Phi(B)\).

The signed squarefree part of an integer \(N\) is \(\mathrm{sqf}(N)=\operatorname{sign}(N)\prod_{p:\,v_p(N)\text{ odd}}p\), and that of a rational \(x=a/b\) in lowest terms (\(b>0\)) is \(\mathrm{sqf}(x)=\mathrm{sqf}(ab)\). For \(x\ne0\), \(\mathrm{sqf}(x)\) is squarefree, \(x=\mathrm{sqf}(x)\,t^2\) for some nonzero rational \(t\), and it is the only squarefree integer with this property; \(\mathrm{sqf}(0)=0\).

A signed divisor of \(2730=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\) is an integer \(m\), of either sign, with \(m\mid2730\). For a rational \(B\) and such an \(m\) put $\(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB),\qquad\theta=\mathrm{sqf}\bigl(m(m-B)\bigr).\)$

docs.title: The multiplier lemma
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.exists_multiplier_pos ZInQ.RouteK.exists_multiplier

Let \(B\) be a nonzero rational. Then there is a positive divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) such that \(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\) is odd and \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\). In particular every admissible \(B\) has a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) with \(\beta\) odd and \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\).

Proof sketch. Write \(B=\mathrm{sqf}(B)\,t^2\) and \(\mathrm{sqf}(B)=2^fb'\) with \(f\in\{0,1\}\) and \(b'\) odd. Multiplication by an odd class permutes the odd classes modulo \(8\), so some \(m_0\in\{1,3,5,7\}\) has \(m_0|b'|\equiv7\pmod8\); put \(m=2^fm_0\). Then \(mB=m_0b'\,(2^ft)^2\), so \(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(m_0b')\) is odd. Since \(m_0\) is \(1\) or a prime, \(\beta\) differs from \(m_0b'\) at most by an odd square factor, and odd squares are \(\equiv1\pmod8\), so \(|\beta|\equiv m_0|b'|\equiv7\pmod8\). Admissibility is not needed beyond \(B\ne0\).

docs.title: The properties (θ1)–(θ4)
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.theta_props ZInQ.RouteK.theta1 ZInQ.RouteK.theta2 ZInQ.RouteK.theta2_isCoprime ZInQ.RouteK.theta3 ZInQ.RouteK.theta4

Let \(B\) be admissible, \(m\) a signed divisor of \(2730\), \( eta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\) and \( heta=\mathrm{sqf}(m(m-B))\). Then:

  • (θ1) \( heta>0\), \( heta\equiv1\pmod8\) and \(\gcd( heta,2730)=1\);
  • (θ2) no prime divides both \( eta\) and \( heta\);
  • (θ3) \(( eta/\ell)=1\) for every prime \(\ell\mid heta\);
  • (θ4) \(( heta/p)=1\) for every odd prime \(p\mid eta\).

Property (θ4) also holds at \(p=2\), since \( heta\) is odd.

Proof sketch. Write \(B=a/k^2\) in lowest terms, so \(0<2a<k^2\) and, for \(p\in S_0\), \(p mid k\) and \(p^4\mid a\). With \(M=mk\) there are nonzero integers \(s,c\) with $\(ma= eta s^2,\qquad heta c^2=M^2-ma,\)$ the integer form of \( heta c^2=1- eta t^2\), \( eta t^2=B/m\). The local computation is one lemma: if \( heta c^2=(p^eM_1)^2-X\) with \( heta\) squarefree, \(p mid M_1\) and \(p^{2e+j}\mid X\) for some \(j\ge1\), then \(p mid heta\) and \( heta c_1^2\equiv M_1^2\pmod{p^j}\) for some \(c_1\) prime to \(p\). At \(p\in S_0\) it applies with \(j=3\) (\(p^4\mid a\), and \(p^2 mid m\)), which gives \(p mid heta\) and, at \(p=2\), \( heta\equiv1\pmod8\), because odd squares are \(\equiv1\pmod8\); and \( heta>0\) because \(M^2-ma=m^2k^2(1-B/m)\) with \(|B/m|\le B<1/2\). This is (θ1). At a prime \(p\mid eta\) outside \(S_0\): \(p\mid ma\) and \(p mid m\), so \(p\mid a\) and \(p mid k\); the lemma applies with \(e=0\), \(j=1\), so \(p mid heta\) and \( heta\) is a nonzero square modulo \(p\); at a prime of \( eta\) in \(S_0\) the first case gives the same. This gives (θ2) and (θ4). At a prime \(\ell\mid heta\): \(\ell otin S_0\) by (θ1), so \(\ell mid m\); \(\ell mid k\), since otherwise \(\ell\mid M^2- heta c^2=ma\) would give \(\ell\mid a\); hence \( eta s^2=ma\equiv M^2 ot\equiv0\pmod\ell\), and \( eta\) is a nonzero square modulo \(\ell\), which is (θ3).

docs.title: The slots
docs.text: The auxiliary primes are chosen by Dirichlet's theorem with prescribed residue bits: one prime \(q_0\equiv3\pmod8\), glue primes \(r_p\equiv1\pmod8\) that glue the primes of \(\beta\) into one virtual prime of class \(7\), and glue primes \(r_\ell\equiv1\pmod8\) that hang the primes of \(\theta\) on \(q_0\).

docs.title: The slot lemma
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.exists_prime_slot ZInQ.RouteK.exists_prime_slot_bits

Let \(S\) be a finite set of odd primes with signs \(\varepsilon_p\in\{\pm1\}\) (\(p\in S\)), let \(a\) be an odd integer and \(A\) a finite set of natural numbers. Then there is a prime \(q\notin A\) with \(q\equiv a\pmod8\) and \((q/p)=\varepsilon_p\) for every \(p\in S\).

Equivalently, in residue bits: for prescribed bits \(b_p\in\mathbb F_2\) (\(p\in S\)) there is a prime \(q\notin A\cup S\) with \(q\equiv a\pmod8\) and \([q/p]=b_p\) for every \(p\in S\).

Proof sketch. Every odd prime \(p\) has \((p-1)/2\ge1\) nonzero squares and as many non-squares modulo \(p\), so some residue \(r_p\) prime to \(p\) has \((r_p/p)=\varepsilon_p\). By the Chinese remainder theorem the conditions \(q\equiv a\pmod 8\) and \(q\equiv r_p\pmod p\) (\(p\in S\)) define one invertible class modulo \(8\prod_{p\in S}p\), and by Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions it contains a prime larger than every element of \(A\) (and of \(S\)).

docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Slots ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.sum_q₀_sym ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.card_primes ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.rev_q₀ ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.rev_rP ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.rev_rT

Let \(\beta,\theta\) be odd coprime integers, \(P=P(\beta)\) and \(T=P(\theta)\) their sets of primes, \(p_0\in P\), \(G=P\setminus\{p_0\}\), \(s=s(\beta)=[\beta<0]\) and \(x=s+1\in\mathbb F_2\). Slot data for \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) are pairwise distinct primes \(q_0\), \(r_p\) (\(p\in G\)) and \(r_\ell\) (\(\ell\in T\)), none dividing \(2\beta\theta\), such that:

  • \(q_0\equiv3\pmod8\), \([q_0/p]=1+\lambda_px\) for \(p\in G\), \([q_0/p_0]=x+\sum_{p\in G}(1+\lambda_px)\), and \([q_0/\ell]=0\) for \(\ell\in T\);
  • for \(p\in G\): \(r_p\equiv1\pmod8\), \([r_p/p]=[r_p/p_0]=1\), and \([r_p/y]=0\) for every \(y\in(P\setminus\{p,p_0\})\cup T\cup\{q_0\}\) and every \(y=r_{p'}\) with \(p'\in G\setminus\{p\}\);
  • for \(\ell\in T\): \(r_\ell\equiv1\pmod8\), \([r_\ell/\ell]=[r_\ell/q_0]=1\), and \([r_\ell/y]=0\) for every \(y\in P\cup(T\setminus\{\ell\})\), every \(y=r_p\) with \(p\in G\), and every \(y=r_{\ell'}\) with \(\ell'\in T\setminus\{\ell\}\).

For slot data, \(\sum_{p\in P}[q_0/p]=x\); the slots number \(|P|+|T|=\omega(\beta)+\omega(\theta)\); and the reverse bits follow by reciprocity: \([y/r]=[r/y]\) for the glue slots \(r\equiv1\pmod4\) and \([y/q_0]=[q_0/y]+\lambda_y\) for every odd prime \(y\ne q_0\).

The prime \(q_0\) breaks the symmetry and forms the base configuration with the glued prime of \(\beta\); the \(r_p\) glue the primes of \(\beta\) into one virtual prime; the \(r_\ell\) hang the primes of \(\theta\) on \(q_0\). The condition \([q_0/\ell]=0\) is never used by the proof.

docs.title: The slots exist
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.exists_slots ZInQ.RouteK.exists_slots_of_admissible ZInQ.RouteK.exists_multiplier_and_slots

Let \(\beta,\theta\) be odd coprime integers and \(p_0\in P(\beta)\). Then slot data for \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) exist: primes \(q_0\), \(r_p\) (\(p\in P(\beta)\setminus\{p_0\}\)) and \(r_\ell\) (\(\ell\in P(\theta)\)) satisfying the slot conditions.

For an admissible \(B\) these hypotheses hold: by the multiplier lemma there is a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) with \(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\) odd and \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), so \(P(\beta)\ne\emptyset\), and \(\theta=\mathrm{sqf}(m(m-B))\) is odd and coprime to \(\beta\) by (θ1) and (θ2); so the slots exist for every \(p_0\in P(\beta)\).

Proof sketch. Choose \(q_0\), then the \(r_p\) one after the other, then the \(r_\ell\) one after the other, each by the slot lemma: each condition fixes the class modulo \(8\) and the residue bit modulo finitely many odd primes already fixed, and the new prime avoids all primes already used and the primes of \(2\beta\theta\). The conditions \([r/r']=0\) between two glue slots, imposed against the earlier one only, hold in both directions by reciprocity, since both are \(\equiv1\pmod4\).

docs.text: With \(n=|\beta|q_0\prod r_p\prod r_\ell\), the partner and gluing lemmas reduce the configurations of \(|n|\) and \(|n\theta|\) to the base configuration, and the class \(\beta\) survives every step.

docs.title: The realization: both curves reduce to the base configuration
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.selmerCertified_d₁ ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.selmerCertified_d₂ ZInQ.RouteK.Inputs ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.d₁ ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.d₂ ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.d₁_eq' ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.d₂_eq ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.squarefree_d₁ ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.squarefree_d₂ ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.d₁_mod ZInQ.RouteK.Slots.β_dvd_d₁ ZInQ.RouteK.selmerCertified_of_primeCfg

Let \(\beta,\theta\) be integers such that \(\beta\) is odd and squarefree with \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\); \(\theta>0\) is squarefree with \(\theta\equiv1\pmod8\); \(\beta\) and \(\theta\) are coprime; \([\beta/\ell]=0\) for every prime \(\ell\mid\theta\); and \([\theta/p]=0\) for every prime \(p\mid\beta\). Let \(p_0\in P(\beta)\), let \(q_0\), \(r_p\) (\(p\in G=P(\beta)\setminus\{p_0\}\)) and \(r_\ell\) (\(\ell\in T=P(\theta)\)) satisfy the slot conditions, and put $\(d_1=|\beta|\,q_0\prod_{p\in G}r_p\prod_{\ell\in T}r_\ell,\qquad d_2=d_1\theta .\)$ Then \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) are squarefree, \(d_1\equiv5\pmod8\), \(\beta\mid d_1\), and both \((d_1,\beta)\) and \((d_2,\beta)\) carry Selmer certificates: \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_{d_1})\) and \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_{d_2})\) have exactly \(8\) solutions each, and each has a solution with first coordinate the class of \(\beta\). (So \(d_2\equiv5\pmod8\) too.)

The hypotheses on \(\beta,\theta\) are those that the multiplier lemma and (θ1)–(θ4) give for an admissible input, in residue bits.

Proof sketch. Both numbers are products of distinct odd primes, so their configurations are those of the families of their primes, and a solution of the family's system with first coordinate \((s(\beta),0,[\,\cdot\mid\beta])\) is a certificate for the product. Let \(s=s(\beta)\) and \(x=s+1\).

The first curve (\(d_1\), on \(P\cup\{q_0\}\cup R_P\cup R_T\)). 1. Each \(r_\ell\) has exactly one nonzero bit inside this set, at its partner \(q_0\); the partner lemma removes all of them and identifies \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_{d_1})\) with \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_\Sigma)\), \(\mathcal C_\Sigma\) the configuration on \(P\cup\{q_0\}\cup R_P\). 2. The gluing lemma applies to \(\mathcal C_\Sigma\) with \(g=p_0\), \(G=P\setminus\{p_0\}\), glue primes \(r_p\) and \(S'=\{q_0\}\). The glued configuration lives on \(\{p^*,q_0\}\) with \(c_{p^*}=|\beta|\bmod8=7\), \(c_{q_0}=3\) and \([q_0/p^*]=\sum_{p\in P}[q_0/p]=x\). 3. By the base configuration lemma it has \(8\) solutions; hence so do \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_\Sigma)\) and \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_{d_1})\). 4. Lift the solution \(\sigma_0\) with \(a_0=s\): through the gluing lemma, \(u_P=\mathbf 1_P\), \(u_{q_0}=0\), and by (2.1) \(u_{r_p}=[q_0/p]+1+\lambda_px=0\) by the choice of \([q_0/p]\); through the partner lemma, \(u_{r_\ell}=u_{q_0}=0\). The first coordinate is \((s,0,\mathbf 1_P)\), the class of \(\beta\).

The second curve (\(d_2\), on \(P\cup R_P\cup\{q_0\}\cup T\cup R_T\)). 5. The gluing lemma applies with \(g=q_0\), \(G=T\), glue primes \(r_\ell\) and \(S'=P\cup R_P\). The glued vertex has class \(q_0\theta\equiv3\pmod8\) by (θ1). For \(p\in P\), \(\sum_{\ell\in T}[\ell/p]=[\theta/p]=0\), because \(\theta=\prod_{\ell\in T}\ell\); and \(\sum_{\ell\in T}[p/\ell]=[\theta/p]+\lambda_p\sum_{\ell\in T}\lambda_\ell=0\) by reciprocity prime by prime, since \(\sum_\ell\lambda_\ell=\lambda(\theta)=0\). The bits between \(R_P\) and \(T\) vanish by construction. So the glued configuration is \(\mathcal C_\Sigma\) with \(q_0^*\) in place of \(q_0\), and \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_{d_2})\) has \(8\) solutions by steps 1–3. 6. Lift the solution of step 4 through this gluing: \(u_T=u_{q_0}=0\), \(v_{q_0}=s+x+1=0\), and by (2.1), for \(\ell\in T\), \(u_{r_\ell}=\sum_{p\in P}[p/\ell]+\lambda_\ell s=[|\beta|/\ell]+\lambda_\ell s =([\beta/\ell]+s\lambda_\ell)+s\lambda_\ell=0\), using \([\beta/\ell]=0\). The first coordinate is again the class of \(\beta\).

docs.title: The descent lemma
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.descent_lemma ZInQ.RouteK.inputs_of_admissible

For every admissible \(B\) there are a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) and an integer \(n\) such that, with \(\beta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\) and \(\theta=\mathrm{sqf}(m(m-B))\):

  • \(\beta\mid n\), \(|n|\equiv5\pmod8\) and \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\);
  • \(n\) and \(n\theta\) are squarefree, and \(|n\theta|\equiv5\pmod8\);
  • \((|n|,\beta)\) and \((|n\theta|,\beta)\) carry Selmer certificates: the systems \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_{|n|})\) and \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_{|n\theta|})\) have exactly \(8\) solutions each, and each has a solution with first coordinate the class of \(\beta\).

Through Proposition 0 this says that \(C_n\) and \(C_{n\theta}\) have 2-Selmer groups of dimension \(3\) in which \(\beta\) is a first Kummer coordinate. The construction uses \(\omega(\beta)+\omega(\theta)\) auxiliary primes.

Along the way: for admissible \(B\), a signed divisor \(m\) of \(2730\) with \(\beta\) odd and \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), and a prime \(p_0\) dividing \(\beta\), the triple \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfies the hypotheses of the realization: \(\beta\) is squarefree, \(\theta>0\) is squarefree with \(\theta\equiv1\pmod8\), \(\beta\) and \(\theta\) are coprime, \([\beta/\ell]=0\) for every prime \(\ell\mid\theta\), and \([\theta/p]=0\) for every prime \(p\mid\beta\).

Proof sketch. By the multiplier lemma choose \(m\) with \(\beta\) odd and \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\); then \(P(\beta)\ne\emptyset\), and by (θ1)–(θ4) the pair \(\beta,\theta\) satisfies the hypotheses of the realization (with \(\beta\), \(\theta\) squarefree as squarefree parts of nonzero rationals, and (θ3), (θ4) in residue bits). Fix \(p_0\in P(\beta)\), choose the slots and take \(n=d_1\). Then \(|n\theta|=d_1\theta=d_2\), and the realization gives every assertion; \(d_2\equiv5\cdot1\pmod8\).

docs.title: From points to pole completeness
docs.text: Two points with abscissas in \(\beta\mathbb Q^{*2}\) on \(C_N\) and \(C_{N\theta}\) rescale to the witnesses of the pole polynomial. With CR₃ applied to the two certified curves this proves pole completeness, which the main theorem therefore no longer assumes. The proof applies CR₃ to these two curves only; the two-curves section proves pole completeness from positive rank on curves of the same kind: the two curves of some slot choice, for every triple \(\beta,\theta,p_0\) satisfying the hypotheses of the realization (CR₃^DL,Rk), or, for each admissible input, for some multiplier, prime \(p_0\mid\beta\) and slot choice (CR₃^DL,Adm,Rk).

docs.title: Points on two congruent number curves give pole solubility
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.poleSoluble_of_points ZInQ.RouteK.exists_multiplier_bits

Let \(B\) be a nonzero rational, \(m e B\) a signed divisor of \(2730\), \( eta=\mathrm{sqf}(mB)\), \( heta=\mathrm{sqf}(m(m-B))\), and \(N\) a nonzero rational. Suppose that \(C_N:y^2=x^3-N^2x\) has a rational point \((x_1,y_1)\) with \(x_1 e0\) and \(x_1/ eta\) a square, and that \(C_{N heta}:y^2=x^3-(N heta)^2x\) has a rational point \((x_2,y_2)\) with \(x_2 e0\) and \(x_2/ eta\) a square. Then \(\Phi(B)\) holds: the pole polynomial has a rational zero with input \(B\).

Proof sketch. Every signed divisor of \(2730\) is the multiplier \((1-2b_0)(1+b_1)(1+2b_2)(1+4b_3)(1+6b_4)(1+12b_5)\) for some bits \(b_i\in\{0,1\}\): the sign gives \(b_0\), and \(|m|=\gcd(|m|,2)\gcd(|m|,3)\gcd(|m|,5)\gcd(|m|,7)\gcd(|m|,13)\) gives the others. Then \(A=mB= eta t^2\) and \(H=A(A-B^2)=B^2m(m-B)= heta h^2\) with \(t,h e0\). Write \(x_1= eta s^2\), \(x_2= eta s'^2\). Scaling the first point by \(\lambda=t/s\) gives the point \((A,\lambda^3y_1)\) on \(C_e\) with \(e=N\lambda^2\), so \(r_1=\lambda^3y_1\) satisfies \(r_1^2=A(A-e)(A+e)\). Then \(eH=N heta(\lambda h)^2\), and scaling the second point by \(\lambda h\) gives \((Az^2,(\lambda h)^3y_2)\) on \(C_{eH}\) with \(z=s'h/s\); so \(r_2=(\lambda h)^3y_2/z\) satisfies \((zr_2)^2=Az^2(Az^2-eH)(Az^2+eH)\), that is \(r_2^2=T_2\). Finally \(w=(eHz)^{-1}\), which exists because \(e,H,z e0\). Every summand of the pole polynomial vanishes.

docs.title: Pole completeness from the certified rank hypothesis
docs.text:
ZInQ.poleCompleteness_of_certifiedRank

Assume the certified rank hypothesis CR₃. Then pole completeness holds: every admissible \(B\) satisfies \(\Phi(B)\), for the pole polynomial with the congruent number curves \(y^2=x(x-\ell)(x+\ell)\).

Proof sketch. Let \(B\) be admissible. The descent lemma gives \(m\) and \(n\). Apply CR₃ to \(d=|n|\) and to \(d=|n\theta|\), with \(a=\beta\) in both cases: \(d\) is squarefree with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), \(\beta\) is squarefree (a squarefree part of the nonzero rational \(mB\)), divides \(n\) and \(n\theta\), has \(|\beta|\equiv7\pmod8\), and the Selmer certificates are the remaining hypotheses. This gives rational points with nonzero abscissas in \(\beta\mathbb Q^{*2}\) on \(C_{|n|}\) and on \(C_{|n\theta|}\), which is \(C_{N\theta}\) for \(N=|n|\) since only \(d^2\) enters. Since \(0<B<1/2\), the integer \(m\) is not \(B\), so the lemma on points and pole solubility gives \(\Phi(B)\).
