docs.title: Proposition 0: the explicit system is the 2-Selmer group
Proposition 0: the explicit system is the 2-Selmer group
docs.text:
The certified rank hypothesis CR₃, which the main theorem derives from four statements about L-series, is stated on the explicit linear system \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) of the Route K chapter, built from classes modulo \(8\) and Legendre symbols. Proposition 0 says that for squarefree \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) the solutions of this system are, in coordinates, the 2-Selmer group of the congruent number curve \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\), defined by the local solubility of its 2-coverings. This chapter proves it, and so replaces CR₃ by the narrower hypothesis CR₃^Sel, stated on the Selmer group itself: when \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has dimension \(3\) and contains a class with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\), every Selmer class comes from a rational point.

Throughout, \(C_d\) is \(y^2=x(x-d)(x+d)\), and \(u\equiv v\) means that \(u/v\) is a nonzero square.

15 fully proved

docs.title: Coverings
docs.text: The 2-coverings \(D_{a,b}\) of \(C_d\) are written in an x-form, which depends only on the square classes of \(a\) and \(b\); over any field of characteristic not \(2\) a covering is soluble exactly when \((a,b)\) is a Kummer image of a point.

docs.title: The 2-coverings of a congruent number curve
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.Cov ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.Loc ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.SqEq ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.SqEq.refl ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.SqEq.symm ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.SqEq.trans ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.SqEq.mul ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.sqEq_iff_isSquare_mul

Let \(K\) be a field and \(d,a,b\in K\). The 2-covering of \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) attached to \((a,b)\) is the curve in \(\mathbb P^3\) $\(D_{a,b}:\qquad az_1^2-bz_2^2=dw^2,\qquad az_1^2-abz_3^2=-dw^2 .\)$ Say that \(D_{a,b}\) is soluble over \(K\) when it has a \(K\)-point, that is a solution \((z_1,z_2,z_3,w)\ne(0,0,0,0)\) in \(K\).

Its x-form is the condition that either \(a\) and \(b\) are squares in \(K\), or there is \(x\in K\) such that \(x/a\), \((x-d)/b\) and \((x+d)/(ab)\) are squares in \(K\) (zero counts as a square).

For \(u,v\in K\) write \(u\equiv v\) when \(u=vs^2\) for some nonzero \(s\in K\). This is an equivalence relation compatible with products, and for nonzero \(u,v\) it says that \(uv\) is a square.

docs.title: The x-form of a covering
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.cov_iff_loc

Let \(K\) be a field and \(d,a,b\in K\) with \(a,b e0\). Then the 2-covering \(D_{a,b}\) of \(C_d\) is soluble over \(K\) if and only if its x-form holds: \(a\) and \(b\) are squares, or some \(x\in K\) makes \(x/a\), \((x-d)/b\) and \((x+d)/(ab)\) squares.

Proof sketch. Let \((z_1,z_2,z_3,w)\) be a point. If \(w=0\), then \(az_1^2=bz_2^2\) and \(z_1^2=bz_3^2\); here \(z_1 e0\), since otherwise every coordinate vanishes, so \(z_3 e0\), \(b=(z_1/z_3)^2\) and \(a=(z_2/z_3)^2\). If \(w e0\), put \(x=a(z_1/w)^2\); then \((x-d)/b=(z_2/w)^2\) and \((x+d)/(ab)=(z_3/w)^2\). Conversely, if \(a=s^2\) and \(b=t^2\) then \((1/s,1/t,1/(st),0)\) is a point, and if \(x/a=r_1^2\), \((x-d)/b=r_2^2\), \((x+d)/(ab)=r_3^2\) then \((r_1,r_2,r_3,1)\) is a point, because \(ar_1^2-br_2^2=x-(x-d)\) and \(ar_1^2-abr_3^2=x-(x+d)\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.loc_torsion ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.loc_mul_sq_iff ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.loc_congr_sq ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.loc_of_sqEq_torsion

Let \(K\) be a field with \(2\ne0\) and \(d,a,b\in K\), \(d,a,b\ne0\).

  1. (Inv) The x-form of \(D_{a,b}\) depends only on the classes of \(a\) and \(b\) modulo nonzero squares: if \(a\equiv a'\) and \(b\equiv b'\), it holds for \((a,b)\) if and only if it holds for \((a',b')\).
  2. (Tor) If \(x/a\), \((x-d)/b\) and \((x+d)/(ab)\) are squares, then either \(x=0\), \(a\equiv-1\), \(b\equiv-d\); or \(x=d\), \(a\equiv d\), \(b\equiv2\); or \(x=-d\), \(a\equiv-d\), \(b\equiv-2d\); or \(x\), \(x-d\), \(x+d\) are all nonzero, \(x\equiv a\), \(x-d\equiv b\), \(x+d\equiv ab\) and \(x(x-d)(x+d)\) is a square.
  3. For \(i,j\in\{0,1\}\), if \(a\equiv d^i(-1)^j\) and \(b\equiv2^i(-d)^j\) (one of the four torsion classes \((1,1)\), \((-1,-d)\), \((d,2)\), \((-d,-2d)\)), the x-form of \(D_{a,b}\) holds.

Proof sketch. (1) Divide the three squares by \(s^2\), \(t^2\) and \((st)^2\); the witness \(x\) is the same. (2) If \(x=0\) then \(-d/b\) and \(d/(ab)\) are nonzero squares, so \(b\equiv-d\) and \(a\equiv-1\); the cases \(x=\pm d\) are alike; otherwise the three quotients are nonzero squares and their product is \(x(x-d)(x+d)/(ab)^2\). (3) By (1) take the class representatives; the witnesses are the first alternative for \((1,1)\) and \(x=0\), \(d\), \(-d\) for the others.

docs.title: Coverings and the Kummer map
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.loc_iff_kummer ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.kummer

Let \(K\) be a field with \(2 e0\) and \(d e0\) in \(K\). The Kummer map of the complete 2-descent on \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) sends the point at infinity to \((1,1)\), the 2-torsion points \((0,0)\), \((d,0)\), \((-d,0)\) to \((-1,-d)\), \((d,2)\), \((-d,-2d)\), and every other point \((x,y)\) to \((x,x-d)\); its values are read modulo squares. Then for \(a,b e0\) the x-form of \(D_{a,b}\) holds if and only if there is a point \(P\in C_d(K)\) whose Kummer image \((\alpha, eta)\) has \(a\equiv\alpha\) and \(b\equiv eta\).

Proof sketch. (⇐) By the invariance under squares it suffices to treat the image of \(P\) itself: the point at infinity and the torsion points give the torsion classes; for \(P=(x,y)\) with \(x otin\{0,\pm d\}\) the witness is \(x\), since \(x/x=1\), \((x-d)/(x-d)=1\) and \((x+d)/(x(x-d))=(y/(x(x-d)))^2\). (⇒) If \(a,b\) are squares take the point at infinity. Otherwise, with \(x=ar_1^2\), \(x-d=br_2^2\), \(x+d=abr_3^2\), the point \((x,abr_1r_2r_3)\) lies on \(C_d\); by the torsion analysis, either \(x\in\{0,\pm d\}\) and \((a,b)\) is the image of the corresponding 2-torsion point, or \((a,b)\equiv(x,x-d)\).

docs.title: Local solubility
docs.text: At each place the soluble classes are computed: by sign at the real place, by Hensel's lemma and square classes at the finite places. At odd primes not dividing \(d\) every unit pair is soluble, through a residue witness over \(\mathbb F_p\) found with Jacobsthal's bound on cubic character sums (and a kernel check for \(p<29\)); at odd primes dividing \(d\) only the four torsion classes are soluble; at \(2\), for odd \(d\), the torsion classes and their products with \((1,5)\).

Let \(p\) be a prime and \(x\in\mathbb Q_p\) nonzero, \(x=p^ku\) with \(u\) a unit of \(\mathbb Z_p\).

  1. (SQ) For odd \(p\), \(x\) is a square if and only if \(k\) is even and the residue of \(u\) in \(\mathbb F_p\) is a square. For \(p=2\), \(x\) is a square if and only if \(k\) is even and \(u\equiv1\pmod8\).
  2. (Hensel) Every \(u\in\mathbb Q_p\) with \(|u-1|<|2|^2\) is a square.
  3. (P) For odd \(p\) and \(|y|<|x|\), \(x+y\equiv x\) modulo nonzero squares; for \(p=2\) the same holds when \(|y|\le|x|/8\).
  4. (RT) For odd \(p\), a quotient \(m/n\) of integers prime to \(p\) with \(mn\) a square modulo \(p\) is a square in \(\mathbb Q_p\), and so is a rational number whose numerator and denominator are prime to \(p\) and whose product is a square modulo \(p\). For \(p=2\), \(m/n\) with \(n\) odd and \(m\equiv n\pmod8\) is a square in \(\mathbb Q_2\), and so is a rational number with odd denominator and numerator congruent to the denominator modulo \(8\).

Proof sketch. (2) is Hensel's lemma for \(X^2-u\) at \(1\): \(|F(1)|=|u-1|<|F'(1)|^2=|2|^2\). A square has even valuation; a unit square root of a unit reduces modulo \(p\), resp. an odd square is \(\equiv1\pmod8\); conversely a unit with square residue is a square by Hensel's lemma at a lift of the residue square root (odd \(p\)), resp. by (2) at \(1\) (\(p=2\), since \(|u-1|\le2^{-3}<2^{-2}\)). This gives (1). (3) applies (2) to \(1+y/x\). (4) applies (1) to the unit \(m/n\).

Let \(d>0\) and \(a,b\ne0\) be real numbers. Then the covering \(D_{a,b}\) of \(C_d\) is soluble over \(\mathbb R\) (in its x-form) if and only if \(a\) and \(b\) have the same sign. In particular this holds for integers \(d>0\) and \(a,b\ne0\).

Proof sketch. If \(a,b>0\) take \(x=d\); if \(a,b<0\) take \(x=0\). If \(a>0>b\), a witness would have \(x\ge0\), \(x-d\le0\) and \(x+d\le0\), impossible; if \(a<0<b\), it would have \(x\le0\) and \(x-d\ge0\), impossible as \(d>0\). The first alternative forces \(a,b>0\).

Let \(p\) be an odd prime and \(d,a,b\) nonzero elements of \(\mathbb F_p\). Then either \(a\) and \(b\) are squares in \(\mathbb F_p\), or there is \(\xi\in\mathbb F_p\) such that \(\xi/a\), \((\xi-d)/b\) and \((\xi+d)/(ab)\) are squares (zero allowed).

Over any finite field \(F\) of odd characteristic with \(q\) elements and quadratic character \(\chi\), the proof uses:

  • (Lemma Q) \(\sum_\xi\chi((\xi-e)(\xi-e'))=-1\) for \(e e e'\);
  • (Jacobsthal) with \(S(n)=\sum_\xi\chi(\xi^3-n\xi)\), \(S(1)^2\le4q\), and \(S(n)^2\le4q\) for every nonzero square \(n\);
  • (the count) for \(d e0\) and signs \(\alpha, eta\in\{\pm1\}\), the number \(N\) of \(\xi otin\{0,\pm d\}\) with \(\chi(\xi)=\alpha\), \(\chi(\xi-d)= eta\), \(\chi(\xi+d)=\alpha eta\) satisfies \(8N\ge q-15-|S(d^2)|\); so \(N\ge1\) once \(q\ge26\).

Proof sketch. Lemma Q is the Jacobi sum \(J(\chi,\chi^{-1})=-\chi(-1)\) after the substitution \(\xi=e+(e'-e)t\). Jacobsthal: \(S(nt^2)=\chi(t)S(n)\), \(S(0)=0\) and \(\sum_nS(n)^2=q(q-1)(1+\chi(-1))\) (by Lemma Q), which bounds \(S(1)^2\) by \(4q\). The count expands \(8N=\sum'(1+\alpha\chi(\xi))(1+ eta\chi(\xi-d))(1+\alpha eta\chi(\xi+d))\): the constant term is \(q-3\), the linear and quadratic sums are bounded by Lemma Q, and the cubic term is \(S(d^2)\). Since \((q-15)^2>4q\) for \(q\ge26\), \(N\ge1\), and with \(\alpha=\chi(a)\), \( eta=\chi(b)\) such a \(\xi\) is the witness. For the primes \(3\le p\le23\) the statement is a finite check over all \(d,a,b\), done by the kernel.

docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.loc_padic_good_iff ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.loc_padic_good_even ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.loc_padic_good_of_units

Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(d\) a natural number with \(p mid d\), and \(a,b\) integers.

  1. (Lemma G1) If \(a,b e0\) and \(D_{a,b}\) is soluble over \(\mathbb Q_p\), then \(v_p(a)\) and \(v_p(b)\) are even.
  2. (Lemma G2) If \(p mid a\) and \(p mid b\), then \(D_{a,b}\) is soluble over \(\mathbb Q_p\).
  3. Consequently, for squarefree \(a\) and \(b\), \(D_{a,b}\) is soluble over \(\mathbb Q_p\) if and only if \(p mid a\) and \(p mid b\).

(Solubility is meant in the x-form.)

Proof sketch. (1) The first alternative and the torsion witnesses give unit classes. Otherwise \(x\equiv a\), \(x-d\equiv b\), \(x+d\equiv ab\); compare \(|x|\) with \(|d|=1\): for \(|x|>1\) all three have valuation \(v(x)\), for \(|x|<1\) both \(x\mp d\) are units, and for \(|x|=1\) at most one of \(x\mp d\) is a non-unit since their difference \(2d\) is a unit; in each case \(v(a)\) and \(v(b)\) are even. (2) Take the residue witness \(\xi\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) for the residues of \(d,a,b\); lift it to an integer \(x\), taken to be exactly \(0\), \(d\) or \(-d\) when \(\xi\in\{0,\pm ar d\}\); the nonzero quotients are units with square residues, hence squares in \(\mathbb Q_p\). If \( ar a, ar b\) are squares, so are \(a,b\). (3) A squarefree integer with even \(v_p\) is prime to \(p\).

Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(d\) a squarefree natural number divisible by \(p\), and \(a,b\) nonzero integers. Then \(D_{a,b}\) is soluble over \(\mathbb Q_p\) (in its x-form) if and only if there are \(i,j\in\{0,1\}\) such that \(ad^i(-1)^j\) and \(b\,2^i(-d)^j\) are squares in \(\mathbb Q_p\); that is, \((a,b)\) is one of the four torsion classes \((1,1)\), \((d,2)\), \((-1,-d)\), \((-d,-2d)\).

Proof sketch. (⇐) The torsion classes are soluble. (⇒) After the torsion analysis, compare \(|x|\) with \(|d|=p^{-1}\). If \(|x|>|d|\), (P) gives \(x\pm d\equiv x\) and \((a,b)\equiv(1,1)\); if \(|x|<|d|\), \(x-d\equiv-d\), \(x+d\equiv d\) and \((a,b)\equiv(-1,-d)\). If \(|x|=|d|\), write \(x=dt\) with \(t\) a unit: \(t-1\) and \(t+1\) are not both non-units (their difference is \(2\)) and not both units (then \(|x(x-d)(x+d)|=p^{-3}\) is not the norm of a square); \(p\mid t-1\) gives \((d,2)\) and \(p\mid t+1\) gives \((-d,-2d)\).

Let \(d\) be an odd natural number (in particular \(d\equiv5\pmod8\)) and \(a,b\) nonzero integers. Then \(D_{a,b}\) is soluble over \(\mathbb Q_2\) (in its x-form) if and only if there are \(i,j,k\in\{0,1\}\) such that \(ad^i(-1)^j\) and \(b\,2^i(-d)^j5^k\) are squares in \(\mathbb Q_2\): the four torsion classes and their products with \((1,5)\).

Proof sketch. (⇐) The torsion classes are soluble; the classes with \(k=1\) have the rational witnesses \(x=1/4\), \(d(1+4d)/(1-4d)\), \(-4d^2\), \(-d(1-4d)/(1+4d)\), for which the three quotients are even powers of \(2\) times rationals \(\equiv1\pmod8\), hence squares by the rational test. (⇒) After the torsion analysis, split on \(v=v_2(x)\). For \(v\le-3\) and \(v\ge3\), (P) gives \((1,1)\) and \((-1,-d)\). For \(v=\pm1\) the norm of \(x(x-d)(x+d)\) is an odd power of \(2\). For \(v=-2\), \(x\mp d\equiv5x\), giving \((1,5)\); for \(v=2\), \(x-d\equiv-5d\), \(x+d\equiv5d\), giving \((-1,-5d)\). For \(v=0\) one of \(x\mp d\) has norm \(1/2\) and the other norm at most \(1/8\), which gives \(x\equiv\pm d\) and \(x\mp d\equiv\mp2d\) or \(\mp10d\). Only "two 2-adic numbers of equal norm have a sum of smaller norm", the discreteness of the norm and (P) are used.

docs.title: The Selmer group and Proposition 0
docs.text: The 2-Selmer group is the set of pairs of squarefree integers whose covering is soluble at every place. Reading the local classes off in residue bits turns the local conditions into the rows of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\).

docs.title: The 2-Selmer group of a congruent number curve
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.Sel2 ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.classInt ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.selPair ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.selPair_injective ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.squarefree_classInt

For a natural number \(d\), the 2-Selmer group \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) is the set of pairs \((a,b)\) of squarefree integers (signs allowed) such that the 2-covering \(D_{a,b}\) of \(C_d:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) is soluble (in its x-form) over \(\mathbb R\) and over \(\mathbb Q_p\) for every prime \(p\), \(p=2\) included.

For odd \(d\) and unknowns \(\sigma=(a_0,a_1,b_0,b_1,u,v)\) of the Selmer system on the primes of \(d\), put $\(a(\sigma)=(-1)^{a_0}2^{a_1}\prod_{p\mid d}p^{u_p},\qquad b(\sigma)=(-1)^{b_0}2^{b_1}\prod_{p\mid d}p^{v_p}.\)$ These integers are squarefree, and \(\sigma\mapsto(a(\sigma),b(\sigma))\) is injective: the sign, \(v_2\) and the \(v_p\) recover the unknowns.

By the Kummer-map lemma over each completion, \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) says that the class of \((a,b)\) in \((\mathbb Q^*/\mathbb Q^{*2})^2\) lies locally everywhere in the image of the Kummer map. With the standard identification of \(H^1(\mathbb Q,C_d[2])\) with \((\mathbb Q^*/\mathbb Q^{*2})^2\), under which the connecting map of the complete 2-descent is the Kummer map (Silverman, Proposition X.1.4), and with each square class written by its squarefree integer representative, this is the textbook 2-Selmer group. That identification is used to read the definition, not formalized.

Let \(d\) be an odd squarefree natural number, \(\mathcal C_d\) the configuration of its primes, and \(\sigma\) unknowns of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\), with the pair \((a(\sigma),b(\sigma))\).

  1. At an odd prime \(p\mid d\): \(D_{a(\sigma),b(\sigma)}\) is soluble over \(\mathbb Q_p\) if and only if \(\sigma\) satisfies the rows \(\mathrm E1_p\) and \(\mathrm E2_p\).
  2. At the real place (\(d e0\)): it is soluble over \(\mathbb R\) if and only if \(a_0=b_0\), the row (R).
  3. At \(2\), for \(d\equiv5\pmod8\): it is soluble over \(\mathbb Q_2\) if and only if \(a_1=0\), \(b_1=\mu\cdot u\) and \(a_0+\lambda\cdot u=b_0+\lambda\cdot v\); given (R) this is the pair of rows (D) for the product class \(5\).
  4. At an odd prime \(p mid d\), \(p\) divides neither \(a(\sigma)\) nor \(b(\sigma)\).

Consequently, for \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) squarefree, \(\sigma\) solves \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) if and only if \((a(\sigma),b(\sigma))\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\), provided every pair of integers prime to \(p\) is soluble over \(\mathbb Q_p\) at the odd primes \(p mid d\) (Lemma G2).

Proof sketch. Write \(a(\sigma)d^i(-1)^j\) and \(b(\sigma)2^i(-d)^j\) as \((-1)^s2^t\prod_{q\mid d}q^{e_q}\) and read the square class off the exponents. At \(p\mid d\) the valuation forces \(i=u_p\), \(j=v_p\) and the residue bit \(s\lambda_p+t\mu_p+\sum_{q e p}e_q[q/p]\) must vanish; by multiplicativity of the residue bits the two conditions are \(\mathrm E1_p\) and \(\mathrm E2_p\). At \(2\) the conditions on \(v_2\) and on the characters \(\lambda,\mu\) modulo \(8\) of the odd parts give \(a_1=0\), \(b_1=i\), \(\mu\cdot u=i\), \(j=a_0+\lambda\cdot u=b_0+\lambda\cdot v\), with \(k\) free. The real place is the sign lemma. Assembling the places gives the equivalence.

docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.prop0Statement ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.Prop0Statement ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.prop0 ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.sel2_subset_range_selPair ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.exists_classInt_eq

Let \(d\) be a squarefree natural number with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\), and \(\mathcal C_d\) the configuration of its primes. Then:

  1. unknowns \(\sigma\) solve the Selmer system \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) if and only if \((a(\sigma),b(\sigma))\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\);
  2. every element of \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) is \((a(\sigma),b(\sigma))\) for some unknowns \(\sigma\).

With the injectivity of \(\sigma\mapsto(a(\sigma),b(\sigma))\), the map is a bijection from the solutions of \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) onto \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\); in particular \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has as many elements as \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) has solutions. The second part needs only \(d\) odd.

Proof sketch. (1) The local conditions are the rows of the system, at \(\infty\), at \(2\) and at the primes of \(d\); at the remaining odd primes \(a(\sigma)\) and \(b(\sigma)\) are prime to \(p\) and Lemma G2 gives solubility. (2) For \((a,b)\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\), Lemma G1 at the odd primes \(p\nmid d\) shows that \(p\) divides neither \(a\) nor \(b\); being squarefree, \(a=\pm2^{a_1}\prod_{p\mid d}p^{u_p}\) and \(b=\pm2^{b_1}\prod_{p\mid d}p^{v_p}\) with exponents in \(\{0,1\}\), which defines \(\sigma\).

docs.text: CR₃^Sel also follows from its positive-rank form CR₃^Rk, which under the same premises asks only that \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) have a point of infinite order, by RK9 and Mordell–Weil for \(C_d\), both proved (the positive-rank chapter).

docs.title: The certified rank hypothesis in Selmer form
docs.text:
ZInQ.RouteK.Selmer.CertifiedRankSel

The hypothesis CR₃^Sel is the following assertion. Let \(d\) be a squarefree positive integer with \(d\equiv5\pmod8\). Suppose that the 2-Selmer group \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has exactly \(8\) elements and contains a pair \((a,b)\) with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\). Then for every \((a',b')\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) the 2-covering \(D_{a',b'}\) is soluble over \(\mathbb Q\) (in its x-form).

Unlike CR₃, it mentions no Legendre symbols, configurations or linear system: those enter only through Proposition 0, which is proved. In the literature's terms, by the Kummer-map lemma over \(\mathbb Q\) and the identification of the Kummer map with the connecting map of the complete 2-descent (Silverman X.1.4), the conclusion says that every Selmer class comes from a rational point, that is \(Ш(C_d)[2]=0\). Since \(C_d(\mathbb Q)[2]\) has order \(4\), the image of \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has dimension \(2+\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\), so when \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) has \(8\) elements, \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\ge1\) gives the conclusion (with Mordell–Weil); the converse is not formalized here. It rests on:

  • for exactly the shape \(d\equiv5\), \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\), Tian–Yuan–Zhang (Theorem 3.5 and the argument of the proof of Theorem 3.5(2), as completed by Proposition N), which gives that \(L(C_d,s)\) vanishes to order one at \(s=1\) (their hypothesis, an odd genus sum, follows from the premises by Corollary 4.4, Theorem 3.6 and Rédei's formula), and Gross–Zagier over an auxiliary imaginary quadratic field (Bump–Friedberg–Hoffstein), which gives \(\operatorname{rank}C_d(\mathbb Q)\ge1\); then the image of \(C_d(\mathbb Q)\) has dimension at least \(3=\dim\mathrm{Sel}_2\), which forces \(Ш(C_d)[2]=0\);
  • as an alternative that is not needed, Kriz's 2-converse theorem (Theorem 10.13, a preprint whose publication status was not checked) for \(C_d\) at \(p=2\), whose standing assumption holds since \(d\ge21\) (by Proposition 0 the class \(a\) is a signed divisor of \(d\), so \(d=|a|m\) with \(m\equiv3\pmod8\)), together with the corank lemma (Cassels–Tate: the pairing on \(Ш/Ш_{\rm div}\) is nondegenerate and alternating, so \(\dim(Ш/Ш_{\rm div})[2]\) is even, with no finiteness of \(Ш\) assumed), giving rank one and \(Ш(C_d)[2]=0\).

Neither rank theorem is formalized here, so CR₃^Sel is a hypothesis, not proved; the step from positive rank to every Selmer class is a theorem (RK9). CR₃^Sel implies CR₃ by Proposition 0, so the main theorem holds with CR₃^Sel in place of CR₃. A sufficient condition in the terms of Smith's matrices is the row-5b hypothesis. With Mordell–Weil for \(C_d\), which is proved, CR₃^Sel also follows from its positive-rank form CR₃^Rk.

docs.text:

The hypothesis CR₃^Sel implies the certified rank hypothesis CR₃.

Proof sketch. Let \(d\equiv5\pmod8\) be squarefree, \(a\) a squarefree divisor of \(d\) with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\), and suppose \(\Sigma(\mathcal C_d)\) has \(8\) solutions, one of them \(\sigma\) with first coordinate the class of \(a\).

  1. By Proposition 0 and the injectivity of \(\sigma\mapsto(a(\sigma),b(\sigma))\), \(\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) is the image of the solutions, so it has \(8\) elements.
  2. Since \(a\) is a squarefree divisor of \(d\), its class gives \(a(\sigma)=a\); so \((a,b(\sigma))\in\mathrm{Sel}_2(C_d)\) with \(|a|\equiv7\pmod8\).
  3. CR₃^Sel gives the x-form of \(D_{a,b(\sigma)}\) over \(\mathbb Q\). The first alternative would make the squarefree \(a\) a square, so \(a=1\), against \(|a|\equiv7\). So there is \(x\) with \(x=ar_1^2\), \(x-d=b r_2^2\), \(x+d=abr_3^2\).
  4. \(x\ne0\): otherwise \(-d/b\) and \(d/(ab)\) are nonzero squares, which forces \(a=-1\).
  5. \(y=abr_1r_2r_3\) satisfies \(y^2=x^3-d^2x\), and \(x/a=r_1^2\) is a square.

This is the conclusion of CR₃.

docs.title: The cutoff and polynomial size
docs.text:
This chapter supplies the quantitative half of input B: the fixed constants of the specification are bounded, the guard cutoff \(T\) is identified with a closed expression below \(2^{2^{2^{9013}}}\), and the specified polynomial \(P_*\) is shown to have degree below \(2\uparrow\uparrow7\) and coefficients below \(2\uparrow\uparrow8\). The constants \(D\), \(T\), \(H_{\rm cat}\), \(N_s\), \(M_0\), \(c_*\), \(\ell\) and the program literal \(c_3\) are astronomically large. None of them is ever evaluated: every statement about them is proved symbolically from their defining expressions, by monotonicity of powers and elementary logarithm estimates. The finite computations that remain are small, closed comparisons and congruences, and one traversal of the template library that computes syntax heights.

The fixed constants are those of the specification: \(P_s=\prod_{p\le324}p\), \(W=4P_s\), the catalogue product \(H_{\rm cat}\) and maximum \(H_{\max}\), \(N_s=P_sH_{\rm cat}\), the least formal multiple \(M_0=\mathrm{LFM}(N_s)\), \(c_*=4M_0\), \(\ell=12P_s^{2916}H_{\rm cat}^{732}\), \(F_0=324!\), \(D=F_0\,3^{256F_0^4}\), \(G_0=116064000000\), \(E_0=10(DG_0)^2\), \(R=\max(D,H_{\max},c_*,10^{12})\), \(Q=R^{RE_0}\), \(B_{\rm cm}=D^2\,3^{21000D^2}+1\), \(C_{\rm cm}=2B_{\rm cm}+4096(1028+5D+84000D^2)\), \(A_{\rm ht}=2\cdot10^{13}\max(1,C_{\rm cm},Q^{17})\) and \(T=(48A_{\rm ht})^{13}\).

2 fully proved

docs.title: The literal cutoff
docs.text:
Proposition 12.1 has three ingredients. First, the prime catalogue is controlled by the catalogue bound: every unit class modulo \(W\) has twenty-two primes above \(324\) below \(X=2^{W^8}\), so \(H_{\max}<X\), \(H_{\rm cat}\le X^{22W}\) and \(\log_2N_s<2^{4613}\). The manuscript derives the same statement with the cutoff \(2^{W^3}\) from the explicit progression estimate of Bennett, Martin, O'Bryant and Rechnitzer; here the cutoff is \(2^{W^8}\), and the catalogue bound is proved from an effective Dirichlet theorem in the progressions chapter. Second, the least formal multiple has a successful index at most \(N_s^{10}\): multiplying \(P_0\) by the product of its reduction orders at the odd places above \(N_s\) puts it in the kernel of reduction there, and a further factor \(N_s^4\) pushes it deep into the filtration at every place above \(N_s\), including the place above \(2\), where \(P_0\) already starts in the third filtration subgroup. Third, a chain of symbolic estimates gives \(c_*<2^{2^{4617}}<2^{2^{8008}}<D\), hence \(R=D\), identifies the maximum in \(A_{\rm ht}\) as \(Q^{17}\), and bounds \(T\).

The small explicit bounds and the catalogue estimates, then the constants derived from them, are in their own section.

The existence of a successful formal multiple, with the reduction and filtration facts it needs, forms the next section.

Assume the catalogue bound. Then the fixed constants of the specification satisfy

  1. \(R=\max(D,H_{\max},c_*,10^{12})=D\);
  2. \(T=(48A_{\rm ht})^{13}=(96\cdot10^{13})^{13}\,D^{2210G_0^2D^3}\), where \(A_{\rm ht}=2\cdot10^{13}\max(1,C_{\rm cm},Q^{17})=2\cdot10^{13}Q^{17}\) and \(Q=R^{RE_0}=D^{10G_0^2D^3}\);
  3. \(T<2^{2^{2^{9013}}}\).

Moreover, the least formal multiple search succeeds: \(N_s\ge1\), \(1\le M_0\le N_s^{10}\), and the normalized representation \(\xi([M_0]P_0)=(a+bs)/c\) satisfies \(N_s^4\mid a\), \(N_s^4\mid b\) and \(\gcd(c,N_s)=1\). This part uses the catalogue bound only through \(N_s\ge1\) (every catalogue entry is then a prime above \(324\)); Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions gives \(N_s\ge1\) as well, so this part also holds without the hypothesis.

Here \(F_0=324!\), \(D=F_0\,3^{256F_0^4}\), \(G_0=116064000000\), \(E_0=10(DG_0)^2\), \(B_{\rm cm}=D^2\,3^{21000D^2}+1\) and \(C_{\rm cm}=2B_{\rm cm}+4096(1028+5D+84000D^2)\). This is a statement about the prescribed integers, independent of the role of \(T\) in excluding false multiplication triples; none of these integers is evaluated.

Proof sketch. The catalogue bound puts the catalogue below \(X=2^{W^8}\), so \(H_{\max}<X\), \(1\le N_s\) and \(\log_2N_s<2^{4613}\). The successful formal multiple, applied to \(N=N_s\ge1\), gives \(1\le M_0\le N_s^{10}\) and the divisibility conditions, and hence \(c_*<2^{2^{4617}}\), while \(2^{2^{8008}}<D<2^{2^{9010}}\); so \(R=D\). Then \(C_{\rm cm}<2^{50000D^2}<Q^{17}\) identifies the maximum and gives the closed form of \(T\), and the closed form is below \(2^{D^8}<2^{2^{2^{9013}}}\).

docs.title: Degree and coefficient bounds
docs.text:
Section 12.1 bounds \(P_*\) without expanding it. Integer polynomials carry the coefficient \(\ell^1\) norm and the total degree; pairs representing elements of \(\mathbb Z[X][\sqrt2]\) carry the weighted norm \(\|a\|_1+2\|b\|_1\). Both are submultiplicative, and substitution multiplies degrees and raises norms to the power of the outer degree. The division polynomials then satisfy \(\deg f_n\le(n+1)^3\) and \(\|f_n\|\le2^{100(n+1)^3}\), the coordinates of \(\iota(n)\) for \(|n|\le T\) have height at most \(2^{2^{30}(T+1)^3}\), and each of the three finite constructors has degree at most \(B^4\) and norm at most \(2^{B^8}\) for \(B=T+1\).

  • Norms, division polynomials and the finite constructors

A syntax height is attached to every node of every template and to every recipe. At height \(h\) a polynomial has degree and logarithmic norm at most \(B^{8h}\); the library traversal gives template heights at most \(249\), the recipe rules give root height \(256\), and the final comparison with the towers uses only \(T<2^{2^{2^{9013}}}\).

docs.title: Bounds for the fixed constants
docs.text:
Only a few small facts are computed: the size of the primorial, the factorial \(324!\) to within its binary length, and \(G_0<2^{37}\).

The symbolic estimates of the whole chapter also use a handful of closed comparisons between explicit numbers of at most a few thousand binary digits; they are collected in one place.

The catalogue bound puts every catalogue prime below \(X=2^{W^8}\). This bounds the catalogue maximum and product, hence \(N_s\) and the pole clearing constant \(\ell\).

The least formal multiple is at most \(N_s^{10}\) (proved in the next section), so \(c_*=4M_0\) is below \(2^{2^{4617}}\), far below \(D\), whose double logarithm lies between \(8008\) and \(9010\).

Hence \(D\) dominates the other entries of \(R\), and with \(R=D\) the maximum defining \(A_{\rm ht}\) is attained by \(Q^{17}\). This identifies \(T\) with a closed expression in \(D\) and \(G_0\), which is bounded by monotonicity alone.

docs.title: The catalogue below the progression cutoff
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.catalogue_bounds

Assume the catalogue bound. Let \(W=4P_s\) and \(X=2^{W^8}\). For every residue \(r\) with \(1\le r<W\) and \(\gcd(r,W)=1\) and every \(j\) with \(1\le j\le22\), the catalogue prime \(p_{r,j}\) (the \(j\)-th prime \(p>324\) with \(p\equiv r\pmod W\)) satisfies $\(324<p_{r,j}<X .\)$ Consequently $\(H_{\max}=\mathrm{catalogue\_max}(W,22,324)<X,\qquad 1\le H_{\rm cat}=\mathrm{catalogue\_product}(W,22,324)\le X^{22W}.\)$

Proof sketch. Fix such \(r\). The hypothesis gives at least \(22\) primes \(p\) with \(324<p<X\) and \(p\bmod W=r\); these are exactly the elements below \(X\) of the set \(S_r=\{p\text{ prime}:p>324,\ p\equiv r\pmod W\}\), whose elements in increasing order are \(p_{r,1}<p_{r,2}<\cdots\). So at least \(22\) elements of \(S_r\) are below \(X\), and the \(j\)-th element for \(j\le22\) is below \(X\) (if \(\#(S_r\cap[0,X))\ge22>j-1\), then the element of index \(j-1\), counting from \(0\), is below \(X\)). It is above \(324\) by definition of \(S_r\). The maximum of finitely many numbers below \(X\) is below \(X\) (an empty maximum is \(0<X\)). The product has \(22\,\varphi(W)\le22W\) factors, each in \([1,X)\), so it lies in \([1,X^{22W}]\).

The manuscript reaches the same conclusion at the smaller cutoff \(2^{W^3}\) through the progression estimate, which gives more than \(X/(2W^4)>22\) primes in each unit class and notes that no prime at most \(324\) lies in a unit class. Here the cutoff is \(X=2^{W^8}\), the range of the effective Dirichlet theorem, and the catalogue bound states the needed count directly.

docs.title: The least formal multiple
docs.text:
The constant \(M_0=\mathrm{LFM}(N_s)\) is the least \(m\ge1\) for which the normalized representation \((a+bs)/c\) of \(1/x([m]P_0)\) has \(N_s^4\mid a\), \(N_s^4\mid b\) and \(\gcd(c,N_s)=1\), with inverse abscissa \(0\) at the identity. The specification only defines it; this section shows that the search succeeds at an index at most \(N_s^{10}\). The argument works for every integer \(N\ge1\) in place of \(N_s\) and does not use the catalogue bound.

7 fully proved

docs.title: Places of \(K_0\)
docs.text: Above an odd prime \(p\) there are one or two primes of \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]\), each unramified with residue field of at most \(p^2\) elements, and conjugation permutes them (the primes above an odd prime, in the multiplication chapter). This lets one read off \(p\)-adic valuations of the two rational coordinates of an element from its valuations at these primes. At the prime \((s)\) above \(2\) the model chapter's formula \(v_s(c_0+c_1s)=\min(2v_2(c_0),2v_2(c_1)+1)\) does the same.

docs.title: Rational coordinates at odd primes
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.padicValRat_coords_ge

Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(k\in\mathbb Z\), and \(u=u_0+u_1s\in K_0\) with \(u_0,u_1\in\mathbb Q\). If \(v_{\mathfrak p}(u)\ge k\) for every prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) containing \(p\) (with \(v_{\mathfrak p}(0)=+\infty\)), then $\(v_p(u_0)\ge k\qquad\text{and}\qquad v_p(u_1)\ge k\)$ (with \(v_p(0)=+\infty\)).

Proof sketch. Let \(\bar u=u_0-u_1s\). Conjugation permutes the primes above \(p\), so \(v_{\mathfrak p}(\bar u)=v_{\bar{\mathfrak p}}(u)\ge k\) for every \(\mathfrak p\mid p\). Then \(u_0=(u+\bar u)/2\) and \(u_1=(u-\bar u)/(2s)\), and \(v_{\mathfrak p}(2)=v_{\mathfrak p}(s)=0\) since \(p\) is odd, so \(v_{\mathfrak p}(u_0),v_{\mathfrak p}(u_1)\ge k\) for any one prime \(\mathfrak p\mid p\). For a rational number \(c\), \(v_{\mathfrak p}(c)=v_{\mathfrak p}(p)\,v_p(c)=v_p(c)\) because \(v_{\mathfrak p}(p)=1\).

The manuscript performs the same extraction ("both rational coefficients lie in \(N_s^4\mathbb Z_{(N_s)}\)") without spelling it out.

docs.title: Reduction and the filtration
docs.text:
Reduction modulo a prime not above \(2\) is a homomorphism from the points with nonsingular reduction onto the nonsingular points of the reduced curve, with kernel the points of negative abscissa valuation. Over a finite field of odd characteristic the reduced curve has at most \(2|k|+1\) points, which replaces Hasse's bound used in the manuscript.

The points with \(v(x)\le-2r\) form subgroups \(W_r\) (the formal neighbourhood and its filtration), and multiplication by \(n\) moves \(W_r\) into \(W_{r+v(n)}\) as long as the residue characteristic has valuation at most four (multiplication in a formal neighbourhood). This replaces the manuscript's formal group and logarithm isometry by elementary statements about valuations on \(K_0\) itself.

Let \(A\in\mathbb Z[s]\), \(W:y^2=x^3+Ax\) over \(K_0\) and \(\widetilde W:y^2=x^3+ ho(A)x\) over \(k\). Let \(\widetilde W_{ m ns}(k)\) be the group of nonsingular points of \(\widetilde W\) over \(k\) together with \(O\), under the chord-and-tangent law. Put $\(W_1(\mathfrak p)=\{O\}\cup\{(x,y)\in W(K_0):x otin\mathcal O_{\mathfrak p}\},\)$ $\(W_0(\mathfrak p)=W_1(\mathfrak p)\cup\{(x,y)\in W(K_0):x\in\mathcal O_{\mathfrak p},\ ( ho(x), ho(y)) ext{ is a nonsingular point of }\widetilde W\}.\)$ (If \(x\in\mathcal O_{\mathfrak p}\) then \(y\in\mathcal O_{\mathfrak p}\), since \(y^2=x^3+Ax\).) Define \(\operatorname{red}:W_0(\mathfrak p) o\widetilde W_{ m ns}(k)\) by \(\operatorname{red}(Q)=O\) for \(Q\in W_1(\mathfrak p)\) and \(\operatorname{red}(x,y)=( ho(x), ho(y))\) otherwise. Then:

  1. \(W_0(\mathfrak p)\) is a subgroup of \(W(K_0)\) and \(\operatorname{red}\) is a group homomorphism with kernel \(W_1(\mathfrak p)\);
  2. if \( ho(A) e0\), then \(\widetilde W\) is nonsingular and \(W_0(\mathfrak p)=W(K_0)\).

Consequently, if \(Q\in W_0(\mathfrak p)\) and \(n\ge1\) is the order of \(\operatorname{red}(Q)\) in the finite group \(\widetilde W_{ m ns}(k)\), then \([n]Q\in W_1(\mathfrak p)\), and so \([mn]Q\in W_1(\mathfrak p)\) for every integer \(m\).

Proof sketch. This is Silverman, Proposition VII.2.1, applied after embedding \(K_0\) in its completion at \(\mathfrak p\) (the local ring \(\mathcal O_{\mathfrak p}\) is the intersection of \(K_0\) with the completed valuation ring, and the residue fields agree). The model is integral at \(\mathfrak p\), and the proof of VII.2.1 uses only integrality: the group law is given by the chord-and-tangent construction, a line through points of \(W_0(\mathfrak p)\) reduces to the line through their reductions, and the third intersection point reduces accordingly; points with \(x otin\mathcal O_{\mathfrak p}\) reduce to \(O\). For (2), the discriminant of \(y^2=x^3+ax\) is \(-64a^3\), nonzero in odd characteristic when \(a e0\); then every point with integral coordinates has nonsingular reduction. The final statement follows from (1) since \(W_1(\mathfrak p)\) is a subgroup.

The manuscript cites VII.2.1 for the nonsingular reduction group at the bad place and uses the same homomorphism at the good places. The model chapter's reduction statement for split primes of good reduction is the special case of (1) with residue degree one.

docs.title: The trivial point count
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.card_affineSolutions_le ZInQ.Size.card_points_le ZInQ.Size.addOrderOf_le_two_card_add_one ZInQ.Size.odd_prime_count_bounds

Let \(k\) be a finite field of odd characteristic and \(a\in k\). Then $\(\#\{(x,y)\in k^2:y^2=x^3+ax\}+1\le2|k|+1,\)$ so every element of the nonsingular group \(\widetilde W_{\rm ns}(k)\) of \(y^2=x^3+ax\) has order at most \(2|k|+1\). Moreover, for every odd prime \(p\), $\(2p^2+1\le p^6\qquad\text{and}\qquad(2p+1)^2\le p^6 .\)$

Proof sketch. For each \(x\in k\) the equation \(y^2=c\) has at most two solutions in a field, so there are at most \(2|k|\) affine points. The nonsingular group is a subset of the affine points together with \(O\), and the order of an element of a finite group is at most the order of the group. For \(p\ge3\): \(2p^2+1\le3p^2\le p^6\) and \(2p+1\le p^3\).

This replaces Hasse's bound \((p+1)^2<p^3\) in the manuscript: with at most two primes above \(p\), a residue field of \(p\) elements at each of two split primes contributes at most \((2p+1)^2\le p^6\), and the single inert prime with \(p^2\) elements at most \(2p^2+1\le p^6\).

docs.title: The point \(P_0\) at the special places
docs.text: At the prime \((d)\) above \(7\) the curve has a cusp, and \(P_0\) reduces to the nonsingular point \((2,6)\) of \(y^2=x^3\); at every other prime not above \(2\) the reduction is good. At the prime \((s)\), \(v_s(x(P_0))=-6\) and \(v_s(y(P_0))=-9\), so \(P_0\) lies in \(W_3\) (the generator in the dyadic formal group).

docs.title: Congruences for \(P_0\) modulo seven
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.bad_place_congruences ZInQ.Size.bad_place_congruences_zmod

The following closed statements about integers hold: $\(1641-1160\cdot3-2\cdot8\equiv0,\qquad -123720+87483\cdot3-6\cdot32\equiv0,\qquad -11243+7950\cdot3\equiv0,\qquad 6^2-2^3\equiv0\pmod 7,\)$ $\(2\cdot6 ot\equiv0,\qquad 3\cdot2^2 ot\equiv0,\qquad 8 ot\equiv0,\qquad 32 ot\equiv0\pmod 7 .\)$

This is a finite computation on integers below \(3\cdot10^5\).

Proof sketch. Direct evaluation: the four left-hand sides are \(-1855=-7\cdot265\), \(138537=7\cdot19791\), \(12607=7\cdot1801\) and \(28=7\cdot4\), while \(12\), \(12\), \(8\) and \(32\) are congruent to \(5\), \(5\), \(1\) and \(4\) modulo \(7\).

The manuscript records the outcome (the reduction of \(P_0\) at the bad place is \((2,6)\) on \(y^2=x^3\) and is nonsingular) without listing the congruences.

Let \(E:y^2=x^3-d^2x\) with \(d=75-53s\), \(A=-d^2=-11243+7950s\), and \(P_0= igl( rac{1641-1160s}{8}, rac{-123720+87483s}{32} igr)\).

  1. At the prime \((d)\), with residue map \( ho:a+bs\mapsto a+3b mod7\) onto \(\mathbb F_7\): \( ho(A)=0\), so the reduced curve is \(y^2=x^3\); the coordinates of \(P_0\) lie in \(\mathbb Z[s]_{(d)}\) (their denominators are powers of \(2\)) and reduce to \((2,6)\); and \((2,6)\) is a nonsingular point of \(y^2=x^3\) over \(\mathbb F_7\). Hence \(P_0\in E_0((d))\).
  2. For every other prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) with \(2 otin\mathfrak p\), \(A otin\mathfrak p\), so \(E\) has good reduction at \(\mathfrak p\) and \(E_0(\mathfrak p)=E(K_0)\).

Proof sketch. (1) \( ho\) is the residue map of \((d)\) (model chapter). The congruences modulo seven (a separate finite computation) give \( ho(8x(P_0))= ho(8)\cdot2\) and \( ho(32y(P_0))= ho(32)\cdot6\) with \( ho(8), ho(32) e0\), so \(8,32 otin(d)\), the coordinates lie in \(\mathbb Z[s]_{(d)}\), and \( ho(x(P_0))=2\), \( ho(y(P_0))=6\); also \( ho(A)=0\) and \(6^2=2^3\) in \(\mathbb F_7\). A point of \(y^2=x^3\) is singular exactly when \(2y=0\) and \(3x^2=0\); here \(2\cdot6=12 ot\equiv0\). (2) \(d\) is a prime element and \(A=-d^2\), so \(A\in\mathfrak p\) only for \(\mathfrak p=(d)\); then apply the good-reduction case of reduction on the nonsingular part.

The manuscript records the reduction to \((2,6)\), its nonsingularity, and good reduction at the other place \(s\equiv4\pmod7\) above \(7\).

docs.title: The successful index
docs.text: Let \(m_0\) be the product of the orders of the reductions of \(P_0\) at the primes above the odd prime divisors of \(N\). Each order is at most \(2|k|+1\), so \(m_0\le N^6\), and \([m_0]P_0\) lies in the kernel of reduction at every such prime. Multiplying further by \(N^4\) gives \(v(1/x)\ge2+8v_p(N)\) at those primes and \(v_s(1/x)\ge6+16v_2(N)\) at \((s)\), which is the required divisibility.

docs.title: Reduction orders of \(P_0\)
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.exists_reduction_multiple

For every integer \(N\ge1\) there is an integer \(m_0\) with \(1\le m_0\le N^6\) such that for every odd prime \(p\mid N\) and every prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(\mathbb Z[s]\) containing \(p\), $\([m_0]P_0\in E_1(\mathfrak p),\quad\text{that is, }[m_0]P_0=O\text{ or }v_{\mathfrak p}\bigl(x([m_0]P_0)\bigr)<0 .\)$

Proof sketch. For each such \(\mathfrak p\), \(P_0\in E_0(\mathfrak p)\): at \((d)\) by the bad-place computation, elsewhere by good reduction. Let \(n_{\mathfrak p}\ge1\) be the order of \(\operatorname{red}_{\mathfrak p}(P_0)\) in the finite group \(\widetilde E_{\rm ns}(k_{\mathfrak p})\); by the trivial point count \(n_{\mathfrak p}\le2|k_{\mathfrak p}|+1\). Put $\(m_0=\prod_{p\mid N,\ p\text{ odd}}\ \prod_{\mathfrak p\ni p}n_{\mathfrak p}.\)$ Since \(n_{\mathfrak p}\mid m_0\), reduction on the nonsingular part gives \([m_0]P_0\in E_1(\mathfrak p)\) for every \(\mathfrak p\) in the product. For a fixed odd \(p\) there are either two primes with residue fields of \(p\) elements or one with \(p^2\) elements, so the inner product is at most \((2p+1)^2\le p^6\) or \(2p^2+1\le p^6\). Hence \(m_0\le\prod_{p\mid N}p^6\le N^6\), the last step because the product of the distinct prime divisors of \(N\) divides \(N\). For \(N=1\), or \(N\) a power of \(2\), the product is empty and \(m_0=1\).

The manuscript takes the same product of actual reduction orders, bounds the orders at good places by Hasse (\((p+1)^2<p^3\)) and the order at \((d)\) by the order seven of the nonsingular group of the cusp over \(\mathbb F_7\); the trivial count suffices for \(m_0\le N^6\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.exists_formal_multiple ZInQ.Size.leastFormalMultiple_bounds ZInQ.Size.leastFormalMultiple_formalCondition ZInQ.Size.M0_bounds

For a point \(Q\in E(K_0)\) let \(\xi(Q)=1/x(Q)\) if \(Q e O\) and \(x(Q) e0\), and \(\xi(Q)=0\) otherwise. For every integer \(N\ge1\) there is an integer \(m\) with \(1\le m\le N^{10}\) such that the normalized representation \(\xi([m]P_0)=(a+bs)/c\) (\(a,b,c\in\mathbb Z\), \(c>0\), \(\gcd(a,b,c)=1\)) satisfies $\(N^4\mid a,\qquad N^4\mid b,\qquad \gcd(c,N)=1 .\)$ Consequently \(1\le\mathrm{LFM}(N)\le N^{10}\) and \(\mathrm{LFM}(N)\) itself satisfies these three conditions. In particular, whenever \(N_s\ge1\) (which holds under the catalogue bound, and also by Dirichlet's theorem, since every catalogue entry is then a prime), \(1\le M_0\le N_s^{10}\) and \(M_0\) is a successful index. The positivity of \(N_s\) is needed: for \(N=0\) the conditions force \(a=b=0\) and \(c=1\), that is \(\xi([m]P_0)=0\).

Proof sketch. Take \(m_0\) from the reduction orders and \(m=N^4m_0\), so \(1\le m\le N^{10}\). If \([m]P_0=O\) or \(x([m]P_0)=0\), then \(\xi=0=(0+0s)/1\) and the conditions hold. Otherwise write \(u=\xi([m]P_0)=u_0+u_1s\) with \(u_0,u_1\in\mathbb Q\).

Odd \(p\mid N\). At every prime \(\mathfrak p i p\), \([m_0]P_0\in E_1(\mathfrak p)=W_1\) and \(v_{\mathfrak p}(N^4)=4v_p(N)\), so multiplication in the formal neighbourhood (item 3) gives \([m]P_0\in W_{1+4v_p(N)}\), that is \(v_{\mathfrak p}(u)=-v_{\mathfrak p}(x)\ge2+8v_p(N)\). By the extraction at odd primes, \(v_p(u_0),v_p(u_1)\ge2+8v_p(N)\ge4v_p(N)\).

\(p=2\), if \(N\) is even. \(P_0\in W_3\) at \((s)\), and \(v_s(m)=2v_2(m)\ge8v_2(N)\), so \([m]P_0\in W_{3+8v_2(N)}\) and \(v_s(u)\ge6+16v_2(N)\). By \(v_s(u_0+u_1s)=\min(2v_2(u_0),2v_2(u_1)+1)\), \(v_2(u_0)\ge3+8v_2(N)\) and \(v_2(u_1)\ge3+8v_2(N)\), both at least \(4v_2(N)\).

Normalization. The normalized representation has \(c=\operatorname{lcm}(\operatorname{den}u_0,\operatorname{den}u_1)\), \(a=u_0c\), \(b=u_1c\). For \(p\mid N\), \(v_p(u_i)\ge0\), so \(p mid c\); thus \(\gcd(c,N)=1\) and \(v_p(a)=v_p(u_0)\ge4v_p(N)\), \(v_p(b)=v_p(u_1)\ge4v_p(N)\) for every \(p\mid N\), i.e. \(N^4\mid a\) and \(N^4\mid b\). The set of successful indices is therefore nonempty, so its least element \(\mathrm{LFM}(N)\) is successful and at most \(m\).

No property of \(P_0\) beyond those cited is needed; in particular the argument does not use that \(P_0\) has infinite order (the conventions for \(\xi\) cover the identity). The manuscript loses up to three units of \(v_s\) when extracting \(u_0,u_1\); the exact valuation formula at \((s)\) avoids this.

docs.title: Syntax heights and the final comparison
Syntax heights and the final comparison
docs.text:
The specified polynomial is a compact syntax, not an expanded monomial list: node lists share nodes, templates call earlier templates, and three constructors insert huge polynomials without expanding them. Its size is bounded by an induction on this syntax.

9 fully proved

docs.title: Heights and majorants
docs.text:
Variables have height zero, constants and fixed nodes height one, an operation or constructor one more than its highest argument, and a call one more than the callee's height plus its highest argument. Recipes add three levels for a substituted callee in a model-evaluation recipe, then two for the final sum of squares; composition recipes only rename variables, so they add two levels for a sum of squares and one for a product.

At height \(h\ge1\) a polynomial has degree and logarithmic norm at most \(B^{8h}\), provided \(B\ge2^{20}\) exceeds every occurring constant, constructor index and guard cutoff. The six closure rules (operations, substitution, constructors, renaming, sums of squares and products) carry this majorant through templates and recipes.

docs.title: Syntax heights
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.Maj ZInQ.Size.nodeHeight ZInQ.Size.nodeHeights ZInQ.Size.templateHeight ZInQ.Size.libraryHeights ZInQ.Size.recipeHeight ZInQ.Size.recipeHeights

Nodes and templates. For a template \(\tau\) with node list \(n_0,\dots,n_{k-1}\) in a library whose calls refer to earlier templates, the height \(h(n_j)\in\mathbb N\) is defined in node order:

  • \(h(\mathrm{var}\ i)=0\);
  • \(h(\mathrm{const}\ c)=1\) and \(h(\mathrm{fixed}\ e)=1\);
  • \(h(\mathrm{add}\ j\ j')=h(\mathrm{mul}\ j\ j')=1+\max(h(n_j),h(n_{j'}))\);
  • \(h(\mathrm{psi}\ e\ (a_0,\dots,a_3)\ c)=1+\max_ih(n_{a_i})\) and \(h(\mathrm{guard}\ e\ (a_1,\dots,a_{15}))=1+\max_ih(n_{a_i})\);
  • \(h(\mathrm{call}\ \tau'\ (a_0,\dots,a_{p-1})\ w)=1+H(\tau')+\max\bigl(0,\max_ih(n_{a_i})\bigr)\).

The intrinsic height of \(\tau\) is \(H(\tau)=h(n_{\mathrm{root}})\).

Recipes. For a model-evaluation recipe \(\rho\) whose calls have callees \(\kappa\) (the natural, raw-addition, multiplication and fixed-scalar templates and the power recipe that actually occur), $\(H(\rho)=\max\Bigl(4,\ \max_\kappa\bigl(H(\kappa)+3\bigr)\Bigr)+2 .\)$ For a composition recipe with callees \(\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_k\), \(H(\rho)=\max_iH(\kappa_i)+2\) for a sum of squares and \(H(\rho)=\max_iH(\kappa_i)+1\) for a product.

Majorant. For an integer \(B\ge2\), an integer polynomial \(P\) satisfies the height-\(h\) majorant, written \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(h,P)\), if $\(\deg P\le1\text{ and }\|P\|_1\le1\quad(h=0),\qquad \deg P\le B^{8h}\text{ and }\|P\|_1\le2^{B^{8h}}\quad(h\ge1).\)$

This is a definition. The height is a majorant for the compact syntax, not the depth of an expanded expression; it deliberately overestimates (shared nodes and unused nodes are counted). For the model-evaluation wrappers the safe value four bounds the generator equations and root differences, as in the manuscript, rather than the literal height two of the companion proof.

docs.title: Closure rules for the height majorant
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.Maj.mono ZInQ.Size.Maj.X ZInQ.Size.Maj.C ZInQ.Size.Maj.add ZInQ.Size.Maj.mul ZInQ.Size.Maj.bind₁ ZInQ.Size.Maj.constructor ZInQ.Size.Maj.rename ZInQ.Size.Maj.bind₁_of_maj_zero ZInQ.Size.Maj.sum_sq ZInQ.Size.Maj.prod

Let \(B\ge2^{20}\) be an integer and write \(\mathrm{Maj}(h,P)\) for \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(h,P)\).

  1. Monotonicity and atoms. \(\mathrm{Maj}(h,P)\) and \(h\le h'\) imply \(\mathrm{Maj}(h',P)\). Every variable satisfies \(\mathrm{Maj}(0,X_i)\), and every integer constant \(c\) with \(|c|\le2^{B^8}\) satisfies \(\mathrm{Maj}(1,c)\).
  2. Operations. \(\mathrm{Maj}(h_1,P)\) and \(\mathrm{Maj}(h_2,Q)\) imply \(\mathrm{Maj}(1+\max(h_1,h_2),P+Q)\) and \(\mathrm{Maj}(1+\max(h_1,h_2),PQ)\).
  3. Substitution. If \(\mathrm{Maj}(H,P)\) and \(\mathrm{Maj}(k,Q_i)\) for every \(i\) such that \(X_i\) occurs in \(P\), then \(\mathrm{Maj}(H+k+1,P(Q))\).
  4. Constructors. If \(\deg C\le B^4\), \(\|C\|_1\le2^{B^8}\) and \(\mathrm{Maj}(k,Q_i)\) for all arguments, then \(\mathrm{Maj}(k+1,C(Q))\).
  5. Renaming. \(\mathrm{Maj}(h,P)\) implies \(\mathrm{Maj}(h,P(Y_\sigma))\) for every map \(\sigma\) of variables.
  6. Sums of squares. If \(1\le m\le B\) and \(\mathrm{Maj}(h,c_i)\) for \(i=1,\dots,m\), then \(\mathrm{Maj}(h+2,\sum_ic_i^2)\).
  7. Products. If \(1\le m\le B\) and \(\mathrm{Maj}(h,c_i)\) for \(i=1,\dots,m\), then \(\mathrm{Maj}(h+1,\prod_ic_i)\).

Proof sketch. Throughout, \(B^{8h}\ge B\ge2^{20}\) for \(h\ge1\), and the height-zero case has norm at most \(1\). (1) Degrees: \(\max\le B^{8m}\) and \(2B^{8m}\le B^{8m+8}\) for \(m=\max(h_1,h_2)\) (for \(m=0\), \(\deg\le2\le B^8\)). Norms: \(\|P+Q\|_1\le2\cdot2^{B^{8m}}\) and \(\|PQ\|_1\le2^{2B^{8m}}\), both at most \(2^{B^{8m+8}}\). (2) By the substitution bounds with \(d=B^{8k}\) (or \(1\)) and \(M=2^{B^{8k}}\) (or \(1\) when \(k=0\)): \(\deg\le B^{8H}B^{8k}\le B^{8(H+k+1)}\) and \(\log_2\|P(Q)\|_1\le B^{8H}+B^{8H}B^{8k}\le B^{8(H+k+1)}\); for \(k=0\) simply \(\|P(Q)\|_1\le\|P\|_1\). (3) Likewise \(\deg\le B^4B^{8k}\le B^{8k+8}\) and \(\log_2\|C(Q)\|_1\le B^8+B^4B^{8k}\le B^{8k+8}\) for \(k\ge1\); for \(k=0\) the arguments have norm at most \(1\) and \(\log_2\|C(Q)\|_1\le B^8\). (4) By the renaming bound. (5) \(\deg\le2B^{8h}\) and \(\|\sum c_i^2\|_1\le m\,2^{2B^{8h}}\le2^{B+2B^{8h}}\le2^{B^{8h+16}}\). (6) \(\deg\le mB^{8h}\le B^{8h+8}\) and \(\|\prod c_i\|_1\le2^{mB^{8h}}\le2^{B^{8h+8}}\) (for \(h=0\): degree at most \(m\le B^8\), norm at most \(1\)).

These are the manuscript's rules: positive height \(h\) gives degree and logarithmic norm at most \(B^{8h}\); a call charges one level beyond the callee and argument heights; and a renaming retains the callee's height.

ZInQ.Size.ConstructorBounds ZInQ.Size.NodeAdmissible ZInQ.Size.nodes_majorant ZInQ.Size.library_majorant

Let \(B\ge2^{20}\) and let \(L\) be a template library, each call referring to an earlier template, such that, in every template of \(L\):

  • every node \(\mathrm{const}\ c\) has \(|c|\le B-1\);
  • every node \(\mathrm{fixed}\ e\) has \(|\mathrm{val}(e)|\le B-1\);
  • every node \(\mathrm{psi}\ e\ a\ c\) has \(|\mathrm{val}(e)|+1\le B\);
  • every node \(\mathrm{guard}\ e\ a\) has \(0\le\mathrm{val}(e)\le B-1\).

Suppose moreover that the constructors satisfy the uniform bounds at \(B\): \(\deg\Psi_{n,c}\le B^4\) and \(\|\Psi_{n,c}\|_1\le2^{B^8}\) whenever \(|n|+1\le B\), and \(\deg G_T\le B^4\) and \(\|G_T\|_1\le2^{B^8}\) whenever \(0\le T\le B-1\). (The constructors of the specification satisfy them at every \(B\ge2^{20}\).)

Then for every template \(\tau\) of \(L\) and every node \(n_j\) of \(\tau\), \(\mathrm{Maj}_B\bigl(h(n_j),[\![n_j]\!]\bigr)\); in particular \(\mathrm{Maj}_B\bigl(H(\tau),[\![\tau]\!]\bigr)\).

Proof sketch. Induction over the library in stored order and, within a template, over the nodes in stored order. Variables: rule (0). Constants and fixed nodes: rule (0), since \(|c|\le B\le2^{B^8}\). Additions and multiplications: rule (1). Constructor nodes: the hypothesis on the constructors gives \(\deg\le B^4\) and \(\|\cdot\|_1\le2^{B^8}\) for \(\Psi_{\mathrm{val}(e),c}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{val}(e)}\); apply rule (3) with \(k\) the maximum argument height. Calls: the call polynomial is \([\![\tau']\!]\) with parameters replaced by the argument polynomials (height at most \(k=\max(0,\max_ih(n_{a_i}))\)) and witnesses by fresh variables (height \(0\le k\)); the induction hypothesis for the earlier template \(\tau'\) gives \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(H(\tau'),[\![\tau']\!])\), and rule (2) gives \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(H(\tau')+k+1,\cdot)\). The values \(\mathrm{val}(e)\) enter only through the four hypotheses and are never computed.

docs.title: Recipes satisfy the height majorant
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.model_majorant ZInQ.Size.composition_majorant

Let \(B\ge2^{20}\).

  1. Let \(\rho\) be a model-evaluation recipe with at most \(B\) constraints, and suppose every callee \(\kappa\) occurring in its calls satisfies \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(h_\kappa,[\![\kappa]\!])\) with \(h_\kappa\ge1\). Then \(\mathrm{Maj}_B\bigl(\max(4,\max_\kappa(h_\kappa+3))+2,\ [\![\rho]\!]\bigr)\).
  2. Let \(\rho\) be a composition recipe with \(m\) calls, \(1\le m\le B\), whose callees satisfy \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(h_i,[\![\kappa_i]\!])\). Then \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(\max_ih_i+2,[\![\rho]\!])\) if \(\rho\) is a sum of squares and \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(\max_ih_i+1,[\![\rho]\!])\) if it is a product.

Proof sketch. (1) The constraints are the three generator equations \(8X_{g_0}-1641\), \(4X_{g_1}+15465\), \(32X_{g_2}-87483\), the calls, and the five root differences. Every point reference is a variable, a constant \(0\), \(1\) or \(-145\), or the negative of a variable, so each argument polynomial has degree at most \(1\) and norm at most \(145\), and satisfies \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(2,\cdot)\). A call is a substitution of such arguments (and fresh variables) into \([\![\kappa]\!]\), so it satisfies \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(h_\kappa+3,\cdot)\) by rule (2). The generator equations and root differences have degree at most \(1\) and norm at most \(87515\), so they satisfy \(\mathrm{Maj}_B(4,\cdot)\). By monotonicity every constraint satisfies the majorant at \(\max(4,\max_\kappa(h_\kappa+3))\), and rule (5) for the sum of at most \(B\) squares adds two. (2) The arguments of every call are coordinate variables, so each constraint is a renaming of \([\![\kappa_i]\!]\) followed by moving witnesses to fresh variables, again a renaming: rule (4) keeps \(h_i\); then rule (5) or rule (6).

The manuscript calls the renaming case the reason why composition calls retain the callee's height, and charges the model wrappers the safe height four.

docs.title: The specified library
docs.text:
One traversal of the constructed library computes the twenty-three template heights and checks the constants and constructor indices that occur. The recipe rules then give the seven recipe heights \(228,233,235,251,252,254,256\), using the constraint counts from the shape of the natural circuit.

The cutoff \(B=T+1\) is admissible: every occurring constant and index is far below \(D\le T\). The root height \(256\) gives degree at most \((T+1)^{2048}\) and coefficients at most \(2^{(T+1)^{2048}}\).

docs.title: Template heights
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.templateHeightTable ZInQ.Size.LibraryAdmissible ZInQ.Size.templateLibrary_maj

Let \(B\ge2^{20}\), and suppose that the constructors satisfy the uniform bounds at \(B\), that every index \(n\) of a division-polynomial constructor of the library satisfies \(|n|+1\le B\), and that \(|\ell|+1\le B\) and \(0\le T\), \(T+1\le B\). Then the polynomial of every template of the constructed library has a majorant of order \(B\) at the following height:

Template Height Template Height member 18 multiply.guard 4 raw_add 21 multiply 214 raw_z 12 natural 223 raw_inverse_x 12 value.signed_encode 230 log25 25 value.abs 9 pole 24 value.close_coordinates 34 test_group 79 value.test 249 slope 169 value.exceptions 43 height_certificate 207 scalar.integer_constant_\(k\) (\(k=0,\dots,4\)) 17 multiply.scalar 17

The division-polynomial constructors of the library occur only in the fixed-scalar templates \(S_\varepsilon\), with indices \(\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon+1\), \(\varepsilon-1\) and \(2\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon\in\{c_*,4,2,3,c_3,1399\}\); the guard constructor occurs at \(T\), and the fixed constant \(\ell\) only in multiply. Every other constant of the library is an explicit integer literal and needs no hypothesis.

The manuscript states the table for the intrinsic heights of the node lists of the saved specification, with \(173\) constant nodes below \(2^{69}\) and \(50\) constructor nodes. The templates here are explicit constructions without node lists, so the statement is made for their polynomials.

Proof sketch. Apply the majorant rules to each template in library order, along its construction, with the bounds of the templates it calls and the constructor bounds. Each literal constant \(c\) is bounded as \(|c|\le2^{2^k}\) for a small explicit \(k\), and \(B\ge2^{20}\) absorbs these bounds; no fixed value is computed. The construction gives much smaller heights, at most \(8\) (\(1\) for the templates without calls, \(6\) for multiply); the tabulated heights follow by monotonicity.

docs.title: Recipe heights
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.recipe_heights

Let \(B\) satisfy the hypotheses of the template heights: \(B\ge2^{20}\), the constructors satisfy the uniform bounds at \(B\), every index \(n\) of a division-polynomial constructor of the library satisfies \(|n|+1\le B\), \(|\ell|+1\le B\), and \(0\le T\), \(T+1\le B\). Let the natural precision circuit have the shape of the compiler chapter, in the form of upper bounds: five inputs, at most \(54{,}056\) explicit variables of which at least five are inputs, at most \(125{,}327\) additions, \(98{,}382\) multiplications and \(15{,}845\) calls, and constants among \(0,1,-1,c_3,2,4,1399\). Then $\(\mathrm{Maj}_B(228,[\![\mathtt{power\_value}]\!]),\quad\mathrm{Maj}_B(233,[\![\mathtt{precision}]\!]),\quad \mathrm{Maj}_B(235,[\![\mathtt{close}]\!]),\quad\mathrm{Maj}_B(251,[\![\mathtt{main}]\!]),\)$ $\(\mathrm{Maj}_B(252,[\![\mathtt{value\_union}]\!]),\quad\mathrm{Maj}_B(254,[\![\mathtt{value}]\!]),\quad \mathrm{Maj}_B(256,[\![\mathtt{integers}]\!]).\)$

Proof sketch. By the template majorant and the template heights (with monotonicity), every template satisfies the majorant at its tabulated height. Then apply the recipe rules in recipe order.

  • \(\mathtt{power\_value}\) has \(3+79+3+196+190+5=476\) constraints (generator equations, natural rows for the \(79\) witnesses, three constant definitions, \(196\) additions, \(190\) multiplications, root differences); its callees are \(\mathtt{natural}\) (\(223\)), \(\mathtt{raw\_add}\) (\(21\)), \(\mathtt{multiply}\) (\(214\)) and three fixed-scalar templates (\(17\)): height \(\max(4,223+3)+2=228\).
  • \(\mathtt{precision}\) has at most \(3+54056+4+125327+98382+15845+5=293622\le2^{20}\) constraints; its callees add the power recipe (\(228\)): height \(228+3+2=233\).
  • \(\mathtt{close}\) (sum of squares, \(7\) calls: five signed encodings (\(230\)), the precision recipe (\(233\)), the coordinate window (\(34\))): \(233+2=235\).
  • \(\mathtt{main}\) (sum of squares, \(\mathtt{close}\) and \(\mathtt{value.test}\) (\(249\))): \(249+2=251\).
  • \(\mathtt{value\_union}\) (product, \(\mathtt{value.exceptions}\) (\(43\)) and \(\mathtt{main}\)): \(251+1=252\).
  • \(\mathtt{value}\) (sum of squares, \(\mathtt{member}\) (\(18\)) and \(\mathtt{value\_union}\)): \(252+2=254\).
  • \(\mathtt{integers}\) (sum of squares, one call of \(\mathtt{value}\)): \(254+2=256\).

All constraint counts are at most \(2^{20}\le B\). The counts for the two model-evaluation recipes come from the translation and the shape of the natural circuit.

docs.title: The cutoff is an admissible bound
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.admissible_cutoff ZInQ.Size.D_le_T

Assume the catalogue bound, and let the program literal satisfy \(|c_3|<2^{2^{24}}\) (as it does, by the size of the program literal). Then \(B=T+1\) satisfies the hypotheses of the template heights for the constructed library with the constructors of the specification:

  1. \(B\ge2^{20}\), and the division-polynomial and guard constructors satisfy the uniform bounds at \(B\);
  2. the fixed constant \(\ell\) satisfies \(1\le\ell\le T\), so \(|\ell|+1\le B\);
  3. every index \(n\) of a division-polynomial constructor of the library has \(|n|+1\le T+1\);
  4. the guard constructor has cutoff \(T\), and \(0\le T\le B-1\).

Moreover \(D\le T\). The literal constants of the templates need no hypothesis.

Proof sketch. By the definitions, \(D\le R\le Q\le Q^{17}\le A_{\rm ht}\le T\), and \(D>2^{2^{8008}}\), so \(B\ge2^{20}\). (1) The uniform constructor bounds hold at every \(B\ge2^{20}\). For (2), \(\ell\ge1\) since \(P_s,H_{\rm cat}\ge1\), and \(\ell<2^{2^{4623}}<D\le T\). For (3), by construction every index is \(\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon\pm1\) or \(2\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\in\{c_*,4,2,3,c_3,1399\}\) (the values of \(\mathrm{integer\_constant}_0,\dots,\mathrm{integer\_constant}_4\) are \(4,2,3,c_3,1399\)), so \(|n|+1\le2|\varepsilon|+2\). Here \(c_*<2^{2^{4617}}\) and \(|c_3|<2^{2^{24}}\), so \(|n|+1\le2\cdot2^{2^{4617}}\le2^{2^{4618}}<D\le T\). (4) is immediate. Nothing is evaluated: each comparison is between symbolic bounds.

The manuscript lists "the absolute values of all literal fixed constants and all occurring division-polynomial indices are at most \(T\)" among the checked facts. The indices and the fixed value \(\ell\) (used by the companion proof) are bounded symbolically here. The literal constants of the templates need no bound, since the majorant rules absorb them at every \(B\ge2^{20}\); for comparison with the manuscript's constant nodes, \(2^{69}<T\).

docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.tower_bounds ZInQ.Size.degree_lt_tower_seven ZInQ.Size.coefficient_lt_tower_eight

Let \(2\uparrow\uparrow0=1\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow(n+1)=2^{2\uparrow\uparrow n}\), so \(2\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow4=65536\). For every natural number \(T<2^{2^{2^{9013}}}\), $\((T+1)^{2048}<2^{2^{2^{9014}}}<2\uparrow\uparrow7\qquad\text{and}\qquad 2^{(T+1)^{2048}}<2\uparrow\uparrow8 .\)$

Proof sketch. \(T+1\le U=2^{2^{2^{9013}}}\), so \((T+1)^{2048}\le U^{2048}=2^{2^{2^{9013}}\cdot2^{11}}=2^{2^{2^{9013}+11}}\), and \(2^{9013}+11<2^{9014}\); thus \((T+1)^{2048}<2^{2^{2^{9014}}}\). Next \(2\uparrow\uparrow7=2^{2^{2^{2\uparrow\uparrow4}}}=2^{2^{2^{65536}}}\), and \(9014<65536\) with strict monotonicity of \(k\mapsto2^{2^{2^k}}\) gives the first chain. The second follows by applying \(k\mapsto2^k\): \(2^{(T+1)^{2048}}<2^{2\uparrow\uparrow7}=2\uparrow\uparrow8\). Only monotonicity of exponentiation and the value \(2\uparrow\uparrow4=65536\) are used.

docs.title: Norms, division polynomials and the finite constructors
Norms, division polynomials and the finite constructors
docs.text:
Integer polynomials are measured by total degree and coefficient \(\ell^1\) norm, and pairs \((a,b)\) representing \(a+bs\) over a polynomial ring by the weighted norm \(\|a\|_1+2\|b\|_1\). Every coefficient is bounded by the \(\ell^1\) norm, so a norm bound is a coefficient bound.

The normalized division polynomials, evaluated at the formal point \((x_0+x_1s,y_0+y_1s)\), satisfy \(\deg f_n\le(n+1)^3\) and \(\|f_n\|\le2^{100(n+1)^3}\) by strong induction: the cubic exponents leave a slack of at least nine in the even recurrence and ten in the odd one, which absorbs the fixed factors.

The guard is a product over the false triples in the box \([-T,T]^3\) of sums of squares whose coefficients are the reduced coordinates of \(\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(c)\). These are obtained from division polynomials at \(P_0\) by a few field operations, each taking a size \(H\) to at most \(3H^4\), which bounds every coordinate by \(2^{2^{30}(T+1)^3}\).

For any \(B\ge2^{20}\) that exceeds the occurring indices and cutoffs, each of the three finite constructors has degree at most \(B^4\) and norm at most \(2^{B^8}\).

9 fully proved

docs.title: Coefficient norms and degrees
docs.text:
ZInQ.Syntax.l1 ZInQ.Size.PairRing ZInQ.Size.pairNorm ZInQ.Size.pairDeg

For a polynomial \(f=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha X^\alpha\in\mathbb Z[X_i:i\in I]\) (finitely many nonzero \(c_\alpha\)), its coefficient \(\ell^1\) norm is $\(\|f\|_1=\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|\in\mathbb N,\)$ and \(\deg f\) is its total degree (\(\deg0=0\)).

Let \(S=\mathbb Z[X_i:i\in I]\) and \(S[s]=S[t]/(t^2-2)\), whose elements are pairs \((a,b)\), written \(a+bs\), with \((a,b)+(c,d)=(a+c,b+d)\) and \((a,b)(c,d)=(ac+2bd,\ ad+bc)\). The weighted pair norm and degree are $\(\|a+bs\|=\|a\|_1+2\|b\|_1,\qquad\deg(a+bs)=\max(\deg a,\deg b).\)$

This is a definition.

docs.title: Elementary estimates for the coefficient norm
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.l1_estimates

For \(f,g\in\mathbb Z[X_i:i\in I]\), \(c\in\mathbb Z\), \(i\in I\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\):

  1. \(|[X^\alpha]f|\le\|f\|_1\) for every monomial \(X^\alpha\), and \(\|f\|_1=0\) only for \(f=0\);
  2. \(\|c\|_1=|c|\) for the constant \(c\), \(\|X_i\|_1=1\), \(\|-f\|_1=\|f\|_1\), \(\|cf\|_1=|c|\,\|f\|_1\);
  3. \(\|f+g\|_1\le\|f\|_1+\|g\|_1\) and \(\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_1\), hence \(\|f^k\|_1\le\|f\|_1^k\), and the same for finite sums and products;
  4. \(\deg(f+g)\le\max(\deg f,\deg g)\), \(\deg(fg)\le\deg f+\deg g\), \(\deg f^k\le k\deg f\), \(\deg c=0\) and \(\deg X_i\le1\).

Proof sketch. (1)-(2) from the definition. For the product, the coefficient of \(X^\gamma\) in \(fg\) is \(\sum_{\alpha+\beta=\gamma}a_\alpha b_\beta\), so \(\|fg\|_1\le\sum_\gamma\sum_{\alpha+\beta=\gamma}|a_\alpha||b_\beta|=\|f\|_1\|g\|_1\). Degrees are standard.

docs.title: Substitution and renaming bounds
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.substitution_bounds ZInQ.Size.rename_bounds ZInQ.Size.l1_rename_eq

Let \(P\in\mathbb Z[X_i:i\in I]\) and \(Q_i\in\mathbb Z[Y_j:j\in J]\) for \(i\in I\), and let \(P(Q)\) be the image of \(P\) under the ring homomorphism \(X_i\mapsto Q_i\). If \(d\ge1\) and \(M\ge1\) satisfy \(\deg Q_i\le d\) and \(\|Q_i\|_1\le M\) for every \(i\) such that \(X_i\) occurs in \(P\), then $\(\deg P(Q)\le d\cdot\deg P,\qquad\|P(Q)\|_1\le\|P\|_1\,M^{\deg P}.\)$ In the manuscript's notation, \(\deg P(Q)\le\deg P\cdot\max(1,\max_i\deg Q_i)\) and \(\|P(Q)\|_1\le\|P\|_1\max(1,\max_i\|Q_i\|_1)^{\deg P}\).

For a renaming \(Q_i=Y_{\sigma(i)}\) with any map \(\sigma:I\to J\) (not necessarily injective), $\(\deg P(Y_\sigma)\le\deg P,\qquad \|P(Y_\sigma)\|_1=\sum_\beta\Bigl|\sum_{\alpha\mapsto\beta}c_\alpha\Bigr|\le\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|=\|P\|_1 .\)$

Proof sketch. Write \(P=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha X^\alpha\). Then \(P(Q)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha\prod_iQ_i^{\alpha_i}\); by the elementary estimates each monomial image has degree at most \(\sum_i\alpha_i\deg Q_i\le d|\alpha|\le d\deg P\) and norm at most \(\prod_i\|Q_i\|_1^{\alpha_i}\le M^{|\alpha|}\le M^{\deg P}\) (as \(M\ge1\)); sum over \(\alpha\). For a renaming each monomial \(X^\alpha\) maps to a single monomial of the same degree, and coefficients of monomials with the same image add, which can only decrease the \(\ell^1\) norm.

docs.title: The weighted pair norm
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.pair_norm_estimates

For \(u=a+bs\) and \(u'=a'+b's\) in \(S[s]\), \(S=\mathbb Z[X_i:i\in I]\), and \(c\in\mathbb Z\):

  1. \(\|u+u'\|\le\|u\|+\|u'\|\), \(\|u-u'\|\le\|u\|+\|u'\|\) and \(\|cu\|=|c|\,\|u\|\);
  2. \(\|uu'\|\le\|u\|\,\|u'\|\), hence \(\|u^k\|\le\|u\|^k\);
  3. \(\deg(u+u')\le\max(\deg u,\deg u')\) and \(\deg(uu')\le\deg u+\deg u'\);
  4. \(\|a\|_1\le\|u\|\) and \(\|b\|_1\le\|u\|\);
  5. for integers \(e,f\), the constant \(e+fs\) has norm \(|e|+2|f|\) and degree \(0\), and the variable pair \(X_i+X_js\) (\(i\ne j\)) has norm \(3\) and degree \(1\).

Proof sketch. (2): \(uu'=(aa'+2bb')+(ab'+a'b)s\), so by the elementary estimates \(\|uu'\|\le\|a\|\|a'\|+2\|b\|\|b'\|+2\|a\|\|b'\|+2\|a'\|\|b\|\le(\|a\|+2\|b\|)(\|a'\|+2\|b'\|)\). The rest is immediate from the scalar estimates.

The manuscript states that both norms are submultiplicative; the companion proof adds subadditivity under the field operations.

docs.title: Size of the division polynomials
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.normDiv_size ZInQ.Size.psiComponent_size

Work in \(S[s]\) with \(S=\mathbb Z[x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1]\), put \(x=x_0+x_1s\), \(y=y_0+y_1s\) and \(A=-11243+7950s\), and let \(F_n=f_n(x)\in S[s]\) for the normalized division polynomials \(f_n\) of \(y^2=x^3+Ax\). Then for every \(n\ge0\) $\(\deg F_n\le(n+1)^3,\qquad\|F_n\|\le2^{100(n+1)^3}.\)$ Consequently, for every \(n\in\mathbb Z\) and \(c\in\{0,1\}\), the component polynomial \(\Psi_{n,c}\in S\) (the coefficient of \(s^c\) in \(\psi_n(x,y)\)) satisfies $\(\deg\Psi_{n,c}\le2(|n|+1)^3,\qquad\|\Psi_{n,c}\|_1\le2^{101(|n|+1)^3}.\)$

Proof sketch. Norms: \(\|x\|=\|y\|=3\), \(\|A\|=11243+2\cdot7950=27143<2^{15}\), and \(D_0=16(x^3+Ax)^2\) has degree \(6\) and \(\|D_0\|\le16(27+3\cdot27143)^2<2^{38}\).

Base cases. \(F_0=0\), \(F_1=F_2=1\). \(F_3=3x^4+6Ax^2-A^2\) has degree at most \(4\le64\) and norm at most \(3\cdot3^4+6\cdot27143\cdot3^2+27143^2<2^{30}\). \(F_4=2(x^6+5Ax^4-5A^2x^2-A^3)\) has degree at most \(6\le125\) and norm at most \(2(3^6+5\cdot27143\cdot3^4+5\cdot27143^2\cdot3^2+27143^3)<2^{46}\).

Even step, \(n=2m\), \(m\ge3\): \(F_{2m}=F_m(F_{m+2}F_{m-1}^2-F_{m-2}F_{m+1}^2)\), all indices below \(2m\). By induction the first product has exponent sum \((m+1)^3+(m+3)^3+2m^3=4m^3+12m^2+30m+28\) (including the factor \(F_m\)), the second \((m+1)^3+(m-1)^3+2(m+2)^3=4m^3+12m^2+30m+16\), smaller. Since \((2m+1)^3-(4m^3+12m^2+30m+28)=4m^3-24m-27\ge9\) for \(m\ge3\), the degree is at most \((2m+1)^3-9\) and \(\log_2\|F_{2m}\|\le100((2m+1)^3-9)+1<100(2m+1)^3\) (the \(+1\) for the difference of two terms).

Odd step, \(n=2m+1\), \(m\ge2\): \(F_{2m+1}=D_0L-R_m\) (\(m\) even) or \(L-D_0R_m\) (\(m\) odd) with \(L=F_{m+2}F_m^3\) and \(R_m=F_{m-1}F_{m+1}^3\), all indices below \(2m+1\). The exponent sums are \((m+3)^3+3(m+1)^3\) and \(m^3+3(m+2)^3\), whose differences from \((2m+2)^3\) are \(4m^3+6m^2-12m-22\ge10\) and \(4m^3+6m^2-12m-16\ge16\) for \(m\ge2\). The factor \(D_0\) costs at most \(6\) in degree and \(38\) in \(\log_2\) of the norm, the difference one more bit, and \(6\le10\), \(38+1\le1000\).

Components. For odd \(n\ge0\), \(\psi_n=F_n\); for even \(n\ge0\), \(\psi_n=2yF_n\) with \(\|2y\|=6<2^3\) and degree one more; and \(\psi_{-n}=-\psi_n\). So \(\deg\psi_n\le(|n|+1)^3+1\le2(|n|+1)^3\) and \(\|\psi_n\|\le2^{100(|n|+1)^3+3}\le2^{101(|n|+1)^3}\) for \(n\ne0\) (\(\psi_0=0\)). Each component has \(\ell^1\) norm and degree at most those of the pair.

These polynomials are never expanded at the astronomical indices; the bound is proved by strong induction on \(n\) from the recurrences.

docs.title: Sizes under quadratic-field operations
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.QRep ZInQ.Size.QRep.exists_add ZInQ.Size.QRep.exists_sub ZInQ.Size.QRep.exists_mul ZInQ.Size.QRep.exists_two_mul ZInQ.Size.QRep.exists_div ZInQ.Size.QRep.coord_bounds

Say that an integer triple \((a,b,c)\) with \(c e0\) represents \(u=(a+bs)/c\in K_0\) and has size \(\max(|a|,|b|,|c|)\). Let \(H\ge2\), and let \(u,u'\in K_0\) be represented by triples of size at most \(H\). Then:

  1. \(u+u'\), \(u-u'\), \(uu'\) and \(2u\) are represented by triples of size at most \(3H^4\);
  2. if \(u' e0\), then \(u/u'\) is represented by a triple of size at most \(3H^4\);
  3. if \((a,b,c)\) represents \(u=u_0+u_1s\) (\(u_0,u_1\in\mathbb Q\)) with size at most \(H\), then \(u_0=a/c\) and \(u_1=b/c\), and their reduced numerators have absolute value at most \(H\) and their positive reduced denominators are at most \(H\).

Proof sketch. With \(u=(a+bs)/c\) and \(u'=(a'+b's)/c'\): \(u\pm u'= igl((ac'\pm a'c)+(bc'\pm b'c)s igr)/(cc')\) has size at most \(2H^2\); \(uu'= igl((aa'+2bb')+(ab'+a'b)s igr)/(cc')\) has size at most \(3H^2\); \(2u=(2a+2bs)/c\) has size at most \(2H\). For the quotient multiply by the conjugate: $\( rac uu'= rac{c' igl((aa'-2bb')+(a'b-ab')s igr)}{c\,(a'^2-2b'^2)},\)$ where \(a'^2-2b'^2 e0\) because \(a'+b's e0\) and \(\sqrt2\) is irrational; the size is at most \(3H^3\). All these are at most \(3H^4\). For (3), reducing a fraction does not increase the absolute values of its numerator and denominator.

docs.title: Heights of the codes in the guard box
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.iota_coord_height

Let \(T\ge0\) be an integer and \(K=2^{30}(T+1)^3\). For every integer \(n\) with \(|n|\le T\), each of the five coordinates of \(\iota(n)\) is a rational number whose reduced numerator has absolute value at most \(2^K\) and whose positive reduced denominator is at most \(2^K\).

Proof sketch. For \(n=0\), \(\iota(0)=(1,0,0,0,0)\). Let \(1\le|n|\le T\). By the fixed point codes (which use that \(P_0\) has infinite order and the multiplication-by-\(n\) formulas), for \(n\ge1\), \(\psi_n(P_0)\ne0\) and $\(x([n]P_0)=x(P_0)-\frac{\psi_{n+1}(P_0)\psi_{n-1}(P_0)}{\psi_n(P_0)^2},\qquad y([n]P_0)=\frac{\psi_{2n}(P_0)}{2\psi_n(P_0)^4},\)$ and \(\iota(-n)\) differs from \(\iota(n)\) only in the signs of the ordinate coordinates.

Values of \(\psi_m(P_0)\). The coordinates of \(P_0\) over the denominator \(32\) are \(x_0=6564/32\), \(x_1=-4640/32\), \(y_0=-123720/32\), \(y_1=87483/32\), with numerators below \(2^{17}\) in absolute value. For \(|m|\le2T\) put \(\delta=2(|m|+1)^3\ge\deg\Psi_{m,c}\). Then \(c_m=32^\delta\), \(a_m=32^\delta\Psi_{m,0}(P_0)\) and \(b_m=32^\delta\Psi_{m,1}(P_0)\) are integers with \(\psi_m(P_0)=(a_m+b_ms)/c_m\), and each monomial of \(\Psi_{m,c}\) contributes at most \(2^{17\delta}\) after clearing, so \(|a_m|,|b_m|\le\|\Psi_{m,c}\|_1\,2^{17\delta}\le2^{135(|m|+1)^3}\) and \(c_m=2^{10(|m|+1)^3}\). With \((|m|+1)^3\le(2T+1)^3\le8(T+1)^3\) all these triples, and the triple \((1641,-1160,8)\) of \(x(P_0)\), have size at most \(H_0=2^{1280(T+1)^3}\).

Field operations. \(x([n]P_0)\) and \(y([n]P_0)\) are obtained from these values by at most eight successive levels of additions, subtractions, products, doubling and quotients (in fact four: \(\psi_n^2\) and \(\psi_{n+1}\psi_{n-1}\), their quotient, the difference with \(x(P_0)\); and \(\psi_n^4\), \(2\psi_n^4\), the quotient). Each level takes a size bound \(H\) to \(3H^4\). With \(h_k=\log_2H_k\), \(h_{k+1}\le4h_k+2\), so \(h_8\le4^8(h_0+1)\le65536\,(1280(T+1)^3+1)<2^{27}(T+1)^3\le K\). By the component part of the size lemma, the four rational coordinates of \([n]P_0\) have reduced numerators and denominators at most \(2^K\); the first code coordinate is \(0\).

docs.title: Size of the guard polynomial
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.guardPoly_size

For every integer \(T\ge0\), the false-triple product \(G_T\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\dots,X_{15}]\) satisfies $\(\deg G_T\le16(T+1)^3,\qquad\|G_T\|_1\le2^{2^{39}(T+1)^6}.\)$

Proof sketch. \(G_T\) is a product of at most \((2T+1)^3\le8(T+1)^3\) factors, one for each false triple \((a,b,c)\in[-T,T]^3\). Fix one, with coordinates \(A_j/B_j\) of \((\iota(a),\iota(b),\iota(c))\) and \(D=\prod_{j=1}^{15}B_j\). With \(K=2^{30}(T+1)^3\) the heights of the codes give \(|A_j|,B_j\le2^K\), so \(D\le2^{15K}\) and \(|(D/B_j)A_j|\le2^{15K}\). Each \((DX_j-(D/B_j)A_j)^2\) has degree \(2\) and norm at most \((2\cdot2^{15K})^2=2^{30K+2}\), so the factor \(\sum_{j=1}^{15}(DX_j-(D/B_j)A_j)^2\) has degree at most \(2\) and norm at most \(15\cdot2^{30K+2}<2^{30K+6}\). Multiplying: \(\deg G_T\le2\cdot8(T+1)^3\) and \(\log_2\|G_T\|_1\le8(T+1)^3(30K+6)\le8\cdot31\cdot2^{30}(T+1)^6<2^{39}(T+1)^6\). The empty product (\(T=0\), where there is no false triple) is \(1\).

The polynomial is never expanded; the bound uses only the product structure.

docs.title: Uniform bounds for the finite constructors
docs.text:
ZInQ.Size.psi_uniform ZInQ.Size.guard_uniform ZInQ.Size.const_uniform

Let \(B\ge2^{20}\) be an integer.

  1. For \(n\in\mathbb Z\) with \(|n|+1\le B\) and \(c\in\{0,1\}\): \(\deg\Psi_{n,c}\le B^4\) and \(\|\Psi_{n,c}\|_1\le2^{B^8}\).
  2. For an integer \(T\) with \(0\le T\le B-1\): \(\deg G_T\le B^4\) and \(\|G_T\|_1\le2^{B^8}\).
  3. For an integer \(c\) with \(|c|\le B-1\), the constant polynomial \(c\) (the value of a \(\mathrm{fixed}\) node) has degree \(0\le B^4\) and norm \(|c|\le2^{B^8}\).

Proof sketch. (1) \(2(|n|+1)^3\le2B^3\le B^4\) and \(101(|n|+1)^3\le101B^3\le B^8\). (2) \(16(T+1)^3\le16B^3\le B^4\) and \(2^{39}(T+1)^6\le2^{39}B^6\le B^8\) because \(B^2\ge2^{40}\). (3) is immediate.

The manuscript states these bounds with \(B_*=T+1\); the companion proof uses the maximum of \(2^{20}\), \(T+1\) and one plus every occurring constant and index, which is shown to equal \(T+1\).
