ZInQ.Syntax.closeTemplate ZInQ.Syntax.close_facts

The template \(\mathtt{value.close\_coordinates}\) has \(16\) parameters and \(53\) witnesses (\(69\) variables). Parameters: points \(A=(X_0,\dots,X_4)\), \(L=(X_5,\dots,X_9)\), \(J=(X_{10},\dots,X_{14})\) and \(t=X_{15}\). Witnesses in allocation order: pairs \(\zeta_A=(X_{16},X_{17})\), \(\zeta_L=(X_{18},X_{19})\), \(\zeta_J=(X_{20},X_{21})\); the ratio pair \(q=(X_{22},X_{23})\) and its inverse witness \(v=X_{24}\); \(a_0=X_{25}\), \(a_1=X_{26}\), the distance \(\delta=X_{27}\); the positivity variables \(z_1,\dots,z_4=X_{28},\dots,X_{31}\); \(\mathtt{member}\) blocks \([32,39)\), \([39,46)\), \([46,53)\); the inverse witnesses \(X_{53},X_{54},X_{55}\) of the gadgets \(Z(A,\zeta_A)\), \(Z(L,\zeta_L)\), \(Z(J,\zeta_J)\); \(\mathtt{value.abs}\) blocks \([56,60)\) and \([60,64)\); the inverse witness \(u_\epsilon=X_{64}\); and a \(\mathtt{value.abs}\) block \([65,69)\).

With \(\epsilon=a_0+a_1\), \(r=q_0\) and \(\mu=\epsilon-\delta\), the formula is the conjunction of, in this order: \(\langle\mathtt{member}[A]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{member}[L]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{member}[J]\rangle\), \(\mathrm{fin}(A)\), \(\mathrm{fin}(L)\), \(Z(A,\zeta_A)\), \(Z(L,\zeta_L)\), \(Z(J,\zeta_J)\), \(\bigwedge(N(\zeta_A)\,v\doteq1,\ \zeta_A\cdot q\doteq\zeta_J)\), \(\langle\mathtt{value.abs}[(\zeta_L)_0,a_0]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{value.abs}[(\zeta_L)_1,a_1]\rangle\), \(\epsilon\,u_\epsilon\doteq1\), \(\langle\mathtt{value.abs}[t-r,\delta]\rangle\) and \(\mu\,(z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2+z_4^2)\doteq1\). The polynomial is \(\kappa\) of it, squared.

It expresses the strict window \(|t-\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}(z(J)/z(A))|<|u_L|+|v_L|\), where \(z(L)=u_L+v_Ls\), for codes \(A,L\) of nonzero points.

docs.title: The value-test template
docs.text:
ZInQ.Syntax.valueTestTemplate ZInQ.Syntax.valueTest_facts

The template \(\mathtt{value.test}\) has \(11\) parameters and \(35282\) witnesses (\(35293\) variables). Parameters: points \(N=(X_0,\dots,X_4)\), \(K=(X_5,\dots,X_9)\) and \(t=X_{10}\). Witnesses in allocation order:

  • points \(C_1,H,U,V_0,V_1\) at \(X_{11},\dots,X_{35}\) (five each);
  • \(\mathtt{member}\) blocks for \(N,K,C_1,H,U,V_0,V_1\) at \(36,43,50,57,64,71,78\);
  • a \(\mathtt{multiply}\) block \([85,35219)\) and \(\mathtt{raw\_add}\) blocks \([35219,35225)\), \([35225,35231)\);
  • for \(i=0,\dots,3\) and \(\Pi=(H,U,V_0,V_1)\), with base \(b=35231+5i\): pairs \(w_i=(X_b,X_{b+1})\), \(\zeta_i=(X_{b+2},X_{b+3})\) and the inverse witness \(X_{b+4}\) of \(Z(\Pi_i,\zeta_i)\);
  • ratio pairs \(\rho_0=(X_{35251},X_{35252})\) with inverse witness \(X_{35253}\) and \(\rho_1=(X_{35254},X_{35255})\) with inverse witness \(X_{35256}\);
  • \(\eta=X_{35257}\), \(q=X_{35258}\), \(R_0=X_{35259}\), \(a_0=X_{35260}\), \(R=X_{35261}\), inverse witnesses \(u_F=X_{35262}\), \(u_a=X_{35263}\);
  • normalized pairs \(C'_0,\dots,C'_5\) at \(X_{35264},\dots,X_{35275}\);
  • \(\omega=(X_{35276},X_{35277})\) with inverse witness \(v_W=X_{35278}\); \(\Theta=X_{35279}\), \(B=X_{35280}\), \(u_\Theta=X_{35281}\); and a \(\mathtt{pole}\) block \([35282,35293)\).

Let \(F=(t-0)(t+15)(t+20)(t+24)(t+30)(t+60)\) (left to right), \(\Delta=(w_0,\ w_1,\ \bar w_2,\ \bar w_3,\ \rho_0-(t,0),\ \bar\rho_1-(t,0))\) and \(W=\prod_{i=0}^5(1+R\,C_i'^{\,2})\) in pair arithmetic. The formula is the conjunction of, in this order:

  1. \(\langle\mathtt{member}[N]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{member}[K]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{member}[C_1]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{member}[H]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{member}[U]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{member}[V_0]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{member}[V_1]\rangle\);
  2. \(\mathrm{fin}(K)\), \(\langle\mathtt{multiply}[K,N,C_1]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{raw\_add}[H,\mathrm{neg}(K),V_0]\rangle\), \(\langle\mathtt{raw\_add}[U,\mathrm{neg}(C_1),V_1]\rangle\), \(\mathrm{fin}(H)\), \(\mathrm{fin}(V_0)\);
  3. for \(i=0,\dots,3\): \(I\!X(\Pi_i,w_i)\) and \(Z(\Pi_i,\zeta_i)\);
  4. \(\bigwedge(N(\zeta_0)\,v_0'\doteq1,\ \zeta_0\cdot\rho_0\doteq\zeta_1)\) and \(\bigwedge(N(\zeta_2)\,v_1'\doteq1,\ \zeta_2\cdot\rho_1\doteq\zeta_3)\), with \(v_0'=X_{35253}\), \(v_1'=X_{35256}\);
  5. \(F\,u_F\doteq1\), \(\eta^2\doteq1\), \(R_0\doteq\eta\cdot2730^6\cdot F\), \(a_0\doteq1-R_0q^2\), \(a_0u_a\doteq1\), \(R\doteq R_0a_0^2\);
  6. \(F\,C_i'\doteq\Delta_i\) for \(i=0,\dots,5\) (pair equations);
  7. \(\bigwedge(N(W)\,v_W\doteq1,\ W\cdot\omega\doteq(1,0))\), \(\Theta\doteq2\omega_0\), \(\Theta u_\Theta\doteq1\), \(B\Theta^2\doteq R\), \(\langle\mathtt{pole}[B]\rangle\).

The polynomial is \(\kappa\) of this conjunction, squared. Here \(2730^6=413976684737889000000\).

These are the six raw field-valued tests and the single pole predicate of the variable-shift relation (Section 11).

docs.title: The exceptional-values template
docs.text:
ZInQ.Syntax.exceptionsTemplate ZInQ.Syntax.exceptions_facts

The template \(\mathtt{value.exceptions}\) has \(6\) parameters and \(406\) witnesses (\(412\) variables). Parameters: the point \(N=(X_0,\dots,X_4)\) and \(t=X_5\).

Chains. For a point \(p\) and an integer \(k\ge0\), the double-and-add chain is built as follows: start with \(\mathrm{out}=O\) (the literal code), \(\mathrm{base}=p\), \(i=0\); while \(k>0\): if \(k\) is odd, take a fresh point \(\sigma_i\), call \(\langle\mathtt{raw\_add}[\mathrm{out},\mathrm{base},\sigma_i]\rangle\) (a block of \(6\)) and set \(\mathrm{out}=\sigma_i\); replace \(k\) by \(\lfloor k/2\rfloor\); if now \(k>0\), take a fresh point \(\delta_i\), call \(\langle\mathtt{raw\_add}[\mathrm{base},\mathrm{base},\delta_i]\rangle\) and set \(\mathrm{base}=\delta_i\); increase \(i\). The chain's formula is the conjunction of its calls (the empty conjunction for \(k=0\)) and its value is the final \(\mathrm{out}\).

Variables. In allocation order: the rational constants \(c_1,c_2,c_3=X_6,X_7,X_8\) of the generator point \(G=(0,c_1,-145,c_2,c_3)\); the chains, in the order \(c=0,-15,-20,-24,-30,-60\), for \(k=|c|\) on \(G\) (for \(c=0\)) or \(\mathrm{neg}(G)\) (for \(c<0\)), each raw addition taking its fresh point and then its block; and a \(\mathtt{member}\) block \([405,412)\). The chains have \(0,7,6,6,8,9\) raw additions, \(36\) in all, occupying \(X_9,\dots,X_{404}\).

Formula. With \(\beta_c=\bigwedge(\text{chain formula},\ \mathrm{eq}(N,\text{chain value}),\ t\doteq c)\), the formula is $\(\varphi=\bigwedge\Bigl(\langle\mathtt{member}[N]\rangle,\ \bigvee(\beta_0,\beta_{-15},\beta_{-20},\beta_{-24},\beta_{-30},\beta_{-60})\Bigr),\)$ and the polynomial is $\((8c_1-1641)^2+(4c_2+15465)^2+(32c_3-87483)^2+\kappa(\varphi)^2 .\)$ The generator equations stay outside the disjunction. The template expresses exactly the six branches \(N=\iota(c)\) and \(t=c\) for \(c\in\{0,-15,-20,-24,-30,-60\}\).

ZInQ.Syntax.templateLibrary ZInQ.Syntax.templateLibrary_witnesses ZInQ.Syntax.templateLibrary_wf

The template library is the list of \(23\) templates, in this order (index: name): \(0\) \(\mathtt{member}\), \(1\) \(\mathtt{raw\_add}\), \(2\) \(\mathtt{raw\_z}\), \(3\) \(\mathtt{raw\_inverse\_x}\), \(4\) \(\mathtt{log25}\), \(5\) \(\mathtt{pole}\), \(6\) \(\mathtt{test\_group}\), \(7\) \(\mathtt{slope}\), \(8\) \(\mathtt{height\_certificate}\), \(9\) \(\mathtt{multiply.scalar}=S_{c_*}\), \(10\) \(\mathtt{multiply.guard}\), \(11\) \(\mathtt{multiply}\), \(12\) \(\mathtt{natural}\), \(13\) \(\mathtt{value.signed\_encode}\), \(14\) \(\mathtt{value.abs}\), \(15\) \(\mathtt{value.close\_coordinates}\), \(16\) \(\mathtt{value.test}\), \(17\) \(\mathtt{value.exceptions}\), and \(18+k\) \(\mathtt{scalar.integer\_constant}_k=S_{\mathrm{integer\_constant}_k}\) for \(k=0,\dots,4\).

The constants \(\mathrm{integer\_constant}_k\) are the distinct integer constants other than \(0,1,-1\) met by the model-evaluation translation, numbered in the order in which they are first met: first in the power template, then in the precision circuit. They are \(4,2,3,c_3,1399\), where \(c_3\) is the program literal of the natural precision polynomial. Equivalently, the list \((4,2,3,c_3,1399)\) is fixed in advance and the translation looks up each constant's index in it; the shape of the natural precision circuit shows that these five values are exactly the constants met, in order of first occurrence.

Every call in a template refers to a template of smaller index, so the library is denoted in this order. The parameter and witness counts are as follows. The manuscript's table also lists the root node index of each template's node list (\(149,308,68,54,229,106,515,2681,260,136,22,83,79,138,23,271,775,487\) and \(136\) for each scalar-constant template); these are properties of the node encoding, checked by the external comparison with the saved specification, and play no role in the proof.

docs.title: Saved precision polynomial
docs.text: Project-authored: construction/precision-natural-polynomial.json (cross-check only). Its structure, read with a JSON parser: \(54056\) explicit variables (inputs code_0..code_4 at \(0..4\), tuple_0..tuple_3 at \(5..8\)), \(293620\) nodes (\(10\) constants, \(54056\) variable nodes, \(125327\) additions, \(98382\) multiplications, \(15845\) calls), \(15845\) witness blocks of length \(79\), one power template with \(3\) parameters, \(79\) witnesses and \(474\) nodes; node \(0\) is the program literal (\(3{,}181{,}317\) decimal digits); the first \(293568\) nodes are the universal halting circuit with variable \(0\) replaced by that literal, variable \(1\) by variable \(5\) and every other variable and block start shifted by \(7\); the last \(52\) nodes form the four pairing equations and the final sum of squares. Decoding the literal with the numbering gives \(w=18\) and a primitive program of \(146{,}779\) encoded states plus the implicit final halt, using \(23{,}633\) registers. The universal interpreter program (\(1{,}399\) instructions: \(1{,}022\) decrements, \(376\) increments, the final halt; \(204\) registers) is recovered from the variable names and state equations of the universal part, and recompiling it with compileRegisterMachine in hierarchical mode reproduces those \(293568\) nodes exactly.

docs.title: Section 3.1 natural predicate
docs.text: Section 3.1, lines 362-371: raw addition has the narrow contract on canonical codes; every later use supplies canonical input codes; multiplication imposes membership of its three roots and is sound on arbitrary rational tuples; in the natural predicate four initially untyped tuples enter multiplication calls, so are typed before their squares are added; Lagrange's theorem then gives exactly \(\iota(\mathbb N)\); this uses multiplication completeness.

Line 968: \(S_{\rm ht}=\{p:p\le324\}\).

docs.title: Section 10 opening
docs.text: Section 10 (sec:compiler), lines 5745-5789: the signed encoding \(\operatorname{enc}(n)=2n\) for \(n\ge0\) and \(-2n-1\) for \(n<0\) (lines 5746-5749); the input order \((n,\kappa,a,l,j)\) and the early rejections \(n\notin\mathcal C\), \(\kappa\ne0\), \(a,l\ge1\), \(j=na\) (lines 5750-5751); \(z=-x/y\), \(z([l]P_0)=u_l+v_ls\), \(\epsilon_l=|u_l|+|v_l|\), \(r(a,j)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(z([j]P_0)/z([a]P_0))\) (lines 5752-5757); \(A^{(0)}_{\rm ht}=H_6(S_{\rm ht})\) and the two strict final tests (lines 5758-5763); the reference program S21 and the ideal IR S22 with its all-input argument (lines 5766-5775); the integer form \(4\epsilon<4^{-B}\iff 4^B\le\lfloor(V-1)/(4U)\rfloor\) and the saturation \(\sigma(x)=\min(x,L+1)\) (lines 5777-5788).

docs.title: Section 10.1 Cantor wrapper and acceptance
docs.text: Section 10.1, lines 5790-5815: the saved precision polynomial has \(1\,305\,811\) natural variables, the first five inputs (lines 5791-5792); S23 specializes a universal natural halting polynomial at the code of a wrapper that inverts four Cantor pairs (lines 5796-5798); the pairing equations \(2t_i=(c_i+t_{i+1})(c_i+t_{i+1}+1)+2t_{i+1}\) (\(0\le i<4\)), \(t_4=c_4\), and the new polynomial as the sum of the squared old polynomial and the four squared differences (lines 5799-5804); acceptance of a fixed increment/decrement/branch program means reaching the unique final halt with all registers zero, with a finite cleanup stage (lines 5807-5809).

docs.title: Section 10.3 program numbering
docs.text: Section 10.3, lines 5977-5982: the universal numbering \(e+1=2^w(2D+1)\); \(w=0\) halts; otherwise the four base-\(2^w\) digits at positions \(4p,\dots,4p+3\) give opcode, register and two targets of state \(p\); opcode one increments, opcode two decrements or takes its zero branch, every other opcode halts; missing digits are zero, so decoding is total.

docs.title: Section 10.3 interpreter
docs.text: Section 10.3, lines 5984-5997: the tape code \(0\) or \(\operatorname{cons}(h,t)=2^h(2t+1)\); decoding by repeated halving, the tail smaller than the code; register update by saving the reversed prefix; absent entries are zero; the reserved jump register stays zero; copies restore their source; aliased addition snapshots its operand; division maintains \(x=qy+r\) and subtracts only when \(r\ge y\), with divisors at least two; one interpreter loop executes exactly one decoded instruction with finite work; a simulated halt enters cleanup; an infinite simulation never does; the all-zero halt is equivalent to virtual halting.

docs.title: Section 10.3 precision IR
docs.text: Section 10.3, lines 5999-6016: normalized signed pairs and pairs over \(1,\sqrt2\); norm zero implies zero (a primitive solution of \(a^2=2b^2\) would have both entries even); every division guarded by that test; the Jacobian formulas satisfy the curve equation and the affine chord and tangent formulas after multiplying denominators; equal abscissas split into doubling and opposite points; zero ordinate doubles to the identity; the fixed projective point is \(P_0\); these identities are independent of the generator theorem; the scalar loop halves, the precision loop divides by four; capped arithmetic computes \(\min(x,L+1)\) with zero bases, unit bases and zero exponents separate; the ideal IR terminates and agrees with the predicate on all five natural inputs.

docs.title: Section 10.3 lowering
docs.text: Section 10.3, lines 6018-6025: each primitive lowering uses fresh auxiliary registers, snapshots overlapping sources and preserves the live-register map at the end of each finite block; saturating decrement gives natural subtraction; repeated addition gives multiplication; variable divisions are guarded; induction on completed loop iterations handles loops; acceptance enters cleanup, rejection a permanent self-loop; the primitive machine halts exactly on acceptance.

docs.title: Section 10.3 unpairing wrapper
docs.text: Section 10.3, lines 6027-6034: \(\operatorname{pair}(a,b)=(a+b)(a+b+1)/2+b\); the unpairing loop invariant \(\text{remainder}=\text{input}-s(s+1)/2\), subtracting \(s+1\) while \(s<\text{remainder}\); at exit \(b=\text{remainder}\), \(a=s-b\); four repetitions put the five codes into registers zero to four; fresh scratch above the old register range, cleared; relocation of every target by the prefix length.

docs.title: Section 10.3 specialization
docs.text: Section 10.3, lines 6036-6050: the polynomial specialization fixes the universal program input to the wrapper code, maps the old packed input to variable five and every old variable \(i\ge2\) and private-block start by \(i\mapsto i+7\); the pairing variables occupy five to eight; the four squared equations force the Cantor values; equation (C.4) (lines 6042-6047); the natural compiler proof has no height, restricted-converse or rational-model premise (lines 6048-6050).

docs.title: Section 10.4 typing order
docs.text: Section 10.4, lines 6052-6076: the typing order (membership, raw addition on canonical inputs, fixed scalars on \(D\), the root membership conjuncts inside the height certificate, the natural predicate only after globally typed multiplication, canonical outputs by the raw-addition postcondition, generator equations outside internal products); induction on the source DAG gives each node the code of its signed integer value; natural guards constrain source variables, not intermediate sums or products; scalar templates supply constants.

docs.title: Section 10.4 power value and precision parent
docs.text: Section 10.4, lines 6078-6086: the power-value recipe (three signed code inputs, seventy-nine private natural witnesses, an output code for the value of the power-template polynomial, not required to vanish, root equality \([17751579,15]\)); the precision parent (\(54056\) explicit variables, \(15845\) disjoint private blocks of seventy-nine variables, no parent variable node accessing a private coordinate); replacing each block by its private power-value call preserves the existential assignment; only the final parent root is equated to the identity.

docs.title: Section 10.4 primitive formulas
docs.text: Section 10.4, lines 6088-6092: equality is a difference, conjunction a sum of squares, disjunction a product; a topological induction including the globally conjoined fixed equations proves equality of polynomial values under substitution.

docs.title: Section 11 precision contract
docs.text: Section 11 (sec:bridge), lines 6103-6114 and 6236-6252: \(\mathrm{Close}\) links the five signed codes to the precision inputs in the order \((n,\kappa,a,l,j)\); the precision contract is used with \(B(n,\kappa)=H_6(S_{\rm ht})|\kappa F(n)|^{24}\).

docs.title: Section 12 literal constants
docs.text: Section 12 (sec:size), lines 6372-6381: for the saved expression, the absolute values of all literal fixed constants and all occurring division-polynomial indices are at most \(T\); the check covers the 173 scalar constant nodes. Appendix C (app:literal), lines 6778-6781: the five scalar-constant templates use the values in library.fixedConstants, and large program literals (the constant \(c_3\)) are retained byte for byte. The manuscript gives no explicit bound on \(c_3\); the bound \(c_3<2^{2^{27}}\) is introduced in this chapter.

docs.title: Appendix C.2 model recipes
docs.text: Appendix C.2, lines 6722-6730: a model-evaluation recipe sums the squares of the generator equations, the natural calls, the scalar-constant calls, the add, multiply and power-value calls and the five root differences; source-node and provenance fields add no equations.

docs.title: Lagrange four squares
docs.text: Classical: every natural number is a sum of four squares of integers (Lagrange, 1770). Used in Section 3.1, line 370, and Section 2.1, lines 190-197.

docs.title: Locators for the Proposition D chapter
Locators for the Proposition D chapter
docs.text: Proposition D is not in the manuscript. The manuscript's Proposition 6.2 (the twenty-two-prime pattern) is replaced by route AP, whose input needs long arithmetic progressions of good slope primes; these come from Szemerédi's theorem in the primes once the good slope primes are known to have positive relative density. That density statement is Proposition D. Its proof is written in the project-authored research note docs/research/pd-paper.md of this repository (a specification written for this project, refereed by a model run in docs/research/rv-pd-paper.md, not a published source). Section numbers below are those of pd-paper.md. The Selberg sieve is vendored from PrimeNumberTheoremAnd (last section).

docs.title: The target statements
docs.text: docs/research/pd-paper.md §0: the relative upper density statement for the good slope primes (Proposition D, weak form), Theorem D (a positive lower Dirichlet density) and the route through Proposition 5.3; the full natural density of nt-22p.md §2.2 is not needed.

docs.title: Character sums
docs.text: docs/research/pd-paper.md §1.2: Lemmas 1.1 (point count), 1.2 (scaling), 1.3 (shifted products), 1.4 (Jacobsthal's identity, with evenness) and 1.5 (divisibility by four through the involution \(x\mapsto-D^2/x\)).

docs.title: The description of good primes
docs.text: docs/research/pd-paper.md §1.3: Proposition 1.6, the description of the good slope primes in the class \(p\equiv1\pmod 8\), \((p/7)=-1\) through \(c_p=\varphi_p(1)/2\).

docs.title: The residue set
docs.text: docs/research/pd-paper.md §2.1 (the sets \(C_L\), \(T_L\), \(G^*_L\), Lemma 2.1 and remark 3, the residue set \(A_L\) and \(\delta_L\)) and §2.3 (the Frobenius conditions are congruences).

docs.title: The main term
docs.text: docs/research/pd-paper.md §3.2: Lemma 3.1, the lower bound for the Dirichlet series of \(C_L\) from Dirichlet's theorem in residue classes (Mathlib's lower bound for the von Mangoldt series of a residue class near \(s=1\)).

docs.title: The lattice count
docs.text: docs/research/pd-paper.md §4.2: Proposition 4.1, the primes bad at a large \(\ell\), counted by lattice points.

docs.title: The sieve
docs.text: docs/research/pd-paper.md §4.3 (the sieve set-up, inequality (4.1), Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4), §4.4 (the Selberg bound and the error terms) and §4.5 (Lemma 4.5, the lower bound for the Selberg sum, with Claims A and B). The Lean proof uses a fixed box \([-K,K]\times[-K-1,K]\) and the constant \(A=14402\) in place of the note's interval \(I_2\) and \(A_1=16003\).

docs.title: Assembly
docs.text: docs/research/pd-paper.md §5: Lemma 5.1 (prime tail), Lemma 5.2 (Abel summation), Proposition 5.3 (Dirichlet density gives upper natural density) and Theorem D.

docs.title: The vendored Selberg sieve
docs.text: The Selberg sieve bound is the theorem selberg_bound_simple of the PrimeNumberTheoremAnd project (https://github.com/AlexKontorovich/PrimeNumberTheoremAnd, files Mathlib/NumberTheory/Sieve/{AuxResults,Basic,Selberg,SelbergBounds}.lean, tag v4.35.0, by Arend Mellendijk), built on Mathlib's BoundingSieve and SelbergSieve structures. It is vendored in this repository under the Apache License 2.0 with only its import lines changed; the license is ZInQKernel/Sieve/LICENSE. For the mathematics see H. Halberstam and H.-E. Richert, Sieve Methods, Academic Press, 1974, Chapter 3.

docs.title: Locators for the Green–Tao chapter
docs.text: The Green–Tao chapter is not in the manuscript. It supplies, in Lean, the input of route AP: Szemerédi's theorem in the primes, for sets of primes of positive relative upper density. The plan is a project-authored research note, docs/research/gt-dense.md; it is a specification written for this project, not a published source. The proof for the set of all primes is a vendored third-party Lean development, and the published theorems are cited at the end.

docs.title: The vendored proof
docs.text: ThirdParty/GreenTao/NOTICE.md: the Lean proof of the Green–Tao theorem for the set of all primes, from the repository Vilin97/Autoformalization (directory green-tao/, commit 0dc67d87416c19690dd641a178ada32cca95c651), produced under the direction of Vasily Ilin as a submission to the green_tao target of the lean-eval benchmark, distributed under the Apache License 2.0 (ThirdParty/GreenTao/LICENSE). It was ported to the Lean and Mathlib versions of this repository with proof edits only; no statement was changed. The trusted statement is ThirdParty/GreenTao/ChallengeDeps.lean.

docs.title: Where the primes enter
docs.text: docs/research/gt-dense.md §1: the assembly chain of the vendored proof, the W-tricked prime weight, density selection, majorization, diagonal negligibility, extraction and small lengths; §2: the relative counting step holds for every weight below the majorant.

docs.title: The proof for a dense set
docs.text: docs/research/gt-dense.md §3: the seven steps (window lemma, density, transference for every large prime modulus, Bertrand modulus selection, residue pigeonhole for the set, count and extraction, small lengths) and the table §3.1 of the places where the original proof uses a property of the set of all primes.

docs.title: The Lean statements
docs.text: docs/research/gt-dense.md §4–§5: the weight of a set of primes, the transference for every large prime modulus and every sub-weight, density selection for the set, the window lemma and the modulus selection, extraction and the final assembly. The Lean files are ZInQKernel/External/GreenTaoDense/ (Window.lean, SetWeight.lean, PrimeModulusTransference.lean, Assembly.lean); the files adapted from the vendored proof carry Apache License notices naming their source files. The window lemma in Lean uses only Chebyshev's lower bound for the prime counting function, with the tail of the dyadic decomposition bounded trivially (module docstring of Window.lean).

docs.title: Green and Tao
docs.text: B. Green and T. Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Ann. of Math. 167 (2008), 481–547: Theorem 1.1 (the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions) and Theorem 1.2 (Szemerédi's theorem in the primes: every set of primes of positive relative upper density contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length). Theorem 1.2 is proved there in outline (section 11 of arXiv math/0404188v6).

docs.title: Tao and Ziegler
docs.text: T. Tao and T. Ziegler, The primes contain arbitrarily long polynomial progressions, Acta Math. 201 (2008), 213–305: a complete proof of Szemerédi's theorem in the primes, as a special case.

docs.title: Locators for the j-form of the height hypothesis
Locators for the \(j\)-form of the height hypothesis
docs.text: Line numbers refer to diophantine_zq.tex in this repository (the 11/5 manuscript, SHA-256 cb1148cd6c7769d2af3f1636b60ff0ada4b40431978d1e98d0c339274b3d792b, as in the manuscript entry); the notes in docs/research/ and KERNEL_PLAN.md are project-authored, not published sources; docs/research/rv-lit.md is a model review of the \(j\)-form and its return to \(u\), not a referee report.

docs.title: The Hauptmodul value
docs.text: Section 4 (sec:height), lines 377-383, the definitions before thm:height (line 404): the contact set \(\mathcal C=\{0,-15,-20,-24,-30,-60\}\), \(F(u)=u(u+15)(u+20)(u+24)(u+30)(u+60)\) and \(G(u)=7u^2+300u+3600\). Line 510, in the proof: "Pull back by \(J(u)=-57600F(u)^2/G(u)^6\)". Lines 949-950: with \(j=a/b\) in lowest terms, the polynomial \(-57600bF(X)^2-aG(X)^6\) has \(u\) as a root, so the \(j\) of the last steps is \(J(u)\). docs/research/rv-lit.md §4, paragraph "\(J\) is the value F2 bounds": the polynomials and the map match these lines, and \(J(u)\) is finite because \(G\) has no rational root. docs/research/h-b1.md M7 records the same map.

docs.title: The j-form of H
docs.text:
The manuscript's steps whose combination gives the \(j\)-form: lines 900-905 (step E4, \(\max(1,h_F(A))\le\max(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_R^{17})M_S(u)^{24}\)), lines 908-926 (step F1, \(j=3779136(\prod z_m)^4/(\sum z_m^8)^5\) in the even theta constants; the manuscript cites Lin–Yang eq. (2) at line 911, which the trust statement replaces, see The trust statement for H), lines 927-932 (step F2, \(h(j)\le40h([z_m])+22\)) and lines 934-947 (step F3, \(h([z_m])\le10^4\cdot2^{24}X\) with \(X=\max(1,h_F(A))\)). The manuscript does not display the combined bound on \(h(J(u))\); docs/research/rv-lit.md (a model review of the \(j\)-form, not a published source) §4, paragraph "The constant", combines E4, F2 and F3 with \(X\ge1\) into \(h(J(u))\le(40\cdot10^4\cdot2^{24}+22)\max(1,C_{\rm cm},Q_R^{17})M_S(u)^{24}\), and its paragraph "Strength" records that this bound implies the minimal height hypothesis, so it is the stronger hypothesis with the shorter justification.

docs/research/wk-h.md, Summary item 4 and §4.1 (the \(j\)-form as the residual hypothesis and the proved return to \(u\)), and §6 (verdict: adopting it is the cheap win; it removes step F4 and the final numerics from what is assumed, and the hypothesis is still a project statement). KERNEL_PLAN.md, section "What can and cannot be formalized", the last two sentences of the paragraph that contains the sentence beginning "ZInQKernel/MainLiterature.lean splits CR₃ further": the \(j\)-form is a bound on the height of the Hauptmodul value \(J(u)\), it implies the minimal height hypothesis (step F4 and the final numerics), and its trust statement is steps A1-F3 of h-trust.

docs.title: Step F4
docs.text: Lines 949-954: the manuscript's last step, the rational-root theorem applied to \(-57600bF(X)^2-aG(X)^6\), giving \(h(u)<h(j)+74\). Lines 956-964: the final numerics, \(40\cdot10000\cdot2^{24}+96<10^{13}\), and the conclusion \(h(u)\le\tfrac12H_6(S;R)M_S(u)^{24}\). docs/research/h-trust.md §1, Part F, step F4 (content and status). docs/research/wk-h.md §4.1: the two polynomial identities expressing \(3a^7\) and \(2^{10}3^85^6b^7\) through \(F_h\) and \(G_h\) (resultant \(2^{18}3^{13}5^{10}\)), the bound \(C_0\) on the cancellation, the lower bound \(\max(|a|,|b|)^{12}\le10^{48}\max(57600F_h^2,G_h^6)\), and \(12h(u)\le h(J(u))+450\), which replaces the manuscript's inequality. docs/research/rv-lit.md §4, the paragraph on \(12h(u)\le h(J(u))+450\): it is a different inequality from the manuscript's, checked on 30 values of \(u\) (the six contact values and 24 others), with largest value of \(12h(u)-h(J(u))\) equal to \(49.1\), and every cancellation divides \(C_0\).

docs.title: The trust statement for H
docs.text: docs/research/h-trust.md, as amended on 11-11 by task h-v16-adopt. h-trust Summary item 1: of its 36 steps, 7 rest only on refereed theorems and scripts, 5 apply refereed theorems through bookkeeping with only a model review, and 24 are manuscript or project arguments reviewed by models only (F4, which the \(j\)-form does not assume, is one of them). Summary item 4 and §2 list what stays outside refereed sources: the manuscript's own descent, conductor and transfer arguments, the project replacements NoCM and Lemma PR, and the identification in step A4. Its §1 steps A1-F3 are the justification of the \(j\)-form (docs/research/rv-lit.md §4: the \(j\)-form variants assume steps A1-F3 and nothing else); step F4 and the final numerics are replaced by the proofs of the \(j\)-form section. As amended: step F1 cites Lin–Yang Example 29 of arXiv:1807.00466v1, the discriminant-six example (cited as Example 30 before the locator audit docs/research/locators.md, AI agents, 2026-11-12; v1's Example 30 treats discriminant fourteen, and the journal number is unverified), and eqs. (13)-(14), with the theta expressions of Lauter–Naehrig–Yang and Igusa, and no longer Lin–Yang eq. (2) (Part F, F1); step C8's finiteness of the twist is the determinant argument of the upstream manuscript's Version 14 (Weil pairing, Kronecker–Weber; cited in h-trust by Version 16 line numbers, V16 L660-667), replacing local algebraicity of Hodge–Tate characters (Part C, C8); Versions 13-16 are later unpublished revisions, not the 11/5 text above, and the argument is checked in docs/research/rv-up.md §2.3, a model review. Kato, Astérisque 295 (2004), is a third option for the \(p\)-adic Hodge theory of eigenforms, proposed for all levels from upstream's Version 14 on (V16 L618-650); whether its §9.4 covers levels divisible by 5 is still to be checked (§2.5 item 3). Four (not five) unrefereed editions cited by the manuscript are replaced (§2.4). The same task amended steps A2, A4, C3, C8, E4 and F1 (h-trust preamble and changelog): among them, Deligne 1971 locators for A4, the Galois choice of field in C3, and a second locator for E4 (Gaudron–Rémond, Comment. Math. Helv. 89 (2014), §2.3 and Cor. 8.4, read only by upstream's model reviewer, by no one here). Upstream context: docs/research/up-h.md §2-§4, verified in docs/research/rv-up.md §2-§3. docs/research/wk-h.md §5-§6 explains why the steps before F4 cannot be stated here.
